I strongly oppose the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). As someone who works directly with international students at a U.S. college, I believe these fees are unreasonable, unnecessarily burdensome, unfair, and would create significant barriers for international graduates seeking to obtain practical experience related to their degrees.

International students already face significant financial barriers throughout their education in the United States. They pay substantial tuition and fees, often without access to the same financial aid opportunities available to domestic students, while also paying the costs associated with maintaining their immigration status. Adding another substantial financial burden at graduation is deeply concerning.

What makes this proposal particularly troubling is that international students' opportunities to gain practical experience during their studies have already been severely limited. The majority of U.S. colleges and universities do not require an internship or other practical experience component for every student. Following the August 12 SEVP directive, many institutions have stopped authorizing CPT for students whose academic programs do not require an internship as part of the curriculum. As a result, international students at these institutions have effectively lost internship opportunities that remain available to their domestic classmates.

This makes OPT even more important. For many international students, OPT is now one of the only meaningful opportunities to obtain practical, degree-related experience. Adding a substantial new fee to OPT therefore does not simply increase the cost of an existing benefit; it places an additional financial barrier on a pathway that has become increasingly important as opportunities for CPT have been restricted

I am also deeply concerned by the proposal's approach to who ultimately bears this cost. The proposed rule would require educational institutions to pay the fee while allowing them to pass that financial obligation on to the F-1 student or an employer.

This is particularly problematic in practice. If the cost is passed to an employer, an employer may simply decide not to hire an international student rather than absorb an additional immigration-related expense. If the cost is passed to the student, the student must pay another substantial fee precisely when they are graduating and attempting to establish themselves financially. If the institution absorbs the cost, colleges and universities are forced to take on another significant unfunded obligation.

There is no realistic outcome in which this proposal does not create a new barrier. The cost will ultimately have to be borne by someone. This structure effectively forces colleges, students, or employers to subsidize a federal immigration program, despite the fact that none of these parties should reasonably be expected to absorb a substantial new cost simply because a qualified graduate seeks employment authorization.

It is difficult to reconcile this proposal with the significant investment international students have already made in the United States. These students have spent years paying U.S. tuition, housing, living expenses, and other costs. They have earned degrees from U.S. institutions and are seeking an opportunity to apply the education they received. At that point, imposing another significant charge simply to access authorized practical training is unreasonable.

The proposal also risks creating an additional hiring barrier. Employers should make hiring decisions based on a candidate's qualifications, experience, and ability to contribute—not on whether hiring that graduate creates an additional immigration-related financial obligation. If employers are expected to absorb the fee, international graduates may face fewer employment opportunities for reasons unrelated to their qualifications.

Even if the broader objective is to reduce the number of foreign nationals remaining in the United States, imposing substantial costs on students who have already completed U.S. degrees is an unnecessarily punitive approach. The students have come here lawfully and legally. DSOs and PDSOs at colleges/universities ensure that. Students should not be placed in a position where they must choose between abandoning their professional plans and paying another significant fee simply to access an existing employment authorization that they were told would be available to them before coming to the US to study.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. Whatever the government's broader immigration objectives may be, imposing substantial additional costs on students who have completed U.S. degrees is an unreasonable and disproportionate burden. The current system is already complex and restrictive enough. Students should not face yet another financial barrier simply to access an employment authorization for which they are otherwise eligible.

​The impact on the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries will be equally damaging. ​Surrendering to International Competition

I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees rule, particularly the $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation outlined in Section V.A. I am concerned that the proposed fees would impose disproportionate financial burdens on American universities, undermine their ability to attract international talent, and potentially harm U.S. higher education and economic competitiveness.

First, the proposed fees could negatively affect international enrollment and university finances.

According to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report, U.S. higher education institutions hosted approximately 1.18 million international students during the 2024–2025 academic year. Second, the financial burden could disproportionately affect smaller universities and institutions with limited resources.

The proposed rule formally places payment responsibility on SEVP-certified educational institutions, although these costs may be passed on to students or employers.

Universities with smaller budgets may be unable to absorb substantial fees for individual students. This could create unequal access to OPT depending on institutional financial resources rather than students' academic qualifications or legitimate training opportunities.

The consequences could include reduced international enrollment, diminished tuition revenue, and fewer resources available for educational programs serving both domestic and international students.

Third, the proposal risks weakening research capacity and the broader economic contributions of American higher education.

Restrictions on access to practical training could also make it more difficult for American universities to recruit and retain talented graduate students and researchers, potentially weakening research programs and academic-industry collaboration.

Fourth, the proposed fees do not appear sufficiently targeted to the stated objective of preventing fraud.

I support appropriate oversight and enforcement against fraudulent OPT arrangements. However, a uniform financial requirement does not directly distinguish legitimate educational training from fraudulent activity.

Students participating in legitimate employment related to their academic fields, as well as institutions with strong compliance records, would face the same substantial fees regardless of their individual risk profiles.

Finally, the proposal could undermine reasonable educational planning expectations.

International students and universities make educational and financial commitments years in advance. Students currently enrolled in U.S. institutions may have reasonably considered existing practical training opportunities when deciding where to study.

Introducing substantial new financial obligations with limited transition time could disrupt these plans and create uncertainty for students, university administrators, and prospective employers.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees because DHS lacks the authority to impose them. A charge unrelated to cost or value to the payer is a tax, and the power to tax belongs to Congress (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 1974). Federal courts have already applied this principle to a parallel measure: in June 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the policy implementing the $100,000 H-1B payment, treating it as an unlawful tax. DHS itself benchmarks the OPT fee to H-1B fees. Following notice-and-comment procedures does not cure a lack of authority. INA 214(a)'s general "time and conditions" clause cannot support an exaction of this size, and after Loper Bright (2024) DHS receives no deference. DHS should withdraw this proposal unless and until Congress expressly authorizes such a charge.

1. The fee bears no relationship to the cost of the service. USCIS fees exist to recover the cost of adjudicating an application. An OPT application is a Form I-765, which currently costs $470 to $520 and requires no more work than any other employment authorization request. A fee that is hundreds of times higher than the processing cost is not cost recovery. It is a tax on a category of people, and DHS has not identified any authority from Congress to levy one. A federal court has already described the similar $100,000 H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax. DHS should explain, with actual cost data, what adjudication expense this fee is meant to cover.

2. It turns a training program into a test of wealth, not talent. OPT is designed for new graduates in entry-level roles. For many of them, the proposed fee would exceed their entire first-year salary. International students have already paid full tuition, often over $100,000 for a graduate degree, with no access to federal financial aid. Charging a second fee of this size after graduation means the only students who can use OPT are those from wealthy families, regardless of their skill or the value of their work.

3. OPT is part of the education students were promised. Practical training is built into F-1 status and is a key reason students choose U.S. universities over those in other countries. Changing the cost this drastically, after students have already enrolled and committed years and savings to their degrees, is unfair to people who made decisions based on the existing rules.

4. It harms U.S. employers, especially small ones. Employers use the OPT period to evaluate graduates before deciding whether to sponsor them. Combined with the separately proposed H-1B fee, this rule would roughly double the cost of hiring a graduate. Large companies may absorb that. Startups and smaller firms cannot, and they will simply stop recruiting international graduates. That reduces competition for talent and concentrates it in a few large companies.

5. It costs the United States more than it raises. OPT participants pay federal and state income taxes and fill roles in fields like data science, engineering, and research where U.S. employers report shortages. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany all offer post-study work options at a small fraction of this cost. A prohibitive fee will push top students to study and build their careers elsewhere, and U.S. universities will lose tuition revenue that supports domestic students and research.

6. The proposal lacks adequate analysis. DHS should publish a full analysis of how many applicants it expects to be priced out, the projected loss in tax revenue and university enrollment, and the effect on employers by size. Without that, the public cannot meaningfully evaluate the rule.

Re: Comments on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees
Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Proposed Rule titled "Optional Practical Training Fees" (Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100). The proposed imposition of a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions on SEVP-certified institutions is economically unviable, legally flawed, and deeply detrimental to the scientific and economic leadership of the United States.
1. Violation of Statutory Authority and Administrative Principles
Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA) and the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), administrative fees imposed by federal agencies must reflect the actual, reasonable cost of providing a specific service or oversight. Imposing a fee of $70,000 or $30,000 per student vastly exceeds any legitimate administrative cost associated with processing or monitoring OPT participation. The proposed fees operate not as a cost-recovery mechanism, but as an exorbitant penalty designed to functionally eliminate the OPT program. This exceeds the statutory authority granted to DHS by Congress and constitutes an arbitrary and capricious action under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
2. Severe Economic and Financial Harm to U.S. Higher Education
American higher education institutions—including non-profit universities and state colleges—do not possess the resources to absorb tens of thousands of dollars in fees per international student. If finalized, this policy will force universities to drastically scale back or terminate their support for practical training programs. This will disincentivize international students from pursuing degrees in the U.S., cutting off a vital stream of revenue and talent that supports university research funding, faculty positions, and academic infrastructure nationwide.
3. Degradation of U.S. Innovation and Global Competitiveness
OPT and the STEM OPT extension serve as critical pipelines for top global talent educated at U.S. universities to gain practical experience in key high-tech sectors, including artificial intelligence, engineering, cybersecurity, and biotechnology. Pricing universities and students out of OPT will directly advantage peer nations—such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia—which maintain streamlined post-study work policies to attract global talent. Depriving U.S. industries of highly skilled STEM graduates will diminish American competitiveness and innovation capacity on the global stage.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
Respectfully submitted,
A Concerned Higher Education Stakeholder

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. However, blaming international students for these problems oversimplifies a complex labor market. There is no justification for treating every international graduate as a threat to American workers simply because of their nationality or immigration status.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorizations and a $30,000 fee for subsequent extensions.
While the stated purpose of this rule is to combat fraud and abuse within the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), the mechanism chosen by the agency is deeply flawed, economically destructive, and represents an arbitrary abdication of core federal responsibilities. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal immediately based on the following grounds:

1. Inappropriate Shifting of Federal Law Enforcement Duties

The enforcement of immigration law, national security compliance, and the vetting of domestic employers are exclusive, core responsibilities of the federal government, specifically U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Shifting the burden of employer verification onto academic institutions through extreme financial coercion is both inappropriate and ineffective.
Colleges and universities are educational institutions, not federal investigative agencies. Designated School Officials (DSOs) possess neither the legal authority, the investigative resources, nor the field personnel required to audit private employers, detect sophisticated corporate fraud, or verify physical workplace conditions. Penalizing universities and international students for the existence of bad actors is an admission of regulatory laziness and a failure of the agency’s own enforcement mandates.

2. Failure to Effectively Address Fraud (Arbitrary and Capricious Logic)

The agency’s justification that extreme fees will create "institutional selectivity" to deter fraud is logically contradictory. Impousing a $70,000 barrier does not stop sophisticated, well-funded illicit operations; instead, it merely prices out legitimate, law-abiding students and small businesses. If the agency has identified "phantom employees" or illegitimate shell companies, it should utilize its existing enforcement powers to audit, fine, and prosecute those specific entities rather than shutting down a vital, legal pathway for hundreds of thousands of legitimate students. Punishing an entire population for the crimes of a few bad actors is the definition of an arbitrary and capricious regulatory action.

3. Severe Economic and Academic Devastation

By explicitly acknowledging that universities may pass these astronomical costs down to students or employers, DHS is effectively dismantling the OPT program. A $70,000 upfront fee creates an insurmountable wealth barrier for middle- and low-income international talent, completely undermining the meritocratic nature of higher education. Furthermore, American employers—particularly in critical STEM and technical sectors—will be severely disincentivized from hiring top-tier global talent due to these artificial, prohibitive costs. This will directly damage U.S. innovation, reduce the competitiveness of American universities, and drive the world's best minds to competitor nations.

Conclusion

DHS has failed to provide a rational connection between the facts found—isolated instances of employer fraud—and the choice made—a blanket, financially catastrophic fee on all OPT applicants. The agency must fulfill its duty to vet employers at the federal level using its existing budget and enforcement tools, rather than outsourcing its job to universities and students through extortionate fees.
I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

**Supplemental Public Comment**

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I recognize the interests of American workers and the need to investigate fraudulent employment. What remains unproven is that these fees would protect workers, deter fraud effectively, or serve America's long-term interests.

First, educational exchange has consequences beyond immediate employment opportunities. Some international students will eventually make fundamental contributions to science, industry, public affairs, or even the national defense of their home countries. Whether they remember America with sympathy or resentment can matter when future international cooperation is needed. In *The Problem of China*, Bertrand Russell praised the American decision to return surplus Boxer Indemnity funds for Chinese higher education, observing that America's gain from the friendship of educated Chinese people was incalculable. That example does not prove the value of OPT in dollars; it illustrates why goodwill and long-term relationships deserve consideration alongside labor-market concerns. Policies that needlessly alienate people who once studied in the United States may impose costs difficult to measure until circumstances become unfavorable.

Second, I neither deny fraudulent employment nor excuse those responsible. The cited 2020 scheme involving approximately 2,693 customers is a serious example. DHS also reports more than 10,000 OPT participants linked to highly suspect employers in a later investigation. But a prosecuted scheme and suspected arrangements represent different evidentiary stages. The issue is not that the reports logically contradict each other; it is whether they establish the need for this nationwide measure. Why is the older case now used to justify so substantial a fee? How many recent suspicions have been confirmed, and what direct actions have followed? Why would a universal charge identify shell companies more effectively than examining employers and employment records? The public deserves answers before lawful students and schools bear potentially severe consequences.

Third, the proposed instrument appears poorly matched to the misconduct. DHS acknowledges that initial OPT applicants may receive school recommendations without having secured employment. Schools may therefore be unable to examine the employer whose future conduct would supposedly justify the fee. DHS argues that high fees will encourage school scrutiny and deter abuse; yet financial ability is not equivalent to honesty. A compliant student may be excluded while a fraudulent employer with sufficient funds remains undetected. DHS further states that receipts will go to the U.S. Treasury rather than being retained by ICE for enforcement. If the objective is better detection, DHS should explain why targeted employer verification, site visits, reporting requirements, and sanctions would not achieve it at lower social cost.

The consequences make that question especially important. DHS's primary regulatory analysis estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs and $12.8 billion in annualized transfers at a 3 percent discount rate. Schools are the direct payers, but the burden may fall on students and employers. DHS should estimate the actual gains to American workers and explain why those gains would outweigh educational, economic, and diplomatic costs, including effects difficult to quantify.

Finally, a policymaker's responsibility differs from the understandable reactions of a citizen who feels powerless or unfairly treated. Questions of preference and unequal advantage, whether involving labor, gender, race, or nationality, deserve scrutiny and reform where warranted. But public policy cannot simply submit to one group's wish to see another suffer. It must weigh short- and long-term consequences and seek a durable balance in which everyone's well-being matters. Defending lawful rights is compatible with a kind of love that wishes others well. In an interconnected world, cooperation and mutual respect are not substitutes for enforcement; they are values that enforcement should not unnecessarily destroy.

I therefore request that DHS reconsider the fees, disclose a fuller basis for their amounts and expected effectiveness, and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures directed at actual misconduct rather than broadly burdening lawful participation.

References: DHS, *Optional Practical Training Fees*, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026), sections IV and V; Bertrand Russell, *The Problem of China*, Chapter III (1922).

Second, the rule invites foreign money. DHS says it won't restrict how schools fund the fee, and it even says the fee "could expose attempts by foreign adversaries to subsidize these costs." In other words, DHS expects foreign governments or companies might pay for their own nationals' OPT, and its answer is to hope someone notices afterward. The rule contradicts itself on the states. Section VII.F says the rule would not have substantial direct effects on the states and skips a federalism impact statement. None of this is a technicality. Re: Optional Practical Training Fees — Opposition

I am a second-year international student. I write in opposition to the proposed rule.

1. The charge is a tax, not a fee, and exceeds the agency’s authority.

The rule provides that collected amounts be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt under 31 U.S.C. 3302, and that ICE will neither retain nor use them. A charge that funds no agency function and recovers no agency cost is not a fee. Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act, 31 U.S.C. 9701, a user charge must be based on the cost to the Government of providing the service. There is no conceivable relationship between $70,000 and the administrative cost of a Designated School Official entering a recommendation in SEVIS, an action measured in minutes.

This defect is not hypothetical. In California v. Trump, the District of Massachusetts vacated a $100,000 charge on H-1B petitions on precisely this ground, holding it an unlawful tax (8 June 2026). That ruling is stayed pending appeal, but its reasoning applies with equal force: money to the Treasury, no cost nexus, no congressional authorization.

INA 214(a) permits DHS to prescribe the time and conditions of admission. It does not confer the power to tax.

2. The amounts are arbitrary and capricious.

The rule offers no cost study, no economic analysis, and no empirical foundation for $70,000 or $30,000. The figures appear chosen for deterrent effect rather than derived from any methodology. DHS states it expects schools to cease recommending pre-completion OPT as a result. An agency may not set a charge for the express purpose of suppressing participation in a lawful program and characterize it as a fee. To do so concedes the amount is untethered from cost.

3. The instrument does not match the stated rationale.

DHS cites fraud — shell employers, falsified employment — as justification. A flat charge on every recommendation by every SEVP-certified institution does nothing to detect or deter fraud. It imposes identical cost on scrupulous institutions and bad actors alike, and falls hardest on compliant students. Targeted employer verification addresses fraud. This rule does not.

4. DHS has not analyzed the effect on students whose institutions do not permit CPT.

My university does not permit Curricular Practical Training. Pre-completion OPT is therefore the only lawful route by which I can hold a summer internship. The rule would attach a $70,000 charge to a ten-week internship undertaken while I remain enrolled and paying full tuition. DHS has not examined how many institutions restrict CPT, nor what becomes of their international students when the only remaining route is priced beyond reach. That is a failure to consider an important aspect of the problem.

5. Concrete effect.

I am recruiting for a 2028 summer intern position. I hold a 4.0 grade point average and was selected this year for a competitive scholars program at my school. None of that will matter if the only authorization route available to me carries a $70,000 charge — an amount neither I nor my family could pay, and which my university would reasonably decline to absorb. Where the cost is passed to students, as the rule expressly permits, the result is not a fee but an exclusion.

6. Requested action.

I ask that the rule be withdrawn. In the alternative, that DHS (a) tie any charge to documented administrative cost, (b) exempt pre-completion OPT, which is short in duration, institutionally supervised, and undertaken during an ongoing course of study, and (c) publish the cost analysis supporting any amount proposed.

Respectfully submitted,

I respectfully oppose the proposed OPT fee structure. While I support DHS's legitimate goals of preventing fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and maintaining program integrity, imposing a substantial financial barrier on legitimate students and schools is not a sufficiently targeted or effective mechanism to achieve these objectives.
1. OPT Serves an Essential Educational Purpose
Practical training allows F-1 students to apply knowledge acquired through their degree programs in real-world settings directly related to their fields of study. DHS must distinguish this legitimate educational function from isolated abuses of the program. Preventing exceptional cases of fraud should not result in making critical practical training inaccessible to qualified, rule-abiding graduates.
2. Financial Capacity is Not a Measure of Merit
If DHS seeks greater selectivity in OPT, financial capacity is the wrong criterion. A student's qualifications are demonstrated through a legitimate degree, academic achievement, specialized skills, employment relevance, and strict compliance with program requirements. A qualified student of limited financial means is no less capable because they cannot overcome an artificial financial barrier. Conversely, the ability to bear a large fee does not make an applicant more talented or qualified. The proposal risks replacing a merit-based opportunity with a wealth-based threshold.
3. Entry-Level Compensation Must Be Distinguished from "Cheap Labor"
New graduates naturally enter the labor market at junior levels compared to experienced workers. Compensation depends on numerous legitimate factors, including occupation, experience, location, and specific job roles. If DHS has evidence that employers systematically underpay workers due to OPT status, it should address those practices directly through targeted wage safeguards, enhanced reporting, audits, and strict enforcement. A large fee applied to the student does not determine or regulate whether an employer is engaging in wage suppression.
4. Fraud Prevention Should Target the Source of Misconduct
I strongly support preventing fraudulent degrees, non-compliant schools, sham employment relationships, and misuse of OPT. However, a blanket financial barrier fails to distinguish legitimate participants from fraudulent ones.
• If fraudulent credentials or schools are the issue: Strengthen school certification, targeted audits, and rigorous degree verification.
• If fraudulent employment is the problem: Enhance employer verification and site enforcement.
• If university oversight is inadequate: Establish stronger objective oversight requirements and severe penalties for non-compliant institutions.
These measures directly correct misconduct; a large fee does not.
5. The Proposed Approach Creates Counterproductive Incentives
If DHS intends for schools to exercise greater selectivity, it should require selectivity based on legitimate educational and compliance criteria. A high financial threshold will instead exclude highly qualified students without substantial financial resources while permitting less-qualified students with greater resources to participate. This achieves financial selectivity, not educational selectivity or enhanced security.
6. Deterring International Talent Harms U.S. Global Competitiveness
Genuine international students who invest their time, energy, and financial resources into American higher education contribute heavily to U.S. technological advancement and economic growth. Implementing an excessive financial barrier will disincentivize top talent, driving qualified students to competing nations for higher education, research, and long-term innovation.
Employment opportunities should remain tethered to professional qualifications. The ILO Declaration of Philadelphia recognizes the importance of pursuing material well-being under conditions of dignity, economic security, and equal opportunity. Financial capacity should not become a substitute for professional merit.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee structure and instead pursue targeted alternatives, including:
• Stronger verification of participating schools and degree legitimacy;
• Risk-based audits of institutions demonstrating abnormal OPT patterns;
• Enhanced verification that employment relates directly to the student's field of study;
• Targeted employer audits and workplace enforcement;
• Appropriate regulatory safeguards against demonstrated wage abuse; and
• Robust penalties against institutions, employers, or individuals who commit fraud.

Before finalizing this rule, DHS should explicitly demonstrate how the proposed fee is logically connected to the specific fraud or labor-market harm it seeks to prevent, and why the aforementioned targeted measures are insufficient. Program integrity, worker protection, educational opportunity, and merit-based employment are not competing objectives and can be balanced effectively.

To Whom It May Concern:

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. The government has a legitimate interest in preventing fraud, maintaining program integrity, and protecting U.S. workers. However, this proposal is not a properly tailored means of achieving those aims and risks imposing substantial, long term harm on U.S. competitiveness, higher education, and innovation.

1. The fee is an overinclusive substitute for enforcement. Sections IV.A and IV.C identify real instances of fraud, including sham employers and improper documentation. Yet the rule charges the same amount for every OPT recommendation, without regard to an employer's compliance history, a school's risk profile, the nature of the work, or the student's record. A uniform fee of this magnitude measures financial capacity, not fraud risk. It may exclude compliant participants while better resourced institutions and sophisticated bad actors can absorb or pass through the cost.

2. The rule does not cure the stated enforcement deficiency. DHS acknowledges that compliance resources have not kept pace with OPT's growth and that site visits are resource intensive. At the same time, the proposal states that fees would be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and that ICE could not retain or use them directly. Thus, the rule creates an enormous financial burden without ensuring that the resulting revenue funds more investigators, stronger employer verification, or risk based inspections. Targeted compliance measures would bear a clearer relationship to the identified problem.

3. The rule threatens the United States' long term talent and innovation pipeline. OPT is not merely a temporary work benefit. It is a principal part of the value proposition for international students deciding where to study, conduct research, and launch careers. The proposal itself recognizes that reduced OPT availability may deter enrollment and cause opportunity costs for institutions, students, and employers, but it does not quantify the downstream effects on research capacity, entrepreneurship, local economies, or U.S. technological leadership. Competitor countries will benefit if capable students and future founders choose more predictable post graduation pathways elsewhere.

4. The claimed benefit to U.S. workers is not adequately demonstrated. Reduced OPT participation does not necessarily mean that U.S. workers will fill the affected positions. Employers may reduce hiring, delay projects, automate work, or move work abroad. This risk is especially acute for startups, research labs, hospitals, nonprofit organizations, and small businesses that cannot absorb a large fixed fee. If DHS is concerned about a specific cost advantage arising from FICA treatment, it should consider a targeted response to that incentive rather than an inflexible fee that is unrelated to wage level, employer size, job type, or actual compliance risk.

5. The rule will create wealth based access to a training pathway and impose disproportionate effects. Although schools are the formal payers, the proposal expressly permits them to shift the cost to students, employers, or other students. The practical result is likely to favor wealthy students, elite institutions, and large employers over smaller colleges, regional universities, startups, and students without comparable resources. DHS's own small entity analysis recognizes that a material share of small affected institutions could face significant revenue impacts. This is not a selection system based on merit, educational value, or public benefit. It is a selection system based on who can finance an extraordinary fee.

Finally, the regulatory analysis acknowledges substantial uncertainty about participation declines and opportunity costs, even while estimating annual transfers in the billions of dollars. A thirty day comment period and a proposed sixty day effective date are inadequate for students and institutions that made multi year educational and financial decisions in reliance on the existing OPT framework.

DHS should withdraw or substantially revise the proposal. Any final rule should use targeted, evidence based compliance tools, provide meaningful transition protection, and include a rigorous analysis of effects on American innovation, higher education, regional economies, and long term national competitiveness.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)) would not stop the fraud DHS describes, would harm U.S. workers and universities, rest on doubtful legal authority, and are supported by a flawed economic analysis.

1. Harm to U.S. workers and employers (Sec. IV.B, VII.A). The rule offers no analysis showing that OPT displaces U.S. workers. A 2026 study of the 2016 STEM OPT extension (Kwon, Lee and Monras) found areas receiving more OPT workers gained about 1% more firms, higher native employment, and about 1% higher wages for high-skilled native workers. The fee is also not calibrated to the FICA incentive DHS cites: at a $90,000 salary that saving is about $6,900 a year, one-tenth of the $70,000 fee. A flat fee falls hardest on lower-paying employers such as university labs, hospitals, startups, and nonprofits.

2. Harm to universities and domestic students (Sec. VI, VII.B). International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25, and NAFSA already projects up to 111,000 fewer students in fall 2026. Their tuition also helps fund aid and programs for U.S. students. Research finds the STEM OPT extension raised international enrollment by about 18% (bachelor's) and 30% (master's). DHS's claim that only 20% of F-1 students use OPT compares one year's participants to all enrollees; about 72% of graduates use OPT (Demirci 2019). DHS's own Table 17 shows 841 of 1,389 small institutions would bear first-year costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 above 20%. Because DHS acknowledges schools may pass the fee to students, OPT would go to those who can pay, not the most promising.

3. The fee misses the fraud (Sec. IV.A, IV.C, V.A). The fraud DHS describes is employer-side: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. Yet the fee is charged to schools and is not tied to any employer, so a shell company pays nothing. DHS's 10,000 suspect cases are about 2.8% of the 360,078 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024; the fee charges the other 97%. Footnote 56 calls the figure 10,000 employers, the text 10,000 students, and the data are not in the docket. CPT, which DHS admits has prevalent fraud, carries no fee, so abuse will shift there. STEM OPT, already subject to E-Verify, training plans, and site visits, still pays $30,000. Fee revenue goes to the general Treasury and funds no enforcement.

4. Lack of legal authority (Sec. III.A, IV.C). A charge set to deter participation, unrelated to any service cost, and deposited in the Treasury is a tax, not a fee (National Cable Television Ass'n v. U.S., 415 U.S. 336). DHS designed it to align with the $100,000 H-1B payment, which a federal court vacated on June 8, 2026 as a tax lacking congressional authorization (California v. Mullin, D. Mass.); a second court vacated the implementing policies Sept. 30, 2026. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee it enacted one, the $500 H-1B fee in 2004. Authority over the "time and conditions" of admission (INA 214(a)) is not a taxing power, and after Loper Bright DHS's reading gets no deference.

5. Flawed analysis (Sec. VI, VII). The high scenario assumes no response to a $70,000 price. Costs are capped at the fee and omit lost tuition, jobs, and tax revenue. Sec. VII.D says the rule would not reach the UMRA threshold, then says it does. Sec. VII.F finds no substantial direct effect on States, yet 1,044 state institutions would pay. STEM OPT for 2024 is 165,524 in Sec. IV.B but 95,384 in Sec. VII.A.3. The baseline treats the Duration of Status rule as in effect, but a court blocked it on Sept. 14, 2026. A 30-day comment period is too short for a rule with up to $16.9 billion in annual transfers; Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 generally call for 60 days.

6. Better alternatives. Require E-Verify and a validated EIN for all OPT employers; match SEVIS employer data against IRS, SSA, and state business records; target site visits at flagged employers; bar fraudulent employers and decertify noncompliant schools; and ask Congress for a modest, cost-based fee funding SEVP oversight. Unlike attestations, these checks rely on independent government records.

Requested actions: withdraw the rule; if not, extend the comment period to 60 days, docket the underlying fraud data, publish a revised impact analysis, and identify specific statutory authority for this charge.

Fraud in OPT is real and deserves a serious response, but this rule charges hundreds of thousands of compliant students, schools, and employers while the fraudulent employers it describes pay nothing. Please withdraw it.

I respectfully and unequivocally oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. As a higher education administrator with responsibilities involving international student advising and regulatory compliance, I recognize the importance of preventing fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and maintaining program integrity. However, these proposed fees are disproportionate, financially untenable, and fundamentally inconsistent with the educational purpose of OPT.

First, the proposal makes financial capacity a condition of access to an established educational training opportunity. OPT allows eligible international students to apply their academic learning in professional settings directly related to their fields of study. Under this proposal, access would depend not simply on eligibility, compliance, and educational merit, but on whether an institution can pay tens of thousands of dollars for a recommendation. The ability to pay $70,000 is not evidence of program integrity, just as the inability to pay is not evidence of fraud. Institutional wealth should not determine whether an eligible student can pursue authorized practical training.

Second, the proposed fees impose an unreasonable burden on colleges and universities. Institutions already devote considerable resources to SEVIS reporting, eligibility verification, student advising, and federal regulatory compliance. Requiring an institution to pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation, before employment authorization is even granted, creates an extraordinary financial obligation unrelated to the administrative cost of making that recommendation. For many institutions, particularly smaller private colleges and universities, these expenditures would be unsustainable. Such costs would divert resources from instruction, student support, and other educational priorities. Colleges should not be expected to finance federal enforcement objectives through punitive fees imposed on legitimate educational activities.

Third, transferring these costs to students is equally indefensible. International students already make significant financial commitments to pursue higher education in the United States, including tuition, housing, insurance, and immigration-related expenses. Practical training allows students to translate academic preparation into professional experience. An additional $70,000 financial barrier would effectively exclude many eligible students, regardless of their qualifications, academic achievements, or compliance histories. Neither students nor institutions should bear extraordinary financial penalties simply for participating in a lawful program.

Fourth, the proposed approach fails to establish a reasonable connection between the fees and DHS's stated objective of preventing fraud. Concerns about fraudulent employers, improper employment arrangements, and immigration violations warrant serious attention. However, charging compliant institutions extraordinary amounts does not directly address the misconduct DHS seeks to prevent. Targeted investigations, employer verification, risk-based institutional oversight, SEVIS data analysis, and enforcement against demonstrated violations would offer more direct and proportionate responses. Financial barriers are not a substitute for evidence-based regulatory oversight.

Fifth, the proposal threatens the competitiveness of American higher education. The opportunity to gain professional experience is an important consideration for international students selecting where to study. Making OPT financially inaccessible would diminish the attractiveness of U.S. colleges and universities, potentially reducing international enrollment and associated economic contributions. It would disproportionately disadvantage smaller institutions lacking the financial resources of larger universities. These consequences for institutional sustainability, local economies, and workforce development deserve serious consideration.

Finally, I am troubled by the precedent this proposal establishes. Educational institutions have a responsibility to comply with immigration regulations, exercise appropriate judgment when recommending students for practical training, and cooperate with government oversight. Those responsibilities should be evaluated through established compliance standards, not an institution's ability to make extraordinary payments. 

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and pursue targeted, evidence-based alternatives that address documented fraud while preserving legitimate educational opportunities. Any reform should demonstrate a clear relationship between regulatory burdens and intended outcomes, distinguish compliant participants from those engaged in misconduct, and avoid shifting unreasonable federal enforcement costs to colleges, universities, and students

To the U.S. Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong concerns regarding DHS’s proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation for an F-1 student and an additional $30,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation. With 14 years of experience in international education, I have witnessed firsthand the significant value OPT provides to students, educational institutions, employers, and the United States.

OPT Is an Essential Extension of Education

International education extends beyond the classroom. OPT allows students to apply their academic knowledge in professional settings, gain relevant experience, and develop skills essential to their careers. It also enables employers to access talented graduates and strengthens the connection between American higher education and the workplace.

Throughout my career, I have seen how practical training helps students translate their education into meaningful professional contributions. These experiences are an important part of the value of an American education.

The Proposed Fees Would Make OPT Financially Unsustainable

Fees of $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation are beyond what most educational institutions could reasonably absorb. Schools must balance tuition revenue, staffing, student services, and compliance costs. These additional expenses could force institutions to discontinue OPT participation, effectively eliminating this opportunity for many legitimate students.

Students who have invested substantial time and money in earning a U.S. degree could lose access to valuable professional experience. Institutions could also become less attractive to prospective international students.

Addressing Fraud Through Proportionate Measures

I recognize DHS’s responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system, address fraud, and protect U.S. workers. However, in my 14 years working in international education, I have witnessed the substantial benefits of OPT without observing widespread intentional deception that would justify fees of this magnitude.

This does not mean fraud never occurs. Rather, policy should distinguish between those who abuse a program and students and institutions that participate in good faith. If DHS has identified specific patterns of fraud, targeted, evidence-based oversight and enforcement would be more proportionate than fees that could make legitimate participation financially impossible.

Potential Economic Consequences

International students contribute significantly to American colleges and universities, local businesses, and communities. Access to practical training is also an important consideration for students choosing where to pursue higher education.

If schools discontinue OPT participation because of these fees, the United States risks losing international students, tuition revenue, and valuable talent. Institutions could face declining enrollment and budget pressures, while local communities could lose economic benefits. These consequences warrant careful consideration before adopting this policy.

Recommendations

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fees and:

- Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.
- Assess the actual scope of documented OPT fraud and abuse.
- Implement targeted compliance and enforcement measures that address misconduct without preventing legitimate participation.
- Evaluate the potential effects on institutions of different sizes, international enrollment, and the broader U.S. economy.
- Consider feedback from educational institutions, international student advisers, employers, students, and other professionals with direct OPT experience.

Conclusion

After 14 years in international education, I remain convinced of OPT’s tremendous value in helping F-1 students develop professional skills and apply their academic learning. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue reasonable, evidence-based alternatives that protect program integrity while preserving legitimate educational opportunities.

Thank you for considering my comments.

America’s strength has never come from shutting out different perspectives. It has come from bringing them together. A country that celebrates diversity and equal opportunity should not make those opportunities dependent on wealth or nationality. That contradiction is what makes this proposal so deeply disappointing.

This proposal is completely unrealistic and financially impossible for the vast majority of international students.
For many students, this proposed fee is significantly higher than the entire cost of our tuition for a full four-year degree. While I understand the agency's desire to cover administrative costs or prevent fraud, the size of this increase is entirely disproportionate. It does not make sense to charge an exorbitant penalty to students who are simply looking to gain entry-level practical experience in their fields of study.
If the agency needs to adjust its funding, a reasonable, minor increase to the standard form application fee would be understandable. However, a $70,000 fee will effectively destroy the OPT program, preventing qualified students from building their careers and hurting U.S. employers who rely on our talent.

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am a Principal Designated School Official (PDSO) from Florida, and I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial post-completion OPT and $30,000 for the second year of practical training. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

1. The fees would effectively eliminate OPT.
OPT is a benefit F-1 students earn by completing a U.S. degree. These fees exceed the annual cost of attendance at most institutions and, for many students, the first-year salary of an OPT position. Few students could pay them, and few employers would pay them for an entry-level hire when domestic candidates carry no such cost. A prohibitive fee does not regulate a program; it ends it, without the process that repeal would require.

2. The fees bear no relationship to the cost of adjudication.
DHS user fees are generally grounded in recovering the cost of adjudication. The current Form I-765 fee is a few hundred dollars; the proposed fees are hundreds of times higher. Combating fraud and protecting workers are enforcement and policy goals, not service costs. DHS has not shown that processing an OPT application costs anything near these amounts. A charge that functions as a penalty or tax raises serious questions about statutory authority and whether the rule is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. I request that DHS publish its cost methodology, data, and legal analysis.

3. The rule would devastate international enrollment.
OPT is among the strongest factors in a student’s decision to study here. Families often borrow heavily, expecting practical training to let students apply their education. Without it, students will choose Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Germany, and other competitors. At our institution, we have 350 enrolled international students, 100 of whom are currently in OPT or in pending OPT application status, and approximately 50% of them are in STEM fields. Enrollment declines would hurt tuition revenue, graduate programs, research capacity, and the campus community, and would reach local housing, retail, and service businesses. Nationally, international students contribute significantly to the economy and support jobs.

4. The rule would harm U.S. employers and workers.
Employers in technology, healthcare, engineering, finance, and hospitality rely on OPT graduates as a talent pipeline, especially in STEM fields with persistent shortages. Research has not shown the worker displacement the proposal presumes, and STEM OPT already requires training plans, wage standards, and site oversight. Ending the program in practice would send talent, and the companies that employ it, elsewhere.

5. Targeted enforcement is the better approach.
DHS already has SEVIS reporting, employer verification, site visits, unemployment limits, and enforcement against sham employers. The vast majority of students, employers, and DSOs comply carefully. A blanket fee punishes every participant while doing little to deter bad actors, who can be addressed through stronger employer vetting, data-sharing, and enforcement.

6. The rule is inequitable and the comment period is inadequate.
Such a fee would limit OPT to students from the wealthiest families, undermining diversity and the principle that opportunity should reflect merit. A 30-day comment period is insufficient for a rule of this magnitude, and I request an extension.

Conclusion
OPT has been a cornerstone of U.S. higher education for decades, benefiting students, employers, communities, and the economy. These fees would end it. I urge DHS to withdraw the rule, and my colleagues and I stand ready to work with the Department on proportionate solutions to program integrity concerns.

Respectfully submitted,

TWG

I am a U.S. citizen and Texas resident. OPT should be ended, not merely priced. If DHS does not end it here, I support the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee and ask that neither be reduced.

1.  OPT should be terminated.
F-1 status is for temporary entry solely for a full course of study. Post-completion OPT and the 24-month STEM extension turn it into open-market work authorization of up to three years, with no cap, no labor-market test, and no prevailing-wage rule.

ICE’s 2024 SEVIS data counted 194,554 OPT participants with an EAD who reported an employer, up 21.1 percent from 2023, plus a large STEM OPT population. Open Doors reported 294,253 graduates on OPT in 2024–25, including 106,504 on the STEM extension. Unlike H-1B, this flow has no ceiling.

OPT also has a cost advantage. Nonresident F-1 students are generally exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes on OPT wages, and the employer skips the matching 7.65 percent FICA contribution. An OPT hire can be cheaper than a citizen graduate before wages are compared. DHS itself calls OPT a pipeline around H-1B caps, fees, and wage rules. A fee does not fix that.

This NPRM says that without these fees DHS may shut OPT down. Ending post-completion OPT and the STEM extension should be the preferred outcome. If that cannot be done here, adopt the fees as an interim control, not a substitute.

2.  The $70,000 initial fee is justified.
The fee is owed by the SEVP-certified school before a DSO recommends the student for any OPT, and USCIS may not grant work authorization if it is unpaid. Schools now make that recommendation at little direct cost. The hiring effects fall on American workers.
DHS sized the fee to match the H-1B fee in Proclamation 10973. That is the right benchmark, because OPT is already used as a substitute for H-1B. A lower fee would keep the arbitrage. If a school or employer cannot justify $70,000 to place one foreign graduate into the U.S. labor market, the placement should not happen. Tuition is the wrong comparison. The right one is the cost of hiring an American with no payroll-tax break and no uncapped multi-year permit.

3.  The $30,000 subsequent fee is justified.
Post-completion OPT plus a STEM extension would cost $100,000. That is appropriate. The STEM extension functions as a three-year work visa and should not be cheaper, in total, than ordinary employment authorization. Pre-completion plus post-completion should also cost $100,000, so schools cannot split authorization to dodge the fee.
Keep $30,000 on every later recommendation, including each STEM extension. Reject a STEM discount, a per-student cap, or a “critical field” waiver. Real shortages can use H-1B, O-1, or employment-based immigrant visas, which have wage and petition controls OPT lacks.

4.  Workers, wages, and hiring.
OPT expands early-career labor, especially in STEM, with no cap and a FICA advantage worth several thousand dollars a year to the employer. The advantage is largest for recent master’s graduates, who often remain nonresidents for most of OPT. Employers will prefer that hire to a citizen who triggers full payroll taxes.
The fee protects workers. It is not a revenue measure. Collections go to the Treasury and are not tied to a named employer. Its value is fewer uncapped foreign graduates in the same junior jobs.

5.  Fraud and abuse.
DHS reports that HSI found more than 10,000 F-1 students at suspect OPT employers, including shell companies, residential worksites, and pay-to-stay schemes. GAO has found OPT job records too incomplete to show where participants worked or to judge technology-transfer risk. Reported OPT employment also rose more than 21 percent in one year.
An upfront fee deters abuse that site visits cannot cover. A school putting a student into nominal employment must risk $70,000, then $30,000. Do not add hardship waivers. Fraudulent actors will claim them first.

6.  Who bears the cost.
The duty belongs on the school. Schools will pass the cost to the student, the employer, or both. That is a feature. The school marketing OPT, the graduate receiving work authorization, and the employer getting a FICA-advantaged hire should pay, not the American worker and not the taxpayer.

Do not move the fee to an appropriation, allow a recommendation before payment, or exempt small schools. Most SEVP-certified schools are small. An exemption would leave most of them outside the rule.

Please end post-completion OPT and the STEM extension, or commit to a rule that does so. If the program continues, adopt both fees with no cut, waiver, or STEM discount; require payment before the DSO recommendation and the EAD; do not let staffing firms spread one fee across many workers; and deposit collections in the Treasury.

Respectfully submitted, 
Sherry Monk, Houston, TX

1. Introduction
I am submitting this comment to address a fundamental legal and policy flaw in the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking concerning Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. Relying exclusively on exorbitant financial extractions—while ignoring all qualitative, academic, and merit-based criteria—transforms administrative oversight into a transactional monetization scheme that damages regulatory integrity.

2. Background
This comment targets the proposed provisions under Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100 that mandate a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 extension fee for OPT recommendations. The agency frames these extractions as necessary to maintain program integrity, reduce fraud, and offset operational costs.

3. Analysis: Monetization of Oversight vs. Merit-Based Regulation
Replacing Qualitative Standards with Monetary Extraction: Under standard administrative practice, regulatory compliance is measured through objective, qualitative benchmarks—such as academic standing, field-of-study alignment, background checks, and institutional accreditation. By conditioning work authorization primarily on the payment of a massive fee, the agency effectively establishes a "pay-to-play" model. This creates the appearance of an administrative buy-in, where authorization is granted not based on merit or rule compliance, but on financial capacity.

Failure to Curb Actual Fraud: A flat fee does not evaluate whether an applicant or institution is engaging in fraudulent activity. High-wealth bad actors or predatory operations can easily absorb or finance a $70,000 fee to maintain access, while fully compliant, highly qualified candidates at top research institutions are excluded simply due to cost. Monetizing administrative recommendations fails to separate legitimate applicants from fraudulent ones.

Arbitrary and Capricious Standard Under the APA: Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency actions must show a rational connection between the facts found and the choices made. Demanding tens of thousands of dollars for a routine administrative endorsement without linking the fee amount to actual individualized processing costs or qualitative screening metrics fails the standard of reasoned decision-making.

4. Recommendations
Withdraw the Flat Fee Framework: Rescind the $70,000 and $30,000 fee proposals entirely.

Re-establish Merit-Based Compliance: Replace monetary barriers with strict, qualitative compliance standards, including mandatory GPA baselines, verified institutional performance audits, and direct field-of-study alignment.

Limit Cost Recovery to Actual Administrative Expenses: If processing fees are assessed, cap them strictly at the demonstrated, itemized cost of conducting background checks and SEVP system maintenance, as required by standard fee-setting guidelines.

5. Conclusion
Administrative oversight should evaluate compliance, academic rigor, and merit—not financial liquidity. Replacing regulatory standards with a massive flat fee undermines public trust and fails to address actual program integrity. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and return to targeted, qualitative enforcement.

1. A deterrent charge of this size is a tax, and only Congress can impose taxes.

The proposal sets a substantial charge whose stated purpose is to deter participation in OPT. A charge designed to discourage conduct, and set at a level far above the cost of administering the program, operates as a revenue-raising measure. The power to tax belongs to Congress under the Constitution (Article I, Section 8). An agency cannot create a tax through a fee label, and the Department should not assume authority that the statute does not clearly grant.

2. The revenue is not tied to the stated purpose.

The proposal says the charge is meant to address fraud, but the funds would be deposited in the general Treasury and would not be used for fraud prevention or enforcement. A fee whose proceeds are disconnected from its justification fails to show a reasonable relationship between the charge and the government service or regulatory cost it is supposed to cover. The rule should explain how the money would be used, and it should not rely on a fraud rationale that the revenue structure does not support.

3. The fraud is on the employer side, but the costs fall on schools and students.

Where fraud occurs, it is typically committed by employers, such as those who create sham training positions or fail to provide the required training. Yet the proposal places the financial burden on students and on the schools that sponsor them. The rule does not target the parties responsible for the misconduct. Imposing costs on those who are not the wrongdoers is neither effective nor fair as a fraud-prevention measure.

4. The economic burden on current students is unfair.

Many students have already enrolled, planned their finances, and made decisions based on the program rules in place. Applying a new charge to them, or to those who entered under prior terms, shifts costs retroactively and without adequate notice. Students with limited resources would be disproportionately affected, which could effectively bar them from completing their degrees or accepting legitimate training positions.

5. Less burdensome alternatives were dismissed too quickly, and the comment period is inadequate.

The proposal does not adequately consider alternatives to a financial deterrent, such as strengthened employer compliance audits, improved information sharing, targeted enforcement against bad-actor employers, and clearer reporting requirements. These options are dismissed in a few sentences without meaningful analysis of their costs, benefits, or effectiveness. For a rule of this significance, the comment period of [X days] is too short for stakeholders, including schools, students, and employers, to analyze the proposal and submit detailed data. The Department should extend the comment period and give the public a real opportunity to respond.

6. The loss estimate is circular.

The proposal treats fees that schools did not collect as a "loss" caused by fraud, but the amount of that "loss" depends on the fee the Department itself sets. The analysis therefore assumes its conclusion: a higher fee produces a higher estimated loss, which in turn justifies the fee. The Department should not measure the harm of fraud using a number that its own pricing decision determines. A valid cost-benefit analysis would estimate actual losses from documented fraud cases, independent of the proposed charge.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees do not target the fraud DHS describes. They impose costs DHS’s own analysis cannot justify. And they would unfairly harm students who came here relying on long-standing rules.

1. The fee does not target fraud (Sections IV.A, V.A).
The fraud described in Section IV.A comes from employers: shell companies, fake worksites, and “phantom employees.” Yet the fee is paid by schools, and Section V.A says it is “not tied to a specific employer.” A fraudulent employer pays nothing, while an honest student with a real job offer pays the full fee. A charge that falls equally on the honest and the fraudulent is not a fraud control.

2. DHS’s own analysis shows billions in costs and no measured benefits (Section VII.A, Table 1).
DHS estimates fee transfers of $8.4–16.5 billion per year and opportunity costs of up to $8.2 billion per year. In Table 1, the benefits are listed as “Not Estimated.” Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 require agencies to choose approaches that maximize net benefits. A rule with billions in quantified costs and no quantified benefits does not meet that standard.

3. The fee does not fund enforcement (Section IV.C).
Section IV.C states that the fees go to the Treasury and cannot be used by ICE. The fee therefore adds no investigators, site visits, or SEVP staff, even though DHS identifies the lack of these resources as the core problem. Because the fee has no relationship to the cost of administering OPT, it raises serious questions about whether INA 214(a) authorizes it.

4. Better, targeted alternatives exist (Sections IV.C, VII.B.6).
DHS’s own investigation identified more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers. That result shows targeted enforcement works. DHS could instead:

require employers to verify they are real businesses (for example, through E-Verify and proof of business),
extend training plans and site visits to all OPT, or
bar flagged employers from hiring OPT students.

DHS rejected these options mainly because a fee is faster. Speed is not a valid reason to burden hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students.

5. The rule is a de facto ban on non-STEM OPT (Section VII.A.3).
DHS’s low-participation scenario assumes schools would stop paying for non-STEM students entirely. Congress has never eliminated OPT, and DHS should not eliminate it indirectly through a price few can pay. IntroductionI am submitting this comment to highlight fundamental administrative and legal flaws in the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. Conditioning post-graduation work authorization on an exorbitant flat fee replaces qualitative regulatory enforcement with a pure monetization mechanism, violating basic administrative fee-setting standards under federal law.   2. BackgroundThis comment addresses the proposed provisions under Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100, which mandate a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 extension fee for OPT recommendations. However, the proposed fee magnitude far exceeds legitimate administrative cost recovery.   3. Analysis: Regulatory Extraction vs. Statutory Fee AuthorityViolation of Full Cost-Recovery Standards Under OMB Circular A-25: Under 31 U.S.C. 9701 and OMB Circular A-25, administrative user fees must be strictly tied to the actual, itemized cost of providing a specific government service or adjudication. High wealth individuals or bad-actor entities can easily absorb financial burdens, while high-performing, compliant scholars from modest backgrounds are excluded based solely on liquidity.   Unfunded Administrative Burden Shifting: DHS relies heavily on DSOs to execute SEVIS reporting, data entry, and compliance verification without providing direct federal compensation to institutions. Imposing massive fee collection and confirmation mandates onto university DSOs adds significant administrative burden without improving the qualitative evaluation of applicants.   4. RecommendationsRescind Flat $70,000 and $30,000 Fees: Fully withdraw the proposed fee structure, as it bears no rational connection to the actual cost of SEVP administration or SEVIS maintenance.   Align Fees with Actual Itemized Cost Recovery: If an administrative processing fee for OPT is deemed necessary, restrict the assessment strictly to the itemized costs of system maintenance, background checks, and verification, in full compliance with OMB Circular A-25 and 31 U.S.C. 9701.   Focus Oversight on Qualitative Merit and Risk-Based Audits: Enhance program integrity through targeted SEVP audits of non-compliant programs and objective academic standards (e.g., degree alignment and institutional performance) rather than monetizing benefit access.   5. Transforming OPT authorization into a transactional extraction fails to address actual program integrity and exceeds standard administrative fee authority. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule

That means the proposal could indirectly raise tuition or reduce academic services for domestic students as well. Reducing their enrollment would weaken universities financially and could increase costs for everyone.
The proposal would also harm U.S. scientific, technological, and economic competitiveness. OPT is one of the key reasons talented international students choose to study in the United States rather than in Canada, Europe, Australia, or Asia. It allows graduates to apply the education they received in the United States, gain practical experience, contribute to research and industry, and often become part of the U.S. high-skilled workforce. Making OPT effectively unaffordable would send a clear message that the United States is less welcoming to global talent. Competitor countries would benefit from the students, researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs trained in U.S. universities.
The structure of the fee is also poorly tailored to fraud prevention. A legitimate student at a reputable university would trigger the same $70,000 fee as a student at an institution or employer presenting a high fraud risk. A flat fee does not distinguish between low-risk and high-risk cases, and wealth becomes a proxy for legitimacy. Well-funded institutions and wealthy students may retain access to OPT, while equally qualified students at public, regional, or smaller nonprofit institutions may lose access. That is neither an efficient anti-fraud tool nor a fair way to protect program integrity.
The proposal may also produce unintended labor-market effects. DHS could also strengthen employer verification, require business documentation, increase audits, impose penalties on bad actors, and use risk-based screening. These tools directly address fraud without imposing a massive financial barrier on every legitimate OPT participant.
Finally, the rule conflicts with the broader national interest in maintaining a strong U.S. higher-education system. American universities are a major source of global influence, research output, innovation, and talent recruitment. Weakening their ability to attract international students would reduce tuition revenue, research capacity, entrepreneurship, tax revenue, and long-term economic growth. The costs would extend well beyond foreign students.
For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. If DHS determines that additional anti-fraud measures are necessary, it should adopt targeted, evidence-based, risk-focused enforcement tools that punish fraud without undermining legitimate students, universities, employers, and U.S. competitiveness.
