I strongly oppose the proposed rule. The fees are legally unsupported, disproportionate to the problem DHS describes, and would cause serious harm to U.S. universities, employers, and the economy.

1. DHS lacks clear statutory authority to impose these fees.
DHS relies on INA § 214(a) (the “time and conditions” provision) and general rulemaking authority (Section III.A). Nothing in these provisions authorizes a fee of this size. A user fee must be tied to the cost of a service or the value conferred on the payer (see 31 U.S.C. § 9701; National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). The NPRM does neither. It states that the fees would be deposited as miscellaneous receipts in the Treasury and that ICE “would not maintain or use” the funds. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service, set to deter participation and raise revenue for the general Treasury, is a tax, and the power to tax belongs to Congress. A fee of this magnitude, which DHS itself says may reduce or end a program that has existed for decades, also raises a major-questions problem: Congress has never clearly delegated authority to price a lawful, long-standing program out of reach.

2. The fee is set by reference to the H-1B fee, not by any measure of cost or harm.
DHS says it chose an amount “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” (Section IV.C). OPT and H-1B are different programs with different purposes. OPT is authorized practical training directly related to a student’s degree; it is not a work visa. Setting the fee to mirror another program’s fee is arbitrary and is not a reasoned basis under the APA.

3. The fee does not fit the fraud problem DHS describes.
DHS cites a probe identifying “more than 10,000” students working for suspect employers. By DHS’s own 2024 figures, 194,554 students were on pre-/post-completion OPT and 165,524 on STEM OPT, about 360,000 in total. The cited suspect cases are a small fraction of participants. DHS proposes to impose a $70,000 charge on every student to address misconduct by a few shell employers and a small number of bad-actor schools. Targeted tools are available and more effective: employer verification, site visits, better use of data DHS already collects through SEVIS and the I-983, and enforcement against identified fraudulent employers and schools. DHS has not explained why these alternatives are insufficient, and it has not analyzed them.

4. The fees do not fund the enforcement DHS says it needs.
The NPRM argues that OPT growth has outpaced DHS’s compliance resources, yet admits that none of the fee revenue would go to ICE or SEVP. The stated rationale and the actual mechanism are disconnected.

5. The labor-market justification is not supported by evidence.
The NPRM relies mainly on a presidential proclamation, a 2017 study about 2001 wages, and the assertion that displacement is “indisputable.” It offers no analysis of whether OPT participants actually displace U.S. workers in the occupations at issue. The 2016 STEM OPT rule already requires employer attestations of no displacement and wage parity. If DHS believes enforcement of those requirements is weak, the remedy is enforcement, not a prohibitive charge on students.

6. The rule would hurt U.S. universities, employers, and competitiveness.
OPT is a core reason international students choose U.S. institutions. International students support tuition revenue, research capacity, and local economies, and many go on to found companies or fill roles that employers cannot fill domestically. Under the proposal, schools must pay before a DSO can recommend OPT. Schools will either pass the cost to students and employers (DHS acknowledges this) or stop recommending OPT. Either result makes the U.S. less attractive than Canada, the U.K., Australia, and other competitors, and the damage falls hardest on students without independent wealth, on smaller institutions, and on startups and small employers that cannot absorb a five- or six-figure cost per hire.

7. The regulatory analysis is inadequate.
The NPRM does not meaningfully quantify the effect on enrollment, tuition revenue, employer costs, tax receipts, or innovation. It does not adequately consider the burden on small entities (schools, startups, small businesses) as the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires, and it does not evaluate less burdensome alternatives. DHS’s own statement that the program may be shut down entirely absent these fees is not a substitute for analysis.

8. Recommendation.
DHS should withdraw the proposed fees. If DHS has legitimate fraud concerns, it should pursue narrowly targeted measures aimed at fraudulent employers and schools, supported by a transparent, data-based analysis, and, if a fee is ever warranted, tie it to the actual cost of administering OPT.

Thank you for considering this comment.

oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.
1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.
2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).
3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.
4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.
5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).
6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).
7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.
8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.
9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee on schools for a student’s first period of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension (DHS, 2026). I urge DHS to withdraw it. The rule rests on an assumption that OPT harms U.S. workers, which the available evidence does not support, and it would damage the research base that U.S. technological leadership depends on.

1. The best available evidence shows OPT does not harm U.S. workers, and STEM OPT helps them.

DHS justifies the fee as protecting U.S. workers, yet the proposed rule cites no empirical study showing that OPT participants displace American workers or depress their wages.

No sign of displacement. An analysis of OPT data from 2008 to 2016 found no evidence that OPT students reduce job opportunities for U.S. workers. Employers hired more OPT workers where U.S. workers were scarce, and more OPT participants relative to U.S. workers was associated with lower unemployment (NFAP, 2019). OPT participants were also a very small share of the workforce: less than 1% of U.S. workers with a STEM bachelor’s degree (NFAP, 2019).
Gains from the 2016 STEM OPT extension. A 2026 study by Kwon, Lee and Monras used a synthetic difference-in-differences design. It found that keeping international STEM graduates in the U.S. “stimulated firm creation and the demand for native high-skilled workers,” and that the extension may have boosted innovation and startup investment, especially near top research universities. In other words, the very program this rule would make unaffordable created demand for American workers.
More U.S. students in STEM. Research summarized by Zavodny for NFAP finds that each additional 10 bachelor’s degrees awarded to international students is associated with about 15 additional STEM bachelor’s degrees earned by U.S. students (Anderson, 2026).
DHS’s own numbers show the cost. The proposed rule estimates costs to the U.S. economy of about $40 billion over ten years in its primary estimate, and up to $80 billion in its high estimate, without quantifying any offsetting economic benefit (DHS, 2026; Anderson, 2026). Independent estimates suggest a fee of this size could reduce OPT participation by up to 84% at the bachelor’s level and 99% at the master’s level (Clemens, as cited in Anderson, 2026).

A rule that admits multibillion-dollar costs, quantifies no benefits, and contradicts the peer-reviewed and working-paper evidence on U.S. workers fails the basic requirement of reasoned decision-making.

2. The rule would weaken U.S. research and AI competitiveness at a critical moment.

International students are not at the margins of American science and technology. They are central to it.

AI and computing depend on them. In 2021, international students made up 70% of full-time graduate students in AI-related fields at U.S. universities: 71% in computer and information sciences and 73% in electrical and computer engineering (National Science Foundation data, as analyzed in NFAP, 2023).
Practical training keeps that talent here. OPT is the bridge from U.S. training to U.S. employment. Without it, graduates trained in American labs at American expense would apply their skills at firms and universities in competing countries such as China.
The losses would compound. The STEM OPT extension spurred firm creation and innovation in local economies (Kwon, Lee, & Monras, 2026). Pricing students out of practical training would reverse those gains and weaken U.S. leadership in AI and other strategic fields.

3. The fee does not match its stated purpose. DHS presents the rule as a fraud-prevention measure. Yet the fees go to the U.S. Treasury rather than to fraud detection or enforcement (DHS, 2026). If shell employers and “pay-to-stay” schemes are the problem, the right remedy is targeted investigation of those actors. A flat fee on every student penalizes the large majority who use OPT exactly as Congress and DHS intended.

4. The fee selects for wealth, not merit. The rule lets schools pass the cost to students or employers (DHS, 2026). Few students can absorb $70,000 to $100,000, and almost no PhD students living on modest research stipends can. The result would not be a selection of “the most promising” students, as DHS claims. It would be a selection of those whose families or employers can pay.

If the fees are intended to support administrative or enforcement activities, DHS should explain how the amounts were calculated and how the methodology is consistent with the statutory authority governing those charges.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency must examine relevant evidence and articulate a rational connection between the facts it finds and the policy it adopts.

A final rule that retains these extraordinary amounts without adequately addressing their methodology, necessity, and foreseeable consequences would raise serious concerns about reasoned decision-making.

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024-2025. Section VII.A.5.b uses unpaid proposed fees as a proxy for opportunity costs and reasons that affected parties could share costs when OPT benefits exceed the fee. [1] An agency-selected price is not independent evidence of the value lost when participation becomes unaffordable.

Students may lack access to financing even when future benefits exceed the upfront charge. Universities, landlords, retailers, and future employers may collectively benefit from a student's presence, but they cannot necessarily coordinate payment or capture enough of those benefits individually to justify financing it. DHS should evaluate these constraints and use independently supported enrollment and participation assumptions.

The proposal states that collections would enter the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than be retained by ICE. DHS should separately assess transfers, administrative costs, lost output, and distributional effects, while avoiding double counting.

If DHS proceeds, it should exempt students already enrolled when the final rule is published, including otherwise-eligible subsequent OPT and STEM extensions.

DHS should compare the proposal with risk-based audits, verification of actual training, enforcement against fraudulent schools and employers, and proportionate, legally authorized fees supported by transparent cost analysis.

Subject: The Proposed OPT Fees Are an Overbroad Response to Fraud Concerns

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

DHS identifies fraud prevention and program integrity as important objectives. However, the proposed fee structure does not adequately demonstrate how imposing extraordinarily high charges on all covered participants will identify, prevent, or punish the specific forms of misconduct that concern the agency.

A student working for a legitimate employer at a genuine worksite is materially different from a participant relying on fabricated employment documentation or a nonexistent employer.

Likewise, a school with a strong compliance record is materially different from an entity that has repeatedly violated program requirements.

The proposed fees do not adequately explain why these different circumstances warrant the same extraordinary financial burden.

DHS should identify the evidence supporting the conclusion that the proposed charges will reduce the particular types of fraud identified in the NPRM.

The agency should explain whether the fees are expected to deter fraudulent operators, reduce legitimate participation, or achieve both outcomes. It should also explain how it will determine whether the proposal has improved program integrity rather than merely reduced the number of students participating in OPT.

A decline in OPT participation would not, by itself, demonstrate that fraud had been reduced. It could simply mean that legitimate students and employers can no longer afford to participate.

DHS should therefore evaluate whether the proposal is likely to improve compliance rates and fraud detection, rather than relying solely on an expectation that higher costs will discourage participation.

I urge DHS to consider more directly targeted measures, including employer verification, worksite inspections, risk-based audits, enhanced reporting requirements, and meaningful penalties for established fraud.

The agency should explain why these alternatives would not adequately address its concerns and why a uniform, extraordinarily high fee is preferable.

I strongly oppose imposing severe financial barriers on compliant participants without a demonstrated connection between the amounts charged and the fraud risks the agency seeks to address.

PUBLIC COMMENT: Major Questions Doctrine and Lack of Clear Statutory Authorization

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule. The regulation impermissibly asserts regulatory authority over an issue of major economic and political significance without explicit, unambiguous congressional authorization.

I. The Proposed Rule Unmistakably Triggers the Major Questions Doctrine
Under West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022), and Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477 (2023), when an executive agency claims the authority to issue decisions of "vast economic and political significance," courts require clear, specific statutory delegation from Congress.

The proposed rule restructures an international student pipeline that generates an estimated $109 billion in annual economic output, directly altering the regulatory framework for over 294,000 F-1 nonimmigrants, 1,044 accredited academic institutions, and employers nationwide. DHS’s own Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) quantifies this economic footprint, estimating annualized costs of $4.1 billion and a ten-year net economic impact exceeding $35.1 billion (at a 3% discount rate). This massive structural reallocation falls squarely within the core threshold of the Major Questions Doctrine.

Furthermore, this exact Treasury-deposit extraction mechanism was rejected in Global Nurse Force v. Trump, No. 4:25-cv-08454 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2026), where the court enjoined a comparable $100,000 fee on the ground that routing unauthorized revenue extractions into the general fund of the Treasury exceeds executive statutory authority.

II. INA § 214(a)(1) Contains No Clear Congressional Delegation
ICE attempts to ground this vast undertaking in the general provisions of Section 214(a)(1) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1), which permits the Secretary to establish the "time and conditions" of nonimmigrant admission.

An ancillary "time and conditions" clause cannot be stretched to support multi-billion-dollar fee extractions or structural workforce restrictions. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), courts exercise independent judgment when reviewing statutory authority and grant zero deference to an agency's expansive interpretation of its own jurisdiction.

The preamble exposes this fatal statutory flaw: DHS acknowledges (at 91 FR 64576) that "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected." As highlighted in Global Nurse Force, an agency cannot claim clear congressional authorization to extract fees under an ancillary admission provision while simultaneously admitting it lacks statutory authority to retain or administer those proceeds.

III. Legislative History and Executive Admissions Confirm Unlawful Circumvention
The Supreme Court considers whether an issue has been repeatedly debated—and left unpromulgated—by Congress as decisive evidence of a major question. Congress has repeatedly considered and declined to restrict or eliminate Optional Practical Training (OPT).

This administrative bypass was confirmed by Vice President JD Vance on September 16, 2026, stating: "Congress is not going to pass a law changing this, there just isn't the political will to do it... so what are the things that we can do administratively?" Using administrative rulemaking as a pretextual substitute for unpassed legislation is a textbook violation of the separation of powers.

IV. Conclusion
Because ICE lacks clear, explicit statutory authorization from Congress to execute a rule of this economic and political magnitude, the proposed rule violates the APA and must be immediately withdrawn.

1. Introduction
As a resident, taxpayer, and passionate well-wisher of the United States, I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I care deeply about the economic vitality, technological leadership, and security of our nation. Watching our immigration framework be converted into an exorbitant, transactional roadside tollbooth is deeply alarming, prompting me to question what kind of message this sends to the global community about American fairness and merit.
2. Background
This comment addresses the proposed rule published under Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100, which mandates a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and a $30,000 fee for extensions (including STEM OPT). The agency attempts to justify these massive financial extractions under statutory fee authorities like Section 286(m) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and OMB Circular A-25, framing them as necessary measures to secure program integrity and curb fraud. 
3. Analysis: Sarcastic Realities vs. Flawed Agency Logic
•	The "Just Pay Us $70k and Everything is Settled" Business Model: Let’s be completely honest about what this rule actually implies. Under this framework, the federal government is effectively signaling that a student's GPA, academic rigor, research contributions, university ranking, and hard work no longer matter one bit. Want to study and work hard? Doesn't matter. Just drop $70,000 on the table, and poof—all paperwork problems and compliance questions magically vanish. It turns legitimate oversight into a "pay-to-play" legal bribe system where only the wealthy get a free pass.

•	Absurd Administrative Math vs. Actual Cost Recovery: DHS claims these fees are necessary to cover administrative overhead. Yet, according to the agency’s own supporting documentation (OMB Control No. 1653-0038), a Designated School Official (DSO) takes roughly 7 minutes to process an OPT recommendation and about 5 minutes to confirm fee payment data in SEVIS. That is a grand total of 12 minutes of computer data entry. Charging $70,000 for 12 minutes of keyboard work values government paperwork at over $350,000 an hour. Under OMB Circular A-25, user fees must reflect the actual, itemized cost of providing a service—not function as a ransom note that turns a federal database into a massive profit center. 

•	Misinterpreting Program Growth & Modern Tech Needs: DHS points to the growth in OPT participation (~294,000 students) and total international enrollment (~1.2 million) as a sign of system abuse. In reality, this growth mirrors the explosive evolution of our own digital economy. We are living through an era of acute talent shortages in Artificial Intelligence, data architecture, and advanced technologies where local pipelines cannot keep pace.
•	Destroying America’s Startup & Innovation Engine: International graduates contribute tens of billions of dollars to our economy and support hundreds of thousands of jobs. Crucially, one-quarter (25%) of all U.S. billion-dollar startup companies ("unicorns") were founded or co-founded by former international students trained right here in our universities, each creating hundreds of local jobs. Slapping a $70,000 tax on OPT doesn't protect American workers—it strangles the very startup ecosystem and innovation pipeline that keeps America ahead of global competitors.
4. Recommendations
To protect our nation's reputation, economy, and technological leadership, I urge DHS to take the following steps:
1.	Withdraw the Flat Fee Structure Immediately: Completely rescind the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 extension fees, as they bear zero relation to actual administrative costs. 
2.	Align Fees with Actual Itemized Expenses: If administrative cost recovery is required, strictly limit fees to the actual itemized cost of system overhead and database maintenance in compliance with federal guidelines. 
3.	Deploy Targeted, Risk-Based Audits Instead of Blanket Taxes: Address program integrity through focused SEVP audits of non-compliant institutions and objective academic standards rather than monetizing benefit access. 
5. Conclusion
Turning our immigration system into a roadside tollbooth where anyone with deep pockets can buy past oversight does not protect American workers or stop fraud—it undermines the integrity of U.S. higher education and starves our economy of essential talent. As a U.S. well-wisher who wants our country to remain a beacon of innovation and merit, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this counterproductive proposed rule.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes new Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees to combat fraud, protect U.S. workers, and cover SEVP administrative costs. However, levying this fee on universities instead of employers or students is a fundamentally flawed approach that places an unmatched burden on academic institutions while failing to address the root causes of the agency's concerns.

I strongly urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure based on the following:

1. Misplaced Burden and Labor Market Realities
DHS argues the fee will protect American workers. Yet, the proposal penalizes schools rather than addressing the actual labor market dynamics. Currently, employers are exempt from paying FICA payroll taxes (roughly 7.65%) for some F-1 students on OPT, creating a direct financial incentive to hire them over domestic workers. If DHS genuinely wants to level the playing field, it should require employers to pay a fee equivalent to this FICA exemption. Burdening universities does nothing to alter the hiring incentives of U.S. corporations.

2. Fees on Schools Will Not Prevent Employer Fraud
The proposal suggests that charging schools will help combat fraudulent activities by "shell" employers. While universities maintain SEVIS records, they are not law enforcement agencies and lack the jurisdiction to audit off-campus corporations. Charging a university a fee does not prevent bad actors from setting up fake businesses. If DHS needs funds to investigate fraud, it should implement an employer-side registration fee.

3. A Sensible Mechanism Already Exists
DHS cites the need to cover SEVP administrative costs. The infrastructure for this already exists: the I-901 SEVIS fee, which international students pay before obtaining their F-1 visa. If SEVP requires more funding to monitor students through the OPT lifecycle, the most logical administrative action is to raise the existing I-901 fee. Creating a completely new fee aimed at university administrators introduces unnecessary bureaucratic friction.

Conclusion
To achieve its objectives, DHS must align its fees with the parties actually participating in the labor market. I urge the agency to revise this proposal by burdening the right party for this fee, or by adjusting the existing I-901 SEVIS fee.

It surrenders American innovation to competitors. Nearly 6 in 10 billion-dollar startups were founded or co-founded by immigrants, and a quarter have a founder who first arrived as an international student; two-thirds of top AI companies have immigrant founders (NFAP). International students are roughly 80% of full-time graduate students in computer and information sciences. Fraud deserves targeted enforcement, not a blanket tax. DHS already has SEVP audits, SEVIS data analysis, employer verification, and STEM training-plan requirements. A flat fee punishes legitimate students, universities, and employers exactly as much as the fraudsters it claims to target.

Re: Public Comment in Strong Opposition to Proposed $70,000 Initial OPT Fee and $30,000 Extension Fee ,A Pay-to-Play Tollbooth That Harms America’s Future
To Whom It May Concern at the Department of Homeland Security:
1. Introduction
As a resident, taxpayer, and passionate well-wisher of the United States, I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I care deeply about the economic vitality, technological leadership, and security of our nation. Watching our immigration framework be converted into an exorbitant, transactional roadside tollbooth is deeply alarming, prompting me to question what kind of message this sends to the global community about American fairness and merit.
2. Background
This comment addresses the proposed rule published under Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100, which mandates a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and a $30,000 fee for extensions (including STEM OPT). The agency attempts to justify these massive financial extractions under statutory fee authorities like Section 286(m) of the Immigration and Nationality Act and OMB Circular A-25, framing them as necessary measures to secure program integrity and curb fraud. 
3. Analysis: Sarcastic Realities vs. Flawed Agency Logic
•	The "Just Pay Us $70k and Everything is Settled" Business Model: Let’s be completely honest about what this rule actually implies. Under this framework, the federal government is effectively signaling that a student's GPA, academic rigor, research contributions, university ranking, and hard work no longer matter one bit. Want to study and work hard? Doesn't matter. Just drop $70,000 on the table, and poof—all paperwork problems and compliance questions magically vanish. It turns legitimate oversight into a "pay-to-play" legal bribe system where only the wealthy get a free pass.

•	Absurd Administrative Math vs. Actual Cost Recovery: DHS claims these fees are necessary to cover administrative overhead. Yet, according to the agency’s own supporting documentation (OMB Control No. 1653-0038), a Designated School Official (DSO) takes roughly 7 minutes to process an OPT recommendation and about 5 minutes to confirm fee payment data in SEVIS. That is a grand total of 12 minutes of computer data entry. Charging $70,000 for 12 minutes of keyboard work values government paperwork at over $350,000 an hour. Under OMB Circular A-25, user fees must reflect the actual, itemized cost of providing a service—not function as a ransom note that turns a federal database into a massive profit center. 

•	Misinterpreting Program Growth & Modern Tech Needs: DHS points to the growth in OPT participation (~294,000 students) and total international enrollment (~1.2 million) as a sign of system abuse. In reality, this growth mirrors the explosive evolution of our own digital economy. We are living through an era of acute talent shortages in Artificial Intelligence, data architecture, and advanced technologies where local pipelines cannot keep pace.
•	Destroying America’s Startup & Innovation Engine: International graduates contribute tens of billions of dollars to our economy and support hundreds of thousands of jobs. Crucially, one-quarter (25%) of all U.S. billion-dollar startup companies ("unicorns") were founded or co-founded by former international students trained right here in our universities, each creating hundreds of local jobs. Slapping a $70,000 tax on OPT doesn't protect American workers—it strangles the very startup ecosystem and innovation pipeline that keeps America ahead of global competitors.
4. Recommendations
To protect our nation's reputation, economy, and technological leadership, I urge DHS to take the following steps:
1.	Withdraw the Flat Fee Structure Immediately: Completely rescind the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 extension fees, as they bear zero relation to actual administrative costs. 
2.	Align Fees with Actual Itemized Expenses: If administrative cost recovery is required, strictly limit fees to the actual itemized cost of system overhead and database maintenance in compliance with federal guidelines. 
3.	Deploy Targeted, Risk-Based Audits Instead of Blanket Taxes: Address program integrity through focused SEVP audits of non-compliant institutions and objective academic standards rather than monetizing benefit access. 
5. Conclusion
Turning our immigration system into a roadside tollbooth where anyone with deep pockets can buy past oversight does not protect American workers or stop fraud—it undermines the integrity of U.S. higher education and starves our economy of essential talent. As a U.S. well-wisher who wants our country to remain a beacon of innovation and merit, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this counterproductive proposed rule.

International enrollment could decline, further eroding tuition revenue that helps sustain campuses and the surrounding communities. American students, faculty, local businesses, and taxpayers would feel the consequences. A policy advertised as protecting Americans should not ignore these burdens on Americans.

Fourth, the rule could undermine the research and innovation ecosystem. American universities train engineers, scientists, and other specialists whose knowledge can be applied in laboratories, businesses, and public-sector projects. OPT offers a limited period to put that training into practice. Removing this opportunity through an unaffordable financial barrier may encourage students to study and build careers elsewhere from the outset. The United States pays a long-term price when ideas, future companies, and highly trained people move to competing economies. A policy aimed at preventing misuse must account for what the country gives up when lawful talent is driven away.

Fifth, the proposal's economic justification is unconvincing. DHS's own regulatory analysis assigns no estimate to annualized monetized benefits, while its primary estimate puts annualized costs at approximately $4.1 billion. It also recognizes the possibility of reduced international enrollment, lost graduate earnings, and lost employer productivity. Without a credible estimate of how much fraud the fee would prevent, it is impossible to conclude that the expected benefits justify such extraordinary costs. Nor does a reduction in OPT participation, by itself, demonstrate a corresponding reduction in fraud.

Sixth, the proposed payment does not directly finance the promised oversight. DHS explains that collected fees would enter the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, rather than being retained by ICE or earmarked for OPT compliance investigations. That raises a basic question: how does collecting billions of dollars from universities strengthen enforcement if the funds are not dedicated to investigators, employer verification, or better monitoring systems? The proposal appears to rely mainly on exclusion rather than more effective detection.

The more rational approach is to improve the rules where abuse actually occurs. DHS could prioritize investigations of shell employers, validate actual worksites and payroll records, apply meaningful penalties to repeated violators, and expand targeted compliance checks. It should evaluate these alternatives against the proposed fee using measurable outcomes, including fraud identified, enforcement costs, effects on tuition and enrollment, and lost economic activity.

America's universities and research institutions are national assets. They should not be forced to choose between supporting legitimate graduates and protecting their own financial health. DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue evidence-based enforcement that safeguards program integrity without sacrificing the nation's education system and economic future.

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule that would impose a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT. This proposal is fundamentally destructive to the concept and value of a US degree for international students.

The proposed rule operates on a flawed assumption that OPT students are systematically used to undercut American workers and depress wages. My personal experience directly contradicts this narrative. I work at a university that makes absolutely no distinction between a US citizen and an international student regarding compensation. I am the only international student working in my department, and I am paid the exact same fixed standard wage as my peers. Nobody reduced the wage to hire me, and I am not cheap labor. I was hired for my skills, not my visa status.

Furthermore, the economic rationale of this rule is disproportionate and punitive.

In 2024, 194,554 F-1 students were granted OPT employment authorization.

If the $70,000 initial fee were applied to that exact population, it would extract over $13.6 billion from the higher education and training ecosystem.

The Department of Homeland Security explicitly acknowledges that institutions may pass this massive financial obligation directly onto students or employers.

International students already pay exorbitant international tuition rates to attend US universities. Adding a $70,000 fee simply to utilize the practical training component of that education makes a US degree mathematically unviable for most. OPT is a crucial program that allows students to gain hands-on, real-world experience directly related to their major area of study. Stripping this opportunity away through prohibitive fees will not protect US workers. It will simply drive top global talent to competing countries.

I urge DHS to withdraw this harmful proposal and protect the integrity and global competitiveness of the US higher education system.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, particularly the proposed fee structure in Section V, the consideration of reliance interests in Section VI, and the economic impact analysis in Section VII. As an international PhD student currently studying and conducting research at a U.S. university, I am deeply concerned about the consequences this proposal would have for international students, American universities, and the future of U.S. research and innovation.

Optional Practical Training has been an established part of the U.S. education and immigration system for more than three decades. OPT regulations were formalized in 1992, and the STEM OPT program was subsequently expanded in 2008 and 2016. Over these decades, countless international students have made substantial academic, financial, and professional commitments based on this established regulatory framework. Introducing fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation would fundamentally disrupt these reasonable expectations. Such a dramatic policy change requires compelling evidence, careful consideration of its consequences, and a proportionate justification.

I am particularly concerned about the impact on international students who are already pursuing their degrees in the United States. Many students commit several years to undergraduate, master's, or doctoral education, often making significant financial sacrifices to study and contribute to American academic institutions. Although OPT authorization has never been guaranteed, its longstanding availability has understandably influenced students' educational and professional planning. Providing only a 60-day transition period after the publication of a final rule would be insufficient for students and universities to adjust to such an extraordinary financial burden. Students who entered the United States under the existing framework deserve meaningful consideration of their reliance interests.

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers. However, imposing an exceptionally high financial barrier on legitimate students and educational institutions is a disproportionate response to those concerns. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of academic merit, research ability, or compliance with immigration regulations. The proposed fees could disproportionately affect students from less wealthy backgrounds, smaller universities, and research institutions with limited budgets. More targeted compliance inspections, stronger employer verification, and improved monitoring of actual violations would address potential abuse without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational opportunities.

The proposed rule could also undermine America's long-term competitiveness in scientific research, engineering, technology, and other critical fields. International graduate students contribute to university laboratories, federally supported research projects, technological development, and the broader American economy. Discouraging these students from pursuing professional training in the United States may weaken the country's ability to attract and retain talented researchers. The Department should carefully evaluate these broader economic and academic consequences before imposing costs of this magnitude.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and preserve reasonable access to practical training. If additional oversight is necessary, I encourage the Department to pursue evidence-based and proportionate measures while providing meaningful protections for students who have already committed to their education under the existing framework. Maintaining a fair, predictable, and accessible educational system is essential to preserving the United States' reputation as a global leader in higher education, research, and innovation.

End all foreign worker programs.  These programs are killing the experienced american worker. The Optional Practical Training (OPT) was created out of thin air and needs to be eliminated. Increasing OPT fees would create unnecessary financial barriers for talented graduates and could discourage skilled individuals from contributing to the U.S. Please keep OPT accessible and affordable.

I oppose the proposed rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees,” Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, and urge DHS to withdraw it.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. However, DHS should pursue those objectives through measures that are proportionate, supported by evidence, and directed at actual misconduct.

1. Labor-market benefits should be demonstrated rather than assumed.
Reducing OPT participation does not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in employment for U.S. workers. Outcomes depend on qualifications, geography, employer needs, and whether affected positions would be filled, eliminated, or relocated. DHS should assess these possibilities and account for potential effects on university enrollment, local spending, and employers’ operations.

2. A large fee does not reliably distinguish legitimate participation from fraud.
Financial resources are not a measure of compliance. Law-abiding students and institutions with limited resources could lose access to OPT, while participants engaged in misconduct could still afford the fees. Verification of genuine employment and training, investigations of fraudulent employers, and enforcement against institutions with documented violations would address abuse more directly.

3. Charging institutions does not eliminate the economic burden.
Schools may transfer the costs to students or employers, or decline to recommend OPT. This could make access to practical training depend on personal wealth or institutional resources rather than eligibility and compliance. DHS should evaluate these responses, including their effects on smaller institutions and employers, before adopting the rule.

4. Currently enrolled students deserve meaningful transition protections.
Students who enrolled under the existing framework have already committed substantial time and money to their education. Although OPT authorization is not guaranteed, imposing an exceptionally large new fee after those commitments have been made would materially alter their practical training options. If DHS proceeds with any new fee, it should protect currently enrolled students and allow them to complete otherwise eligible OPT and STEM OPT periods under the prior fee framework.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they make a student's eligibility depend on a third party's budget. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii), USCIS will deny OPT if the school has not paid the fee, even when the student meets every regulatory requirement. DHS declines to define which OPT has "genuine educational value" and leaves selection to schools, with no published criteria, no notice, and no appeal for the student. Because the fee is charged per student, schools gain a financial incentive to recommend fewer students regardless of merit. Two equally qualified students could receive different outcomes based solely on their schools' finances. A federal benefit should turn on the applicant's eligibility, not on an institution's willingness to pay $70,000. DHS should withdraw this proposal.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because DHS contradicts its own positions without explanation. To claim authority, DHS describes OPT as part of an educational F-1 admission; to set the price, it aligns the fee with H-1B employment-visa fees. In 2024, DHS amended the cap-gap rules specifically to ease the transition from OPT to H-1B status; it now calls that same pathway "circumvention" of the H-1B cap. In 2016, DHS justified STEM OPT as beneficial to the U.S. economy; it now reverses course with no new OPT-specific labor data, relying on a study of 2001 wages. FCC v. Imposing fees of this magnitude would effectively make that opportunity inaccessible to many qualified students, regardless of their academic achievements, professional abilities, or potential contributions.

DHS argues that these fees would combat fraud and protect American workers. However, **financial barriers are not fraud prevention measures.** A legitimate student with limited financial means is not more likely to commit fraud than a wealthy student. If fraud is the concern, DHS should pursue targeted enforcement, improved verification, and meaningful penalties for actual violations instead of imposing indiscriminate financial barriers on law-abiding students.

Furthermore, the proposal risks undermining America's competitiveness in attracting international talent. Students choose American universities partly because of the opportunity to translate their education into meaningful professional experience. Making that opportunity prohibitively expensive would discourage talented students from studying in the United States and could deprive American employers, universities, and communities of valuable contributions.

International students should be evaluated based on their qualifications, compliance with immigration requirements, and professional potential—not their wealth or their university's ability to pay an extraordinary fee.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures that address actual fraud without financially excluding legitimate international students.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would undermine the educational purpose of practical training. OPT must be directly related to a student's field of study. DHS acknowledges that students will abandon pre-completion OPT rather than pay twice, eliminating training during studies, much of it in university research labs. Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because American students may end up paying for them. DHS expressly acknowledges that schools may pass the fee on to "all students." Meanwhile, the fee proceeds go to the Treasury rather than to SEVP oversight, so taxpayers gain no added enforcement. DHS should withdraw this proposal and analyze its impact on domestic students and small institutions.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees, and I object to the process. I strongly oppose the proposed rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).

As a graduate student of a U.S. university, I am deeply concerned that imposing fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation would place practical training beyond the reach of many international students, undermine American universities, and weaken the United States' long-term scientific and economic competitiveness.

First, the fees create a major financial barrier for international students who already contribute substantially to the U.S. economy. International students often pay higher tuition than domestic students and have limited, if any, access to federal aid. They also spend on housing, goods, and services that support local communities and the broader U.S. economy. A fee as large as $70,000-$10,000 would effectively block many students from accessing OPT, an integral part of the F-1 program they relied on when they chose to pursue their education in the United States.

Second, the proposed rule would undermine research and teaching at U.S. universities. International students, especially graduate students, are integral to American research institutions, contributing as researchers, teaching assistants, and mentors. Their work supports scientific discovery, classroom instruction, and the training of future generations of scientists and engineers. Restricting post-graduation opportunities would make U.S. universities less attractive to talented students worldwide, ultimately weakening the research ecosystem that has helped sustain America's leadership in science and technology.

Third, the rule threatens America’s ability to attract global talent. U.S. universities draw exceptional students in AI, biotechnology, engineering, and other critical fields, and many leading researchers and founders in the U.S. began as international graduate students here. The United States gained enormously from scientists who fled Europe before and during World War II. In the age of nations competing aggressively for top talents, training the world’s brightest minds and then pricing them out would hand that advantage to competing nations.

Fourth, the fees are disproportionate to their stated goals. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate aims, but DHS has not shown why fees of this size, estimated at about $12.4 billion a year in its primary scenario, are necessary. Targeted measures such as better verification, audits, and enforcement against actual violations would address abuse without penalizing legitimate participants.

Finally, the proposal raises serious concerns about fairness and reasonable reliance. Many students chose U.S. universities partly because of OPT and made years of financial and personal commitments based on it. Imposing these fees midway through their studies, with only a 60-day implementation period, unfairly changes the terms they relied on. DHS should at minimum consider lower fees, phased implementation, and exemptions for current students and recent graduates.

The United States has built its scientific and economic strength in no small part by attracting ambitious people from around the world and giving them opportunities to contribute. OPT has been an important part of that system. Making it prohibitively expensive would not strengthen American competitiveness; it would undermine one of the country's most enduring advantages.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and pursue more targeted, proportionate measures that protect program integrity without sacrificing America's ability to attract and retain global talents.
These regulations are so important to protect our educational institutions and promote education among Americans

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because DHS relies on a factor Congress controls. DHS cites the FICA tax exemption as giving employers an incentive to hire OPT students. An agency may not use a fee to offset tax policy it disfavors; doing so relies on a factor Congress did not intend it to consider (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 1983). DHS should withdraw this proposal and remove any reliance on the FICA exemption as a justification.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because DHS failed to adopt obvious, less burdensome alternatives. Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because the economic analysis cannot support them. Docket ICEB-2026-0100: I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would effectively close practical training to entire fields of study. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

A fee should reflect the actual cost of administering a program, not be used to discourage eligible students from participating.

But instead of directly targeting those employers, it places the financial burden on universities and students. Third, this would cause serious financial harm to American universities and unfairly punish international students. Many schools simply cannot afford these fees, and students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses. This could discourage international enrollment, reduce university revenue, and hurt research and innovation in the United States.

Finally, there seems to be a disconnect between the stated purpose of preventing fraud and how the fees would actually be used. If the money goes into the general Treasury rather than being specifically dedicated to fraud investigations, employer verification, and enforcement, how would these charges improve OPT integrity?

I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud, but this proposal creates enormous costs without clearly demonstrating how those costs would solve the problem. It would harm universities, discourage talented international students, and undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and focus on targeted enforcement against actual fraud rather than imposing excessive financial barriers on legitimate students and universities.

This proposal is extremely unappealing as well as unjust towards international students that have worked very hard in addition to spending a lot of money over many years toward their education. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and request withdrawal of the fee structure. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but DHS has not shown that these charges effectively target misconduct or justify their burdens.

1. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance or merit.

Tables 1 and 10 report approximately $4.1 billion in primary annualized costs, while monetary benefits are not estimated. **Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees**

I am an international PhD student conducting research at a U.S. institution. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation, and respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

**1. The fees are disproportionate to the stated goals.**

Preventing immigration fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals. But imposing extraordinary fees on legitimate graduates and universities is not a targeted solution. Financial resources do not measure academic merit, professional qualifications, or immigration compliance. A qualified graduate could lose access to practical training simply because their institution cannot afford the fee.

DHS should explain why employer verification, compliance audits, stronger reporting, and enforcement against fraudulent entities would not achieve these objectives at substantially lower cost.

**2. The proposal undermines investment in American education and research.**

American universities, faculty, and funding agencies invest years in training international students. Students also contribute substantial time, research, and resources. It makes little economic sense to educate skilled graduates and then create a financial barrier to their participation in the U.S. workforce.

According to the NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, temporary visa holders earned approximately 61% of U.S. doctorates in computer and information sciences, 54% in engineering, and 51% in mathematics and statistics in 2024. Restricting their ability to apply this training in the United States could reduce the return on American educational and research investments.

**3. The fees would disproportionately burden early-career researchers and nonprofit institutions.**

Although the proposed fees would initially be paid by educational institutions, they could be passed to students or employers. Universities, nonprofit research institutions, and laboratories often operate under tight budgets. The public value of research and early-career scientific work is not measured by starting salaries or an institution's ability to finance a $70,000 or $100,000 charge.

This approach could exclude qualified graduates based on institutional wealth rather than professional ability.

**4. The proposal threatens U.S. competitiveness.**

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–2025 academic year. Post-graduation practical training is an important consideration for prospective students. A major financial barrier to OPT could discourage applications to U.S. institutions and push talented graduates toward other countries, affecting universities, employers, research programs, and local communities.

**5. The proposal fails to adequately address reliance interests and economic costs.**

Students entered multi-year U.S. degree programs under a framework that offered OPT as practical training. PhD programs frequently take five years or longer. A short implementation period does not adequately protect students who have already invested years and cannot readily change their plans.

DHS also acknowledges substantial potential economic costs and reduced OPT participation, while indicating that fee revenue would not be specifically dedicated to ICE enforcement. The agency should substantiate the fee amounts and explain why projected benefits outweigh the costs.

**Conclusion**

Protecting American workers and maintaining immigration integrity matter. But these goals should be pursued through evidence-based, targeted enforcement rather than sweeping financial barriers that keep qualified graduates from contributing to the United States.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees and urge DHS to withdraw this rule in favor of proportionate, effective alternatives.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal.

Seeking this experience does not, by itself, demonstrate immigration abuse.

My educational decisions involved years of commitment, relocation, and significant opportunity costs. Although OPT was not the sole purpose of my education, its availability was a meaningful part of my decision. The fact that training requires approval does not eliminate the importance of having a financially accessible opportunity to apply.
Current students cannot recover those years or easily restart their education elsewhere. DHS should preserve the existing framework for currently enrolled students and current OPT participants, including their otherwise eligible STEM extensions.
3.	Consider the loss of research and industrial contributions.
Regarding Section VII, these fees could discourage prospective international students from choosing U.S. institutions and prevent graduates from applying their specialized education here.
Doctoral research requires sustained effort, technical preparation, and persistence. International students contribute alongside American students to demanding research programs. Policy should support the development of qualified researchers from both groups.
In my field, practical experience connects university research with steel manufacturing challenges. Excluding graduates because they or their institutions cannot afford a large upfront fee risks losing useful expertise. DHS should assess these effects across disciplines, including specialized manufacturing fields, rather than treating every occupation as having the same labor-market conditions.

• Enforce compensation and non-displacement protections and provide accessible channels for reporting abuse.
• Improve DSO training and electronic reporting, with reasonable correction opportunities for minor errors and meaningful consequences for deliberate fraud.
• Evaluate any additional administrative charge through a transparent cost analysis and applicable legal authority, while preserving affordability.
• Protect currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants through their otherwise eligible training periods.

I respectfully request withdrawal of the proposed fees and adoption of proportionate safeguards that protect American workers while preserving legitimate practical training.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. Imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and a $30,000 fee for subsequent authorization represents an unprecedented barrier that will decimate the OPT program, causing severe harm to American students, the domestic workforce, and U.S. geopolitical leadership. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

1. Severe Financial Impact on Domestic U.S. Students
The premise that restricting international students prioritizes domestic students ignores the structural realities of university funding. International students typically pay full, non-resident tuition, which directly subsidizes the operational costs of American universities and lowers the overall baseline cost of education for domestic students. Furthermore, these tuition dollars fund vital institutional financial aid, merit-based scholarships, and work-study programs reserved strictly for American citizens. Forcing a precipitous drop in international enrollment will leave significant funding gaps, forcing universities to reduce financial assistance or hike domestic tuition.

2. Devastating Economic Consequences and Local Job Losses
International education is a multi-billion-dollar export sector that acts as a vital driver of the U.S. economy. According to data from NAFSA: Association of International Educators, international students are projected to contribute $38.3 billion to the U.S. economy and support over 294,000 American jobs during the 2026–2027 period alone. This consumer spending sustains small businesses, housing markets, and local services nationwide. Forcing international talent out will choke off billions from local economies and lead to campus-wide budget shortfalls and layoffs.

3. Unacceptable Geopolitical and Technological Risks
International graduates make up roughly 50 to 70 percent of all STEM graduate students in the United States, particularly within critical sectors like electrical and industrial engineering. These students form the backbone of advanced research and laboratory work. If global talent is discouraged from coming to or staying in the U.S. due to these cost structures, they will redirect their innovations to geopolitical rivals like China, which are actively expanding pathways to retain high-skilled researchers. Squeezing the supply of high-skill workers impairs long-term U.S. productivity, innovation, and technological leadership.

Balanced Alternatives to Prevent OPT Exploitation
DHS can accomplish its enforcement goals through targeted, non-financial alternatives that preserve the program's immense benefits:
• Enhanced Digital Reporting and Audits: Utilize existing SEVIS tracking data to execute targeted, risk-based electronic audits of employers offering OPT placements, stopping fraudulent entities without penalizing legitimate students.
• Mandatory E-Verify Alignment: Require all participating OPT employers to use the USCIS E-Verify system to confirm employment eligibility, standardizing compliance without charging massive upfront fees.
• Stricter Employer Placement Attestations: Mandate that employers electronically sign specific legal certifications verifying that the training program directly aligns with the student’s major course of study and does not displace an existing U.S. worker.

2. The fee bears no relation to program costs and is arbitrary and capricious.

Federal fee-setting must be grounded in the cost of providing the service. DHS's own estimates describe $8.7 to $16.9 billion in annual transfers under this rule. A charge two orders of magnitude above adjudication costs, generating multi-billion-dollar transfers, is revenue-raising — not cost recovery. The proposal offers no credible methodology tying $70,000 and $30,000 to any actual government cost, which renders it arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and beyond the Department's lawful authority. Respectfully submitted,
Felix Liu
University of Chicago, Master of Public Policy

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but the principal arguments supporting these fees do not establish that this approach will achieve those goals.

1. Ability to pay does not establish compliance.

A large payment does not verify that an employer exists, that training is genuine, or that compensation is appropriate. A well-financed fraudulent operation could pay, while a legitimate student or resource-constrained institution could be excluded. DHS should explain why financial capacity is a reliable indicator of integrity and compare the fee with targeted employer verification, audits, and penalties for actual misconduct.

2. Restricting OPT does not necessarily create more jobs for American workers and may encourage offshore hiring.

Employers make hiring decisions based on skills, experience, productivity, and cost. At a given salary budget, a company may seek the candidate who best meets its needs. If the proposed fee prevents a U.S.-educated graduate from working locally, the employer will not necessarily fill that position with a U.S. worker.

For roles that can be performed remotely, the company may instead recruit abroad or move the work to an overseas team. It could even employ the same graduate after that person returns to their home country. In such cases, the work would continue outside the United States rather than become an opportunity for an American worker.

This possibility does not mean every OPT position would move offshore. It means DHS cannot assume that each reduction in OPT participation creates a corresponding domestic job. The agency should evaluate how many positions would be filled by U.S. workers, moved abroad, left vacant, or eliminated, and assess whether the proposed fee could unintentionally encourage employers to expand overseas hiring instead of maintaining jobs in the United States.

3. Wage concerns call for enforceable wage protections.

For STEM OPT specifically, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)(8) requires comparable employment conditions and compensation, and subsection (10)(ii) requires an employer assurance against replacing U.S. workers. These protections should be enforced and any gaps addressed. Charging a school does not itself verify an employer's wages or prevent displacement. DHS should explain how a payment produces those outcomes beyond simply reducing participation.

4. Payroll-tax differences do not justify this fee.

IRS guidance recognizes a Social Security and Medicare tax exemption for certain qualifying F-1 nonresident aliens. It does not cover every OPT participant or exempt students from all applicable income taxes. The proposed fee would not change those tax rules or ensure comparable pay. DHS should quantify any claimed tax-related hiring advantage and explain why a large school-paid fee is a proportionate response.

5. Revenue is not the same as funding oversight.

Section IV.C states that these receipts would go to the Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or earmarked for SEVP enforcement. A possible future congressional appropriation is not a funded inspection plan. Supporters therefore should not assume that paying this fee will purchase better verification or additional investigations.

6. Educational purpose and institutional accountability require substantive standards.

Current regulations authorize temporary OPT employment connected to the student's field of study. Where that connection is missing, DHS should investigate and enforce the requirement. Likewise, schools should be accountable for accurate recommendations and reporting. A financial barrier does not distinguish meaningful training from sham training, or academic merit from wealth.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fees. DHS should pursue targeted safeguards against documented abuse and explain the legal, economic, and administrative basis for any necessary fee. Any replacement proposal should evaluate effects on compliant participants, actual benefits for U.S. workers, and less burdensome alternatives.
