I am a recent graduate in computer science and business, and I have worked as a software engineer at both a large technology company and early-stage fintech startups. I write to respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees for Optional Practical Training.

DHS cites fraud and worker protection as the basis for this rule, but a flat fee does not target fraud. It falls equally on every student, compliant or not, and does not identify a single bad actor. Fraud is better addressed through enforcement aimed at noncompliant employers and schools, using tools DHS already has, such as SEVIS reporting, site visits, and E-Verify enrollment for STEM OPT employers. Likewise, worker protections are already in place: STEM OPT requires a formal training plan, E-Verify enrollment, and wages comparable to those paid to similarly situated U.S. workers. If DHS has found gaps in these safeguards, the appropriate remedy is stronger enforcement, not a fee on every participant.

The amount of the fee also appears untethered from any stated cost. DHS estimates the rule would collect $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year, and it should explain how that figure relates to the actual cost of administering OPT. A fee far above administrative cost functions less as a user fee and more as a restriction on a program DHS has chosen to keep.

In practice, the rule would end OPT at most schools. A STEM student who completes initial OPT and the extension would cost a school $100,000, more than a year of tuition at nearly any U.S. university, and DHS itself acknowledges that schools may decline to pay. Large, well-endowed institutions might absorb the cost, while public universities and smaller colleges likely could not, so access to OPT would depend on a school’s endowment rather than a student’s merit. The proposal also states that schools may pass the fee on to students or employers. Passed to students, it would exclude anyone without substantial family wealth. Passed to employers, it would favor large companies over startups. From my own work at early-stage companies, I know a small team cannot absorb $70,000 per hire, while a large firm can, and the rule would steer talent toward incumbents and away from the companies that create new jobs. For the same reasons, DHS should reject the alternative of re-charging the $70,000 fee at each degree level, which would penalize the advanced-degree graduates the United States most wants to retain.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. If some fee is necessary, it should be set at the documented cost of administering OPT, and fraud should be addressed through targeted enforcement against noncompliant employers and schools. Before issuing any final rule, DHS should also publish an analysis of the expected decline in OPT participation and its effects on schools of different sizes and types. OPT keeps trained graduates contributing to the U.S. economy, and I urge DHS to protect it.

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. These fees risk causing significant economic harm to the United States by making it more expensive for American employers to hire qualified graduates, weakening the talent pipeline from American universities to U.S. businesses, and encouraging skilled talent to contribute to competing economies instead.

1. The proposed fees would impose substantial costs on American employers.

A proposed fee of $70,000 for initial OPT participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation could make hiring an otherwise qualified graduate financially impractical. For many employers, particularly startups, small businesses, and research-driven organizations, these amounts could exceed what they can reasonably allocate to hiring a single entry-level employee.

American businesses should be able to compete for talent based on skills, qualifications, and economic value. A hiring-related cost of this magnitude could discourage employers from considering qualified candidates, even when those candidates could contribute meaningfully to business growth and productivity.

The consequences would extend beyond individual graduates. Fewer viable hires could mean slower product development, reduced research capacity, fewer new ventures, and missed opportunities for American businesses to grow.

2. The United States risks losing talent it has already invested in educating.

American universities attract talented students from around the world. These students pay tuition, contribute to university research, support local economies, and spend money on housing, transportation, food, and other goods and services.

When graduates are unable to pursue practical employment opportunities because of prohibitively high fees, the United States risks losing part of the economic return on that investment. The education and training take place in America, but the resulting skills, productivity, innovations, and future business activity may benefit other countries instead.

This is not simply a question of individual employment opportunities. It is a question of whether the United States wants to retain the economic value generated by the education system it has worked to build.

3. The proposed fees could weaken American innovation and entrepreneurship.

Innovation depends on access to qualified people who can turn research, technical knowledge, and new ideas into useful products and services. Re: ICEB-2026-0100 — Economic Concerns About Proposed OPT Fees

To the Department of Homeland Security:

As an American citizen and taxpayer, I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. Immigration enforcement and protecting U.S. workers are important goals, but the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT could impose substantial costs on American jobs, universities, businesses, and taxpayers without a demonstrated net benefit [1].

1. American jobs and local spending are at stake. NAFSA estimates international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–25 [2]. Their spending sustains jobs in education, housing, retail, food service, and transportation. Colleges and surrounding towns could lose customers and revenue if prospective students decide that studying in the United States is no longer worth the cost and uncertainty.

2. Enrollment already faces pressure. IIE reported that new international enrollments at 828 surveyed U.S. institutions fell 17% in fall 2025 [3]. Separately, an August 2026 NAFSA scenario projected as many as 111,000 fewer international students, up to $3.4 billion in lost economic contributions, and nearly 40,000 jobs at risk because of pressures existing before this proposal [4]. These estimates are NOT forecasts of losses caused by this rule. They nevertheless show why DHS must evaluate whether very large OPT fees would worsen an already challenging situation.

3. Hiring international graduates does not automatically displace Americans. A 2024 peer-reviewed study in MIS Quarterly found that increased supply of foreign STEM professionals through a STEM OPT extension boosted employment among domestic STEM workers, especially in information technology [5]. This does not prove that every OPT job benefits Americans, but it challenges the assumption that restricting OPT necessarily creates equivalent employment for U.S. citizens. DHS should evaluate empirical effects on U.S. wages, jobs, innovation, and business expansion.

4. U.S. universities could face damaging tradeoffs. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), a university issuing 100 initial OPT recommendations would owe $7 million [1]. Schools could refuse recommendations, pass costs to students or employers, or divert funds otherwise available for teaching, research, and student support. Domestic students and university employees could also be affected. Smaller universities, startups, and nonprofit employers may be especially unable to bear these costs.

5. American technological competitiveness matters. NSF reports that temporary visa holders earned 61% of U.S. computer and information sciences doctorates and 54% of engineering doctorates in 2024 [6]. The United States invests in educating and training highly skilled researchers. Making practical training prohibitively expensive could encourage some of them to develop technology and build careers in competing economies instead of contributing to U.S. firms and institutions.

6. Fee revenue is not an economic benefit by itself. DHS's own analysis estimates about $12.4 billion in annual fee collections under its primary scenario and classifies these payments as transfers to the federal government [1]. Transfers are not equivalent to increased national output. DHS also acknowledges uncertainty about reductions in OPT participation and related opportunity costs. It should quantify impacts on employment, university budgets, tuition, employer productivity, and tax receipts before proceeding.

I support targeted antifraud enforcement, audits, and protections against worker exploitation. But broad, exceptionally high fees may punish legitimate schools and undermine the U.S. economy without effectively distinguishing fraud from compliance. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, assess less burdensome enforcement alternatives, and publish a fuller economic analysis that accounts for American workers and communities.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I understand DHS's goals of preventing fraud, protecting American workers, and ensuring that practical training is genuine. These goals matter. But requiring a university to pay $70,000 before recommending an eligible student for OPT does not establish whether that student's eventual employment is legitimate. For initial post-completion OPT, students do not even need a job offer when their school recommends them. A large payment is therefore a poor substitute for verifying employers, worksites, training arrangements, and compliance after employment begins.

The proposal places an extraordinary cost on SEVP-certified institutions, and DHS acknowledges that schools could pass that cost to students or employers. Many schools may simply stop recommending otherwise qualified students. A student's chance to use their education would then depend less on eligibility or merit than on a school's budget. This is particularly troubling for public universities and smaller institutions. DHS's own economic analysis estimates roughly $4.1 billion in annualized costs and $12.8 billion in annualized transfers under its primary scenario (3% discount rate). I urge DHS to explain why costs on this scale are necessary and proportionate to the fraud risks identified.

OPT is also an important reason students choose American universities. It allows graduates to apply classroom and laboratory learning in the U.S. economy. The National Science Board's The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026 reports that temporary visa holders received 42% of U.S. science and engineering master's degrees and 38% of doctoral degrees in 2024, including 61% of doctorates in computer and information sciences. These students help sustain research in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, medicine, and engineering. Restricting their ability to gain practical experience could weaken the appeal of U.S. universities and their research ecosystems.

I am particularly concerned about what happens to innovation when highly trained graduates cannot remain and contribute. Some international graduates hope to start companies, commercialize research, and hire workers in the United States. If post-graduation opportunities become financially inaccessible, they may instead build those startups in India or other countries. That would mean potential U.S.-based investment, intellectual property, and future American jobs being created elsewhere. This is a foreseeable risk, not a claim that every graduate would leave. A policy meant to protect U.S. workers should account for the jobs and businesses it might discourage from being created here.

Section VII.A should examine these longer-term effects more carefully, including possible reductions in international enrollment, university research capacity, startup formation, and employer access to specialized skills. The impact may not be captured fully by estimates of immediate OPT participation or fee transfers. DHS can address fraud more directly through risk-based audits, verification of employers and actual worksites once employment is reported, stronger reporting requirements, data-sharing, and meaningful penalties for fraudulent schools or employers. These measures should be designed to avoid unnecessary burdens on legitimate participants. DHS should compare their costs and expected effectiveness with the proposed fees rather than treating payment capacity as evidence of integrity.

America's universities attract talent because they offer both excellent education and opportunities to apply it. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure, reject the higher-degree repeat-fee alternative, and adopt proportionate measures that target fraud without driving away the researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs who could help build America's future.

Neither rules out displacement, but both caution against assuming that excluding an international graduate creates an equivalent opportunity for an American worker. DHS should assess effects on business formation, complementary employment, and the relocation of work abroad.

Second, requiring schools to pay does not resolve who bears the burden. DHS acknowledges that costs may be passed to students, employers, or the broader student body. University funding could divert resources from teaching and research; student funding could make access depend on wealth; employer funding could disadvantage startups and smaller organizations. Ability to pay does not establish educational merit or compliance.

Smaller employers may need specialized skills yet lack resources to absorb these costs. Restricting their ability to hire graduates with the skills they need could delay projects, constrain expansion, and reduce opportunities for American colleagues and future hires. Reduced OPT participation should not itself be treated as evidence of improved worker protection.

Third, the proposal could weaken American higher education and workforce preparation. Prohibitive fees could discourage international students from choosing U.S. universities and encourage graduates to take their skills elsewhere. Over time, this could narrow the pool of researchers and future faculty, weaken research programs, and limit courses, mentorship, and research opportunities for American students. Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. Although schools would legally owe these fees, the resulting barriers could fall on students, universities, and employers. I ask DHS to withdraw the fees and use targeted oversight.

OPT’s educational purpose.

OPT is temporary practical training directly related to an F-1 student’s field of study. It lets graduates apply what they learned at U.S. institutions. Under the proposal, eligibility alone would no longer suffice: a university would first need to pay $70,000 for an initial recommendation. DHS itself states that an initial OPT recommendation does not require a prior job offer (DHS, 2026). Thus, students could lose access to training before any employer has assessed their abilities. Financial capacity is not a measure of educational merit or program compliance.

Effects on students and universities.

In a peer-reviewed study of past STEM-OPT expansions, Amuedo-Dorantes et al. (2023) found increases of 18% in international bachelor's matriculation and 30% in master's matriculation. These past effects are not predictions for this rule. They nevertheless show that access to practical training shapes enrollment decisions. A large fee could undermine the expected value of degrees for enrolled students and deter future applicants.

Shih (2017) also found that, in the graduate programs studied, 10 additional international students increased domestic enrollment by approximately eight, consistent with tuition revenue cross-subsidizing places for U.S. students. Reduced international enrollment may therefore harm domestic students too.

Effects on workers and employers.

Not every international graduate simply replaces a U.S. worker. Beine et al. (2023) estimated that each additional international master's student increased the U.S. skilled labor supply by 0.23 workers in the graduation year (0.08 for bachelor's students), using 2003–2017 data. Employers could lose access to graduates trained in U.S. programs.

Research also finds mixed distributional effects: Demirci (2020) documented reduced employment for some recently graduated U.S.-born master's workers but higher earnings for experienced U.S.-born master's workers in the same fields. These findings warrant focused labor safeguards—not an undifferentiated $70,000 barrier for every first OPT recommendation.

In a separate study of international enrollment rather than OPT specifically, Dang (2026) estimated that one extra international student per 1,000 working-age residents increased the local employment-to-population ratio by 0.19 percentage points and hourly wages by 0.48%.

Disproportionate costs and inadequate targeting.

DHS estimates $8.4–$16.5 billion in annual fee transfers under its modeled participation scenarios and acknowledges possible losses of student earnings, employer productivity, and international enrollment (DHS, 2026).

The proposal does not establish that a $70,000 payment identifies fraudulent training more accurately than verification of academic relevance, risk-based employer inspections, or meaningful penalties for abuse. Existing STEM OPT training plans already require commensurate compensation and prohibit replacing U.S. workers.

I support protecting American workers and preventing fraud. DHS should publish evidence connecting its proposed fee levels to measurable enforcement benefits, consider less burdensome alternatives, and preserve lawful access to supervised, degree-related work experience. I respectfully request withdrawal of the proposed OPT fee structure.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed OPT fees, because DHS seeks to recast a lawful program as abusive without the reasoned explanation the law requires. 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A).

DHS itself cites Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (D.C. Cir. 2022), which upheld OPT and STEM OPT as a lawful exercise of DHS authority. Sec. III.A. DHS maintained and expanded practical training through rulemaking in 2008 and 2016, and as recently as 2024 amended the cap-gap provisions to facilitate the transition from OPT to H-1B status. Sec. III.B.

The proposal now characterizes participation in that same lawful program as "circumvention" of the H-1B cap and describes the program as "flooded with participants seeking to exploit" it. Secs. III.B, IV.A. Use of a pathway that DHS designed, defended, and recently expanded is not circumvention. An agency changing course must acknowledge the change and offer good reasons for it, and must provide a more detailed justification where its new policy rests on factual findings that contradict those underlying its prior policy. FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515-16 (2009). DHS identifies no new evidence that the program's lawful operation has changed; its evidence concerns a minority of fraudulent employers.

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I am submitting this comment as an individual directly affected by this proposal, and I strongly oppose the rule as written.

1. The fees are arbitrary and bear no relationship to the government's cost. An OPT recommendation is a brief SEVIS entry made by a university Designated School Official. It costs the federal government essentially nothing to process. A $70,000 fee for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one cannot be justified as cost recovery — it is a punitive charge. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agency action that is arbitrary and capricious or unsupported by the record cannot stand, and a fee thousands of times greater than any plausible processing cost fits that description.

2. The rule would functionally eliminate OPT. DHS itself estimates $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual fees across roughly 2,478 schools. No university can absorb $70,000 per student, and few students can pay it on top of tuition. Schools will either stop recommending OPT or pass the cost to students, which means OPT becomes available only to the wealthiest — or to no one. A fee set so high that it destroys the program it purports to administer is not regulation; it is a ban by another name, and it goes beyond what Congress authorized.

3. The economic damage falls on the United States. OPT allows US-educated graduates — particularly in STEM fields facing documented workforce shortages — to contribute their skills to the American economy rather than taking them elsewhere. If OPT becomes financially impossible, those graduates will go to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries that actively recruit them. American employers, universities, and the communities around them lose; competitor nations gain. The rule trades long-term US competitiveness for a short-term Treasury deposit.

4. The fees are deposited into the general Treasury rather than used to administer the student visa program. That design confirms this is a revenue measure, not a user fee tied to services rendered — which further undermines any claim that the amounts reflect the cost of adjudication.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. At a minimum, any fee must be tied to actual processing costs, be structured so it does not fall on students or schools as a barrier to participation, and be supported by analysis showing it will not destroy the OPT program.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I am submitting this comment as an individual directly affected by this proposal, and I strongly oppose the rule as written, on the following additional grounds.

1. The fee has no rational connection to the problems DHS claims to address. DHS cites fraud and worker-protection concerns as justification. But a flat $70,000/$30,000 charge does not distinguish legitimate OPT use from fraudulent use — it prices out both equally. Fraud is addressed through compliance reviews, site visits, and enforcement, not through a toll that honest students and schools must also pay. A rule whose chosen tool does not logically advance its stated goals is arbitrary.

2. The rule upends the reliance interests of students already in the pipeline. International students currently enrolled in US degree programs made multi-year commitments — often at great personal and family expense — with the reasonable expectation that OPT would be available on the terms in place when they enrolled. A 60-day effective date gives these students no meaningful opportunity to adjust. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that agencies must account for serious reliance interests before changing course; this proposal does not.

3. A 30-day comment period is inadequate for a rule of this magnitude. DHS's own estimate puts the annual burden at $8.4 to $16.5 billion across nearly 2,500 schools — plainly a major rule with sweeping consequences for higher education, employers, and the labor market. Thirty days is not enough time for universities, employers, and affected students to analyze the proposal and respond with the data-driven comments the APA process is meant to produce. The truncated timeline undermines meaningful public participation.

4. The flat fee falls hardest on smaller institutions and less-wealthy students. A per-student charge of this size is regressive: well-funded elite universities may find workarounds, while regional public universities, HBCUs, and smaller colleges — and the first-generation and lower-income international students they serve — will simply lose access to OPT. The result is a less diverse talent pool and a further concentration of opportunity among the already privileged.

5. The proposal is administratively unworkable. It turns university Designated School Officials into payment gatekeepers, blocking SEVIS recommendations until a fee clears. Universities are educators, not tax collectors — they have no systems for this, and the inevitable payment delays, errors, and disputes will strand students whose employment authorization timing is critical. The rule creates a bureaucratic failure point with no corresponding benefit.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

**1. U.S. competitiveness and innovation (Sections IV.C and VII.A)**

America benefits when graduates of its universities can apply their education in U.S. laboratories, companies, and startups. **2. American universities and students (Section VII.B)**

The proposed fees would be imposed on U.S. educational institutions, which may pass them to students or employers. Universities compete globally for talented students, researchers, and tuition revenue. Making practical training financially inaccessible could lead applicants to study elsewhere. Lower enrollment may reduce funds for academic programs, research positions, course offerings, and services that also benefit American students.

**3. American jobs and communities (Section VII.A)**

International education supports Americans far beyond campus. These figures reflect the broader international-student economy, not a prediction of this rule's precise effects, but they show the importance of assessing indirect consequences.

OPT participants also pay taxes, spend locally, and work alongside American colleagues. Excluding qualified graduates from legitimate employment does not automatically create equivalent jobs for U.S. workers: hiring depends on skills, industry, geography, and employers' needs. I support protecting U.S. workers and preventing sham employers, fraudulent job offers, and misuse of student status. Yet the fee applies regardless of whether an individual student, school, or employer presents any specific risk. Ability to pay is not evidence of immigration compliance. More proportionate alternatives include risk-based audits, employer verification, targeted site visits, better reporting, and enforcement against proven violations.

The proposed fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury rather than earmarked for OPT oversight. DHS should therefore explain, with evidence, why this particular fee structure would better prevent fraud than targeted oversight with fewer adverse effects.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee rule, complete a fuller assessment of economic, educational, and community impacts, and adopt narrowly tailored anti-fraud measures. Immigration integrity and American economic strength should reinforce each other.

I am very encouraged to see this Administration taking steps to address what I believe has become an unfair imbalance between the employment opportunities available to international students and those available to U.S. workers.

When international students evaluate the cost of studying in the United States, the possibility of obtaining practical training and employment in the United States after graduation is widely considered part of the value of a U.S. education. This helps explain why many international students are willing to pay very high tuition and living expenses.
However, the opportunity to work in the United States is not something created by the university itself. It exists because U.S. immigration policy authorizes employment through programs such as OPT and because American employers are willing to provide those employment opportunities. A useful question is: if post-graduation employment opportunities such as OPT were eliminated, how many international students would still be willing to pay the same tuition to study in the United States?
My view is that the costs of education and the costs associated with access to practical training and employment opportunities should be separated more clearly. Universities should charge students for education, academic services, and the credential they provide. Students who seek the additional privilege of accessing the U.S. labor market through OPT should separately bear an appropriate cost for that opportunity.
Such a system could have another important benefit: it could help bring the price of academic credentials closer to their underlying educational value. This is particularly relevant to many graduate programs. International students may rationally be willing to pay a substantial premium because a degree can also provide a pathway to U.S. work authorization and potentially longer-term employment opportunities. American students, by contrast, receive no additional immigration or work-authorization benefit from earning the same degree. As a result, the same tuition may represent a much less attractive value proposition for a U.S. student. By implementing the new policy, this could make some programs more accessible and attractive to American students. Over time, greater participation by American students in advanced STEM education could expand the domestic talent pipeline for highly technical occupations.
I also believe the scale of OPT deserves serious consideration when evaluating its effects on entry-level employment and internships. When a temporary employment program operates at a very large scale relative to the number of new employment opportunities being created, policymakers should carefully examine its effects on U.S. students and workers, particularly recent graduates competing for entry-level positions.

I think the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee should not be approved . The proposal does not adequately establish that this fee structure is an effective or proportionate way to prevent fraud, protect American workers, or improve program administration.

First, the proposed fees are an imprecise mechanism for identifying legitimate participants. Regarding Sections IV.C and V.A, financial capacity is distinct from compliance with OPT requirements. A legitimate student or employer may lack the resources to pay, while a fraudulent participant may have sufficient funding. Although higher fees could discourage some abuse, they would also discourage lawful participation. DHS should estimate these effects separately and demonstrate why the selected amounts would improve compliance more effectively than targeted verification and enforcement.

Second, the economic benefits to American workers cannot be inferred directly from a reduction in OPT participation. Regarding Sections IV.B and VII.A, employers do not necessarily replace each departing OPT participant with an American worker. They may instead leave positions vacant, reduce production, or move work abroad. Conversely, some positions may be filled by American workers. An adequate analysis should estimate these different responses and their effects on wages, employment, and complementary jobs. Broad trends in unemployment or foreign-worker participation do not establish the causal effect of OPT.

Third, the opportunity-cost analysis in Section VII.A.5.b requires a stronger economic foundation. Using unpaid fees as a proxy for the value of lost participation does not adequately distinguish willingness to pay from ability to pay. Students may face credit constraints, and prospective employers may be unwilling to finance authorization before assessing a candidate. Research and innovation can also produce benefits beyond the student, school, and immediate employer. Those benefits may not be captured through private cost-sharing. DHS should evaluate financing constraints and economic spillovers explicitly.

Fourth, requiring educational institutions to make the payment does not determine who ultimately bears the cost. If schools absorb the fees, fewer resources may be available for instruction, research, or student services. If they pass the fees to students, access depends more heavily on personal wealth. If employers pay, smaller businesses and research organizations may face greater hiring constraints than larger employers. The analysis should assess these distributional effects, including possible costs to American students and workers.

Fifth, the proposed funding mechanism does not directly expand enforcement capacity. Section IV.C states that receipts would be deposited in the Treasury rather than retained by ICE for OPT oversight. Reduced participation could lower administrative workload, but that effect should be compared with the educational and economic activity forgone. DHS should evaluate whether targeted audits, employer verification, and sanctions for documented violations would achieve comparable compliance improvements at lower overall cost.

Finally, Sections V.C and VI do not adequately address students already enrolled. A rule applied to future recommendations can still disrupt decisions made years earlier under existing regulations. A 60-day transition provides limited opportunity to adjust lengthy educational commitments. If DHS proceeds with changes, it should protect currently enrolled students and their otherwise eligible subsequent OPT periods.

Before adopting these fees, DHS should provide evidence supporting the specific amounts, a causal assessment of labor-market effects, and a comparison with less costly enforcement alternatives. Without that analysis, the proposal risks restricting legitimate training without demonstrating corresponding improvements in compliance or outcomes for American workers.

Observability and load testing need no physical presence. If a team cannot fill the position here, the work goes to an offshore contractor or to a team the company already has abroad, and the job is gone from the U.S. labor market entirely rather than transferred to an American worker. The rule does not analyze this substitution, and it should, because it undercuts the premise of Section IV.B.

A second thing the rule misses is where OPT people actually work. The preamble's fraud examples are IT staffing companies and shell firms. That is not the whole program. A large share of OPT and STEM OPT participants work on public-facing infrastructure, including health information systems, hospital software, and clinical research tooling. A rule aimed at the first should not be written so that it takes out the second, and it would be straightforward to target: employer verification, worksite requirements, scrutiny based on an employer's history. DHS lists those options in Section IV.C and sets them aside without pricing them.

Third, the fee is charged to the party with the least information. A school's DSO has never seen the codebase, the team, or the training plan. The employer has. Putting a $70,000 decision on the office that knows least about whether the training is real is a strange way to improve screening, and it predicts the outcome: schools will not try to judge quality, they will simply stop recommending, because the cheapest way to avoid a $70,000 mistake is to make no decision at all. Section VI says a student who received a DSO recommendation before the effective date will not trigger the initial fee, but that a subsequent OPT request on or after the effective date is covered. Harm to American universities and students
International students help sustain American higher education. Many pay full tuition, which supports financial aid, faculty, research labs, and programs that domestic students rely on. OPT is a major reason students choose the U.S. An Institute for Progress survey found 80% fewer students would likely try to stay if these fees took effect; among OPT-eligible STEM students, only 15% would. Just 100 initial participants would expose a school to $7 million in fees, a burden regional public universities, community colleges, and small colleges cannot absorb. Harm to American companies and jobs
U.S. employers compete for talent against companies in Canada, the UK, Germany, Australia, and Asia, all of which offer accessible post-study work pathways. High-skilled immigrants found companies and drive innovation that creates jobs for Americans, and cutting off this pipeline reduces American job creation.

Illegal and unconstitutional
Federal fee authority, including 31 U.S.C. § 9701 and 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m), permits fees that recover the cost of a service. This $70,000 charge bears no relation to the cost of processing an OPT recommendation, would be deposited in the general Treasury rather than fund the program, and is openly designed to deter participation. A charge meant to raise revenue and discourage lawful activity is a tax, not a fee. Article I, Section 8 gives the taxing power to Congress alone. In National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States (1974), the Supreme Court read agency fee authority narrowly precisely to avoid unconstitutionally delegating that power to agencies.

Fraud calls for targeted enforcement
Shell-employer fraud should be addressed. But this fee punishes every legitimate student and school for a few bad actors, and because the money goes to the Treasury, it funds no enforcement at all. DHS has better tools: require E-Verify for OPT employers, expand site visits, strengthen SEVP verification, and penalize the specific employers and schools engaged in abuse.

Contrary to American ideals
America became the world leader in science, technology, and education by welcoming talented people from everywhere and letting them prove themselves through hard work. Generations of immigrants arrived as students and went on to found companies, cure diseases, teach in our classrooms, and become proud Americans. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to introduce unprecedented, exorbitant fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). This cost-prohibitive fee will inflict severe harm on the American higher education system and the domestic innovation ecosystem. For the following critical reasons, the proposed fee should be entirely abandoned:
1.Severe Financial Hardship for Startups and AI Innovation: Early-stage startups rely heavily on finite venture capital funding and operate with zero or razor-thin profit margins in their foundational years. Their limited capital is strictly allocated toward research and development (R&D) and core payroll. This is particularly true for the surging artificial intelligence (AI) sector. If the United States is to maintain its global leadership in AI, domestic startups must have an accessible pathway to hire highly skilled, foreign-born professionals. A fee of this magnitude will effectively lock startups out of the global talent pool, stifling innovation where it is needed most.
2.Disincentivizing Outstanding International Students: This fee creates a massive artificial barrier for exceptional international students considering U.S. higher education. If post-graduation experiential training becomes economically unfeasible for potential employers or students, these top minds will choose to study, graduate, and build their careers in competing jurisdictions, severely weakening the pipeline of American-educated talent.

Alternative Regulatory Mechanisms to Combat Fraud of OPT
While the agency’s stated goal of integrity is important, implementing a cost-prohibitive fee is an blunt tool that punishes legitimate actors rather than targeting bad ones. DHS can achieve more effective fraud mitigation through targeted, data-driven administrative compliance enforcement, such as:
1.Enhanced Employer Vetting: Implementing stricter verification protocols, including mandatory site visits to an employer’s physical office or operational address.
2.Tax Compliance Verification: Cross-referencing employer tax records to verify the legitimacy, capitalization, and payroll capacity of the hiring entity.
3.Student Tax Reporting Requirements: Mandating that OPT participants submit proof of tax compliance (such as initial paystubs or local tax filings) within the first month of employment, followed by periodic validation checks during their training period.

For these reasons, the proposed fee is arbitrary, capricious, and economically destructive. I strongly urge the agency to withdraw this fee proposal in its entirety.

I write to urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. The rule would require SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 before recommending any F-1 student for Optional Practical Training (OPT) for the first time, and $30,000 for every later OPT recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension. These amounts are not fees in any ordinary sense. They exceed a year of tuition at most American universities, they bear no relationship to the cost of any service DHS provides, and DHS concedes the money would go to the general Treasury rather than to the program it claims to protect.

I am an international undergraduate at an Ivy League university. Like many elite schools that are need-blind for American applicants, mine is not need-blind for international applicants. Because applying for aid can significantly hurt an international applicant's chances of admission, very few international students I know receive any scholarship. Most of us pay the full sticker price, far more than American classmates from similar family backgrounds.
DHS asserts that the F-1 visa "was never intended to provide a pathway to employment" (91 FR 64578). But OPT is training that, by regulation, must relate directly to what we studied. Charging tens of thousands of dollars more before we may practice the skills we already paid so much to learn has no sound basis.

Other countries understand this. The United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia all offer post-study work permits, because graduates of their universities help fill high-skill gaps in their labor markets. Under this rule, the United States would stand out among major destinations: it charges international students full price for their education, then demands a six-figure sum before they may train in their field.

That approach overlooks what educated immigrants have built here. A 2022 National Foundation for American Policy study found that immigrants founded 319 of 582 U.S. startups valued at $1 billion or more (55 percent), and that 143 of those companies had a founder who first came to the U.S. as an international student. SpaceX, Stripe, Databricks, OpenAI, and Anthropic each have at least one foreign-born founder, and leading U.S. firms depend on highly educated immigrants to keep their edge.

I may not seek U.S. employment right after my bachelor's degree. But the accumulation of rules aimed at foreign students, including the fixed admission period final rule (91 FR 44976), the $100,000 H-1B payment, this proposal, and DHS's stated intent to scrutinize CPT and the loss of opportunities that has been around for decades, signals a novel form of hostility that is hard to ignore. Had I known such changes were possible, I would have seriously reconsidered studying in the United States. Prospective students abroad are weighing that same question now, and the rule's economic analysis does not count the cost of those who choose to go elsewhere.

Above all, DHS has no right to impose this fee. Under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. 9701, agency charges must be fair and based on the cost to the government and the value of the service to the recipient. The proposed charge has every feature of a tax and none of a fee. No statute authorizes it, and the power to levy a charge of this size, designed to deter rather than to pay for any service, belongs to Congress alone.

1. The fee has no reasonable relationship to the cost of the service.
The current OPT application costs students a few hundred dollars. The proposal would raise this cost by more than a hundredfold, and the money would go to the general Treasury instead of funding the administration of the program. A charge of this size, unconnected to processing costs, works as a penalty on students. It does not recover a cost.

2. The rule would hit non-STEM and creative-field students hardest.
As a student in the creative field, I am eligible for only 12 months of OPT, with no STEM extension. The creative industries where graduates like me start our careers, such as design studios, film and media companies, and agencies, are often small or mid-sized. They cannot absorb a $70,000 cost for a one-year entry-level hire. In practice, the rule would end OPT for students in the arts and humanities while doing little to address the concerns DHS describes.

3. The fee shifts an impossible burden onto schools.
The proposal requires schools to pay before a DSO can enter a recommendation. Small, specialized institutions like mine cannot fund $70,000 per graduating international student. Students would be forced to pay it themselves, or schools would stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, students would lose access to a benefit that existing regulations provide.

4. Fraud concerns should be addressed through targeted enforcement.
If specific schools or employers are misusing OPT, DHS already has the tools to investigate them, deny certification, and penalize bad actors. A uniform fee on every student punishes the large majority who use OPT exactly as intended: to gain practical experience directly related to their field of study. DHS should consider less burdensome alternatives, such as stronger SEVIS reporting and employer verification or audits of noncompliant institutions.

5. Practical training is part of an American education.
Hands-on work after graduation is how students in my field build portfolios and professional skills. During my studies, I have worked as a brand creative intern at a U.S. media company, and OPT is the natural next step in that training. Making OPT unaffordable would push international students toward countries that welcome graduates, and it would weaken the U.S. creative industries that benefit from our work.

6. If any fee is finalized, students must have adequate notice.
At a minimum, DHS should keep the provision that exempts recommendations dated before the effective date. It should also give students and schools a long enough transition period to plan, since students who are already enrolled made their decisions under the current rules.

As a U.S. citizen, taxpayer, and advocate for American higher education and innovation, I strongly oppose the proposed rule Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01) and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

Harm to the U.S. Economy and American Workers
According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs in 2024–2025, and Fall 2025 declines already cost more than $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs. A $70,000 fee would compound this decline. Although DHS frames the rule as protecting American workers, it would harm Americans directly through budget pressure on universities serving domestic students, losses to U.S. employers, and reduced activity in communities that depend on international enrollment.
Exporting U.S.-Trained Talent to Competitors
Practical training is how America captures the return on its investment in educating these students. Without it, U.S.-trained graduates, often in STEM and finance, would take their skills to Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, which actively recruit them through post-study work pathways. The rule would transfer American-developed skills and innovation capacity to firms and nations that compete directly with the United States.
Ignored Alternatives
The fee falls identically on compliant students and schools with no indication of fraud. DHS considered targeted alternatives, such as site visits and training-plan requirements, but rejected them largely because of the government’s own administrative burden. Convenience does not justify billions in costs on regulated parties. At a minimum, DHS should exclude students with verified full-time offers from legitimate employers and focus on auditing employers directly.
Failure to Consider Reliance Interests
Under DHS v. Regents, 140 S. Ct. 1891 (2020), an agency acts arbitrarily and capriciously under 5 U.S.C. § 706 when it fails to consider substantial reliance interests. Students, universities, and employers have made multi-year commitments in reliance on OPT as it has existed for decades under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)–(11). The NPRM does not adequately account for them.
The Fee Exceeds DHS’s Authority and Is an Unauthorized Tax
Congress has authorized DHS immigration fees only on a cost or service basis: INA § 286(m) and the IOAA, 31 U.S.C. § 9701 (see National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). The NPRM invokes neither, relying instead on INA § 214(a), which authorizes the “time and conditions” of admission but no monetary charges; the only monetary condition it mentions is a refundable bond. By DHS’s own account, the fee is not based on any cost, will be deposited in the general Treasury under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, and is meant to deter participation. Under San Juan Cellular Tel. Co. v. Public Service Comm’n, 967 F.2d 683 (1st Cir. 1992), a charge paid into the general fund for broad public purposes is a tax, and the taxing power belongs to Congress (U.S. Const. art. I, § 8). Where Congress wanted non-cost-based immigration surcharges, it enacted them expressly, as in INA § 214(c). At $8.4 to $16.5 billion annually, the major questions doctrine requires clear congressional authorization, and under Loper Bright v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), DHS’s reading of § 214(a) receives no deference.
Inadequate Comment Period
A 30-day period is inadequate for a multi-billion-dollar rule, especially one where DHS threatens to end OPT entirely. Executive Order 12866 generally calls for at least 60 days. I request an extension and full responses to substantive comments.

I am writing as an F-1 international graduate student in STEM (Mechanical Engineering) currently engaged in advanced academic and engineering research at an accredited U.S. research institution, to express my strong and unequivocal opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding the establishment of exorbitant fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT).

Imposing an unprecedented, punitive fee of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent STEM OPT extensions is substantively flawed, economically destructive, and legally indefensible under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). I urge the Department to immediately withdraw this proposed rule on the following grounds:

1. Lack of Statutory Authority and Violation of IOAA Principles

Under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA, 31 U.S.C. 9701), user fees charged by federal agencies must be reasonably related to the actual costs incurred by the government in providing a specific service to an identifiable recipient. The administrative burden of issuing an SEVIS recommendation (Form I-20) requires negligible marginal effort from designated school officials (DSOs). Imposing a mandatory transfer of $70,000 and $30,000 bears zero rational connection to the administrative processing costs of SEVP. Instead, these amounts represent an ultra vires punitive tax designed to eliminate a legally authorized training program without congressional authorization, violating the core tenets of the APA by acting arbitrarily and capriciously.

2. Catastrophic Disruption to Academic Research and STEM Innovation

Doctoral candidates and graduate researchers in critical STEM fields—such as clean energy infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, power systems resilience, and artificial intelligence—rely on OPT and STEM OPT to bridge academic research with hands-on industrial collaboration, national laboratory research, and practical field implementation. Neither non-profit research universities nor graduate students earning modest academic stipends can absorb or finance a $70,000 fee. By effectively abolishing the practical training pipeline, this rule will throttle the domestic pipeline of high-skilled researchers and severely undermine the United States' competitive technological advantage.

3. Devastating Burden on Higher Education and Flawed Economic Assumptions

The proposed structure mandates that SEVP-certified institutions directly remit these fees to the Department. This places an intolerable financial and administrative liability on public universities, community colleges, and private non-profits alike. Institutions will be forced to either slash vital academic programming or transfer these crippling costs to students, effectively pricing international talent out of U.S. higher education. Consequently, top-tier global scholars will divert to competing international destinations (such as Canada, the UK, Germany, and Australia) that offer clear, accessible post-study pathways, causing billions of dollars in economic losses to local college towns and regional economies.

4. Misguided Means to Address Fraud and Disproportionate Impact

While DHS cites combating fraud and "pay-to-stay" abuses as justifications, levying universal, crippling penalties across all legitimate accredited institutions punishes bona fide degree earners rather than targeting bad-faith actors. Strict compliance frameworks (such as the Form I-983 training plan, E-Verify requirements, and rigorous SEVP accreditation reviews) already exist to enforce compliance. Collective financial punishment across legitimate university graduates is completely disproportionate to the stated regulatory objectives.

For these reasons, the proposed fee schedule represents an irrational, counterproductive barrier to national innovation and educational exchange. I respectfully request that DHS fully rescind this proposed rule.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation.

I understand the government's interest in protecting employment opportunities for U.S. citizens and preventing abuse of the immigration system. However, these objectives should be pursued through policies that directly address employment practices and program integrity, rather than imposing extraordinary financial barriers on international graduates.

Employers already have the ability to establish hiring policies that limit visa sponsorship. By contrast, imposing fees of this magnitude on OPT participation does not meaningfully distinguish between qualified and unqualified applicants, nor between legitimate employment and fraudulent arrangements. Instead, it creates a financial barrier that disproportionately disadvantages students from less affluent backgrounds.

**This proposal does not select international graduates based on merit, qualifications, or compliance with immigration law. It selects them based on their ability, or their institution's willingness, to pay.**

Such a policy raises serious concerns about proportionality, fairness, and whether the proposed fees are reasonably connected to their stated objectives. If the goal is to protect American workers and prevent fraud, more targeted measures, such as strengthened employer verification, compliance monitoring, and enforcement against fraudulent employment arrangements, would address those concerns more directly.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and adopt measures that protect U.S. workers without making access to practical training dependent on financial privilege.

Thus, charging the school a fee would not hit the root of the problem, as the school cannot know what job the student will take at the time of OPT recommendation and does not play an active role in the student's career decisions. 

An effective alternative solution would be increasing fines for businesses found to be committing employment fraud. This alternative solution would focus on the primary concern that DHS states (fraudulent businesses) and provides a consequence for the primary actor in such cases (the business owner).

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee because DHS has not adequately demonstrated that these charges would prevent fraud or protect American workers in proportion to their economic costs.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. For decades, the original statutory intent of the F-1 nonimmigrant student visa classification under 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F) has been perverted by academic institutions seeking to maximize external funding streams while evading the natural labor market pressures that protect domestic students. Graduate research positions across critical disciplines including computer science, chemical engineering, materials science, and biotechnology are overwhelmingly underwritten by federal taxpayer dollars disbursed through competitive grants from agencies such as the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, and the National Institutes of Health.

The public investment of American tax dollars is explicitly intended to cultivate a domestic scientific and technical elite that secures the nation's long-term economic competitiveness and technological sovereignty. Yet, university admissions committees and principal investigators systematically bypass qualified American applicants in favor of international graduate students. This preference is not driven by objective academic superiority, but by a predatory labor incentive: international students represent a captive workforce whose legal residency, visa continuity, and post-graduation mobility are entirely controlled by their academic advisors.

This power dynamic fosters institutionalized exploitation. Foreign graduate students can be and routinely are compelled to work 70 to 80 hours per week, forced to perform menial labor outside the scope of their dissertation research, and subjected to sub-market stipends that fail to cover local inflation and cost-of-living increases. Because their legal status depends on maintaining active student or practical training status, they lack the leverage to report labor abuses, hazardous laboratory conditions, or wage stagnation. DHS possesses clear and unassailable statutory authority under 8 U.S.C. 1184(a) to regulate the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission, and this rule and its eventual progression toward full OPT cancellation will withstand any judicial challenge brought by special-interest lobbies seeking to preserve subsidized foreign labor.

I write in robust support of Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, establishing significant fees for Optional Practical Training. Under current statutory and regulatory interpretations, F-1 students working on OPT enjoy a profound financial advantage over American citizens and lawful permanent residents through an exemption from Federal Insurance Contributions Act taxes under Internal Revenue Code Section 3121(b)(19). By sparing employers the mandatory 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare contributions (a cumulative 7.65% payroll savings), the federal government effectively provides corporations with a direct financial incentive to discriminate against domestic workers in favor of temporary OPT holders.

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). Although combating fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee represent a misguided approach. Rather than addressing specific misconduct, this rule would reshape American higher education and the labor market through financial barriers with little demonstrated connection to immigration compliance.

A central weakness of the proposal is its assumption that enormous fees will improve program integrity. DHS identifies fraudulent employers, fabricated job offers, and shell companies as major concerns. Yet charging universities tens of thousands of dollars does not verify whether employment is genuine. A student with a legitimate job offer faces the same fee as someone associated with a suspicious organization. Reducing participation is not equivalent to preventing fraud. DHS should explain why targeted investigations and stronger employer verification would not be more effective.

The proposed fees would also distort university decision-making. Academic institutions should evaluate students based on qualifications, achievement, and regulatory compliance. Under this proposal, however, financial considerations could determine whether a student receives an OPT recommendation. Universities might prioritize students whose employers can provide financial support or restrict opportunities regardless of merit. This would transform practical training into a privilege determined largely by wealth.

Another overlooked consequence is the damage to American students and university communities. International enrollment generates revenue supporting academic departments, faculty positions, laboratories, and student services. If prospective students conclude that practical training in the United States is financially unrealistic, enrollment may decline. Universities would then face reduced tuition revenue and increased financial obligations. To compensate, institutions could raise tuition, reduce scholarships, eliminate courses, or limit research expenditures. American students could ultimately bear significant costs for a policy supposedly designed to benefit them.

The proposal also threatens smaller American businesses and research organizations. Large corporations may have the resources to support international graduates, while startups, small engineering firms, nonprofit laboratories, and regional employers often operate with limited budgets. If OPT becomes prohibitively expensive, these organizations may lose access to graduates with specialized expertise. This could discourage entrepreneurship, slow innovation, and strengthen the advantages of dominant corporations.

Equally troubling is the proposal's treatment of students who have already invested years and substantial resources in an American education. Many enrolled with the reasonable expectation that OPT would remain potentially available under established eligibility rules. Although authorization is never guaranteed, introducing extraordinary fees after students have committed to their education could radically alter their opportunities. A short transition period does not adequately address decisions made years earlier.

The consequences for American competitiveness deserve attention. The United States has historically benefited from educating talented individuals who contribute to scientific research, technology development, and entrepreneurship. International students support university research and develop skills valuable to American industries. Making practical training financially inaccessible would encourage future students to choose competing countries. Once these individuals establish careers elsewhere, the United States may permanently lose their contributions.

Finally, DHS's own regulatory analysis raises questions about whether the rule serves the public interest. The agency estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario but does not estimate annualized monetized benefits. It also acknowledges potential losses in enrollment, earnings, and productivity. Before imposing such extensive burdens, DHS should provide credible evidence that the fees would prevent enough fraud to justify their costs. The possibility of deterrence cannot substitute for a meaningful assessment of effectiveness.

Fraud should be addressed through investigations, compliance monitoring, and penalties against responsible parties, not by forcing legitimate universities to choose between financial stability and students' educational opportunities.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity while preserving affordable American higher education, competitive American businesses, and the nation's ability to attract global talent.

I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. I have three major concerns regarding the economic consequences, the rationale for charging educational institutions, and the justification for the proposed fee amounts.

1. International students make substantial contributions to the U.S. economy.

According to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report, 1,177,766 international students studied at U.S. higher education institutions during the 2024–2025 academic year. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs during the same period.

These figures demonstrate the substantial economic value of international education. International students contribute through tuition payments, housing, transportation, consumption, and other economic activities. OPT also provides opportunities for graduates to apply their U.S. education in professional settings and contribute their skills to the American workforce.

Imposing substantial additional financial barriers to OPT could discourage international students from choosing U.S. universities and reduce their economic contributions. I urge DHS to carefully consider whether the proposed fees could undermine the very economic interests and employment opportunities the rule intends to protect.

2. The rationale for imposing these fees on universities is unclear.

I question the logic of requiring educational institutions to pay substantial fees for students to participate in OPT. Universities provide education and verify students' eligibility for practical training, but they are not necessarily the employers benefiting from the students' work. Why should universities bear the financial responsibility for employment authorization associated with graduates' professional activities?

Furthermore, if the objective is to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers, it is unclear how charging universities $70,000 per student would directly achieve these goals. Universities that follow all applicable immigration regulations would face the same financial burden as institutions with documented compliance problems.

For an institution with 100 students seeking initial OPT, the proposed fees would total $7 million. Such expenses could substantially affect institutional budgets and force universities to limit OPT recommendations, regardless of students' qualifications or compliance with immigration requirements.

Although the proposed rule allows institutions to pass these costs to students or employers, this would merely transfer the financial burden rather than resolve the underlying concern. I request that DHS provide a clearer justification for assigning these costs to universities and explain how this approach would specifically reduce fraud.

3. The proposed fee amounts lack a sufficiently clear and proportionate justification.

The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT raise serious questions about how these specific amounts were determined.

What empirical evidence supports these figures? Are they based on the actual administrative costs of reviewing OPT applications, documented costs associated with fraud prevention, or an analysis demonstrating that these particular amounts would reduce fraudulent participation?

DHS states that the fees are intended to encourage institutions to be more selective in their OPT recommendations. However, reducing participation through financial barriers is not equivalent to identifying or preventing fraud. A university's ability to pay does not necessarily reflect the legitimacy of a student's employment or compliance with immigration regulations.

I urge DHS to provide a transparent, evidence-based explanation of the fee calculations, demonstrate their proportionality to the stated regulatory objectives, and consider whether more targeted and less financially burdensome measures could achieve the same goals.

I am a U.S. citizen writing to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT. The proposal is disproportionate to any legitimate administrative purpose, harmful to American workers and employers, and legally vulnerable. I urge DHS and ICE to withdraw it.
1. The fee bears no reasonable relationship to the cost of administering the program.
Federal user fees are generally expected to recover the government’s cost of providing a service. Processing OPT involves reviewing school recommendations, updating SEVIS records, and conducting compliance oversight. It is difficult to imagine any credible cost analysis showing that these functions cost $70,000 per student. A fee set this far above administrative cost works as a penalty or a de facto ban, not a user fee. If DHS intends to restrict OPT, it should say so directly and defend that policy on the merits, rather than achieving it through a fee schedule.
2. The stated goal of combating fraud does not justify a fee charged to every student.
The notice cites fraud as a primary rationale. Fraud should be addressed through targeted enforcement: auditing employers, verifying the legitimacy of positions, and strengthening SEVIS reporting. A flat fee on every lawful participant punishes thousands of compliant students for the misconduct of a few. It also does nothing to stop fraud by participants who can afford the fee. A measure this broad and this poorly targeted is likely arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
3. The proposal would hurt American workers, not protect them.
OPT participants are concentrated in STEM fields where U.S. employers report persistent shortages. Many work in research labs, hospitals, startups, and engineering firms, where their work creates and sustains jobs for Americans. International graduates have founded or co-founded a large share of America’s most valuable startups. Pushing this talent out means those jobs, patents, and companies will be created in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, or Germany instead. These are countries actively competing for the same graduates.
4. The economic damage would extend well beyond universities.
International students contribute tens of billions of dollars to the U.S. economy each year and support hundreds of thousands of American jobs, according to NAFSA’s annual estimates. For many students, the opportunity to gain practical experience through OPT is a central reason for choosing the United States. A $70,000 barrier would sharply reduce enrollment. The effects would fall on tuition revenue, which cross-subsidizes domestic students, and on local economies that depend on student spending, including housing, retail, and services. Small businesses and startups would be hit hardest, because they cannot absorb or reimburse a fee of this size. The Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis should account for that impact.
5. The fee would make access to OPT depend on wealth, not merit.
A $70,000 fee means only the wealthiest international students could participate. Talented students from modest backgrounds, often the most driven and innovative, would be excluded. That outcome serves neither American employers nor the integrity of the immigration system.

I am writing to express my concerns regarding the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026.
The proposal would require educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an international student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT recommendation. These requirements would apply to both pre-completion and post-completion OPT, including STEM OPT extensions.
I am concerned that these fees would create substantial financial barriers to practical training opportunities that are directly relevant to students' academic programs and professional development.
First, the proposed fees could significantly restrict access to internships during graduate school. Recent changes to Curricular Practical Training (CPT) eligibility have already made internships less accessible to students whose academic programs do not require internships for graduation. For these students, pre-completion OPT may be the primary available pathway to gain professional experience outside their universities. Imposing a $70,000 institutional fee for an initial OPT recommendation could make that pathway financially impractical.
Second, the proposal could undermine opportunities for international graduates to apply their specialized training in the United States. OPT enables students to obtain practical experience in fields related to their degrees. Graduate students often develop highly specialized expertise through years of academic research, and opportunities to apply that knowledge in industry, government, or research institutions can be important components of their professional development.
Third, the proposal places a substantial financial burden on educational institutions, with the possibility of costs being transferred to students or employers. Although the rule would require institutions to pay the fees, it does not prohibit them from obtaining funding from other parties. This creates uncertainty regarding who would ultimately bear these costs and whether universities would continue recommending eligible students for OPT.
I recognize DHS's stated objectives of preventing fraud, protecting the integrity of immigration programs, and ensuring compliance with employment authorization requirements. These are legitimate subjects for regulatory oversight. However, I encourage DHS to evaluate whether the proposed fees are proportionate to these objectives and whether more targeted compliance measures could achieve similar results without substantially restricting access to authorized practical training.
I also encourage DHS to consider the combined effects of recent CPT eligibility restrictions and the proposed OPT fees, particularly for students in degree programs where internships are academically relevant but not mandatory.
I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate less financially burdensome alternatives, and fully account for the consequences for students, universities, employers, and the broader research and education community before issuing a final rule.
Thank you for considering this comment.

Without the proposed fee structure the Department cannot adequately resource its oversight operations or prevent bad actors from exploiting practical training as an informal and unlimited employment benefit.

Furthermore, historical enforcement actions validate the immediate necessity of this rule. Federal authorities previously convicted individuals who operated shell companies providing false employment verification documents and fake offer letters to thousands of foreign students in exchange for illegal fees. These criminal enterprises directly facilitated visa fraud and compromised national security. The proposed fees of seventy thousand dollars for initial authorization and thirty thousand dollars for subsequent extensions create a vital and rational financial deterrent. This fee structure ensures that participating institutions exercise proper oversight and selectivity rather than rubber-stamping applications for profit.

Beyond the immediate implementation of these robust fees, the Department must recognize that incremental financial barriers remain an incomplete remedy for a fundamentally flawed program. The systemic displacement of American workers, the ongoing evasion of statutory H-1B visa caps and the persistent structural incentives for cheap foreign labor demonstrate that the Optional Practical Training program should be canceled altogether. Practical training was originally conceived as a limited and supervised educational adjunct rather than an open-ended corporate labor pipeline. Because administrative oversight can never fully eliminate shell companies, proxy employment schemes and the systematic suppression of entry level wages for domestic graduates, the complete revocation of the program under 8 U.S.C. 1184(a) represents the only permanent solution to protect national economic security.

In the context of judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Department has established an unimpeachable rational connection between the empirical evidence of fraud and the chosen regulatory remedy. The Secretary of Homeland Security possesses broad and unambiguous statutory authority under section 214 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 to administer immigration laws and prescribe the time and conditions of alien admission. Establishing conditions that combat fraud, protect domestic labor markets and ensure economic security falls squarely within the primary mission of the Department. Any legal challenge brought against this rule or subsequent actions toward program cancellation would fail to recognize that the agency has acted reasonably and proportionately to safeguard the integrity of the immigration system against pervasive abuse. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 bil. rule but 60 days on a 5-min paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days

Our school is a small private Christian university (est. 1922), who has been privileged to host F1 students since 1961 (66 years).
