I strongly oppose this rule.
I. Failure to Comply with Executive Order 12866 and OMB Circular A-4
Executive Order 12866 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-4 require federal agencies to promulgate regulations only upon a reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs, and to quantify both direct and indirect economic effects using sound empirical methodologies. In the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) for Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) estimates that imposing a $70,000 fee on initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee on subsequent or STEM OPT extensions will impose net economic costs on the United States of $40 billion to $80 billion over 10 years, while quantifying $0 in monetized economic benefits. Proceeding with an economically significant rule that produces tens of billions of dollars in net societal deadweight loss without a single quantified benefit violates the core mandate of E.O. 12866.
II. Omitted Fiscal, Tax, and Multiplier Costs
Even at $40 billion to $80 billion, DHS’s Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) severely understates the true macroeconomic cost of the proposed rule by omitting three major categories of quantifiable harm:
Lost Federal, State, and Local Tax Revenues: Approximately 418,000 F-1 students participate in OPT and STEM OPT annually. While initial F-1 students are exempt from FICA taxes during their first five calendar years, all OPT participants pay federal, state, and local income taxes as well as sales and excise taxes, and many STEM OPT participants who transition past their fifth calendar year pay Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes. DHS fails to model the net present value of lost federal and state income tax receipts resulting from the projected collapse in OPT participation.

Loss of Domestic Tuition Cross-Subsidization: International students frequently pay full out-of-state or unsubsidized tuition rates at public and private universities, which institutions use to cross-subsidize financial aid and instructional costs for domestic U.S. students. Survey data across more than 800 higher education institutions demonstrates that 92% of institutional leaders expect international students to choose competing nations if OPT is eliminated or priced out of reach. DHS fails to quantify the resulting tuition increases and program reductions that will fall directly on U.S. citizen students.

Downstream R&D Spillover and Multiplier Effects: Peer-reviewed labor economics literature consistently demonstrates that foreign-born STEM graduates on OPT are complements, not substitutes, for native-born U.S. workers—generating patents, university spin-outs, and local service-sector jobs in college communities. DHS cites zero empirical labor-market studies showing that OPT depresses domestic wages, rendering its qualitative assertions of "protecting U.S. workers" unsupported by the administrative record.

III. Arbitrary Selection of the $70,000 and $30,000 Fee Levels
OMB Circular A-4 requires agencies to evaluate alternative regulatory stringency levels and justify the marginal cost of the chosen threshold. DHS provides no mathematical, actuarial, or economic derivation explaining why $70,000 (initial) and $30,000 (subsequent)—or the even more punitive alternative of charging $70,000 repeatedly at each degree level—were selected. Because median first-year earnings for recent bachelor’s and master’s graduates across most academic disciplines are lower than or comparable to the $70,000 fee itself, the fee functions as a de facto prohibition rather than a regulatory fee.
IV. Less Burdensome Alternative & Request for Data Disclosure
Before finalizing any rule, DHS must model a cost-recovery alternative in which any institutional OPT oversight fee is capped strictly at the marginal administrative cost of Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) compliance audits (e.g., $150 to $350 per recommendation). Furthermore, DHS must disclose in the final rule: (a) the exact price-elasticity parameters used to project OPT demand under a $70,000 fee disaggregated by Bachelor’s, Master’s, and Ph.D. levels, and (b) the ten-year projected loss in federal income tax revenues.

I strongly oppose this proposed rule, for the following reasons:

I. The Proposed Charges Are an Unconstitutional Tax, Not a Lawful Regulatory Fee
Under Article I, Section 8 of the U.S. Constitution, the power to lay and collect taxes resides exclusively with Congress. In National Cable Television Ass’n, Inc. v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), the Supreme Court established that an executive agency may only charge a "fee" that reflects the cost of providing a specific service or conferring a specific benefit on an identifiable recipient; when an agency assesses a punitive charge untethered to service costs to raise general revenue or achieve broad public policy objectives, it crosses the line into unauthorized taxation.
Here, the NPRM explicitly states that the $70,000 and $30,000 fees collected from SEVP-certified institutions will not be retained by DHS or ICE to fund SEVP adjudication or fraud-prevention operations, but will instead be deposited directly into the general fund of the U.S. Treasury. Depositing a $70,000–$100,000 exaction into the general Treasury confirms as a matter of law that the charge is a revenue-raising tax and a punitive deterrent, not a lawful user fee.
II. Violation of the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701) and INA § 286(m)
Neither the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m), nor 8 U.S.C. § 1372 (which governs SEVP institutional and student fees), nor the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA), 31 U.S.C. § 9701, authorizes DHS to levy a $100,000 surcharge on educational institutions:
8 U.S.C. § 1372 Limits SEVP Fees to Program Costs: Congress specifically legislated the fee structure for monitoring F-1 students and SEVP-certified schools under 8 U.S.C. § 1372, tying fee collection to the actual costs of administering the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) and SEVP enforcement. Nothing in § 1372 authorizes a $70,000 or $30,000 general-revenue levy per student.

8 U.S.C. § 1356(m) Does Not Authorize General Treasury Exactions: INA § 286(m) permits fees only at a level that recovers the costs of providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services and deposits them into the Immigration Examinations Fee Account (IEFA)—not the general Treasury. Moreover, OPT applicants already pay the Form I-765 adjudication fee ($470–$520) to USCIS to cover EAD processing costs.

Binding Federal Precedent Invalidating the $100,000 H-1B Fee: Federal district courts—including the District of Massachusetts in June 2026 and the Northern District of California on September 30, 2026 in Global Nurse Force v. Trump—have already held that the Executive Branch lacks statutory authority under the INA to impose a $100,000 fee designed to deter foreign worker participation or raise general revenue without explicit congressional authorization. The Major Questions Doctrine (West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)) similarly bars DHS from using ancillary fee provisions to effectively abolish or restructure the 418,000-person OPT program without clear congressional direction.

III. Legal Questions DHS Must Address in the Final Rule
To comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C)), the Office of the General Counsel must explain on the record:
Which specific statutory subsection permits DHS to assess a fee under 8 U.S.C. § 1372 or § 1356(m) that exceeds the marginal cost of SEVIS processing by more than 10,000% and deposits those funds into the general Treasury?

How does DHS distinguish the statutory basis of this $100,000 OPT fee from the $100,000 H-1B fee invalidated in Global Nurse Force v. Trump?

This rule should be retracted, because:

I. Failure to Properly Analyze Impacts Across All Affected "Small Entities" Under 5 U.S.C. § 601
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA), 5 U.S.C. §§ 601–612, as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA), requires agencies to prepare a comprehensive Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) and Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) whenever a rule will have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of "small entities." Under 5 U.S.C. § 601(4)–(6), the statutory definition of "small entity" encompasses three distinct groups impacted by this rule:
Small Not-for-Profit Organizations (including private non-profit liberal arts colleges, faith-based colleges, seminaries, arts conservatories, and specialized technical institutes that are independently owned and operated and not dominant in their field);

Small Governmental Jurisdictions (including regional community college districts and municipal educational institutions serving populations under 50,000); and

Small Businesses (including early-stage technology startups, community hospitals, rural healthcare clinics, and small engineering or architecture firms meeting SBA size standards that rely on F-1 OPT and STEM OPT graduates).

II. Flawed Pass-Through Assumptions That Devastate Small Colleges and Small Businesses
In the NPRM, DHS places the direct legal obligation to pay the $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee on SEVP-certified educational institutions, while casually asserting that schools may pass these costs on to F-1 students or their prospective employers. This assumption ignores economic reality for small entities:
Impact on Small Non-Profit Colleges: Hundreds of SEVP-certified small colleges operate on thin tuition margins and enroll 50 to 300 international students. If a small college must pay $70,000 upfront before its Designated School Official (DSO) can even enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS, sponsoring just 100 graduating seniors would require $7,000,000 in upfront liquidity—exceeding the entire annual operating surplus of many small institutions. If small colleges pass that $70,000 fee on to students, international enrollment at small colleges will drop to near zero, threatening institutional insolvency.

Impact on Small Businesses and Startups: While cash-rich multinational corporations might absorb a $70,000 or $30,000 fee for a specialized hire, small businesses and early-stage university spin-out startups cannot pay a $70,000 surcharge BEFORE an OPT candidate even receives a USCIS Employment Authorization Document (EAD)—especially when the candidate has not yet worked a single day for the firm and when initial OPT lasts only 12 months. The rule therefore creates a severe anti-competitive barrier that entrenches monopolies at the expense of small U.S. employers.

III. Mandatory RFA Alternatives DHS Must Evaluate Under 5 U.S.C. § 603(c)
Under 5 U.S.C. § 603(c), an agency’s analysis must evaluate regulatory alternatives that minimize significant economic impacts on small entities, including differing compliance standards or exemptions. DHS must explicitly analyze and adopt the following alternatives in the final rule:
A Complete Small-Entity Exemption: Exempting all SEVP-certified institutions that qualify as small non-profit organizations or small governmental jurisdictions under 5 U.S.C. § 601, as well as any OPT placement where the verified employer qualifies as a small business under Small Business Administration (SBA) North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) size standards.

A Revenue-Capped Tiered Fee Structure: Capping institutional OPT fees at no more than 0.5% of an institution's per-student instructional expenditure or $250 for small entities.

I. Binding Supreme Court Precedent Requires DHS to Weigh Reliance Interests
In Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the U.S. Supreme Court held that when an agency alters a longstanding immigration policy, the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)) requires the agency to assess whether there were "legitimate reliance" interests on the prior policy, weigh those reliance interests against competing policy concerns, and consider transition measures or partial accommodations. Failing to meaningfully consider cognizable reliance interests renders an agency rule arbitrary and capricious.
II. Three Distinct Cohorts With Concrete, Quantifiable Reliance Interests
Under the proposed text of Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100, the $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent/STEM OPT fee would take effect just 60 days after publication of the final rule, with no grandfathering protection for students already in the United States. Only students whose OPT has already been approved prior to the effective date are spared the initial fee, and even those approved initial OPT holders will be hit with the $30,000 fee when they apply for their 24-month STEM OPT extension after the effective date. This retroactive disruption destroys massive, good-faith investments across three distinct cohorts:
Currently Enrolled Multi-Year F-1 Degree Students (Bachelor’s, Master’s, and Ph.D.): Hundreds of thousands of F-1 students matriculated at U.S. universities between 2022 and Fall 2026 in reliance on the longstanding federal regulatory framework (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)), under which post-completion OPT required only a standard Form I-765 filing fee ($470–$520). Comment on Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100: Operational Contradictions Between SEVIS and USCIS Adjudications and Lack of Procedural Due Process in Fee Refund Determinations

I. Fatal Operational Mismatch Between SEVP Recommendation Gatekeeping and USCIS Form I-765 Adjudication
The NPRM proposes a bifurcated operational mechanism under which a SEVP-certified educational institution must remit the $70,000 (initial) or $30,000 (subsequent) fee—and have that payment verified by DHS—before a Designated School Official (DSO) is permitted to enter an OPT recommendation into SEVIS, which in turn is a prerequisite for the student to file Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization) with USCIS. This workflow ignores fundamental statutory and regulatory deadlines governing F-1 status and creates unworkable administrative bottlenecks:
Collision with Strict Regulatory Filing Windows (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)): Under existing regulations, a student applying for post-completion OPT must file Form I-765 with USCIS within 30 days of the DSO entering the OPT recommendation in SEVIS (60 days for STEM OPT), and no later than the end of the 60-day post-graduation grace period (or prior to the expiration of initial OPT for STEM extensions). However, Institutional wire transfers, Automated Clearing House (ACH) daily limits for $70,000+ transactions, university procurement approvals, and federal payment clearing through Pay.gov routinely take days or weeks, and bank holds or payment reconciliation errors are common for high-dollar transactions. DHS provides zero safeguard to toll the regulatory filing deadline when SEVIS payment verification is delayed.

Pre-Employment Timing Paradox for Initial Post-Completion OPT: Unlike STEM OPT, initial 12-month post-completion OPT does not require a job offer at the time the DSO recommends OPT in SEVIS or when the student files Form I-765. Thus, DHS’s suggestion that "employers" can pay or reimburse the $70,000 fee before the DSO enters the SEVIS recommendation is operationally impossible for any graduating student who does not yet have an employer at the moment of DSO recommendation, or who changes employers during their 12-month OPT period.

II. Arbitrary, Standardless, and Non-Appealable Refund Determinations Violate the APA
The NPRM states that if an F-1 student is ultimately denied an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) by USCIS after the $70,000 or $30,000 fee has been paid, DHS will determine whether to issue a refund on a "case-by-case basis" and that such refund determinations cannot be appealed. This provision is unlawful and arbitrary for three reasons:
Retention of $70,000 When No Benefit Is Conferred: If USCIS denies Form I-765 (or if a student withdraws the application before adjudication due to a medical emergency or departure from the United States), the student never receives OPT authorization. Retaining a $70,000 or $30,000 sum when the underlying benefit is denied constitutes an unlawful forfeiture penalty without statutory authorization.

Complete Absence of Articulable Standards: Granting agency officials unfettered "case-by-case" discretion over whether to return $70,000—without codifying objective regulatory criteria in the Code of Federal Regulations specifying when a refund is mandatory—violates basic administrative law principles against standardless agency action.

Denial of Administrative Review: Prohibiting any administrative appeal of a $70,000 refund denial deprives educational institutions and payers of procedural due process and forces every disputed refund directly into federal court under the Tucker Act or the Administrative Procedure Act.

III. Operational Revisions Required Before Any Final Rule
DHS must explain on the record: (a) how an employer can fund a pre-SEVIS-recommendation fee for initial OPT when no job offer is required at the time of DSO recommendation; (b) why automatic 100% refunds are not mandated whenever a Form I-765 is denied, rejected, or withdrawn prior to EAD issuance; and (c) what formal administrative appeals mechanism will govern disputed fee payments.

Comment on Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100: Violation of Executive Order 13132 (Federalism), the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C. § 1532), and State Constitutional Fiscal Constraints on Public Universities

I. Failure to Conduct a Federalism Assessment Under Executive Order 13132
Under Executive Order 13132 (Federalism), federal agencies are prohibited from promulgating any regulation that has "federalism implications" and imposes substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments unless the agency consults early and meaningfully with State officials and publishes a formal Federalism Summary Impact Statement. In the United States, public flagship universities, land-grant universities, state university systems, and community colleges are arms and instrumentalities of State governments, governed by state-appointed regents or trustees and funded through state legislative appropriations.
By placing the direct legal obligation on SEVP-certified public universities to remit a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent OPT fee per student—and threatening the loss of tens of billions of dollars in nonresident tuition revenues paid to state public university systems—this rule directly commandeers and burdens state fiscal administration. DHS’s failure to conduct formal consultations with State Governors, State Attorneys General, and State Higher Education Executive Officers (SHEEO) violates Executive Order 13132.
II. Conflict With State Constitutional "Gift of Public Funds" Clauses and State Appropriations Laws
DHS asserts in the NPRM that educational institutions must pay the $70,000 and $30,000 fees directly to the federal government prior to entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS, and suggests that schools may either absorb the cost or pass it along to students or employers. However, DHS completely ignores State constitutional law:
State Constitutional Anti-Gift Clauses: Nearly every U.S. state constitution contains a strict "Gift Clause" or "Public Purpose Doctrine" (e.g., prohibiting state agencies and public universities from using public treasury or state-appropriated funds to pay a $70,000 post-graduation federal employment fee on behalf of an individual graduate or a private commercial employer). State universities are legally barred under state law from absorbing these fees.

Statutory Tuition and Fee Caps: At most public university systems, setting or collecting a new $70,000 mandatory student fee requires explicit statutory authorization from the State Legislature or formal notice-and-comment rulemaking by a State Board of Regents across a multi-year budget cycle. State universities cannot lawfully invent and collect a $70,000 pass-through fee within 60 days of a federal final rule.

III. Noncompliance With the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C. §§ 1501–1571)
Under the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA), 2 U.S.C. § 1532, whenever a federal rule may result in the expenditure by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (adjusted for inflation) in any one year, the agency must prepare a written statement assessing the qualitative and quantitative costs to State and local governments and must select the least costly, most cost-effective, or least burdensome alternative under 2 U.S.C. § 1535. Because the rule imposes $40 billion to $80 billion in costs—much of it borne directly by state public university systems—DHS must complete a full intergovernmental UMRA consultation and exempt state public institutions of higher education from the rule.

Declining to pay could instead undermine the institution's ability to recruit talented students. None of these outcomes should be treated as a cost-free way to protect Americans.

It makes little economic sense to train talented graduates in American institutions and then make it financially impractical for American organizations to benefit from their skills. The proposal risks shifting the subsequent benefits of that training to other countries. A university laboratory, startup, nonprofit, or small professional firm should not have to abandon an otherwise valuable graduate because it cannot absorb an enormous upfront charge. 1. The fee amounts are unexplained. Section IV.C says the $70,000 fee is "designed to closely align with the H-1B fees." The H-1B fee under Proclamation 10973 (cited in fns. 84, 116-117) is $100,000, so $70,000 and $30,000 miss the stated benchmark by 30% and 70%. That is not the "rational connection between the facts found and the choice made" required by State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), which the rule itself cites (fn. 125).

2. The structure contradicts DHS's risk theory. The initial fee ($70,000) exceeds the subsequent fee ($30,000), yet STEM OPT carries the I-983 training plan, employer attestations, and the only site visits (Section III.D.2, fns. 53-54). The stage with the most oversight costs less.

3. It is a tax, not a fee. Section IV.C says the money goes to Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt and ICE keeps none of it. Table 5 puts actual processing costs near $15.7 million a year, while Table 3 projects $12.4 billion in annual collections, about 800 times the cost. INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), authorizes "time and conditions" of admission, not general revenue. Taxation belongs to Congress under Article I.

4. The "school pays" framing is a shell game. DHS admits schools "may pass the financial obligation... onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers" and says pass-through "would further discourage misuse." DHS cannot claim the charge falls on schools while relying on it reaching individuals. Spreading it to "all students" raises tuition for Americans who never use OPT.

5. The "shut down the program" claim (Sections IV.A, IV.B) has no support. SEVP is already fee funded. Its own director has said it "does not receive any appropriated funding from Congress," and DHS's FY2026 budget justification lists SEVP at $216.5 million. The rule's $12.4 billion annual take is about 57 times that, with no shortfall shown.

6. No benefits were quantified. Table 1 lists monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" against $4.1 billion in annualized costs, contrary to E.O. 12866 and 13563.

7. The burden misses the fraud it targets. Section IV.A describes organized shell networks and offshore money. Table 17 shows 60.5% of small schools would see impacts above 1% of revenue and 98 above 20%. Section VII.B.6 rejects a small-entity exemption without showing fraud is concentrated there.

8. It will hurt American students and research. About 67% of international master's students are self-funded and 38.6% of science and engineering master's students are international (NSF). Research in Economics of Education Review (Shih, 2017) finds their tuition cross-subsidizes domestic students. Hechinger Report documents U.S. students facing "program cuts and higher prices" as international enrollment falls, and a UCSB economist warns of "a really big hole in the budget." Temporary visa holders earned 58% of computer science doctorates in 2024 (ITIF/NSF), so fewer of them means less federally funded research.

9. OPT drives enrollment. The Presidents' Alliance reports "wide consensus that OPT is a critical factor in attracting international students," and a 2024 AECC survey found 79% rate post-study work rights "extremely important." Canada, the UK, and Australia are recruiting these students now.

Sundar Pichai came on an F-1 visa, used OPT, and now leads Alphabet. Section VI calls reliance on OPT "speculative," yet fn. 88 cites Washington Alliance of Tech. Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164, 176 (D.C. Cir. 2022), finding OPT measurably expanded STEM labor supply.

DHS should withdraw the rule or, at minimum, disclose how the amounts were derived, quantify benefits, and analyze effects on domestic students, research, and small institutions.

I offer the following observations respectfully, in the hope that they are useful to the agency's analysis.

1. F-1 students on OPT have already passed through several independent screenings.
To obtain an F-1 visa, a student must first be admitted to an SEVP-certified institution through a competitive admissions process, demonstrate the financial ability to support their studies, and satisfy a consular officer at a visa interview. To reach OPT, the student must carry a full course load, maintain lawful status throughout, receive authorization from a Designated School Official, and be approved by USCIS. Employment under OPT additionally requires passing an employer's hiring process. Each of these steps is an independent filter, and the resulting population is therefore already narrowly selected.

2. F-1 students contribute to the U.S. economy and workforce during their authorized period.
In 2024, F-1 and other international students contributed $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy and supported approximately 378,000 jobs, making them the second-largest contributors to GDP among education-related sectors. Employers hire OPT participants for the specialized skills they bring, often in fields where domestic demand exceeds supply, and these students are estimated to increase the U.S. skilled labor supply by approximately 0.23 percent. Studies examining cities and states as labor markets generally find that immigration increases local innovation and productivity, with stable or rising native employment and wages. 

3. OPT itself confers no path to permanent residence.
OPT provides a fixed, time-limited period of work authorization. It creates no eligibility for permanent residence, and any later status requires a separate petition judged against independent standards. The primary work visa for degree holders, the H-1B, requires employer petition and sponsorship and is numerically capped. Transition rates from student visas to work visas have steadily declined, because student visa numbers increased while new H-1B numbers stayed roughly constant. Restricting OPT would therefore have limited effect on permanent immigration, which is decided through an entirely separate and capped process.

4. DHS data indicate that F-1 students are not a primary source of unlawful presence.
In Fiscal Year 2024 there were 482,954 Suspected In-Country Overstays out of 46,657,108 expected departures, an overall rate of 1.04 percent. Business and pleasure visitors accounted for roughly 349,738 of these, about 72 percent of the national total, while students and exchange visitors in the F, M, and J categories accounted for 34,540, about 7 percent. The rate for the F visa category was 2.44 percent, essentially the same as the 2.22 percent rate for non-Visa Waiver B-1 and B-2 visitors, a population roughly nine times larger. CBP also notes that student records are document-centric, since each Form I-20 carries its own identification number, so one person may hold multiple active and inactive records. The F visa figure should therefore be read as an upper bound.

5. Restricting OPT would forfeit skills the United States has already helped develop.
If fees or compliance costs rise substantially, many employers will decline to hire OPT participants. F-1 students who cannot find work in which their training applies generally return home. In rapidly advancing technical fields, those skills often cannot be fully applied elsewhere, because the necessary infrastructure, industry base, and demand do not yet exist in their home countries. Reduced work authorization also discourages prospective students at a time when universities in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom have substantially expanded their capacity. Arrivals have already fallen by approximately 19 percent, and more than 250,000 F-1 visa denials have been associated with an estimated $7 billion in direct economic loss.

I hope these words convey the genuine respect and sense of purpose behind our presence here.

Thank you for considering this comment.

If the purpose is funding oversight, DHS should publish the cost basis. If the purpose is deterrence, the fee will screen by ability to pay, not by academic merit or legitimacy of the training.

3. In practice, the rule would end OPT for most lawful participants. The NPRM reports about 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, the large majority of whom are not implicated in fraud. Few schools can absorb $70,000 per student and few students can pay it. DHS should analyze the proposal for what it is likely to be: a de facto termination of the program.

4. OPT is a central part of the value of a U.S. degree. Applied training directly related to the field of study is a key reason international students, especially in STEM, choose the United States. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and others offer post-study work periods without comparable fees. A fee at this level would shift qualified students to those countries, with effects on U.S. university finances, graduate research capacity, and the pipeline of skilled workers and company founders that U.S. employers rely on.

Before finalizing, DHS should quantify: the expected decline in international enrollment; tuition revenue losses, especially at public and smaller institutions; effects on research labs that depend on international graduate students; effects on U.S. employers, including small businesses; and changes in tax revenue. Claimed labor-market benefits should rest on evidence that OPT participants displace U.S. workers in specific occupations, not on aggregate trends with many causes.

6. Predictability and international standing. Students make multi-year, high-cost decisions based on the rules in place when they enroll. A change of this size, applied to students already enrolled, reduces confidence in U.S. policy and weakens the standing of U.S. higher education as a reliable destination.

Recommendations:

- If any fee is retained, set it at a cost-recovery level with a published methodology.
- Address fraud through employer verification, I-983 verification, site visits, and enforcement against bad actors.
- Exempt students enrolled before the effective date.
- Publish a full regulatory impact analysis before any final rule.

I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). Its most troubling feature is that it replaces a compliance question—whether an OPT opportunity is lawful and educationally appropriate—with a financial question: who can afford to pay for it? Those are not the same question, and confusing them could create new problems while leaving existing fraud risks unresolved.

DHS describes schemes involving fake job offers, shell companies, and nonexistent worksites. These abuses demand verification and enforcement. Yet a $70,000 initial fee, followed by $30,000 for subsequent OPT, would be due because a school recommends a student, not because DHS has identified suspicious conduct. A university could pay the fee for an entirely legitimate graduate and still have no additional assurance that an employer is compliant. Conversely, a school could refuse a qualified student solely to protect its budget. Neither outcome demonstrates better fraud prevention.

The proposal may also create an incentive to make decisions based on money rather than educational quality. Schools with limited resources may reserve recommendations for students with access to outside funding, rather than those whose training best matches their field. Employers may favor candidates whose institutions can absorb the expense. The result could be fewer opportunities for capable graduates from modest backgrounds or smaller universities. A system that selects for financial resources is not necessarily a system that selects for integrity.

The timing of the payment makes matters worse. Under the proposal, schools generally must pay before a designated school official can enter an OPT recommendation. Yet initial post-completion OPT does not require a student to have secured a job beforehand. Schools would thus be asked to commit an extraordinary sum without knowing whether the graduate will obtain employment. Although refunds may be requested if an employment authorization document is not issued, the proposal makes refund decisions discretionary and final. Such uncertainty would discourage even responsible institutions from participating.

DHS also acknowledges that the fee can be shifted to international students, other students, or employers. This is not a harmless accounting choice. If universities absorb the payments, resources that could fund teaching, scholarships, or research will instead be diverted. If they pass the burden through, tuition or other educational costs could rise for American students as well. If they simply stop supporting OPT, prospective international students may enroll elsewhere, reducing tuition revenue and putting additional pressure on campus budgets. These are foreseeable consequences for American higher education, not merely costs to foreign nationals.

That financial damage would extend to communities surrounding colleges. Universities support jobs, housing demand, local businesses, and research partnerships. A decline in international enrollment can affect more than university accounts; it can reduce spending in college towns and weaken the resources available to domestic students. Smaller regional institutions may be especially vulnerable. DHS should examine these effects before advancing a rule that could substantially alter where students choose to study.

The policy also raises a basic fiscal question. DHS states that the new payments would enter the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and would not be earmarked for ICE's OPT enforcement operations. If the central concern is limited capacity to investigate fraudulent employers, it is difficult to see how collecting billions from educational institutions—without directing those funds to stronger enforcement—resolves that problem. Reducing legitimate participation may lighten administrative workloads, but a smaller program is not necessarily a safer one.

Finally, the United States risks undermining its own investments in education and innovation. American universities train people in engineering, computing, and many other fields. OPT offers an opportunity to apply that training in the domestic economy. Pricing graduates out of this opportunity could send knowledge, entrepreneurial activity, and future research collaborations to competing countries. DHS's analysis estimates substantial costs but does not quantify monetized benefits sufficient to demonstrate that this tradeoff is justified.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and instead identify higher-risk employers and institutions, verify actual employment, expand focused audits, and impose meaningful consequences for proven violations. Effective immigration enforcement should distinguish legitimate participation from fraud. An expensive barrier that largely distinguishes those who can pay from those who cannot is not an adequate substitute.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and the $30,000 fee for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. I agree that DHS should combat fraud and protect US workers, but this proposal does neither effectively, and would impose heavy costs on students, schools, employers and communities that follow the rules.

1. The fees are not tied to any cost of service.
Section IV.C says the fees are meant to make schools more selective and deter participation. DHS itself says that they “are not nominal amounts” and would “[produce] a smaller pool of participants.” A charge set at tens of thousands of dollars in order to shrink a lawful program is not a fee for a service, it’s a barrier. DHS should publish the reason for the $70,000 and $30,000 cost, if there is one at all.

2. The fees do not target the fraud DHS describes.
Section IV.A focuses on specific schemes: sham employers, suspect worksites, and a small number of bad actors. The fee applies to every student at every school. A graduate working at an established employer with a verified worksite and training plan, pays the same as a participant in a sham. Also, one’s ability to pay says nothing about their willingness to comply with the law. DHS has more specific tools to target violators that should be used before imposing a universal charge that affects everyone. I urge DHS to not punish the many for the deeds of the few.

3. The cost will fall on students and employers, or students will be shut out.
DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fee onto individual students, all students, or employers. Few recent graduates can pay $70,000, especially those who are just starting their first jobs. Additionally, few schools or small employers can absorb this cost. A school recommending 100 students would owe $7 million. The likely result of this is that OPT becomes available mainly to the wealthy, or that schools stop recommending students at all. That outcome does not select “the most promising students.” It selects those with the most money, who will then enter these shams the proposal aims to deter anyway, regardless of merit or genuine training value.

4. The $30,000 STEM extension fee penalizes the most accountable part of the program.
STEM OPT students are already working, have already been vetted at least once, and have employers who have signed formal training plans. A fee that discourages this path pushes students and employers away from the better supervised option.

5. The costs would reach American students and the broader economy which this proposal does not account for.
Again, DHS knows that schools may pass the fee to “all students,” which would raise costs for American students directly. Schools that decline to pay would instead lose international enrollment, and research suggests that revenue matters to domestic students. Shih (2017, Journal of Public Economics) found that foreign students’ high net tuition payments help subsidize the cost of enrolling additional domestic students. Bound, Braga, Khanna, and Turner (NBER) found that public research universities expanded international enrollment as state funding fell. I ask DHS to quantify the projected effects on enrollment, university budgets, tuition for domestic students, small businesses and employers, research, and US competitiveness before moving forward with this proposal.
Students and families make major financial and life decisions on the promise that following the rules leads to a fair opportunity. A student who has maintained lawful status, earned a degree and secured a legitimate job should not be priced out of using that education to contribute to the country that allowed them that opportunity. I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based measures against actual fraud that do not harm American and international students alike.

I am submitting this comment in my individual professional capacity as a higher education international enrollment and student services administrator with extensive experience supporting international students and administering F-1 student programs.

1.The proposed fees are disproportionate and would create significant barriers to OPT participation. A $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation is an extraordinary financial burden for a higher education institution. The additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation further increases the burden for students who seek additional authorized practical training, including STEM OPT extensions. These amounts are disconnected from the ordinary administrative function of recommending a student for OPT and maintaining the associated student record. The proposal would require institutions to make substantial financial commitments before a designated school official can enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. Institutions would have to decide whether they can absorb these costs, restrict access to OPT, or reconsider the enrollment and program populations they serve. The consequences would extend beyond the international student office to institutional budgets, academic programs, enrollment planning, and employers seeking qualified graduates.
2.The proposal could undermine international enrollment and U.S. workforce development. Practical training is an important consideration for many international students deciding where to pursue higher education. The opportunity to apply academic learning in a professional setting helps students develop skills, gain relevant experience, and connect their education to career opportunities. The proposed fees could make OPT financially impractical for institutions to support, reducing the availability of these opportunities regardless of a student's academic performance, qualifications, or the legitimacy of the employment. Students may choose to pursue their education in other countries, and U.S. employers may lose access to qualified graduates educated at American institutions. These effects could be especially difficult for institutions with limited financial flexibility and for academic programs that depend on international enrollment. The Department should carefully evaluate these potential consequences before advancing a policy of this magnitude. 
3.The proposal does not adequately demonstrate that the fee amounts are necessary or appropriately calibrated to address fraud. The Department identifies fraud prevention, program integrity, and protection of U.S. workers as the objectives of the proposal. These are important objectives. However, the Department should demonstrate how fees of $70,000 and $30,000 were determined, how the amounts relate to the actual costs of administering and overseeing OPT, and why such substantial fees are necessary to achieve the stated objectives. A fee of this magnitude does not, by itself, establish that an OPT recommendation is legitimate or illegitimate. The Department should evaluate whether targeted compliance measures, improved reporting and oversight, risk-based enforcement, and appropriate penalties for demonstrated violations could address program-integrity concerns without imposing a prohibitive financial barrier on institutions and students. 
4.The Department should consider the operational and reliance impacts on institutions and students. Institutions have established enrollment strategies, academic programs, staffing models, and student support processes around the existing OPT framework. The proposed fees could force significant changes to those plans and could create uncertainty for prospective students, current students approaching program completion, and employers planning to recruit graduates. Before adopting any fee structure, the Department should provide a more complete assessment of the effects on institutions of different sizes and financial capacities, international enrollment, student access to practical training, and U.S. employers. It should also explain how it would address students and institutions that have made educational, enrollment, and workforce decisions in reliance on the existing framework.

I urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule. If the Department continues to consider changes to OPT fees, it should provide a transparent, evidence-based justification for any fee, demonstrate a reasonable relationship between the fee and the costs or regulatory objectives it is intended to support, assess the impact on international students and higher education institutions, and consider less burdensome alternatives. Protecting the integrity of the OPT program and protecting the educational and workforce benefits of international education should not be treated as mutually exclusive goals. The proposed fee structure risks restricting legitimate participation without adequately demonstrating that fees of this magnitude are necessary or proportionate.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee associated with Optional Practical Training (OPT). Requiring payment before a designated school official can recommend OPT in SEVIS would also create serious procedural and administrative difficulties. Even where payment is possible, the proposal would increase costs for universities and for the government offices responsible for collecting and verifying the fee. In practical terms, the proposal risks ending OPT for many otherwise eligible students without meaningfully advancing program integrity.
Employers that are unable or unwilling to incur costs exceeding $100,000 for an H-1B petition are even less likely to pay $70,000 for an OPT student whose performance they have not yet had an opportunity to evaluate. The likely result is not better oversight, but fewer lawful training opportunities and reduced access to the U.S. talent pipeline.
OPT helps address critical workforce needs, particularly in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and research. The Keep Innovators in America Act (H.R. 8013) reflects broader concerns that the United States does not currently produce enough graduates to meet demand in parts of the knowledge economy. International graduates can help fill documented skills gaps while complementing, rather than displacing, U.S. workers. A fee that effectively blocks participation in OPT would weaken this pipeline without addressing the underlying sources of program abuse.
International enrollment at U.S. institutions has already declined, creating financial pressure on colleges and universities and affecting U.S. jobs supported by international education. NAFSA reports that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs during the 2024 2025 academic year. NAFSA has also projected potential losses of $3.4 billion and 40,000 jobs in Fall 2026. A prohibitively high OPT fee would compound these economic harms by making the United States a less attractive destination for talented students.
Restricting practical training would also reduce the global competitiveness of U.S. higher education and weaken fields supported by universities, including science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and artificial intelligence. International students and scholars contribute substantially to U.S. innovation and economic vitality. According to NAFSA research cited in this comment, international student immigrants account for 25 percent of U.S. start-up companies valued at more than $1 billion, 42 percent of founders of leading artificial intelligence companies, and 40 percent of U.S. Nobel Prize winners in chemistry, medicine, and physics. The United States should retain this talent and provide lawful pathways through which international graduates can contribute. For many students, that pathway begins with OPT.
Universities share government interest in preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the OPT program. Established public and private institutions already maintain policies for identifying and rejecting fraudulent documentation. Enforcement efforts should therefore focus on employers that exploit OPT participants; for example, by offering unpaid or underpaid work, charging students for purported employment, or providing false evidence of employment. Students may be victims of such schemes and should not be broadly penalized for misconduct committed against them.
SEVP field representatives regularly engage with universities and are positioned to assess institutional compliance within their areas of responsibility. Institutions that comply with reporting and oversight requirements should not be treated as complicit in fraud carried out by sham or abusive employers. A more targeted enforcement strategy would better protect students, preserve legitimate training opportunities, and direct government resources toward the actors responsible for misconduct.
For these reasons, I respectfully request that the agency withdraw the proposed $70,000 OPT fee and pursue narrower, evidence-based measures to prevent fraud and improve program oversight. As drafted, the proposal would impose disproportionate costs on students, institutions, employers, and the government; reduce access to lawful practical training; weaken U.S. universities; and undermine the nation’s competitiveness in STEM and other high-demand fields. The proposed fee is unlikely to achieve its stated purpose and would create substantial economic and administrative harm.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on what happens after American schools stop recommending OPT — because the students do not simply disappear. They go somewhere else, and right now the world's other leading study destinations are actively competing to take them.

Canada's post-graduation work permit lets international graduates work for up to three years with no fee charged to their schools and no employer sponsorship hurdle. The United Kingdom's Graduate route grants two years of unrestricted work rights — three for PhD graduates. Australia's post-study work stream offers up to four years depending on the qualification. These are programs designed to attract global talent, and they are growing: each of these countries has publicly committed to expanding international enrollment as part of its economic strategy.

The United States already asks more of international students than any of these competitors — higher tuition, no federal financial aid, strict enrollment and work limits during study. OPT has been the one competitive advantage that keeps American schools in the race: a practical bridge from graduation to employment that convinces a talented student in Shanghai, Hyderabad, or Lagos to choose Ohio or Texas over Ontario or Manchester.

A $70,000 fee on schools for each OPT recommendation erases that advantage in one stroke. The moment American universities begin capping or suspending OPT recommendations, recruiting agents in every sending country will notice, and the pitch from Canadian, British, and Australian universities — "come here, work legally after graduation, no fee, no gamble" — will sell itself. The students the United States loses are not the marginal ones; they are the highest-performing graduates in engineering, computer science, and the life sciences, the exact people every advanced economy is trying to recruit.

DHS frames this fee as protecting American interests. In practice, it is an export subsidy for our competitors' talent strategies. The graduates, the startups they would have founded, and the tax revenue they would have generated will enrich Toronto, London, and Sydney instead of American cities — a transfer this rule would accomplish at the stroke of a pen, without any of those countries having to lift a finger.

The United States spent decades building the world's most attractive higher-education system. This rule hands that advantage to its rivals. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I am a U.S. citizen and a current PhD candidate in biomedical science at an American medical school. I am writing to express my serious concern regarding the proposed Optional Practical Training fee rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).

I am not personally dependent on OPT or an international student visa. I am commenting because, as an American scientist in training, I am deeply concerned about what this proposal could mean for the future of science in my country.

Every day, I work alongside talented scientists who came to the United States from around the world to pursue doctoral training and conduct biomedical research. They are our labmates, collaborators, mentors, and colleagues. Together, we investigate disease, develop new technologies, and produce discoveries that benefit American patients and the public.

The proposed fees—$70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation—would create an extraordinary financial barrier between scientific training and scientific employment. In academic biomedical research, where early-career scientists are often employed as postdoctoral researchers and laboratories operate on finite grant budgets, costs of this magnitude cannot simply be absorbed without consequences.

I am especially concerned about the incentive this creates for American research institutions. Faced with two qualified young scientists, an employer could have a powerful financial reason to avoid the candidate requiring OPT. That decision would have nothing to do with scientific ability, creativity, productivity, or the needs of the research. It would be driven by a financial penalty attached to immigration status.

The consequences extend beyond individual researchers. Biomedical research depends on continuity and specialized expertise. Scientists spend years learning techniques, developing experimental systems, generating datasets, and acquiring knowledge that cannot simply be replaced when they leave. Making it prohibitively expensive to retain scientists whom American institutions have already spent years educating and training risks wasting scientific talent as well as investments made by universities, federal research agencies, and American taxpayers.

I am also concerned about the long-term signal this sends to future scientists. The United States has benefited enormously from being a place where talented people from around the world want to study and conduct research. But talented students have choices. If pursuing a PhD here increasingly means facing extraordinary financial barriers to continuing one's research after graduation, some will choose to train elsewhere. Other countries are investing heavily in science and competing for the same talent. American scientific leadership should not be taken for granted.

I recognize that the federal government has legitimate responsibilities to prevent fraud, ensure compliance, and protect American workers. Appropriate oversight of OPT is reasonable. But fees of this magnitude are an exceptionally blunt instrument. A $70,000 fee does not distinguish between a fraudulent employment arrangement and a legitimate scientist joining a research laboratory at an American medical school. DHS should consider more targeted approaches—such as employer verification, auditing, reporting requirements, and enforcement against actual violations—that address abuse without imposing enormous costs on legitimate students and research institutions.

I urge DHS to consider not only anticipated fee revenue, but also the downstream effects on international student recruitment, federally funded research, universities' ability to recruit specialized talent, and the long-term competitiveness of the U.S. biomedical research enterprise.

International scientists are not an abstraction to those of us working in American laboratories. They are the people standing at the bench beside us. They teach us techniques, challenge our ideas, co-author our papers, and help us solve difficult scientific problems.

I am proud to be an American scientist. I want my country to remain a place where the world's most talented young scientists want to come because extraordinary science happens here. Policies that make it dramatically harder for American institutions to retain those scientists put that advantage at risk.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed OPT fee structure and pursue targeted approaches to program integrity that do not undermine American scientific research, innovation, and competitiveness.

I am writing to submit my formal comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions. While the stated intent of this rule is to protect domestic workers and prevent program reliance, an empirical, data-driven analysis of the international student ecosystem demonstrates that this astronomical fee structure will severely damage U.S. higher education, stifle critical talent pipelines, and cause net harm to local and national economies.

1. The Financial Stabilization of U.S. Higher Education
International students act as a critical financial pillar for American universities. The vast majority of international undergraduates and master's students pay full, out-of-state tuition entirely out-of-pocket, with virtually no access to federal financial aid or state subsidies. According to data from NAFSA: Association of International Educators, during the 2022-2023 academic year alone, international students contributed $40.1 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 368,000 jobs. This massive influx of out-of-state tuition directly subsidizes institutional infrastructure, research facilities, and financial aid budgets that make higher education more affordable for domestic, in-state American students. Imposing a massive financial barrier at the post-completion stage will cause a sharp decline in international enrollment, leaving universities with severe budget shortfalls.

2. Direct Contributions to Local Businesses and Consumer Markets
International students do not live in an economic vacuum. During their years of study and subsequent operational training, they spend billions of dollars directly supporting local economies. This includes housing rentals, grocery stores, automotive purchases, utilities, consumer electronics, and local services. By discouraging international students from choosing the United States, DHS is effectively draining consumer capital out of college towns and metropolitan areas across the country, directly harming small businesses that rely on student populations to sustain their operations.

3. Fiscal Contributions Through Taxation and Work-Authorized Spending
When international graduates transition to OPT and STEM OPT, they become highly productive, tax-paying contributors to the U.S. labor force. I oppose the proposed rule, which misclassifies costs, assumes behavior that contradicts basic economics, and omits the effects most relevant to the rule's goals. It cannot support a finding under E.O. 12866 and OMB Circular A-4 that benefits justify costs.

1. A poorly targeted instrument
DHS's largest fraud figure, 10,000 OPT participants with suspect employers, is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 participants, yet the fee hits all of them. To deter fraud, a fee must exceed the rents of those who commit it. "Pay-to-stay" buyers and shell employers already pay for false documents and can absorb or pass on a fee. Honest students of modest means cannot. A uniform price therefore drives out legitimate low-wealth participants before high-rent fraudulent ones. That is adverse selection, not "selectivity." DHS never estimates how much fraud any fee level would deter, so there is no benefit per dollar to weigh.

2. Lost OPT is mismeasured
DHS treats the fees as transfers and sets the cost of lost participation at the unpaid fee, because if OPT were worth more, parties "could collectively cost share." That assumption fails three ways.
a. Coordination: value is split among a student, a school and an employer who may not exist yet; initial OPT requires no job offer. Bargaining among them is costly or impossible.
b. Credit constraints: the fee is due upfront. Students and small schools that cannot finance $70,000 lose OPT even when its value exceeds the fee. DHS's own RFA finds 116 small institutions would face year-one costs above 20% of revenue.
c. External value: much of OPT's value goes to third parties no payer captures: income tax revenue, innovation spillovers, local spending. Peri, Shih and Sparber (J. Labor Econ. 2015) attribute a large share of 1990-2010 U.S. productivity growth to foreign STEM workers. The fee proxy omits all of it.

3. Implausible behavioral assumptions
The high scenario assumes no change in participation despite a $70,000 charge. The low scenario assumes every STEM participant stays and every non-STEM participant leaves. Neither draws on elasticity evidence, and neither models enrollment, though DHS concedes OPT "may contribute to increased enrollment." NAFSA estimates international students contribute over $40 billion a year to the economy, and their tuition cross-subsidizes domestic students at many schools. The analysis values enrollment losses at zero.

4. Predictable substitution ignored
DHS expects a shift from pre- to post-completion OPT but not the larger one: a shift to Curricular Practical Training, which carries no fee and which DHS says has "historically prevalent" fraud. Taxing one channel and not its substitute relocates fraud rather than reducing it. Firms may also offshore work rather than hire U.S. workers; Glennon (Mgmt. Sci. 2024) finds H-1B restrictions raised foreign-affiliate employment.

5. Labor-market benefits asserted, not estimated
DHS assumes jobs held by OPT participants pass to U.S. workers. The evidence is mixed. Doran, Gelber and Isen (J. Polit. Econ. 2022) find some crowd-out at firms winning H-1B lotteries. Mayda et al. (Eur. Econ. Rev. 2018) find tighter H-1B caps did not raise native employment. DHS engages neither. Its only quantitative wage evidence is a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, quoted from a Presidential Proclamation. It counts gained FICA revenue as a benefit but ignores income taxes lost when participants leave.

6. Internal data inconsistencies
The preamble cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants; the analysis uses 95,384 authorizations. The NPRM counts 6,186 certified schools; the PRA statement counts 6,778. The PRA burden assumes 226,200 fee payments; footnote 143 uses 289,938. Estimates built on these figures cannot be checked.

7. Competitiveness
Canada, the UK and Australia grant post-study work rights for a small fraction of $70,000. A fee this size raises the relative price of a U.S. degree for the most mobile, highest-skilled students, the people DHS says it wants to keep. The analysis includes no comparison.

8. Required corrections
DHS should:
(a) estimate fraud reduction per dollar of fee;
(b) model participation and enrollment using empirical elasticities;
(c) value external benefits and tax effects;
(d) analyze substitution to CPT and offshoring;
(e) reconcile its data;
(f) evaluate targeted alternatives, such as employer verification and risk-based audits, which address the employer-side fraud DHS documents at far lower social cost.

The Immigration and Nationality Act does not authorize DHS to impose fees of this magnitude for student work authorization. Mass., June 8, 2026), U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee, ruling it constituted an unconstitutional tax the President lacked authority to impose—because employing H-1B workers is lawful conduct and the fee bore no reasonable relationship to administrative costs. The same reasoning applies here: participating in OPT is lawful, and a $70,000 charge untethered to actual costs is a tax requiring Congressional authorization. On September 30, 2026, a California federal court further blocked agency implementation of the $100,000 H-1B fee, reinforcing that executive overreach on immigration fees will not stand.

On September 14, 2026, in *Presidents' Alliance et al. v. DHS* (D. Mass.), a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS's rule eliminating Duration of Status (D/S) for F-1 and J-1 visa holders—a rule that would have imposed four-year caps on student admissions. DHS must withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Many go on to obtain long-term sponsorship, buy homes, start businesses, and raise families here — their children become the next generation of American contributors. That compounding, multi-generational return is worth orders of magnitude more than a fee that, in practice, almost no one will pay. Meanwhile, the signal this policy sends — that the U.S. is closing its doors to educated talent — will accelerate brain drain among skilled professionals already here and redirect future talent to Canada, the UK, and Australia. Worse, when legal pathways become prohibitively expensive, they do not deter bad actors; they create a larger market for immigration fraud and exploitation, breeding exactly the instability DHS claims to prevent.

For students: this eliminates the primary reason to study in America.

International students choose U.S. universities in large part because of the post-graduation work pathway. Remove that pathway, and there is no rational reason to pay American tuition over more affordable — and now more welcoming — alternatives abroad. The students shut out will not be fraudsters; they will be qualified graduates who played by the rules and invested years of effort in a system that changed the terms at the finish line. The frustration this breeds among hundreds of thousands of educated young people is a social cost no fee can offset.

For universities: this triggers a vicious cycle.

No school will quietly absorb $70,000–$100,000 per student. Schools will stop recommending OPT. International enrollment will decline. The tuition revenue these students bring — revenue that funds research, faculty, and program quality — disappears with them. Weaker programs attract fewer students, which means less revenue, which means weaker programs. This is not a fee; it is the first domino in a cycle that hollows out the university system that made America a global academic destination.

For employers: this cuts off a talent pipeline with no replacement.

U.S. companies — from startups to Fortune 500 — rely on OPT and STEM OPT to access skilled graduates they have already invested in recruiting on campus. There is no alternative pipeline that delivers job-ready, U.S.-educated talent at this scale. Eliminating OPT does not free up these roles for domestic workers; it forces employers to offshore the work entirely or lose the capability. The result is less innovation, less output, and less growth — all originating from a fee that was never going to be collected.

RE: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566)

I oppose this proposed rule. A close reading of DHS's own preamble reveals fundamental deficiencies that render the rule arbitrary and unsupported by its own analysis.

The Fee Generates No Enforcement Capacity

DHS states the fees "would be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302" and that "ICE would not maintain or use the funding collected" because "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds." A rule justified by combating fraud, whose revenue cannot fund a single additional site visit or investigator, is not a fraud-prevention measure. It is a punitive extraction with no operational connection to the stated problem.

Billions in Costs, Zero Monetized Benefits

The OMB A-4 Accounting Statement (Table 1) lists annualized monetized benefits as "Not Estimated." DHS projects annualized costs of $4.1 billion (primary, 3% discount), with 10-year costs up to $69.9 billion. Every claimed benefit — fraud deterrence, worker protection — appears only qualitatively. Under EOs 12866 and 13563, agencies must select approaches that maximize net benefits. A rule imposing tens of billions in quantified costs against zero quantified benefits fails this standard on its face.

The Fee Is Reverse-Engineered, Not Evidence-Based

DHS states it "selected a fee amount comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" to "reduce students and employers from using OPT to circumvent H-1B program fees." The fee is set at $70,000 not because it bears any relationship to OPT administration or fraud prevention costs, but to price-match H-1B. No methodology explains why $70,000 — rather than $7,000 or $700,000 — achieves the stated goals. Arbitrary fee-setting untethered to any cost analysis is vulnerable to challenge as arbitrary and capricious under the APA, 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A).

False Binary: This Fee or Program Shutdown

DHS twice states it "may shut down the program entirely" without these fees. Yet DHS identifies alternatives — expanded site visits, increased reporting, stricter procedural mandates — and rejects all of them not as ineffective, but because a fee "can be implemented quickly and uniformly" with "minimal administrative burdens on the government." Administrative convenience is not a legally sufficient basis for choosing the most destructive option while dismissing targeted alternatives that directly address fraud.

Fraud Is Concentrated, Not Systemic

DHS cites ~10,000 students at "highly suspect employers" against ~290,000 total OPT/STEM OPT participants (Table 2) — roughly 3.5%. DHS proposes fees on 100% of participants to address misconduct in 3.5%. The preamble describes specific shell companies, identifiable phantom worksites, and named prosecutions — enforcement targets, not evidence of systemic failure. Targeted enforcement would address the problem at a fraction of the cost and collateral damage.

Inadequate Comment Period

DHS classifies this rule as economically significant with 10-year costs up to $69.9B and significant impact on 56% of affected institutions. A 30-day comment period for a rule of this magnitude is inconsistent with standard practice for economically significant rulemakings, which routinely receive 60–90 days.

Fee Structure Penalizes Pre-Completion OPT

DHS acknowledges the fee creates a $30,000 penalty for splitting OPT between pre- and post-completion ($100,000 total vs. $70,000 post-only). Pre-completion OPT integrates training into coursework — the program's foundational purpose. A rule that financially eliminates this component contradicts the program's stated objectives.

DHS should withdraw this rule and pursue targeted enforcement against the identified bad actors rather than imposing program-destroying fees on the entire OPT population.

I am writing in my personal capacity. The proposed fee for optional practical training (OPT) is not allowed under law. This proposal must be abandoned.  31 USC 9701(b), requires that fees must be commensurate with the cost or value or the services rendered among other criteria. Note that the statute provides several factors and uses the word “and” to join them, meaning all of those conditions must be satisfied.  E.g., fair and based on the cost of the services, the value to the recipient, “public policy or interest served”, and “other relevant facts.”   

The current fee imposed on most students of $470 supports the existing program’s administration.  Thus, a fee of $70,000 is unlawful under that statute because it will far exceed (by almost 150x) the cost of providing the service. The proposal to fund enforcement through the new fee does not justify a 14,793.62% increase. Given the likelihood that this will be deemed a tax (based on how Judge Sorokin analyzed the proposed increase in H1b fees) this would mean that the administration could be publicly characterized as attempting to create a new tax.

Given the statements that the funds would be deposited into the general treasury instead of being limited exclusively to OPT processing further solidifies the characterization of this proposal as a new tax.  Fees funds go to pay for the service provided, while tax funds go to the general treasury and can be used for other purposes.   The Constitution specifies that taxes must be enacted by Congress.

The distinction between a tax and a fee often turns on who receives a benefit or service from the government and also how the government uses the funds. 

In the case of the proposed “fee” for OPT, the government seeks to charge educational institutions, rather than the students, for each students’ application for OPT.  

Per the Supreme Court in National Cable Television Assn., Inc. v. United States, 415 U. S. 336 (1974), Fees “bestow a reciprocal benefit on the [payor], not shared by other members of society.” For contrast, the funds received from taxes, “inure to the [wider public’s] benefit.” Here, the enforcement aims of the administration are used to justify this proposal. These aims are aimed at benefiting the broader public of US citizens, not the recipient of the gov’t service.  

Further, problems arise because these fees (almost certainly taxes) are aimed at Universities, many of which are tax exempt. Thus, the proposed rule attempts to violate an existing statute, 26 USC  501(c)(3) which, in this case, prevents the taxation of tax-exempt universities and other educational institutions.
Additionally, even if the rule were to survive challenge, however briefly before appeal, the economic incidence, or burden, would likely fall on US students.  Universities may not discriminate on the basis of national origin. Students are the ones who elect to incur this charge. Universities can approve or deny OPT applications on the basis of whether it relates to their field of study and they are in good academic standing, but if Universities deny OPT to avoid the fees, they may open themselves to civil suits and claims of national origin discrimination.

Finally, the Supreme Court has repeatedly held under the “major questions doctrine” that Congress must set major national policy or economic decisions.  In this instance, the proposed rule would drastically reshape the US labor market, the US educational system, and would drastically change the rules which foreign-citizen students relied upon when they came to the US to study. The billions of dollars that these students would have spent here will stay in their home countries instead of coming to the US, thus weakening the dollar.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on educational institutions recommending F-1 students for Optional Practical Training (OPT). This measure functions as a punitive ban rather than a legitimate user fee, failing administrative law standards and harming the U.S. economy.

I. Fundamental Flaws in the Proposed Policy
Unauthorized Tax and Administrative Overreach: Administrative fees under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701) must reflect the actual cost of providing a regulatory service. Routine SEVIS updates and I-20 processing do not cost $70,000. Depositing these funds into the U.S. Treasury as general miscellaneous receipts rather than funding SEVP enforcement confirms that this is an unauthorized tax enacted without congressional approval.

Punishing Educational Institutions for Enforcement Gaps: The cited issues of shell companies and fraudulent worksites stem from a lack of physical site inspections and employer verification by enforcement agencies. Imposing crushing financial burdens on accredited, non-profit academic institutions shifts agency oversight failures onto educators who hold no legal authority over post-graduate commercial entities.

Harm to Academic and Early-Stage Innovation: Large corporations with deep capital reserves may absorb or transfer these costs, but university research laboratories, public hospitals, and early-stage startups will be priced out of retaining top STEM graduates trained in the United States.

Market Inversion and Ineffective Fraud Deterrence: Bona fide universities and legitimate students will be priced out, while illicit "pay-to-stay" brokers operating outside legal boundaries will simply pass elevated costs onto black-market participants, deepening illicit underground activity rather than eliminating it.

II. Rebuttal to Arguments in Favor of the Rule
Some argue that international graduates displace entry-level American workers and depress domestic wages.

However, modern technical fields do not operate on a fixed sum of jobs. Skilled STEM talent enables startups to build core products and secure capital, which in turn creates domestic operational, managerial, and marketing roles. Barring these graduates does not transfer those engineering roles to local candidates; companies instead offshore entire development teams to technological centers in Canada, Europe, or Asia, eliminating peripheral domestic jobs entirely.

Some argue that employers prefer OPT workers because of the FICA payroll tax exemption.

However, if tax parity were the objective, targeted adjustments to tax regulations would address it. Imposing a $70,000 fee on an entry-level professional adds an immediate surcharge of nearly 90% onto a typical starting salary—wildly disproportionate to a 7.65% payroll differential. Employers already spend significant resources on legal onboarding, compliance, and work authorization management.

Some argue that OPT functions as an uncapped loophole to circumvent H-1B visa limits.

However, practical training has been a legally recognized component of the student visa framework since the Immigration Act of 1924, repeatedly upheld in federal court as an integral extension of academic instruction. STEM OPT already mandates structured I-983 training programs and E-Verify employer participation. Confusing educational training with permanent nonimmigrant work visas ignores established legal frameworks.

Some argue that if graduates or their sponsors have true merit, paying $70,000 should not be an obstacle.

However, groundbreaking research and clinical studies typically occur within state hospitals, university research facilities, and early-stage ventures with lean operating budgets. A $70,000 gatekeeper fee does not evaluate technical merit; it evaluates corporate capitalization, giving entrenched tech monopolies a structural hiring advantage while choking off fundamental academic research.

The proposed rule does not resolve regulatory integrity issues and instead damages American research output, university viability, and economic competitiveness. DHS should withdraw this proposed rule.

Universities that cannot absorb a $70,000 fee per OPT student will be forced to reduce international admissions — shrinking this economic contribution, eliminating American jobs, and weakening the institutions that depend on it.

I request DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
