I firmly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. I submit this comment as a faculty member at a research university. I focus on how this rule would further reduce university research output by discouraging international students from applying to and enrolling in PhD programs. International students earn a majority of new doctorates in computer science, engineering, and mathematics and statistics and are a large part of the doctoral research workforce. The fee would also harm graduate education without directly addressing fraud.

1. Financial burden on graduate students
DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fee on to F-1 students (NPRM Secs. IV.C and VI). Graduate students cannot absorb it. $70,000 is nearly twice the $37,000 annual stipend of an NSF Graduate Research Fellow (NSF 26-526), a prestigious national fellowship. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion or STEM OPT would trigger $100,000 in fees. Few departments can budget that, so the likely result is that schools stop recommending OPT, including for legitimate students.

2. Loss of U.S.-trained talent
Foreign-born individuals are 43% of doctorate-level scientists and engineers in the U.S. (National Science Board, 2024). Temporary visa holders earned 38% of U.S. S&E doctorates in 2024 (16,738 of 45,929; NSF NCSES Survey of Earned Doctorates), and in 2023 they earned 62% of computer and information sciences doctorates, 56% of engineering, and 53% of mathematics and statistics (NSF NCSES, NSF 25-300). Most stay: NCSES found that 32,650 of 44,450 temporary-visa S&E doctorate recipients who graduated in 2017-2019 were living in the U.S. in 2023. These graduates are trained in U.S. labs with federal and university research funding, and OPT is a key bridge to staying and contributing. A fee of this size would push many toward countries that are actively recruiting researchers.

3. Postdoctoral and academic careers
Not every graduate takes an industry job; many move into postdoctoral research. The NIH NRSA minimum for a new postdoc in FY2026 is $63,480 (NOT-OD-26-044), less than the $70,000 initial fee. A department cannot reasonably pay more than a postdoc's annual salary for permission to employ them. Research funding is also under pressure: the FY2027 President's budget request proposes cutting NSF 54% (to $3.9 billion) and NIH 12% (to $41.43 billion) (AAU, April 3, 2026). Congress rejected similar FY2026 cuts, but funding uncertainty and immigration policy have contributed to 55 AAU institutions admitting 15% fewer PhD students for fall 2026, following an 11% drop in new PhD enrollment at the 42 institutions reporting fall 2025 data (AAUDE, via AAU, July 2026). Reducing funding on the input side while imposing a prohibitive fee on the output side squeezes students and universities from both directions.

4. Discouraging international PhD applicants and reducing research output
Doctoral students run experiments, write code, publish, and teach undergraduates in STEM labs, so fewer incoming students means less research and teaching capacity at the university itself. Because the fee falls on the school at the point of recommendation, departments may hesitate to admit international students they might later be unable to afford to recommend for OPT, and applicants may not apply to a path that ends in a $70,000 barrier. DHS itself expects schools to become more selective, producing a smaller pool of participants (NPRM Sec. IV.C). The early data point the same way: international applications to PhD programs at those 55 institutions fell 21% this cycle, while domestic applications rose only 3% (AAUDE, 2026). Universities' capacity to fund students has shrunk, so even rising domestic demand led to fewer admissions. Domestic students are already a minority of new doctorates in several STEM fields (see item 2), and the temporary-visa share of S&E doctorates has risen from about 36% (2010-2017) to 38-39% since (NSF NCSES). Domestic students cannot fill that gap on their own, and a prohibitive fee on the path international students rely on would further shrink research output and the future faculty these programs produce.

Requests
(a) Withdraw the proposed rule. (b) If DHS proceeds, exempt master's and doctoral students, postdoctoral and research positions, and nonprofit and public institutions of higher education. (c) Address fraud directly with employer verification, site visits, and SEVP school audits, as DHS did for STEM OPT, rather than a charge on all participants. (d) Extend the comment period to at least 60 days.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Major impacts and takeaways if this proposed rule is enacted:

1) USCIS will lose substantial revenue

They’re initial impressions are that this will kill OPT and make it essentially unattainable for all but a very few international students. Using Florida as an example, according to an economic value statistics analysis from NAFSA, nearly 44,767 international students enroll in Florida colleges and universities, contributing $1.5 billion to the economy and supporting 12,555 jobs. This data clearly demonstrates international students’ financial contribution to our Florida communities, but their influence goes far beyond just economics.

At the national level, international students studying at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 jobs to the U.S. economy during the 2024-2025 academic year.

The Institute for Progress outlines the specific effects to STEM:

The lost STEM talent will cost about $362 billion in annual GDP after ten years. That is the average estimate of a number of scenarios. After a decade, the high-skill STEM workforce will shrink by 6.3% and GDP will be 1.2% smaller. This would cost $2,680 per household per year on average.

DSOs and international advisors are already over-worked and under-supported across the country. It will not happen, plain and simple.

Conclusion:

The negative consequences of this proposed rule would dire. Rescind this rule and allow our students to continue to live, work, and contribute to our country within the strict systems already in place. If students from around the world are prevented from coming here and encouraged to pursue their studies elsewhere, they will. The world of the future—full of technological advances, groundbreaking art, scientific discoveries, innovative businesses, and global problem-solving—will leave the US behind.

To Whom It May Concern: I write to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and the related information collection under OMB Control No. 1653-0038. Imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for STEM extensions is arbitrary, economically unfeasible, and legally indefensible. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m) and OMB Circular No. A-25, administrative fees must reasonably reflect the actual cost of service delivery; here, assessing tens of thousands of dollars for maintaining SEVIS records bears zero rational connection to agency adjudication costs, violating the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)). Furthermore, the Paperwork Reduction Act supporting statement severely miscalculates institutional impact: allocating merely 5 minutes per transaction ignores the complex compliance infrastructure, escrow accounting, fraud auditing, and advising caseloads that SEVP-certified institutions must establish to handle transactions of this magnitude. Functionally, this exorbitant levy operates as an insurmountable financial exclusion that will devastate international student recruitment, penalize non-corporate academic disciplines, compromise university research productivity, and diminish U.S. economic competitiveness by diverting global talent elsewhere. Practical training is an indispensable continuation of academic curricula, not a commodified luxury. DHS should immediately withdraw this unworkable proposal and adhere strictly to standard, cost-grounded administrative fee frameworks.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT recommendation, including STEM OPT. I support strong enforcement against fraud and abuse, but these extraordinary fees are not a reasonable or well-targeted way to achieve that objective.
First, the proposal would punish legitimate students and educational institutions for misconduct committed by a small subset of bad actors. DHS identifies concerns involving fraudulent employers, false employment arrangements, and inadequate oversight. Those problems should be addressed directly through employer investigations, site visits, SEVIS data analysis, audits, verification requirements, and penalties against schools, employers, or individuals that violate the law. A blanket $70,000 charge for every legitimate student recommended for OPT does not distinguish a compliant university, student, or employer from a fraudulent one.
Second, the magnitude of the fees is disconnected from the administrative burden associated with reviewing OPT. DHS estimates approximately $15.7 million in annual review and payment-processing costs, yet estimates that the proposed fees would generate roughly $12.4 billion in annual payments under its primary scenario, with annualized transfers of about $12.8 billion. This enormous disparity shows that the fees are not simply designed to recover the cost of administering OPT. DHS expressly states that the fee is intended to deter participation and is modeled in part on H-1B-related fees. A fee imposed primarily as a deterrent, rather than one reasonably related to the cost of administering the program, would unnecessarily eliminate lawful practical-training opportunities.
Third, DHS itself recognizes serious economic harm. The Regulatory Impact Analysis acknowledges that students could lose work experience and earnings, employers could suffer productivity losses, and universities could experience lower international enrollment and tuition revenue. DHS estimates annualized costs as high as $8.2 billion and acknowledges that it cannot precisely quantify the lost societal benefits. These are not incidental consequences. OPT is the bridge between U.S. education and practical experience in the field of study. Making that bridge financially inaccessible undermines the value of a U.S. education, particularly in STEM fields.
The proposal would also place an unrealistic financial obligation on universities. A school recommending only ten students for initial OPT could face $700,000 in fees; one hundred students would mean $7 million. DHS's own small-entity analysis estimates an average maximum post-transition fee impact of approximately $5.7 million among affected small institutions, and identifies institutions for which the impact could exceed 20 percent of estimated annual revenue. Many universities simply cannot absorb costs of this magnitude. The predictable result would not be better compliance; it would be that otherwise-qualified students are denied OPT because their school cannot afford to recommend them.
I am also concerned by the assumption that reducing OPT participation will necessarily protect U.S. workers. STEM OPT already contains safeguards: employers must participate in E-Verify, complete Form I-983 training plans, attest that the student will not replace U.S. workers, provide compensation commensurate with similarly situated U.S. workers, and remain subject to DHS site visits. If DHS believes these protections are insufficient, it should strengthen and enforce them directly rather than effectively pricing students out of the program.
Finally, DHS states that without these fees it may be unable to operate OPT consistent with its enforcement priorities and may shut down the program. That statement does not establish that fees of $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary. DHS should analyze less restrictive alternatives, including reasonable cost-based fees, increased targeted compliance fees for high-risk or noncompliant institutions, expanded employer verification and site visits, enhanced SEVIS analytics, and meaningful penalties for proven fraud.
I therefore urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. If additional resources are necessary to administer and protect the integrity of OPT, DHS should adopt a reasonable, evidence-based, cost-related fee structure and targeted enforcement measures that preserve lawful OPT and STEM OPT opportunities while addressing actual fraud.
Thank you for considering my comment.

DHS asks the public for "alternatives that would accomplish the same objectives" with less burden. This comment offers one. It uses tools DHS already has and aims them at the employers its own evidence identifies. DHS should withdraw the fee proposal and re-propose this design or one like it.

1. The fraud DHS describes is visible in employer records
The NPRM's red flags are facts about employers: residential addresses listed as worksites with no employees present, multiple employers claiming one address with none on the lease, "identical websites and shared personnel," tax liens, "phantom employees," and multi-state networks placing students with unreported third parties. A school that pays $70,000 learns none of this. A records check and a site visit can. DHS found these patterns through HSI investigations and site visits, not through schools.

2. Element one: verify the employer at reporting
OPT students already report employer information to SEVP. DHS should require an Employer Identification Number and a physical worksite address for every OPT employer report, as Form I-983 already asks of STEM OPT employers. SEVP should screen each new employer automatically for the signals listed above: a residential address, an address shared by many unrelated employers, a newly formed entity reporting many OPT workers, or officers shared across a cluster of companies. The NPRM notes that STEM OPT employers "are not required to submit any business documents" and that DHS does not verify attestations "unless and until there is a site visit."

3. Element two: risk scoring to direct site visits
DHS says a smaller OPT pool would let it "focus its investigative efforts on high-risk industries and sectors." Risk scoring reaches that focus without shrinking the pool. Employers flagged in Element one would be ranked and visited first. DHS's recent investigation already found the "coordinated employer clusters" and shared addresses that a scoring model would flag.

4. Element three: STEM-style safeguards for flagged employers only
DHS rejected extending site visits, training plans and reporting to all OPT because they "may require substantial time and resources." A tiered rule answers that objection. Apply the Form I-983 training plan, document submission (tax records, proof of business, a lease) and site visits only to employers that score as high risk. Most employers would see no change. DHS says self-attestation is insufficient "without more." Requiring flagged employers to produce documents is the "more."

5. Element four: consequences for the parties who commit fraud
The fee charges the school, which DHS's evidence does not show to be the main source of fraud. Sanctions should follow the conduct. An employer found to have filed false OPT reports should be barred from employing OPT and STEM OPT students for a set period. Students should be told promptly when an employer they reported is flagged, so honest students placed by a sham company can move before they lose status. Schools with a pattern of recommending students to flagged employers can be addressed through existing SEVP oversight and certification review.

6. The fee does not pay for oversight
A main reason DHS gives for choosing a fee is that it "does not require DHS to deploy significant additional resources for enforcement or oversight." But the problem DHS cites, from the CIS Ombudsman's 2020 report, is that "agency compliance resources are not scaled to (or keeping pace with) the size of the program." The fee does nothing for that. The money goes to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt, and ICE "would not maintain or use the funding." If oversight needs money, DHS should request appropriations or set any charge at the documented cost of the verification it performs.

7. This approach produces evidence. A fee does not.
DHS calls the fee "a crucial first step" and "an immediate first step in a graduated strategy" that will provide "valuable data." A fee yields a count of who paid. It cannot show whether fraud fell or honest students left. A risk-based program yields hit rates: how many flagged employers were confirmed as fraudulent, and how many unflagged ones were. That is the kind of evaluation OMB Circular A-4 expects.

8. Requested action
DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and re-propose a rule that:
(a) requires an EIN and physical worksite address for every OPT employer report;
(b) screens new employers automatically and directs site visits by risk score;
(c) applies I-983 plans, document submission and site visits to high-risk employers;
(d) bars employers found to have filed false OPT reports, with notice to affected students;
(e) starts with a published pilot that reports confirmed-fraud rates per visit.

I want to put a simple question to DHS: what service, exactly, does a university receive in exchange for $70,000?

When a Designated School Official recommends a student for OPT, the school does the work — verifying enrollment, entering data in SEVIS, issuing the updated I-20. The government then adjudicates the student's employment authorization for about $520, the current Form I-765 fee. That is the measure of legitimate fee authority: under the Immigration and Nationality Act, DHS may set fees to recover the costs of providing adjudication services. Nothing about processing one work-permit application costs $70,000. This fee is roughly 135 times the price of the service it supposedly funds — and it is charged to the school, which is not even the applicant.

That mismatch matters because Congress never gave the executive a general power to raise revenue through immigration programs. When the administration tried the same approach with a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, federal courts blocked it — in California, for bypassing required rulemaking and lacking statutory authority; in Massachusetts, for usurping Congress's power to tax. This fee repeats the same legal error on a larger scale: a charge designed to extract $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year from universities, by DHS's own estimate, is not cost recovery. It is a revenue measure, and revenue measures are Congress's to enact.

The proposal's own framing gives this away. If the fee were genuinely about covering the cost of administering OPT, it would track those costs. Instead it is set at a level DHS concedes will push schools to stop recommending OPT at all — a de facto shutdown of the program, priced to look like a fee. The executive branch does not get to abolish a congressionally created program by making it unaffordable.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate government objectives, the proposed rule fails to establish that these extraordinary fees are a necessary, proportionate, or effective means of achieving those objectives.

1. The proposed fees lack a demonstrated relationship to administrative or enforcement costs.

The proposed rule acknowledges that the collected fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE for OPT enforcement. DHS should explain how collecting up to $70,000 per student would directly improve fraud detection when the revenue is not specifically allocated to enforcement.

DHS should publish a transparent cost calculation justifying both fee amounts and demonstrate why substantially lower fees, combined with targeted enforcement, would be insufficient.

2. Financial barriers do not establish immigration compliance.

A student’s or university’s ability to pay $70,000 is not evidence that an employment arrangement is legitimate. Conversely, inability to pay is not evidence of fraud.

The proposed fee primarily measures financial resources rather than compliance. Fraud prevention would be better served through employer verification, targeted audits, enforcement against fraudulent institutions, and investigation of documented violations.

DHS should provide empirical evidence demonstrating that the proposed fees would reduce fraud more effectively than these alternatives.

3. The rule creates substantial economic burdens without demonstrating corresponding benefits.

According to DHS’s regulatory analysis, the proposed fees could generate billions of dollars annually. These payments represent substantial costs to educational institutions, students, or employers.

The rule should evaluate not merely fee revenue, but also reduced international enrollment, lost tuition revenue, reduced university research capacity, reduced employment opportunities, and potential displacement of investment and skilled employment outside the United States.

Revenue transferred to the Treasury should not be treated as a net economic benefit without accounting for the corresponding burden on those paying it.

4. The proposal undermines the educational purpose of practical training.

OPT permits eligible international students to gain practical experience directly related to their academic studies. The existing framework generally allows 12 months of post-completion OPT, with an additional 24-month extension for qualifying STEM graduates.

Under the proposed fee structure, an initial OPT period followed by a STEM OPT extension could require $100,000 in total fees.

This creates a financial barrier unrelated to academic qualifications, professional competence, or regulatory compliance. It particularly disadvantages students and smaller employers without substantial financial resources.

5. The rule does not adequately establish benefits for U.S. workers.

Reducing the number of international graduates authorized to work does not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in employment for U.S. workers.

DHS should provide evidence demonstrating the degree to which OPT participants directly substitute for domestic workers, accounting for differences in skills, occupations, geographic labor markets, and employer demand.

The economic analysis should also examine whether restricting access to international graduates could cause employers to relocate research, development, or engineering activities outside the United States.

6. Less burdensome alternatives deserve serious consideration.

DHS should evaluate targeted employer audits, improved SEVIS reporting, enhanced verification of employment arrangements, stronger enforcement against fraudulent institutions, and fees reasonably related to documented administrative costs.

These alternatives address specific compliance risks without imposing extraordinary financial barriers on legitimate students and institutions.

Conclusion

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.

At minimum, DHS should provide a rigorous, evidence-based justification for the fee amounts, demonstrate their effectiveness in reducing fraud, quantify their broader economic consequences, and meaningfully evaluate less burdensome alternatives.

Immigration enforcement should target actual violations, not use financial capacity as a substitute for evidence of compliance.

I am writing as a current F-1 student to strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.

1. A blanket fee on all students is not a reasonable response to fraud committed by a small minority.

The proposed rule’s own justification (Section IV.A) rests on fraud involving shell companies, fake worksites, and “visa mill” schemes. These are serious problems and should be prosecuted. But by DHS’s own figures, the investigation it cites identified roughly 10,000 students working for suspect employers, out of nearly 195,000 OPT participants in 2024. The overwhelming majority of OPT participants are legitimate students working in jobs related to their degrees. The proposed rule punishes all of them, and all of the schools that educate them, for the conduct of a few bad actors. A fee that every student must bear, regardless of employer, field, or conduct, is not targeted at fraud. It does not distinguish a fraudulent “pay-to-stay” scheme from a genuine research or engineering role.

2. The fee penalizes lawful pathways and does not reduce fraud.

OPT and H-1B are lawful, established channels through which U.S. employers hire talented graduates of U.S. universities. These students have already been vetted when issued visas, admitted to accredited institutions, and recommended by school officials. Placing a prohibitive cost on a lawful pathway will mainly deter the honest participants who respond to price signals and follow the rules. Operators of sham employers and visa mills, by contrast, have shown they will adapt. DHS provides no evidence that a fee will stop them, and the proposed rule contains no new mechanism for identifying or sanctioning fraudulent employers or schools. The result is that capable graduates who would otherwise contribute to U.S. employers, research, and innovation are driven away, while the fraud the rule claims to target is left largely untouched. This reverses cause and effect.

3. DHS acknowledges the cost will be passed on to international students.

Although the fee is assessed on schools, DHS states in the proposed rule that schools may pass the obligation on to F-1 students, all students, or employers (Sections IV.C and VI). In practice, a $70,000 to $100,000 charge per student cannot be absorbed by most institutions. Students will bear it directly or indirectly, through higher tuition, program-specific surcharges, or being denied OPT recommendations altogether. This is effectively a very large new cost on international students, for a benefit (work authorization related to their own degree) that they have lawfully qualified for. I note that DHS’s own regulatory impact analysis estimates annualized costs of about $4.1 billion, and projects that participation will fall.

4. The loss of international students will significantly harm U.S. universities and communities.

OPT is a major factor in where international students choose to study. If it becomes unaffordable or unavailable, many prospective students will choose other countries. DHS dismisses this concern (Section VI) as “speculative,” but the impact on enrollment is predictable, and the rule’s own analysis identifies 2,478 affected schools, 56 percent of them small entities. International students contribute tuition revenue that supports graduate programs, research, and faculty positions, and they spend in the local economies around campuses. Reduced international enrollment will force some programs to shrink or close, which also affects American students and the communities that rely on these institutions.

5. Recommendations.

If DHS wishes to address OPT fraud, I urge it to withdraw the fee proposal and instead:

focus enforcement on employers and schools with documented violations, including site visits and verification of employer existence;
strengthen training and accountability for Designated School Officials;
use existing reporting tools such as SEVIS and Form I-983 to detect high-risk patterns, rather than imposing costs on all participants.

I also oppose the alternative DHS raised in Section V.A of charging the $70,000 fee again at each new education level, which would compound these harms.

Finally, the proposed rule would apply to students who enrolled and invested in U.S. degrees expecting access to OPT. DHS’s treatment of these reliance interests is inadequate.

I respectfully urge DHS not to finalize this rule.

Respectfully,
Anonymous

Employers benefit too. Students on OPT are generally exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes, so an employer saves 7.65% of wages on an OPT hire compared with an American graduate paid the same salary. That saving gives companies a cost reason to prefer OPT graduates for entry-level jobs.

A student visa is meant for study, and OPT has grown well beyond that purpose. I support these fees as a step, and I would support ending OPT altogether. Any practical training should happen within the degree program itself, unpaid or with a modest stipend, much like a summer internship.

I support the proposed rule and urge DHS to finalize it. I also support the alternative in Section V.A, which would reapply the initial fee at each new degree level.

1. The program has outgrown what Congress designed (Sec. IV.B).
Congress capped H-1B visas at 85,000 a year. OPT has no cap. In 2016, DHS projected that STEM OPT would reach about 92,000 participants by 2026. By 2024 it already exceeded 165,000, alongside 194,554 participants in regular OPT. A regulatory training benefit now produces more work authorizations than the statutory work visa Congress actually created. An uncapped side door that dwarfs the front door is not "practical training." It is a parallel guest worker program that no statute authorizes. A fee set in line with H-1B costs restores parity and removes the incentive to route around the cap.

2. Fraud is documented, large, and growing faster than enforcement (Sec. IV.A).
DHS identified more than 10,000 OPT students tied to highly suspect employers, including phantom worksites and residential addresses with no employees present. One convicted defendant supplied false employment documents to 2,693 students. About 60 SEVP field representatives cover 6,186 certified schools. In 2020, the CIS Ombudsman warned that compliance resources were not scaled to the size of the program. Site visits only catch problems after the fact. A fee prevents them, because it changes incentives before a fraudulent authorization is ever issued.

3. Charging schools puts accountability where the gatekeeping happens (Sec. IV.C).
Designated school officials recommend OPT, often with no job offer in hand for the initial 12 months, and they currently pay no price for bad recommendations. Requiring payment before a SEVIS recommendation gives each institution a direct financial stake in every placement. Programs that function as visa mills will be priced out. Schools confident in their students will pay, or will partner with employers who value those students.

4. The rule levels the field for American graduates (Sec. IV.B).
OPT workers are generally exempt from FICA taxes for up to five years. That saves employers 7.65 percent of wages and gives them a built-in reason to prefer foreign hires over U.S. graduates. Recent computer science and computer engineering graduates face unemployment rates of 6.1 and 7.5 percent. The fee offsets a tax-driven cost advantage that U.S. workers cannot match.

5. Reliance interests are properly protected (Sec. VI).
The rule applies only going forward. It exempts anyone who receives a DSO recommendation before the effective date, delays the effective date by 60 days, and refunds the fee if no employment authorization is issued. By statute, the F-1 classification is for people coming "solely" to study. Only about 20 percent of F-1 students used OPT in 2024, so the core educational benefit of the visa is untouched.

6. Recommendations to strengthen the final rule:
a. Adopt the Section V.A alternative, so the $70,000 initial fee applies at each new degree level. This closes the "degree-hopping" pattern used to extend work authorization.
b. Expressly bar schools from recovering the fee through tuition charged to U.S. students. The cost should fall on the participants and employers who benefit.
c. Publish annual data on fee collections, refunds, OPT participation by school, and employer compliance findings, so the public can judge whether the rule is working.
d. Strengthen the record on legal authority under INA 214(a) and HSA 102. Document how the fee amount relates to the deterrence goal and to existing H-1B costs, so the rule holds up on judicial review.
e. Pair the fee with mandatory E-Verify and I-983-style training plans for all post-completion OPT, as DHS indicated it may do in later phases.

This rule is a measured first step. It does not abolish OPT. It requires that participation be worth paying for. I urge DHS to finalize it promptly.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and ask DHS to withdraw this proposal.

The analysis should distinguish reduced fraudulent participation from the loss of legitimate educational opportunities and evaluate how costs would be distributed among schools, students, and employers.

Please preserve meaningful access to lawful, educationally relevant practical training while addressing specific misconduct through proportionate measures.

International students enter American universities under a set of published terms, and OPT is one of them. The proposed rule — $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one — rewrites those terms after the bargain has been struck, and it is the students who followed every rule that pay the price.

Consider the timing. A student graduating in May 2027 enrolled two to four years ago, chose a program, paid tens of thousands in tuition, signed a lease, and accepted an internship — all with OPT as a known feature of the deal. Under the proposal, a final rule would take effect 60 days after publication, and the fee would attach to the Designated School Official's recommendation date. A rule finalized in spring could therefore pull the rug from students whose graduation is weeks away. They cannot re-enroll elsewhere, recover the tuition they paid, or undo the decisions they made under the old terms.

Universities cannot bridge the gap. Institutional budgets are set a year in advance; a school facing millions in unplanned OPT fees in the spring semester cannot reprice tuition or invent new revenue mid-year. The only lever available on short notice is to stop recommending OPT — which punishes the students closest to graduation, the ones with the least time to adjust.

DHS could have offered a real transition: grandfather students already enrolled, tie the fee to enrollment cohorts after the effective date, or phase it in over several admission cycles. It did none of these. Instead the proposal treats four years of good-faith reliance as irrelevant.

Changing the rules on people mid-course is the hallmark of an arbitrary regulation. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal, or at a minimum to exempt every student already enrolled from its reach.

I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it or substantially revise it.
1. The fee is a revenue measure, not a fee for service, and DHS’s authority is doubtful.
DHS relies on its “time and conditions” authority under INA 214(a). Yet the NPRM states that the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and that ICE “would not maintain or use” them. A $70,000 charge that funds no service, and is justified only as a deterrent, operates as a tax. Narenji v. Civiletti and Washington Alliance of Technology Workers upheld conditions “reasonably related” to F-1 status. Neither addressed a multi-thousand-dollar levy. A charge of this size, with estimated transfers of $12.8 billion annually, raises serious questions about whether Congress delegated it.
2. The remedy does not match the problem.
The fraud described involves shell companies, staged worksites, and “pay-to-stay” employers. The fee falls on schools, which are not the alleged wrongdoers, and applies equally to every student at every institution. DHS cites about 10,000 suspect employers against roughly 195,000 OPT participants in 2024. A flat levy on all participants is not tailored to that problem. A fraudulent employer or visa-mill school may simply pass the cost to the student or ignore it. Legitimate institutions bear the burden.
3. DHS’s own analysis shows severe and unmitigated harm.
The primary estimate of annualized costs is $4.1 billion, with a high estimate of $8.2 billion.
Of 1,389 small institutions, 841 (60.5%) would see impacts above 1% of revenue in the transition year, and 116 would see impacts above 20%.
DHS cannot predict participation or enrollment effects, and it declines to quantify costs for budgeting, refunds, or financial administration.
Opportunity costs are proxied by the unpaid fee itself, which is an arbitrary figure with no empirical basis. Meanwhile the claimed benefits (fraud reduction, protection of U.S. workers, wage effects) are entirely unquantified. For an economically significant rule, Executive Order 12866 requires a reasoned comparison of costs and benefits. This analysis does not provide one.
4. The rule signals an intent to end the program without Congress.
DHS states twice that without the fees it “may shut down the program entirely.” That suggests the fee is designed to price OPT out of existence. Regulations must not circumvent the limits on agency power or the stability Congress and employers have relied on for decades.
5. The enforcement rationale contradicts the funding design.
DHS says the fee will relieve its resource burden. But because the money goes to the Treasury and not to SEVP, enforcement capacity does not grow. The agency also says schools “may pass” the fee to students or employers, which defeats the stated aim of making schools the accountable gatekeepers.
6. The fee conflicts with OPT’s educational purpose.
OPT is training “directly related” to a student’s field of study. Under the proposal, a student who does pre-completion and post-completion OPT triggers $100,000 in fees versus $70,000 for post-completion alone. DHS itself expects pre-completion OPT to decline. This discourages integrated work-based learning. The $70,000 initial fee, benchmarked to the H-1B fee, treats students as if they were employer-sponsored workers, which they are not.
7. Alternatives were dismissed without real analysis.
DHS considered only no action, a small-school exemption, and heavier procedures, then rejected them in a few sentences. It did not evaluate:
risk-based or tiered fees tied to school or employer risk profiles;
E-Verify or employer-registration requirements for all OPT employers;
fees that fund SEVP enforcement and are retained for that purpose;

I oppose this proposal. The NPRM says the amount "is designed to closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees." That benchmark cannot carry the rule. Other comments address statutory authority and cost recovery. This one looks only at the H-1B link.

1. The NPRM never states its benchmark
The rule cites the proclamation in footnotes 116 and 117. It does not state the H-1B amount, who pays it, or which petitions it covers. Commenters must look elsewhere to learn what the OPT fee is meant to match. A rule that borrows a number should explain the number.

2. The H-1B payment does not apply to F-1 graduates
USCIS guidance issued October 20, 2025 says the payment applies to new petitions for beneficiaries outside the United States without a valid H-1B visa. It does not apply to an F-1 student in the United States who is eligible to change status to H-1B. So an OPT graduate who moves to H-1B owes nothing under the proclamation. That is the policy as implemented. The NPRM calls the same path "circumvention" and charges schools an amount the proclamation's implementers chose not to charge these students. DHS does not mention the exemption or say why it disagrees with it.

3. DHS built the OPT-to-H-1B bridge
The 2008 and 2016 STEM OPT rules both provided cap-gap relief for students with pending H-1B petitions. In 2024 DHS extended cap-gap coverage to April 1 of the fiscal year for which H-1B status is requested (89 FR 103054). Footnote 102 says the 2008 extension was adopted to address the "competitive disadvantage" U.S. high-tech industries faced from H-1B limits. A student who uses OPT, then cap-gap while a petition is pending, is following a route DHS wrote. The NPRM does not reconcile that history with its claim that OPT is a channel "to circumvent employment visa caps."

4. Wrong payer, wrong time
The H-1B payment falls on an employer that has chosen a specific worker for a specific job. The OPT fee falls on a school, before the DSO enters a recommendation. Initial post-completion OPT does not require a job offer. If the concern is employers using OPT to avoid H-1B costs, the employer is not the one charged. The school pays for a hiring choice it does not make and cannot see.

5. The terms do not match
An H-1B petition can support up to three years of work, renewable to six. A non-STEM graduate gets at most 12 months of OPT, yet the school would pay $70,000 for it. DHS's own low scenario assumes schools stop paying for non-STEM students because of "the limited benefit of paying $70,000 for only a single year compared to paying $100,000 for up to three years with STEM OPT eligibility." One year of training is a poor substitute for an H-1B. The benchmark falls hardest on the students least able to use OPT as one.

6. A temporary benchmark for a permanent rule
Proclamation 10973 was a 12-month entry restriction. A proclamation signed September 18, 2026 extended it to September 21, 2027. In June 2026 a federal district court in Massachusetts vacated the USCIS policy implementing the payment, and USCIS has said it is not collecting it while that order stands. The NPRM, published October 8, 2026, discusses neither the extension nor the litigation. Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) has no sunset and no tie to the proclamation. If the H-1B payment ends or is struck down, the OPT fee would stay at a level whose only stated basis is matching it.

7. No joint analysis
The regulatory analysis treats the OPT fee alone. It does not estimate how the OPT fee and the H-1B payment together affect the number of F-1 graduates employers sponsor, or how the two rules interact for students who leave and return on a new petition.

8. Requested action
DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it re-proposes any fee, it should:
(a) drop the H-1B benchmark and justify any amount on its own record;
(b) explain why F-1 graduates exempt under USCIS's guidance should bear an equal charge through their schools;
(c) address its own cap-gap rules and the 2008 and 2016 findings on the OPT-to-H-1B transition;
(d) state what happens to the fee if the proclamation expires or is set aside; and
(e) analyze the combined effect of both charges on F-1 graduates and their employers.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for a student's first participation in Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for any subsequent participation. DHS has not adequately shown that these amounts are lawful, cost-based administrative fees or a properly targeted way to combat fraud.

The charges appear designed to deter lawful participation, not recover administrative costs.

DHS says the fees would make schools more selective and discourage OPT use, including use it believes avoids costs and restrictions associated with the H-1B program. The amounts are not based on the cost of processing an OPT recommendation, monitoring a student, or investigating a particular employer or school. The initial fee is instead linked to estimated education costs, while the subsequent fee applies to later OPT, including STEM OPT. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,575–77 (Oct. 8, 2026).

This raises a basic legal question: is this a genuine regulatory fee, or a tax-like or punitive exaction intended to deter conduct that is otherwise lawful? In National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–43 (1974), the Supreme Court distinguished regulatory fees from taxes and cautioned against treating general fee authority as a general taxing power. DHS cites broad immigration and rulemaking authorities, including 8 U.S.C. §§ 1103(a) and 1184(a), but does not adequately explain how those provisions authorize a charge of this magnitude whose stated purpose includes deterrence rather than cost recovery.

DHS should identify clear statutory authority for this fee structure and explain why each amount is proportionate to the government service or regulatory burden involved. If the real purpose is to impose a financial penalty or discourage OPT use, DHS should not assume general rulemaking authority alone permits it.

The revenue is not tied to the stated anti-fraud purpose.

DHS says the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302. ICE would not retain the money, and it would not be specifically earmarked for SEVP or immigration enforcement. Future congressional appropriations are uncertain. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,576.

A Treasury deposit does not by itself prove a fee unlawful. But it weakens the claim that these amounts reimburse OPT administration or anti-fraud enforcement. DHS acknowledges that the deterrent effect would remain even if the revenue were never appropriated to enforcement. This suggests the central mechanism is to price people out of lawful participation, not finance additional investigations.

DHS should explain why a large across-the-board charge is more effective than targeted audits, employer inspections, verification, and investigations. Reducing lawful OPT participation is not the same as detecting or preventing fraud.

The fee burdens schools and students without tying liability to misconduct.

Schools must pay before their designated officials recommend students for OPT. The fee is not linked to a particular employer, a finding of fraud, or the student's or school's compliance history. The same amount applies to compliant and noncompliant participants alike. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,575–77.

If misconduct occurs at the employment stage, schools may have limited ability to monitor an employer's day-to-day conduct. Imposing a large burden on a school does not establish that it caused the risk or should bear the cost of every potential violation. Schools may seek contributions from students or employers, but that does not eliminate the risk that students will bear the cost or lose access to OPT.

DHS should prioritize measures directed at parties responsible for documented violations, including risk-based employer audits, verification of training and employment arrangements, and meaningful penalties for proven fraud. Any retained fee should be transparent, proportionate to substantiated administrative costs, and not operate as an indiscriminate barrier to lawful OPT.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. DHS has not adequately assessed the effects on students and educational institutions, demonstrated that less burdensome alternatives would be ineffective, or supported its estimates of the economic losses caused by reduced OPT participation.

The economic analysis risks circular reasoning.

To estimate opportunity costs from reduced OPT participation, DHS uses unpaid fees as a proxy for the value lost when a student does not participate. DHS acknowledges that this proxy may overstate or understate actual costs, but assumes opportunity costs equal the unpaid fees. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,588–90 (Oct. 8, 2026).

The fee is a government-selected price, not an independent measurement of an OPT opportunity's value. If a school declines to pay $70,000 and a student cannot participate, that does not establish that the student, institution, employer, or U.S. economy lost exactly $70,000. Actual effects depend on wages, productivity, employment alternatives, educational outcomes, and enrollment. Using the fee to measure the loss caused by the fee risks circular reasoning.

DHS estimates a primary 10-year cost of about $35.1 billion at a 3% discount rate and a separate primary 10-year transfer of about $109.4 billion. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,579–80. These are different concepts: a transfer to government is not automatically a net social cost of the same amount, and a foregone fee is not necessarily the value of a lost work opportunity. DHS should independently estimate lost earnings, productivity, educational outcomes, and institutional impacts; separate transfers from real resource costs; disclose supporting data; and show how results change under alternative assumptions.

The proposal inadequately accounts for reliance and transition costs.

Students make decisions about tuition, borrowing, degree programs, and careers under existing rules. A new fee may eliminate a planned opportunity after years of study, even where the student, school, and employer complied with all requirements. Schools unable to absorb it may cut services, seek funds from students or employers, or stop recommending eligible students for OPT.

DHS estimates that, among 1,389 affected small institutions, 841 could experience transition-year impacts exceeding 1% of estimated revenue, including 116 with estimated impacts exceeding 20%. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,595–96. These estimates deserve serious consideration. Although schools formally pay the fee, costs may be passed on to students or opportunities may disappear altogether.

DHS should assess reliance interests more carefully and provide meaningful transition protections, especially for students already enrolled who made substantial educational and financial commitments in reliance on the existing framework.

DHS has not justified rejecting less burdensome alternatives.

DHS discusses site visits, reporting requirements, training plans, and other safeguards, but rejects them in part because they are more complex, require agency resources, or take longer to implement. 91 Fed. Reg. 64,575–76, 64,596–97. These considerations do not establish that a blanket fee is more effective or proportionate.

DHS should compare alternatives using evidence about fraud prevention, costs, and effects on compliant participants. Risk-based audits, employer verification, targeted site visits, and stronger reporting could focus resources on demonstrated risks rather than impose the same charge on everyone. The possibility of fraud at some small institutions does not establish that all such institutions should bear the same burden.

The comment period is inadequate.

The rule was published October 8, 2026, with comments due November 9—a period of only 32 calendar days. The proposal raises complex legal issues and forecasts enormous economic effects. Executive Order 12866, § 6(a)(1), generally contemplates at least 60 days for public comment, although the Administrative Procedure Act does not impose a universal 60-day minimum. DHS should extend the period to at least 60 days so students, schools, employers, and researchers can evaluate the data and provide meaningful feedback.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal, improve its economic analysis, evaluate targeted anti-fraud alternatives, extend the comment period, and protect students and institutions that relied on existing rules. A sound anti-fraud policy should address actual misconduct rather than use a government-selected fee as a proxy for both deterrence and the economic loss caused by deterrence.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. This comment addresses the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) in section VII.B. Others have noted its headline results: in the transition year, 841 small institutions face costs above 1 percent of revenue. The method behind those numbers understates the harm, and DHS skipped most of the alternatives the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires it to consider.

1. Every public institution is excluded without evidence
DHS assumes all 1,044 public institutions are not small "as they are run by states whose jurisdictions are larger than 50,000 people." Footnote 137 rests this on "a sample of the data" showing "state-run colleges and universities." The RFA counts school districts and special districts with populations under 50,000 as small governmental jurisdictions (5 U.S.C. 601(5)). Many community colleges are run by local districts, not states. DHS does not say how large the sample was or whether it included any community colleges. Locally governed colleges serving small districts are the public schools least able to pay $70,000 per student, and the IRFA counts none of them.

2. Revenue is estimated two different ways, and both overstate it
The IRFA says DHS estimated private receipts by "multiplying the approximate annual cost of room, board, and tuition by the average number of total students." Later it compares fees to "estimated annual revenue as reported on their I-17 in SEVIS." Elsewhere it refers to "revenue derived from tuition and other student-related sources." The reader cannot tell which measure drives Tables 15 and 17. The room-board-tuition method also uses list prices. It ignores institutional aid and treats housing and meal charges as money free to pay a federal fee. Inflated revenue shrinks every impact percentage. It may also push for-profit schools above the SBA size standard. DHS found only 95 of 140 for-profit institutions to be small, using this same receipts estimate.

3. The real small-entity effect is not estimated
DHS admits that some small institutions "may be unable to secure" outside funding and that it "cannot accurately predict how many schools or OPT participants would be affected." It then uses unpaid fees as a proxy for lost enrollment and tuition. For a small college, the question that matters is whether losing OPT costs it enough international students to cut programs or close. The IRFA gives no estimate, range or scenario for that outcome. It also keeps 2022-2024 OPT participation constant after a $70,000 price is added.

4. The small-entity exemption is rejected on a count, not on risk
DHS rejects a small-entity exemption because 56 percent of institutions are small, so "fraud could still continue." That figure is 1,389 of the 2,478 schools that recommended OPT, not of all 6,186 certified schools. More important, a share of schools is not a share of fraud. The NPRM presents no data showing that small schools generate more OPT fraud per student than large ones. If fraud tracks volume, large schools matter more. DHS's reasoning would defeat any small-entity relief for any rule where most regulated parties are small, which is the case the RFA was written for.

5. Three of the four statutory alternative types are never considered
Section 603(c) names four kinds of alternatives: differing compliance requirements or timetables that reflect small entities' resources; simplification; performance rather than design standards; and exemption from all or part of the rule. DHS considered no action, a full exemption, and expanded oversight. Its fourth listed "alternative," charging the $70,000 fee again at each degree level, would raise costs. It considered no fee scaled to revenue or enrollment, no cap, no installment or post-placement payment schedule, no delayed effective date for small schools, and no exemption for schools with clean SEVP compliance records. A clean-record exemption is a performance standard and targets the stated fraud goal directly.

6. Why this matters now
A final rule must respond to significant issues raised about the IRFA (5 U.S.C. 604(a)(2)), and compliance with section 604 is subject to judicial review (5 U.S.C. 611). Fixing the analysis at the proposed stage, with public input, is the lawful and efficient path.

7. Request
I ask DHS to withdraw the rule. If DHS continues, it should publish a corrected IRFA for comment that (a) identifies locally governed public colleges and counts those that are small; (b) uses one documented revenue measure net of institutional aid and pass-through charges; (c) estimates enrollment losses and closure risk at small schools; (d) presents any data on fraud rates by institution size; and (e) analyzes revenue-scaled fees, caps, deferred payment, delayed timetables, and a clean-compliance exemption under section 603(c).

The NPRM says the fee will “protect American workers” by shrinking OPT. That treats every OPT job as a theft from a U.S. graduate. It is not. Re: Comment Opposing Proposed Rule Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — "Optional Practical Training Fees"

I write to oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT, and urge the Department to withdraw it rather than finalize it.

1. The fees are a de facto ban on OPT, not a fee. OPT participation currently costs students roughly $500 in filing fees. A 140-fold increase cannot be justified as cost recovery. A fee that is deliberately set to price nearly every participant out of the program is not a "condition of admission" — it is a prohibition dressed as a fee, and should be evaluated honestly as such under the Administrative Procedure Act.

2. The burden falls on schools and cannot be passed through fairly. The proposal makes SEVP-certified schools the payor. An estimated $16.5 billion in potential annual costs across ~2,500 institutions would be crushing for small and mid-sized colleges. Schools that absorb the cost will raise tuition for all students — including American students — while schools that pass it to F-1 students will simply watch their international enrollment collapse.

3. It will drive international talent to competing countries. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and disproportionately fill STEM research and graduate roles. Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia are actively recruiting these students with post-study work routes that cost a fraction of this fee. This rule would hand America's competitors a generation of scientists, engineers, and entrepreneurs.

4. It punishes legitimate students for fraud they did not commit. DHS cites fraud by bad actors — exploitative worksites and "pay-to-stay" schemes. The answer to targeted fraud is targeted enforcement against those actors, not a blanket six-figure tax on every international student. Punishing the compliant majority for the misconduct of a few is neither fair nor effective at combating fraud.

5. The rule reaches even pre-completion OPT, meaning a student seeking a brief, degree-related internship while enrolled would trigger the same $70,000 fee. That severs the link between OPT and its stated educational purpose.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS believes OPT enforcement needs strengthening, it should do so through evidence-based, targeted measures — not a fee schedule that effectively ends the program.
