These are precisely the graduates in artificial intelligence, semiconductor design, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing — the fields where a decade of federal policy has aimed to onshore talent and capacity. This proposal taxes the very pipeline those policies were built to create.

University research labs feel it first. Principal investigators plan postdoc and research-scientist hiring on multi-year grant budgets set years in advance; a six-figure fee attached to the training authorization of a foreign-born postdoc is not a line item any grant can absorb. Labs will do what budgets force: stop hiring international postdocs, or relocate the positions to partner labs abroad. The research does not wait — it continues, but it continues somewhere else, under someone else's patent regime.

Private employers face a simpler calculus. A company hiring new graduates does not need OPT to exist at all; it needs a workable start date. If universities stop recommending OPT, entry-level technical hiring does not reroute to an equal supply of domestic graduates — it reroutes to offices in the countries where the talent is and where no university pays six figures for the privilege of employing them. The administration has said American leadership in AI and advanced technology is a national priority; a fee structure that places a $30,000 surcharge on retaining STEM graduates is inconsistent with that goal. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

This proposed rule does not make any sense. The explanation for the need of the increased fee is that it would prevent fraud, which it would in no way do, and even if it did, the cost does not make any sense. The rational given is that if an employer truly believed in the talents of an international student above an American Worker than they would pay this incredibly high fee. But the employer is not asked to pay the fee and in fact students do not need to have an employer lined up to apply for OPT. Instead, colleges and universities are being asked to pay the fee. So on the face of it, the rule will not accomplish it's aim. Additionally schools are funded by state, federal, donation, and tuition dollars. It is not the aim of the federal government to see its money go to these OPT fees or to see tuition hikes to compensate for the number of international students who would need OPT work authorization. School may become unaffordable to the poorest students who stand to benefit the most from a degree and often these are the students who get degrees in practical matters such as engineering and project management. So again, not only is the rule not structured to work as a screening to test to see if International Students are desirable to employers, but this will have undesirable effects when it comes to tuition costs for students. So this enormous additional burden on the school would just make this so called fraud that is being claimed even worse because schools would be paying huge amounts of money for International Students to go on OPT but they could do all the same things the government has claimed that they did already.  Also its important to keep in mind that even if employers did need to pay a fee in order to hire a student on OPT, it would not make sense for that fee to be this high. As an example, colleges and universities charge an application fee to prospective students to prevent students from applying to every school they could apply to even when woefully underqualified or when they already know they would not go to that school, which creates a huge burden on schools to review all of those applications for students who would never end up even having a likelihood of attending. Studies show that these fees don't need to be that high to prevent application spamming. They could only be $15 dollars as that amount would really add up for any student who wants to send applications out to lots of schools and because every application now has weight to them. The federal government could do something similar and I don't think there is any argument that charging an employer or a school more than a year's salary on the federal minimum wage makes any sense. More than most college students make in a year in their first role after college. It is admirable that the government wants to prevent fraud and abuse and wants to make sure that American workers have the opportunities they deserve and I want that too but this proposed rule would fail in that mission. I hope you all can go back to the drawing board on this one and put out a rule that would have the stated desired outcome.

I strongly oppose the proposal. I understand that DHS wants to prevent fraud and protect American workers. Those are reasonable goals. But after reading this proposal, I have to ask: how does making universities pay up to $100,000 for a student's practical training actually solve the problems DHS is worried about?

DHS talks about fake employers, fraudulent job offers, and shell companies. If those are the problems, shouldn't the government focus on investigating those companies? Charging a university $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation does not prove that a job is real or that an employer is following the law. It only proves that someone can afford the fee. An honest student at a small public university could lose their OPT opportunity, while a dishonest operator with enough money might still find a way around the rules. How is that an improvement?

Another thing that makes little sense is where the money goes. The proposal says these fees would go to the U.S. Treasury, not directly to ICE for OPT enforcement. So the government says it needs to fight fraud, but the billions collected would not automatically pay for more investigators, inspections, or employer verification. If DHS really needs more resources to catch fraudulent employers, why not invest in enforcement instead of making legitimate universities pay enormous amounts?

And let's talk about who actually pays the price. Universities do not have unlimited money. Many public universities already struggle with tight budgets. Asking them to pay tens of thousands of dollars per student could force them to stop supporting OPT entirely. Others might raise tuition, reduce scholarships, cut research budgets, or eliminate positions. In the end, American students, university employees, and taxpayers could suffer. How does making college more expensive protect American families?

The damage could be even worse in smaller towns. In many rural communities, the local university is a major source of jobs and economic activity. International students rent apartments, shop at grocery stores, eat at restaurants, buy cars, and support local businesses. If fewer international students come to the United States, local landlords, shop owners, and workers lose customers. These are real American businesses and real American jobs. The proposal seems to overlook how much these communities depend on university enrollment.

It also seems strange that America spends so much money building world-class universities and research facilities, only to make it harder for the people trained there to contribute to the economy. International students work on medical research, engineering projects, scientific discoveries, and new technologies. Many contribute alongside American researchers in laboratories supported by public funding. Why would we want to push those talented graduates toward countries that are competing with us? America benefits when talented people choose to study, work, innovate, and build businesses here.

DHS also argues that schools can simply pass these fees on to students or employers. But that is not a solution. It just moves the financial burden somewhere else. Many graduates cannot afford $70,000, and smaller employers certainly cannot justify paying that much for every new hire. If the government wants to protect American workers, making it harder for American startups, research institutions, and small businesses to hire qualified people seems counterproductive.

Perhaps the biggest problem is that DHS has not shown that this policy is worth its cost. Its own analysis estimates about $4.1 billion in annualized costs under the primary scenario, while monetized benefits have not been estimated. That is a huge amount of economic damage to risk without clear evidence of how much fraud will actually be prevented. Simply reducing the number of people participating in OPT is not proof that the system has become more secure.

I am absolutely in favor of stopping immigration fraud. Investigate fake companies, verify employment records, inspect suspicious worksites, and punish people who break the law. But please do not confuse making a program unaffordable with making it more secure.

This proposal could hurt American universities, increase costs for American families, weaken local economies, and drive away the scientists and innovators America needs. I urge DHS to withdraw it and pursue practical, targeted solutions that actually address fraud without damaging the country's economic future.

TO: Policy Division, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE); Office of Policy and Strategy, USCIS; Department of Homeland Security (DHS)
SUBJECT: Interstatutory & Ultra Vires Defect Brief: OPT Fee Regime Contradicts Congressional Classification Under 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19) and IOAA Fee Limits

This comment demonstrates that the proposed OPT fee regime is ultra vires, unconstitutional, and arbitrary and capricious under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)), State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983), and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024).

I. CONGRESS SPECIFICALLY EXCLUDED OPT FROM "EMPLOYMENT" UNDER 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19)
The Internal Revenue Code explicitly establishes that services performed by F-1 nonimmigrants under INA § 101(a)(15)(F) to carry out their educational purpose are excluded from the statutory definition of "employment." 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19); see also 26 U.S.C. § 3306(c)(19) (FUTA). The IRS has repeatedly confirmed this exclusion covers Curricular Practical Training (CPT) and Optional Practical Training (OPT). IRS Info. Ltr. 2002-0041; IRS Pub. 519.
Neither student nor host employer pays FICA/FUTA taxes because Congress determined practical training is an inherent extension of academic study, not commercial employment. The D.C. Circuit affirmed this in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164, 178–82 (D.C. Cir. 2022), holding post-completion OPT is lawful precisely because it directly advances the pedagogical purpose of F-1 student status.

II. THE PROPOSED FEE RULE RECHARACTERIZES OPT AS EMPLOYMENT IN DIRECT STATUTORY CONFLICT
The NPRM levies massive fees on SEVP institutions and students based on an administrative premise that OPT constitutes commercial employment subject to revenue extraction and labor policing. DHS invokes general admission authority under INA § 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1). But broad authority over nonimmigrant conditions cannot override a specific statutory classification. Morales v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 504 U.S. 374, 384–85 (1992) (the specific governs the general). Post-Loper Bright, courts owe no deference to DHS's reinterpretation. Whether OPT can be administratively reclassified as commercial employment to justify fees is a pure legal question reviewed de novo. Under § 3121(b)(19), OPT is academic training, not employment.

III. UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAXATION & VIOLATION OF IOAA LIMITS (31 U.S.C. § 9701)
To the extent DHS/ICE attempts to levy fees generating $8.4 to $16.5 billion annually, the rule violates the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA), 31 U.S.C. § 9701. Under National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–42 (1974), and FPC v. New England Power Co., 415 U.S. 345 (1974), user fees must be calibrated to the specific value of the agency service conferred upon the recipient. Levying billions in fees far exceeding the nominal cost of adjudicating Form I-765 or updating SEVIS converts an administrative fee into an unconstitutional, unauthorized tax. Under Article I, Section 8, the taxing power belongs exclusively to Congress. An agency cannot transform F-1 training into a general revenue engine.

IV. FAILURE TO ANALYZE INTERSTATUTORY CONFLICTS VIOLATES STATE FARM
The NPRM is silent regarding 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19). Promulgating an economy-wide fee regime without analyzing how its core employment premise conflicts with the Internal Revenue Code is a fatal administrative failure. An agency acts arbitrarily when it "entirely fail[s] to consider an important aspect of the problem" or adopts contradictory legal positions across federal statutory schemes. State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43; Burlington Truck Lines v. United States, 371 U.S. 156, 168 (1962).

V. MAJOR QUESTIONS DOCTRINE: RECLASSIFICATION REQUIRES CLEAR CONGRESSIONAL GRANTS
Legislative efforts—such as proposals to strip § 3121(b)(19)'s exclusion from OPT—confirm Congress recognizes reclassifying OPT requires affirmative legislation. Under West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 721–23 (2022), and Biden v. Nebraska, 600 U.S. 477, 501 (2023), DHS cannot invoke vague organic authority under INA § 214(a) to extract billions from 2,478 academic institutions and upend settled statutory baselines.

REQUIRED ACTION:
DHS, ICE, and USCIS must: (1) reconcile the proposed fee scheme with 26 U.S.C. § 3121(b)(19) and WashTech; (2) demonstrate compliance with IOAA fee limitations (31 U.S.C. § 9701); and (3) identify express statutory authority authorizing a multi-billion dollar fee regime on academic training; or withdraw the NPRM.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose this rule as a resident of the Houston area.

International students and OPT alumni are not an abstraction here. University of Houston reported 1,839 F-1 alumni on OPT in fall 2024, on top of thousands of enrolled nonimmigrants. ICE’s 2024 campus table listed UH with 1,639 students employed on OPT authorizations, Texas A&M with 2,036, and UT Austin with 1,519. UNT, UT Dallas, and UT Arlington are among the highest OPT campuses in the country.

Those graduates rent apartments in the Energy Corridor, Midtown, and near campus. They buy used cars, carry auto insurance, shop at grocery stores, and pay Texas sales tax. A rule that DHS’s low-participation scenario uses to end ordinary (non-STEM) OPT and that prices STEM OPT at $100,000 per person will empty those leases mid-year. Landlords in student corridors do not collect from a “U.S. worker” who never moves in. They collect vacancy.

If schools pass the fee to students, families wire money that never becomes local rent and tuition for the next sibling. If schools refuse to pay, students leave at graduation instead of working a year in Houston’s energy, medical, and engineering employers. Either way, the city loses people who already live here, already passed visa screening, and already paid U.S. tuition.

Section IV.C says the national interest outweighs reliance by “state and government employers.” Harris County, the Texas Medical Center, and public universities are those employers. Charging a public university $70,000 per graduate is a charge on Texas taxpayers. I request withdrawal of ICEB-2026-0100.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose the fee structure in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) and the participation model in Section VII.A.3.

OPT is not only for STEM. Accounting, architecture, nursing (where not STEM-listed), education, hospitality, and business students use the same 12-month OPT. DHS’s low scenario assumes institutions “would pay the initial OPT fee for only F-1 nonimmigrant students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension,” because $70,000 for one year is not “worth it.” That is a deliberate sacrifice of every non-STEM graduate.

The NPRM even invites comment on an alternative that would charge another $70,000 each time a student starts OPT at a higher degree level. A student who did bachelor’s OPT and later master’s OPT could face $70,000 twice, plus $30,000 for STEM. That is not integrity. That is stacking penalties on people who follow the rules and keep studying.

Pre-completion OPT is treated even worse. If a student uses any pre-completion OPT, the school pays $70,000; post-completion then costs another $30,000 for the same 12-month lifetime cap. DHS expects pre-completion OPT to decline for that reason. Summer internships that are the legitimate academic purpose of practical training would vanish because the fee design makes them irrational.

Congress did not limit F-1 study to STEM. 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F) does not say “engineering only.” A rule whose own economic analysis treats non-STEM OPT as disposable is arbitrary. Withdraw the NPRM. Do not adopt the per-degree-level $70,000 alternative.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose using the fraud examples in Section IV.A to justify a blanket fee in 8 CFR 214.13(i).

The NPRM describes real crimes: shell companies, fake offer letters, empty buildings, pay-to-stay schemes. Those cases should be prosecuted. They do not describe a teaching hospital, a CPA firm in busy season, or a university lab that hires its own graduate.

The proposed fee is not tied to the employer. It is triggered when a school recommends OPT. A DSO at an accredited medical center’s affiliated university must pay $70,000 to recommend a student whose worksite DHS could visit tomorrow. Meanwhile, the shell shop in Section IV.A does not pay the fee unless some school is willing to recommend that student—and if schools stop recommending everyone, the fraudsters and the hospitals are cut off together.

STEM OPT already requires Form I-983, E-Verify, commensurate-wage attestations, and site visits. DHS says those tools are not enough, then refuses to extend them because they require staff, then proposes a fee it cannot spend on staff. That is circular.

If DHS wants to stop empty-building employers, condition OPT on a real EIN, a commercial lease, and a site visit before the EAD for employers that have never been verified—not a $70,000 invoice to every SEVP school. I request that DHS withdraw this NPRM and use existing HSI and SEVP authorities against the specific fraud networks it has already identified.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose the 30-day comment period described in the DATES section and Section VI.

OMB designated this a significant regulatory action that is economically significant under E.O. 12866. DHS estimates annual fee transfers of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion, and 10-year transfers up to $144 billion. Implementation costs and opportunity costs add billions more. For a rule of that scale, APA practice and E.O. 12866/13563 call for a meaningful opportunity to comment. Thirty days from October 8 to November 9, with images of tables that many readers cannot parse, is not meaningful for 2,478 schools, state university systems, and hundreds of thousands of students.

Section VII.A.5.d asks the public to supply data DHS does not have: budgeting costs, refund volumes, and the collapse of pre-completion OPT. An agency that needs that information cannot also claim the comment window is ample. Section VI says 30 days plus a 60-day delayed effective date is enough for students to change status or leave the country. Leaving the country is not a comment-period feature. It is an eviction plan.

Refunds under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) are discretionary, case-by-case, and not appealable. Schools would wire $70,000 with no hearing if SEVP later says no. Combined with a 30-day docket, that is not “minimal administrative burden.” It is unreviewable extraction.

I request that DHS withdraw the NPRM, or at minimum reopen the comment period for at least 60 additional days, republish the economic tables in accessible text, and provide a genuine Paperwork Reduction Act discussion of $70,000 payment controls—not five minutes of SEVIS data entry.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose Section IV.C’s suggestion that schools fund the fee by charging “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.”

I am a U.S. student / parent of a U.S. student. If a university cannot pay $70,000 per international graduate, DHS tells it to raise tuition or fees on the whole campus. That means a Texas resident would pay more so ICE can collect a penalty that, again, ICE cannot even keep. That is not protecting American families. That is taxing them.

If the fee is loaded only onto F-1 students, then only the richest international students get practical training. OPT becomes a luxury good. The NPRM says that is a feature: it would “discourage misuse.” Wealth is not a fraud screen. The shell-company cases in Section IV.A involved people who already paid for fake jobs. A $70,000 official fee will not stop a criminal broker. It will stop a middle-class engineering student whose parents already spent their savings on U.S. tuition.

Employers who pay would simply stop using OPT and, where they can, shift to offshore teams. That does not hire the unemployed computer-science graduate in Section IV.B. It moves the work out of the United States.

DHS should not outsource a federal penalty to bursar’s offices. Fraud enforcement is a government function. Charge the violators. Do not put a $70,000 line item on every Form I-20. I request that DHS withdraw ICEB-2026-0100 in full.

Public Comment Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees
To the Department of Homeland Security:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).
I work with international students at the University of California, Berkeley, helping them explore and prepare for graduate education. My students come from universities around the world, and many are considering pursuing master's or doctoral degrees in the United States.
Although the visiting-student program in which I teach does not itself qualify students for OPT, I see firsthand how important future educational and professional opportunities are to students deciding where to pursue advanced degrees.
I am concerned that the proposed fees would create substantial barriers to participation in OPT and could discourage talented international students from choosing American universities for their graduate education.
While the fees would formally be paid by universities, institutions could pass those costs to students or employers, or decide not to recommend otherwise eligible students for OPT. This would potentially make access to valuable professional experience dependent on financial resources rather than a student's academic qualifications, skills, or potential contributions.
I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the immigration system and preventing fraudulent use of employment authorization programs. However, I encourage DHS to consider whether these fees are proportionate to those objectives and to provide clear evidence that they would achieve the intended results.
I urge the Department to withdraw the proposed fee structure and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to program oversight that preserve legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
Thank you for considering my comments.
Respectfully,
Sally Clapper
Educator, UC Berkeley Global Access Program
Submitted in an individual capacity; views are my own.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses to study in the United States. OPT provides an important opportunity for students to gain practical experience, apply their education, and contribute to the U.S. economy.

These extremely high fees would make OPT unaffordable for most international students, regardless of their academic achievements, skills, or potential contributions. They would also place an unreasonable financial burden on universities and employers.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting American workers. However, charging such excessive fees is not a fair or effective solution. Stronger oversight and reasonable, transparent fees would be more appropriate.

Many international students have invested years of hard work and significant financial resources in pursuing an American education. Changing the rules so drastically would undermine their educational and career plans and discourage talented students from choosing the United States.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and consider more reasonable alternatives that protect the integrity of the OPT program without unfairly penalizing legitimate international students.

Thank you for considering my comment.

This is the best way to make America last. The brightest minds are not always from wealthy backgrounds, yet should be welcomed to our country to improve our country's intellectual assets. Making absorbent fees blocks the path to this end.

The proposed rule DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 attempting to update Optional Practical Training fees seems to be a blatant attempt to limit access and opportunity for international students to make a living and support themselves while studying in the United States.

OPT (Optional Practical Training) is a temporary work authorization that allows eligible international students on an F-1 visa to gain hands-on work experience in the United States directly related to their major field of study.

Currently, when a student applies for Optional Practical Training (OPT), the student is recommended for an OPT period by their school's international affairs office, and then the student files an application with USCIS and pays the $470 application fee.

The proposed plan would add a fee that the school pays before recommending a student for OPT. The school would pay $70,000 the first time it recommends a student for any type of OPT, most commonly 12 months of post-completion OPT. Then the school would pay $30,000 for each later OPT recommendation for that student, such as the STEM extension, if applicable. 

This is clearly a disturbing attempt to limit international students' opportunity and ability to learn, make a living, and gain hands-on experiences as well as networking connections in their field. Institutions will not be able to take on these additional fees, and I think DHS knows this. 

I work at an institution comprised of around 30% international students. Our campus represents a breadth of beautiful identities and cultures. We contain multitudes and our country is better because of our inclusion of international learners as well as noncitizens. 

It is shameful to see the ways in which DHS and ICE are dehumanizing and oppressing international learners as well as noncitizens who have sought refuge or found a home in the United States. Please stop this proposal and also stop trying to frame these proposals as a way to protect U.S. workers. If the government actually cared about U.S. workers, you would enforce livable wages, universal healthcare, and retirement benefits. Additionally, you would stop champioining A.I. taking jobs away from workers and start providing more opportunities for your low income citizens to receive access to support, instead of cutting funding for those programs.

I am a clinical neuropsychologist. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation. 

Clinical neuropsychology requires extensive specialized training, including two-year postdoctoral fellowships following doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled, competitive neuropsychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates.

These consequences extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning and linguistic/cultural considerations that strengthen neuropsychological assessment, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and limit the availability of clinical-researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S.'s diverse population.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

Thank you for considering.

Why Protecting Optional Practical Training (OPT) Matters

Optional Practical Training (OPT) plays an important role in maintaining the United States' position as a leading destination for international talent. By allowing international students to gain practical work experience in their fields of study, OPT contributes to American innovation, research, and economic competitiveness. International students bring valuable skills to American employers, contribute to local economies, and support job creation. Protecting OPT helps ensure that the United States continues to attract talented students from around the world and benefit from their contributions. Learn more about the economic contributions of international students (NAFSA).

Research highlights the economic benefits of OPT and provides little evidence that the program negatively affects American workers.

Innovation and wages: A 2023 Niskanen Center analysis found that international STEM students contribute to innovation and higher average earnings without reducing employment opportunities or wages for U.S. workers.

Employment opportunities: A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy study found no evidence that STEM OPT participation reduces job opportunities for American workers.

Economic competitiveness: A 2018 Business Roundtable report warned that restricting OPT could harm the U.S. economy and result in job losses for American workers.

Economic contributions: According to NAFSA, international students and their families contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year.

OPT is particularly important to community colleges, which play a vital role in workforce development, career preparation, and expanding access to higher education. The program allows international students to apply their academic knowledge while gaining valuable professional experience with American employers. For community colleges, particularly those offering career and technical education programs, OPT helps strengthen relationships with local businesses, supports regional workforce needs, and makes their programs more attractive to international students. It also supports international student recruitment and institutional competitiveness by providing opportunities to connect classroom learning with professional experience. Restricting or eliminating OPT could weaken these opportunities and limit the contributions international students make to local economies and communities.

Protecting OPT is not simply about supporting international students. It is about strengthening the U.S. economy, supporting American employers, encouraging innovation, and preserving the country's global competitiveness. Maintaining OPT benefits students, educational institutions, employers, and the communities they serve.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) is an important component of the United States' ability to attract and retain international talent and maintain its global leadership in higher education, research, and innovation. By providing international students with opportunities to gain practical experience directly related to their academic fields, OPT contributes to the nation's economic competitiveness and workforce development. International students bring valuable knowledge, skills, and perspectives to American employers, stimulate economic activity, and support job creation. Preserving OPT is therefore essential to sustaining the United States' attractiveness as a destination for international education and maximizing the economic and societal contributions of international students. Additional information on these contributions is available in NAFSA's report on global talent and U.S. competitiveness.

Existing research provides substantial evidence of the economic benefits associated with OPT, while offering little support for concerns that the program adversely affects employment opportunities or wages for American workers.

Innovation and wages: A 2023 analysis by the Niskanen Center found that international students in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contribute to innovation and higher average earnings without negatively affecting employment opportunities or wages for U.S. workers.

Employment opportunities: A 2019 study by the National Foundation for American Policy found no evidence that participation in STEM OPT reduces employment opportunities for American workers.

Economic competitiveness: A 2018 report by the Business Roundtable projected that restrictions on OPT could have significant adverse consequences for the U.S. economy, including employment losses among American workers.

The program enables international students to apply their academic knowledge in professional settings, thereby strengthening the connection between education and employment. For community colleges, particularly those offering career and technical education programs, OPT provides opportunities to deepen partnerships with local employers, respond to regional workforce needs, and enhance the appeal of their academic programs to prospective international students. Furthermore, the availability of practical training opportunities contributes to international student recruitment and institutional competitiveness by offering a meaningful connection between academic preparation and professional development. Restrictions on OPT could diminish these opportunities, potentially weakening community colleges' capacity to attract international students and limiting their contributions to regional economic development.

Preserving OPT should therefore be viewed not solely as a matter of supporting international students, but as a broader economic and educational priority. The program contributes to workforce development, strengthens the competitiveness of American higher education, supports innovation, and facilitates mutually beneficial relationships among students, educational institutions, employers, and local communities. Maintaining OPT is consistent with the nation's long-term interests in economic growth, educational excellence, and global competitiveness.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. It would require schools to pay $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, up to $100,000 per student. DHS estimates the fees at $8.4–16.5 billion a year, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion.

The charge is a tax that only Congress may impose. Under the Constitution, Congress alone has the taxing power. A charge that is not tied to the cost of a government service, raises general revenue, and is meant to discourage an activity is a tax (NCTA v. United States, 1974). DHS set the amount to match H-1B fees, not to cover any cost of its own. INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" language does not authorize fees. When Congress wanted student or visa fees, it created them by statute, as with the SEVIS fee and the H-1B/L Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee. In Learning Resources v. Trump (2026), the Supreme Court held that a power to regulate does not include a power to tax.

The revenue does not fund anti-fraud work. The fees would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302), and DHS admits ICE would not keep or use them. No site visits, audits or investigations would be funded. DHS rejected expanding enforcement because a fee needs "little new enforcement spending." The only anti-fraud effect is pricing honest students out of OPT along with dishonest ones. That use of the money is inconsistent with the rule's stated purpose.

Employers commit the fraud, but schools and students pay. DHS's own examples involve employers and brokers: "highly suspect employers," shell companies, staged worksites, and an employer claiming 150 student workers when only one was present. Schools are not accused of wrongdoing, yet they pay, and they may pass the cost to honest students. Fraudulent employers pay nothing. Even DHS's 10,000-student figure, which describes only "suspect" employers, is about 3.5% of roughly 290,000 OPT participants.

Universities and states would suffer heavy losses. 2,478 schools would be affected, 1,044 of them public institutions of states. In the transition year, 116 small schools would face costs above 20% of revenue. Yet DHS claims no substantial direct effect on states and did not consult state officials under the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024–25 (NAFSA).

Alternatives were not fully considered, and the comment period is too short. DHS did not seriously analyze targeted options: E-Verify for all OPT employers, matching OPT records against IRS and SSA wage data, risk-based site visits, penalties and debarment for fraudulent employers, or asking Congress for a modest dedicated fee. Executive Order 13563 calls for comment periods of generally at least 60 days. DHS gave 60 days for paperwork comments but only 30 days for a rule with $12.4 billion in yearly transfers.

The loss calculation is circular. DHS measures the lost value of OPT using the fees schools do not pay ($8.07–8.92 billion a year). The loss figure is therefore set by DHS's own price: a lower fee would show a smaller "loss" even if the same students lost the same jobs. DHS also calls fees that are paid costless "transfers" and fees that are not paid real "costs." Real losses are never measured: lost wages, tax revenue, tuition, employer output and local jobs.

Potential losses if finalized: up to $100,000 per student; $12.4 billion a year in fees; $90.6–109.4 billion over 10 years; and $29.0–35.1 billion in real costs over 10 years by DHS's own estimate. About 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants would be exposed. NAFSA already projects a $3.4 billion loss and 39,000 lost jobs from falling enrollment in fall 2026, and this fee would deepen that decline. I’m writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees, and to ask DHS to withdraw the rule.

A fee at this level doesn’t separate bad actors from legitimate students. It prices out nearly everyone. DHS’s own analysis assumes schools may stop recommending most non-STEM students entirely, which suggests the practical effect is to shrink the program, not to make it more honest.

2. Better-targeted tools exist, and DHS acknowledges them.
Section IV.C notes that DHS considered extending STEM OPT safeguards, such as training plans, employer reporting and site visits, to all OPT. Those measures go after the specific problems the rule describes: shell companies, staged worksites and phantom employers. DHS should strengthen enforcement against the employers committing fraud rather than placing a $70,000 cost on every student and school.

3. The money wouldn’t fund anti-fraud work.
Section IV.C states the fees would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP or enforcement. If the goal is fighting fraud, it’s hard to see how a fee that adds no investigative capacity serves that goal. The amount also appears tied to H-1B fees rather than to any cost of administering OPT, which raises the question of whether a charge this size is within DHS’s authority under INA 214(a) to set “time and conditions” of admission. You might want to consider whether a fee functioning mainly as a deterrent or revenue measure needs authorization from Congress.

4. The costs are very large by DHS’s own estimate (Section VII.A).
DHS projects annualized costs of about $4.1 billion and 10-year costs of up to $69.9 billion in its high scenario. Those costs fall on universities, employers and communities, and the proposal offers little quantified benefit in return. Universities rely on international students for tuition and research, and employers rely on OPT graduates in fields where they compete globally for talent. Other countries actively recruit these same students, and a fee of this size would push many of them elsewhere.

5. The reliance analysis understates the harm to current students (Section VI).
Many students now enrolled chose a U.S. school, took on significant costs, and planned their careers with OPT as part of their education. The rule would apply to anyone who hasn’t yet received a DSO recommendation, including students partway through their degrees. At a minimum, DHS should exempt all students enrolled before the final rule takes effect.

6. Small institutions would be hit hardest.
DHS estimates 56 percent of affected institutions are small entities. Many can’t absorb a $70,000 per-student cost and would likely stop offering OPT altogether, putting them at a disadvantage in recruiting international students.

7. The comment period is too short.
This is an economically significant rule with billions in projected costs, yet the public has only about 30 days to respond. DHS should extend the comment period to at least 60 days.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers instead.

To mitigate this litigation risk while still achieving policy objectives, I recommend adjusting the fee structure to a more legally defensible threshold—specifically $30,000 for the initial OPT period and $30,000 for the STEM extension.

A calibrated pricing model of this magnitude offers two main advantages:

Reduces Institutional Resistance: It lowers the legal exposure associated with accusations of arbitrary and capricious rulemaking, making it less likely to trigger coordinated injunctions from educational advocacy groups.

Maintains Deterrence and Filtering: A total commitment of $60,000 remains a significant financial threshold that will naturally discourage marginal applicants, ensuring only high-intent candidates proceed.

Adjusting the fee to this range balances regulatory goals with practical enforceability and legal resilience.

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. Immigration policy should advance American interests. This proposal risks undermining those interests by discouraging skilled graduates from contributing to the U.S. economy and creating financial barriers for institutions and employers.

First, the proposed fees could weaken the United States’ ability to retain internationally trained talent. American universities attract students from around the world and provide advanced scientific, technical, and professional education. Making legitimate practical training prohibitively expensive could encourage graduates to pursue opportunities elsewhere. The United States could consequently lose the benefits of their research, entrepreneurship, and professional contributions while competing economies gain them.

Second, the financial burden could fall disproportionately on smaller institutions, startups, and employers with limited resources. Although schools would be responsible for payment, the proposal acknowledges that costs could be passed to students or employers. Larger organizations may be better positioned to absorb these expenses, while smaller organizations could lose access to qualified candidates regardless of the educational value or legitimacy of the training opportunity. DHS should assess whether the proposed fees would favor financial capacity over merit and compliance.

Third, restricting access to OPT could reduce potential economic contributions from participating graduates. Their employment can support consumer spending, tax revenues, research, and business development. DHS should evaluate these potential losses alongside its asserted benefits, including whether reduced participation would actually improve outcomes for American workers or instead constrain productive activity.

Protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud are legitimate objectives. However, a substantial financial barrier does not reliably distinguish compliant training from abuse. DHS should compare the proposal with targeted enforcement, employer accountability, and measures addressing demonstrated misconduct.

American competitiveness benefits from an environment where qualified people can develop skills, conduct research, and contribute through lawful employment. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate, evidence-based measures that protect workers while preserving access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw it in its current form.

1. Disproportionate financial burden

The proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation could create substantial financial barriers for educational institutions, employers, and eligible international students. International students already pay significant tuition, housing, insurance, and living expenses. Universities may be unable to absorb these fees and could pass costs to students or employers, or stop supporting OPT recommendations altogether.

DHS should explain how these specific amounts were calculated and demonstrate their connection to documented administrative and enforcement costs.

2. Impact on students and employers

Optional Practical Training allows eligible F-1 students to gain practical experience related to their academic fields. An exceptionally high institutional fee could discourage universities from supporting eligible graduates and employers from hiring them. This could make access to professional opportunities depend more on an institution's financial resources than on a student's qualifications and merit.

Students who have already invested substantial resources in U.S. education could also face unexpected uncertainty about their post-graduation plans.

3. Supporting economic data

According to ICE's *2024 SEVIS by the Numbers* report, 194,554 students with OPT employment authorization who reported working for an employer were recorded in 2024, a 21.1% increase from 2023.

Sources:

https://www.nafsa.org/fall-2025-international-student-enrollment-snapshot-economic-impact

Before finalizing this proposal, DHS should publish a detailed cost justification, assess the likely effects on universities, students, small businesses, and employers, estimate how costs might be passed on, and compare the proposal with less burdensome alternatives. Federal immigration fees exist to recover what it costs the government to process a request. Congress said so in 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m), and the general user-fee statute, 31 U.S.C. § 9701, says much the same. Nothing about reviewing an OPT application costs $70,000. DHS’s justification gives the game away. The agency does not say the fee reimburses a service. It says the financial cost would deter schools from recommending students with questionable qualifications. That is a penalty, and a price designed to discourage participation is not a fee. When revenue is the effect, the picture is clearer still. One analysis estimates the rule could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually. A charge of that size, detached from any cost of service, is a tax.

The Constitution gives the power to tax to Congress alone, and the Supreme Court has been careful to keep agencies from quietly claiming it. In National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States and Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., the Court drew the line between a charge for a particular benefit, which an agency may set, and a general revenue measure, which it may not. DHS points to no clear statement from Congress authorizing a multibillion-dollar levy on student work authorization. Without one, the rule fails.

Even if the statute were ambiguous, the question is too big to answer by implication. When an agency claims power of vast economic and political significance, the Supreme Court demands clear authorization from Congress. West Virginia v. EPA and Biden v. Nebraska say so plainly. And after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, courts no longer defer to an agency’s convenient reading of a vague statute. DHS leans on the broad language in 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1), which lets it set conditions on nonimmigrant admission. But a general power to set conditions is not a power to charge $70,000 for a benefit the program has long offered at modest cost.

The rule also fails basic reasoned decision-making. The APA requires agencies to explain why a rule fits the problem it claims to solve. DHS cites a few enforcement incidents, such as the arrest of 15 international students in 2020. A flat charge on every student does nothing to find or punish those cases. Fraud calls for audits, investigations, and school-level accountability. It does not call for a price that most students and many schools cannot pay. DHS does not seriously consider those alternatives. The rule also ignores the people who relied on the system as it stood. Students chose American universities, paid tuition, and planned careers on the understanding that OPT was available. DHS v. Regents requires agencies to weigh that kind of reliance before changing course. And the costs are real. A survey by the Institute for Progress found 80% fewer students said they would likely try to stay if the fees were implemented. DHS itself acknowledges that schools could pass the charge on to students, to all students, or to employers. So a fee billed to schools is, in practice, a fee billed to the students and the employers who want them.

This is not only about international students. Their tuition funds scholarships and programs that American students use. Their work fills roles that American employers struggle to fill. A rule that makes the United States a worse place to study will send the next generation of engineers, designers, and scientists to Canada, Britain, and Australia.

DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it believes OPT needs more oversight, it can tighten enforcement, require better school reporting, and set any fee at a level that reflects the actual cost of the service. It should not price access out of reach and call the result integrity.

In fairness to the other side, DHS and supporters of the rule argue that OPT has been misused and that existing oversight is weak, and that schools should bear more responsibility for who they recommend. Some also argue that OPT competes with American workers, and that the agency’s broad authority over F-1 conditions reaches this kind of charge. The government will lean on the D.C. Circuit’s decision in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, which upheld OPT itself as within DHS’s authority, to argue that the agency has wide latitude to set the program’s terms. Courts have not yet resolved whether that latitude includes a fee of this size.

As a U.S. citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and reconsider its potentially devastating long-term consequences for American innovation, economic competitiveness, and national strength.

1. Excessive Fees Will Reduce Participation and Undermine Revenue Projections

DHS estimates that the proposed fees could generate billions annually. However, these projections raise a fundamental economic concern: increasing a fee does not necessarily increase total revenue when the fee becomes so expensive that people can no longer afford to participate.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about declining participation and includes a reduced-participation scenario. However, it does not address the possibility that the overwhelming financial burden will cause many STEM students and their institutions to abandon OPT altogether.

If participation declines far more sharply than DHS anticipates, actual fee collections could fall substantially below projections. The government would sacrifice an enormous amount of potential economic activity, innovation, and future tax revenue without necessarily achieving its projected financial returns.

2. America Cannot Remain Number One Without Attracting the World's Best Talent

The U.S. has ~316 million citizens. Our citizens are the foundation of America's strength. But in an increasingly competitive world, relying exclusively on domestic talent would limit our potential.

America's greatest advantage has never been simply its population. It has been its ability to attract exceptional minds from around the world, give them opportunities, and transform their ideas into breakthroughs that benefit the entire country.

According to the National Science Board's State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026, foreign-born workers accounted for 46% of U.S. science and engineering workers with doctoral degrees in 2023. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned 61% of the doctoral degrees awarded by American institutions in computer and information sciences. These figures demonstrate how deeply international talent contributes to America's technological leadership.

We are competing with Canada, Europe, China for the same brilliant minds. If we make it financially impossible for talented graduates to build their careers here, those individuals will not simply disappear. They will take their knowledge, ambition, and innovations elsewhere.

3. We Are Educating Tomorrow's Innovators Only to Send Them to Our Competitors

The most concerning part is that OPT participants are already being educated and trained in the U.S. These students have chosen American universities, learned from American professors, conducted research in American laboratories, and become familiar with American industries and institutions. They represent an extraordinary opportunity for the future of our country.

Why would we invest years in developing this talent, only to create a financial barrier that encourages graduates to take their skills to competing nations?

The consequences may not be immediately visible. But 10 or 20 years from now, the United States could face the enormous cost of losing researchers who might have developed groundbreaking technologies. The next generation of breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, semiconductor manufacturing, advanced computing, and medicine will help determine which countries lead the world.

We cannot afford policies that encourage the world's best minds to develop those breakthroughs outside the United States.

4. Protect American Workers Through Targeted Enforcement

I fully support protecting American workers, enforcing immigration laws, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of our immigration system. However, DHS should prioritize investigating actual immigration violations and documented fraud rather than imposing financial barriers on international students who have pursued legitimate educational and professional opportunities in the United States. Protecting American workers and attracting outstanding international talent are not mutually exclusive objectives. 

5. America's Future Must Come Before Short-Term Revenue

Ultimately, the issue is much larger than OPT fees or projected government revenue. It is about whether the United States intends to remain the world's leading destination for innovation, entrepreneurship, and technological advancement. We should not sacrifice our long-term national competitiveness for a speculative short-term financial return.

Every talented individual we push away represents an opportunity that another country may gain. Over the next two decades, the cumulative cost of losing those opportunities could be far greater than any fee revenue collected today. 

We want the United States to remain number one. We want our companies to lead, our universities to excel, our economy to grow, and our country to remain strong. Achieving those goals requires the best talent in the world.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.

Clinical neuropsychology requires extensive specialized training, including two-year postdoctoral fellowships following doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled, competitive neuropsychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates.

These consequences extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning and linguistic/cultural considerations that strengthen neuropsychological assessment, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and limit the availability of clinical-researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S.'s diverse population.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

I am writing to oppose DHS's proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. The fee is identical for every school, and that is exactly why it will hit different schools so differently. DHS itself counted 2,478 institutions with students on OPT between 2022 and 2024 — 194,554 students starting OPT and 95,384 starting STEM OPT in 2024 alone. Treat all 2,478 schools as interchangeable payers of $70,000 per recommendation, and the rule will quietly sort them into survivors and casualties.

A wealthy research university with an endowment of $2 million per student can absorb the fee or ration recommendations at the margins and keep its OPT program largely intact. Now consider a community college or a small regional school whose endowment per student is measured in the low thousands — or nothing at all. Recommending OPT for fifty graduates costs $3.5 million: more than the entire budget of the international office that runs the program, and money no mid-year tuition increase can produce. These schools do not have a margin to absorb the cost; they face a binary choice, and the rational answer is to stop recommending OPT.

The predictable result is concentration. International students will be herded toward the few dozen richest campuses, while the schools that depend most on international enrollment to keep their doors open — regional public universities, liberal arts colleges, schools in college towns where foreign students sustain local housing and retail — will be priced out of the program. DHS's own concession that some schools would "simply stop recommending OPT" will happen first where the budget is thinnest.

Inside those schools, the Designated School Official becomes a rationing officer. With fees unaffordable for every student, which twenty get recommended this year and which two hundred are turned away? No criterion can make that choice fair: students in revenue-generating STEM programs will be favored over students in the humanities; students who can self-pay over those who cannot. A federal training program becomes an auction, rigged toward the already-advantaged.

International students already pay full tuition, receive no federal aid, and subsidize American students at many of these institutions. A uniform fee that wealthy schools can shrug off and small schools cannot is not neutral policy — it is a transfer of opportunity from modest schools to elite ones, paid for by the students who trusted the program most. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. While protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud are important national priorities, these fees are excessive, disproportionate, and likely to harm American universities, scientific research, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

1. Financial Burden on American Universities

Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 per student before recommending OPT would impose an extraordinary financial burden, particularly on smaller universities, public institutions, and research programs with limited funding. Many universities and academic laboratories cannot afford these costs. As a result, qualified graduates could lose access to legitimate practical training regardless of their academic achievements or compliance with immigration laws.

This policy would financially penalize American educational institutions without necessarily addressing the underlying causes of OPT fraud.

2. Harm to Scientific Research and Innovation

The United States has maintained global leadership in biotechnology, genomics, medicine, engineering, artificial intelligence, and other scientific fields partly by attracting talented students and researchers from around the world.

International graduates contribute to research laboratories, biomedical discoveries, technological development, and scientific collaboration. Restricting their access to practical training could disrupt research projects, reduce scientific productivity, and discourage talented individuals from pursuing advanced education in the United States.

Such outcomes could weaken American research institutions and benefit competing countries seeking to attract highly trained scientists.

3. Fraud Prevention Through Targeted Enforcement

I support DHS efforts to investigate fraudulent employers, fictitious employment arrangements, and institutions that abuse immigration regulations. However, imposing exceptionally high fees on all legitimate OPT participants does not effectively distinguish fraudulent activity from lawful training.

A better approach would involve stronger employer verification, risk-based inspections, improved reporting requirements, and meaningful penalties against organizations engaged in fraud.

Targeted enforcement would protect the integrity of the immigration system without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational opportunities.

4. Protecting American Workers Through Evidence-Based Policies

Protecting American jobs and fair wages is essential. However, DHS should demonstrate that the proposed fees would actually improve employment opportunities for U.S. citizens rather than simply impose additional financial burdens on American institutions.

The economic effects of OPT may vary considerably across industries and occupations. Specialized scientific research positions, for example, should not automatically be treated the same as employment arrangements associated with documented program abuse.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the proposed fees' effects on domestic employment, university finances, research productivity, and economic growth.

5. Disproportionate Fees and Long-Term Economic Consequences

The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees appear disproportionate to the administrative and oversight activities associated with OPT. DHS should provide a transparent, evidence-based explanation for these specific amounts and evaluate whether less burdensome alternatives could achieve the same regulatory objectives.

These fees could also discourage international enrollment at American universities, reduce research collaboration, and encourage highly trained graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries.

Rather than strengthening American competitiveness, the proposal risks undermining institutions that contribute to scientific progress, technological innovation, and economic development.

Conclusion:

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

I support strong immigration enforcement, protection of American workers, and meaningful measures against fraud. However, these objectives should be achieved through targeted oversight, employer verification, appropriate penalties, and proportionate regulations rather than excessive financial barriers.

America's economic strength depends not only on protecting its workforce but also on maintaining world-class universities, encouraging scientific innovation, and attracting talented researchers.

Thank you for considering this public comment.

I strongly oppose this proposed policy for the following 3 reasons.

International students typically pay more than three times the tuition of local resident students, serving as a vital financial pillar for American universities. If policies restrict international enrollment, institutions will inevitably face severe budget deficits. To make up for this shortfall, universities will have no choice but to raise tuition fees for domestic students. Far from helping local families, such restrictions will only make higher education even more expensive and burdensome for American citizens.

2. Misconceptions Regarding Job Market Competition
The Optional Practical Training (OPT) program already enforces exceptionally strict limitations, preventing international graduates from posing a substantial threat to local workers:

-Strict Duration Limits: Non-STEM graduates receive only a 1-year work authorization, and STEM graduates are capped at 3 years.
-Rigid Employment Requirements: OPT authorization requires individuals to work strictly in roles directly related to their major, with employers willing to hire under short-term authorization constraints.
-Low H-1B Lottery Selection Rates: With H-1B lottery selection rates hovering around just 30%, the vast majority of international graduates who do not secure a visa are ultimately forced to leave the U.S. labor market.

Given these formidable barriers, average international graduates do not engage in unfair or substantial competition with domestic workers.

3. Economic Value and Net Fiscal Contributions of High-Skilled Immigrants
Those who manage to navigate these stringent hurdles, secure long-term employment, and transition from OPT to H-1B and eventually permanent residency represent an exceptionally elite group. Their ability to overcome these obstacles proves their extraordinary capabilities and competitiveness.

-High Economic Value: Retaining these top-tier talents fuels innovation and generates broader economic growth for the United States.
-Net Fiscal Benefit: As highly educated, high-earning professionals, they do not burden public welfare systems—such as unemployment benefits or Medicaid. Instead, their substantial tax contributions provide significant net revenue for local, state, and federal governments.

Ultimately, retaining these qualified individuals yields far more economic benefits than costs for the United States.
