Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (FR Doc. 2026-20660)

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal for three reasons.

1. The proposal is not supported by evidence.

DHS's central evidence is an ICE finding that more than 10,000 students claimed to work for "highly suspect" employers.  The only citation for this figure is a YouTube video of a press conference.  No report, data, or methodology is provided.  The figure is also inconsistent: the preamble describes 10,000 students, while footnote 56 describes 10,000 suspected employers.  DHS should publish the underlying investigation, define "highly suspect," and state how many cases have led to charges, convictions, or status terminations.  In 2020, DHS estimated that about 1,100 of 220,000 OPT permits involved fraud, roughly half a percent.  DHS should provide a current fraud rate and explain why a $70,000 charge on every OPT student is proportionate to it.

The proposal's own data contradicts its labor-market claims.  The preamble states that 165,524 students were on STEM OPT in 2024, "nearly double" the annual H-1B cap.  Yet Table 2 reports 95,384, and DHS uses that lower figure throughout its cost analysis.  At 95,384, STEM OPT participation is only modestly above the 85,000 H-1B limit.  Table 2 also undercuts the claim of "exponential" growth: participation fell every year from 2017 to 2021, and the 2024 figure is about 27 percent above the 2017 level.

Finally, DHS's accounting statement (Table 1) lists monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" and effects on wages and economic growth as "N/A."  A proposal justified as protecting American workers offers no estimate of its effect on their wages, and it quantifies no benefit against annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion.

2. Better options exist to stop fraud.

DHS describes fraud driven by shell companies and employer networks, yet the fee falls on schools and students who have done nothing wrong.  It does not target the employers DHS says it has already identified.  More focused alternatives include:

- Requiring OPT employers to submit proof of a legitimate business, such as tax records or a lease, which DHS admits it does not currently collect
- Requiring E-Verify enrollment for all OPT employers, not only STEM OPT employers
- Prioritizing site visits and enforcement at the top 25 employers ICE has already flagged
- Expanding the DSO fraud training SEVP launched in November 2025

DHS rejected these options in part because a fee is faster and requires fewer government resources.  Administrative convenience is not evidence that a fee will reduce fraud more effectively.

3. The proposal will harm the US economy.

DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion and up to $82 billion over ten years.  Under its own low scenario (Table 3), roughly 106,000 students each year would lose access to OPT as schools stop recommending non-STEM students.  Even this estimate is incomplete.  Table 9 assumes each lost OPT placement is worth no more than the fee, and DHS acknowledges the true cost may be higher.  The analysis does not measure lost wages, tax revenue, local spending, or tuition revenue.

Small institutions would be hit hardest.  All 1,294 private nonprofit colleges with OPT students qualify as small entities, and their average fee bill in the first year would be about $7.3 million.  In that year, 116 small institutions would face costs above 20 percent of their annual revenue.

DHS also fails to consider the shrinking pipeline of US college graduates.  According to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education (WICHE), the number of US high school graduates peaked in 2025 and is projected to fall 13 percent by 2041, with the Northeast and Midwest already seeing declines.  International graduates on OPT help employers fill roles in fields and regions where domestic talent is limited.  Restricting OPT just as the domestic pipeline begins to shrink risks leaving employers short of qualified workers.

International students choose where to study based in part on post-study work opportunities.  The UK, Canada, and Australia all offer post-study work routes with no comparable charge.  This proposal would push talented students toward those countries, reducing tuition revenue, local spending, and the skilled graduates US employers depend on.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue enforcement aimed at fraudulent employers instead.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

I am an F-1 international student pursuing a STEM degree at a U.S. university. I entered the United States expecting to participate in the existing practical training framework after completing my education. The proposed fees would fundamentally change that framework and could make OPT inaccessible to many legitimate students.

First, DHS has not adequately demonstrated that a $70,000 fee is reasonably connected to its stated objectives of combating fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and strengthening OPT integrity. If the concern is fraudulent employers, nonexistent employment, or violations of OPT requirements, enforcement should target those specific violations. Imposing a $70,000 burden on every legitimate student seeking OPT does not distinguish compliant students from those engaging in fraud.

The proposed amount is also extraordinarily large compared with the nature of OPT administration. A $70,000 charge is not merely an administrative fee; it can exceed a student’s annual tuition and living expenses. DHS should explain how this amount was calculated and why substantially less burdensome enforcement mechanisms would be insufficient.

Although the proposed payment obligation is placed on educational institutions, DHS acknowledges that schools may recover the cost from students, employers, or other sources. Therefore, calling it a university fee does not eliminate its economic effect on students. Universities could pass the cost to students, increase other charges, reduce OPT support, or reconsider whether they can continue recommending students for OPT.

The proposal could exclude legitimate students based primarily on their ability to pay rather than their compliance with immigration law. A student who has never violated an OPT requirement could lose access to practical training simply because the student, employer, or university cannot absorb such a large cost.

The proposal also risks harming the competitiveness of U.S. higher education. International students make educational decisions years before becoming eligible for OPT. A potential $70,000 charge could cause prospective students to choose universities in countries with more predictable post-graduation pathways. This could reduce international STEM enrollment and negatively affect U.S. research institutions and employers.

DHS should also consider the reliance interests of students already enrolled in U.S. degree programs. International students make multi-year financial and educational commitments based on the immigration framework available when they begin their programs. They cannot reasonably restructure years of education shortly before graduation because practical training has suddenly become tens of thousands of dollars more expensive.

If additional enforcement is necessary, DHS has more targeted alternatives. It could increase employer verification, conduct risk-based audits, impose stronger penalties for fraudulent employers and intentional violations, require additional documentation for high-risk cases, and increase oversight of institutions with unusually high violation rates. These measures would address misconduct without imposing an extraordinary cost on every compliant student.

I am also concerned about applying the proposed fees when a student advances to a higher educational level. Requiring another large fee when a student progresses from a bachelor’s degree to a master’s or doctoral program could discourage international students from pursuing advanced STEM education in the United States. These students can become researchers, teaching assistants, and contributors to U.S. universities and scientific institutions.

If DHS determines that an OPT fee is necessary, I respectfully request a substantially lower, evidence-based amount proportionate to actual administrative and enforcement costs. DHS should also demonstrate why less burdensome alternatives cannot achieve the same objectives.

Most importantly, DHS should evaluate who will actually bear the economic burden. Whether the payment is formally assigned to a university is less important than its real-world effect on students, employers, universities, and OPT participation. A policy that makes lawful practical training financially inaccessible to compliant students risks undermining U.S. educational and workforce interests.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. At minimum, I urge DHS to substantially reduce the amounts and adopt targeted enforcement measures addressing actual violations rather than imposing an extraordinary financial barrier on legitimate OPT participants.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees. The proposal departs from the judgments DHS made in the 2016 STEM OPT rule (81 FR 13040) and does not identify which of those judgments were wrong or what evidence shows it.

1. The standard
An agency changing course must acknowledge the change and give good reasons. More detailed justification is required when the new policy rests on factual findings that contradict those behind the old one, or when the old policy created serious reliance. FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009). Both conditions apply here.

2. What DHS decided in 2016
In 2016 DHS extended STEM OPT to 24 months and added duties for schools, students and employers. As the NPRM itself recounts, DHS based that rule on "the widely accepted proposition that educational and cultural exchange, a strong post-secondary education system, and a focus on STEM innovation are, on the whole, positive contributors to the U.S. economy and U.S. workers and in the overall national interest." The D.C. Circuit upheld the 2016 rule. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022). The NPRM never says that proposition is false. It says DHS "believes" the programs have "widely drifted." The proposed rule keeps STEM OPT and its 24 months and only puts a price on them.

3. Growth is the only new fact offered, and it is not comparable
DHS says participation "far surpassed" its 2016 estimate that eligible students could "be almost 50,000 in year one and grow to approximately 92,000 in year 10," and cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024. The NPRM does not say whether the two figures measure the same thing. A 24-month program holds two years of entrants at once. DHS's own cost analysis uses 95,384 STEM OPT participants for 2024. And the 2016 rule set no cap. Growth in a program DHS found beneficial is a harm only if the added participants are disproportionately fraudulent. The NPRM gives no fraud rate per participant for any year.

4. The 2016 safeguards were never tested
The STEM OPT rules as revised in 2016 set the protections now in force: the Form I-983 training plan, employer attestations that the student will not replace a U.S. worker and will be paid commensurately, E-Verify, reporting duties, student self-evaluations, and DHS site visits. The NPRM says these "have not sufficiently addressed the shortfalls" and that "Experience with STEM OPT" shows procedural requirements "do not eliminate the risk." It reports no data on that experience: no count of site visits since 2016 and no violation rate. The fraud DHS does describe was found by HSI site visits at STEM OPT worksites, which is the 2016 tool working. The gap DHS names is volume: it "does not generally verify the employer attestations unless and until there is a site visit." That is a choice about enforcement resources. It is not evidence that the 2016 design failed.

5. The labor-market evidence does not address the 2016 period
DHS notes that the 2016 rule had no quantified estimate of harm to U.S. workers. The NPRM quantifies none either. Its benefits section rests on what DHS "believes" and what "could" or "may" happen. Its wage evidence is a 2017 study of 2001 conditions, quoted from a proclamation. It says nothing about the years since 2016. The FICA exemption DHS cites is set by the tax code and predates the 2016 rule, so it is not a changed circumstance.

6. The fee misses the concern DHS states
The NPRM's labor-market concern is STEM: computer science unemployment and the foreign share of STEM jobs. Yet DHS's low scenario assumes schools would stop paying for non-STEM students and keep paying for STEM students, because $100,000 buys up to three years. By DHS's own model, the fee falls hardest on the group its labor rationale does not concern. The 2016 rule placed duties on employers, who control wages and training. The fee charges schools instead.

7. Reliance on the 2016 rule
Schools, employers and students have built programs, training plans and hiring around the 24-month framework for a decade. That is the second Fox trigger. The court in Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), found DHS likely acted arbitrarily in the companion Duration of Status rule, citing "statements of 'belief' without supporting reasoning." The same pattern appears here.

8. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. Any re-proposal should:
(a) identify each 2016 finding DHS now rejects and the evidence for rejecting it;
(b) publish STEM OPT compliance data since 2016: site visits, findings, and I-983 violations;
(c) compare the 2016 projection and current participation on the same basis;
(d) evaluate enforcing the existing 2016 safeguards before adding any fee; and
(e) explain how a fee expected to cut mainly non-STEM OPT serves a STEM labor-market goal.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (comments on Sections IV.A, IV.B, and IV.C)

I am a computer science PhD student at a U.S. university, graduating soon, with research expertise in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

1. The fee would push out the very talent the rule says it wants to keep (Section IV.C). DHS states that the fee would lead schools to recommend only "the most promising students." In practice, a $70,000 fee per student, paid before a DSO can even enter a recommendation, is more than a typical PhD stipend for an entire year. Most universities cannot pay this for every graduate, and passing it on to students would put OPT out of reach for most PhD graduates regardless of merit. The fee screens for ability to pay, not for talent or legitimacy.

2. It would weaken U.S. capacity in AI safety and cybersecurity. After graduation, I hope to work in the United States on preventing the misuse of AI systems and strengthening cybersecurity. These are national-security priorities where the U.S. needs more experts, not fewer. OPT is the practical bridge that allows PhD graduates like me to begin this work while longer-term visa processes run their course. Without it, I and many of my peers would have to take our U.S.-trained expertise to other countries, including countries that compete with the U.S. in AI and cyber capabilities.

3. It wastes the investment already made in our training. A U.S. PhD typically takes five or more years and is frequently supported by U.S. research funding. Making it prohibitively expensive for graduates to apply that training in the U.S. means other countries capture the return on that investment.

4. The fee does not target the fraud the NPRM describes (Section IV.A). The examples cited involve shell companies, nonexistent worksites, and fraudulent employers. A flat fee charged to universities does nothing to identify those employers; it mainly burdens legitimate students and schools. Targeted measures would address the problem directly: verifying employers and Form I-983 training plans, more site visits to high-risk employers, and penalties for employers and schools that abuse the program.

5. OPT for new graduates is not a substitute for H-1B (Section IV.B). Recent PhD graduates in specialized fields like AI security are not low-wage labor displacing U.S. workers; we help build the research and security capabilities that create U.S. jobs.

Requested action: I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. At a minimum, DHS should exempt graduates of advanced-degree STEM programs, or limit any fee to the actual cost of administering and overseeing OPT, and rely on targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers instead.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. While protecting American workers and preventing immigration fraud are important national priorities, these fees are excessive, disproportionate, and likely to harm American universities, scientific research, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

1.⁠ ⁠Financial Burden on American Universities

Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 per student before recommending OPT would impose an extraordinary financial burden, particularly on smaller universities, public institutions, and research programs with limited funding. Many universities and academic laboratories cannot afford these costs. As a result, qualified graduates could lose access to legitimate practical training regardless of their academic achievements or compliance with immigration laws.

This policy would financially penalize American educational institutions without necessarily addressing the underlying causes of OPT fraud.

2.⁠ ⁠Harm to Scientific Research and Innovation

The United States has maintained global leadership in biotechnology, genomics, medicine, engineering, artificial intelligence, and other scientific fields partly by attracting talented students and researchers from around the world.

International graduates contribute to research laboratories, biomedical discoveries, technological development, and scientific collaboration. Restricting their access to practical training could disrupt research projects, reduce scientific productivity, and discourage talented individuals from pursuing advanced education in the United States.

Such outcomes could weaken American research institutions and benefit competing countries seeking to attract highly trained scientists.

3.⁠ ⁠Fraud Prevention Through Targeted Enforcement

I support DHS efforts to investigate fraudulent employers, fictitious employment arrangements, and institutions that abuse immigration regulations. However, imposing exceptionally high fees on all legitimate OPT participants does not effectively distinguish fraudulent activity from lawful training.

A better approach would involve stronger employer verification, risk-based inspections, improved reporting requirements, and meaningful penalties against organizations engaged in fraud.

Targeted enforcement would protect the integrity of the immigration system without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational opportunities.

4.⁠ ⁠Protecting American Workers Through Evidence-Based Policies

Protecting American jobs and fair wages is essential. However, DHS should demonstrate that the proposed fees would actually improve employment opportunities for U.S. citizens rather than simply impose additional financial burdens on American institutions.

The economic effects of OPT may vary considerably across industries and occupations. Specialized scientific research positions, for example, should not automatically be treated the same as employment arrangements associated with documented program abuse.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the proposed fees' effects on domestic employment, university finances, research productivity, and economic growth.

5.⁠ ⁠Disproportionate Fees and Long-Term Economic Consequences

The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees appear disproportionate to the administrative and oversight activities associated with OPT. DHS should provide a transparent, evidence-based explanation for these specific amounts and evaluate whether less burdensome alternatives could achieve the same regulatory objectives.

These fees could also discourage international enrollment at American universities, reduce research collaboration, and encourage highly trained graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries.

Rather than strengthening American competitiveness, the proposal risks undermining institutions that contribute to scientific progress, technological innovation, and economic development.

Conclusion:

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

I support strong immigration enforcement, protection of American workers, and meaningful measures against fraud. However, these objectives should be achieved through targeted oversight, employer verification, appropriate penalties, and proportionate regulations rather than excessive financial barriers.

America's economic strength depends not only on protecting its workforce but also on maintaining world-class universities, encouraging scientific innovation, and attracting talented researchers.

Thank you for considering this public comment.

I submit this comment as a professional in international education who advises F-1 students and works with the Designated School Officials (DSOs) who administer Optional Practical Training (OPT) under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)–(12). I share the Department's interest in OPT integrity: fraudulent employers, fabricated job letters, and "pay-to-stay" schemes harm legitimate students, the schools that enroll them, and U.S. workers alike. Schools and DSOs are the first to want those actors removed from the program.

The proposed rule, however, would not accomplish that goal. It would require each SEVP-certified school to pay the federal government $70,000 before a DSO may recommend any F-1 student for OPT for the first time, and $30,000 for every subsequent recommendation, including the 24-month STEM OPT extension (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). The Department estimates transfers of approximately $12.4 billion per year and $109.4 billion over ten years (91 FR 64579, 64583). The fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and would not fund SEVP, fraud investigation, or employer oversight (91 FR 64576).

I respectfully request that the Department:

1. Withdraw the proposed OPT fees in their entirety.
2. 3. Reject the alternative of charging the initial fee again at each educational level.
4. At a minimum, if any fee is retained: tie it to the documented cost of a specific service; exempt pre-completion OPT and STEM extensions; exempt current OPT participants and currently enrolled students; define "previously participated"; provide that cancellation, correction, or re-filing does not trigger a new fee; establish objective refund criteria with a decision timeframe and an appeal; and specify payment mechanics that do not jeopardize regulatory filing deadlines.

**Re: Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees**
**Docket ICEB-2026-0100**

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw these provisions. They would weaken U.S. competitiveness, discourage investment in American higher education, and unfairly burden students, universities, and employers.

**1. The United States risks losing talent when international recruitment is already weakening.**

The Institute of International Education's Fall 2025 Snapshot reported a 17% decline in new international enrollment among 828 responding U.S. institutions. NAFSA projected in August 2026 that further declines could mean up to 111,000 fewer international students, $3.4 billion in lost economic activity, and nearly 40,000 fewer jobs supported. These are projections, not confirmed losses.

Meanwhile, Germany projected approximately 420,000 international students for winter 2025–26, and France reported 443,500 in 2024–25, a 17% increase over five years. These figures do not establish a direct migration from U.S. to European institutions, but demonstrate that students have attractive alternatives. Access to practical experience after graduation is a meaningful factor in where they choose to study.

**2. International students support American jobs and educational opportunities.**

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 355,000 jobs during 2024–25.

International students also often pay higher tuition. Research by Kevin Shih (Journal of Public Economics, 2017) found that international students' tuition payments can subsidize additional domestic enrollment. Bound and colleagues (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020) documented how international tuition revenue helps public universities respond to funding constraints. Discouraging international enrollment threatens these benefits for American students.

DHS recognizes that universities may pass OPT fees to international students, employers, or their broader student populations. In other words, the proposed rule could raise costs for Americans while reducing the economic contributions of international students.

**3. OPT strengthens research, innovation, and STEM education.**

OPT connects American degrees to professional experience. Amuedo-Dorantes, Shih, and Xu (Economic Inquiry, 2023) found that earlier OPT reforms increased international bachelor's and master's enrollment. Research in AEA Papers and Proceedings (2026) reported that OPT expansions increased STEM degree completions by about 14–15%, including increases among domestic students.

These findings challenge the notion that opportunities for international graduates necessarily come at Americans' expense. Graduates contribute to laboratories, hospitals, universities, and businesses. Excessive fees risk sending talent trained in the United States—and its future innovations—elsewhere.

**4. The fees are disproportionate and inequitable.**

A $70,000 initial fee, potentially followed by $30,000 for additional OPT, is far beyond what many graduates or institutions can reasonably afford. Although formally imposed on universities, these costs could be passed on or prompt schools to stop offering OPT recommendations. Access would depend on financial resources rather than merit or eligibility. DHS's own low-participation scenario assumes schools would pay for STEM-eligible students only, potentially excluding non-STEM graduates from OPT.

Research, public health, and education graduates could be especially affected. I also oppose charging another $70,000 when a student advances to a higher degree.

**5. Address fraud directly rather than penalizing legitimate students.**

Fraud prevention matters, but an extraordinary fee is a blunt and counterproductive response. DHS should prioritize employer verification, targeted audits, stronger oversight of documented abuses, and penalties for violations. Before adopting sweeping barriers, DHS should fully evaluate effects on university budgets, enrollment, American student costs, employment, and research capacity.

American higher education has flourished by attracting talented people from around the world. International students are not merely beneficiaries; they are investors in universities, contributors to local economies, and participants in American innovation. The United States should protect this advantage, not price it out of reach.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and pursue targeted, proportionate measures against fraud.

Finding a job on top of that in this job market? University students should be allowed to be university students without any barriers.

I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. My comments address Sections III.A, IV.A-C, VI, and VII.A.

1. The rule exceeds DHS's statutory authority (Secs. III.A, IV.C).
INA section 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of nonimmigrant admission. A $70,000 to $100,000 per-student charge is not a condition of admission; it is a revenue measure. When Congress wants immigration fees, it says so, as in 8 U.S.C. 1356(m), which ties fees to the cost of services. This rule is not cost-based. DHS states the money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, that ICE cannot retain it, and that the amount was chosen to align with the H-1B fee, itself the subject of pending litigation. A charge unconnected to cost, projected to transfer roughly $109 billion over ten years, functions as a tax, and an agency cannot impose one without clear congressional authorization. See National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974). A change of this economic magnitude to a program in place since 1992 also raises major-questions concerns, and after Loper Bright, DHS's "reasonably related" theory gets no deference. The cited WashTech decision addressed whether DHS may allow OPT, not whether it may price it at $70,000.

2. The fee does not fit the problem DHS describes (Secs. IV.A, IV.C).
The fraud DHS documents involves shell employers and a minority of bad-actor schools. The fee falls uniformly on roughly 2,478 schools, including public universities and community colleges, regardless of employer or compliance history. DHS acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Operators who already sell "pay-to-stay" arrangements can do the same, so the deterrent is weak where it matters. The burden lands on legitimate students, who far outnumber the roughly 10,000 DHS flagged among hundreds of thousands of OPT participants. Targeted measures, such as decertifying bad schools, expanding employer verification, and cost-based site-visit funding, address the actual conduct.

3. DHS did not reasonably weigh alternatives (Sec. IV.C).
DHS rejected expanded reporting, training plans, and site visits mainly because a fee is quick and uniform. Administrative convenience is not a reasoned basis for a measure DHS itself expects to shrink participation sharply and warns could end the program. DHS also declined a small-institution exemption because 56 percent of institutions are small entities; that is a reason to study tiered or cost-based options, not to skip them. DHS's own model assumes schools would stop paying for non-STEM students, effectively ending OPT for non-STEM majors, a major policy change DHS neither acknowledges nor justifies.

4. The economic analysis cannot support the rule (Sec. VII.A).
DHS's annualized cost estimates range from $32 million to $8.2 billion, and DHS says it cannot confidently predict behavior. A range spanning more than two orders of magnitude cannot show that benefits justify costs, particularly when benefits are described mostly qualitatively. The evidence for U.S. worker displacement (aggregate unemployment figures, a proclamation, and a single study on 2001) does not show that OPT participants cause those outcomes. The FICA exemption DHS cites as an employer incentive is a tax-law issue a school-paid fee does not address. The analysis gives no weight to lost international tuition revenue, to employers and startups that depend on OPT talent, or to U.S. competitiveness in attracting STEM talent.

5. Reliance interests are dismissed (Sec. VI).
Students enrolled in multi-year programs, and the schools that recruited them, relied on OPT as an established feature of F-1 study. Calling that reliance speculative does not satisfy DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), which requires the agency to assess serious reliance interests and consider mitigation. A 60-day effective date and application to every student without a prior OPT recommendation leave current students no way to adjust. At minimum, DHS should exempt all students enrolled before publication of a final rule.

6. The comment period is too short (Secs. I, VII).
For an economically significant rule with over $100 billion in projected transfers, a roughly 30-day comment period is inadequate, especially when the information-collection comment period runs to December 7. I request an extension to at least 60 days.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

1. The rule would damage American public research. OPT lets researchers continue publicly funded work after finishing their degrees. Many labs depend on OPT researchers to complete federally funded projects. Public universities cannot pay $70,000 per student, and DHS’s own small-entity analysis shows many institutions would lose OPT entirely. Losing these researchers delays work that U.S. taxpayers have already invested in. It also pushes trained talent to competitor countries.

2. The fee does not fund fraud prevention (Section IV.C). DHS says that fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and that ICE will not keep them. The estimated $8.4 to $16.5 billion collected each year would pay for no site visits, no SEVP staff, and no investigations. A charge of this size that funds no service is a barrier, not a fee. DHS has not shown that INA 214(a) authorizes it.

3. It targets the wrong party (Sections IV.A, V.A). The fraud examples in the preamble involve shell employers and fake worksites, yet DHS states the fee is not tied to any employer. Well-funded fraud networks can still pay. Legitimate researchers at public universities cannot. The rule screens for wealth, not merit.

4. Targeted alternatives were rejected without evidence. DHS rejected employer verification, training plans, and site visits mainly because a fee has “minimal administrative burdens on the government.” It offers no data showing those tools failed, and its own preamble shows site visits are how fraud was found.

5. The benefits are not quantified (Section VII.A.6). DHS estimates up to $69.9 billion in ten-year costs. It provides no estimate of fraud prevented, U.S. jobs gained, or wage effects. That falls short of what E.O. 12866 and Circular A-4 require for an economically significant rule.

6. It penalizes training during study. Pre-completion OPT followed by post-completion OPT costs $100,000, versus $70,000 for post-completion alone. DHS itself predicts schools will discourage training during study, which undermines OPT’s educational purpose.

7. It disregards reliance interests. I chose a U.S. university and committed years to my program on the understanding that OPT would be available. DHS’s statement that it “may shut down the program entirely” is not a reasoned response to those interests.

Requested action: Withdraw the rule. If DHS has fraud concerns, it should target employers through verification and site visits, and set any fee based on the actual cost of administering the program.

Alternative approaches such as enhanced compliance reviews, targeted enforcement actions, and stronger oversight mechanisms may address fraud concerns without imposing severe financial barriers on legitimate participants.

I respectfully request that Department of Homeland Security reconsider the proposed fee levels and pursue less burdensome methods of achieving its stated objectives.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees. A school must pay $70,000 before a DSO can enter a recommendation. The rule then gives it no clear right to a refund, no standards, no deadline, no reasons and no appeal.

1. The fee is paid before anything is known
Under proposed 214.2(f)(11)(ii), the fee must be paid before the DSO recommends OPT. At that point USCIS has not acted on the Form I-765. For post-completion OPT, the student often has no job offer yet. Current rules allow up to 90 days of unemployment during post-completion OPT (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(E)). So a school pays $70,000 for a student who may never start work.

2. After the EAD issues, the money is gone "under any circumstances"
The rule says the fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document." That covers cases with no fraud at all: an offer rescinded after the EAD arrives, an employer that closes, a student who finds no job within the unemployment limit, a student who changes to another status before starting, or a serious illness or death. DHS says refunds exist for cases "when OPT does not proceed as initially intended." In each of these cases OPT did not proceed. The text still bars a refund.

3. Before the EAD, refunds are pure discretion
Even when USCIS denies the application, a refund is not owed. SEVP "may exercise discretion to grant a refund request ... on a case-by-case basis." The rule names no factors. It sets no time limit for a request or a decision. It does not require a written explanation. It says SEVP "may issue further guidance" on its website. Criteria that decide who keeps $70,000 belong in the regulation, adopted after notice and comment, and not in website guidance that can change without notice.

4. The school must give up the application to ask
The DSO "must remove the student's OPT recommendation in SEVIS before requesting a refund." A school cannot keep a pending application alive and also protect its money. If USCIS is slow, the school must either wait with no assurance or cancel the student's request.

5. The text does not say what happens on refiling
If a first application is denied and the student is recommended again, which fee applies? Paragraph (1) charges $70,000 "the first time that the alien is recommended." Paragraph (2) charges $30,000 only if the student "has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee." A student whose first application was denied has paid but never participated. The rule does not say whether the first payment carries over, whether a second $70,000 is due, or whether either fee applies.

6. No appeal and no law to apply
"Refund request determinations are not subject to any administrative appeals." The APA requires prompt notice of a denied request and a brief statement of the grounds (5 U.S.C. 555(e)). With no standards in the rule, a court may find there is "no law to apply" (Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe, 401 U.S. 402 (1971)), leaving the decision effectively unreviewable. Deciding a $70,000 question with no criteria, reasons or review invites inconsistent results. Under the Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) factors, a large private interest and a high risk of error weigh toward more process.

7. DHS has not said how refunds would be paid
Fees are deposited "as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302," and ICE "would not maintain or use the funding." Yet DHS says ICE "would also bear the burden of transferring funds back." The NPRM does not identify what account refunds would come from. DHS also admits it "does not have sufficient information to estimate the number of refund applications or the associated costs."

Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. If DHS proceeds in any form, it should re-propose for comment a rule that:
(a) makes refunds mandatory, not discretionary, when USCIS denies or rejects the I-765, when the school withdraws before the EAD issues, when employment never begins, when the student changes status before starting, or when a government error causes the loss;
(b) puts refund criteria in the regulation text;
(c) sets deadlines for requests, decisions and payment, with written reasons;
(d) allows one level of administrative appeal to an official who did not make the first decision;
(e) lets a school keep an application pending while a refund request is considered, and credits a prior payment on refiling;
(f) identifies the account from which refunds are paid; and
(g) as a simpler option, collects any fee only after the student begins OPT employment, which removes most refund cases.

I respectfully oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals. However, the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation are disproportionate, poorly targeted, and insufficiently justified by the agency's own analysis.

The proposal does not establish why these particular amounts are needed to prevent fraud. It identifies abuses involving fictitious employers, false job offers, and nonfunctional worksites, yet requires payment from schools whether or not there is any indication of wrongdoing. Paying a large fee does not verify a job, establish an employer's legitimacy, or demonstrate that a graduate's training is related to a degree. Nor does an institution's inability to pay imply misconduct. The rule would therefore restrict lawful participation based largely on financial capacity rather than actual compliance risk. DHS should explain, with evidence, why the chosen fee levels would prevent more fraud than substantially less burdensome alternatives.

The design also undermines the claimed incentive for institutional accountability. DHS expressly allows schools to obtain funds from students or employers and acknowledges that costs may even be spread across all students. If the cost is passed on, it is not clear why schools would necessarily perform more effective reviews. If schools absorb it, the payment competes with instruction, scholarships, research, and student services. Neither outcome is a reliable substitute for verifying employment records or investigating suspicious employers.

The timing and refund provisions create additional unjustified risks. Schools would have to pay before issuing an OPT recommendation, although an initial post-completion OPT applicant need not have a job offer at that stage. Once an employment authorization document is issued, the fee is not refundable even if the anticipated training fails to materialize. Where an authorization document is not issued, refunds are subject to discretionary review. Such uncertainty may cause universities to refuse recommendations for qualified students simply to avoid financial exposure.

The proposed rule's economic justification is especially weak. DHS estimates roughly $4.1 billion in annualized costs in its primary scenario at a 3 percent discount rate, while its accounting statement lists annualized monetized benefits as not estimated. It also acknowledges that reduced OPT participation could mean lower international enrollment, lost student earnings, and lower employer productivity. These are substantial consequences. The agency cannot reasonably treat a smaller OPT population as proof of reduced fraud or assume that the unmeasured benefits necessarily outweigh the identified costs. Its own text further states that the fees would be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for OPT enforcement.

American universities and communities would bear much of the burden. International students support campuses through tuition and support nearby businesses through housing, food, transportation, and daily purchases. A decline in enrollment could strain smaller and regional institutions, with consequences for American faculty, staff, students, and local employers. Universities seeking to maintain OPT opportunities might instead increase tuition or reduce services. These foreseeable domestic impacts deserve analysis, not dismissal as costs borne only by foreign students.

The long-term effects on innovation are equally important. International graduates contribute to research in medicine, engineering, computing, and the physical sciences. Making practical training prohibitively expensive may steer prospective students and researchers toward competing countries, reducing the return on investments in American universities and laboratories. Employers, including startups and public research institutions, may lose access to specialized talent. Protecting American workers should include strengthening the institutions and industries that create American jobs.

DHS should instead use risk-based employer verification, targeted site visits, payroll and worksite checks, and meaningful sanctions against proven fraud. Those measures would address the conduct described in the proposal without imposing extraordinary charges on every legitimate participant. Until DHS can demonstrate that these fees are necessary, effective, and proportionate, the proposed rule should not proceed. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

I am a clinical neuropsychologist practicing in California, and I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.

Clinical neuropsychology requires extensive specialized training, including two-year postdoctoral fellowships following doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled, competitive neuropsychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates.

These consequences extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning and linguistic/cultural considerations that strengthen neuropsychological assessment, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and limit the availability of clinical-researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S.'s diverse population.

I support aggressive enforcement against fraudulent employers, shell companies, fake employment letters, nonexistent worksites, and "pay-to-stay" schemes. However, this proposal does not target those activities. It uses financial capacity as a proxy for legitimacy.

DHS itself states that the $70,000 fee is not tied to a specific employer. Therefore, a legitimate engineering PhD joining a semiconductor company, research organization, startup, or advanced-manufacturing firm triggers the same fee as an individual associated with a fraudulent employer. Ability to pay $70,000 is not evidence of legitimate employment, and inability to pay it is not evidence of fraud.

DHS also states that schools may pass the financial obligation to students or employers and claims the fee will encourage schools to recommend only the "most promising" students. But financial capacity is not technical merit. This system could favor wealthy students, wealthy universities, and large corporations over highly qualified graduates working with startups, smaller companies, or research organizations.

The proposed fees are enormous. DHS estimates annual collections of approximately $8.4-$16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. During the transition period, DHS estimates that 116 affected small entities could experience costs exceeding 20% of annual revenue.

More importantly, DHS states that these billions of dollars would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. ICE would not retain them for OPT investigations or enforcement. DHS also acknowledges that it considered more targeted approaches—site visits, additional reporting, training plans, and enforcement—but selected a fee partly because it creates less administrative burden for the government.

Administrative convenience should not replace precise enforcement.

The proposed rule also risks harming U.S. technological competitiveness. The National Science Board reports that temporary visa holders earned 42% of U.S. science and engineering master's degrees and 38% of S&E doctorates in 2024, including 61% of computer and information-science doctorates, 54% of engineering doctorates, and 52% of mathematics/statistics doctorates.

Recent research also challenges the assumption that reducing STEM OPT automatically benefits U.S. workers. A 2026 AEA Papers and Proceedings study found previous STEM-OPT expansions increased STEM degree completions by 14%-15%, including increased domestic completions. A 2024 MIS Quarterly study found STEM-OPT expansion increased domestic STEM employment, particularly in IT.

International graduates also contribute to entrepreneurship. A 2024 NBER study found that a 10-percentage-point increase in foreign master's graduates produced approximately 0.4 additional startups per cohort, with 30%-45% of the startup effect attributable to positive spillovers to U.S.-origin founders.

The United States is also competing globally for this talent. The National Science Board reports that internationally mobile enrollment decreased about 3% in the United States from 2017-2023 while increasing 85% in Canada, 72% in the United Kingdom, and 63% in Germany. International S&E enrollment in the United States then fell another 9% from 2024-2025, including a 24% decline at the master's level.

DHS should target fraud directly through employer verification, E-Verify where authorized, business and worksite verification, risk-based inspections, stronger training requirements, payroll/employment verification, and severe penalties for fraudulent employers.

If DHS proceeds with any substantial OPT changes, current students should at minimum be grandfathered, and any fee should be reasonably tied to actual administrative or enforcement costs.

The solution to fraud is better enforcement—not an indiscriminate $70,000 barrier that can drive legitimate scientists, engineers, researchers, entrepreneurs, and future employers out of the United States.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee on the most basic fiscal grounds: no adjudication process costs $70,000 per applicant. OPT recommendations are processed through paperwork universities and DHS already handle — forms, SEVIS records, and employment authorization documents. Whatever the true administrative cost is, it is orders of magnitude below $70,000. A fee must bear some relationship to the cost of the service, or it stops being a fee and becomes something else: a barrier, a deterrent, a deliberate end to the program by pricing. I want to return to the justification DHS offers for charging schools $70,000 per initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 per subsequent one: fraud. Fighting fraud is a legitimate goal, so the question is whether this fee actually fights it. It does not — and a serious anti-fraud measure would look nothing like this.

International students and their schools already pay to fund the Student and Exchange Visitor Program: the I-901 SEVIS fee, currently $350 per student, exists precisely to pay for SEVP's operations, monitoring, and enforcement. If DHS believes its fraud-fighting capacity is underfunded, the remedy is to adjust that fee or request appropriations — not to impose a separate charge two hundred times larger on a different party for a different act. There is no showing that $70,000 per recommendation bears any relationship to the cost of investigating the fraud it claims to target.

Look at how OPT fraud has actually been detected and stopped. The major cases — fraudulent employers, sham staffing arrangements, schools selling records — were broken by investigators, audits, whistleblowers, and prosecutions, not by pricing honest participants out of the program. That is because fraudsters do not fear fees; they fear enforcement. A six-figure charge does not deter someone already breaking the law. It deters the Designated School Official at a compliant college who must now weigh whether recommending a legitimate student's OPT is worth $70,000 of institutional money.

The fee even creates a perverse incentive against enforcement's own interests. Honest small schools that run OPT by the book are the ones most likely to stop recommending it, which means SEVP loses reporting, oversight, and visibility into exactly the corner of the system where compliance is highest. Meanwhile a bad actor with enough margin to keep operating simply builds the fee into its business model. Enforcement agencies normally want more compliant participants inside the tent, generating records and tips — not fewer.

DHS already has the tools that actually work: SEVP certification and revocation authority, site visits, records audits, criminal referrals. This fee is not an enforcement measure. It is a tax on compliance, and it will shrink the honest program while leaving the dishonest one intact. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

From the U.S. perspective, I understand the reasoning behind OPT fees. Processing applications and maintaining oversight require resources, and policymakers have a responsibility to consider both program costs and the interests of American workers. International students’ desire for work experience does not remove those responsibilities.

However, the deeper issue is how financial risk is distributed. International students have already invested heavily in an American education, yet they must pay for work authorization without knowing whether they will find a job or whether an employer will consider them given their temporary status. Paying the fee buys the opportunity to seek employment, not the security of employment itself. The same fee can therefore be manageable for a wealthy student but a serious barrier for an equally qualified student with limited resources.

A fair approach should distinguish between recovering administrative costs and using price to restrict access. If protecting American workers is the goal, fees alone are a blunt tool: they select applicants by their ability to pay rather than by their qualifications or potential contributions. The challenge is to respect U.S. priorities while recognizing that international students bear substantial costs with limited control over the outcome.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I am an F-1 chemistry Ph.D. student at a U.S. research university and expect to graduate in 2027. My research involves mass spectrometry, laser spectroscopy, vacuum instrumentation, and the electronic structure of actinide-containing molecules. OPT would allow me to apply this specialized training in a practical setting directly related to my degree. The proposed fees would create a serious barrier to that educational opportunity.

The proposal does not adequately protect students already pursuing their degrees (Sections V.C and VI).

Doctoral education requires years of sustained work. Students approaching graduation have already invested substantial time and effort in specialized training and are making plans under the existing regulatory framework. A 60-day transition after publication of a final rule cannot reasonably accommodate the disruption caused by a new financial requirement of this magnitude.

I recognize that OPT requires authorization and is not guaranteed. However, the opportunity to apply for an established training program is materially different from an opportunity conditioned on a new $70,000 payment. Applying the fee only to recommendations issued after the effective date would still disrupt students who enrolled years earlier. DHS should preserve access under the existing fee framework for currently enrolled students, including their subsequent STEM OPT extensions.

Requiring schools to pay does not eliminate the burden on students (Sections V.A and VI).

The proposal requires educational institutions to pay before recommending students for OPT. If institutions cannot absorb these costs, they may limit recommendations or pass costs to students or other parties. Either outcome could prevent otherwise eligible students from participating for reasons unrelated to the legitimacy or educational value of their training.

For a graduate student, a $70,000 charge would be an extraordinary financial burden. Nor can I assume that my university or a prospective employer would pay it. Access to legitimate practical training should not depend on a student's personal wealth or an institution's ability to make such a large payment.

A uniform financial barrier is poorly targeted to fraud prevention (Section IV).

I support meaningful oversight, verification of legitimate training, and enforcement against fraudulent schools and employers. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training opportunity is genuine, and inability to pay does not establish fraud.

DHS should explain, with evidence, why these specific fee amounts are necessary and how they would distinguish fraudulent participation from compliant participation. It should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including risk-based audits, verification of employers and training activities, and enforcement focused on documented violations. Any oversight fee should be transparent, proportionate, and supported by the actual cost of administering that oversight.

DHS should give greater weight to the loss of legitimate scientific training opportunities (Section VII.A).

My doctoral work has developed skills in experimental design, instrument troubleshooting, and analysis of complex scientific data. Practical training would help me extend those skills beyond my dissertation research. A financial barrier that prevents participation could also deprive U.S. research teams and employers of relevant expertise. DHS should evaluate these effects rather than treating reduced participation as evidence that program integrity has improved.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. I also oppose the alternative of charging the $70,000 initial fee again at each higher educational level. If DHS proceeds with changes, it should protect currently enrolled students and adopt targeted, evidence-based oversight measures that preserve access to legitimate OPT and STEM OPT.

I believe this proposal would cause significant harm to international students, American universities, U.S. employers, and the long-term competitiveness of the United States.

First, these fees are unreasonable and would effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for many qualified international students. International students already make substantial financial investments in American higher education, often paying full tuition without access to federal financial aid. Requiring an additional $70,000 or $100,000 to gain practical work experience would make OPT financially inaccessible to most students. Career opportunities should be based on qualifications and merit, not the ability to pay an extraordinary fee.

The opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation is an important reason why talented students choose to study in the United States. The United States should continue to attract and retain talented graduates, not discourage them from contributing to its economy and future.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees — Request for Full Withdrawal
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. DHS should withdraw the proposal entirely, not merely reduce the amounts. These charges would add a major barrier to an already difficult path from American education to lawful professional experience, with consequences far beyond the students affected.
1. Post-graduation opportunities are already uncertain.
Students invest years and substantial savings in U.S. education without any guarantee of later employment. Graduates face limited work authorization periods, employer constraints, and uncertain future status. OPT offers valuable training in its own right and can bridge graduation and later H-1B employment. But H-1B has caps and filing constraints; it cannot simply replace OPT. Making OPT unaffordable would compound existing obstacles and weaken the appeal of an American degree.
2. These fees amount to another enormous education bill.
College Board reports average 2025–26 out-of-state undergraduate tuition and fees of $31,880 per year at public four-year colleges. The $70,000 charge exceeds two years of that benchmark. Initial OPT plus a later STEM extension could total $100,000. DHS acknowledges that universities could pass fees to students, employers, or other students. Schools unable to absorb the costs may simply stop recommending OPT. Labeling it a university fee does not protect students from the burden.
3. America is already losing prospective students.
IIE's Fall 2025 Snapshot reported a 17% decline in new international enrollment among responding institutions. In August 2026, NAFSA projected that existing pressures could mean up to 111,000 fewer international students in fall 2026, costing up to $3.4 billion and nearly 40,000 jobs. These changes and forecasts predate this proposal and are NOT attributable to it. They show how damaging an additional deterrent could be.
An October 2026 Institute for Progress survey of 734 current or former international students found that 70% of STEM-eligible respondents said they would not have enrolled in a U.S. program had these fees existed. This is stated intent, not an exact forecast. DHS must assess the risk of further enrollment losses.
4. Current students could feel that the rules changed after they paid.
International students often commit years of tuition, savings, and family resources in reliance on established practical-training opportunities. A 60-day transition cannot undo those investments. Someone already on ordinary OPT could face the first $70,000 fee when seeking a STEM OPT extension after the rule takes effect. Students who followed the rules may feel betrayed and leave disappointed; their experiences may influence future applicants. Such a loss of trust could damage America's international reputation long after the fees are collected.
5. The economic harm would reach American workers and communities.
NAFSA estimates international students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024–25. These are existing contributions, not projected losses from this rule. Enrollment declines could affect universities, domestic students, housing, businesses, research, and jobs. Fewer OPT participants do not automatically mean equivalent jobs for Americans: employers may cancel projects or move them abroad. DHS should assess these indirect impacts, not just the fees it expects to collect.
6. Wealth is not a test of merit or compliance.
The ability to pay $70,000 does not establish honesty or qualifications, and inability to pay does not indicate fraud. DHS has not shown why these specific sums are necessary or effective against misconduct. Revenue would enter the Treasury rather than directly finance ICE's OPT oversight. That raises serious questions about proportionality and legal authority.
America competes for global talent through educational excellence, opportunity, and trust. Adding a massive financial barrier to already uncertain lawful training risks driving away future students and alienating those already here, with lasting economic and reputational costs.
DHS should WITHDRAW the proposed rule IN FULL.
Sources: DHS, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (2026), §§ IV–VII; College Board, Trends in College Pricing 2025; IIE, Fall 2025 Snapshot; NAFSA, Fall 2026 Outlook and Economic Value 2024–25; Institute for Progress, OPT Fee Analysis (Oct. 2026).

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. My comment addresses Section III.A (Legal Authority) and the proposed fee structure. The central question is not whether DHS may regulate practical training. It plainly may. The question is whether the authorities identified in the notice permit DHS to impose charges of this magnitude, with the practical effect of excluding otherwise eligible students based on wealth rather than compliance or educational merit.

DHS relies on 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a), and general homeland-security authorities. Those provisions confer substantial regulatory powers, but the notice should distinguish authority to establish conditions of nonimmigrant status from authority to raise revenue or impose a prohibitive financial condition. Calling a payment a "fee" does not answer that distinction. If the charge is intended to reimburse government expenses, DHS should identify the relevant services, their costs, the allocation method, and why the amount charged to each applicant reasonably corresponds to those costs. If instead the charge is intended to deter participation or reshape the OPT labor market, DHS should identify the statutory basis for that different policy instrument and explain its limits.

The Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. 9701, reflects a cost-and-benefit framework for federal user charges. I do not assume that statute exclusively governs every charge DHS may impose. Rather, its framework highlights the need for DHS to specify which fee-setting authority it invokes and how the proposed amounts are justified under that authority. The notice should explain whether the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts represent adjudication costs, monitoring costs, projected enforcement costs, deterrence targets, or some combination. These are materially different rationales requiring different evidence.

The proposed distinction between initial and subsequent OPT also needs an explanation grounded in actual administrative burdens. Why should the first authorization cost $40,000 more than a later one? Does DHS expect first-time applicants to require more than twice the expenditure or oversight? If not, what non-cost criterion produces these precise figures? A reasoned rulemaking should provide a reproducible calculation, not merely assert that high charges promote program integrity.

There is also a mismatch between the stated anti-fraud objective and the chosen mechanism. A student who has complied with status requirements, obtained a school recommendation, and submitted truthful information would pay the same extraordinary amount as an applicant presenting heightened risk. Meanwhile, ability to pay is not evidence of compliance. DHS should explain what evidence shows that imposing a uniform financial barrier on lawful applicants will identify or prevent fraud more effectively than targeted audits, employer verification, SEVIS data analysis, or enforcement against fraudulent schools and employers. It should compare these options on effectiveness, administrative cost, and burdens imposed on compliant students.

Under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), courts review whether agency action is arbitrary or capricious. Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983), requires reasoned consideration of important aspects of the problem and relevant alternatives. These principles do not dictate any particular fee, but they make the evidentiary bridge between DHS's objectives and its chosen amounts especially important. DHS should also address whether an enormous uniform charge effectively changes access to an existing training program in ways not adequately explained by the cited authority.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and, before pursuing any replacement, publish: (1) an itemized cost basis for each fee; (2) the statutory provision authorizing any amount exceeding service-related costs; (3) the empirical basis for the $40,000 difference; (4) evidence connecting the charges to measurable fraud reduction; and (5) a comparative assessment of narrower enforcement alternatives. If the agency cannot provide these explanations, it should not finalize this proposal. Immigration compliance should be evaluated through lawful conduct and verifiable program requirements, not presumed from an applicant's capacity to pay an extraordinary sum.

Public Comment on Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. As an international helicopter pilot who has invested significant time, money, and personal sacrifice into pursuing an aviation career in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the impact this proposal would have on students and pilots like me and the American flight schools that train us.

1. The personal and financial investment of international students
Many international students leave their families, friends, and home countries, take on significant financial burdens, and dedicate years of their lives to pursuing flight training in the United States. Some invest well over $100,000 in their education. For us, this is not simply a training course; it is a major life decision and an investment in a future aviation career. Yet earning a pilot certificate alone is not enough to qualify for professional employment. We need real-world experience to develop our skills, build flight hours, and become safe, competent, and employable pilots.

2. One year of CPT is not enough
In helicopter aviation, gaining meaningful experience takes time. One year of CPT alone is by far not enough for newly qualified pilots to build the experience and professional competence employers require. The opportunity to continue working through OPT, often as a flight instructor, is a crucial step toward becoming a valuable pilot. Without it, students may complete expensive U.S. training but be unable to gain the experience needed to secure employment in their home countries or elsewhere. This risks undermining the very purpose of their investment.

3. Serious consequences for American flight schools and aviation
Many FAA Part 141 flight schools depend heavily on international students and the substantial revenue they bring to the United States. If OPT becomes financially inaccessible, international enrollment could fall sharply, threatening schools, instructor jobs, and local economies. The rotorcraft industry also needs pathways to develop the next generation of pilots as experienced pilots retire and others transition to airline careers.
I support strong measures against fraud, but a flat fee of this magnitude punishes legitimate students and employers rather than targeting misconduct. DHS should prioritize risk-based employer verification, site inspections, and stronger documentation requirements instead.

In the name of all international students who have left their homes, families, and countries behind to pursue their dreams in American aviation, I respectfully ask DHS to reconsider this proposal. We are not here looking for shortcuts or taking opportunities away from American workers. We are here to learn, work hard, and become skilled professionals. We have invested our time, savings, and years of our lives in the belief that the United States offers a fair opportunity to turn our education into a career. Please do not let these sacrifices be in vain. Give us the opportunity to gain the experience we need and to make our investment in American aviation training worthwhile.

The rule would require SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 before recommending a student for OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including the STEM OPT extension. Each defect below is independent, and each alone would require vacatur of a final rule:

1. No statute authorizes it. INA 214(a) governs the time and conditions of an alien's admission. It is not a revenue power, and the schools being charged are not admitted at all. Congress legislates immigration fees expressly (8 U.S.C. 1372(e), 1356(m), 1184(c)(9), 1184(c)(12)) and has never enacted an OPT fee. Under Loper Bright, DHS's reading gets no deference.

2. It is a tax. It recovers no cost, compensates no service, and is not retained to run OPT. A federal court vacated a similar six-figure H-1B charge as an unauthorized tax in State of California v. Mullin (D. Mass. 2026), stay denied, No. 26-1699 (1st Cir. 2026).

3. It is arbitrary and capricious. The fraud the NPRM describes is employer conduct, yet employers pay nothing. The NPRM excludes CPT entirely. No analysis supports $70,000 over any lower amount, and no employer-targeted alternatives were considered.

4. Its stated reasons do not match what it does. DHS acknowledges the fee could reduce participation and warns it may shut down OPT without it. That is a plan to curtail a program Congress has declined to restrict.

5. It ignores reliance and reaches backward. Students enrolled under existing rules are caught by the recommendation-date trigger. Worse, a student whose initial OPT predates the rule would owe $70,000, not $30,000, at the STEM extension. The rule charges the most to those with the strongest reliance.

6. It is procedurally deficient. DHS allowed 30 days for comments on an economically significant rule, while allowing 60 days for paperwork comments on the same rule.

If DHS proceeds in any form, it should exempt every student enrolled before any final rule, including later STEM extensions, and never apply the $70,000 rate to a STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT predates the rule.

Under Ohio v. EPA (2024), DHS must respond to each of these points, and to the questions in the attachment, in any final rule.

I am a US professional writing in support of stronger OPT oversight. I am concerned, however, that the proposed fees target the wrong part of the system and will not correct the program’s central harm: US graduates are being shut out of the entry-level training that starts a career.

1. OPT has displaced the first rung of the career ladder. Employers increasingly fill entry-level roles with OPT participants and later sponsor the strongest for H-1B status. When positions requiring two to four years of experience open, US graduates lack that experience because they were never given the first opportunity to gain it. The resulting gap is then cited as evidence of a domestic shortage, even as many qualified US graduates remain unemployed or underemployed. The shortage is produced by the pipeline, not by a lack of capable Americans.

2. Entry-level hiring should be a fair competition. An employee’s value is more than credentials. It includes initiative, adaptability, and willingness to step in where needed, qualities that can only be demonstrated on the job. When cost and status incentives tilt entry-level hiring toward one pool of applicants, US graduates never get the chance to show those qualities.

3. The incentives favor OPT hires even at equal pay. The FICA exemption lowers employer costs at any salary. OPT has no labor market test and no requirement that employers consider qualified US applicants. Workers whose status depends on their employer are also less able to change jobs or negotiate.

4. Fees on schools will be passed on rather than change behavior. The proposal acknowledges that schools may recover these costs from students or employers. A fee that can be absorbed or passed along becomes a cost of doing business, not a deterrent.

5. The harm extends beyond individual careers. Graduates who cannot establish careers delay forming households and families, carry unmanageable debt, and lose confidence that effort leads to opportunity. International students are harmed too. Many take on significant debt expecting a pathway the system cannot reliably provide.

I urge DHS to consider:

- Employer-side obligations: an attestation that an OPT hire did not take the place of a qualified US applicant or displace US workers.
- Limits on the share of an employer’s entry-level hires that may be OPT participants.
- Penalties for misuse scaled so they cannot be absorbed as a routine cost.
- Requirements that schools disclose OPT employment and conversion outcomes to prospective international students before enrollment.

2. DHS's stated mechanism does not follow from its own evidence

DHS premises the rule on schools paying or absorbing the fee and therefore recommending only "the most promising students" (section IV.C). The rule does not establish that universities can absorb fees of this scale. The predictable outcome is that the cost passes to students, or that institutions stop issuing OPT recommendations entirely. In either case the effect is the functional end of OPT and STEM OPT for students at non-wealthy institutions and in non-wealthy families, which the rule does not analyze as a cost.

The fraud evidence DHS cites concerns employers: shell companies, staged worksites, residential addresses listed as worksites, coordinated employer clusters with shared personnel, and the 10,000-student investigation described in section IV.A. In nearly every example, the wrongdoing sits with employers or document vendors, not with students paying tuition at accredited universities. A fee charged at the student-and-school gate does not reach those employers. It removes the compliant majority from the program while leaving the described networks intact and unexamined.

Use the data DHS already holds. Flag employers in SEVIS with implausible student-to-revenue or student-to-address ratios, shared ownership, or the duplicate-address patterns described in section IV.A, and audit those first.
Penalize the actors found at fault. Debar employers and decertify schools found to have filed false attestations on Form I-983.
If a fee is retained, set it at cost. A fee tied to documented administrative cost, with a hardship waiver and installment payment, would preserve access while funding integrity work.
