Statement:
The Asian and Pacific Islander Diaspora Special Interest Group (API SIG) of the American Psychological Association’s Division of Rehabilitation Psychology (APA Division 22) respectfully opposes the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation.

Rehabilitation Psychology requires extensive specialized training, including one- to two-year postdoctoral fellowships following doctoral education, to prepare highly skilled, competitive psychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on institutions that could employ international trainees. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates.

These consequences extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning and linguistic/cultural considerations that strengthen assessment and therapy, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could undermine workforce development and limit the availability of clinical-researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S.'s diverse population.

We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

I submit this comment as an F-1 STEM OPT participant currently employed in the U.S. technology sector in California. I chose to pursue my graduate education and begin my career in the United States in reliance on the OPT framework as it existed when I enrolled. Although the proposed rule would not apply to recommendations already entered in SEVIS, it would effectively end OPT for future students — including anyone who later returns for further study — and I write to ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee schedule.

1. The fee bears no relationship to the cost of the service. An OPT recommendation is a data entry made by a designated school official in SEVIS. A charge of $70,000 for that act — $100,000 in total for a student who later uses the STEM OPT extension — cannot plausibly reflect the administrative cost of processing a recommendation. User fees are supposed to be commensurate with the cost of the service provided to the payer. A five-figure charge of this kind, deposited into the general fund of the Treasury, functions in substance as a tax on education and employment — one that Congress has never enacted.

2. In practice, the fee operates as a ban achieved through pricing. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to students or employers. Very few students can pay $70,000 on top of tuition, and many institutions — particularly smaller schools — will simply stop issuing OPT recommendations rather than assume this cost and liability. The predictable result is not a better-funded OPT program; it is the end of OPT for most participants, accomplished without any congressional vote to terminate the program.

3. The fee is not tailored to the stated anti-fraud purpose. Combating fraud is a legitimate goal, but fraud is the conduct of a small minority of bad actors and is properly addressed through enforcement against them. A blanket fee punishes compliant students, schools, and employers alike. OPT — and STEM OPT in particular — is already among the most heavily supervised employment categories in the immigration system, with SEVP school certification, DSO reporting, employer training plans (Form I-983), site visits, and periodic evaluations. DHS has not explained why these existing tools are inadequate.

4. The economic cost to the United States is substantial. OPT and STEM OPT participants fill engineering, research, and technology roles, pay federal and state income taxes, and form the first link in an innovation pipeline that begins at American universities. Pricing OPT out of reach will divert exactly these graduates to Canada, the United Kingdom, and other countries that actively compete for them, while reducing the enrollment revenue on which U.S. institutions depend.

5. The proposal disregards reliance interests. Students make multi-year educational investments — frequently six figures — based on the rules in place when they enroll. I respectfully submit this comment regarding the proposed fee structure for Optional Practical Training (OPT). While maintaining program integrity, preventing fraud, and ensuring regulatory compliance are important objectives, imposing substantial fees on OPT recommendations is not the most effective to achieve these goals.

I encourage the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to consider the following alternative approaches that would strengthen oversight and preserve the educational and economic purposes of the OPT program.

1. Implement Risk-Based Compliance Monitoring Instead of Broad Financial Barriers

Rather than imposing substantial fees across the program, DHS should adopt a risk-based enforcement framework that focuses additional oversight on employers and participants presenting identifiable compliance risks.

This approach could involve conducting targeted audits based on documented indicators of potential fraud, strengthening verification procedures for employers with repeated reporting violations, and using existing government data to identify inconsistencies in employment reporting. Enforcement resources should be directed toward substantiated risks rather than imposing uniform financial burdens.

2. Strengthen Employer Verification and Accountability

DHS should consider enhanced employer verification requirements as an alternative to substantial OPT fees.

This could include establishing standardized procedures to verify employer legitimacy and business operations, improving verification of employment arrangements and training opportunities, and requiring timely reporting of material employment changes.

DHS could also introduce proportionate penalties for employers found to have knowingly submitted fraudulent information. These measures would address potential misuse more directly by focusing regulatory attention on identifiable sources of noncompliance.

3. Adopt a Transparent, Cost-Based Fee Structure

If additional administrative funding is necessary, DHS should consider a reasonable fee structure based on the actual costs of administering and monitoring the OPT program.

Any proposed fees should be supported by a publicly available explanation of the administrative expenses being recovered and a transparent methodology demonstrating how fee amounts are calculated.

DHS should also assess the financial impact on educational institutions and program participants, consider lower-cost alternatives, and conduct periodic reviews to ensure that fees remain proportionate to actual administrative expenses.

Administrative fees should support necessary government functions rather than serve as financial barriers to otherwise eligible participation.

4. Improve Reporting Systems and Interagency Coordination

DHS could further strengthen program oversight by modernizing existing employment reporting systems, standardizing electronic reporting procedures, and improving appropriate information sharing among government agencies and educational institutions.

Clearer reporting requirements, more accessible procedures for correcting inaccurate records, and better data coordination could help identify potential violations while reducing unnecessary administrative burdens.

Investments in reporting accuracy and administrative efficiency would provide a practical alternative to relying primarily on substantial financial requirements.

5. Conduct a Comprehensive Impact Assessment Before Implementation

Before adopting substantial new fees, DHS should conduct a detailed assessment of their potential consequences.

This assessment should examine how the proposed fees could affect access to practical training, educational institutions' administrative and financial responsibilities, employer participation, research activities, and workforce development.

Importantly, DHS should evaluate whether the proposed fee structure would meaningfully improve compliance compared with targeted employer verification, risk-based audits, and enhanced reporting requirements.

A phased implementation or pilot program could also allow DHS to test alternative compliance measures and assess their effectiveness before adopting broader regulatory changes.

6. Establish Measurable Outcomes and Periodic Policy Review

DHS should establish clear performance indicators for evaluating any new OPT oversight measures.

These indicators could include verified compliance violations, processing efficiency, administrative costs, employer verification outcomes, and reporting accuracy.

Regular public reporting and periodic evaluations would help determine whether new requirements are achieving their stated objectives and whether adjustments are necessary.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure and thoroughly evaluate these alternative approaches before finalizing the rule.

I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). This comment addresses one question the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) does not answer: what the rule does to the federal budget. Other comments have covered the rule's legal basis and its labor-market economics. This one looks only at the fiscal ledger.

1. The fee does not fund the oversight it is meant to replace

DHS projects annual fee collections of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion, and 10-year transfers of $109.4 billion (primary, 3 percent). Every dollar would go to the Treasury "as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302." DHS states that ICE "would not maintain or use the funding." The NPRM says the "deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these funds are appropriated." The same NPRM quotes the CIS Ombudsman's 2020 finding that compliance resources are "not scaled to (or keeping pace with)" the program. The rule would collect more than $100 billion and route none of it to site visits, DSO training or SEVP staff. DHS should explain why a fee that cannot pay for oversight is the right response to a shortage of oversight.

2. The revenue estimate and the deterrence theory cannot both hold

In the high scenario, schools recommend exactly as many students as today. That scenario yields the largest collections and, by DHS's own logic, no added screening. In the low scenario, schools drop non-STEM OPT. That scenario yields the most screening and much less revenue. The primary estimate averages the two. If the fee changes school behavior as DHS predicts, the $12.4 billion figure overstates receipts. If receipts reach that figure, the fee did not screen anyone. The RIA should say which outcome DHS expects and report receipts and benefits from the same scenario.

3. The tax ledger counts only one side

The RIA says that if OPT students are replaced by FICA-subject workers, "there could be additional transfers for federal taxes collected." It does not count taxes lost. OPT students are generally exempt from FICA under 26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19) for their first five calendar years, as NPRM footnote 108 notes. They generally still owe federal income tax on U.S. wages, subject to any tax treaty, and state income tax where it applies. Students past the five-year period, including some on STEM OPT, generally owe FICA as well. DHS concedes that employers "may face productivity losses" when they cannot replace these workers. A position that goes unfilled, moves abroad, or is lost when a graduate leaves produces no tax at all. DHS should estimate net federal tax effects: income and payroll tax lost from forgone OPT employment, minus any gain from replacement hires.

4. Enrollment and tuition effects are left unquantified

DHS acknowledges that schools "could also experience declines" in F-1 enrollment and "reduced enrollment revenue," and then uses unpaid fees as a stand-in for those losses. In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court preliminarily postponed DHS's companion Duration of Status rule. It found DHS likely acted arbitrarily in part because it "made no real effort to quantify" enrollment and revenue effects and "provided no counter-estimate." This RIA repeats that gap. It also tells schools they may pass the fee to "all students." That means domestic tuition payers, and state budgets at public institutions, could end up funding a Treasury receipt. The RIA does not estimate how much of the $12.4 billion would come from them.

5. Federal collection costs are not estimated

DHS says Treasury may need to modify systems and ICE must confirm payments and process refunds. It states it "is unable to estimate the cost impacts of these processes." A program expected to collect about $12 billion a year should come with at least a rough estimate of what collecting it costs the government.

6. Request

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. Any new proposal should include (a) a net federal fiscal estimate covering fee receipts, income and payroll taxes, and collection costs; (b) receipts and benefits drawn from the same participation scenario; (c) an estimate of how much of the fee would be passed to domestic students and public budgets; and (d) an explanation of why DHS prefers a fee it cannot spend to oversight measures it could fund through the normal appropriations process.

The federal government has a legitimate interest in preventing immigration fraud, maintaining the integrity of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, ensuring compliance with employment requirements, and protecting U.S. workers. These are reasonable policy objectives, and universities have a responsibility to support lawful and accountable participation in the program.

However, recognizing these objectives does not automatically mean that the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are the most effective or proportionate means of achieving them. A policy of this magnitude should be supported by a clear explanation of how the fees were calculated, how they are expected to reduce fraud, and how their effectiveness will be measured.

There is an important distinction between deterring fraudulent participation and discouraging legitimate students, universities, and employers from participating in a lawful educational and employment pathway. Although substantial fees might encourage institutions to scrutinize OPT recommendations more carefully, they could also create significant financial barriers for public universities and students with limited resources, regardless of whether their employment arrangements are legitimate.

A more targeted approach could include stronger employment verification, risk-based audits, increased institutional oversight, and meaningful penalties for documented violations. These measures could strengthen program integrity while focusing enforcement on identifiable risks and misconduct. Reasonable administrative fees, supported by transparent cost calculations, could also be considered.

Ultimately, the question is not whether OPT should be subject to oversight. It should. The question is whether this particular fee structure is necessary, effective, and proportionate to the problems it seeks to address. A balanced policy should protect the integrity of the immigration system and U.S. workers while preserving fair access to legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule. DHS has a legitimate responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect U.S. workers. Those goals, however, do not justify a measure whose financial burdens are extraordinary and whose connection to the stated problems remains unproven.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee appear designed primarily to discourage participation. But lower participation is not necessarily evidence of better compliance. The fraud cases described by DHS involve fabricated employment, shell companies, and misleading records. None of those practices is established or disproved by a university's ability to pay a fee. A financially constrained institution could decline to support a fully qualified student, while an adequately funded bad actor might still pursue fraudulent arrangements. DHS should demonstrate why these particular charges would meaningfully reduce misconduct, rather than simply reduce the number of lawful participants.

The method used to set the amounts is also questionable. Aligning an OPT charge with fees associated with another visa program does not establish that $70,000 reflects the cost of administering OPT, the risk posed by a given application, or the cost of detecting fraud. OPT is a temporary form of training connected to a student's education, not an interchangeable substitute for every other employment visa. A sound fee policy should be justified by evidence specific to the program it regulates.

The proposal also places universities in a contradictory position. It expects schools to be more careful because they must pay, while expressly allowing them to pass that expense to students, employers, or the wider student body. Shifting the bill does not improve the quality of employment verification. Absorbing the bill, meanwhile, diverts resources from instruction, financial aid, and research. A university should not have to choose between supporting an eligible graduate and maintaining essential educational services.

The practical details create further uncertainty. An initial post-completion OPT application need not be tied to an existing job offer, yet the institution would have to pay before entering its recommendation. Refunds would be limited and, in qualifying cases, subject to agency discretion. These risks would predictably discourage schools from making otherwise legitimate recommendations, particularly public universities and smaller nonprofit institutions with limited financial flexibility.

DHS's own economic analysis underscores the need for caution. It estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario, but does not estimate annualized monetized benefits. It acknowledges potential declines in international enrollment and resulting losses for institutions, students, and employers. The analysis does not establish that preventing fraud through this fee would outweigh the damage to education, research, and economic activity. Furthermore, the fee receipts would go to the Treasury rather than being specifically allocated to OPT investigations or oversight. That makes it harder to understand why the proposed financial burden is the appropriate response to enforcement shortfalls.

These consequences would reach beyond international graduates. Universities support employment and spending in communities across the country, especially smaller towns where campuses are major economic anchors. International students pay tuition and spend locally on housing, groceries, transportation, and services. Declining enrollment could weaken university budgets and nearby businesses, and pressure schools to raise tuition or reduce services for domestic students. These are real costs to American communities.

The longer-term losses could be greater still. International students and graduates contribute to medical research, engineering, technology, and other fields that sustain U.S. innovation. If the United States makes legitimate practical training inaccessible, competing countries will have stronger opportunities to attract the talent educated here. A rule presented as protecting American interests should not undermine the universities, employers, and research institutions on which American competitiveness depends.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. A more defensible approach would focus on verifiable fraud indicators, employer and worksite checks, targeted audits, and meaningful penalties for violations. Program integrity should be measured by actual compliance outcomes, not by how many students and universities have been priced out of participation.

I strongly oppose the proposed change. The OPT program is one of the best mechanisms the US has for keeping talent in the country. Those people go on to work in research labs, industry, and other technical organizations that make the US economy stronger and more resilient. The proposed change would significantly harm US economic growth for years.

I am writing to voice my vehement opposition to the proposed rule imposing an exorbitant, unprecedented fee structure on Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extensions. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this catastrophic proposal immediately. Beyond its blatant legal vulnerabilities under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), this rule will systematically dismantle U.S. academic research and cripple the American startup ecosystem.

1. The "Death Spiral" for U.S. Academic Research and University Funding
The OPT program is the primary mechanism that makes U.S. higher education attractive to the world's brightest minds. International students pay full out-of-state tuition, effectively subsidizing domestic education, while serving as the backbone of university STEM research labs. By attaching a $100,000 employment penalty to these graduates, DHS completely destroys the return on investment for studying in the United States.

Top-tier students will immediately divert to universities in Canada, the U.K., and Australia, which offer seamless and affordable post-graduation work pathways. This will trigger a massive revenue collapse for U.S. universities and a severe shortage of graduate research assistants. Critical federal and privately funded research in artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced computing will stall simply because universities will no longer have the international talent required to staff their labs.

2. Crippling the American Startup Ecosystem and Innovation Pipeline
While massive tech conglomerates might possess the capital to offshore their R&D to foreign subsidiaries, American startups do not. Startups rely heavily on the OPT program to recruit hungry, brilliant, entry-level STEM graduates without the immediate administrative friction of H-1B sponsorship.

A $70,000 to $100,000 fee for an OPT hire is a death sentence for early-stage companies. It acts as an insurmountable financial barrier that deprives U.S. startups of essential technical talent. By pricing out small and medium-sized enterprises, DHS is effectively handing a monopoly on global talent to foreign competitors and a few mega-corporations. This will stifle the very entrepreneurial innovation that drives long-term U.S. economic growth and job creation.

3. Unlawful Taxation Disguised as an Administrative Fee
Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA) and INA § 286(m), agency fees must rationally correlate to the actual cost of providing the adjudication service. Processing an I-765 application costs USCIS a fraction of this proposed fee. Imposing up to $100,000 is not cost recovery; it is an unauthorized, punitive tax designed to bypass Congress and effectively nullify the OPT program. This constitutes an arbitrary, capricious, and ultra vires action under the APA.

This proposal is economically destructive and legally indefensible. It will defund American universities, starve startups of critical talent, and offshore the next generation of technological innovation. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Support for Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an American worker and union-represented employee at the University of California. I recently received an email from UAW Local 4811 urging members to oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. I fundamentally disagree with my union's position and am submitting this comment anonymously in support of the proposed rule.

1. Protecting American Workers

As a union member, I believe protecting American workers, their wages, and their employment opportunities should be a central priority of organized labor.

For too long, American universities have emphasized attracting international talent without sufficient consideration for American workers and graduates competing for those same opportunities. Publicly supported universities have a responsibility not only to advance research, but also to serve the American public whose investment makes that research possible.

I question a system in which American research institutions become dependent on foreign labor without demonstrating comparable commitments to developing, recruiting, and employing American talent.

2. Support for the Proposed Fees

I support the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee as substantial financial incentives for universities to scrutinize their reliance on foreign labor.

Section IV.B of the proposed rule, "Protecting American Workers," identifies legitimate concerns regarding worker displacement, wage competition, insufficient labor protections, and payroll-tax advantages associated with OPT employment. These concerns deserve serious consideration from policymakers and labor organizations alike.

I also support the broader principle behind substantial H-1B employment fees. Employers and institutions should have compelling reasons to recruit internationally rather than choosing foreign labor simply because it is cheaper or more convenient.

Temporary education and employment programs should operate under clear, enforceable rules, not serve as alternative pathways around the requirements established for employment-based immigration.

I recognize that international students and researchers make valuable contributions to American universities. However, those contributions do not eliminate the government's responsibility to prioritize American workers and safeguard domestic employment opportunities.

3. Implementation and Accountability

I support finalizing substantial OPT fees while ensuring that universities cannot simply transfer those costs to American students or taxpayers.

The financial responsibility should reinforce institutional accountability and encourage universities to invest in domestic talent rather than externalizing the costs of their international recruitment decisions.

4. Union Dissent and Representation

I support collective bargaining because I believe in securing better wages, working conditions, and economic opportunities for myself, my family, and my fellow American workers. That support should not be mistaken for an endorsement of my union's broader political agenda.

UAW Local 4811's appeal portrays opposition to this rule as a united position among workers. I reject that characterization. I am confident that my views are not unique.

I am submitting this comment anonymously because I believe expressing these views publicly could expose me to professional retaliation within my institution. The absence of visible dissent should not be mistaken for unanimous agreement.

I urge DHS to consider that union leadership's stated position does not necessarily represent the views of all union-represented American workers.

I support the proposed rule and its objective of protecting American workers.

Spring Arbor University is writing in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)'s proposed rule to impose a $70,000 fee on institutions for each initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. 

First, the proposed fee structure is disproportionate and financially unsustainable. A fee of $70,000 per student bears no reasonable relationship to the administrative action being performed by institutions. Most colleges and universities, particularly small private institutions such as Spring Arbor University, would be unable to absorb such costs. As a result, institutions would likely be forced either to discontinue support for OPT participation or pass costs on to students, creating a substantial barrier to educational opportunity.

Second, the proposal would harm U.S. higher education and reduce the attractiveness of the U.S. as a destination for international students. Many international students choose U.S. institutions because of the opportunity to gain practical experience through OPT. Eliminating or severely restricting access to OPT would place U.S. institutions at a competitive disadvantage compared to universities with English-speaking academic programs in Canada, France, Germany, and other countries that actively encourage international graduates to remain and contribute to their economies.

Third, the proposed rule would have significant economic consequences beyond higher education. International students contribute billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, consumer spending, and local economic activity. They also help address workforce shortages in fields such as healthcare, engineering, technology, and scientific research. OPT allows employers to benefit from graduates who have already been trained in U.S. institutions and who possess desired skills. 

Fourth and very importantly, the proposed fee structure places responsibility for alleged program abuses on institutions that already operate under extensive federal oversight. Designated School Officials are required to monitor student status, maintain SEVIS records, and comply with numerous reporting obligations. Institutions should not be subjected to punitive financial penalties based on fraud concerns that could be addressed through targeted enforcement measures against bad actors. A broad fee imposed on all institutions, regardless of compliance history, is neither fair nor effective. DHS itself states that the rule is intended to address fraud and abuse concerns within the OPT program; however, imposing extraordinary costs on compliant institutions is not the most narrowly tailored approach to achieving that objective.

Finally, the proposed rule would create inequitable outcomes among institutions and students. Wealthier institutions may be able to continue supporting OPT, while smaller colleges and universities would be unable to do so, limiting opportunities based on institutional resources rather than student merit. Students who have invested substantial time and resources in pursuing a U.S. education would see the value of that investment significantly reduced.

For these reasons, we respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS believes reforms are necessary to address program integrity concerns, the Department should consider targeted compliance measures, enhanced oversight of identified bad actors, improved reporting requirements, or reasonable cost-recovery fees that are proportionate to actual administrative expenses.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a regulatory program that allows foreign students to work in the United States after completing their studies, with the STEM extension allowing employment for up to three years. What began as practical training connected to a course of study has grown into a major foreign-worker pipeline. In 2024, according to DHS’s SEVIS by the Numbers report, 194,554 students participated in pre- and post-completion OPT, and 165,524 participated in STEM OPT.
 
Unlike the H-1B program, OPT has no annual cap, generally requires neither a labor condition application nor a prevailing wage, and does not require employers to seek American workers first. A program of this size, with direct consequences for the American labor market, demands meaningful oversight, transparent reporting, and accountability—particularly for its impact on American students and recent college graduates seeking entry-level employment.
 
OPT also gives employers a financial incentive to hire foreign graduates over Americans. F-1 students on OPT are often exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes, depending on their tax status and circumstances. Employers hiring eligible OPT workers avoid their share of those payroll taxes, an advantage they do not receive when hiring American graduates.
 
OPT also serves as a pathway to the H-1B program. Foreign students can complete their degrees, work through OPT and STEM OPT for up to three years, and then seek H-1B sponsorship. Universities benefit from international enrollment and can market post-graduation employment opportunities to prospective students, while American students face increased competition for university places and American graduates face increased competition for jobs.
 
The training issue is equally important. When employers claim that American graduates lack the experience or specialized skills needed for available positions, the appropriate response should be to invest in training American workers—not to create incentives to recruit foreign graduates on temporary visas instead. American graduates can be told they lack the qualifications for the jobs their education was intended to prepare them for, while employers have pathways to recruit foreign workers and provide them with practical experience. If Americans need more training, public policy should expand those opportunities for Americans rather than redirect them toward temporary foreign labor.
 
American universities, particularly public institutions receiving federal taxpayer support, have a responsibility to serve the students and communities that fund them. They should be preparing American graduates to enter the workforce, not helping create financial incentives for employers to choose foreign workers over equally qualified Americans. American taxpayers should not be required to subsidize a system that can make American workers more expensive to employ than foreign graduates competing for the same positions.
 
The proposed fees place a cost on institutions that benefit from OPT and recommend students for the program. Schools that profit from international enrollment and promote post-graduation work authorization should bear a share of the program’s costs and have an incentive to recommend OPT responsibly. DHS cites fraud and worker-protection concerns in support of the rule. These concerns warrant serious attention in a program of this size.
 
We therefore urge DHS to:
 
1. Finalize the proposed OPT fees.
2. Strengthen oversight of OPT and STEM OPT employers, including site visits and enforcement of STEM OPT training plan requirements.
3. Publish regular data on OPT and STEM OPT employment, including employers, job titles, wages, and the share of participants who later transition to H-1B status.
4. Evaluate the combined effect of OPT, STEM OPT, and H-1B on entry-level employment opportunities for American graduates.
 
The future of the American workforce depends on developing the skills, experience, and productive capacity of Americans entering the labor market. Pushing American graduates toward unemployment or underemployment while expanding the supply of foreign workers risks undermining that goal.
 
A student visa should be a student visa. Post-graduation work authorization should be limited, accountable, and paid for by the institutions that benefit from it, not subsidized at the expense of American workers. The purpose of workforce policy should be to give Americans a fair opportunity to learn, work, and build careers in their own country. Immigration programs should not undermine that objective by expanding foreign labor supply without adequate safeguards, transparency, or accountability to the American public.
 
We urge DHS to finalize this rule.

A Washington, D.C. university education is uniquely enhanced by its focus on international relations and global business, which depends entirely on classrooms shaped by diverse geopolitical perspectives. As a pediatric neuropsychologist, I oppose the proposed fees for initial and subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT). These fees could jeopardize the training of future healthcare professionals, exacerbate existing workforce shortages, and ultimately limit access to specialized care for children and families.

Becoming a pediatric neuropsychologist requires extensive education, including a two-year postdoctoral fellowship in which trainees develop the specialized skills needed to assess and address children’s cognitive, behavioral, and emotional needs. OPT provides an essential pathway for international trainees to complete this required training in the United States. Additional fees could discourage institutions from accepting international fellows or make these training positions financially unsustainable, ultimately limiting the number of qualified professionals available to meet the growing demand for pediatric neuropsychological services. These added costs may be particularly burdensome in a field already facing significant financial pressures due to stagnant reimbursement rates and insurance-related limitations on clinical practice.

International trainees and professionals strengthen our healthcare and research communities by contributing specialized knowledge, clinical expertise, and diverse perspectives. Their work supports advances in understanding brain development and functioning and helps improve care for children with neurological conditions, cancer, developmental differences, and other complex needs.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to preserve access to OPT by eliminating the proposed fees. Creating additional financial obstacles to specialized clinical training would be counterproductive, particularly when children and families already face significant barriers to accessing appropriate care. Maintaining accessible OPT pathways is an important investment in the future healthcare workforce and in the well-being of the children and communities that workforce serves.


Clinical neuropsychologists are required to complete two-year fellowships following doctoral education to prepare for competent practice.  OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships.  The proposed fees would impose financial burdens on institutions employing international trainees, restricting their access to required training. The likely outcome would be the loss of talented international trainees who could be serving many unmet health needs in our communities.



International professionals contribute to the United States through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to brain-behavior functioning that improves the health of American children and adults.



For the benefit of all Americans, DHS needs to maintain the status quo by not imposing any  OPT fees on international students.  Fees would create barriers to professional development that would be counterproductive for our economy and harmful to preserving and treating the health of our families and friends.

Comment on DHS Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fee structure, including the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT periods.

I submit this comment as a naturalized U.S. citizen and as an educator in Speech-Language Pathology. I came to the United States as an international student on an F-1 visa, then went through the H-1B process, became a lawful permanent resident, and ultimately became a U.S. citizen. I understand personally how complex, expensive, and uncertain the immigration process can be. I also understand how important practical training opportunities are for international graduates who want to contribute their skills to the United States.

In Speech-Language Pathology, OPT is not simply an optional employment benefit. For many graduating international students, it is the only realistic way to complete the required clinical fellowship year after graduation. This supervised professional experience is essential for entering the field, gaining licensure, and becoming fully qualified to serve patients, students, families, schools, hospitals, clinics, and communities.

The proposed fees would create an impossible barrier for many international graduates in Speech-Language Pathology and other health and education professions. A $70,000 fee is far beyond what most new graduates can afford. It is also far beyond what most healthcare and education employers can absorb, especially for a clinical fellowship or training year. These employers have not traditionally had the capacity to pay for work visa sponsorship during this stage, and many already operate under significant financial and staffing constraints.

The likely result is that qualified international graduates would be unable to complete their clinical fellowship year in the United States. This would harm not only those graduates, but also the communities they would otherwise serve. Speech-language pathologists are needed in schools, early intervention programs, hospitals, rehabilitation settings, skilled nursing facilities, and community clinics. Many areas of the country already face shortages in access to speech-language pathology services. Creating a fee structure that blocks trained graduates from entering the workforce would worsen these shortages.

International students invest years of study, tuition, clinical education, and professional preparation in U.S. universities. In fields like Speech-Language Pathology, they also prepare to meet rigorous professional standards and serve populations with communication, swallowing, language, literacy, and developmental needs. OPT provides a bridge between academic training and professional practice. Removing that bridge through unaffordable fees would undermine the value of U.S. graduate education and reduce the ability of health and education systems to recruit needed professionals.

My own pathway from F-1 student to H-1B worker, permanent resident, and U.S. citizen allowed me to build a career, teach future clinicians, and contribute to the United States. I am deeply grateful for that opportunity. I am concerned that this proposal would close the door on future students who are ready and willing to contribute in the same way, particularly in professions where the public need is significant and the financial margins are limited.

I urge DHS not to finalize this proposed fee structure. At minimum, DHS should fully consider the disproportionate impact on health professions, education professions, clinical training years, and shortage fields. Any fee policy should be reasonable, evidence-based, and structured in a way that does not prevent qualified international graduates from completing required professional training or serving U.S. communities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

I am writing regarding the proposal regarding the following fees to apply for each F-1 nonimmigrant student to engage in OPT through a Student and Exchange Visitor Program-certified institution: $70,000 for initial OPT; and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT. The proposed rule would create a significant systemic barrier to completing this required training, as many programs would be unable to absorb the proposed fees and there may not be an alternative visa pathway available to these trainees.

As a former international student myself (for a bachelor's degree and a doctorate), and now a U.S. citizen, I have spent my entire educational and occupational career in the U.S. (25 years!). Having used OPT for my own training, I feel well-equipped to discuss how essential an accessible OPT program is. 

OPT is often essential for completing training specific to certain degrees, such as internships and fellowships. For doctoral level psychology trainees specifically, internship and fellowship are often requirements and OPT is the primary  mechanism through which international trainees obtain authorization to complete this training in the U.S. Interns and fellows are paid employees and contribute taxes, as well as social security and medicare payments to the U.S. economy. There is currently no fee for hiring a trainee who is an OPT work authorization and a jump to $70K hiring fee will make this impossible for the vast majority of employers (many who are in the health sector) to hire international students to complete these vital parts of training. 

International students contribute heavily to the U.S. economy (up to $43 billion annually) via their tuition, paying for housing, and general purchasing power during the years they study. If they are able to do authorized work during their training, they also contribute taxes, as well as medicare and medicaid payments. It seems only right that they should have accessible means to completing vital parts of their training (internships, fellowships) after contributing to the U.S. economy and training within the U.S. system. 

An alternative is H1B/J1 sponsorship, but this is not a viable option for many fellowship programs. Preliminary work by the Asian Neuropsychological Association suggested that only ~35% of fellowship programs accepted international trainees and either had a known visa mechanism in place or indicated that some form of sponsorship might be possible but not guaranteed. International trainees already face significant barriers under the current system, and this proposal would compound these existing visa-related barriers, likely leaving trainees without a viable pathway to complete our field's required training in the U.S.

While I support the need to reduce fraud, I ask respectfully that alternative measures are considered that would not limit hundreds of thousands of international students from completing their educational requirements, after many years of study and contribution to the U.S. economy.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to implement a $70,000 fee for Initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT or STEM extensions.
While the stated intent may involve administrative cost recovery, the exorbitant and unprecedented scale of this proposed fee represents a prohibitive barrier that will severely damage the United States’ ability to attract and retain global talent. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal based on the following critical points:

1. The Fee is Financially Prohibitive and Outpaces Tuition Costs

A $70,000 fee is completely disconnected from the financial reality of most international students and higher education institutions. This fee often exceeds the entire cost of annual tuition at many elite U.S. undergraduate and graduate programs, and doubles or triples the cost at public universities. Expecting students—or universities already facing tight budgets—to pay a fee of this magnitude prior to a SEVIS recommendation is fundamentally unrealistic. It transforms a standard post-graduation training authorization into an unattainable luxury, effectively pricing out highly qualified students from diverse economic backgrounds.

2. Draining Global Talent from the U.S. Workforce

The primary value of the OPT program is that it allows the brightest minds educated at U.S. institutions to transition their academic knowledge into practical expertise within the American economy. By imposing a financial penalty of up to $100,000 for a student to complete their training and STEM extension, the U.S. government will effectively shut the door on thousands of skilled graduates. Instead of being absorbed into the U.S. workforce, these individuals will be forced to take their talents, innovations, and tax contributions to competing nations with more welcoming immigration frameworks.

3. Long-Term Damage to U.S. Global Competitiveness

For decades, the ability to work temporarily post-graduation through OPT has been a primary selling point for U.S. higher education. If this fee is finalized, international enrollment will sharply decline as prospective students choose destinations like Canada, the UK, or Australia, where post-study work pathways remain accessible. Over time, this self-imposed talent drain will erode the United States’ competitive advantage in critical, high-growth fields like artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and engineering. American businesses will lose access to the domestic talent pipeline they rely on to lead global innovation.

Conclusion

A regulatory fee should never act as a de facto ban on a vital economic and educational program. The proposed OPT fees are disproportionate, economically counterproductive, and harmful to the nation's long-term interests. I strongly encourage DHS to reconsider this approach and explore sustainable, equitable administrative funding mechanisms that do not jeopardize America's standing as the premier destination for global innovation.
Sincerely,
Anonymous

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule, which would impose fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent participation.

As a higher education executive with extensive experience overseeing international university partnerships, enrollment strategy, and academic operations, I have witnessed firsthand the contributions international students make to American universities, local communities, and the broader U.S. economy.

I recognize the importance of program integrity and protecting American workers. However, these extraordinary fees would undermine U.S. competitiveness while threatening the economic benefits international students and OPT participants provide.

Economic Contributions to the United States

According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs during the 2024–25 academic year. These contributions extend beyond university campuses, supporting housing, transportation, hospitality, retail, and other industries.

NAFSA also estimated that declining international enrollment in Fall 2025 resulted in $1.1 billion in lost economic activity and nearly 23,000 fewer American jobs. While these figures reflect international education broadly rather than OPT specifically, post-graduation employment opportunities influence students' decisions to study in the United States.

OPT Supports American Jobs

A central argument against OPT is that international graduates take jobs that would otherwise be filled by American workers. However, economic research challenges this assumption.

A 2026 study by Kwon, Lee, and Monras examining the STEM OPT extension found that greater access to international STEM graduates stimulated business formation and increased demand for U.S.-born high-skilled workers.

The Economic Innovation Group's analysis reports employment gains equivalent to approximately 450 additional American workers per 100,000 residents in areas with greater STEM OPT exposure, alongside an approximately 1% increase in local firms, without declines in average wages.

These findings challenge the assumption that every international graduate displaces an American worker. International graduates can help businesses expand and create additional opportunities for domestic workers.

OPT Strengthens Innovation and Entrepreneurship

Forthcoming research by Johns Hopkins economist Michael Clemens, reported by Inside Higher Ed in October 2026, highlights OPT's potential economic benefits.

Preliminary findings associate every 100 current and former STEM OPT workers with approximately eight approved patents and two high-growth technology startups. The research also identifies increased patent activity among American colleagues, illustrating the benefits of collaboration and knowledge exchange.

These economic effects extend beyond STEM occupations, supporting additional jobs across industries.

The Proposed Fees Would Undermine U.S. Competitiveness

OPT is an important component of the value of an American education. International students invest substantial resources to earn U.S. degrees, often expecting to gain practical experience after graduation.

Requiring universities to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation would make participation financially unsustainable for many institutions, potentially eliminating access for eligible students based on institutional resources rather than qualifications.

In my professional experience, immigration policy uncertainty and post-graduation opportunities directly influence international student recruitment. The United States competes with countries offering attractive educational and professional pathways. Policies that diminish the value of a U.S. degree risk redirecting talented students, tuition revenue, and future economic contributions elsewhere.

Recommendation

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures to strengthen oversight and prevent fraud without undermining legitimate participation.

Protecting American workers and maintaining a competitive international education system are not mutually exclusive goals. Research suggests international graduates can stimulate innovation, entrepreneurship, and employment opportunities for Americans.

The United States should seek to retain the talent it educates, rather than introduce financial barriers that drive talent and economic contributions to competing economies.

Sources: NAFSA Economic Value Tool (2024–25); Kwon, Lee & Monras, CEPR DP21224 (2026); Economic Innovation Group OPT Analysis (2026); Inside Higher Ed (Oct. 23, 2026).

The OPT Fee Is Not a National Security Measure

I oppose the proposed OPT fees (FR Doc. 2026-20660). DHS says the fee, together with foreign-gift reporting under 20 U.S.C. 1011f, will help law enforcement detect "foreign governments or threat actors that may seek to use OPT to steal US technology." The design does not support that claim.

1. A payment is not a background check
DHS sets the initial fee higher because students "may not have been vetted by the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa." Paying $70,000 adds no check of identity, affiliations, funding or field. USCIS still decides the Form I-765 on the DSO recommendation and existing criteria. Footnote 115 points to extension-of-stay vetting under the Duration of Status rule, which the court in Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), postponed. If DHS sees a vetting gap at the OPT stage, the answer is a vetting step. The rule adds none.

2. A price screen favors sponsored applicants
The NPRM imposes no "limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source the requisite funds" and acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students or employers. So OPT goes to students whose fee someone covers. A student backed by a foreign government, a state-linked company or a well-funded intermediary can pay. An independent student cannot. A security screen should make sponsored access harder. This one makes it easier.

3. The money trail is not in the rule
DHS says schools "would need to track how they are funding the OPT fees" and that large foreign contributions "could serve as red flags." The proposed text of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i) requires only proof that the fee was paid. It does not ask who paid it. Section 1011f reaches foreign gifts and contracts totaling $250,000 or more from one source in a year, so a single $70,000 payment may never be reported. The NPRM does not say whether a fee paid by a family, a foreign employer or a foreign scholarship agency is a reportable gift or contract.

4. The fee ignores field and employer
DHS says a smaller pool would let it focus on "technology and critical infrastructure." The fee is the same for a nursing graduate at a local clinic and an engineering graduate at a defense supplier. DHS's own low scenario assumes schools will keep paying for STEM students, where technology-transfer concerns sit, and stop paying for non-STEM students, where they mostly do not. By DHS's model, the fee mainly removes the participants least relevant to security and sorts the rest by who can pay.

5. The record has one anecdote and no estimate
The only security case the NPRM describes is a student, helped by a shell company, who was convicted of acting as an agent of the PRC. He was caught and convicted under existing law. The benefits section of the economic analysis lists no national security benefit. In Presidents' Alliance, the court found DHS likely failed the rational-connection test for the companion rule because it relied on anecdotes and gave no reason why its mechanism "would prevent, deter, or mitigate" the incidents. The same gap is present here.

6. Better tools exist
DHS already holds the data a risk-based screen needs. Its PRA supporting statement calls SEVIS "a primary resource for conducting counterterrorism and counterintelligence threat analysis." Export control rules already require a license before controlled technology is released to a foreign national in the United States (15 CFR 734.13(b)). Proclamation 10043 (2020) already targets PRC graduate students tied to military-civil fusion. Targeted tools focus on high-risk cases. A flat fee charges everyone.

7. Security also means keeping talent
The proclamation DHS quotes in footnote 84 says H-1B abuse made it harder "to attract and retain the highest skilled subset of temporary workers," with the largest impact "in critical science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields." A fee on every OPT graduate raises the cost of retaining that same group.

8. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. If national security is a basis for any future rule, DHS should:
(a) identify the specific risks and the evidence for them;
(b) screen by risk factors such as sensitive field, critical-technology employer and foreign-government funding, using SEVIS and USCIS adjudication;
(c) if any charge remains, require disclosure of who paid it and bar payment by foreign governments and entities of concern; and
(d) state and estimate the security benefits in the regulatory impact analysis, or drop the claim.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment focuses on the economic impact analysis and the consideration of less burdensome alternatives. Even if DHS has authority to impose these charges, it must reasonably evaluate how institutions, students, and employers would respond to fees of this magnitude.

First, fee revenue is not a measure of the rule's full economic impact. Payments to the government are transfers, but reduced OPT participation could also cause real losses: foregone employment matches, reduced research activity, lower demand for U.S. educational programs, and disrupted hiring. DHS should estimate these effects separately, without double counting them as both transfers and costs. In particular, it should assess how lower participation could affect university enrollment, tuition revenue, employer recruitment costs, and economic activity associated with graduates working in the United States.

Second, the proposal's outcome depends heavily on whether educational institutions can and will pay the charges. Past OPT participation does not reliably predict institutional behavior when each recommendation carries an extraordinary new cost. DHS should publish sensitivity analyses for low, moderate, and high reductions in recommendations, explain the evidence supporting each scenario, and identify which conclusions change across scenarios. Without that analysis, projected revenues and economic impacts may create a misleading impression of precision.

Third, the burdens may fall unevenly on smaller institutions. Schools with limited budgets may be unable to fund recommendations, while wealthier institutions may retain that option. The result could be unequal access to practical training based on institutional resources rather than students' eligibility or compliance. DHS should assess impacts on small educational institutions and evaluate meaningful alternatives, including lower or graduated fees, exemptions, phased implementation, and risk-based oversight. The Regulatory Flexibility Act's framework for considering significant alternatives is relevant to this inquiry.

Fourth, the assumption that reduced OPT participation necessarily benefits U.S. workers requires evidence. An employer unable to hire a particular graduate might hire another worker, but might instead leave a position vacant, reduce a project, or move work elsewhere. DHS should examine occupation-specific substitution, hiring delays, and effects on research-intensive activities. Potential gains to some workers should be assessed alongside potential losses to employers, institutions, and local economies, rather than assumed to offset them automatically.

Finally, DHS should compare the proposal with targeted fraud-prevention tools: risk-based audits, employer verification, better use of existing reporting data, and enforcement against proven misconduct. Such alternatives could address abuse without imposing the same blanket financial burden on compliant programs. A meaningful comparison would estimate implementation costs, expected enforcement benefits, and burdens on legitimate participants.

I request withdrawal of the proposed rule. Before adopting any replacement, DHS should provide transparent participation scenarios, disaggregated institutional and labor-market impacts, and a quantitative or otherwise evidence-based comparison of reasonable alternatives. These questions go directly to whether the rule's predicted benefits justify its foreseeable costs.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and request withdrawal of the rule. My concern is the gap between the proposal's stated program-integrity objectives and evidence that the chosen financial mechanism would actually achieve them. A charge of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT may sharply reduce participation, but reduced participation is not itself proof of reduced fraud.

The agency should distinguish three outcomes: fewer applications, fewer fraudulent applications, and a lower rate of fraud among remaining applications. These are not interchangeable. A high fee could deter compliant schools and students while leaving better-funded bad actors able to continue. If DHS uses the number of OPT recommendations as a proxy for integrity, it risks mistaking exclusion for enforcement success. DHS should identify the outcome it intends to improve and the evidence connecting the fee amounts to that outcome.

A sound analysis should begin with a baseline. How many substantiated instances of OPT-related fraud have been identified, what forms did they take, and which weaknesses allowed them to occur? Allegations, referrals, confirmed violations, and enforcement actions should not be grouped together as if they establish the same facts. Where confidentiality prevents disclosure of case-level details, DHS could publish aggregate figures and explain their limitations. Without a clear baseline, the public cannot assess whether this proposal is tailored to an identified problem.

DHS should also explain why ability to finance a recommendation is a useful indicator of compliance. Financial capacity may reflect institutional wealth, fundraising ability, or budget priorities; none necessarily establishes whether a training placement is genuine. Conversely, an institution unable to pay an extraordinary charge may maintain strong oversight and a record of compliance. A uniform fee therefore risks creating false positives by excluding lawful activity without identifying the conduct that actually warrants investigation.

The proposal also raises a displacement question. If fraud is concentrated in particular practices or intermediaries, a broad fee may move misconduct into other channels rather than eliminate it. DHS should assess whether the rule could incentivize opaque financing arrangements, improper cost shifting, or attempts to circumvent recommendation procedures. Such risks are reasons to design targeted safeguards, not to assume that the most expensive option is the most effective one.

Before finalizing a rule, DHS should compare measurable outcomes under less restrictive tools. These include risk-based site visits, verification of training placements, focused audits of institutions with documented irregularities, and better coordination of existing reporting systems. For each option, DHS should discuss expected detection rates, false-positive rates, staff requirements, and procedural safeguards. Where evidence is insufficient to quantify an effect, DHS should acknowledge that uncertainty rather than substitute a deterrence assumption for demonstrated results.

Finally, DHS should describe how it would evaluate success after implementation. Would the agency track substantiated fraud per recommendation, the share of investigations resulting in confirmed violations, or the time needed to identify misconduct? Would it examine whether legitimate training opportunities were lost? A policy that measures only collections or falling application counts cannot establish that program integrity improved.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and develop a fraud-prevention approach tied to documented risks and verifiable performance measures. If DHS continues to consider a financial requirement, it should first publish the evidence supporting its expected effectiveness, analyze foreseeable unintended consequences, and explain why targeted oversight cannot achieve comparable integrity benefits with fewer burdens on compliant participants.

Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Yuanzhao Zhang, and I'm a faculty member in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Rochester, where I lead a research group working on nonlinear dynamics, complex networks, and machine learning for scientific forecasting. I teach graduate courses and mentor graduate students, and I'm submitting this comment in my personal capacity.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

I'm not an international student, but these fees would directly harm my research group, my department, and my field. Many of the PhD students I train and the colleagues I work with are international. For physics and data-science PhDs, OPT and the STEM OPT extension are often the bridge from graduation to a first postdoc or industry research job, and pre-completion OPT makes summer research internships possible.

A $70,000 fee per student, more than a year of a typical graduate stipend, plus $30,000 for each STEM OPT extension, would force universities either to absorb costs they cannot afford or to ration OPT recommendations. Either way, students we have spent years training would lose the chance to put their skills to work here. The strongest international applicants would choose programs in Canada, Europe, or Asia instead. When I recruit PhD students, the chance to gain U.S. work experience after the degree weighs heavily in where they decide to go.

My field sits at the intersection of physics, applied mathematics, and machine learning, and it depends on attracting top talent from around the world. A flat fee on every student does nothing to target fraud. It simply makes the U.S. a less attractive place to train and build a scientific career.

International students are part of the core workforce of American science. In physics and astronomy, they have made up about 42% of first-year graduate students for two decades and earn nearly half of U.S. PhDs (American Institute of Physics). Most of them stay. More than three-quarters of recent international physics and astronomy PhDs remained in the U.S. for work the year after their degree, and for many, OPT is how that transition happens. These fees would make it harder for that talent to stay, after U.S. universities and taxpayers have already invested years in training it.

The long-run stakes are large. Since 2000, immigrants have won 45% of the U.S. Nobel Prizes in physics (National Foundation for American Policy). Other countries are competing hard for the same students, and making the U.S. the most expensive place to begin a scientific career would hand them that advantage.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Yuanzhao Zhang

PUBLIC COMMENT OPPOSING OPTIONAL PRACTICAL TRAINING FEES
DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01; 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)  

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this rule imposing a $70,000 fee on schools for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT. Payment is required before recommendation; refunds are discretionary. DHS estimates 2,478 affected schools, $8.7–$16.9 billion in annual transfers, and annualized costs of about $4.1 billion. These costs may be passed to students or employers and are intended to deter participation.

1. Authority and fee design

The charge is imposed on schools, is unrelated to a specific service or demonstrated administrative cost, and goes to the general Treasury. A deterrent charge far exceeding processing costs resembles a tax, requiring congressional authorization. See 31 U.S.C. § 9701; *Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co.*, 490 U.S. 212 (1989). Its scale also raises the major-questions concern in *West Virginia v. EPA*, 597 U.S. 697 (2022). DHS should identify clear authority or withdraw the rule.

2. Evidence and fit

DHS cites suspected fraud and more than 10,000 students associated with “highly suspect” employers, but suspicion is not confirmed misconduct. The notice provides no underlying data or substantiated fraud rate. DHS reports 194,554 OPT participants in 2024; participation growth alone does not prove fraud.

The fee is poorly targeted: initial recommendations may occur before a student has an employer, potentially allowing shell-company operators to evade it while compliant schools pay. The cited concerns involve employers or brokers, yet the rule burdens every school and eligible student. Existing prosecutions demonstrate that targeted enforcement is possible.

DHS’s labor rationale relies largely on computer-science material, while the fee covers all fields. The notice does not quantify OPT’s effects on U.S. workers. STEM OPT already includes training plans and employer attestations. Address proven problems directly instead of imposing a blanket fee.

3. Arbitrary reasoning and inadequate analysis

DHS portrays schools as both the problem and gatekeepers, without defining what they must do to avoid a $70,000 charge. The rule adds no investigators, audits, or site visits despite DHS’s stated oversight limits; it also charges STEM OPT despite additional safeguards.

DHS says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet calls this a first step in a broader strategy. It must explain the connection between evidence and action. See *Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm*, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

The analysis inadequately considers students’, schools’, and employers’ reliance interests. A 60-day transition is unrealistic for institutions to budget or secure funding. DHS estimates 56% of affected institutions are small entities but does not meaningfully assess exemptions, tiered fees, phase-ins, or risk-based alternatives. Costs are substantial; benefits are not comparably quantified.

4. Harm and alternatives

Pre-completion and post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000; a STEM extension adds $30,000. Schools may refuse recommendations or pass costs to students. This screens by ability to pay—not eligibility, training value, or risk—may harm small institutions, non-STEM fields, and less-resourced students and employers. It could reduce enrollment, research, hiring, and economic activity while pushing trained graduates abroad.

DHS should instead verify employer identities and addresses, conduct risk-based audits, investigate and penalize proven misconduct with fair procedures, and address substantiated labor-market concerns directly. If fees are necessary, base them on actual administrative costs; tier them by risk; exempt or reduce them for small institutions; provide reviewable refunds; protect current students; allow at least two academic years for transition; and evaluate outcomes publicly.

I also oppose charging $70,000 again when a student begins OPT after moving to a higher degree level. DHS provides no evidence that this transition presents greater fraud risk.

5. Requests

Withdraw the fees. At minimum, extend the comment period 60 days after posting underlying data; publish the evidence behind the “more than 10,000” figure and any confirmed fraud rate; analyze cumulative effects with the July 17, 2026 rule on fixed periods of admission; and hold a public hearing.

Program integrity and worker protection are legitimate goals. But a universal charge is not targeted enforcement, is not shown to recover costs, and may exclude lawful participants without distinguishing them from wrongdoers. DHS should adopt focused, evidence-based, proportionate measures.

Respectfully,  
Anonymous commenter
