I want to put DHS's own answer to the test. The proposal acknowledges that universities cannot absorb $70,000 per initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 per subsequent one, and suggests schools can simply pass the cost to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers. That suggestion is the load-bearing wall of this rule — and it does not bear weight.

Take the F-1 student first. The fee is triggered when the Designated School Official enters the recommendation in SEVIS — before the student has an offer, an employer, or any U.S. income. A student who splits twelve months of OPT between pre-completion and post-completion use would trigger $100,000 for a single training allowance. International students already pay full tuition with no access to federal aid, and F-1 rules tightly limit their ability to work or borrow while enrolled. Demanding a six-figure sum from someone with no guaranteed income is not cost-sharing; it is a barrier most students cannot cross.

Spreading the fee across all students fares no better. DHS considered an exemption for small schools and rejected it — so the charge lands hardest on the institutions least able to spread it. And no university can mid-cycle levy a new charge on every enrolled student for a federal immigration fee: public schools answer to legislatures and boards, private ones to markets. Billing American students for DHS's program tax would punish the domestic population this rule claims to protect.

Employers are the least plausible channel of all. A recruiter hiring through ordinary campus recruiting has no contract with the graduate's university and no budget line for a SEVIS-entry surcharge. A school would have to invoice a stranger — "pay us $70,000 so we can recommend our own alumnus to work for you" — and when the employer declines, as it will, the recruiter simply hires the candidate who carries no surcharge.

The fees are even deposited into the general Treasury, which betrays the cost-recovery story. A fee no one can pass along, no school can absorb, and no small institution can escape is not a user fee — it is the end of OPT by another name. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT). DHS should withdraw the proposal or substantially revise it after providing stronger evidence and analysis. I support addressing fraud and protecting U.S. workers, but the proposed fee does not show how a particular OPT placement involves fraud or displaces a U.S. worker.

Labor-market effects require evidence. Immigrant workers can compete with U.S. workers for similar jobs, especially within the same occupation and location. But the broader research does not support treating every immigrant hire as a job taken from a U.S. worker. The National Academies found that immigration’s long-run effect on native-born workers’ wages overall was “very small,” and found little evidence of significant effects on overall employment. It also noted that effects can be greater for workers whose skills most closely match those of new arrivals. These findings concern immigration generally, not OPT specifically, and should not be presented as proof that OPT never displaces workers. [National Academies, *The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration* (2017)](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/23550/chapter/2).

Immigration can also expand labor demand. A Census Center for Economic Studies working paper, using U.S. administrative data on firms and founders, concluded that immigrants appear more like “job creators” than “job takers” when counted as both workers and entrepreneurs. That study is not an OPT-specific causal analysis, but it illustrates why labor-supply counts alone do not establish net job displacement. [Azoulay et al., CES Working Paper 20-44 (2020)](https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2020/adrm/CES-WP-20-44.html).

The proposed fee is not tailored to the alleged harm. The fee is imposed on a school for an OPT recommendation, is not tied to a particular employer, and may be passed to the student, employer, or other students. DHS estimates annual fee transfers of $8.4–$16.5 billion, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. Yet DHS acknowledges it cannot confidently predict the resulting decline in participation. Its claim that the rule “may provide job opportunities” to U.S. workers is a possibility, not a quantified estimate of displacement prevented. [91 Fed. Reg. at 64,575–76, 64,583–84, 64,591](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm).

DHS should explain how the proposed amounts are connected to the specific risks and costs it identifies. The rule relies on DHS’s authority to regulate the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission under [8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-120/t8/s1184/). If DHS also treats these assessments as user charges, it should explain their relationship to [31 U.S.C. § 9701(b)](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-118/t31/s9701/) and [OMB Circular A-25](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/Circular-025.pdf), which address fairness and the basis for federal user charges, to the extent applicable. The NPRM states that collections will go to the Treasury and will not be retained by ICE for OPT oversight. [91 Fed. Reg. at 64,576](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm).

Hiring decisions are not a test of anyone’s worth. A U.S. worker’s inability to obtain a particular job does not establish that the worker lacks talent; nor doesn OPT hire, by itself, establish displacement. Hiring can reflect qualifications, job fit, location, timing, and employer costs. DHS itself identifies a possible FICA tax incentive for some OPT hiring, which makes it especially important to assess actual wages and displacement rather than assume hiring is based on talent alone. [91 Fed. Reg. at 64,574](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/html/2026-20660.htm).

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agency action may be set aside if arbitrary or capricious, and the Supreme Court has required agencies to provide a reasoned explanation connecting the evidence to the action. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); *Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.*, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) ([opinion](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-463/pdf/USREPORTS-463-29.pdf)). I urge DHS to provide OPT-specific evidence on fraud prevalence, wages, and displacement; explain the basis for the fee amounts; and assess less burdensome alternatives, including risk-based audits, employer documentation, and penalties for proven violations.

As a stakeholder in the U.S. higher education and innovation ecosystem, I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed fee increases for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. International students already make a massive financial commitment to the United States, spending tens of thousands of dollars on tuition and living expenses. Imposing excessive additional fees on graduates seeking practical training places an unreasonable financial hurdle on individuals who have already heavily invested in their education.
If enacted, these changes will undermine the core purpose of the OPT program and discourage top global talent from choosing American universities. The negative impacts of a weakened talent pipeline will extend far beyond individual students, creating a damaging ripple effect across the country. U.S. universities risk losing their competitive edge in attracting bright minds from around the world, and American employers will face steeper challenges in recruiting highly skilled graduates to fill critical technical gaps.

I have worked in international education for 17 years and serve as the Principal Designated School Official (PDSO) at a small university. In that role, I would be the official required to confirm payment of a $70,000 fee before recommending a student for OPT. I oppose the proposed rule becuase of the economic and societal harms that other commenters have addressed. However, my comment will focus on this reason for opposing this rule: the proposed charge appears to be a tax, not a fee, and DHS has identified no statute that authorizes it. The views expressed here are my own and do not represent the positions of my institution. 

The proposed charge is a tax that Congress has not authorized (Section III.A)
•DHS cites no fee statute. The NPRM relies on general rulemaking authority and the authority to set the "time and conditions" of nonimmigrant admission (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1184(a)). Neither provision mentions fees.
•DHS acknowledges that it cannot retain the funds. Section IV.C states that collections will be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 because the statute "does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected." None of the $70,000 per participant cost would support SEVP's fraud investigations. DHS's primary estimate is $12.8 billion per year in transfers. A charge of that size that funds no service functions like a revenue measure.
•The Supreme Court has long distinguished fees from taxes. In National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), the Court explained that a fee is tied to a benefit conferred on the payer and is measured by its "value to the recipient," while assessments set to serve public policy are "in the nature of 'taxes,'" which are for Congress to levy. DHS describes this charge as a deterrent and ties it to no agency cost.
•Congress legislates immigration fees expressly. It created the SEVIS fee, based it on program costs, and directed where it is deposited (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)). It set the H-1B fraud prevention and detection fee at $500 (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12)). It has enacted nothing comparable for OPT.
•Recent decisions point the same way. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that authority to regulate does not carry authority to tax. In California v. Mullin (D. Mass. June 8, 2026), the court vacated the $100,000 H-1B payment as an unauthorized tax. The NPRM states that the OPT amount was chosen to be comparable to H-1B fees. 
The record does not support the amount or the target (Sections IV.A and IV.C)
•Scale. The largest fraud figure in the NPRM is an investigation that flagged more than 10,000 students at suspect employers. DHS counts 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024. Even if every single flagged case were fraud, that represents about 3 percent of OPT participants, yet the charge applies to all participants.
•The fraud described is employer fraud. The examples DHS cites focus on shell companies, staged worksites, and false offer letters. As the NPRM acknowledges, a student does not need a job offer when I recommend post-completion or pre-completion OPT. As a PDSO, I have no employer or direct connection between job duties and degree to review at that stage, and the fee proposal does not change that.
•Unworkable operational mandate. The rule misunderstands the administrative role of the PDSO and the OPT reporting functionality in SEVIS. Forcing a campus administrator to verify a $70,000 payment transaction before issuing an OPT I-20 recommendation In SEVIS —at a stage where no OPT employment is even allowed or can be recorded in the SEVP Portal or SEVIS for both pre-completion and post-completion OPT — places a new administrative and high-liability burden on the sponsor.
•No basis for the amount. DHS offers no cost study and no deterrence analysis. The figures are pegged to H-1B fees and to the cost of one or two years of education. DHS does not explain why the $70,000 is appropriate, or why a the fee would deter fraudulent actors instead of compliant schools.
•The fee funds no enforcement. DHS set aside site visits, training plans, and added reporting as too resource-intensive, then chose a mechanism that gives SEVP no additional resources.
In sum, the rule penalizes schools and students, the vast majority of whom comply with current regulations, while setting aside none of the money collected to prevent the fraud that is the rule’s stated rationale.
At an institution of my size, a per-student charge on the scale of a year's tuition would end OPT for students who have followed the rules, while leaving the fraudulent employers DHS describes without any additional oversight. I respectfully ask DHS to consider the issues I have addressed in this letter and withdraw the proposed rule. 
Sincerely,
Hunter Swanson, PhD

As a current international student, I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

I am a Professor of Engineering and the Engineering Undergraduate Program Chair at The Polytechnic School, Ira A. Fulton Schools of Engineering, Arizona State University. I strongly oppose this proposed rule. A $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee would not meaningfully reduce fraud. They would damage engineering education and weaken the U.S. technical workforce that universities like mine exist to build.

1. The rule would push talent we educate to our competitors. U.S. universities invest years of faculty mentorship, research funding, and lab infrastructure in international engineering students. International students make up a large share of U.S. STEM graduate enrollment, 54% of master’s and 44% of doctoral enrollments, and OPT is the primary pathway that keeps these graduates working in U.S. industry and research. Peer nations offer post-study work rights without six-figure barriers. Pricing OPT this way means the United States pays to train engineers and then exports them. 
icef

2. The fee is a wealth test, not an integrity test (Sections IV.C and V.A). DHS says the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students.” In practice, it selects students by whether an institution, employer, or family can pay $70,000. DHS itself acknowledges that costs may be passed on to students (Section IV.C). That fee exceeds a year of tuition at many institutions. Talented students from modest backgrounds, and the institutions that serve them, would be shut out first.

3. It effectively eliminates pre-completion OPT, which is core to engineering education (Section VII.A.5.d(3)). DHS anticipates that institutions will steer students away from pre-completion OPT to avoid paying $100,000 instead of $70,000. Internships and co-ops during the degree are central to how engineering programs develop professional competencies, especially at polytechnic, hands-on programs like ours. The rule treats this educational loss as a side effect rather than a cost.

4. The fee targets the wrong actors. The fraud cases DHS cites in Section IV.A involve shell employers, staged worksites, and sold offer letters. These are employer-side abuses. A fee charged to universities does nothing to stop a fraudulent employer. DHS also rejected targeted enforcement, such as expanded site visits and employer verification, mainly because a fee is quicker (Section IV.C). Speed is not a justification for a policy aimed at the wrong party.

5. The fees would not fund oversight. Section IV.C states that the fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to SEVP. The rule therefore does nothing to address the resource gap that DHS identifies as the core problem.

6. DHS’s own analysis does not support the rule (Section VII.A, Table 1). DHS lists monetized benefits as “Not Estimated.” Meanwhile, it estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion and transfers of up to $16.9 billion. It also finds that 841 of 1,389 small institutions, about 60%, would bear impacts above 1% of revenue in the transition year (Table 17). A rule with unquantified benefits and multibillion-dollar costs should not proceed.

7. Public universities and states were not considered (Sections VII.B.3 and VII.D.5). DHS excludes all 1,044 public institutions from its small-entity analysis. It also states that it did not consult state governments, even though state universities would bear these costs. This omission is significant for states like Arizona that depend on engineering talent for semiconductor and advanced manufacturing growth.

8. Reliance interests are dismissed (Section VI). Current students chose U.S. programs, and often took on debt, with a reasonable expectation that OPT would be available. DHS calls that expectation “speculative.” A comment period of roughly 30 days is also inadequate for a rule of this economic significance.

I also oppose the alternative of re-imposing the $70,000 fee at each degree level (Section V.A). It would further discourage students from pursuing the graduate study that our research enterprise relies on.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted, employer-focused enforcement instead.

I submit this comment in my individual capacity; my title and affiliation are provided for identification only, and these views do not necessarily represent those of Arizona State University.

Respectfully,
Dr. Nadia Kellam, Professor of Engineering; Engineering Undergraduate Program Chair, Associate Director for Strategic Initiatives, The Polytechnic School, Arizona State University

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training Fees rule. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee are excessive, poorly justified, and likely to cause substantial harm to American higher education and the economy.

First, DHS has not provided convincing evidence that fees of this magnitude are necessary to prevent fraud. The proposal identifies problems such as fraudulent employers, fabricated job offers, and shell companies. However, charging universities enormous fees does not verify whether an employer is legitimate or whether a student is complying with immigration regulations. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of compliance. A university unable to afford the fee may be entirely legitimate, while fraudulent organizations with sufficient resources may continue their activities. DHS should focus on investigating actual misconduct rather than imposing financial barriers on legitimate participants.

Second, the proposed rule could seriously weaken American universities. International students contribute substantial tuition revenue that supports faculty positions, academic programs, research, and campus operations. Making OPT financially inaccessible would discourage prospective students from choosing American institutions, reducing enrollment and university revenue. Meanwhile, universities attempting to preserve OPT opportunities would face significant additional expenses. These financial pressures could force institutions to reduce scholarships, cut academic programs, or increase tuition. American students and families could ultimately bear some of these costs.

The damage would extend beyond university campuses. In many rural communities and smaller cities, universities are major employers and important drivers of economic activity. International students rent apartments, purchase groceries, use transportation, and support local restaurants and businesses. Fewer international students would mean less revenue for landlords, retailers, and service providers, potentially harming American jobs and local economies. These consequences deserve serious consideration.

The proposal also threatens America's scientific and technological competitiveness. International students contribute to medical research, engineering, technology, and other fields critical to economic growth. OPT allows graduates educated in the United States to apply their skills and contribute to American innovation. If these opportunities become prohibitively expensive, talented individuals may choose to study and work in competing countries. The United States risks losing valuable researchers, entrepreneurs, and future technological advances.

DHS's economic analysis raises further concerns. The agency estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario, yet does not estimate annualized monetized benefits. Without demonstrating that the proposed fees would meaningfully reduce fraud, it is difficult to justify imposing such substantial costs on universities, students, and employers. Reducing OPT participation should not automatically be treated as evidence of successful fraud prevention.

A more reasonable approach would strengthen employer verification, expand targeted investigations, conduct risk-based inspections, and impose meaningful penalties on fraudulent organizations. These measures would address misconduct directly without undermining legitimate educational and employment opportunities.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Protecting immigration integrity should not come at the expense of American universities, educational affordability, local economic stability, scientific innovation, and the nation's long-term competitiveness.

American higher education does more than provide academic credentials; it develops specialized expertise, supports scientific innovation, and creates a pipeline of skilled professionals who contribute to American industries. Rather than strengthening American workers, a blanket financial barrier risks encouraging companies to move certain activities overseas, where qualified talent may be more accessible.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i). DHS should withdraw these fees and address fraud through targeted, risk-based enforcement.
Fraud should be investigated and punished. But a flat fee of this size does not distinguish a legitimate graduate, employer, or university from a fraudulent one. It distinguishes only who has access to money. Because the fee must be paid before a school can recommend a student, it will exclude capable graduates from less wealthy institutions, startups, smaller employers, and regions outside the largest technology hubs. That is a wealth test, not a fraud test.
The rule would sharply reduce the United States’ capacity to innovate, commercialize discoveries, and develop new technologies. OPT lets U.S.-educated graduates apply specialized knowledge in American laboratories, startups, manufacturers, hospitals, and technology companies. Destroying that bridge after the United States has trained these graduates hands their skills—and the inventions, companies, and jobs they may create—to competing countries.
The National Science Board reports that foreign-born workers account for 46 percent of U.S. science and engineering workers with doctorates, including 57 percent of doctoral-level computer and mathematical scientists and 58 percent of doctoral-level engineers. Temporary visa holders earned 38 percent of U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2024 and 61 percent of doctorates in computer and information sciences. These are precisely the fields in which the United States faces intense global competition.
Research published by the American Economic Association finds that immigrants are 16 percent of U.S. inventors but author 23 percent of patents and, including spillovers to U.S.-born collaborators, account for an estimated 32 percent of aggregate U.S. innovation. Research specifically on OPT finds that expansions increased STEM degree completions by 14–15 percent, including increases among domestic students rather than displacement. A 2026 STEM OPT study also finds large increases in first-time immigrant inventors near research universities, with no evidence of displacement of first-time native inventors.
The proposal’s own analysis confirms the danger. DHS estimates annualized costs as high as $8.2 billion. Its low-participation scenario assumes schools would stop recommending non-STEM graduates for OPT, and it estimates approximately $8.07 billion in annual opportunity costs after transition. DHS acknowledges that these losses include foregone output, contributions to the U.S. economy, employer productivity, and educational benefits. Its proxy still cannot capture lost patents, startups, research spillovers, future tax revenue, reduced enrollment, or long-run damage to America’s ability to attract talent.
The fee is poorly matched to its stated purpose. DHS acknowledges that the revenue would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and would not fund ICE, SEVP, investigations, or site visits. The proposal offers no evidence that a legitimate school paying $70,000 makes employment more genuine. A uniform financial barrier will deter legitimate participation at enormous scale while leaving the underlying verification problem unresolved.
DHS should instead use measures tied directly to risk: data matching across SEVIS, payroll, tax, corporate-registration, and worksite records; targeted and randomized site visits; employer attestations and training plans; rapid investigation of shared addresses, shell companies, phantom employees, and pay-to-stay arrangements; and meaningful sanctions against actors that knowingly facilitate fraud. Dear Docket Manager,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, 91 FR 64566). 

As an alumna of Virginia Tech with an advanced background in computing and human-centered technology, and as a practitioner working in the American technology sector, I have witnessed firsthand how essential Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the 24-month STEM OPT extension are to maintaining America's technological leadership, supporting world-class university research, and driving industry innovation. 

Imposing a $70,000 fee on institutions for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation (an aggregate of $100,000 per STEM graduate) is arbitrary, economically destructive, and exceeds statutory authority. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety for the following reasons:

1. Unprecedented Financial Burden on Public Land-Grant Institutions Like Virginia Tech
Under the proposed rule, the legal obligation to pay these exorbitant fees falls squarely on SEVP-certified institutions prior to entering an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. Public institutions like Virginia Tech cannot absorb these costs within state-allocated budgets and research funding. 

In premier computing and engineering programs, international graduate students play an indispensable role: they conduct groundbreaking research in artificial intelligence, robotics, and cybersecurity; staff labs; and serve as graduate teaching assistants. Forcing institutions to either absorb millions of dollars or pass these prohibitive fees onto students will decimate international student recruitment. Prospective students will simply choose peer institutions in the UK, Canada, Australia, or Germany, severing the academic talent pipeline that underpins American engineering excellence.

2. Severe Harm to U.S. Industry and Innovation Leadership
In the technology industry, OPT is not a loophole; it is the primary bridge allowing top U.S.-educated graduates to immediately apply their specialized technical skills in domestic industry. 

The proposed fees—representing a more than 150-fold increase over existing filing costs—will severely bottleneck early-career hiring in high-demand, cutting-edge technical sectors. Forcing these graduates out of the domestic labor market will not increase domestic employment; rather, it will handicap American research and development velocity and incentivize companies to expand their engineering and R&D operations abroad.

Setting fees intentionally designed to induce an estimated 80% contraction in program participation represents a de facto administrative dismantling of a program authorized under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Using disproportionate financial penalties to suppress legitimate program usage constitutes arbitrary and capricious agency action.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fee rule will irrevocably harm American higher education, cripple institutional research programs at universities like Virginia Tech, and compromise the competitive advantage of the United States tech sector. 

I strongly urge DHS to rescind this proposed rule.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees (FR Doc. 2026-20660). The rule moves the real OPT decision from federal eligibility rules to a school's budget choice, and it gives that choice no standards, no reasons, no review and no protection against discrimination.

1. A recommendation becomes a purchase
Today a DSO "must ensure that the F-1 nonimmigrant student is eligible for the type and period of OPT." Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), no DSO may enter a recommendation until the school pays $70,000, or $30,000 for a later OPT period. Eligibility is no longer enough. DHS says schools "would need to consider both the costs of OPT participation and the value each F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT participation brings to the institution," and that a DSO "can elect not to pay the fee for a particular F-1 nonimmigrant who is not a strong candidate." The rule never defines "strong candidate." DHS also declines to define "genuine educational value," saying schools are "in a better position" to judge it.

2. The test DHS sets is the school's interest
Value "to the institution" is not program integrity. A school may weigh rankings, employer partnerships, donor ties or whether a student can repay the fee. None of these measures fraud risk. The fraud DHS describes is employer fraud: shell companies, staged worksites, "phantom employees." For initial OPT the student need not have an employer when the DSO recommends. The school is asked to screen for a risk it cannot see.

3. DHS hands a bigger job to staff it calls overwhelmed
The NPRM says DSOs are "often overwhelmed by the program responsibilities and not fully trained." The rule adds a discretionary $70,000 decision per student. It offers no training, criteria or model policy for making them.

4. Discrimination risk with no guidance
With no neutral criteria required, schools may reach for proxies. DHS's lead fraud example involved false documents sold primarily to Chinese students. A school that rations recommendations by country, or by a student's ability to reimburse, invites claims under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. 2000d, which bars national-origin discrimination by recipients of federal financial assistance. DHS does not discuss this risk or tell schools how to avoid it. Schools will face legal exposure whether they ration or pay.

5. Students get no process at all
A student who meets every regulatory requirement can be refused because the school chose not to pay. The rule requires no written reasons, no internal review and no appeal. USCIS never sees the case, because no recommendation is entered. Timing makes this worse. Post-completion OPT must be requested within a set window after the program ends. A late or silent refusal can end the option for good. A separate comment addresses review of SEVP refund decisions. This gap comes earlier and falls on the student.

6. Equal cases, unequal results
Two graduates with the same degree, field and record will get different answers based on their schools' budgets and internal politics. Nothing in the rule promotes consistent treatment across 6,186 certified schools. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), a rule is arbitrary if the agency failed to consider an important aspect of the problem. Here DHS did not consider how private, conflicted, standardless decisions will be made, or by whom.

7. Requests
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any role for schools beyond today's eligibility check, it should:
(a) require a school to enter a recommendation for any student who meets the regulatory criteria, with no added payment condition;
(b) if any discretion remains, require each school to publish neutral written criteria tied to defined integrity factors;
(c) require written reasons for any refusal, a prompt internal review, and a toll of the OPT filing window while review is pending;
(d) issue civil rights guidance with the Department of Education and the Department of Justice before any rule takes effect; and
(e) place integrity checks at the employer stage, where DHS's own evidence locates the fraud.

I want to focus on who will actually decide the fate of American international enrollment if this rule takes effect — and it will not be DHS. I oppose this proposed rule. I hold an MS in Mechanical Engineering from a U.S. university and work on post-completion OPT. 

1. The rule penalizes students already on OPT. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3), the $30,000 fee applies only if the $70,000 fee was previously paid, so students whose initial OPT predates the rule would owe $70,000 for a STEM extension. The regulatory analysis confirms all Year 1 participants, "including those in STEM OPT," pay $70,000. DHS admits current students are differently situated (fn. 124) but gives them no protection. At minimum, exempt STEM extensions for students whose initial OPT began before the effective date.

2. The fee funds no enforcement. The NPRM states fees go to the Treasury general fund (31 U.S.C. 3302) and ICE cannot retain them. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service operates as a tax, which DHS has not shown INA 214(a) authorizes.

3. It is not targeted at fraud. DHS cites about 10,000 students linked to suspect employers, versus 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, under 3 percent. Yet the fee hits every participant, including employers already subject to E-Verify, I-983 attestations, and site visits. DHS rejected targeted alternatives such as expanded site visits because a fee is faster, not because they are less effective. Refunds are discretionary and unappealable, so even a legitimate student whose job falls through has no assured remedy.

4. There is no evidence of harm to American workers. The OMB A-4 statement lists benefits as "Not Estimated." DHS relies on unemployment rates for computer science majors and offers no data on engineering fields like mine. Research points the other way: Gong et al. (2019) found the 2008 STEM OPT extension raised domestic STEM employment 4.4-5.8% and wages 2.4-3.3%; a study reviewed by DOL's CLEAR database (Mukherjee, 2019) found no link to domestic STEM salaries or labor force participation; NFAP (2019) found more OPT approvals relative to U.S. workers associated with lower U.S. unemployment. STEM OPT employers already attest that trainees will not replace U.S. workers and will be paid commensurately (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C)).

5. The FICA rationale does not fit the remedy. DHS argues the payroll tax exemption makes OPT workers cheaper. That saving is 7.65% of salary, and DHS concedes (fn. 108) many STEM OPT workers already pay FICA after five calendar years. A $70,000-$100,000 fee per student is grossly disproportionate to that saving, and if FICA is the concern, Congress can address it directly.

6. DHS understates reliance. It says only about 20% of 1.4 million F-1 students used OPT in 2024, but that compares OPT users with all enrolled students, many of whom are still studying and not yet eligible. The relevant group is graduates, for whom OPT is a central reason to study in the U.S. Students like me enrolled, paid tuition, and accepted job offers under the current rules.

7. Costs far exceed any demonstrated benefit. DHS estimates $8.7-16.9 billion in annual transfers and up to $8.2 billion in annualized opportunity costs. In the transition year, 841 of 1,389 small institutions face impacts above 1% of revenue, and 116 above 20%. The fee is calibrated to the $100,000 H-1B fee, which a federal court vacated on September 30, 2026.

8. The fee distorts training choices. DHS admits it would push students away from pre-completion OPT because combining pre- and post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for the same 12 months. A rule that discourages legitimate, school-supervised training does nothing to stop fraud.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)
The proposed fee is not rationally connected to the fraud it is meant to address, because it falls on schools and students rather than on the employers the proposal identifies as the problem. DHS should withdraw it.

OPT is a regulated, degree-specific training program. Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii), OPT is "temporary employment for practical training directly related to the student's major area of study." It requires a Designated School Official's recommendation and USCIS employment authorization. Unemployment is capped at 90 days for post-completion OPT and 120 days in total through a STEM extension. The STEM extension adds more requirements. Employers must be enrolled in E-Verify and execute a Form I-983 training plan. They must attest that the student will not replace a U.S. worker and that duties, hours and pay are commensurate with those of similarly situated U.S. workers. They are subject to DHS site visits. The program is concentrated in professional fields: nearly half of 2024 OPT participants held computer science or engineering degrees.

The fraud DHS describes is already unlawful under this framework. The proposal cites shell companies, falsified employment records, and students reporting work for "highly suspect employers." Each is a violation of existing requirements by the employer, the student, or both. DHS already has authority to investigate, terminate status, and refer such conduct for prosecution.

A school-paid fee cannot screen employers. Post-completion OPT does not require a job offer at the time of the school's recommendation. When the proposed fee is paid, there is often no employer to evaluate. The fee therefore cannot distinguish a student who will work for a legitimate firm from one who will report work for a shell company. It applies equally to roughly 290,000 participants, nearly all of whom DHS does not accuse of anything.
The revenue does not fund enforcement. The proposal states that fees will be deposited in the general fund of the Treasury because the statute does not let ICE keep them. DHS justifies the fee partly by citing limited oversight capacity, yet the fee adds none.

This fails the reasoned-decision-making standard. An agency must articulate "a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made" (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). In September 2026, the District of Massachusetts postponed DHS's duration-of-status rule (Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. DHS) after finding no rational connection between the rule and its stated fraud and security goals, which rested on a small number of anecdotes. The OPT fee rests on the same kind of record and has the same gap between problem and remedy.
DHS should withdraw the proposed fee. If it pursues OPT integrity measures, they should be directed at employers. Examples include extending E-Verify and employer attestation requirements to all OPT, increasing site visits, and debarring employers found to have falsified records.

I oppose the proposed rule. 

1. DHS expects students to pay
The NPRM says schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." It says DHS will not impose "specific limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source the requisite funds." It treats pass-through to students as a benefit, because it would increase "the cost of participation for those whose intent is primarily to work." DHS also tells schools they can "mitigate their budgetary impact" this way. A final rule should assume many students will face the charge directly.

2. A price measures ability to pay, not intent
The fee is flat. It is the same $70,000 for every student regardless of field, salary, employer or family means. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1), it must be paid before the DSO recommendation, before USCIS acts, and before any paycheck. A student whose family has the cash can pay. A student with an equally real job offer and no family money cannot borrow against a job that does not exist yet. The RIA assumes "affected parties could collectively cost share to preserve OPT" whenever OPT's benefit exceeds the fee. That is true only for those with money in hand. Earlier comments raised credit constraints as an efficiency problem. The point here is who is excluded: the fee sorts students by family wealth.

3. DHS's own record shows wealth is no proxy for good faith
DHS says the fee will help "distinguish those who are committed to lawful participation from those who may seek to exploit the program." But footnote 82 of the NPRM cites a prosecution titled "Monrovia Man Sentenced to 4 Years in Prison for Scheming to Fraudulently Obtain Student Visas for Wealthy Foreign Nationals." A bad actor with resources pays the fee and proceeds. An honest student without resources is screened out. The rule's filter runs in the wrong direction.

4. Students have already passed a financial test
F-1 applicants must already show documentary evidence of financial support for their studies (8 CFR 214.2(f)(1)(i)(B)). The fee adds a second, much larger means test at the end of the degree, after families have already spent heavily on tuition. DHS reports that only about 20 percent of the 1.4 million F-1 students in higher education used OPT in 2024. It offers no data on the family income of that group, or on how many rely on OPT earnings to cover costs already incurred.

5. The Family Assessment is a one-sentence conclusion
Section N states the rule "would not affect family well-being" under section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999 (Pub. L. 105-277). Section 654 asks whether an action increases or decreases the disposable income of families and whether its benefits justify its financial impact on the family. It requires an adequate rationale for any rule that may harm family well-being. DHS gives no analysis. Yet DHS itself says the fee may be passed to students. A $70,000 charge on a student is a charge on the parents who sponsor that student. It also reaches spouses and children in F-2 status. F-2 spouses may not work (8 CFR 214.2(f)(15)(i)), so OPT may be the only lawful earnings in the household. A conclusion that contradicts the agency's own pass-through statements is not reasoned decision-making.

6. No distributional analysis
E.O. 12866 directs agencies to weigh "distributive impacts" and "equity" when choosing among approaches. The RIA uses unpaid fees as a proxy for all opportunity costs and never asks who bears them. It does not estimate how many students would pay personally, how many would be priced out, or how outcomes differ by family income or country. If the fee is shifted to "all students," domestic students would subsidize it through tuition. That is also unanalyzed.

7. Requests
I ask DHS to withdraw the rule. If DHS proceeds, it should:
(a) publish a real section 654 family assessment and a distributional analysis by income and payer, and re-propose with a new comment period;
(b) prohibit schools from charging the fee, directly or indirectly, to individual students or their families; and
(c) direct integrity resources to the employer-side and visa-fraud risks DHS itself identifies, where the screen measures conduct, not wealth.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)

The proposal does not adequately consider reasonable, less burdensome alternatives that would address OPT fraud more directly. Finalizing it without that analysis would be arbitrary and capricious. DHS should replace the fee with targeted employer-integrity measures.

1. The duty to consider alternatives. An agency acts arbitrarily when it fails to consider an obvious alternative within the scope of its existing policy (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 51 (1983)). In DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the Supreme Court set aside a DHS action in part because the agency did not consider a narrower option. In September 2026, the Northern District of California blocked the $100,000 H-1B fee policy because the agencies "failed to consider any alternatives or the reliance interests" of those affected (Global Nurse Force v. Trump). The Regulatory Flexibility Act separately requires a description of significant alternatives that would minimize the impact on small entities (5 U.S.C. 603(c)).

2. The alternatives the proposal dismisses. The proposal considered applying STEM OPT-style safeguards to all OPT, including site visits, training plans and reporting. It rejected them as insufficient and resource-intensive. It also considered and rejected an exemption for small institutions, which it says make up 56% of SEVP-certified schools. Neither rejection is adequately explained:
• "Insufficient" is asserted without evidence. The proposal does not show that the fraud it describes occurs among STEM OPT employers that already use E-Verify and training plans at rates similar to the rest of OPT.
• "Resource-intensive" compares the cost of enforcement with nothing. The relevant comparison is the full cost of the fee. That includes lost enrollment, lost tuition revenue that supports domestic students, and lost participation by compliant students, which the proposal does not quantify.
• The small-entity exemption is rejected without analyzing how a $70,000 per-student charge affects institutions with small budgets.

3. Alternatives the proposal does not address at all. Each of the following falls within DHS's existing authority over OPT and targets the conduct the proposal describes:
1. Employer verification in SEVIS before a student can report employment, such as matching the employer's identification number and confirming business existence.
2. Mandatory E-Verify enrollment and employer attestations for all OPT employers, not only STEM.
3. Risk-based site visits targeting employers with many OPT workers, no verifiable operations, or unusual reporting patterns.
4. Debarment of employers found to have falsified OPT employment, with criminal referral where warranted.
5. A cost-based compliance fee under IIRIRA section 641 (8 U.S.C. 1372) and INA section 286(m), deposited in the Immigration Examinations Fee Account to fund SEVP oversight.

The last option matters. The proposal's main resource concern is that OPT has outgrown DHS's oversight capacity. Yet the proposed fee goes to the Treasury's general fund and adds no capacity. A cost-based fee designed to fund oversight would address the stated problem. The proposed fee does not.

I support stronger oversight of the Optional Practical Training program to prevent fraudulent placements and protect U.S. workers. DHS should require verifiable employer-employee relationships, confirm that training is directly related to the student’s field of study, conduct risk-based audits and site visits, and impose meaningful penalties for shell placements, benching, or false reporting. I support adopting effective safeguards and urge DHS to finalize a rule that can be consistently enforced.

According to a review by the Institute for Progress, those estimates assume international enrollment does not change. That is implausible for a charge of $70,000 to $100,000 per student, often exceeding a year's tuition. Clemens (2026) estimates that OPT participation would fall 23% to 99%, depending on whether students, universities, or employers bear the fee. International master's enrollment would fall by 5% to 58%. If participation falls this sharply, projected collections fall too, and the forgone tuition, wages and taxes become the dominant costs.

2. Opportunity costs are understated. As NFAP analysts have noted, the analysis counts fee revenue as the main opportunity cost. The real economic loss is the value of training and work that no longer happens, including output, earnings and tax payments.

3. Evidence on U.S. workers is not engaged. The proposal says OPT depresses wages but cites no study showing OPT harms U.S. workers. The research record is mixed but mostly runs the other way:
• Kwon, Lee and Monras (2026) found that the 2016 STEM OPT expansion increased demand for U.S.-born workers with similar skills, apparently through firm creation.
• Zavodny (NFAP, 2019) found no evidence that OPT reduced job opportunities for U.S. workers, and found higher OPT numbers associated with lower STEM unemployment.
• Demirci (2020) found higher wages for U.S.-born STEM workers, but lower employment among recent U.S.-born master's graduates in the same fields.
A reasoned analysis would weigh these findings. The proposal does not mention them.

4. Effects on the H-1B pipeline are ignored. Most international STEM graduates who stay in the United States move from OPT to H-1B. H-1B workers who began as U.S.-educated F-1 students earn about 10% more than those hired from abroad (Sparber, 2026). Outsourcing-firm H-1B workers earn about $9,000 a year less than those who entered as students (Economic Innovation Group, 2026). By pricing U.S. graduates out, the fee shifts H-1B demand toward lower-paid workers hired from abroad. That cuts against DHS's stated aim of protecting U.S. wages.

5. Effects on domestic students are ignored. Shih (2017) found that each 10 additional international graduate students were associated with about 8 additional domestic students, through tuition cross-subsidy. A large drop in international enrollment would reduce domestic seats, particularly in master's programs where international students are a large share. In computer science master's programs, they were about 53% of enrollment in 2025.

6. Small-entity effects are understated. DHS says 56% of SEVP-certified schools are small entities and rejected an exemption. A $70,000 per-student charge is far more burdensome for a small college than for a large research university. The analysis does not quantify how many small institutions would stop recommending OPT, or what that would do to their enrollment.

Recommendation. DHS should withdraw the proposal. Any future proposal should model enrollment and participation responses using published estimates. It should count lost tuition, earnings and tax revenue, and engage the labor-market literature on both sides. It should also analyze effects on H-1B wage composition and domestic enrollment, and quantify small-entity impacts. It should then provide at least 60 days for comment on the revised analysis.

Several comments in this docket, including ICEB-2026-0100-0018, describe real frustrations: struggling with student loans, and feeling that college did not deliver what was promised. Those experiences deserve to be taken seriously. Some of the beliefs about international students in those comments are not accurate, though, and DHS should not rely on them. I want to offer my own experience as one data point.

"Schools fund foreign students with scholarships." I came to the United States on an F-1 visa. F-1 students cannot receive any federal student aid: no Pell Grants and no federal loans. My family and I paid for my bachelor's degree at a public university, at out-of-state rates several times what in-state students paid. Nationally, a majority of international students are funded primarily by personal and family sources. Only six U.S. colleges admit international undergraduates without regard to their ability to pay. Being able to prove the ability to pay, is also a key consideration during F1 visa interviews. 

"International students take jobs Americans need." OPT is limited by regulation to work "directly related to the student's major area of study." Mine was an entry-level software engineering job in my field. For STEM extensions, employers must use E-Verify and pay what similarly situated U.S. workers earn. They must also attest that the student will not replace a U.S. worker. OPT does not give international graduates any hiring preference. If anything, employers take on extra paperwork to hire us.

"How long can students stay?" OPT lasts 12 months, plus up to 24 more months only for STEM graduates. Students who stay unemployed beyond 90 days (120 days with a STEM extension) fall out of status. After OPT, I moved to H-1B, and I now pay well over $40,000 a year in taxes.
"The fee should go to American students." It would not. The proposal sends every dollar to the Treasury's general fund, not to scholarships, loan relief or tuition support. And because international tuition helps fund seats for domestic students, driving international students away would likely leave fewer resources for Americans, not more.

I share the goal of making higher education more affordable for Americans. This fee does not advance it. I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal.

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees (RIN 1653-AB01)

The proposal's central justification is DHS's limited capacity to police OPT fraud, but its fee adds no capacity. That gap undermines the rule's rationality and confirms that the charge is a revenue measure, a tax DHS lacks authority to impose.
The stated problem is resources. The proposal says OPT's growth has outpaced DHS's ability to review and investigate employers. It cites the burden of OPT investigations and suggests the program might have to shut down without new fees. Among the benefits it claims is "alleviating burdens imposed on DHS tied to OPT investigations."

The remedy provides no resources. The proposal states that collections will be deposited in the Treasury's general fund as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302), because "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected." No portion of the projected $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year would fund SEVP oversight, site visits or investigations.

The only remaining mechanism is deterrence of all participants. Without new resources, the fee can reduce DHS's burden only by reducing participation across the board. The proposal does not explain why excluding large numbers of compliant students is a rational way to address fraud by a minority of employers. That is the kind of mismatch between "the facts found and the choice made" that State Farm forbids (463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)).
Congress's approach confirms the problem. When Congress has wanted an anti-fraud charge in a high-skilled program, it has enacted one itself, in a fixed amount and earmarked for fraud prevention and detection (INA section 214(c)(12)). When it authorized a student fee, it limited the use of the fee to SEVP purposes (IIRIRA section 641(e)). DHS's choice to raise general revenue rather than fund oversight is not a choice the statutes leave to it.

The revenue character makes this a tax. A charge not based on any cost, deposited in the general fund, and projected to raise billions annually bears every marker of a tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). In 2026 the Supreme Court held that a general power to "regulate" does not include the power to tax (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump). The District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee policy on similar reasoning (California v. Noem).

Requested action. DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it needs resources for OPT oversight, it may propose a cost-based fee under IIRIRA section 641 or INA section 286(m), supported by a cost study and deposited for program use, or seek appropriations from Congress.

Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed $70,000 OPT Fee

Dear Department of Homeland Security Officials,

I respectfully submit this comment expressing serious concerns regarding the proposed $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT). While I acknowledge the government's responsibility to protect American workers and prevent immigration fraud, this proposal could create significant economic, educational, and workforce challenges.

1. Excessive Financial Burden

International students already make substantial financial investments in American education, often relying on personal savings, family support, and educational loans. Imposing a $70,000 fee, whether directly or indirectly through universities and employers, could make practical training financially inaccessible to many qualified graduates.

2. Negative Impact on the U.S. Economy

International graduates contribute valuable skills to critical industries, including engineering, technology, healthcare, and scientific research. OPT allows graduates to apply their education while supporting American businesses and innovation. Restricting these opportunities through excessive fees could discourage employers from hiring international graduates and reduce access to specialized talent.

3. Reduced Competitiveness of American Universities

The United States attracts international students because of its academic excellence and professional development opportunities. Such substantial fees could discourage prospective students from choosing American universities, potentially reducing international enrollment, tuition revenue, and research contributions. Other countries offering more accessible post-graduation employment pathways may become increasingly attractive.

4. Unfair Impact on Current Students

Many international students are already pursuing degrees after making significant financial commitments based on existing educational and practical training opportunities. Introducing such a substantial fee without transitional protections could undermine their academic and professional plans.

5. More Practical Alternatives

Immigration fraud concerns should be addressed through stronger employer verification, improved compliance monitoring, targeted audits, and stricter penalties for fraudulent activities. These measures would address misuse without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on legitimate students and institutions.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee and adopt a reasonable, evidence-based approach that balances immigration enforcement with economic competitiveness and educational opportunities.

The United States benefits from attracting talented international students who contribute to its workforce, research, and technological advancement. Immigration policies should preserve these contributions while maintaining appropriate oversight and accountability.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Respectfully,  
International Graduate Student in Engineering

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to describe how OPT will actually end if this rule takes effect — not with a vote, a press release, or a Federal Register notice terminating the program, but quietly, office by office, one refused recommendation at a time.

Consider what an OPT recommendation is today. A Designated School Official verifies a student's enrollment, enters a field in SEVIS, and issues an updated I-20. It is a routine administrative act that takes minutes and costs the school almost nothing. That is why OPT works: it is a low-friction bridge between graduation and employment, administered by the people closest to the student.

This rule turns that keystroke into a $70,000 expenditure decision. No DSO has the authority to spend $70,000 on a single student's record. Every recommendation would have to climb the chain — to a dean, a budget officer, a chief financial officer, perhaps a board committee — for approval that no institution will routinely grant. Schools will respond the only way bureaucracies can: they will create rationing committees, set annual caps, screen by major or by ability to pay, and quietly stop recommending OPT for most students. Many will simply suspend recommendations rather than build an approval apparatus for a program the fee has made unaffordable.

The result is a program that dies without ever being repealed. Students will not receive a denial letter they can appeal or a policy change they can debate. They will get silence — a recommendation queue that never moves, a DSO who cannot say yes because no one above them will sign off on the cost. DHS concedes that some schools would "simply stop recommending OPT," as though that were a footnote. It is the mechanism itself.

Congress created OPT and has kept it on the books for decades. If it should end, that decision belongs in the open, by a vote, with reasons stated. Ending it by turning a routine administrative act into a six-figure procurement decision is not regulation. It is repeal by friction, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposing exorbitant fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students. While I recognize the Department’s stated goals of protecting system integrity and combating fraud, these proposed fees are deeply punitive, economically counterproductive, and fundamentally arbitrary. If enacted, this rule will devastate higher education institutions, cripple the U.S. economy's ability to attract top global talent, and effectively abolish the legal pathway for practical training.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule for the following critical reasons:

1. Prohibitive Financial Barriers and Economic Disproportion
The proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent extensions are entirely unmoored from any reasonable administrative cost-recovery model. Most international students invest significant personal and family savings to pursue higher education in the United States. Requiring an upfront or post-graduation payment tens of thousands of dollars higher than the tuition of many degree programs makes OPT financially impossible for the vast majority of qualified students. This transforms a temporary, merit-based work authorization program into an exclusionary luxury available only to the ultra-wealthy.

2. Severe Damage to U.S. Higher Education Competitiveness
U.S. universities rely on international students to enrich academic environments, support research, and contribute billions of dollars to local and national economies. Optional Practical Training, particularly the STEM extension, is a vital, legally established component of the F-1 educational experience, providing students with critical real-world application of their studies. Imposing these crippling fees will cause international student enrollment to plummet as prospective students choose more welcoming destination countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany, where post-study work pathways remain accessible and reasonably priced.

3. Undermining Key U.S. Industries and Workforce Needs
U.S. employers across technology, engineering, healthcare, finance, and advanced manufacturing face chronic talent shortages. OPT serves as a vital bridge allowing graduates to transition into the U.S. workforce, often serving as the primary pipeline for H-1B filings and high-skilled employment. By erecting a $70,000 financial wall, DHS will deny employers access to the world-class graduates trained by American universities. Rather than "protecting U.S. workers," starving vital sectors of specialized talent harms innovation, decreases domestic productivity, and incentivizes companies to offshore research, development, and high-tech jobs.

4. Disproportionate Burden on Entry-Level Workers
OPT is designed for recent graduates who are, by definition, at the very beginning of their professional careers. Entry-level salaries for practical training participants rarely accommodate an immediate out-of-pocket burden of $70,000, nor can standard entry-level employers reasonably absorb such a fee on behalf of temporary interns or junior staff. This fee acts as an absolute market exclusion rather than a regulatory safeguard.

5. Lack of Narrowly Tailored Solutions to Combat Fraud
While DHS cites fraud prevention as a primary justification, imposing a catastrophic, across-the-board financial barrier is an overbroad and disproportionate policy mechanism. Existing enforcement mechanisms, such as enhanced employer validation, SEVIS tracking, and strict reporting requirements through Designated School Officials (DSOs), already exist to police bad actors. Penalizing thousands of legitimate, law-abiding students and hurting American academic institutions to target isolated instances of fraud is neither sound public policy nor an effective regulatory solution.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fee rule threatens to inflict long-term damage on the global preeminence of the U.S. higher education system and weaken the competitiveness of the American economy. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). The rule charges universities $70,000 to let their own new graduates work in university research labs, and the NPRM never considers that case. 

1. The NPRM never discusses research employment

The preamble and the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) do not discuss academic research, laboratories or postdoctoral appointments. The RIA groups everyone who might lose from the rule into three classes: schools, students and "employers." It then says employers "may face productivity losses if they are unable to replace" OPT participants. It does not ask which employers those are. For many graduate-level OPT participants, the employer is a university, a teaching hospital or a nonprofit research institute. DHS should identify how many OPT and STEM OPT participants work for such employers before it sets a fee that applies to them.

2. When the school is the employer, the school-screening theory does not apply

DHS says the fee will make schools "more selective and deliberate" and give them "a direct stake in the integrity of the OPT program." The fraud it describes is employer-side: shell companies, residential addresses listed as worksites, and "phantom employees." Now take a university that hires its own new graduate as a research associate. The recommending school and the employer are the same institution. It is SEVP-certified, it is already subject to SEVP review, and its lab is a real worksite with payroll records. The fee asks that school to screen itself, and charges it $70,000 for doing so. None of the red flags DHS lists apply. The rule text in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) makes no distinction by employer.

3. The H-1B cap rationale does not reach these employers

DHS says the fee is meant to stop students "trying to circumvent the H-1B visa cap and fee requirements." It cites the 65,000 cap and the 20,000 advanced-degree allocation (footnotes 100 and 101). The same statute exempts from those numerical limits workers employed at an institution of higher education, at a related or affiliated nonprofit entity, or at a nonprofit or governmental research organization. 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(A)-(B). An OPT graduate working in a university lab cannot be evading a cap that does not apply to that lab. The NPRM cites 1184(g)(5)(C) but never mentions (A) or (B). DHS should explain why a fee justified by cap evasion should fall on employers Congress placed outside the cap.

4. Grant-funded labs cannot "cost share" around the fee

DHS uses unpaid fees as a proxy for lost value. It assumes that if OPT is worth more than the fee, the parties "could collectively cost share to preserve OPT." Many research positions are paid from fixed sponsored-research budgets. A principal investigator cannot add $70,000, or $100,000 for initial OPT plus a STEM extension, to an award already made. Much of the value of research goes to the public through published results, so no single party can capture enough of it to pay the fee. The NPRM also does not say whether the fee is an allowable cost on federal awards under 2 CFR part 200. If it is, research appropriations would be routed to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302. If it is not, the school must pay from its own funds. Either answer has costs that the RIA leaves out.

5. The labor evidence does not cover research

The labor-market evidence in Section IV.B concerns computer occupations and wages in computer science. DHS's low scenario predicts the fee will mostly remove non-STEM OPT. Neither addresses research staff in the life sciences, physical sciences or engineering. DHS offers no finding that OPT researchers in university labs displace U.S. workers or depress their wages.

6. Request

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds with any fee, it should (a) exempt recommendations where the employer is the recommending institution or an employer described in 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(A)-(B); (b) estimate the number of OPT and STEM OPT participants working for those employers and the effect of the fee on funded research projects; and (c) state whether the fee may be charged to federal awards. These points should be addressed in a re-proposed rule open for public comment.

1. A high price is not proof of compliance.

Fraudulent job offers, wage violations, and misuse of practical training should be investigated and penalized. But a large fee does not determine whether an employer is legitimate, a training position is meaningful, or American workers are protected. Well-funded bad actors might absorb the cost, while compliant schools and smaller employers could lose access to the program. DHS should explain what evidence shows that these fee levels would reduce misconduct more effectively than employer verification, targeted audits, wage enforcement, and penalties for documented violations.

2. The proposed fees could impose significant costs on U.S. institutions and communities.

Ten initial OPT recommendations would cost an institution $700,000. Schools might have to reduce recommendations, divert resources from teaching and research, or attempt to pass costs to students or employers. These outcomes could affect Americans who work at universities and businesses near campuses.

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed about $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. These figures concern international education overall, not OPT alone. Still, they illustrate why federal policy affecting the attractiveness of U.S. universities deserves a careful assessment of possible enrollment and local economic effects.

3. America should evaluate both labor protection and long-term competitiveness.

The United States invests in educating students in engineering, science, business, and other fields. Practical training can enable U.S. employers to use skills developed at American institutions. If access becomes prohibitively expensive, some graduates may seek work elsewhere, and American firms may lose candidates they would otherwise hire. This possibility does not eliminate valid concerns about competition for jobs or wages. It does mean DHS should evaluate both sides with relevant evidence rather than assume that fewer OPT participants necessarily benefit U.S. workers.

4. The economic analysis and fee amounts deserve stronger justification.

DHS acknowledges possible employer productivity losses and university enrollment effects, yet these effects are difficult to quantify. Using the amount of an unpaid fee as a proxy for lost opportunities may not capture the value of lost output, research, tuition revenue, or local spending. DHS should explain why $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary, what measurable reduction in fraud is expected, and how the costs compare with less burdensome alternatives.

5. Enforcement resources should match the stated problem.

The proposal indicates fee revenue would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than directly fund ICE oversight. If gaps in oversight contribute to abuse, DHS should consider whether focused investigations, better reporting, and employer compliance checks would be more effective and more proportionate.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and consider a targeted, evidence-based approach. Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are important goals. They should be pursued in a way that also safeguards American educational institutions, employers, taxpayers, and long-term economic competitiveness.

References: DHS, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026); NAFSA, International Student Economic Value Tool (2024–25).
