I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. I am a student current pursuing my Master in the United States. 

Supporters of the rule, and the preamble itself (Sections IV.B and VI), rely on two claims: that F-1 is a study visa and should carry no work rights, and that restricting OPT will return jobs to American workers. Both are mistaken.

1. Practical training is part of studying, not a departure from it.

Practical training has been part of the F-1 framework since 1947, and Congress has revised immigration law many times since without eliminating it. OPT must be directly related to the student’s major area of study (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)). In engineering, architecture, accounting, public health and many other fields, applied training is how an education is completed, and many professional licenses require supervised experience. The D.C. Circuit upheld OPT and the STEM extension as lawful conditions of F-1 status in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022), and the Supreme Court declined review in 2023.

The rule is also internally inconsistent. If work were truly incompatible with study, a fee would not cure the problem. A $70,000 charge does not make OPT more educational; it only makes it available to students whose schools or families can pay. That rewards wealth, not merit or educational purpose.

Our competitors understand this. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Germany all offer post-study work options as part of international education. Pricing out OPT sends the strongest students to those countries.

2. Restricting OPT will not bring manufacturing or other jobs back to Americans.

OPT is available only to students who have completed at least a full academic year at a U.S. college or university, and the job must relate to their degree. Participants are mostly graduates in STEM and business fields, and most come from India and China. They are not the workforce in factories, construction, agriculture or service industries. The rule’s own labor analysis (Section IV.B) focuses on computer occupations, not manufacturing. Workers from Mexico and other countries in those sectors are in entirely different visa categories, which this rule does not touch.

Manufacturing jobs left largely because of automation, global supply chains and trade, not because of international graduates. Rebuilding domestic manufacturing in semiconductors, batteries and advanced materials requires engineers and scientists, and U.S. universities train many of them on F-1 visas. Driving them out deepens the talent shortage that slows new factories.

When companies cannot hire talent here, they hire it abroad. Work moves to offices in Toronto, Bangalore or London, along with the American support jobs around it. Many major American companies were founded by immigrants who first came as students.

The rule also harms American students directly. DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to “all students” (Section IV.C), meaning higher tuition for Americans. Lost international enrollment also cuts revenue that supports programs, faculty and local jobs.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

Comments of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) on Optional Practical Training Fees, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Secretary Mullin: 

The Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) respectfully urges the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw its proposed rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026). 

FASEB represents 21 scientific societies and more than 100,000 researchers in the biological and biomedical sciences. For more than a century, we have advanced biomedical research and education in the United States. American labs compete for the best scientists in the world. Many scientists who now lead those labs, train American students, and serve in our societies first came here as international students. OPT was often their bridge from a U.S. degree to a U.S. research career. It let the nation keep the return on its investment in their training. Today, our members train, mentor, and work alongside the next generation of international scientists. This rule would decide whether those scientists stay to advance American research. 

FASEB supports DHS's goal of preventing fraud in OPT. The proposed rule does not show that a fee would advance that goal. It would require schools to pay $70,000 to $100,000 or more for each international student who uses OPT, whether or not any fraud is involved. DHS estimates that schools would pay $12.4 billion a year. Under the proposed rule, that money would go to the general Treasury, not to fraud prevention or oversight. The rule reports no fraud rate, and it cites no OPT fraud case involving a research institution.

DHS states that it cannot confidently predict how much OPT participation would decline. However, the available evidence indicates it would fall sharply. If schools pay the fee, independent estimates project that OPT participation among bachelor's and master's graduates would fall by nearly two-thirds at $70,000 and by about four-fifths at $100,000. Doctoral graduates have even more at stake. Two-thirds of international doctoral graduates on F-1 visas are approved for OPT. Temporary visa holders make up 58% of postdoctoral researchers in U.S. science, engineering, and health. This rule would narrow the path that brings these highly skilled, U.S.-trained scientists into our research workforce. More broadly, researchers estimate that a sustained one-third decline in international STEM graduates entering the U.S. workforce could reduce annual U.S. economic output by $240 billion to $481 billion after a decade (Clemens, Neufeld, and Nice, 2026).
 
FASEB's recommendations: 
1.	Withdraw the proposed fees. DHS has not shown that fraud is common or that a fee would reduce it. The fees would go to the Treasury, not to oversight. DHS should pursue targeted oversight of the employers and schools it has already identified. 

2.	Exempt universities and nonprofit research organizations. Congress exempts these employers from the H-1B training fee and the H-1B cap. DHS's concern about avoiding the cap does not apply to them, and none of the OPT fraud cases DHS cites involves a research university or nonprofit research organization. To implement this exemption, schools should not be charged the OPT fee for students employed by universities or nonprofit research organizations. 

3.	Exempt the STEM OPT extension. It already requires E-Verify, a signed training plan (Form I-983), and DHS site visits. DHS's own STEM OPT site visits uncovered some of the fraud it cites. 

4.	Do not extend the $70,000 fee to each new degree level. The rule sets no maximum fee per student. This option would multiply fees for students who pursue advanced degrees.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees for the following reasons:
 
1. These positions can be scientifically valuable without generating enough direct revenue to justify an additional $100,000 cost per person. A principal investigator with a limited grant budget may be unable to retain a talented researcher even if that researcher is essential to the project.

2. DHS says the proposal is intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, protect U.S. workers, and prevent employers from using OPT to circumvent other employment-based visa requirements. However,  the fee is triggered by an institution's OPT recommendation—not by a finding of fraud, underpayment, or displacement of an American worker. Consequently, a legitimate university hiring an exceptionally qualified graduate could face the same fee as an institution whose practices raise serious concerns. A more proportionate approach would target documented violations, improve compliance audits, enforce existing labor protections, and impose penalties where misconduct is established.

3. It treats educational and employment circumstances as interchangeable: OPT is associated with education; it allows students to gain practical experience related to their field of study. The proposed fee, however, is partly designed to prevent OPT from being used to bypass the H-1B system. That rationale risks treating legitimate educational training as an alternative route to ordinary employment-based immigration. Yet a graduate undertaking a research fellowship, for example, may be gaining experience directly connected to their degree rather than exploiting a visa category. The distinction matters because a policy designed around suspected misuse can discourage legitimate educational and scientific activity.

5. It could shift the costs onto people who had no role in the alleged abuse: If a university spreads these expenses across its general budget, domestic students and other research programs could also bear some of the cost. If it passes them to individual students or employers, those parties bear the burden instead.

In other words, the proposal creates a large financial penalty without ensuring that the people who ultimately pay are responsible for any misconduct.


6. It could undermine U.S. competitiveness

International graduates trained in the United States are already familiar with U.S. institutions, research practices, and professional networks. OPT offers a way to retain some of that expertise after graduation. If universities and employers cannot afford to retain these graduates, some may pursue opportunities in other countries. That could weaken the return on U.S. educational investment and make it harder for American institutions to recruit international students in the first place. The magnitude of these effects remains uncertain, but they are legitimate concerns in evaluating the proposal.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations for F-1 international students. **1. Financial Burden on International Students**

OPT allows eligible international students to gain practical experience related to their academic programs. Students and their families invest substantial resources in tuition, housing, insurance, and other educational expenses. Although the proposed fees would be charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, institutions could pass on costs through higher tuition, reduced financial assistance, or fewer OPT opportunities. This could disproportionately affect students from modest-income families.

**2. Harm to Universities and the Economy**

International students contribute to American universities through tuition, research, and academic participation. The proposed fees could discourage institutions, especially smaller colleges, from recommending eligible students for OPT. Reduced enrollment and participation could affect university finances, research programs, employment, and local businesses. DHS should consider these consequences before adopting the proposal.

**3. Loss of Skilled Talent and Innovation**

The United States attracts international students through its educational excellence, research opportunities, and career development pathways. These graduates contribute to technology, healthcare, scientific research, and entrepreneurship. Excessive OPT fees could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, weakening America's ability to attract skilled workers and remain globally competitive.

**4. Impact on Employers and Workforce Development**

OPT helps eligible graduates apply their academic knowledge in professional settings. Employers benefit from their specialized skills and experience. If universities reduce OPT recommendations because of the proposed fees, employers could face recruitment challenges and lose access to qualified graduates. Protecting American workers is important, but this goal should be pursued without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational and workforce opportunities.

**5. Disproportionate Fees and Better Alternatives**

DHS has a responsibility to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, these objectives do not automatically justify fees of $70,000 and $30,000. DHS should explain how these amounts were determined and provide evidence that they are necessary and proportionate.

Less burdensome alternatives include stronger verification procedures, targeted compliance reviews, improved reporting systems, and appropriate penalties for proven violations. These measures could address legitimate concerns without creating excessive financial barriers for educational institutions and eligible students.

**6. Wider Economic and Family Consequences**

Many international students rely on family savings, scholarships, and loans to complete their education. The proposed fees could increase financial pressure on institutions, resulting in reduced student support and fewer practical training opportunities. International students also contribute to local economies through housing, transportation, food, and other spending. Reduced enrollment or OPT participation could harm universities, employers, and local communities.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the proposal's educational, financial, economic, and workforce consequences before proceeding.

**Conclusion and Request**

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, regulations should be evidence-based, proportionate, transparent, and fair to educational institutions and eligible international students.

At a minimum, DHS should reconsider the proposed fees, explain their justification, evaluate their likely consequences, and consider less burdensome alternatives.

The United States should continue promoting educational excellence, research, innovation, and responsible workforce development while protecting the integrity of its immigration system. Excessively high OPT fees could undermine these goals and encourage talented international graduates to contribute their skills to other countries instead.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and adopt a balanced approach that protects American workers without imposing unreasonable financial burdens on universities or restricting legitimate opportunities for eligible international students.

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international student from Sri Lanka, currently in my fourth year of graduate study in the United States. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and the $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a graduate student, I cannot afford these amounts. Using an approximate exchange rate of 330 Sri Lankan rupees per U.S. dollar, the proposed initial fee of $70,000 would equal 23.1 million Sri Lankan rupees. An additional $30,000 fee would equal 9.9 million rupees. If both applied to my training, the combined cost would be $100,000, or approximately 33 million Sri Lankan rupees. For me, these amounts represent an insurmountable financial barrier, not simply an additional application expense.

I understand that the proposal would require schools to submit payment before recommending OPT. However, allowing schools to obtain funding from students, employers, or other sources does not ensure that such funding will be available. If my university could not cover the fee, I could not afford to pay it myself. I also cannot assume that a prospective employer would be willing or able to pay tens of thousands of dollars to support my practical training.

I have already devoted years of effort to my graduate education and professional development. OPT would allow me to apply the knowledge and skills gained through my degree in a practical setting directly related to my field. These proposed fees could prevent me from pursuing that opportunity because of my financial circumstances, regardless of my qualifications or the educational value of the training.

We have invested substantial time and effort in our education. Introducing such a large financial barrier at this stage would create serious uncertainty as we prepare to complete our studies and plan our careers.

I support appropriate oversight to ensure that OPT serves its intended educational purpose. However, I respectfully urge DHS to pursue targeted measures rather than impose fees that make practical training financially inaccessible to students like me. Access to degree-related training should not depend on personal wealth or the ability to find a university or employer willing to pay such large amounts.

I am an international doctoral student in bioengineering at a U.S. research university. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on OPT and STEM OPT recommendations. Doctoral students are in a different position from other OPT participants, and the proposal does not account for that.

1. The fee exceeds what a doctoral graduate would earn in a year.
Most international PhD students are on F-1 visas, and after graduating, most of us go directly into postdoctoral research positions. A first-year postdoc earns roughly $60,000 to $65,000, in line with NIH’s own postdoctoral stipend scale. A $70,000 fee for one recommendation is more than the salary of the position OPT is meant to make possible. No lab or department can reasonably absorb that, and federal research grants are unlikely to cover it. Schools will either decline to recommend doctoral graduates, or pass the cost to students, labs, or employers. I ask DHS to state who is expected to bear this cost for research trainees.

2. OPT is how doctoral graduates enter the U.S. research workforce.
OPT and the STEM extension give up to three years of work authorization, which is the bridge from graduation to a postdoc and then to a permanent position. This pipeline depends on international scientists trained in U.S. labs with public funding. Pricing these graduates out of OPT would send them to Canada, Europe, or Asia, and the U.S. would lose the return on its own investment in their training.

3. The fraud rationale does not fit doctoral students.
DHS cites fraud involving shell companies and suspect employers. Doctoral graduates work at universities, hospitals, and research institutes, under named mentors, with documented STEM OPT training plans. A flat fee on every student penalizes legitimate participants far more than it deters bad actors. Targeted tools such as employer verification, site visits, and SEVP audits address fraud without cutting off research trainees. At minimum, DHS should consider exempting doctoral students, or students employed by accredited institutions of higher education and nonprofit research institutions.

4. The fee amount has no stated relationship to administrative cost.
I ask DHS to explain how $70,000 and $30,000 relate to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation, and what statutory authority supports fees of this size.

5. Enrolled students relied on existing rules.
Doctoral students commit five to six years to a program, often after moving countries, on the understanding that OPT would be available afterward. This public comment is submitted in formal opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the imposition of unprecedented fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. The proposed financial barriers—specifically $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent STEM extensions or pre-completion OPT—would effectively dismantle the OPT program, inflict severe unintended consequences on U.S. higher education, exacerbate domestic economic vulnerabilities, and weaken overall national competitiveness.

DHS should fully withdraw this proposed rule based on the following policy and economic considerations:

1. Arbitrary Disruption to Current Students and Lawful Visa Holders
The proposed fee structure abruptly alters the foundational rules under which current international students and existing OPT participants made their academic and financial investments. International students enter the United States lawfully, adhering strictly to federal regulations and contributing substantial tuition. Imposing prohibitive financial costs at the practical training stage retroactively devalues their education and undermines the reasonable expectations established upon enrollment.

2. Disregard for Lawful Contributions and Fiscal Impact
Participants in the OPT program operate entirely within the legal frameworks established by federal immigration law. During their post-graduation training, OPT employees pay federal, state, and local income taxes while drawing minimally from public benefits. Imposing punitive administrative fees overlooks the fiscal contributions made by these high-skilled, lawful taxpayers.

3. Financial Instability for U.S. Higher Education and Increased Costs for Domestic Students
The steep fee increases will make American universities cost-prohibitive for global talent, leading to a sharp decline in international student enrollment. Because international students frequently pay full tuition, institutions rely heavily on this revenue to maintain academic programs, research infrastructure, and institutional stability. A sudden drop in international enrollment will destabilize university budgets, potentially forcing campus downscaling, program closures, and tuition increases for domestic U.S. students to offset operational shortfalls.

4. Disruption of the High-Skilled Talent Pipeline for U.S. Businesses
The OPT program serves as a critical bridge connecting American industry with top talent educated within the U.S. higher education system. Restricting access to OPT through cost-prohibitive regulations will sever this pipeline, restricting access to specialized skills essential for research, development, and market competition.

5. Mismatch with Domestic Labor Market Needs in Critical STEM Disciplines
The overwhelming majority of OPT participants are concentrated in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields—sectors characterized by chronic domestic labor shortages. OPT graduates fill technical roles that exceed the current supply of domestic graduates. Restricting OPT participation will result in unfilled critical technical positions across sectors vital to economic growth, including information technology, advanced engineering, and healthcare.

6. Offshoring of U.S. High-Tech Jobs and Corporate Capital Flight
If domestic regulations hinder U.S. enterprises from retaining qualified foreign graduates, businesses will not simply absorb the labor deficit locally. Instead, multinational firms will be incentivized to relocate research centers, software operations, and engineering jobs abroad to jurisdictions with predictable, competitive talent acquisition framework (e.g., Canada, Europe, and Asia). This outcome results in a net loss of domestic employment and capital investment.

7. Erosion of Long-Term National Competitiveness and Innovation Leadership
For decades, the accessibility of practical training has made the United States the primary destination for world-class talent. Enacting prohibitive administrative fees sends a signal that damages the global reputation of the U.S. innovation ecosystem. Over time, reducing the inflow of global talent will diminish technological innovation, weaken economic capacity, and permanently erode American leadership in global markets.

Conclusion

The proposed OPT fee increases represent an economically counterproductive approach that burdens U.S. academic institutions, disadvantages domestic businesses, and threatens broader national interest. The Department of Homeland Security should withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the standard operation of the OPT program.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am an international PhD student currently studying in the United States on an F-1 visa. Second, the proposed fees would particularly harm academic research and the postdoctoral workforce. Many PhD graduates pursue postdoctoral positions at universities, medical schools, and research institutions. An International PhD Student in the United States

The proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on Optional Practical Training is completely unworkable, legally vulnerable, and effectively acts as a backdoor ban on practical training. Labeling this astronomical fee structure as a measure to combat fraud or protect American workers completely misses the reality on the ground. The underlying logic of the rule collapses entirely when examining how the funds are actually handled. DHS openly admits that these collected fees will not be retained by ICE or SEVP for administrative oversight or enforcement; instead, they are dumped directly into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302. Slapping a $70,000 price tag on an initial OPT recommendation has zero rational connection to actual administrative costs and functions purely as a punitive deterrent and disguised tax. Furthermore, penalizing hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students, legitimate employers, and accredited universities because of isolated criminal incidents involving a handful of bad actors and shell companies is entirely disproportionate and violates basic administrative law principles against arbitrary and capricious rulemaking.

The broader economic and innovation impacts would be disastrous for the country's competitive standing. In recent years, approximately 200,000 students participated in post-completion or pre-completion OPT, while nearly 100,000 participated in STEM OPT extensions. These graduates fill critical talent shortages across engineering, software development, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced research. Choking off this pipeline does not magically create jobs for American workers; it simply forces global tech and research companies to shift talent acquisition, capital, and innovation overseas to countries like Canada, the UK, and Singapore that are actively courting this expertise. Moreover, the administration's reliance on arguments surrounding FICA tax exemptions ignores that these programs are foundational for bringing top-tier global talent into our ecosystem. Forcing employers and institutions to shoulder an insurmountable $70,000 upfront barrier completely destroys the entry-level hiring market for high-skilled graduates and handicaps American firms against international competitors.

The proposal is equally devastating for educational institutions, especially smaller schools, regional colleges, and non-profit universities. DHS's own Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis reveals that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-certified institutions are small entities, and over 60 percent of small institutions will face severe financial burdens ranging from 1 percent to over 20 percent of their annual revenue. For regional universities and colleges operating on tight margins, absorbing or passing on a $70,000 liability per student is an absolute impossibility. This rule will gut institutional budgets, force massive administrative overhead regarding compliance tracking, and destroy practical training options for students who rely on them to bridge the gap between classroom theory and professional experience.

Furthermore, graduate education—particularly Master's and PhD programs in STEM fields—will suffer catastrophic enrollment declines. International graduate students who fund their education and contribute significantly to university research labs and academic publications will simply look elsewhere if U.S. post-graduate training is placed behind an insurmountable paywall. Even designated school officials are set up to fail under this rigid framework. DSOs will be forced to act as tax collectors and financial auditors, confirming wire transfers, validating institutional funds, and verifying complex ledger entries before entering recommendations into SEVIS. The administrative chaos this introduces—coupled with rigid and unfair refund policies where fees are entirely non-refundable once an Employment Authorization Document is issued—creates an untenable operational nightmare. Docket Number ICEB-2026-0100 fundamentally misdiagnoses the challenges facing the U.S. labor market and immigration system. Rather than enhancing integrity or protecting workers, these punitive fees will drive top-tier global talent away from American shores, cripple institutional budgets, and erode U.S. technological preeminence. DHS must withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

I oppose DHS’s proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation. Fraud involving sham employers and false records is a serious concern, but DHS has not shown that charges this large, imposed on legitimate students and schools, are necessary or effective. DHS should withdraw it and pursue targeted enforcement.

The fees are not tied to an applicant’s risk, employer, training period, or government processing costs. They apply across pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT, regardless of risk. DHS estimates $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers, compared with $15.7 million in annual OPT review and payment-processing costs. The money would go to the U.S. Treasury, not directly fund ICE or SEVP oversight, and would not be reserved for OPT enforcement. DHS has not explained why a fee so far removed from administrative costs is proportionate.

DHS’s economic analysis raises further concerns. It estimates primary 10-year costs of $35.1 billion at a 3% discount rate ($29.0 billion at 7%) and government fee transfers of $109.4 billion ($90.6 billion at 7%), while leaving monetized benefits unestimated. DHS does not quantify how much fraud the rule would prevent, how many jobs it would create for U.S. workers, or what wage gains would result. Without comparable estimates, the public cannot assess whether benefits justify the costs. DHS acknowledges it cannot fully measure the value of lost OPT opportunities. Using fees collected as a proxy for the value of opportunities that disappear risks circular reasoning. Its projections depend on unverified assumptions about how schools will respond.

The fraud cases cited do not establish that lawful OPT participants are responsible for wider labor-market problems. Cases involving sham companies, false documents, and fraudulent job offers justify investigating and penalizing those involved, not imposing a six-figure barrier on every participant. Increasing STEM OPT participation alone does not prove that OPT caused unemployment or wage depression; broader outcomes are also affected by economic cycles, layoffs, and employer demand. Using a lawful training period while pursuing another immigration status is not, by itself, proof of fraud. DHS should demonstrate a measurable connection between lawful OPT participation and the harms it alleges before restricting the program nationwide.

The fee would select for ability to pay, not legitimacy. DHS says schools may seek funding from students, employers, or other sources, but many cannot absorb a $70,000 charge per student. They may pass the cost on, stop recommending qualified students, or experience reduced enrollment. The burden is especially disproportionate for non-STEM graduates eligible for only 12 months of OPT. The proposal can also trigger $100,000 in fees when a student uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT, encouraging schools to discourage legitimate training simply to avoid the extra payment.

DHS estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small institutions would face transition-year fee impacts exceeding 1% of revenue, including 116 facing impacts above 20%. These burdens could harm enrollment, tuition revenue, research capacity, and employers’ access to qualified graduates. It does not adequately assess effects on innovation or U.S. competitiveness. A policy that disproportionately excludes students whose schools lack resources does not reliably identify fraudulent applicants; it risks driving talented people to study and work elsewhere.

The problems DHS describes call for targeted enforcement, not a blanket financial penalty. Its examples involve fake worksites, shell companies, false records, and networks facilitating fraudulent documentation. A flat fee verifies none of these facts. Better measures include risk-based employer site visits, verification of employer identities and payroll records, analysis of suspicious networks and addresses, fraud training for designated school officials, timely school recertification, and meaningful penalties for employers and intermediaries that facilitate fraud. GAO-19-297 identified opportunities to strengthen SEVP oversight and risk management. These measures target warning signs and permit evaluation. Administrative convenience is not enough to justify a fee that could effectively eliminate lawful opportunities.

DHS should withdraw this proposal. Before considering any new fee, it should explain how the amount was calculated, quantify expected fraud-prevention and labor-market benefits, assess effects on students, schools, employers, and U.S. innovation, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Protecting U.S. workers and immigration integrity are legitimate goals. A near-prohibitive fee imposed indiscriminately on legitimate participants, without demonstrated proportionality or dedicated enforcement funding, is not a justified way to achieve them.

I oppose the proposed rule in its entirety and ask DHS to withdraw it. A full comment with citations is attached.
No statutory authority (Sections III.A, IV.C). INA 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of admission. It does not authorize a $70,000 charge on schools deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt. DHS concedes ICE cannot retain the funds and does not claim the amount reflects any cost of service. A charge that raises general revenue beyond the cost of service is a tax. National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States (1974). Congress enacts immigration fees expressly (8 U.S.C. 1356(m), 1372(e), 1184(c)(9), (12)). After Loper Bright (2024), DHS gets no deference, and a rule with $74.6–144.3 billion in ten-year transfers requires clear authorization. West Virginia v. EPA (2022).
The fee does not target fraud (Section IV.A). Every fraud example DHS cites involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. The fee is charged to schools, is not tied to any employer, and is due before initial OPT requires a job offer. DHS's latest probe flagged about 10,000 students, under 3% of the roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. The rule charges all of them.
The enforcement rationale defeats itself (Section IV.C). DHS says compliance resources have not scaled with the program and rejects site visits as too resource-intensive. The fee proceeds, a primary estimate of $12.8 billion a year, fund no enforcement.
The fee selects for wealth (Section IV.C). DHS allows schools to pass the fee to students. The practical selection criterion becomes ability to pay $70,000 to $130,000, which excludes qualified students and leaves well-funded bad actors untouched.
The labor rationale does not fit the amount (Section IV.B). The FICA exemption DHS cites is worth about $6,900 a year on a $90,000 salary. The fees for OPT plus STEM OPT total $100,000. DHS's own low scenario eliminates about 106,000 of 194,554 initial OPT placements. That is abolition of most non-STEM OPT by price, without acknowledgment or justification.
Irrational structure (Section V.A). Part-time pre-completion OPT triggers the full $70,000. Pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT total $130,000. Fees are non-refundable once an EAD issues, even if an offer is rescinded; earlier refunds are discretionary and unappealable.
Change in position unexplained. The 2016 STEM OPT rule rested on findings of benefit to institutions, the economy, and U.S. workers. DHS does not quantify the benefits it would forgo. FCC v. Fox (2009). The repeated statement that DHS "may shut down the program entirely" is not a reason for this rule.
Reliance interests (Section VI). About 280,000 students used OPT in 2024. Students chose STEM programs and borrowed tuition in reliance on OPT. DHS grandfathers only students with a DSO recommendation before the effective date and never considers grandfathering all currently enrolled students. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires that analysis.
Procedure. The rule is economically significant, yet DHS allowed 30 days instead of the 60 days EO 12866 and EO 13563 call for. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption in one sentence although 56% of affected schools are small entities.
Requested action: withdraw the rule. Otherwise: extend the comment period 60 days; limit any fee to administrative cost; target employers through I-983 plans, E-Verify, and site visits; grandfather all enrolled students; exempt pre-completion OPT; reject re-charging $70,000 per degree level; make refunds appealable.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and reconsider its approach to preventing fraud in the OPT program.

1. The proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier to employment.

International students already make substantial financial investments in their education in the United States, including tuition, housing, health insurance, and other living expenses. Many students rely on their personal savings and family support to complete their degrees. An additional fee of $70,000 would make OPT financially inaccessible to an overwhelming number of qualified graduates, regardless of their academic performance, professional skills, or compliance with immigration requirements.

The proposed fee is particularly concerning because OPT is intended to provide eligible international students with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. A fee of this magnitude would effectively prevent many students from accessing this opportunity, undermining the educational and professional value of their U.S. degrees.

2. The proposal would undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.

International students choose the United States because of its educational institutions, research opportunities, and professional development pathways. The opportunity to apply their education in a professional setting is an important consideration when deciding where to study.

If graduates face a $70,000 fee before they can pursue initial OPT, prospective students may increasingly choose universities in other countries that offer more accessible post-study employment pathways. This would weaken the United States’ ability to attract talented students, reduce the international competitiveness of American universities, and potentially diminish the long-term contributions of U.S.-educated graduates to the American economy.

3. The proposal would disproportionately harm small businesses and entry-level employers.

Many industries depend on early-career professionals who bring specialized knowledge, technical skills, and new perspectives. In fields such as architecture and design, graduates often begin their careers at small and mid-sized firms, where entry-level compensation is constrained by business size and project-based revenue.

A $70,000 OPT fee would create a substantial obstacle for graduates seeking entry-level employment and could discourage smaller employers from hiring otherwise qualified candidates. Even if the fee were formally imposed on students, employers would face a narrower talent pool, increased recruitment uncertainty, and greater difficulty filling positions. The resulting burden could be especially severe in industries where professional experience and technical training are essential to career development.

4. Fraud prevention should be proportionate, evidence-based, and targeted.

I recognize the government’s responsibility to maintain the integrity of the immigration system, prevent fraud, and ensure compliance with employment authorization requirements. However, the existence of these legitimate objectives does not establish that an exceptionally high fee is a necessary or effective solution.

A fee of $70,000 risks treating eligible students who comply with immigration rules as though they were responsible for the misconduct of others. The Department should demonstrate, with transparent evidence, why this specific amount is necessary, how it would reduce fraud, and whether less burdensome alternatives could achieve the same objectives.

Potential alternatives include enhanced verification of employment and employer information, targeted investigations of suspected fraud, improved oversight of noncompliant employers, and stronger coordination between educational institutions and the relevant government agencies. These measures would more directly address misconduct without imposing a prohibitive financial burden on the broader population of eligible students.

Optional Practical Training Fees, RIN 1653-AB01

Please consider the attached comment, "Transition Feasibility and Reliance Cohorts for Proposed OPT Fees," including its six analytical appendices. I oppose adopting the proposed fees with the transition arrangements presently described.

DHS expressly considered reliance interests. This comment asks whether its chosen transition adequately addresses distinguishable existing commitments and the legal calendars governing adjustment. It does not claim a right to OPT approval, immutable rules, or automatic grandfathering.

First, the proposed regulatory text uses the DSO recommendation date, while portions of the reliance discussion refer to applications or subsequent requests. DHS should harmonize these terms and expressly preserve an otherwise valid pre-effective-date recommendation through a timely application and adjudication. It should distinguish an unchanged replacement I-20 from an expired recommendation, substantive change, or new recommendation.

Second, the attachment provides an executed, reproducible calendar analysis. Under the operative baseline identified there, initial post-completion filing opens 90 days before completion and must follow a recommendation within 30 days. A usable recommendation therefore cannot precede completion by more than 120 days. The corresponding necessary outer bound for STEM is 150 days before initial OPT expiration. These mathematical bounds do not authorize early recommendations. They show why some enrolled students cannot obtain a usable pre-cutoff recommendation even with timely preparation. Other scenarios are only calendar-compatible and still require school, employer, filing, and eligibility prerequisites.

Third, protecting existing initial OPT does not necessarily protect a defined STEM continuation. A first recommendation after the cutoff can require the $70,000 initial payment even after substantial initial OPT participation. A timely pending-STEM work extension depends on a proper application; it cannot replace the recommendation and payment prerequisites.

Fourth, DHS should reconcile its legal baseline with the September 14, 2026 nationwide postponement of the fixed-admission rule. That was preliminary relief, not final invalidation. The attachment uses the prior baseline, supplemented by the 2025 cap-gap amendment, and identifies variables requiring updating if the litigation posture changes.

I request that DHS:
1. Clarify the controlling trigger and adopt an explicit recommendation savings and correction rule.
2. Assess enrolled, near-completion, recommended, pending, approved, active-OPT, and STEM-window cohorts separately, using aggregate counts and disclosed missing fields.
3. Test transition feasibility across plausible effective dates, distinguishing legal deadlines from uncertain processing intervals and continuous work authorization from permission to remain.
4. Compare finite alternatives: existing-recommendation savings, a specified existing-program cohort, one defined STEM continuation stage, and a longer implementation lead period. Specify cutoffs, proof, transfer and degree treatment, sunsets, anti-gaming safeguards, administrative costs, and integrity tradeoffs.
5. Distinguish delayed receipts from permanently forgone receipts and fiscal transfers from resource costs. Identify evidence supporting or defeating the need for a cohort accommodation.

The legal analysis addresses Fox, Regents, Encino Motorcars, Bowen, and the adverse 2025 FDA v. Wages and White Lion decision. Prospective operation and discretionary approval matter, but they do not alone answer every concrete reliance question. DHS may conclude that supported policy objectives outweigh serious reliance after a reasoned comparison.

The attachment states its October 29, 2026 research cutoff and access limits. It does not claim exhaustive docket review, national cohort estimates, or verified private commitments. Its contribution is a source-grounded cohort map, reproducible boundary tests, and operationally specified alternatives with explicit tradeoffs.

Formal Objection and Request for Withdrawal of Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

To the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE):

This public comment is submitted to formally and register a profound and comprehensive objection to the Department of Homeland Security’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published on October 8, 2026, which proposes exorbitant fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent extensions.

Rather than serving its stated goals, this proposed rule will inflict severe, lasting damage on U.S. higher education, undermine America’s global technological leadership, and trigger widespread economic collateral damage. Because the rule is fundamentally unsupportable from both an economic and a legal standpoint, we urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 in its entirety.

The primary reasons requiring the immediate withdrawal of this proposal include:

1. Severe Destabilization of U.S. Higher Education and Regional Economies
Financial Strain on Non-Profit Institutions: DHS’s own analysis concedes that over 60% of small and regional non-profit educational institutions will face severe budgetary pressures, with impacts ranging from 1% to over 20% of annual revenue. For many institutions, international student enrollment and the associated programs are essential to operational stability. Imposing these prohibitive costs will force many colleges to cut academic programs and face acute financial distress.

Disruption of Regional Innovation Hubs: Academic institutions serve as the economic and intellectual anchors of their local communities. By sharply curtailing practical training opportunities and draining institutional resources, this rule will set off a negative economic ripple effect throughout college towns and regional technology sectors across the country.

2. Undermining U.S. Technological Competitiveness and Talent Retention
Accelerating a Critical "Brain Death" in STEM: The United States is engaged in an intense global race for supremacy in critical sectors such as artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and biotechnology. International graduates from U.S. universities are a vital component of this talent pipeline. By erecting a massive $70,000 financial barrier, DHS is actively driving top-tier scientific and engineering talent away from the United States.

Directly Benefiting Global Competitors: Highly skilled graduates who are priced out of the U.S. labor market will redirect their talents to our primary international competitors—including Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union—all of which actively welcome high-skilled professionals. This policy creates a self-inflicted brain drain that directly harms U.S. long-term economic growth and national security.

3. Undue Burden on Employers and Incentivizing Offshoring
Acute Labor Shortages: From research laboratories and academic medical centers to innovative tech startups and enterprises, employers depend on practical training to address specialized workforce needs. A six-figure financial barrier will severely restrict access to this essential talent pool.

Disincentivizing Domestic R&D: When employers are legally or financially foreclosed from hiring top-tier specialists within the United States, they will not automatically replace them with local workers for specialized technical roles. Instead, companies will be heavily incentivized to relocate their research, development, and high-tech operations overseas, moving valuable economic activity and tax revenue entirely outside of the U.S. economy.

4. Flawed Justifications and Internal Contradictions
Disproportionate Collective Punishment: DHS attempts to justify these sweeping fees by citing isolated instances of fraud and bad actors. However, penalizing thousands of accredited, law-abiding non-profit universities and hundreds of thousands of honest students with a prohibitive financial penalty is an disproportionate and arbitrary regulatory approach.

Contradictory Agency Statements: The rule explicitly acknowledges that these collected fees will be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts and will not be retained by ICE or SEVP to fund enforcement or oversight operations. This internal contradiction undermines the agency’s central premise that the fees are required to sustain program integrity, rendering the rulemaking logically flawed and vulnerable under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Conclusion
This proposed rule miscalculates the immense value of international students and practical training to the United States. Rather than strengthening the immigration system, it inflicts profound, disproportionate harm on the U.S. economy, academic institutions, and technological competitiveness.

We strongly urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 immediately.

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to implement an unprecedented $70,000 fee for the initial 12-month Optional Practical Training (OPT) period and an additional $30,000 fee for the 24-month STEM OPT extension. If finalized, this aggregate $100,000 fee will inflict severe, long-lasting damage on American innovation, compromise our national security, and fundamentally undermine our nation's economic competitiveness.

The United States has long been the premier global destination for the world’s most talented STEM students. OPT and the STEM OPT extension are the primary bridge allowing these high-skilled, domestically trained graduates to enter the American workforce, transition into employment-based visas, and contribute directly to our economy. International students represent nearly half of all physics PhD graduates from U.S. universities, three-quarters of whom choose to remain in the U.S. to work after graduation. Furthermore, over 80% of these foreign-born physics PhDs rely on OPT to begin their careers in industry or academia.
By introducing an insurmountable financial barrier, this rule will deter the world's best minds from seeking education in the U.S. and force existing graduates to leave. 

American industries face significant workforce shortages in leading-edge, physics-relevant sectors, such as semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and quantum computing. Independent economic analyses demonstrate that a one-third reduction in international STEM graduates would lower the high-skill STEM workers in the country, cutting economic productivity growth by an estimated 3% to 6%.
The Department’s justification that universities can simply absorb or selectively fund these fees ignores the rigid financial realities of public and non-profit higher education. Academic institutions cannot legally or ethically redirect research grants, tuition dollars, or taxpayer funds to cover individual post-graduation employment fees. The real-world consequence of this rule will be the immediate elimination of international student participation in vital post-graduate industrial training and postdoctoral research.

Instead of protecting American jobs, this regulation serves as a direct subsidy to foreign competitor nations. Forcing thousands of highly trained, U.S.-educated scientists out of our national ecosystem ensures that their innovations, patents, and entrepreneurial endeavors will benefit economies abroad rather than driving wealth and technological preeminence here at home.

For these reasons, he Department of Homeland Security must withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the integrity of our nation’s scientific enterprise and economic resilience.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (ICEB-2026-0100). A $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT per student would effectively end Optional Practical Training as a workable program.

Although the fee would formally be paid by SEVP-certified schools, no school can absorb tens of thousands of dollars per student. Schools will either pass the cost on to students, who cannot pay it, or stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, the practical effect is the same: the pathway is closed.

OPT is how many international students gain the professional experience that U.S. employers need and that often leads to longer-term employment-based immigration. Eliminating it in practice would push talented graduates trained at U.S. universities to other countries, harming American employers, research labs, and the competitiveness of U.S. higher education.

The stated goal of deterring fraud does not justify a fee of this magnitude. Fraud should be addressed through enforcement against bad actors, not a blanket fee that punishes every legitimate student and school. I urge DHS/ICE to withdraw this proposal.

I strongly oppose the proposed $100,000 fee for OPT. International students already contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through tuition, taxes, and innovation. Imposing such an excessive financial burden would unfairly punish graduates, discourage global talent, and undermine America’s competitiveness. OPT should remain an accessible pathway for international graduates to gain practical work experience and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

The American higher education system truly is one of the world's best places to gain access to advanced research exposure and graduate coursework. I consider myself fortunate to have been a part of it and to have worked closely with American faculty - alums of top-tier U.S. institutions like CMU whose teaching and research credentials are second to none - across advanced facets of Computer Architecture, Computer Networks, and Operating Systems. Without their tutelage, my ability to understand and build reliable systems in this new age of AI would not be what it is today.

I understand I do not speak for everyone, but I have no intention of overstaying my welcome in the United States. All I ask is that genuine students who follow every rule and simply wish to complete their education with real-world practical training in fields like Kernel Development and Distributed Systems get the opportunity to do so lawfully. During OPT, students work alongside American peers, contribute directly to U.S. engineering and infrastructure teams, and fulfill the hands-on training component of degrees they invested heavily to earn at American universities before returning home.

The field of computer science became what it is today because people from multiple backgrounds came together to build innovative solutions. Linus Torvalds from Finland and Richard Stallman from the United States both contributed to giving us GNU/Linux—a platform that powers billions of machines across the world right now, including the one I am typing this on and the government server rack where this comment will be stored. Many of us still care deeply about exchanging ideas and building reliable systems that benefit everyone, including American citizens. The OPT program is the vital bridge that allows students to see how classroom theory maps to production reality.

Therefore, it is my humble request that DHS withdraw or reconsider this proposed rule (ICEB-2026-0100). Even though the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent STEM OPT fee are nominally assessed on universities, DHS's own economic analysis acknowledges that schools will either pass these astronomical costs onto students or cease recommending students for OPT entirely. Turning a $470 application process into a $70,000 to $100,000 burden does not target fraud. It simply prices legitimate universities and honest students out of existence. Heavier scrutiny, site visits, and strict verification of genuine roles, employers, and degrees are completely welcome; those of us who have nothing to hide and have come here with pure, lawful non-immigrant intent are more than happy to comply with rigorous verification requirements.

Thank you for your time.

Finally, this rule encourages universities to reinvest in domestic talent. By attaching a significant cost to the administrative pipeline of foreign student placement, institutions will be incentivized to focus more heavily on the career placement, recruitment, and training of American students, particularly in critical STEM fields.

I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). This comment is about startups and small employers. The NPRM expects employers to help pay the $70,000 and $30,000 fees, but it never counts these employers, sizes them, or asks whether they can pay.

1. DHS relies on employer money it never analyzed

The NPRM says schools "may pass the financial obligation" of the fee onto "F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." The RIA assumes that if OPT is worth more than the fee, "affected parties could collectively cost share to preserve OPT." The IRFA then says school impacts "may be overstated" because schools can obtain funding from "employers or organizations." So employer payments are used to shrink the small-entity findings. Yet the RIA gives employers one line: they "may face productivity losses." It has no count of OPT employers, no size data, and no estimate of what share of the fee they would bear. DHS cannot lower its burden estimate for small schools by assuming payments from small businesses it never studied.

2. Cost sharing works only for large, planned hiring

The initial fee must be paid before the DSO enters the recommendation, and initial OPT requires no job offer. Employers who can commit $70,000 per student months ahead of a start date are large firms with campus recruiting pipelines and steady budgets. A seed-stage startup or a 15-person engineering firm hires when it wins a contract or closes a funding round. By then the student's recommendation window has passed or the fee has already been paid by someone else. The cost-share mechanism DHS relies on is open to big incumbents and closed to most small firms.

3. For STEM OPT, the fee is a per-hire charge on the best-documented employers

For the STEM OPT extension, the employer is known before the fee is due. The student must submit Form I-983, with the employer's attestations, to the DSO "prior to the new DSO recommendation." STEM OPT employers must also use E-Verify (NPRM footnote 52). The $30,000 subsequent fee therefore lands on a specific, identified employer that has signed a training plan, enrolled in E-Verify, and is subject to site visits. A large firm can spread $30,000 across a big payroll. For a small company hiring one graduate, it is a large share of that role's first-year cost. The rule taxes the most transparent hiring channel hardest, and hits small firms hardest within it.

4. The fraud DHS cites is the kind a fee does not stop

DHS's evidence describes shell companies, "phantom employees," shared addresses, and residential worksites. Operations that sell job letters can add the fee to their price. Legitimate small employers cannot pass it to anyone. A flat charge drives out honest small firms and leaves well-funded schemes in place. DHS also concedes that STEM OPT employers "are not required to submit any business documents" and that attestations are not verified "unless and until there is a site visit." Asking for an EIN check or proof of business at the I-983 stage would target the shell-company problem directly. It would cost a real small employer little.

5. DHS already holds the data it says it lacks

The RIA says DHS lacks data "on the value placed on OPT by ... employers." But Form I-983 asks each STEM OPT employer for its EIN, its NAICS code, and its number of full-time U.S. employees. DHS could tabulate STEM OPT employers by size and industry from records it already collects. It did not. It also says employers "can minimize this impact by recruiting U.S. citizens." A small firm cannot easily do that for a specialized role when it competes with large firms for the same graduates. E.O. 12866 asks agencies to consider distributive impacts. A rule that changes which firms can hire STEM graduates calls for that analysis.

6. Entrepreneurship by graduates

[Optional, if the commenter can supply facts: describe a startup founded or staffed by OPT or STEM OPT workers, its size, and how the fee would have affected hiring.] The NPRM does not discuss graduates who start companies on OPT or the small firms that hire them first.

7. Request

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any fee, it should: (a) use I-983 and SEVIS employer data to count OPT and STEM OPT employers by size and industry; (b) estimate what share of the fee small employers would bear and treat that in the RFA and E.O. 12866 analysis; (c) stop counting employer contributions as relief for small schools until it has shown employers can pay; and (d) adopt employer-side verification, such as EIN and proof-of-business checks at the I-983 stage, in place of a flat fee.

I oppose the inference that the reported approximately 20-percent annual OPT participation share demonstrates that reliance on OPT is generally weak. This objection recognizes DHS's authority to change policy and the proposal's existing transition provisions; it requests a better-supported assessment of affected cohorts.

First, annual OPT participation divided by the entire F-1 higher-education population is not a graduating cohort's eventual participation rate. The denominator includes students who have not reached graduation. Nor does the ratio identify how the availability of OPT influenced enrollment choices. DHS should publish cohort-based estimates and distinguish descriptive participation from evidence about the reasons for choosing U.S. education.

Second, OPT need not be the sole reason for studying in the United States to create a substantial reliance interest. Educational quality, degree choice, and opportunities for related practical training can jointly influence commitments. DHS v. Regents explains that temporary or discretionary benefits do not automatically eliminate reliance interests; the agency must assess their existence and significance and weigh them against competing concerns.[1] Regents does not require permanent continuation of OPT or a particular exemption. Here, DHS has discussed reliance, so the question is whether its evidence and accommodations adequately address the affected groups.

Third, relevant public experience varies sharply by field and career stage. AIP reports that 82 percent of surveyed non-U.S.-citizen physics and astronomy PhD recipients from academic years 2022–23 and 2023–24 who remained in the United States to work used OPT.[2] This is a conditional, field-specific survey result, not a participation estimate for all international students or a forecast of departures. It demonstrates the need for disaggregated analysis rather than reliance on one aggregate ratio.

The proposed 60-day delay and protection for recommendations predating the effective date are meaningful. They do not by themselves explain the treatment of already enrolled students who cannot yet seek recommendations. The transition text and transition-year analysis indicate that a later STEM recommendation can trigger the new $70,000 initial fee when no such initial fee has previously been paid (91 FR 64583, 64594; proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), 91 FR 64600). An existing approved OPT period is distinct from a future recommendation.

Please replace the unsupported inference with cohort-, degree-, and field-specific analysis. Compare protection through an already enrolled student's current degree and associated OPT/STEM sequence, a longer transition, and phased implementation, and explain why the selected approach reasonably balances reliance and enforcement objectives.

I oppose finalizing the $70,000 initial charge and $30,000 subsequent charge without a more specific explanation of their statutory basis and calibration. The proposal's general immigration-management authorities and references to H-1B payments do not resolve why these particular OPT amounts are authorized and reasonably suited to their stated purposes.

Likewise, the observation that students already incur substantial tuition does not establish willingness or ability to pay an additional charge for practical training. That makes the connection between authority, amount, deterrence, and collateral effects particularly important. A claim that some participation should be discouraged does not select $70,000 or $30,000 from the range of possible amounts.

Please withdraw the proposed amounts, or publish their specific statutory rationale and a reproducible comparison of lower amounts and designs related to risk or authorized training duration. I oppose the inference that the cited labor-market evidence adequately supports a uniform $70,000/$30,000 OPT charge. Protecting U.S. workers, including recent graduates exposed to competition, is a legitimate objective. The proposal still needs to connect that objective to this instrument across the populations covered.

First, the quoted 2.6–5.1 percent wage and 6.1–10.8 percent employment counterfactuals match Bound, Khanna, and Morales's 2017 study of H-1B immigration, calibrated using 1994–2001 data.[1] The same study reports gains to complementary workers and consumers and an increase in overall U.S.-native welfare. It is a general-equilibrium model of a historical H-1B setting, not an estimate of this OPT fee's effect. DHS should address its full findings and explain their relevance to contemporary OPT rather than rely only on its within-occupation distributional losses.

Second, an increase in foreign labor supply and elevated unemployment do not, by themselves, identify the effect of OPT on U.S. employment. Substitution can differ by age, field, experience, and location, while firms may adjust investment and scale. A uniform school charge also does not directly require higher wages or prevent a particular employer from replacing workers. DHS should compare the proposed instrument with feasible measures directed at the specific labor practices it seeks to change.

Third, evidence unfavorable to blanket defenses of OPT deserves explicit consideration. Demirci's 2020 study of a STEM-related visa-policy change finds lower employment for recently graduated native-born master's holders alongside higher earnings for experienced native-born master's holders in the same field.[2] That evidence supports concern for exposed workers. It also demonstrates that the effects are heterogeneous and cannot simply be treated as uniform harm from every category of OPT participation.

DHS can choose to prioritize particular groups even where aggregate gains exist. The objection is not that aggregate welfare mechanically defeats a distributional objective, but that the rule should explain which groups this charge helps, how much, at whose expense, and why a more targeted approach would be inadequate.

Please publish field-, degree-, career-stage-, and region-specific evidence and evaluate feasible wage, verification, anti-fraud, and non-displacement protections alongside the charge. Identify the benefits and costs to different U.S. workers, consumers, institutions, and employers. The available evidence does not establish that the proposed amounts are an appropriately matched response.

International enrollment is already falling. The costs fall hardest on smaller schools. DHS’s own estimates show about 60.5% of affected small institutions would face costs above 1% of annual revenue, and 116 institutions would face costs above 20% of annual revenue. American students lose too. Research by Kevin Shih (Journal of Public Economics, 2017) finds that at the graduate level, every 10 additional international students bring 8 more American students, because international tuition cross-subsidizes domestic seats. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fees because they would impose an unreasonable financial barrier to degree-related practical training, particularly for students who have already borrowed to finance their education. This comment addresses the student cost impacts discussed in Sections IV.C and VII.A.

Students who finance tuition and living expenses with education loans may reach graduation with substantial debt and little remaining access to credit. Rent, food, health insurance, transportation, and loan obligations continue during the transition from study to practical training. Requiring another large payment at this stage could force otherwise qualified students to take on unaffordable debt or abandon the opportunity to apply their education.

Although schools would make the payments to the government, the proposal expressly allows costs to be passed on to students. Naming the school as the payer therefore does not resolve student affordability. If a school cannot absorb the charge and a student cannot finance it, the practical consequence may be the loss of access to OPT.

The proposal compares the fees with the cost of one or two years of U.S. education. That comparison does not establish affordability. For a student who borrowed to pay those original costs, it describes another major financial burden. The ability to finance a degree does not demonstrate the ability to produce an additional $70,000 before beginning practical training.

For perspective, if the full $70,000 initial fee were passed to a student seeking 12 months of OPT, the charge would be equivalent to approximately $5,833 for each month of potential training, before any financing costs. This would be additional to existing educational debt and necessary living expenses. The payment would be required before the school recommends OPT, so DHS cannot simply assume that future training income will cover the upfront cost.

Neither a suitable position nor a particular level of earnings is guaranteed. Access to legitimate educational practice should not depend on whether a student has wealthy relatives or can obtain another large loan. Making practical learning financially inaccessible to otherwise eligible borrowers would undermine its educational purpose.

Students who have already made a substantial investment in their education should have a financially realistic opportunity to pursue lawful, degree-related practical training. They should not have to jeopardize their ability to meet basic needs or incur another major debt merely to access that opportunity.

I oppose the proposed rule's reliance on unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the social opportunity cost of lost participation. DHS acknowledges that actual benefits may exceed the fee but assumes affected parties could collectively finance participation when benefits are sufficiently large. That assumption needs support before it can anchor the regulatory analysis.

Initial OPT applicants need not already have an employer, and Section VII.A.5.d recognizes additional budgeting, funding, and transaction burdens. An unidentified future employer cannot necessarily commit funds before the school must pay. The ability to pool sufficient funds therefore cannot simply be presumed.

Second, a student's liquidity, a university's recoverable return, an employer's private benefit, and benefits to U.S. society are different quantities. Research spillovers and benefits to other workers or consumers may not be recoverable by the parties required to finance the fee. Even a project with social benefits above $70,000 can disappear when its participants cannot capture or finance those benefits. OMB Circular A-4 discusses externalities, transaction costs, and public goods, including basic scientific research; it does not assume that private bargaining always captures social value.[1]

Third, behavioral effects require explicit incidence assumptions. Clemens's 2026 working paper separately models effects when the economic burden falls on students, universities, or employers.[2] Its estimates are conditional projections, with substantial limitations; they are not observed effects of this proposed rule. They nevertheless illustrate why DHS should test financing and participation responses rather than infer social losses from a chosen fee alone.

DHS reasonably acknowledges that valuation is uncertain and that alternative workers may replace some OPT participants. Those considerations justify transparent ranges, rather than establishing that the fee is an appropriate ceiling or unbiased proxy. This objection does not establish whether the proposal's aggregate cost estimate is too high or too low, and fee transfers should not be double-counted as resource costs.

Please withdraw this unsupported assumption, or publish a revised analysis distinguishing private returns, financing constraints, coordination costs, and domestic spillovers. Include sensitivity and break-even analyses for replacement rates, participation, and unquantified effects, with an opportunity for supplemental comment before finalization.

I oppose the proposition that the proposed uniform fee reliably distinguishes lawful, educationally valuable OPT participation from abuse. Fraud prevention is a legitimate objective. The missing step is evidence that this price-based mechanism improves compliance sufficiently to justify its exclusion of otherwise eligible participants.

Convictions, ongoing investigations, and students associated with highly suspect employers are not interchangeable. These materials establish reasons for investigation; without a sampling frame, denominators, case dispositions, and overlap checks, they do not establish a program-wide fraud rate or the relative effectiveness of a $70,000 charge. Please disclose the evidence needed to evaluate those inferences.

Second, fewer participants do not necessarily mean a lower fraud rate among those remaining. A well-financed violator may pay while a verified, lawful participant at a financially constrained institution cannot. This is a possible mechanism, not a claim that adverse selection will necessarily occur. Moreover, DHS expressly permits schools to pass the charge to students, other students, or employers. Nominal payment by a school therefore does not establish that the school bears the economic stake on which the proposed screening mechanism relies.

Third, GAO-19-297 identifies specific controls, including fraud-risk assessment, network analysis, school recertification, and fraud-specific DSO training.[1] Subsequent implementation updates show that several recommendations have been implemented.
