As an international graduate student at Northwestern University, I support this administration's goals of protecting American workers, strengthening immigration enforcement, preventing fraud, and ensuring that immigration programs serve the national interest. However, I respectfully disagree with the proposed $100,000 OPT fee because I believe it could undermine these same objectives by discouraging American employers from hiring qualified international graduates. I have a background in civil engineering and am pursuing a STEM-designated Master of Science in Organizational Dynamics, combining technical problem-solving with project management, leadership, and organizational change. I want to use my education to contribute to American businesses and the U.S. economy. A fee of this magnitude could make employers reluctant to consider international graduates regardless of their qualifications, the legitimacy of their employment, or the value they could bring to American companies. I believe it is possible to support strong immigration enforcement while recognizing the value of legitimate international students who have invested in American universities and want to contribute their skills after graduation. Rather than imposing a substantial financial barrier on OPT, I encourage DHS to pursue targeted fraud prevention, employer accountability, and effective enforcement against actual violations. I support the administration's broader objectives, but I believe this particular proposal risks harming American businesses, universities, and the country's ability to attract talented graduates.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These excessive fees would effectively deprive many international students of meaningful practical training opportunities and undermine the educational mission of American universities.

Optional Practical Training is not merely an employment benefit. It is an important extension of academic education, allowing students to apply their knowledge, develop professional skills, and gain practical experience in their fields of study.

As an international student studying art and design in the United States, I am particularly concerned about the disproportionate impact on students in creative disciplines. In fields such as fine arts, design, and crafts, professional development often depends on hands-on experience, studio practice, apprenticeships, exhibitions, and collaboration with artists and institutions. These opportunities are essential to artistic and educational development, yet they frequently offer limited financial compensation.

The educational value of such experiences cannot be measured solely through salaries or immediate economic returns. Imposing extraordinarily high fees would make practical training inaccessible to students pursuing careers in fields where professional opportunities are already financially limited. It would effectively favor students in higher-paying industries while excluding those whose educational contributions are equally valuable.

Furthermore, requiring universities to pay tens of thousands of dollars for OPT recommendations would impose an unreasonable financial burden. Whether universities absorb these costs or transfer them to students, access to practical training would become dependent on financial resources rather than educational merit.

A training opportunity that is technically available but financially inaccessible is not a meaningful opportunity.

I urge DHS to obtain and carefully evaluate empirical evidence from U.S. universities before finalizing this rule. Universities should provide data on OPT participation, their capacity to absorb the proposed fees, the anticipated reduction in training opportunities, and the potential consequences for international enrollment, academic programs, and educational outcomes.

DHS should also specifically examine the disproportionate impact on students in art, design, humanities, and other fields where professional training may not generate substantial immediate income.

International students invest years of study and significant financial resources in American higher education. Restricting their access to practical training after they have made these commitments would fundamentally undermine the educational opportunities associated with their academic programs.

While preventing fraud is a legitimate government objective, imposing prohibitively expensive fees on legitimate students is neither a proportionate nor an appropriately targeted solution.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee requirements and pursue evidence-based alternatives that protect program integrity without depriving international students of essential educational opportunities.

More than half of international students in the U.S. rely on substantial home-country loans when scholarships or assistantships are unavailable. Upon graduation, most enter entry-level positions. Imposing an additional $100,000 fee benefits neither party: it exceeds the graduate's net annual salary, while employers cannot find local talent, should face an unsustainable penalty if forced to bear it to hire required talent. Beyond individual employers, this policy creates severe structural losses for the U.S. economy. Firstly, a direct loss to local economies. International students inject over $42–$50 billion annually into the U.S. economy and support upwards of 350,000 American jobs through university tuition, housing, taxes, and local business spending. Pricing them out diverts this massive capital flow to competing host nations like Canada, the UK, Germany, France, Italy and Australia. Secondly, loss of top innovation and high-tech talent. Highly skilled graduates are taxpayers who fill critical workforce gaps. A staggering 25% of all U.S. billion-dollar startup founders entered the country as international students—including tech visionaries like Elon Musk (SpaceX/Tesla/Neuralink/X Corp.), Sundar Pichai (Google), and Jensen Huang (NVIDIA). Restricting this pipeline forfeits the next generation of industry builders. Finally, the brain drain in critical research. Over 40–50% of U.S. STEM graduate degrees are earned by international students. Ditching or penalizing these researchers directly weakens American leadership in AI, biotechnology, clean energy, and defense technology.

I am writing in opposition to the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 international students. Based on my four years of experience working as a Designated School Official (DSO) at Portland Community College (PCC), I have seen firsthand how important practical training opportunities are for students pursuing career and technical education.

During my time at PCC, I supported international students seeking practical training opportunities connected to their programs of study. These students invested significant time, effort, and financial resources into developing the skills necessary to enter their chosen professions. Practical training allowed them to apply their classroom learning in real-world settings, gain relevant experience, and strengthen their preparation for the workforce.

Career and technical education programs are designed to help students develop practical, industry-relevant skills. For students in these programs, the opportunity to gain experience related to their field of study can be an important part of translating their education into professional skills and career readiness. Restricting access to practical training would undermine these educational and professional development opportunities.

I am particularly concerned that the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT could create significant barriers for educational institutions and the students they serve. These costs could discourage institutions from supporting eligible students' participation in OPT, regardless of a student's qualifications, educational achievement, or the relevance of their training to their field of study.

I recognize the importance of maintaining program integrity, preventing fraud, and protecting U.S. workers. However, I encourage DHS to consider approaches that address these concerns without imposing fees that could make practical training inaccessible. Oversight and compliance measures should be proportionate and should preserve legitimate opportunities for students who have followed the rules and completed their academic programs.

Based on my experience supporting F-1 students at a public community college, I believe practical training serves an important educational purpose by helping students connect their academic preparation with real-world professional experience. These opportunities are particularly meaningful for students in career and technical education programs, where applied learning and field-specific skills are central to their preparation.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees or consider a substantially less burdensome alternative that preserves access to legitimate practical training while maintaining appropriate oversight and protections for U.S. workers.

Thank you for considering my comments and for the opportunity to share my professional perspective.

I am a Professor of Astronomy at Columbia University, where for many years I have taught, supervised, and worked alongside graduate students and postdoctoral researchers from the United States and around the world. I am writing to respectfully but firmly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s initial period of Optional Practical Training and a $30,000 fee for subsequent periods, including STEM OPT extensions. A fee of this size bears no relationship to the cost of administering the program. In practice it would end OPT for nearly all students at universities like mine. This would harm American students, American research, and the American economy.

The students who use OPT are among the most talented and best-trained young scientists and engineers anywhere. In my experience, their presence makes the training of domestic students better, not worse. American students in my group and my classes learn from these peers every day. They share techniques, debug code together, co-author papers, and build the collaborative habits that modern science depends on. OPT is often the bridge that lets an international student finish a project they began in graduate school, or move into a postdoctoral or industry position here rather than abroad. One former member of my group used OPT to make exactly that transition. Today that person is a faculty member at the University of Massachusetts, training the next generation of American-born scientists. That is what OPT does: it keeps exceptional talent in this country, where it multiplies. That continuity is a large part of why the best students in the world choose the United States in the first place. Our competitors in Canada, Europe, the UK, and Asia are actively recruiting the same people, and a fee like this sends them an unmistakable signal to go elsewhere. The cost would not stop with the students. Research groups would lose skilled people midway through federally funded projects, universities would lose the international enrollment that helps support their broader educational mission, and the country would lose the startups, patents, and technical leadership that these graduates disproportionately create when they stay.

I also want to address the stated justifications directly. In decades of working with international students and their university sponsors, I have not encountered OPT fraud. University OPT participation is already closely monitored through designated school officials, SEVIS reporting, and, for STEM OPT, formal training plans with employer attestations. Where specific abuses exist, the appropriate response is targeted enforcement against bad actors, not a blanket charge that falls on every legitimate student and institution. Nor are these students a source of cheap labor. In my field, OPT positions are paid exactly the same as positions held by American workers, on the same salary scales and under the same terms. OPT students do not displace Americans. Demand for people with advanced quantitative and computational training far exceeds the domestic supply, and OPT graduates fill roles that would otherwise go unfilled or move offshore, paying taxes and spending in their communities while doing so. Placing this fee on universities would also force institutions to divert funds from teaching and research, including funds that support American students, or else deny opportunities based on a student’s ability to pay rather than their merit. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and to work with universities on measures that address real problems without dismantling a program that has served the nation so well.

The exorbitant OPT fees being considered put our growth and intellectual capital in the US at risk. We are already projected to have a million person shortage for STEM professions over the next decade, and making it impossible for international students to attend American Universities will further exacerbate this problem.

Over 60% of new international graduate students pursue math and computer science degrees, with over 60% to 70% in specific fields like electrical engineering and computer science.

The lack of foresight that this legislation exhibits is disconcerting. It not only restricts technological advancement in the US, it also jeopardizes the fiscal health of universities who specialize in technology related fields. As they lose a substantial number of students in STEM programs, they will have to cut programs and some will need to close altogether. In the long run, there will be far fewer opportunities available to domestic students due to program cuts, lack of funding, and low enrollment. 

If you care about the future of STEM advancement of our country, reconsider this ill-conceived legislation.

I am writing in strong support of the proposed rule to implement high-fee requirements for F-1 Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations.

The primary objective of the U.S. education and labor framework must be to support and protect the future of domestic students and American workers. The OPT program has grown into a parallel guest-worker program that operates with minimal labor market protections, frequently placing recent American graduates at a disadvantage as they enter the workforce heavily burdened by student debt.

By implementing these fee requirements, DHS will properly disincentivize the over-reliance on foreign student labor pipelines for entry-level positions. This rule encourages employers to prioritize the recruiting and hiring of qualified U.S. citizens and permanent residents. Furthermore, it ensures that institutions of higher education bear the administrative costs of the programs they utilize. I urge the agency to finalize this rule as proposed to protect the domestic workforce.

I write to express strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 extension fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This punitive policy harms both international students and the strategic interests of the United States.

1. International Student Perspective: Destroying Equity and Career Pathways

Unbearable Financial Burden: Although levied on universities, the proposal concedes that institutions will likely pass these costs onto students via tuition hikes or administrative fees. Adding $100,000 for temporary work authorization—which guarantees neither a job nor a visa—prices out middle- and working-class global talent.

Erosion of Meritocracy: Employers will not absorb tens of thousands of dollars in fees for entry-level graduates. Conditioning practical training on extreme wealth rather than academic merit undermines the core purpose of F-1 educational exchange.

2. U.S. Government Perspective: Economic Self-Sabotage and Talent Drain

Crippling Higher Education: International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy, subsidizing domestic tuition and university research. Eliminating practical training access will drive prospective students to competing nations like the UK, Canada, and Australia, triggering severe financial crises across American campuses.

Weakening U.S. Innovation: OPT is the primary pipeline for global STEM talent. Blocking this pipeline will not create domestic jobs; instead, it will force U.S. corporations to offshore R&D centers and high-paying roles abroad, directly reducing U.S. tax revenue and technological leadership.

Legal Vulnerability: Following the federal court’s invalidation of the similar $100,000 H-1B fee, imposing an unauthorized, punitive tax via executive rulemaking exceeds statutory authority and will inevitably waste public resources in prolonged litigation.

For the sake of American economic competitiveness and educational integrity, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule immediately.

I truly think that changing OPT regulations and increasing costs for international students is probably one of the worst things this administration could do for not only American culture but also our economy. It would restrict highly motivated and very skilled workers from contributing to our country and our institutions. Additionally, it would limit the number of international people here, our country has been built on the backs of international people from all over the world. It is why our economy was once so strong. I think OPT rules should not increase costs upwards of 100,000 dollars for companies/institutions and subsequently the international students who apply for those opportunities. I hope these new laws don’t ever get passed. Please stop

After reading through this proposed rule, I am appalled by its lack of consistency and basic logic. The administration claims that the purpose of this fee is to combat fraudulent abuse of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, citing examples of fraudulent sponsors collecting illegal fees from international students. But how exactly would charging educational institutions such an extraordinary fee reduce fraud? If the goal is genuinely to combat abuses of the OPT program, the federal government already has substantial investigative resources and legal enforcement mechanisms at its disposal, including the FBI, DHS and ICE. Why not use these existing authorities to investigate and prosecute fraudulent activities rather than impose an enormous financial burden on educational institutions?

Universities collect tuition from students, including international students, in exchange for providing education. In higher education, they also provide the intellectual and institutional environment in which graduate students and PhD researchers conduct critical scientific research. Asking universities to pay an astonishing $70,000 fee to the federal government would establish an extraordinary precedent: that academic and educational institutions must pay the government simply so that individuals who have earned degrees from those institutions can pursue internships, employment, or other opportunities to apply the knowledge and skills they acquired through their education and research. What is the logical justification for such a financial requirement?

I would particularly like to hear the administration explain the actual intent and purpose of requiring universities to pay this OPT fee. No university in its right mind would willingly pay such an exorbitant amount. Is the intended outcome, therefore, to effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for international students, preventing them from pursuing internships or short-term employment, including postdoctoral research positions? If that is the goal, the administration should state it explicitly rather than disguise it as an effort to combat fraud.

And if the financial burden is ultimately shifted from universities to employers, wouldn’t that simply reinforce the very mechanisms that have enabled fraudulent practices in the first place? The administration cites the exploitation of international students by fraudulent sponsors as a justification for this proposal, yet its proposed solution risks creating even greater financial incentives for exploitation. How does that make any sense?

OPT is a temporary program, generally allowing eligible international graduates to work in the United States for up to one year, with a possible two-year extension for qualifying STEM graduates. Why should these individuals be treated as liabilities rather than welcomed as guests and contributors? They are legally present in the United States, have received their education from American institutions, and have invested years of their lives in developing skills, conducting research, and contributing to American society. Many international graduates have gone on to establish successful businesses, advance scientific research, and make lasting contributions to the American economy and technological leadership.

I fear that the ultimate consequence of this proposal will be to drive talented individuals away from the United States. After investing years in obtaining an American education, many will simply choose to pursue their careers elsewhere. And frankly, who would want to build a future in a country that makes it so abundantly clear that their contributions are not welcome?

If the administration genuinely wishes to prevent fraud, it should target those who commit fraud, rather than punish the educational institutions and international graduates who have followed the laws . The proposed rule appears fundamentally disconnected from its stated purpose, and I urge the administration to reconsider both its justification and its potentially devastating consequences for American higher education, scientific research, and international competitiveness.

Subject: Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees - Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT, which together total $100,000 for a student who completes OPT and a STEM extension.

As a former F-1 student who used OPT and STEM OPT to gain practical training in my field, I know OPT is not a loophole. It is how international graduates apply what they studied, contribute to U.S. employers, and pay taxes while building a career.

A $100,000 fee is prohibitive and will end OPT in practice. Schools required to pay before recommending OPT will either stop recommending it or pass the cost to students or employers. That will shut out students without wealth, especially in STEM, and push talent to other countries.

The current EAD fee is already in place. This proposal adds a barrier nearly 200 times that amount, with no proportionate benefit to students, schools, or the U.S. workforce.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01)

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees, particularly for graduates of accredited Doctor of Medicine (MD), Juris Doctor (JD), Doctor of Dental Surgery/Medicine (DDS/DMD), and Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) programs. DHS has legitimate interests in preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers, but uniform fees of this magnitude disregard these professions' oversight and public-service roles.

1. The cited fraud evidence does not establish comparable risk in these fields.

DHS describes shell companies, fictitious employment letters, and questionable worksites, including IT-related arrangements. These are serious concerns. But the rule does not identify widespread substantiated OPT fraud involving MD, JD, DDS/DMD, or DPT graduates, nor provide fraud rates by degree. Absence of cited cases does not mean fraud is impossible; it means DHS has not shown comparable risks.

DHS should disclose substantiated fraud cases and OPT participation totals by degree, distinguish suspected from proven misconduct, and separate employer fraud from student misconduct. It should explain why a fee imposed regardless of risk is preferable to enforcement against fraudulent employers.

2. These are highly regulated professions.

State licensing boards oversee medicine, law, dentistry, and physical therapy. Lawyers face bar examinations and character-and-fitness investigations addressing honesty and suitability. Physicians undergo credential verification, examinations, training requirements, and medical-board scrutiny. Dentists and physical therapists face state-specific education, testing, licensing, and disciplinary requirements; background checks may apply. Practicing without required licensure can carry serious consequences.

Professional regulation is not a substitute for immigration screening, and some graduates pursue supervised OPT before full licensure. Nevertheless, accredited education, credential checks, state oversight, and disciplinary systems provide additional accountability. DHS should evaluate these protections rather than assume all degree pathways pose identical fraud risks.

3. The fees risk harming essential public services.

America needs doctors, dentists, and physical therapists to provide healthcare, including in underserved communities. It also needs lawyers to protect constitutional rights, help businesses operate lawfully, represent vulnerable people, and support government services. These graduates may work in hospitals, community clinics, public-interest law offices, and government institutions unable to absorb a $70,000 cost. Although schools would owe the fee, they may pass on costs or decline OPT recommendations.

DHS should revisit its statement that it anticipates no health or safety impacts. It should assess effects on healthcare access, access to justice, public services, and employers with limited budgets. Many professional graduates, including most JD graduates, cannot rely on a STEM OPT extension, making a $70,000 barrier to a limited training period especially severe.

4. Exempt professional graduates and use targeted safeguards.

I request an exemption from the proposed additional OPT fees for graduates of accredited MD, JD, DDS/DMD, and DPT programs pursuing lawful, degree-related practical training. Alternatively, DHS should establish reduced fees and meaningful waivers, particularly for nonprofit and public-service roles. It should prioritize employer verification, institutional audits, credential checks, and evidence-based investigations, and explain how the proposed fees deter the fraud schemes it cites.

5. Create a lawful green-card pathway.

Beyond this rulemaking, I urge the Administration and Congress to establish a direct, appropriately vetted permanent-residency pathway for qualified graduates of these programs. During his June 20, 2024 All-In Podcast appearance, then-candidate Donald Trump proposed giving international graduates of U.S. colleges green cards upon graduation; his campaign later described vetting conditions. This proposal deserves consideration for graduates who can serve American patients, clients, businesses, and communities. I recognize that a new green-card category may require legislation and cannot simply be created through this OPT fee rule.

DHS should not impose extraordinary uniform fees without degree-specific evidence and analysis of existing professional safeguards and public-service consequences. I urge the Department to exempt these graduates, adopt risk-based enforcement, and support lawful avenues for retaining qualified professionals educated in the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I am an F-1 graduate student in the United States, expected to graduate in 2028, and I plan to apply for Optional Practical Training (OPT) in my field of study. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees.

The proposal would require a school to pay $70,000 before its designated school official recommends a student for initial OPT, and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. For a student who uses initial OPT and a STEM extension, that is $100,000 in total. That amount bears no apparent relationship to the actual cost of entering a recommendation in SEVIS or adjudicating an employment authorization application. DHS should reconsider the proposed fee amounts and provide clear evidence showing how they relate to the actual costs of administering and overseeing OPT.

Although the fee would formally be paid by the school, the proposal expressly contemplates that schools may pass the cost on to F-1 students, to students generally, or to employers. In practice, many schools and employers will not absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per student. The predictable result is fewer OPT recommendations, especially at institutions with fewer resources, and fewer training opportunities for students who have completed their degrees in good faith.

A blanket fee of this size does not target fraud. It penalizes legitimate students and programs along with any bad actors. Fraud and misuse should be addressed through targeted oversight, enforcement against specific schools or employers, and SEVIS controls, not by pricing OPT out of reach.

OPT is practical training directly related to a student's field of study. Making it unaffordable would discourage international students from studying in the United States, reduce the research and STEM workforce available to US universities and employers, and push talented graduates toward other countries. For students like me, who are already enrolled and planning their careers around OPT, the change would be deeply disruptive.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, DHS should not finalize any fee until it publishes a detailed, cost-based justification and considers a fee set at actual administrative cost.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I understand that the motives of this proposed regulation is to limit the number of foreign students who may take away opportunities from American students.  As we need new talented foreign students to come to the US and to remain in the country, a better approach than this would be to create strong incentives for foreign students to remain in the US LONG after graduation... and disincentives to those who might immediately or quickly return to their home countries.  Talented young foreign students have been an important -- even an essential -- part of American prosperity and success.  Let's find ways to pressure them to stay in the US after graduation, rather than discouraging them from coming here at all.

(It's worth remembering that even when they return to their home countries, they also bring a tremendous amount of money into the country... through tuition, living expenses, travel, consumption, etc.)

International students are critical to psychology as they offer new perspective and ability to connect with patients from similar backgrounds.  Just as American students are afforded the opportunity to learn in other countries as part of a global society, we also benefit from students coming to America to both learn and teach us what they know.  Limiting barriers to such a goal is crucial for this kind of international exchange in our profession.

I strongly disagree with the proposed fee because it would place an unnecessary financial burden on international students. Increasing the cost could prevent many students from gaining valuable work experience through OPT, especially those who cannot afford the additional expense. USCIS should ensure that the fee remains affordable for those who have already put so much into their education.
I do not think any new fees should be added.

This is a completely impractical source of revenue. It weeds out visa recipients based on whether or not they can pay $70,000 and not by their merit as students and employees. Do not enact this regulation.

I budgeted for my post-graduation year down to the dollar before this proposal appeared, and an unexpected federal fee was in none of my calculations. Students make housing, loan, and employment decisions years in advance based on the rules as promised, and changing the cost midstream is fundamentally unfair. Please do not move forward with this charge. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid under the terms students relied on when they enrolled.

Some of my classmates support younger siblings or send money home to parents who earn very little, so a new fee does not come out of spare cash; it comes out of a family's food and housing budget. The burden of this proposal would fall on households that have already stretched themselves to the limit for an education. I strongly oppose it for that reason. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled; it should remain in place without shifting new costs onto struggling families.

A delayed start is not a small thing for a new graduate, because training positions are filled on fixed cycles and missing one window can cost a full year. If paying this fee takes time graduates do not have, some will watch the opportunities they qualified for go to someone else. I urge the agency to drop this proposal entirely. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid so career starts are decided by merit, not by who can pay fastest.

I chose a lower-paying research position because the work matters, and I accepted the tight budget that came with that choice. Adding an OPT fee would make positions like mine financially impossible for the next graduate who wants to do this kind of work. The country loses when public-interest science becomes something only the wealthy can afford to pursue. I oppose this rule. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place for graduates in every pay range.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule imposing new OPT fees. While it targets international students, they are an economic asset of the country and is currently losing under those new policies. NAFSA estimates they contributed $42.9 billion and supported more than 355,000 jobs in 2024–25, a 2 percent decline from the prior year’s record, with contributions dropping a further $1.1 billion this fall and costing nearly 23,000 jobs. A six-figure barrier to post-study work would deepen that slide, especially since surveys show 66 percent of students would study elsewhere without post-study work options, draining the tuition that helps fund universities and subsidize domestic programs along with it.
Pushing these students out would not create jobs for Americans. A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy study found no evidence that OPT reduces opportunities for U.S. workers, a 2023 Niskanen Center analysis reached the same conclusion for STEM, and DHS itself offered no research showing that practical training harms U.S. workers. When firms cannot hire the graduates they train here, the roles tend to move abroad rather than convert into openings for U.S. workers, so the likely result is lost economic activity, not gained jobs. This also threatens innovation: more than half of international students are in STEM fields, former international students have founded a quarter of U.S. start-ups worth $1 billion or more, and many pursue OPT in medical and scientific research that sustains U.S. leadership. Cutting off both the talent and the tuition that supports research would weaken universities’ capacity to compete.
Finally, the fee does not even go to the program it claims to protect. DHS frames it as an anti-fraud measure, yet by its own account the revenue would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and would not be retained by ICE or used for OPT oversight or enforcement. A charge that is untethered from the government’s actual cost of administering the program and diverted into the general Treasury cannot be justified as protecting that program’s integrity, and observers note these are the very features that led a court to treat a comparable $100,000 H-1B fee as an unlawful tax. For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. While preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are important, these fees are excessive and would cause significant harm.

Unfair Financial Burden: International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses. These fees would make OPT inaccessible to many qualified graduates, regardless of their academic achievements or professional abilities.

Harm to U.S. Competitiveness: OPT helps American universities attract talented international students and allows U.S. companies to recruit skilled graduates. Excessive fees would discourage international talent from studying and working in the United States, potentially benefiting competing countries.

Negative Economic Impact: International students contribute to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, consumption, and taxes. Restricting OPT could reduce university enrollment, weaken local economies, and limit access to specialized talent.

Ineffective Fraud Prevention: High fees do not prevent fraud. Legitimate students and employers would bear the costs, while bad actors might still find ways to exploit the system. Targeted audits, employer verification, and stronger enforcement would be more effective.

Unreasonable Impact on Current Students: Many international students made major financial and educational commitments based on existing OPT policies. Imposing such extraordinary fees would unfairly disrupt their career plans and financial stability.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue more reasonable, evidence-based measures to protect program integrity without undermining educational opportunities and U.S. economic competitiveness.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Graduates I know are already weighing offers from Canada and Europe against staying here, and each added fee tips the scale further toward leaving. It makes little sense to train people at American universities and then charge them until they take that training elsewhere. This proposal would accelerate a loss the country should be trying to prevent, and I am against it. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid so staying is the natural choice.

Living on a graduate stipend or a first small paycheck leaves no cushion for surprise expenses, and this fee would be exactly that. Many of us will have to put it on a credit card and pay interest on the cost of being allowed to work, which deepens the debt we are trying to escape. That outcome helps no one, and I oppose the rule that produces it. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place free of new financial barriers.

In smaller communities, one graduate engineer or scientist can matter a great deal to a local employer that has searched for years to fill a role. Fees and uncertainty discourage exactly those matches, because neither the small employer nor the new graduate has money to spare for a complicated process. I ask the agency to withdraw this proposal. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled; it should remain valid so small communities can benefit from the graduates willing to build a life there.

I graduated this spring carrying more student loan debt than my first job will pay me in a year, and every dollar of my budget is already spoken for. Adding a government fee on top of OPT at the exact moment I am starting out would force me to choose between paying for work authorization and paying rent. I strongly oppose this proposed rule. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid for the graduates who planned their finances around it.

For many of us, the months right after graduation are the poorest months of our lives, with savings drained by tuition and no paycheck yet in hand. A new OPT fee lands precisely when we have the least ability to pay it, which means some qualified graduates will simply be priced out of working legally. Please withdraw this proposal. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled or weakened; it should remain in place as the bridge from study to work.

My parents sold land back home and borrowed against their own retirement so I could earn a degree in this country. Charging me again for OPT would tell families like mine that the sacrifices were not enough and that the door closes unless we pay one more time. I oppose this rule without reservation. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid so that family sacrifice is met with opportunity, not another bill.
I don’t think it’s reasonable to charge a fee.

Employers already hesitate to hire candidates who need work authorization, and a fee plus added uncertainty will make them hesitate even more. If this rule takes effect, some of us will lose job offers we waited years to earn, not because we lack skills but because the process became more expensive and less predictable. I urge the agency to abandon this proposal. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place for the students who built their plans around it.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. 

I am an F-1 master's student in a STEM field at a U.S. university. Through authorized practical training, I have applied my education to actual supply chain forecasting, inventory planning, and operations. This work has strengthened my professional skills and helped me contribute to a U.S. business. OPT is a temporary, regulated opportunity to build on an American education, not an automatic right to employment or a substitute for other visa classifications.

First, the proposed fees are grossly disproportionate and would restrict access based on ability to pay rather than lawful eligibility. Under Section V.A, schools must pay before recommending a student, but DHS acknowledges in Section VI that they may shift this expense to international students, other students, or employers. Most students could not afford $70,000, and many schools cannot reasonably absorb that amount for every eligible graduate. A qualifying student would be denied an educational opportunity not because of fraud or ineligibility, but because their school cannot finance the recommendation. The rule would also create inequities between wealthy and less-resourced institutions and between STEM and non-STEM students.

Second, the proposal does not establish that these extraordinarily high fees will prevent fraud. I recognize that fraudulent employers and sham employment arrangements require serious enforcement. However, financial capacity is not proof of compliance. Legitimate students may be excluded while dishonest actors able to pay remain. DHS estimates only an additional 0.5 hour of DSO review and 0.5 hour of administrative payment processing per application (Section VII.A.5.a), without demonstrating why fees of $70,000 or $30,000 are necessary to fund these activities. A more direct response would be risk-based employer verification, targeted site visits, stronger action against fraudulent entities, and DSO fraud training. The Government Accountability Office has specifically recommended stronger SEVP fraud-risk assessment and oversight (GAO-19-297).

Third, DHS has not sufficiently justified the economic and educational losses. The proposal's own analysis estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario (Section VII.A.1), and its low-participation scenario assumes that institutions may stop paying for non-STEM OPT entirely. This is a foreseeable loss of lawful training opportunities, not merely a reduction in fraud. International education also contributes to American jobs and communities: NAFSA reports that international students supported $42.9 billion in economic activity and more than 355,000 U.S. jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. DHS should evaluate the damage that reduced enrollment, lost talent, and disrupted employer hiring may cause rather than assume these costs can be transferred without consequences.

Fourth, the transition provisions are inadequate. Under Sections V.C and VI, a student who already received an OPT recommendation may be protected for that period, but a later STEM OPT extension may still trigger a $70,000 initial payment if no fee was paid under the new system. Students already enrolled, or already planning their lawful post-graduation training, cannot realistically redesign their finances or careers within 60 days. Future extensions of previously authorized OPT should not be subjected to new prohibitive fees.

I know graduates who are already preparing to leave the United States because each new cost and restriction makes staying feel impossible. Every departure takes training, research, and tax contributions with it to a competing country that is glad to receive them. This proposed fee pushes in exactly the wrong direction, and I oppose it. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled; it should remain valid so the country keeps the people it educated.

The stress of finishing a degree while wondering whether I can afford to work afterward has been constant, and this proposal makes it worse. Financial anxiety during a job search is not a minor inconvenience; it shapes whether graduates can accept unpaid training periods, relocate for work, or hold out for a job that fits their field. I am firmly against this rule. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place without a price tag attached.

Graduates in rural areas and small cities face thinner job markets and lower starting salaries than those in major tech hubs, yet this fee would hit all of us the same. A flat charge that is manageable for a high earner in a big city can be the deciding barrier for someone starting out in a small community that needs their skills. That is reason enough to reject this proposal. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid everywhere, not just where salaries are high.

I am the first person in my family to attend university, and nobody at home could explain this system to me or help me pay for it. First-generation graduates navigate every form and deadline alone, and adding a fee adds one more way for us to fall out of the process entirely. I oppose this rule because it punishes exactly the students with the least support. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place as an accessible path, not a paywall.

Not every OPT participant goes into a high-paying industry; many of us enter public-interest research, laboratories, and other modestly paid work that serves the public good. A fee designed without regard to field will push talented people out of the low-paying roles where they are needed most. I ask the agency to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain valid for graduates across all fields, including the least lucrative ones.

Between final tuition bills, moving costs, and the deposit on a first apartment, my bank account hit its lowest point the week I graduated. That is the moment this fee would arrive, and for many graduates it will be the expense that breaks the budget completely. Policy should not be timed to hit people at their most financially fragile point. I oppose this rule. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place so graduation is a beginning rather than a billing event.

No one in my family had ever filled out an American immigration form before me, and I learned every step of this process by trial, error, and worry. Adding a payment requirement adds another step where a first-generation student with no guidance can stumble and lose everything. I oppose a rule that makes an already difficult path harder for those with the fewest resources. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place, simple and accessible.

Friends of mine entering teaching-adjacent STEM fields and education research will earn modest salaries for work that schools and communities depend on. A fee that ignores those pay scales tells them their fields are worth less, even though their training is just as long and just as costly. I cannot support a proposal with that effect. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled; it should remain valid for graduates in service-oriented fields as much as for anyone else.

I am an F-1 international student currently in my first year of post-completion Optional Practical Training. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees and respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. My comments address Section V.A on the proposed fees, Section V.C on the transition period, and Section VI on reliance interests.

For me, OPT is an opportunity to connect my education with practical experience in my field. Having reached my first year of OPT, I am concerned that this proposal would make access to legitimate training depend on financial resources rather than educational purpose, eligibility, and compliance.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier. Requiring educational institutions to make the payment does not shield students from its consequences. A school could pass the cost to students or employers, or decide that it cannot afford to recommend otherwise eligible students. Students could therefore lose access to training because of a school's budget or an employer's willingness to pay, even when their training is legitimate.

I am particularly concerned about the treatment of students already studying or participating in OPT. These students have already committed time and resources to their U.S. education. In addressing reliance interests, DHS should not require OPT to have been the sole reason for choosing a U.S. education before recognizing that access to practical training can meaningfully influence a student's plans. Education and the opportunity to apply that education are closely connected.

I recognize that the proposal does not impose a new fee simply because someone is already participating in an authorized OPT period. However, protecting an existing authorization alone does not resolve concerns about future training opportunities. DHS should explicitly protect current students and OPT participants from new fees throughout their remaining eligibility, including a STEM OPT extension where the student qualifies. A short transition period cannot meaningfully address commitments made over years of study.

I support preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate, and an inability to pay does not indicate fraud. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular amounts would distinguish abusive arrangements from legitimate participation. It should also evaluate targeted investigations, employer verification, and enforcement against documented misconduct as alternatives.

DHS should further assess whether these fees could discourage smaller employers, research organizations, and other institutions with limited budgets from offering legitimate training. Reducing participation through financial exclusion should not itself be treated as proof of improved program integrity or a benefit to U.S. workers.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, preserve affordable access to legitimate practical training, and pursue proportionate measures directed at actual misconduct. If DHS proceeds with any new fee, it should provide a transparent justification for the amount and explicitly exempt current students and OPT participants, including their otherwise eligible future extensions.

Thank you for considering the perspective of an international student currently in the first year of OPT.

The months between my last class and my first paycheck were filled with applications, interviews, and the constant fear that money would run out first. This proposed fee would have made that period unbearable, and it will do the same to the class graduating behind me. I am writing in opposition because I remember exactly how thin the margin was. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place so new graduates can focus on finding work, not funding their permission to look.

Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As an international graduate of a U.S. university, I believe this proposal fundamentally misunderstands the economic value international students bring to the United States. International students invest significant financial resources in American higher education, contribute to local economies, and develop skills that American businesses need. OPT provides an essential bridge between education and professional experience, allowing the United States to benefit from the talent its universities have helped develop.

First, this proposal would undermine American economic competitiveness. The United States competes globally for highly educated professionals, entrepreneurs, researchers, and innovators. Imposing fees of up to $100,000 would discourage talented graduates from remaining in the country and encourage them to pursue opportunities in competing economies. America would risk losing skilled workers after investing years in educating them.

Second, the proposed fees would disproportionately harm smaller institutions, startups, and growing businesses. While the proposal places the payment obligation on educational institutions, its economic consequences would extend to students and employers. Universities may become unwilling or unable to recommend otherwise qualified students for OPT. Smaller employers, which often depend on specialized talent but lack extensive recruitment resources, would lose access to qualified candidates.

Third, the proposal does not adequately distinguish legitimate participants from those who abuse the system. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate policy objectives. However, imposing extraordinary fees on all participants is not a targeted solution. Stronger verification, employer accountability, and enforcement against fraudulent employment arrangements would address misconduct more directly without penalizing legitimate students and employers.

Finally, the proposal threatens America’s long-term reputation as a destination for education and innovation. International students make educational and career decisions years in advance. Introducing such substantial financial barriers would weaken confidence in the stability of the American education-to-employment pathway and could discourage future generations of talented students from choosing U.S. institutions.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that strengthen program integrity without compromising America’s ability to attract and retain global talent.

Protecting American workers and maintaining America’s global competitiveness should be complementary objectives, not competing ones. This proposal risks undermining both.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee as a Tech Manager responsible for U.S. hiring and growth.
Global talent drives U.S. tech innovation. Adding financial penalties to OPT will force companies to build and expand teams outside the U.S. instead of keeping that work onshore.
Additionally, suppressing international student enrollment deprives U.S. universities of funding for cutting-edge research, shifting financial burdens to American families through higher tuition and deflating local economies reliant on student spending. Protecting OPT is critical to maintaining U.S. leadership.

My degree cost more than my family home is worth, and I will be repaying that investment for decades. Charging graduates again at the very start of repayment treats education like a toll road with no end, and it discourages future students from attempting the same path. I urge the agency to abandon this fee. OPT should not be charged, and OPT should not be cancelled; it should remain valid as part of the opportunity students were promised when they took on that debt.

When a classmate told me she was leaving for another country because staying had become too expensive to justify, her lab lost a trained researcher it cannot quickly replace. Multiply that story across thousands of graduates and the damage to American research and industry becomes obvious. This proposal hastens those departures, and I oppose it plainly. OPT should not be charged, and it should not be cancelled; it should remain in place so trained graduates build their futures here.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) that would charge SEVP-certified schools $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions.

1. It defunds American universities and the research they produce.
International students overwhelmingly pay full tuition, and that revenue is not profit — it funds research labs, faculty lines, and facilities that American students and American science depend on. Graduate research in this country runs substantially on international students, paid for substantially by international tuition. If a $100,000-per-student toll makes the US the most expensive and least welcoming place to study, enrollment will fall — and university research budgets will fall with it. The schools DHS itself estimates would owe $8.4–16.5 billion a year under this rule are American institutions, and the research they would have to cut is American research.

2. It raises costs for American students.
Full-pay international enrollment is one of the main things keeping tuition lower and programs viable for domestic students, especially at public and regional universities. Lose that revenue and American families make up the difference — through higher tuition, fewer course offerings, or closed programs. A master's program in engineering that loses its international enrollment often doesn't shrink; it closes, and the American students in it lose their program too.

3. It costs American jobs, including far from any campus.
International students contribute on the order of $40+ billion a year to the US economy and support several hundred thousand American jobs — in housing, retail, transportation, health care, and the local businesses of college towns across the Midwest and South, not just in big coastal cities. Every student this rule deters is spending that never happens in an American community.

4. It hands the technology race to our competitors.
The United States is in a direct competition with China for leadership in AI, semiconductors, and advanced engineering. The single greatest structural advantage America has in that race is that the world's best students want to come here, train here, and stay here. This rule taxes exactly that advantage. Students deterred from the US do not vanish — they go to Canada, the UK, and Australia, which are actively recruiting them, or they stay home and build for our competitors. We would be paying to train talent and then charging a toll that pushes it into rival economies.

5. It cuts off a proven pipeline of American founders and employers.
A large share of America's most valuable startups were founded by immigrants, and many of those founders first entered the country as students and stayed through OPT. That pipeline produces American companies, American jobs, and American tax revenue. I urge the DHS to abandon these plans. Their argument rests on these faulty bases:

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages.

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. 

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

I am writing as an F-1 international undergraduate student at a U.S. university to strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.
International students make significant financial, academic, and personal commitments to pursue higher education in the United States. We pay substantial tuition and living expenses, contribute to university communities, and participate in research and other academic activities. For many of us, the opportunity to gain practical experience related to our studies is an important part of the decision to study in the United States.
The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would place an unreasonable financial burden on educational institutions and, ultimately, international students. Although the fees would technically be paid by universities, schools may be unwilling or unable to cover such enormous amounts. Students could consequently lose access to practical training regardless of their academic qualifications, employment opportunities, or compliance with immigration regulations.
I am particularly concerned about the impact on undergraduate students pursuing careers in science, technology, mathematics, and other specialized fields. Internships, research positions, and practical work experience are essential for applying classroom knowledge and developing professional skills. Making these opportunities dependent on whether a university can afford tens of thousands of dollars would undermine the educational purpose of OPT.
I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the immigration system. However, imposing extremely high fees on all participants is not a targeted or proportionate solution. Legitimate students and institutions should not bear such substantial costs because of misconduct by others. More effective alternatives could include stronger verification procedures, targeted audits, and enforcement against institutions or employers that violate existing regulations.
This proposal could also discourage talented students from choosing American universities, reducing the contributions international students make to academic research, innovation, and the broader U.S. economy. The United States benefits from attracting students who want to study, conduct research, and contribute their skills. Restricting access to practical training through excessive fees would weaken that advantage.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and pursue more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing fraud without penalizing legitimate international students.
Thank you for considering my comment.

I oppose the proposed "Optional Practical Training Fees" rule. This comment raises one question the NPRM never asks: which regions, states and communities would carry the cost. A flat national fee lands very differently in different labor markets. DHS has the data to measure that and did not use it.

1. DHS skipped the regional analysis
UMRA section 202(a)(3) asks for estimates of "any disproportionate budgetary effects" on "particular regions of the Nation," on particular state or local governments, and on "urban or rural or other types of communities." DHS answers with two sentences. It says it "has provided compliance costs for the main provisions" and that state and private entities "make the cost-benefit decisions" about OPT. There is no state table, no metro and non-metro split, and no list of the most exposed communities. Circular A-4, which DHS cites in footnote 126, asks agencies to describe distributional effects, including by geography. DHS built its regulated population of 2,478 schools from OPT authorizations with start dates in 2022 to 2024. It knows which schools these are, where they are, and how many students each recommends. The regional analysis was feasible.

2. A flat fee is not a flat burden
The fee is $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, everywhere. Entry pay and tuition are not the same everywhere. Where starting salaries are lower, the fee is a larger share of what the training job pays. DHS names H-1B fees as its benchmark. But the H-1B program sets wage rules by the area of intended employment (20 CFR 655.731). The OPT fee has no locality adjustment at all.

DHS assumes that if OPT is worth more than the fee, the parties "could collectively cost share to preserve OPT." That assumption fits best where employers pay high salaries and hire graduates in volume. It fits worst for a regional manufacturer, a county engineering office or a small-city firm that hires one graduate every few years.

3. The screen sorts by geography, not fraud
DHS says the rule would end OPT "as a pathway for low-paid employment." It asks schools to weigh "the value each F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT participation brings to the institution." Under that test, a school paying $70,000 will favor students with offers in high-wage metros. A normal regional salary will look like "low-paid employment" next to the fee, even when it matches local pay for the job.

DHS's own fraud evidence shows no regional pattern that would justify this. It cites site visits at IT services companies in Northern Virginia, a high-cost metro. It describes the 10,000-student investigation as "nationwide fraud, with problematic worksites across multiple states." A fee that shifts OPT toward a few large metros moves training away from some places. It does not move it away from fraud.

4. The low scenario was never mapped
In DHS's low scenario, schools pay only for students eligible for the 24-month STEM extension, and non-STEM OPT ends. DHS did not check which schools, states or regions place more non-STEM OPT participants. It cannot say whether those losses are spread evenly or concentrated in particular states and kinds of institutions.

5. Labor-market effects are local
DHS says the rule would "alleviate the job market from depressed wages." That is a national claim. The effect of removing a worker depends on the local market. In a tight local market, a lost OPT hire may mean an unfilled job, not a job for a U.S. worker. DHS itself concedes employers "may face productivity losses if they are unable to replace" OPT participants. DHS already uses BLS wage data in this RIA (footnote 131). It should use local data to estimate where replacement is likely and where it is not.

6. State budgets carry part of it
Of the 2,478 schools, DHS counts 1,044 as public. A public university that pays the fee pays from state-supported budgets or from tuition. How much each state's institutions would pay depends on their OPT counts. DHS did not estimate it by state.

7. Request
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. Before proposing any OPT fee again, DHS should:
(a) publish a state-by-state and metro and non-metro table of expected fee exposure and lost OPT placements, built from the SEVIS data it already used;
(b) complete the UMRA section 202(a)(3) estimate of disproportionate regional and community effects;
(c) explain why a fee with no locality adjustment fits a program whose H-1B benchmark adjusts wages by area; and
(d) allow at least 60 days for comment on that analysis.

I am writing this to express my strong opposition to the proposed institution of fees for Optional Practical Training applicants. I will detail below two major points:

1. The American industry and scientific enterprise critically depend on international talent.
2. Attracting and retaining top international talent in the United States is critical for our national security.


The proposed fees will, thus, undermine both our security and the welfare of our industrial and scientific enterprises. The new fees will lead to more talented individuals leaving our country, and will also discourage foreign students for coming to the US since they will no longer see a promising path towards a career in our country.

Before I provide more justification for my points, I want to comment on my own credentials. I have worked in biomedical research for over 25 years both at a private research institute and in a large public research university. In these roles, I have been involved in mentoring scientists, both American and foreign, and have been an active member of recruitment efforts aimed at helping to grow our nation's scientific workforce, and at advancing American leadership in science and technology. These roles give me a unique perspective of the national and international talent landscape, directly relevant to the proposed regulation.

Regarding my first point, that the US needs foreign talent to retain its leadership, I want to make the point that groundbreaking discoveries are rare - much like home runs in baseball. The more "at bats" one gets, the more likely one is to eventually "hit it out of the park. In other words, the more talented, well-trained, and motivated individuals we engage in scientific discovery, the more likely it is that breakthrough discoveries will be made. The United States has become the uncontested scientific and technological leader of the world because our country has been able to attract top talent from around the world, and to retain this talent here. Google, for example, a company that has had an outsized impact on the US economy, was co-founded by the son of Russian scientists who chose the US as their new home.

Importantly, this is not a "US talent" versus "international talent" debate - it's not "either/or" - to remain competitive, we need both. 

My second point, that our national security is critically dependent on foreign talent is related to the first. Threats to our nation, whether military, cyber, or biological, require innovative defenses. The same conditions that promote scientific and industrial innovation, also allow us to rapidly respond to attacks and to develop creative solutions to emerging threats. In the biodefense space, for example, our ability to control, in a record time, the COVID-19 pandemic, was in large part due to the contribution of a Hungarian scientist who had moved to the US - Katalin Karikó. Our nation's advanced military capabilities (such as the Patriot missile interceptors) are also the result, in part, of basic and applied scientific contributions by talented immigrants.

And to close, I want to focus briefly on the risks of pushing talented individuals out of the US. A great example is the great scientific exodus of scientists from Germany during WW2 and from from Soviet Russia and the Eastern bloc during the Cold War, exodus that greatly benefited the United States. This brain drain weakened Nazi Germany and communist Eastern Europe while strengthening the US, eventually leading to the collapse of these regimes.  Pushing international talent out of the US will weaken our country, and strengthen our enemies - this is yet another significant risk of the proposed OPT fees.

In light of all of the above, I strongly urge you to rescind the plan to institute such fees.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. DHS suggests the fee is manageable because schools can pass it along — to students, to employers, or across the student body. That suggestion fails on a point the proposal never addresses: timing. The fee comes due before anyone who could pay it has anything to pay with.

The fee attaches when the Designated School Official enters the recommendation in SEVIS. For a student seeking pre-completion OPT — say, a summer internship between academic years — that moment arrives before the internship begins, before any paycheck, and often before the employer has even finalized the offer. A $70,000 charge for the privilege of a three-month internship is not a cost to be shared; it is a wall. No internship pays enough to justify it, and no student can borrow against wages they have not yet earned.

Post-completion OPT is no better. The recommendation is entered before graduation, before the graduate has a job, and frequently before the graduate has an employer at all. Asking the student to pay presumes savings they do not have; asking the employer to pay presumes a relationship that does not yet exist. And even where an employer is identified, shifting a federal immigration cost onto a worker as a condition of employment raises pay-to-work problems that employers will sensibly refuse to touch — the rational response is to hire someone who does not carry a $70,000 surcharge.

Spreading the fee across all students is the last refuge, and it fails too: public universities operate under state tuition rules, and private schools face a market in which a surcharge on every student's bill is a competitive disadvantage against schools that simply stop recommending OPT instead.

A cost that no one can pay, at a moment when no one has the money, is not a pass-through. It is a shutdown with extra steps, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

Please see my attached public comment concerning the proposed Optional Practical Training fees (Docket ICEB-2026-0100). My comment addresses the proposed rule's effects on American graduate education, federally funded research, domestic students, and the assumptions underlying DHS's economic and fraud-prevention analyses.

I submit these comments in my individual capacity, informed by my experience as a Professor and former Director of Graduate Studies in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Notre Dame.

I oppose DHS's proposed Optional Practical Training fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 for each student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that, so three years of STEM OPT would cost $130,000. OPT is the main bridge from U.S. training to U.S. employment: 82% of international STEM graduates who stay to work use OPT before getting an H-1B. Most international PhDs were trained on assistantships funded by U.S. universities and federal grants. DHS projects $8.416.5 billion in fees a year, and its own analysis shows 60% of affected small schools facing first-year costs above 1% of revenue. Economist Michael Clemens estimates OPT participation would fall 2399%, depending on who bears the cost. Lower international enrollment would mean about 46,000 fewer American students enrolling each year, by the Institute for Progress's estimate. It would also push talent toward competitor countries, whose post-study work visas cost a small fraction of this amount. DHS's own cited investigation found only about 3% of participants at suspect employers. Barring those employers and extending STEM OPT's E-Verify and training-plan safeguards to all OPT would address fraud without these costs. I urge DHS to withdraw the fee and pursue those alternatives.
