A $70,000 charge exceeds a full year of tuition at the large majority of U.S. colleges and universities. For a student who completes post-completion OPT and then a STEM OPT extension, the combined cost would be $100,000. At this level, the charge does not recover the cost of any service; it effectively eliminates OPT for all but the wealthiest students and institutions. The Department has not explained how these amounts relate to the actual cost of administering OPT or SEVIS oversight, nor has it clearly identified its statutory authority to impose a charge of this magnitude on schools. If revenue is deposited into the general treasury rather than used to fund the program, the charge operates as a tax, which is a power reserved to Congress, not an agency fee. At a minimum, the Department must disclose the cost basis for these figures and the legal authority on which it relies.
2. The rule would damage the U.S. economy.

International students are a major U.S. export sector. According to NAFSA’s analysis of Open Doors data, international students contributed roughly $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy in the 2024–25 academic year and supported approximately 355,000 American jobs, in sectors including higher education, housing, dining, retail, transportation, and health insurance. The availability of OPT is a central reason students choose the United States over competitor destinations such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, all of which offer post-study work pathways. Making OPT prohibitively expensive will redirect talented students, along with their tuition and spending, to those competitors. These losses fall heavily on local economies in states such as Massachusetts, California, New York, Texas, and Illinois, where international education activity is concentrated.

OPT participants also contribute directly as workers. Open Doors 2025 reported 294,253 students on OPT, many of them in STEM fields where U.S. employers report persistent shortages. These graduates work in research labs, engineering teams, hospitals, and startups. Some go on to found companies that create jobs for U.S. citizens. Pricing them out of the labor market does not transfer their positions to American workers; in many cases, employers will instead offshore the work or leave positions unfilled.

3. The rule would harm U.S. higher education and American students.

Under the proposal, schools pay the fee before recommending OPT, and the Department itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers. Each option is harmful. Passing costs to all students raises tuition for U.S. citizens. Passing costs to international students makes U.S. degrees uncompetitive. Absorbing the costs drains resources from instruction, financial aid, and research. Tuition paid by international students frequently cross-subsidizes domestic students and keeps graduate programs, particularly in STEM, financially viable. Smaller, regional, and less-resourced institutions, which cannot absorb six-figure charges per student, would be disproportionately affected, raising serious concerns under the Regulatory Flexibility Act about the impact on small entities.

Practical training is an integral component of education, not an add-on. Engineering, computer science, and other applied fields depend on hands-on experience that completes academic learning. Making that experience available only to students who can pay an extra $70,000 converts a merit-based educational system into a wealth-based one.
4.The fee is not an effective means of protecting U.S. workers.

STEM OPT already includes worker-protection safeguards, including the requirement that compensation be commensurate with similarly situated U.S. workers and that the training opportunity not replace a U.S. worker. If the Department believes particular aspects of OPT, such as payroll tax treatment, create unfair cost advantages, those concerns should be addressed directly through targeted policy or legislation, not through a blanket charge that removes skilled graduates from the U.S. economy altogether. Research on high-skilled immigration has generally found that international STEM graduates complement rather than substitute for U.S. workers, contributing to innovation that expands overall employment.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to press on the logic of DHS's fraud justification, because the fee is aimed at the wrong end of the transaction entirely.

Fraud in OPT does not originate with the student who enrolls, studies, and graduates, nor with the Designated School Official who verifies that record and enters a recommendation in SEVIS. The documented abuse lives elsewhere: with shell employers that exist only on paper, staffing firms that farm out OPT workers to jobs unrelated to their field of study, and a small number of schools that sell enrollment records rather than education. Those are the sellers of fraud. The students and the honest schools are its customers, or its victims — not its perpetrators.

A fee on the recommending school cannot tell these actors apart. It is collected before any fraud could be detected, from the institution that did its job correctly, and it is collected in exactly the same amount from the institution that did not. A shell employer does not pay it; a diploma mill that profits from selling records will simply fold it into its price. The only parties who feel it are the compliant schools whose recommendations are legitimate and whose students are real. That is not a fraud measure. It is a toll on honesty.

Worse, the fee degrades the very information enforcement depends on. Honest schools generate SEVIS records, employer reports, and site-visit data that let DHS spot anomalies. When those schools stop recommending OPT, the data stream thins, and the remaining field is proportionally more fraudulent — enforcement gets harder, not easier. A policy that shrinks the visible, compliant program while leaving the shadow program intact is working against its own stated goal.

DHS already has the instruments that target the actual sellers of fraud: employer verification against tax and business records, unannounced SEVP site visits, data matching between SEVIS and employer filings, and criminal prosecution of the operators. Those tools distinguish the guilty from the innocent. A $70,000 blanket charge does not, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

**Strong Opposition to the Proposed OPT Fees — Docket ICEB-2026-0100**

I strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees and urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee raise serious concerns about unconstitutional taxation, executive overreach, lack of statutory authority, and violations of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

**1. The proposed fees raise serious questions about statutory authority.**

Under Article I, Section 8 of the U.S. Constitution, Congress possesses the power to impose taxes. Federal agencies cannot independently impose taxes or extraordinary financial obligations without sufficient congressional authorization.

The proposed OPT fees appear designed to create economic barriers to lawful practical training rather than merely recover administrative costs. DHS must identify the statutory provisions authorizing these specific charges and explain how the proposed amounts fall within the authority delegated by Congress.

**2. Federal courts have rejected the implementation of the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement on statutory and constitutional grounds.**

In *State of California v. Mullin*, No. 1:25-cv-13829-LTS (D. Mass. June 8, 2026), the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts ruled that the policy implementing the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement imposed a tax without the necessary congressional delegation of authority. The court held the implementing policy unlawful and vacated it.

On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the federal government's motion to stay that judgment pending appeal. See *State of California v. Mullin*, No. 26-1699 (1st Cir. July 24, 2026).

Although these rulings concern H-1B rather than OPT, they illustrate a fundamental constitutional principle: executive agencies cannot impose extraordinary financial requirements beyond the authority granted by Congress.

DHS must independently demonstrate that Congress authorized the proposed OPT fees. The existence of other immigration-related payment requirements cannot substitute for such authorization.

I submit the district court's June 8, 2026 Memorandum and Order as supporting evidence.

**3. The proposed OPT fees resemble unauthorized taxation rather than legitimate administrative cost recovery.**

The extraordinary amounts of $70,000 and $30,000 appear disproportionate to the administrative services involved in processing OPT applications.

If the purpose of these charges is to discourage lawful participation, influence immigration policy, or generate government revenue rather than recover legally authorized administrative costs, DHS must explain how such objectives fall within its statutory authority.

Depositing revenue into the U.S. Treasury does not automatically make a regulatory charge a tax. However, the magnitude of these proposed fees, their apparent deterrent function, and the need for a demonstrated connection to administrative costs raise substantial legal concerns.

**4. DHS must satisfy the Administrative Procedure Act.**

Under 5 U.S.C. § 706, agency actions exceeding statutory authority or adopted through arbitrary and capricious decision-making are subject to judicial review.

DHS must provide a reasoned explanation for the proposed fee amounts, identify their statutory basis, justify their relationship to authorized administrative costs, and meaningfully consider the effects on international students, employers, universities, and the U.S. research workforce.

The proposed charges could effectively exclude qualified students from practical training based on financial resources rather than eligibility or merit.

DHS must also explain why existing administrative fees or less burdensome alternatives would be inadequate.

**Conclusion**

I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

The federal courts' treatment of the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement demonstrates the importance of respecting constitutional limits and congressional authority. DHS should not impose similarly extraordinary financial burdens on OPT participants without a clearly established statutory basis.

Administrative agencies must not use regulatory fees as substitutes for unauthorized taxation or as economic barriers beyond the powers delegated by Congress.

**Legal Authorities and Supporting Evidence:**

1. *State of California v. Mullin*, No. 1:25-cv-13829-LTS, Memorandum and Order (D. Mass. June 8, 2026).
2. *State of California v. Mullin*, No. 26-1699, Order Denying Stay Pending Appeal (1st Cir. July 24, 2026).
3. U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 8.
4. Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706.

The United States has long benefited from attracting ambitious international students who contribute their knowledge, skills, and productivity to American society. Policies that make legitimate practical training financially inaccessible risk weakening that competitive advantage.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

Fee Justification: How were the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts determined? What specific cost analysis or empirical evidence supports these figures?

Fraud Prevention: What evidence demonstrates that imposing these fees on educational institutions would effectively reduce OPT fraud? How would higher fees prevent fraudulent activity rather than simply restrict legitimate participation?

Less Burdensome Alternatives: Why are targeted measures, such as employer verification, compliance audits, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent employers, insufficient to achieve the same objectives?

Without clear evidence addressing these questions, the proposed fees appear disproportionate to their stated objectives and risk penalizing legitimate students and educational institutions.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee requirements.

I am a U.S. citizen and a fifth-year PhD candidate and graduate worker in the Department of Immunobiology at Yale University. I study how the RAG recombinase, the enzyme that assembles antibody and T-cell receptor genes, evolved from ancient transposable elements, using biochemistry and structural biology. I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity. I am the kind of U.S. worker this proposed rule says it protects, and I believe it would harm me, my colleagues, and American science. I am writing to oppose the fees proposed at [8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)], [8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)], and [8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)]. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
1. Impact on my research and lab environment. Academic biomedical research depends on trainees. Graduate students and postdocs run most of the experiments in U.S. research labs, and many of them are international. In my lab, I work with 11 different graduate and postdoctoral workers, 8 of whom are working under visas. My own projects have depended on my international postdoctoral colleagues who brought skills and expertise that I did not possess. During my graduate education, I aimed to develop my expertise in protein purification, biochemistry, cryo-EM, bioinformatics, and computational biology. These international colleagues taught me these essential techniques, and my training would not be possible without their support and mentorship. These same colleagues were supported by an F1 visa during their graduate education in the US and the OPT and the STEM OPT extension supported their seamless transitions from their graduate studies towards postdoctoral positions. OPT and the STEM OPT extension let my colleagues finish their projects, publish, and develop their expertise so they can support my training and help me become a strong mentor and leader in the scientific fields of my interest. The proposed fee is $70,000 for a first OPT recommendation. That is more than the NIH’s own FY2026 NRSA stipend for a first-year postdoc ($63,480) and more than twice the NIH minimum predoctoral stipend ($29,364). Many universities and nonprofit research institutes cannot pay a fee of this size for every trainee. Where the fee is passed on, very few trainees will be able to afford to pay it. The predictable result is that projects are abandoned partway through and labs lose people they spent years training, along with the federal research money already invested in them.
2. Impact on academia and my career. DHS argues that OPT competes with U.S. workers. Academic research does not work that way. Research positions are created by grants, and grants are won by productive labs. When a lab loses trained scientists partway through a project, it publishes less, competes worse for funding, and hires fewer people, U.S. citizens included. As I move into postdoctoral work and, I hope, eventually run my own lab, my career will depend on joining and later building teams that can recruit the best scientists anywhere. This rule would shrink that pool and shift it toward people who can afford the fee rather than people with the most scientific promise. It would not make room for me. It would weaken the labs I hope to work in.
3. Impact on universities’ ability to recruit. International students compare U.S. programs against programs in other countries. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctorates (NSF NCSES, Survey of Earned Doctorates). For many students, being able to gain training and work experience after graduation is part of why they choose a U.S. program. Countries competing for this talent offer post-study work pathways with no fee of this kind. Adding $70,000 to $100,000 to the cost of U.S. practical training would steer top applicants toward those countries before they ever apply here.
4. Impact on society and U.S. standing. The rule does not formally bar anyone from OPT, but at these prices it would end OPT for most participants. DHS states its goal is to fight fraud. Yet the fee applies equally to accredited research universities and to the “visa mills” DHS describes, so it does nothing to separate fraud from legitimate training. These fees do not act as a measure to mediate fraud, instead it will simply push trained scientists out of the United States after American institutions have worked and paid to educate them. These scientists will not be able to give back to the institutions and academic systems that have supported their training and these talented scientists will go onto to make their discoveries and new entrepreneurial ventures elsewhere. These fees will contribute to the brain drain that is currently occurring in the US. These fees will contribute to a loss of important talent and source of mentorship and training in the US academic system. If fraud is the concern, DHS should use enforcement aimed at the institutions committing it, not a flat fee on every student. 

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw

I am a PhD student working on an impactful research & technology to improve the healthcare in the US.  I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the fraud evidence in Sec. IV.A does not support the fees and that targeted enforcement fits the problem better.


The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a DSO first recommends a student for any OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including STEM OPT (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). The fees go to the general Treasury. Fraud is DHS's main justification (Sec. IV.A, 91 FR 64570-72).


1. Anecdotes, not analysis. The record is one 2020 conviction of a shell-company operator, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story on about a dozen suspected shell companies, 2025 site visits in Northern Virginia, and a May 2026 ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp (91 FR 64570-71, nn.60-74). DHS gives no fraud rate, no trend, no audit, and no data in the docket.

2. The "10,000" figure is inconsistent. The text says an investigation found more than 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers (91 FR 64571, n.67). Footnote 56 says the same video showed 10,000 highly suspected employers. These are different claims. Suspicion is not a finding, and DHS reports no confirmed cases.

3. Even at face value it is about 3 percent: 3.4 percent of the 289,938 OPT and STEM OPT participants DHS's analysis counts for 2024, or 2.8 percent of the 360,078 its preamble counts. DHS would charge the other 97 percent.

4. The fraud is employer fraud; the fee ignores employers. Every specific finding (shell companies, empty buildings, residential worksites, "phantom employees," employer clusters sharing staff) concerns employers (91 FR 64571). Yet initial OPT needs no employer (91 FR 64569), the fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and changing employers triggers no fee or review (91 FR 64577). A student whose school paid $70,000 can move to a shell employer the next week unchecked.

5. A fee would not have stopped DHS's examples. The 2020 scheme sold false offer letters to at least 2,693 people "in exchange for a fee" (91 FR 64570); such schemes can simply raise their price. The foreign-agent case turned on lying to the U.S. Army, not inability to pay (n.62). On Sept. 14, 2026, a federal court faulted DHS's duration-of-status rule for resting on a few anecdotes the rule would not have prevented (Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-13799). The same flaw recurs here.

6. Existing tools work. Site visits, HSI investigations and prosecutions found every case DHS cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS cites, found OPT oversight had improved; ICE has implemented five of its seven recommendations and partly implemented the rest (91 FR 64570 n.56; 64572 n.81). ICE began DSO fraud training in November 2025 (n.81) and reports no results before turning to a fee.

7. DHS's diagnosis calls for resources the fee does not supply. The Ombudsman report DHS quotes blames compliance resources that have not kept pace with the program (91 FR 64571). About 60 field representatives cover some 6,186 schools (id.). OPT grew 21 percent from 2023 to 2024 (160,627 to 194,554), not "exponentially" (id.). That is a staffing problem, and the fee funds no staff (91 FR 64576).

8. The fee ignores compliance history. A school with a clean record pays the same $70,000 as a visa mill.

9. Fraud is real and should be prosecuted. The question is fit: the fee falls on everyone except the employers where the fraud was found.

RECOMMENDATIONS
- Withdraw the rule.
- Place in the docket the data behind the "10,000" figure, state whether it counts students or employers, and report confirmed cases.
- Extend risk-based site visits to post-completion OPT employers; require prompt employer reporting and E-Verify for initial OPT; use the address, ownership and payroll signals HSI identified to flag employer clusters.
- Act against noncompliant schools under existing SEVP authority (8 CFR 214.3-214.4).

CONCLUSION
DHS's own evidence shows employer fraud caught by existing enforcement. A fee on every student's school, untied to any employer and funding no enforcement, does not address that problem at all. DHS should withdraw the rule and target fraudulent employers.

Sec. IV.B - DHS misreads its own data and the labor-market evidence

I am a PhD Student working in improving the healthcare sector through my research contributions. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the worker-protection rationale in Sec. IV.B rests on inconsistent figures and on evidence that does not measure OPT.


The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). Sec. IV.B says the fees protect U.S. workers (91 FR 64572-74).


1. One number to justify the rule, another to price it. The preamble says STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of about 92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, citing 165,524 participants in 2024 (91 FR 64573). That counts everyone active at any time in 2024 in a 24-month program. DHS's impact analysis uses 95,384 STEM OPT participants in 2024 to compute fees (Sec. VII.A.3). On that basis STEM OPT is near the 2016 projection and about 12 percent above the 85,000 annual H-1B cap, not "nearly double." DHS does not say what the 2016 projection measured. An agency may not rest a rule on figures it contradicts without explanation (Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211 (2016)).

2. The labor claims are borrowed. Every labor statistic in Sec. IV.B comes from Proclamation 10973 on the H-1B program: unemployment of recent computer-science graduates, growth of all foreign-born STEM workers since 2000, and a 2017 study of 2001 data (nn.84, 91-93, 111-112). None measures OPT. DHS's accounting statement lists the rule's effects on wages and growth as "N/A" (Table 1, 91 FR 64580). DHS cannot claim to protect wages while declining to estimate any wage effect.

3. The study DHS cites concludes the opposite. Bound, Khanna and Morales modeled H-1B computer scientists in 1994-2001, before STEM OPT existed. They estimate U.S. computer scientists' 2001 wages would have been 2.6-5.1 percent higher without immigration, but find it raised overall U.S. welfare and U.S. workers' incomes (0.2-0.3 percent), lowered IT prices, and raised IT output 1.9-2.5 percent. DHS quotes the side effect and omits the conclusion.

4. Research on OPT itself finds gains for U.S. workers. A February 2026 study of the 2016 STEM OPT expansion found growing employment gains for native high-skilled and STEM workers and more firm creation (Kwon, Lee and Monras, UPF Economics Working Paper 1940). An NFAP analysis found more OPT approvals relative to U.S. workers associated with lower U.S. STEM unemployment (Zavodny, March 2019). DHS addresses neither. BLS data, as reported, show unemployment in computer and math occupations falling from 3.9 percent (Sept. 2025) to 3.3 percent (Sept. 2026).

5. DHS reverses its 2016 findings without evidence. In 2016 DHS found that education, exchange and STEM innovation benefit the economy and U.S. workers (91 FR 64573, quoting 81 FR 13040). Contrary new findings require a reasoned explanation (FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502, 515-16 (2009)). DHS offers belief.

6. FICA is set by Congress, not changed by the fee. The payroll-tax exemption is statutory (26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19)) and also covers CPT and on-campus work (n.108). A fee paid by a school leaves every employer's FICA savings unchanged. DHS counts possible FICA gains as a benefit but ignores income taxes OPT workers pay.

7. Protections exist; DHS does not verify them. STEM OPT employers attest on Form I-983 that students will not replace U.S. workers and will be paid commensurately, and DHS may verify by site visit (nn.53-54). DHS's complaint is that it rarely verifies (91 FR 64573). That calls for verification, not a fee.

8. "Circumvention" is DHS's own design. DHS gives no data on how many OPT participants later obtain H-1B status or displace U.S. hires. Its cap-gap rules, expanded in 2024, exist to carry OPT workers into H-1B status (91 FR 64568-69).


- Withdraw the Sec. IV.B rationale or support it with OPT-specific wage and employment analysis.
- Reconcile the 165,524 and 95,384 figures and state what the 2016 projection measured.
- Address the OPT-specific research above.
- Enforce Form I-983 attestations with risk-based site visits.


The worker-protection rationale rests on a number DHS's own analysis does not use, statistics about a different program, and a study whose conclusion runs the other way. Research on OPT itself finds U.S. workers gain. DHS should withdraw the rule.

Sec. IV.C - A price is not a screen, and DHS dismissed better alternatives


I am a student at a top university in US. I used my analytical skills to do some digging on the claims used to back this proposal. 
TLDR: I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that a fee cannot do the screening Sec. IV.C expects, creates perverse incentives, and was chosen over alternatives DHS never evaluated.


The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS expects schools to recommend only "the most promising students" (91 FR 64574) and chose a fee over site visits, training plans and reporting because it is faster and cheaper for the government (91 FR 64576).


1. A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit, honesty or the value of a placement. Schemes that already sell job letters can build it into their price. An honest student without $70,000 cannot.

2. Pass-through dissolves the incentive. DHS says schools "may pass the financial obligation" to F-1 students, "all students," or employers (91 FR 64575, 64578). If someone else pays, the school bears no cost and has no new reason to screen. DHS cannot rely on pass-through to soften the burden and on school-borne cost to produce screening.

3. "All students" means American students' tuition could fund a federal levy on international students' training (91 FR 64575).

4. The gatekeepers are unequipped. DHS calls DSOs "often overwhelmed" and "not fully trained" (91 FR 64574), then makes them the screen with no training, staff or criteria, and declines to define the "genuine educational value" they should screen for (91 FR 64575).

5. The school pays before any employer exists. Initial OPT requires no job offer (91 FR 64569), so the fee is paid when there is no placement to evaluate.

6. Perverse incentives DHS does not consider:
- A shift to CPT, which the rule leaves untouched although DHS says CPT fraud has been "historically prevalent" and is growing (91 FR 64576).
- A penalty on work-study: pre-completion ($70,000), post-completion ($30,000) and STEM OPT ($30,000) total $130,000, versus $100,000 for a student who skipped training during school (91 FR 64577).
- An opening for foreign money: DHS warns adversaries may subsidize fees through gifts to schools (91 FR 64575). The rule creates the gap that invites them.

7. Unsupported assertions. DHS says the fees are "on par with" one or two years of tuition, with no data (91 FR 64575), and that the fee "serves as a clear signal to the public" (91 FR 64576). Signaling cannot justify a $109 billion charge.

8. Alternatives dismissed for convenience. Those tools uncovered every fraud case DHS cites, and GAO-19-297 found oversight improving. DHS estimates neither the cost nor the effectiveness of any alternative, and calls the fee only "a crucial first step" (id.), conceding it is not enough. Administrative ease is not a reasoned choice among alternatives (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

9. "Schools can decline to recommend students" (91 FR 64578) is the design: OPT restricted by price instead of by a rule that says so and justifies it.

SUGGESTIONS

- If DHS wants schools to screen, define criteria, fund DSO training, and use SEVP's authority over noncompliant schools (8 CFR 214.3-214.4).
- Evaluate, with cost and effectiveness estimates, risk-based site visits and training plans for post-completion OPT employers.

A price cannot do the screening DHS describes, and DHS's own pass-through provision ensures it will not. The tools that found the fraud DHS cites remain available. DHS should withdraw the rule.

Secs. III.A and IV.C - The fee is a tax Congress has not authorized


I am a working professional interested in pursuing law major. I analysed the rule and here are my conclusions:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the charge is a tax that DHS lacks authority to impose.


Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). The money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302; DHS concedes no statute lets ICE keep it (91 FR 64576). DHS relies on the "time and conditions" power in INA 214(a) (91 FR 64567).

1. The charge has every feature of a tax. It is set to deter, not to recover a cost. It buys no service. It goes to general revenue. Its amount was chosen to "closely align with the H-1B fees," not from any cost study (91 FR 64575). DHS projects $74.6-144.3 billion in transfers over ten years (91 FR 64579).

2. Congress authorizes immigration fees to recover costs. INA 286(m), 8 U.S.C. 1356(m), allows fees that recover the full cost of adjudication services. Congress funded SEVIS through a separate fee (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)), and DHS's 2019 SEVP fee rule set fees to recover program costs (84 FR 23930). The user-fee statute, 31 U.S.C. 9701, ties charges to the value of a service. DHS invokes none of these.

3. INA 214(a) is not a taxing power. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT as a condition of stay; it says nothing about revenue. Narenji v. Civiletti, 617 F.2d 745 (D.C. Cir. 1979), upheld a reporting requirement. A charge exceeding the value of a service to the payer is a tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). Congress may delegate taxing power, but it must do so (Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212 (1989)).

4. INA 274A(h)(1) does not help. DHS cites it (91 FR 64575), but it requires limits on employment to be stated on work documents. It says nothing about fees.

5. The scale demands clear authorization. A levy of this size, reshaping a program used by about 280,000 students a year, is a question of vast economic significance (West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)). DHS's reading of INA 214(a) gets no deference (Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)).

6. A court has called the fee this one copies a tax. On June 8, 2026, the District of Massachusetts held the $100,000 H-1B payment a tax and vacated its implementing policy (State of California et al., D. Mass. No. 1:25-cv-13829); the First Circuit declined to stay that ruling on July 24, 2026. On Sept. 30, 2026, the Northern District of California vacated the agency policies implementing that fee and its renewal, faulting them for ignoring alternatives and reliance interests (Global Nurse Force v. Trump). DHS benchmarks this fee to the H-1B fee (91 FR 64575) without mentioning any of these rulings.

7. "Without the fees, OPT may close" is a non sequitur. DHS says three times it "may shut down the program entirely" without the fees (91 FR 64572, 64574). None of the money reaches OPT oversight (91 FR 64576). The fee works only by reducing participation. If DHS means to restrict OPT, it must propose that directly and justify it.

8. Anticipated responses. A D.C. district court upheld the H-1B fee in the Chamber of Commerce case, now on appeal, but rested on the President's statutory power over entry, which this rule does not invoke. Calling the charge a "deterrent" does not help: a charge untied to cost, designed to suppress an activity, and paid into general revenue is what the Massachusetts court called a tax.

ADVICE
- Withdraw the rule.
- Any OPT-related fee should be cost-based, set under a statute that authorizes it, and retained for SEVP compliance.
- If DHS claims taxing authority, identify the statute and explain why it reaches a $109 billion levy.


DHS concedes it cannot keep the money, admits the amount was copied from a fee a court has called a tax, and identifies no statute authorizing revenue of this scale. DHS should withdraw the rule.

Title/Subject: Public Comment on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-XXXX)
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to charge very high new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extension programs. While DHS has the authority to regulate F-1 students doing temporary practical training, the argument that these extreme fees are necessary to stop fraud and improve the immigration system is wrong and unfair. This proposal should be canceled for the following five reasons:

1. Unfair Punishment for Innocent Students
The proposal punishes the vast majority of law-abiding international students for the wrongdoings of a very small number of bad actors. In a fair legal system, enforcement costs should be paid by the entities committing the fraud—such as fake staffing agencies and shell companies—not by honest students who are the victims, not the creators, of these scams.

2. Driving Away Top Talent While Failing to Stop Criminals
While the goal is to stop fraud, a $70,000 fee will actually do the exact opposite. Excellent, law-abiding students who have real job offers will be forced to give up their practical training because they cannot afford this huge amount of money. On the other hand, criminals backed by wealthy, illegal networks will easily pay this fee just to buy legal status. This rule will push away the best students while failing to stop real fraud.

3. Charging Twice for the Same Service (Double Dipping)
The government claims these fees are needed to pay for company visits and employer background checks. However, this is a form of "double dipping." Employers using the STEM OPT program must already use E-Verify, and employers sponsoring H-1B visas already pay hundreds or thousands of dollars in "Fraud Prevention and Detection Fees." Since these companies are already checked and funded through employer-paid fees, charging students tens of thousands of dollars for the same exact oversight is redundant and unfair.

4. Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), government agency fees must be reasonably close to the actual cost of providing the service. In today's digital age, checking if a company is real by matching information with IRS tax data, Social Security Numbers (SSN), or electronic systems costs less than $10 per case. A $70,000 bill has no connection to actual administrative costs. It acts as a punishment tax designed to stop students from applying, which goes beyond what DHS is legally allowed to do.

5. Hurting the True Educational Purpose of OPT
The legal purpose of OPT is to be an extension of a student’s education; it is not a standard foreign labor program. Putting up an impossible financial wall to post-graduation training will immediately hurt the global appeal of U.S. universities. By driving top global talent to other countries, this rule will hurt America's technological innovation and economic leadership, which goes completely against the goal of keeping America competitive.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this harmful proposal and instead use smart, data-driven methods to catch fraud without punishing innocent students.

Respectfully submitted,

A Concerned F-1 Student

The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to levy a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorizations and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent STEM extensions must be withdrawn. The imposition of a cumulative $100,000 regulatory assessment on international graduates seeking post-completion technical training constitutes an unprecedented financial barrier that operates as a de facto administrative prohibition on high-skilled workforce participation.
This proposed regulatory framework introduces a profound, counterproductive contradiction within broader federal policy objectives. While the administration prioritizes aggressive deregulation and infrastructure fast-tracking to accelerate the domestic artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced technology sectors, this rule simultaneously engineers prohibitive market friction against the specialized human capital essential to sustain those sectors. Advanced hardware, domestic compute campuses, and deregulated frameworks are entirely inert without human intelligence. The rapid scaling of next-generation machine learning, quantum computing, and cryptography requires a concentrated supply of elite technical talent. Weaponizing administrative fee adjustments to choke off the supply of highly skilled technical experts directly undermines the domestic technology pipeline.
For decades, the OPT and STEM OPT extension programs have served as the premier mechanism for retaining top-tier, globally recruited minds educated at leading American research institutions. Forcing these graduates or their prospective employers to absorb exorbitant, non-statutory upfront costs introduces artificial labor market distortions. The predictable macroeconomic consequence of this rule will not be the safeguarding of domestic labor, but rather a severe, self-inflicted contraction of the American innovation ecosystem.
Global technical talent is highly mobile. By artificially inflating the cost of domestic professional integration, this policy creates a powerful economic incentive for elite researchers and engineers to migrate to competing technological hubs in Europe, Canada, and Asia, where high-skilled immigration pathways are actively optimized. Consequently, American universities will suffer a sharp decline in global academic competitiveness, and domestic industries will face acute, structural labor shortages in critical STEM fields.
Furthermore, the allocation of a restrictive 30-day public comment window for a regulatory modification of this magnitude is procedurally deficient. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a 30-day timeline is wholly inadequate for universities, economic analysts, and industry stakeholders to comprehensively quantify the long-term structural and macroeconomic damage this rule will inflict on American industrial competitiveness.
An administration cannot logically seek to outpace foreign adversaries in technological innovation while systematically starving the domestic tech engine of its primary catalyst: elite human capital. Because this proposal is logically inconsistent with stated national security imperatives, economically counterproductive, and procedurally rushed, the Department of Homeland Security must immediately withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment tests the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) in section VII.A against E.O. 12866 and OMB Circular A-4 (2003), which DHS cites in footnotes 126 and 130. 

1. Once transfers are removed, one unquantified benefit is left
The RIA names three benefits: program integrity, protecting U.S. workers, and "alleviating burdens imposed on DHS tied to OPT investigations." DHS then classifies the worker effect as "transfers to other workers" and the FICA effect as "additional transfers for federal taxes collected." Footnote 130, citing A-4, says transfers "do not affect total resources available to society." By DHS's own accounting, those are not benefits. What remains is fraud deterrence, which DHS "believes" will occur, with no estimate. The investigation savings DHS claims are never estimated, though DHS holds its own enforcement cost data.

2. No break-even analysis
When benefits cannot be quantified, A-4 asks for a threshold or break-even analysis. The primary annualized cost is $4.1 billion (3 percent). DHS's largest fraud figure is "more than 10,000" students working for "highly suspect employers." Even if the fee ended every one of those cases, it would need to produce about $410,000 in benefits per case per year to break even. At the $8.2 billion high estimate, about $820,000. DHS does not state the threshold or argue it is met. E.O. 12866 section 1(b)(6) requires a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs. The RIA contains none.

3. The low scenario mixes two baselines
The high scenario uses 2024 counts: 194,554 OPT and 95,384 STEM OPT. The low scenario uses a different base. Footnote 129 multiplies the 2022-2024 average of 157,494 by 56.11 percent to get 88,374 STEM-bound initial fees, and the STEM OPT count drops to the 74,088 average. The scenario's premise is that schools keep paying for STEM-bound students. Yet it removes about 20,790 STEM-bound initial fees (56.11 percent of 194,554 is about 109,164) and 21,296 STEM extensions. Those cuts come from switching baselines, not from the fee. By my arithmetic, about $2.1 billion of the $8.07 billion annual post-transition opportunity cost is a baseline artifact. About $6.0 billion is the assumed loss of non-STEM OPT. The text also calls 88,374 "a low-end future annual OPT population," which conflicts with footnote 129. A-4 calls for one baseline, with baseline uncertainty handled through sensitivity analysis.

4. Two corners are not an uncertainty analysis
A-4 calls for a formal quantitative analysis of uncertainty for rules with annual effects of $1 billion or more. Annualized transfers here are $8.7 to $16.9 billion. DHS offers two corner cases: no behavioral change at all, or every non-STEM student dropped. It calls their midpoint the "primary" estimate without assigning any probability. There is no intermediate case, no participation elasticity and no enrollment response.

5. Alternatives are listed, not analyzed
A-4 asks agencies to compare alternatives, including more and less stringent options. DHS analyzed one fee schedule. It assigns no cost or benefit to any alternative it names: no action, a small-entity exemption, a repeat fee at each degree level, or expanded site visits and reporting. It rejects site visits because they "may require substantial time and resources," with no figure, though it priced DSO time at $50.14 an hour. It never tests a lower fee, a phased-in fee, or a cost-based fee.

6. Costs capped by assumption
DHS assumes opportunity costs are "equal to or less than the proposed fee," so its cost estimate cannot exceed the fee by construction. Refund, Treasury and bank costs are left unestimated. In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court found DHS likely acted arbitrarily in the companion Duration of Status rule partly because DHS used "no principled method" to compare costs and benefits. The court quoted the rule that "a reasoned decision would explain why any unquantified benefits cannot reasonably be quantified."

7. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. Any re-proposal should include an RIA that:
(a) separates benefits from transfers and estimates fraud reduction, or at least presents a break-even analysis;
(b) uses one baseline for every scenario, with baseline sensitivity shown separately;
(c) provides a probabilistic uncertainty analysis with intermediate participation and enrollment responses;
(d) prices at least one less stringent and one more targeted alternative, including a lower or cost-based fee and employer verification; and
(e) estimates the DHS investigation savings it claims as a benefit.

I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT.

I am commenting because I have personally gone through the process this proposal would affect. I came to the US as an international student, used OPT after completing my education, and am now a lawful permanent resident. I received my green card through the National Interest Waiver process, where I had to demonstrate the substantial merit and national importance of my work to the United States.

OPT was an important part of how I got from being an international student to where I am today.

Like many international students, I invested a significant amount of money in an American education. Tuition alone was a major financial commitment. After spending years studying here, OPT gave me the opportunity to apply what I had learned in school and gain real professional experience.

I also saw OPT as an opportunity to give something back. Since graduating, I have worked, paid taxes, developed my expertise, and contributed to the U.S. economy. Eventually, I qualified for permanent residence through the National Interest Waiver process based on the importance of my work.

That contribution did not stop with my own employment. In my current role, I built a new unit within my department. As that unit has grown, I have hired more than 10 interns and over 5 full time employees over the past two and a half years. My unit has also enabled hiring over 3 American vendors/content creation companies for projects.

When I was an international student using OPT, I could not have known that years later I would help build something that would provide opportunities to American students. That is why I don't believe the value of OPT can be measured simply by looking at the first job an international graduate takes.

I understand the argument that employment opportunities in the United States should benefit American workers first. I do not dismiss that concern. American students and workers should have strong opportunities to build their careers in their own country.

But giving an international graduate a limited period of practical training does not necessarily mean taking an opportunity away from an American worker. My own experience shows why it can be more complicated than that. The opportunity I received early in my career helped me develop the experience that eventually put me in a position to help build a new area of business and create opportunities for other people, including American workers.

I am not suggesting there is never competition between international and American workers. There can be competition in any labor market, and protecting American workers is a legitimate concern. But international graduates can also build teams, develop new areas of business, pay taxes, train colleagues, and create additional opportunities for American workers.

I also understand DHS's concerns about fraud and abuse. I support enforcement against employers, schools, or individuals who misuse OPT. People who break the rules should face consequences. But a $70,000 fee does not distinguish between someone abusing the system and a student who has done everything correctly.

Most graduating students simply do not have $70,000 available for the opportunity to begin working in the field they studied. Universities cannot reasonably absorb that amount for every international graduate either. Regardless of who technically pays the fee, I worry that many legitimate students will lose access to OPT.

If there are weaknesses in OPT oversight, DHS should address them directly through employer verification, investigations, audits, and enforcement against those who violate the rules. Those approaches target misconduct rather than creating a financial barrier for everyone.

International students make enormous financial and personal commitments to study in the United States. If obtaining even a limited period of practical experience after graduation effectively requires a $70,000 payment, talented students may choose to study and build their careers elsewhere. The United States could then lose not only those students and their tuition, but also whatever they might have contributed here afterward.

I. Introduction and Overview
I am writing to submit this formal public comment in strong opposition to any proposed rule or policy that would impose an additional "training fee," user surcharge, or substantial fee hike on participants and employer sponsors of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the STEM OPT extension.

Practical training is an indispensable, integral component of higher education in the United States. Instituting cost-prohibitive fees on recent graduates, early-career researchers, and hosting institutions undermines the foundational mission of practical training, harms U.S. academic institutions, damages economic competitiveness in key STEM fields, and creates arbitrary financial barriers for high-skilled global talent.

II. Core Arguments Against the Proposed Fee
1. Incompatibility with the Nature of Practical Training as an Educational Benefit
Direct Extension of Degree Curricula: OPT is not a distinct employment-based immigrant visa; it is a regulatory continuation of F-1 student status authorized under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10). Experiential learning, clinical practice, and laboratory training are natural extensions of graduate and undergraduate curricula.

Double Taxation of Students: International students already make enormous financial contributions to the U.S. higher education system via full tuition, institutional administrative fees, the SEVIS I-901 fee, and standard USCIS Form I-765 application filing fees. Imposing a separate "training fee" is an unjustified financial extraction that mischaracterizes essential experiential training as a commercial luxury.

2. Disproportionate Harm to Academic Research and Early-Career Scientists
Severe Burden on Postdoctoral Scholars and Academic Labs: A substantial share of STEM OPT beneficiaries are postdoctoral researchers, clinical fellows, and research scientists at major universities and biomedical research institutes.

Depleted Research Budgets: Postdoctoral stipends are strictly bounded by federal guidelines (e.g., NIH NRSA scales) and funded through constrained academic grants. Siphoning vital grant capital into administrative training fees shifts resources away from scientific discovery, laboratory supplies, and peer-reviewed research without providing any commensurate administrative benefit.

Risk to Foundational Science: Driving early-career researchers out of U.S. laboratories directly slows down critical work in cutting-edge biotechnology, artificial intelligence, semiconductor physics, and public health.

3. Erosion of U.S. Global Competitiveness in STEM
Global Talent Diversion: The U.S. relies heavily on recruiting the world’s top minds in STEM disciplines. Competing nations—such as the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, and Australia—continue to liberalize and streamline post-study work authorization to actively attract international researchers and engineers.

Economic Bottlenecks: Levying steep financial penalties on post-graduation training signals hostility toward skilled international contributors, accelerating "reverse brain drain" and pushing promising innovators to launch startups or pursue specialized research abroad.

4. Disproportionate Hardship on Startups, Nonprofits, and Small Businesses
Chilling Effect on Early-Stage Hiring: Large technology conglomerates can easily absorb extra administrative costs, but early-stage spin-offs, non-profit think tanks, and local educational institutions cannot.

Distortion of the Talent Market: Adding mandatory fees skews the playing field, effectively pricing small employers and startup ventures out of hiring top talent trained at U.S. universities.

5. Arbitrary Cost Structure and Lack of Regulatory Justification
Lack of Demonstrable Service Delivery: Fees charged by federal agencies must reflect the actual adjudicative and administrative cost of providing the specific service (as mandated under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. § 9701). The SEVIS system and standard Form I-765 fees already fully recover the administrative costs of tracking students and issuing Employment Authorization Documents (EADs).

Regulatory Exceedance: Imposing a punitive, standalone fee detached from direct processing costs exceeds statutory authority and operates as a de facto tariff on international educational exchange.

III. Conclusion and Request
For these reasons, the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS should withdraw any proposed implementation of an OPT training fee. Imposing such a fee places an unjustifiable drag on scientific innovation, damages the recruitment capacity of American universities, and harms the U.S. economy. The agency should instead focus on reducing processing backlogs, modernizing adjudications, and protecting the integrity of post-study practical training.

First: For the majority of small, liberal arts colleges and universities in the United States that serve international students, paying and/or collecting a $70,000 fee to pursue OPT would simply not be possible. Due to the demographic cliff, many such colleges are already strapped for resources. Coming up with these funds for students would simply not be possible. The vast majority of these students–who receive financial aid–would also not be able to pay the fee themselves. And a $70,000 would simply be disqualifying for the majority of employers. (As a comparison, refer to the H-1B fee, which was touted as a money generator and has resulted in few payments.)

Given that the majority of undergraduate students–domestic and international–expect hands on practical training as part of their degree or immediately after completion of their degree, creating an insuperable obstacle to pursuing employment related to the degree would effectively remove it as an option for students, despite their eligibility, as already permitted by law. This would undoubtedly lead to a collapse in international student enrollments in the United States, which have already taken a hit, due to a variety of other challenges to the higher education sector. 

International students in the United States generate a substantial amount of revenue for U.S. businesses during their stay in the United States. Often, the immigration conversation turns to how much non-citizens “take” (e.g. jobs) without a necessary focus on how their needs generate job and economic growth for communities. In Indiana, for example, international students contribute nearly a BILLION dollars to the state economy across a number of sectors, from accommodation and dining to retail and telecomm, among others. In Washington DC alone, that number is a half a BILLION dollars. These needs in turn create jobs for citizens. In other words, putting roadblocks on legitimate, lawful employment and study by nonimmigrants who are studying in the United States ultimately hurts American citizens. Both supply and demand need to be considered together, not in isolation.

It has frequently been said that the non-U.S. citizen population most tracked and surveilled in the United States is the student population, in particular the F student community. The middle-class students attending my current university (and even the average student at a very expensive private I used to work at) would simply not be able to come up with the necessary funding. Given that international talent is directly responsible for such a large number of start-ups in the United States and such a high amount of innovation, it would be self-defeating for the United States to make it even more difficult for international students to participate in the workplace and the economy.

RE: Public Comment Opposing Optional Practical Training Fees — Docket ICEB-2026-0100

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566), requiring SEVP-certified institutions to pay $70,000 for initial and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. While I recognize the government’s legitimate interest in preventing fraud and protecting domestic labor, this fee structure introduces severe economic distortions and lacks the necessary evidentiary basis under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

1. Adverse Economic Impacts and Market Competitiveness
The United States operates in a highly competitive global market for talent. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. OPT provides a vital bridge for these graduates to apply their skills locally. Imposing prohibitive financial burdens risks discouraging institutions from participating, reducing the return on educational investments, and restricting access to high-skilled talent. This disproportionately impacts smaller institutions and businesses with less capital, leading to market consolidation rather than broad-based innovation. High-skilled immigrants and domestic workers act as complementary assets; restricting the former directly limits the growth and hiring capacity of American enterprises.

2. Insufficient Legal and Evidentiary Justification under the APA
Under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 553(c), agencies must examine relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for their actions, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. DHS has not provided empirical evidence demonstrating that $70,000 or $30,000 fees are correlated with fraud reduction. An institution's liquidity is an inaccurate proxy for compliance integrity. By failing to model the broader macroeconomic impacts on university enrollment, research capacity, and employer hiring, the proposed rule lacks the reasoned justification required to withstand judicial review. Capital barriers do not deter sophisticated fraudulent actors; instead, they penalize compliant, high-value participants.

3. Proposed Clear and Effective Solution: Risk-Based Compliance
Rather than implementing arbitrary, economically disruptive financial barriers, DHS should adopt a Risk-Based Enforcement and Cost-Recovery Model. This effective framework consists of:
• Targeted Compliance Audits: Allocate enforcement resources based on historical institutional risk profiles rather than a flat fee.
• Proportionate, Cost-Based Fees: Structure administrative fees strictly around the documented, itemized cost of SEVP oversight and verification activities, ensuring compliance with the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA).
• Enhanced Data Integration: Leverage existing electronic verification databases to flag anomalies automatically without disrupting legitimate participants.

As a professional who entered the U.S. via a lawful academic pathway in cancer research and is expanding expertise in healthcare administration and business analytics, I have directly contributed to the domestic economy through high-skilled labor and tax revenue. I request that federal oversight distinguish compliance risks from lawful, high-value participation. DHS should withdraw the current fee proposal and implement a data-driven, risk-based compliance framework that safeguards system integrity without compromising American competitiveness.

Thank you for your consideration.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to impose substantial mandatory fees—specifically $70,000 for initial recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent periods—on Optional Practical Training (OPT). These proposed fees are disproportionately high and create an unreasonable financial barrier for international students pursuing legitimate experiential learning opportunities in the United States.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal or substantially revise it to implement reasonable, cost-proportionate fees if any fee adjustment is deemed necessary. International students already invest significant financial resources in higher education within the United States. OPT is a core component of this educational investment, enabling eligible F-1 students to obtain temporary practical training directly related to their field of study. Imposing excessive fee requirements on the program threatens to make post-graduation training cost-prohibitive, undermining the primary purpose of the nonimmigrant student framework. While the proposed rule includes provisions allowing institutions to request refunds if an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) is denied or not issued, this mechanism fails to mitigate the immediate harm. USCIS adjudication timelines for OPT applications routinely range from three to six months. 

Requiring the advance deposit and holding of tens of thousands of dollars per student for extended periods imposes an undue financial burden on institutions and students alike, regardless of whether a refund is eventually granted. Furthermore, because the rule explicitly permits institutions to shift these costs onto individual students or employers, shifting the legal responsibility of payment does not remove the underlying financial burden—it merely redistributes it onto parties ill-equipped to absorb such extreme costs.  DHS asserts that these fees are necessary to enhance oversight and curb program misuse. However, an applicant’s or institution's ability to pay high fee amounts bears no rational relationship to program integrity or compliance; financial capacity is not evidence of misconduct, nor does a high price tag ensure compliance. DHS should explain how imposing prohibitive costs improves oversight beyond serving as a blanket financial deterrent.   Instead of establishing financial barriers that penalize compliant participants, the agency should evaluate tailored, less burdensome regulatory alternatives, including:Targeted compliance reviews of participating entities;Enhanced verification of degree-related training plans (such as Form I-983);Direct employer accountability and verification mechanisms; andFocused enforcement against identified bad actors.

Enforcement measures targeted specifically at demonstrated misconduct are far more effective and equitable than punitive financial barriers applied broadly across compliant institutions and students.If implemented as proposed, this fee structure will create severe market distortions. Designated School Officials (DSOs) and institutions may feel compelled to decline recommending otherwise fully qualified students due to liability risks. Employers may withdraw legitimate entry-level training opportunities rather than assume prohibitive fee obligations. Consequently, qualified international graduates will be deprived of practical experience despite fulfilling every academic and regulatory requirement.   

While protecting the U.S. domestic workforce is a legitimate regulatory goal, discouraging global talent from participating in the U.S. economy directly harms American competitiveness. International students on OPT contribute significantly to campus communities, fuel innovation, and support key economic sectors. Restricting their ability to obtain practical training deprives American employers of vital talent in critical fields.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS rescind the proposed fee structure and consider less restrictive alternatives that uphold program integrity without disrupting the U.S. higher education system and talent pipeline.

- Passed to students, it prices practical training out of reach for all but the wealthiest, turning opportunity in America into a privilege of birth rather than merit.
- Passed to employers, it taxes companies for hiring the very graduates American universities trained, and it will fall hardest on startups and smaller employers that cannot absorb a $70,000 surcharge per hire.

I urge rejection of section [V A] based on the lack of guidelines for implementation and asymmetric impact associated with the proposed OPT fee.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01 | 91 FR 64566
DHS should withdraw this proposed rule. A detailed comment is attached; the core objections follow.
1. The rule's central assumption is refuted by DHS's own data. It assumes schools, students, or employers will pay $70,000 for twelve months of work authorization that currently costs about $500. DHS's technical appendix to its H-1B fee rulemaking (91 FR 54817) reports initial Form I-129 petitions for beneficiaries abroad fell from 13,823 to 1,212 in 245 days under the $100,000 H-1B charge, a 91.2 percent decline. This rule neither cites nor distinguishes that finding. Employers unwilling to pay $100,000 for an experienced professional on a multi-year visa will not pay $70,000 for a graduate's first twelve months.
2. The participation estimates are unsupported. The "high" case assumes a 140-fold price increase produces no behavioral response. The "low" case assumes OPT falls 56 percent while STEM OPT falls only 22 percent, implying 84 percent of a shrunken pool pays a second $30,000 charge. The "primary" figure averages the two. No reasoning supports any of them.
3. Revenue and deterrence cannot both occur. DHS projects $12.4 billion annually while stating it intends a smaller participant pool. One claim must be abandoned, and the rule does not say which.
4. Table 9 values forgone labor at the fee amount. The opportunity cost of a deterred graduate is set equal to the fee not collected, so the same graduate would be worth $5,000 under a $5,000 fee. A correct estimate would include wages, downstream H-1B employment, firm creation, and forgone tax revenue. The rule quantifies $40 to $80 billion in costs and no benefits at all.
5. The fraud rationale fails on the rule's own terms. The notice states the fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and that ICE lacks authority to retain them. A measure premised on inadequate enforcement resources that supplies none has no rational connection to its objective. The supporting evidence is two 2020 cases, a 2021 news article, and 2025 site visits, none establishing that deterrence requires $100,000 rather than $5,000.
6. Reasonable alternatives exist under current authority and are not considered: auditing schools with anomalous SEVIS placement patterns; systematic verification of Form I-983 attestations, extended to initial OPT; SEVP certification consequences for documented violators; and a cost-recovery fee the agency may lawfully retain. Each distinguishes compliant institutions from non-compliant ones. A flat fee cannot.
7. The worker-protection rationale is uncited and contradicted. Zavodny finds no evidence OPT reduces U.S. job opportunities, and that 10 additional bachelor's degrees awarded to international students correspond to 15 additional STEM degrees awarded to U.S. students. Kwon, Lee and Monras (2026) find the 2016 STEM OPT expansion produced employment gains for native high-skilled workers. BLS reports computer and mathematical unemployment at 3.3 percent, down from 3.9 percent a year earlier.
8. The rule damages the administration's stated priority. International students are 79.7 percent of full-time graduate students in computer and information sciences (90,570 of 113,633). EO 14363 launched the Genesis Mission as comparable in urgency to the Manhattan Project; EO 14434 directs agencies to call this field Super Intelligence. The preamble never mentions AI competitiveness.
9. The charges exceed the authority Congress granted. 8 U.S.C. 1372 and 1356(m) limit such charges to cost. A compulsory payment untethered to cost and deposited in the general fund is a tax. In California v. Mullin (D. Mass. June 2026) the court vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee as a tax. In Global Nurse Force v. Trump (N.D. Cal. Sept. 2026) the court found a failure to consider alternatives or reliance interests. In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS (D. Mass. Sept. 2026) the court faulted DHS for treating unquantifiable costs as zero, relying on anecdotes, and failing to show a rational connection to its stated objectives. Each defect recurs here.

If substantial OPT fees reduce opportunities for graduates to apply their research training within the United States, some of those potential benefits may instead materialize abroad.

This does not mean that all international students are publicly funded or that every graduate would otherwise remain in the United States. It does mean that the possibility of reduced domestic returns deserves consideration.

Issue 2: Incomplete accounting of indirect costs

A fiscal analysis focused primarily on fee collections and immediate administrative effects may overlook broader economic consequences.

Relevant questions include:

Would reduced OPT participation affect the commercialization of publicly supported research?

Could universities face additional financial pressure that affects research programs?

What are the potential consequences for future business formation, taxable economic activity, and skilled employment?

Have less costly, risk-based enforcement alternatives been adequately evaluated?

Requested Action

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) pending a more comprehensive economic analysis.

That analysis should distinguish direct regulatory costs from potential indirect effects and compare the proposed fees with targeted employer verification and compliance enforcement.

Public policy should consider the full economic consequences of a regulatory decision, including the long-term value of investments already made in American research and workforce development.

I write as an individual to oppose the proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees" (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), under which a SEVP-certified school must pay $70,000 before making a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I have commented on this docket before on the question of statutory authority. This comment addresses a separate defect: the proposed charge bears no relationship to the cost of anything the government does, and by the Department's own estimates it would operate not as a fee but as a prohibitive toll that ends the program in practice.

A fee, as opposed to a tax, is a charge for a service rendered to the payer, measured by the cost of providing it. The service here is a designated school official entering a recommendation in SEVIS — a database transaction — followed by USCIS adjudication of a Form I-765, for which the student already pays a separate filing fee of $470 online. The marginal governmental cost of the SEVIS entry is, on any realistic accounting, a few dollars of system time. DHS proposes to charge $70,000 for it: roughly 150 times the entire I-765 filing fee, and thousands of times the cost of the act being charged for. The mismatch is explained by where the money goes. These receipts would be deposited in the Treasury as general revenue; they do not fund SEVP's administration of OPT. A charge that does not fund the service, is not measured by its cost, and is collected for the general fisc is a tax, and the power to levy it belongs to Congress.

The Department's own estimates confirm that the charge is prohibitory rather than compensatory. DHS projects $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year in collections across some 2,478 schools. No school will pay $70,000 — in many cases more than a year of the student's tuition, and more than the first-year salary in many fields — as a routine cost of entering a recommendation. The predictable institutional responses are to stop recommending, to ration recommendations, or to pass the charge through to students or employers, a pass-through the preamble itself concedes is possible. Each response ends OPT for the affected students as effectively as a direct repeal. But OPT is not the Department's to repeal by pricing: practical training is embedded in the statutory scheme for F-1 students under INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i) and in regulations maintained under INA 214 for decades. An agency that lacks authority to abolish a program outright cannot achieve the same result by setting its price at a level no one can pay.

The worker-protection rationale offered for the rule also runs in the wrong direction. OPT is the bridge by which U.S. employers hire and evaluate foreign graduates before sponsoring them. Close the bridge and the work does not revert to U.S. workers; the employer's practical alternative is to move the function to its offices abroad, where neither the job, nor the payroll taxes, nor any eventual H-1B petition ever touches the United States. A rule that exports the job in order to protect it fails on its own stated terms.

Finally, the compliance machinery is a burden in itself: payment must precede the SEVIS entry, refunds are confined to narrow pre-issuance circumstances, and 2,478 institutions — most of them colleges with only a handful of international students — must build payment and accounting procedures around a per-student charge larger than many of their entire international-program budgets. DHS books the collections as a transfer and moves on; the institutions administering this will not experience it as a formality.

A $70,000 charge for a database entry is not a fee, and $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year is not a paperwork detail. I urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule.

Dennis Ma
