I submit this comment as an individual working in the field of international education for 14 years. Based on my professional experience supporting international students and observing the role practical training plays in higher education, I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw it.

The proposed fee structure is extraordinarily burdensome and appears disconnected from the educational purpose of Optional Practical Training (OPT). While DHS states that the proposal is intended to address oversight and fraud concerns, imposing massive fees on institutions does not target fraud. Instead, it creates financial barriers for institutions and students who are already complying with the law and following established procedures.

OPT is not merely an employment benefit. It is an educational experience that allows students to apply classroom learning in real-world settings related to their academic fields. For many international students, the opportunity to gain practical experience is a primary factor in deciding to study in the United States. Weakening access to OPT makes U.S. institutions less competitive at a time when other countries are actively recruiting international talent.

The proposal would also create inequitable outcomes among students who otherwise meet the same eligibility requirements. Access to practical training should not depend on whether a student's institution, employer, or personal circumstances allow someone to absorb extraordinarily high fees. This proposal would effectively divide students into those who can afford experiential learning opportunities and those who cannot.

Beyond the impact on individual students, international students make significant contributions to universities, local communities, research efforts, innovation, and the broader economy. They support academic programs, contribute diverse perspectives to classrooms, and help prepare all students for participation in a global workforce. Policies that discourage international enrollment ultimately affect domestic students as well.

I am also concerned that the proposal raises significant implementation questions. The structure and timing of the proposed fees are unclear, particularly for students pursuing additional degrees, transferring institutions, or participating in multiple periods of practical training. Before considering a proposal with consequences of this magnitude, stakeholders deserve clear explanations regarding how the requirements would operate in practice.

Finally, I believe the proposed fees are disproportionate to any stated policy objective. Legitimate oversight and enforcement should focus on identifying and addressing misconduct directly rather than creating broad financial barriers that affect all participants regardless of compliance history.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and engage with educational institutions, employers, students, and other stakeholders to identify more effective and less burdensome approaches to maintaining program integrity.

Thank you for considering my comments.

I strongly support the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for the initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT recommendation (including STEM OPT extensions) for F-1 nonimmigrant students. These fees, to be paid by SEVP-certified institutions before a Designated School Official may enter a recommendation in SEVIS, are a necessary and appropriate step to combat fraud and abuse, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect American workers.
Optional Practical Training was created as a limited, temporary opportunity for practical training directly related to a student’s major field of study—not as a broad work-authorization program, a bridge around H-1B numerical limits, or a low-cost labor pipeline. Over time it has grown dramatically and is widely treated as the latter. DHS has correctly identified that this expansion has outpaced effective oversight and produced documented problems, including problematic or nonexistent worksites, “pay-to-stay” schemes, and cases involving highly suspect employers. Recent SEVP findings of thousands of F-1 students on OPT associated with questionable employers underscore the scale of the integrity problem.
High fees address these issues in several concrete ways:
	•	They give schools a direct financial stake in the recommendations they make. Institutions will have a strong incentive to exercise greater selectivity and oversight rather than routinely recommending large numbers of students, many of whom may have only a tenuous connection between the training and the academic program.
	•	They raise the cost of participation enough to deter low-value or fraudulent uses of the program while still allowing employers and students who genuinely value the particular training opportunity to absorb or share the cost. Talent that is truly exceptional will continue to be justified; routine use of OPT as inexpensive, tax-advantaged labor will become far less attractive.
	•	They reduce the overall volume of OPT participation, thereby easing the competitive pressure on U.S. workers and recent American graduates—especially in STEM and other high-demand fields—where the program has functioned as a substantial additional supply of labor outside the statutory frameworks Congress created for temporary workers. American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been converted into a large-scale pipeline for lower-cost foreign labor.
The rule is properly structured. Fees are triggered by the school’s recommendation (not by any particular employer), apply prospectively, and are collected before the process advances to USCIS employment authorization. Depositing the fees into the Treasury is consistent with the dual goals of volume reduction and general revenue; the primary integrity benefit comes from the deterrent and selectivity effects of the fee itself.
Critics will argue that the amounts are too high or that legitimate talent will be lost. The appropriate response is that OPT is a privilege extended by regulation, not a right, and that the program’s original educational purpose does not require open-ended, low-cost access for hundreds of thousands of participants. Employers who can demonstrate that a particular F-1 graduate’s training is worth the cost can still proceed. Those who cannot, or who have relied on the program primarily for labor-cost advantages, should not continue to enjoy the status quo.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to finalize the rule substantially as proposed. The fees will better align OPT with its intended limited purpose, reduce fraud and abuse, and give American workers a fairer opportunity in the labor market.

The Council of University Directors of Clinical Psychology (CUDCP) opposes the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000 fee for subsequent participation. CUDCP represents over 180 programs who provide doctoral education in clinical psychology.

Clinical psychology requires extensive specialized training, often including a one-year postdoctoral fellowship following doctoral education in many states, to prepare highly skilled psychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on CUDCP member programs’ universities, with the costs likely passed on to students or fellowship sites. This could potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified candidates, leading to even more imbalance in provider supply and demand than already exists. Current research (Cicero et al., 2025) indicates that behavioral health care resources are in decline, while demands for services are increasing. This mismatch will reach a peak by 2037, when projected resources will be able to meet only 55% of anticipated demand.

Negative consequences of the proposed rule extend beyond individual trainees. International professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing valuable scientific expertise related to psychological functioning that strengthens the quality of psychological services, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training could further undermine already constrained workforce development and limit the availability of clinical researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S. population.

We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.
Thank you for considering our comments.

Two students graduate with the same degree. Both have followed immigration rules. Both have legitimate opportunities for practical training.

One attends a wealthy university. The other attends a smaller institution with limited financial resources.

Should their access to OPT depend on which university can afford a $70,000 payment?

That is the fairness problem I see in this proposal.

The proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), combined with the payment requirements under § 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and (iii), could create substantial differences in access to practical training based on institutional financial capacity.

OPT is supposed to provide eligible students with training directly related to their academic field. Its educational purpose is to connect classroom knowledge with professional experience.

Whether a student has earned that opportunity should be determined by eligibility, academic preparation, and compliance with applicable requirements.

A university's financial resources do not establish any of those things.

Large institutions may have greater flexibility to absorb extraordinary expenses. Smaller colleges, regional universities, and institutions operating under tight budgets may have far fewer options.

The result could be a system in which equally qualified students face very different opportunities for reasons unrelated to their education or conduct.

There is another problem.

If the objective is to prevent fraud, the proposed fees do not appear to distinguish between institutions with strong compliance records and those presenting documented risks.

An institution that can afford the payment is not necessarily more compliant. An institution that cannot afford it is not necessarily less compliant.

This raises a fundamental question about whether financial capacity is an appropriate substitute for regulatory oversight.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee requirements and evaluate alternatives based on actual compliance risks, such as targeted institutional audits, employer verification, and stronger investigation of fraudulent training arrangements.

The integrity of OPT should depend on whether participants follow the rules, not on the size of a university's budget.

Financial barriers should not be mistaken for effective oversight.

I oppose this rule. DHS should withdraw it.

1. IT IS A TAX, NOT A FEE (Sec. IV.C). DHS says the money goes to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt and ICE cannot keep it. It pays for no service; USCIS already charges its own I-765 fee. DHS set the amount to match the H-1B charge and a year or two of tuition, not any cost, and admits its purpose is deterrence. A charge that raises $8.4-16.5 billion a year for general revenue is a tax. Only Congress can tax (Art. I, Sec. 8; NCTA v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974); 31 U.S.C. 9701). INA 214(a) says nothing about OPT fees.

2. NO CLEAR AUTHORITY (Sec. III.A). DHS projects up to $144 billion in transfers over 10 years. A claim this large needs clear authorization from Congress (West Virginia v. EPA, 2022), and courts no longer defer to agency readings (Loper Bright, 2024). Congress has written specific immigration fees into the INA. It has never written an OPT fee.

3. THE FEE DOES NOT TARGET THE FRAUD (Sec. IV.A). Every example DHS gives is employer fraud: shell companies, empty offices, phantom employees. But initial OPT requires no employer, and DHS says the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." A fee paid before any job exists cannot screen out bad employers. DHS's largest probe found about 10,000 suspect cases among roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT students, under 3%. The fee hits 100%. A fraud ring can afford $70,000; an honest student from a modest family cannot. That screens for wealth, not honesty.

4. DHS'S OWN PREDICTIONS SHOW THE MISFIT (Sec. VII.A). DHS expects schools to stop paying for non-STEM students and to abandon pre-completion OPT to avoid $100,000. Neither outcome has anything to do with fraud. A student who gets an EAD but never finds a job gets no refund.

5. ZERO QUANTIFIED BENEFITS (Sec. VII.A). DHS estimates $35.1 billion in costs (up to $69.9 billion) and quantifies no benefit at all: no fraud prevented, no U.S. jobs gained. DHS faults the 2016 STEM rule for lacking numbers, then does the same. It also ignores the roughly $43 billion international students added to the economy in 2024-25 (NAFSA).

6. THE ANALYSIS CONTRADICTS ITSELF (Sec. VII). DHS says the rule will not cause $100 million in yearly spending under UMRA, yet projects billions in yearly fees. It says states face no direct costs, yet counts 1,044 state-run public schools that must pay. It finds 98 small schools would lose over 20% of revenue, but offers no small-entity alternative.

7. IT IGNORES RELIANCE (Sec. VI). The rule covers nearly every student now enrolled. We chose schools and took on debt relying on rules that have existed since 1992. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires DHS to weigh that seriously. A 60-day effective date gives us no way to adjust.

8. IT HURTS AMERICANS TOO (Sec. IV.B). DHS admits schools may pass the cost to "all students," meaning U.S. students could pay. Lost international tuition cuts aid and programs for domestic students. Top students will go to Canada, the UK and Australia instead.

9. BETTER OPTIONS EXIST (Sec. IV.C). DHS chose a fee because it is quick and cheap for DHS. But the money goes to the Treasury, not to enforcement. Target the fraud directly: require employers to register and use E-Verify, flag shared and residential addresses, extend I-983 plans and site visits to flagged employers, and debar bad actors.

10. 30 DAYS IS TOO SHORT. E.O. 12866 calls for at least 60 days on economically significant rules.

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule requiring schools to pay $70,000 for a student's initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

1. The fee exceeds DHS's fee-setting authority. Immigration fees are authorized to recover the cost of adjudication services. Reviewing a school's OPT recommendation and issuing an employment authorization document is a routine administrative act costing a fraction of the proposed amount. DHS's own estimate that the rule would collect $12.4 billion per year confirms the fee is not calibrated to cost recovery. A charge of this magnitude functions as a revenue measure, not a service fee, and therefore exceeds the authority Congress granted DHS to set fees.

2. The rule would effectively terminate OPT, contrary to its legislative purpose. OPT exists so F-1 students can obtain practical training related to their field of study. Schools that cannot absorb a $70,000 fee will either pass it on to students, most of whom cannot afford it, or stop recommending OPT altogether. Either way, OPT becomes unavailable to the overwhelming majority of students it was designed to serve. An agency may not use a fee schedule to accomplish indirectly what it has no authority to do directly. If OPT should be narrowed or eliminated, that is a decision for Congress, not for a fee rule.

3. The rule harms the American public interest. International students choose the United States in large part because OPT offers post-study work experience. If OPT becomes unaffordable, many will study in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia instead. The United States would lose tuition revenue that sustains its universities, research contributions in university laboratories, and the companies and jobs these graduates would otherwise create here. American employers, especially startups and small businesses that cannot compete with large firms for experienced workers, would also lose a critical entry-level pipeline.

4. DHS has not provided evidence that a fee of this size is needed. The proposal does not demonstrate that fraud or abuse in OPT is of a scale that could justify $70,000, nor does it connect the size of the fee to any identified problem. Its figures describe the revenue the rule would generate, not the harm it would prevent. A fee imposed without an evidentiary basis linking its size to a documented problem is arbitrary: it burdens students, schools, and employers while the agency has not shown that those costs purchase any improvement in program integrity.

5. The burden will fall hardest on public universities and students of modest means. Well-resourced private institutions may absorb or subsidize the fee; public universities under tight budgets cannot, and will be forced to restrict OPT recommendations or shift the cost to students. OPT would thus become a privilege of wealthy institutions and wealthy families, while students at public universities and from modest backgrounds lose the practical training component of their education. This undermines the breadth of American higher education and one of its principal attractions to talented students worldwide.

For these reasons — unlawful fee-setting, inconsistency with OPT's purpose, lack of evidence, and damage to the American public interest — DHS should withdraw the proposal.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. Schools would have to pay them before recommending a student for practical training. DHS has not shown that it has authority to charge them, or that payments this large would separate legitimate training from fraud.

DHS relies on INA § 214(a)(1), which lets it set the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission.[1] That provision says nothing about fees. DHS set the amounts to match the H-1B payment, not to recover a cost. The money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and ICE could neither keep nor use it.[2] Skinner requires Congress to speak clearly before an agency imposes financial burdens, "whether characterized as 'fees' or 'taxes,'" even to recover costs that do not benefit the payer.[3] A charge that recovers no cost at all needs at least as clear an authorization. When Congress authorizes immigration fees, it says so expressly and specifies how the money is collected and used. Examples include the H-1B/L fraud fee, adjudication fees, the SEVIS fee, and the 2025 visa integrity fee.[4] Section 214(a)(1) has nothing comparable. In July, the First Circuit relied on that pattern, on Skinner, and on Learning Resources. It held that the government had not made a strong showing of authority to require the $100,000 H-1B payment, which is the benchmark DHS used here.[5] Washington Alliance upheld DHS's authority over OPT; it did not consider any fee.[1]

The fraud DHS describes involves shell companies and fake worksites. Yet the school pays before recommending OPT, possibly before the student has a job offer, and the payment "would not be tied to a specific employer."[2] A school's willingness to pay says nothing about whether a future employer is legitimate. DHS rejected broader site visits, training plans, and reporting partly because enforcing them would take "substantial time and resources."[2] The fees would not fund that enforcement either. DHS's main evidence is also inconsistent. The text describes more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers, while footnote 56 describes 10,000 suspect employers. Both cite a video.[2] DHS should release the underlying data.

DHS's primary estimate after the transition year is $12.4 billion a year in fees from 2,478 schools, an average of about $5 million per school. Its low-participation scenario still assumes about 88,000 initial OPT participants a year, mostly STEM students, plus about 74,000 STEM extensions.[6] DHS does not explain why schools would keep paying at that scale. Using the unpaid fee as a proxy for lost opportunities does not capture enrollment lost over whole degree programs.[6] The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act discussion says in one paragraph that the rule would not reach the statutory threshold, and in the next that it would exceed it.[6]

DHS should also weigh this proposal together with its pending H-1B fee proposal. If both take effect, one graduate who uses OPT, receives a STEM extension, and is then sponsored for a cap-subject H-1B could trigger $203,265 in new payments by the school and the employer.[7]

Under the transition rule, if a student began OPT before the effective date, the school would owe $70,000 for a STEM extension recommended afterward, because no initial fee was ever paid.[8] DHS acknowledges that current students are differently situated from prospective ones,[2] but gives them no protection. Students enrolled before the final rule takes effect should be exempt for OPT and STEM extensions tied to their current degree.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. Any new proposal should cite specific statutory authority, disclose the fraud data, and support its participation and cost assumptions.

Dear Acting Director Venturella:

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. The proposal would impose a prohibitive barrier that effectively dismantles a longstanding program without clear congressional authorization. I urge DHS to withdraw it for the reasons below.

1. The fees exceed statutory authority and function as a general revenue tax.

Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act and established precedent, a user fee must reasonably relate to the cost of a specific service and the proceeds should support that program. The NPRM states that the projected $8.4 to $16.5 billion in annual collections would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP compliance or anti-fraud work. The preamble also indicates the amounts were set as a deterrent, aligned with proposed H-1B fees, rather than calculated from the marginal cost of a DSO recommendation in SEVIS. Using a prohibitive price to reduce participation, and suggesting the program might otherwise be shut down, amounts to an attempt to curtail a regulatory program and raise general revenue without an Act of Congress.

2. The FICA tax rationale is mathematically implausible.

In the NPRM, DHS points to the FICA exemption (7.65% combined employee Social Security and Medicare) as creating an incentive for employers to prefer F-1 OPT students. For a 7.65% savings to equal the $70,000 initial fee over a 12-month OPT period, an entry-level graduate would need to earn more than $915,000. Typical OPT salaries are far lower. Treating a statutory payroll tax differential that Congress itself created as justification for a $70,000 to $100,000 per-student charge is arbitrary.

3. Requiring universities to pre-pay $70,000 before a DSO recommendation is unworkable.

The obligation falls on the school before any OPT recommendation is entered in SEVIS. At that stage, a student seeking initial post-completion OPT is not required to have an employer. Nonprofit universities are educational institutions, not staffing agencies. Forcing them to front $70,000 per graduate, or to build escrow and pass through arrangements with students or prospective employers before USCIS even adjudicates an EAD, creates an unnecessary administrative and financial burden. Grant-funded labs and early-stage employers often cannot absorb an additional $30,000 to $100,000 surcharge within existing budgets.

4. The rule harms U.S. STEM capacity while failing to target actual fraud.

International graduate students contribute substantially to research and innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, biomedical engineering, and other critical STEM areas. OPT and STEM OPT provide a bridge from graduate training to practical work. DHS has identified concerns about shell companies and other abuse, but ICE and USCIS already have targeted tools such as SEVIS reporting, Form I-983 reviews, and site visits to address bad actors. Applying a six figure charge across all certified institutions and compliant students, rather than focusing enforcement on fraudulent employers, is not a reasoned response.

5. Reliance interests and less burdensome alternatives were not adequately considered.

Hundreds of thousands of current F-1 students entered multi-year programs in reliance on the existing OPT framework. Even with grandfathering of prior recommendations, students who have not yet graduated, and those on initial OPT who will need a subsequent recommendation for a STEM extension after the effective date, face sudden disruption. DHS has not meaningfully evaluated more targeted measures, such as cost based compliance fees or strengthened employer verification, that could address integrity concerns without broadly reducing access to practical training.

For these reasons, the proposed rule is arbitrary, capricious, and in excess of statutory authority. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

Respectfully submitted.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate goals, but the proposed approach imposes broad costs without adequately establishing that these particular fees are necessary or effective. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and evaluate more targeted alternatives.

1. A high fee is not a reliable fraud screen.

DHS expects these fees to deter bad actors and encourage schools to scrutinize OPT requests. Yet ability to pay is not the same as compliance. A legitimate school could be priced out while a well-funded fraudulent operator could pay. DHS should provide evidence linking the proposed dollar amounts to reductions in fraudulent authorizations and distinguish that outcome from a reduction in legitimate participation. What proportion of discouraged applicants is expected to be fraudulent, and on what evidence is that estimate based?

2. The projected costs require a stronger accounting of benefits.

DHS's regulatory impact analysis estimates annualized economic costs of about $4.1 billion in its primary scenario, with substantial uncertainty [1]. The agency should compare these modeled costs with quantified estimates of avoided fraud, enforcement savings, and measurable gains for U.S. workers. Lower OPT participation alone is not proof of better wages or employment outcomes. Without such a comparison, the public cannot assess whether the fees are proportionate to the stated objectives.

3. The fees do not directly finance stronger oversight.

DHS states that fee receipts would go to the U.S. Treasury rather than be earmarked for SEVP enforcement [1]. The agency proposes deterrence and stronger school incentives, but it should demonstrate why those indirect mechanisms would outperform risk-based school audits, employer verification, data-driven fraud detection, and mandatory DSO training. GAO identified specific SEVP oversight vulnerabilities and recommended stronger fraud-risk controls [3]. DHS should compare these alternatives using estimated effectiveness and cost rather than assume a uniform fee is preferable.

4. The effects on U.S. education and research deserve fuller analysis.

OPT can influence where students pursue degrees and where graduates develop their skills. Research on earlier STEM OPT expansions found increases of approximately 14–15% in STEM degree completions, including gains among domestic students [2]. That finding does not directly predict the effect of this proposal, but it cautions against assuming that opportunities for international graduates necessarily disadvantage U.S. students. DHS should evaluate impacts on university enrollment, research capacity, domestic STEM training, and innovation.

5. A uniform charge creates uneven burdens and reliance concerns.

A $70,000 obligation may have vastly different effects on large universities, smaller colleges, and the students they recommend, irrespective of compliance history. Students and institutions also make multi-year educational commitments under existing OPT expectations. DHS should examine these distributional and reliance effects and explain why its proposed 60-day transition is adequate.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and instead evaluate evidence-based, risk-targeted oversight measures, including their expected fraud-reduction benefits, costs, and effects on U.S. workers and universities. An effective rule should target misconduct rather than treat financial capacity as a proxy for program integrity.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published on October 8, 2026 (91 FR 64566). The proposal would impose a fee of $70,000 for an initial period of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT period. I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw this proposal.

1. Disproportionate financial burdens on international students and universities

OPT is an important component of the F-1 student program, allowing international graduates to apply their academic knowledge and skills in professional settings. The proposed fees are so substantial that they risk making OPT practically inaccessible. Although educational institutions would formally bear the payment obligation, these costs could ultimately be passed on to students, employers, or other members of university communities. This would create significant financial barriers for international students, many of whom have already made substantial investments in their education in the United States.

2. Insufficient justification and lack of proportionality

The Department identifies fraud prevention, immigration system integrity, and the protection of U.S. workers as justifications for the proposed fees. While these are legitimate governmental objectives, the Department should demonstrate how fees of this extraordinary magnitude are reasonably related to the actual administrative and enforcement costs of the OPT program. The proposal raises serious questions about the methodology used to calculate these amounts and whether they are necessary to achieve the stated objectives. The Department should provide a transparent, evidence-based justification before imposing such substantial financial obligations.

3. Negative consequences for U.S. higher education and research

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research institutions, and the broader economy. They participate in academic research, support innovation, contribute specialized expertise, and enrich the intellectual life of university communities. OPT provides an important pathway through which these contributions extend beyond the classroom. The proposed fees would disproportionately disadvantage international students with limited financial resources and institutions unable to absorb additional costs. For many graduates, OPT provides an essential opportunity to gain professional experience and establish careers after completing their degrees. Making access to this opportunity dependent on an institution's or employer's capacity to absorb extraordinarily high fees risks creating unequal access to professional development and employment opportunities.

5. Less restrictive alternatives are available

The Department's objectives of preventing fraud and ensuring program integrity do not necessarily require prohibitive fees. More targeted measures, including strengthened institutional oversight, improved verification procedures, risk-based compliance reviews, and enhanced reporting requirements, could address documented abuses without undermining access for otherwise eligible students. The Department should meaningfully consider these less burdensome alternatives.

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed rule. Its extraordinarily high fees are insufficiently justified and risk imposing disproportionate burdens on international students, universities, and employers. The objectives of protecting U.S. workers and maintaining immigration system integrity are important, but they should be pursued through proportionate, evidence-based, and carefully tailored regulatory measures.

OPT should remain an accessible pathway for international graduates to contribute their knowledge, skills, and professional expertise to American society. A regulatory framework that effectively restricts access on the basis of institutional or financial resources would undermine the educational, economic, and research interests that OPT helps advance.

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am a doctoral student in biostatistics, and I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training recommendation and $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations. Protecting U.S. workers and preventing fraud are important objectives. However, the proposed fees could undermine American research, weaken employers’ access to qualified graduates, and restrict legitimate training opportunities without adequately distinguishing them from fraudulent activity. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

My training focuses on statistical methods used to evaluate health interventions and improve the reliability of medical evidence. In biostatistics, the value of a researcher’s work extends beyond an individual position: rigorous study design and analysis help researchers determine whether treatments are effective, identify safety concerns, and draw reliable conclusions from clinical data. These contributions benefit American patients, clinicians, and research teams. A substantial financial barrier to retaining U.S.-trained graduates could interrupt this work and reduce the future domestic benefits of investments in their education and training.

I am particularly concerned about the economic reasoning in Section VII.A.5.b of the proposal. DHS assumes that, when the benefits of OPT exceed the proposed fees, affected parties could collectively share the costs to preserve participation.[1] This assumption overlooks the distinction between social value, private financial returns, and the availability of funds. Patients who may benefit from better medical evidence cannot readily finance a researcher’s employment authorization. A university or nonprofit may recognize the value of a graduate’s contributions while lacking unrestricted funds to cover the fee. An inability to pay therefore does not demonstrate that an opportunity offers insufficient value to the United States. DHS should explicitly evaluate these financing constraints and the benefits of research that extend beyond the student, institution, and employer.

The proposed fee would also make financial resources a major determinant of access to practical training. Two equally qualified graduates pursuing equally legitimate opportunities could face different outcomes because one has access to a wealthy employer or personal resources and the other does not. A flat fee does not directly measure competence, compliance, or educational value. It could disadvantage smaller employers and nonprofit research organizations even when they offer appropriate supervision and competitive compensation.

Protecting American employment also requires examining whether international graduates complement U.S. workers, rather than assuming that excluding one graduate creates one job for an American. A 2024 study by Guo, Gong, and Pang found that an expansion of STEM OPT increased domestic employment in STEM occupations, with stronger effects in information technology.[2] This finding does not establish that every worker benefits or predict the effects of the proposed fee. It does, however, demonstrate why DHS should assess potential effects on team productivity, business expansion, and demand for American workers before imposing a substantial barrier to participation.

Fraud should be addressed through measures that identify and penalize misconduct. Payment of a large fee does not establish that an employer exists, that appropriate training occurs, or that wages and working conditions comply with applicable requirements. DHS should compare the proposal with targeted employer verification, risk-based inspections, and enforcement against documented violations. Reducing legitimate participation alongside fraudulent participation is not sufficient evidence that a policy improves program integrity or benefits the country overall.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate proportionate alternatives supported by evidence. Any future proposal should account for effects on American research, smaller employers, domestic workers, and students already investing years in U.S. education. Preserving legitimate practical training while enforcing meaningful safeguards would better serve the interests of the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent or STEM OPT fee. Although preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, these extraordinary fees threaten America's ability to attract and retain international talent.

OPT participants are highly educated graduates who contribute specialized knowledge to research, technology, and other industries. Protecting domestic workers should involve enforcing wage protections and labor standards rather than imposing blanket financial barriers. Preventing qualified graduates from contributing could reduce U.S. productivity, innovation, and advanced technology development.

V.A - Establishing OPT Fees

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent or STEM OPT fee are excessive and disproportionate to reasonable administrative costs. International students already pay substantial tuition and living expenses. These fees would make practical training accessible primarily to those with exceptional financial resources. Such barriers could drive talented graduates toward competing countries, weakening America's scientific leadership and skilled workforce.

Additional fees associated with higher educational levels would discourage advanced education and professional development. This risks losing future researchers, scientists, and innovators whose contributions could benefit the United States for decades.

Educational Cost Comparisons

Tuition and educational expenses cannot justify extraordinary immigration-related fees. Students pay universities for instruction and educational services, not for the ability to afford an additional $70,000 employment authorization charge. Such policies could undermine America's attractiveness as a global destination for higher education and intellectual talent.

Institutional and Employer Costs

If universities or employers must pay these fees, they may reduce recruitment, employment opportunities, compensation, or research funding. Small businesses and research institutions may be particularly unable to absorb these costs. Reduced access to international researchers could slow American scientific discoveries, technological advancement, and economic growth.

V.C - Transition Period

A 60-day transition period is inadequate for universities, employers, and students to adjust budgets and existing employment commitments. Students have made substantial educational and financial decisions based on the existing OPT framework. Abrupt implementation could disrupt research projects and jeopardize investments in American education and innovation.

The proposed rule risks discouraging international students from attending U.S. universities and encouraging qualified graduates to pursue opportunities abroad. Losing these graduates means losing future entrepreneurs, researchers, inventors, and contributors to America's economic and intellectual leadership.

DHS should thoroughly evaluate impacts on universities, small employers, research organizations, and students and provide transparent evidence supporting the proposed fee calculations.

Fraud prevention and program integrity can be achieved through targeted enforcement, reasonable administrative fees, employer accountability, and improved compliance mechanisms. These alternatives are less burdensome and preserve access to qualified international talent.

OPT should remain accessible through a reasonable, transparent, and proportionate regulatory framework that protects program integrity without creating prohibitive financial barriers.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule and recommend its withdrawal. Preserving access to qualified international graduates is an investment in America's economic prosperity, scientific leadership, and intellectual future.

I write to strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety. A $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee would effectively end Optional Practical Training for most international students. That would harm American science, the American economy, and the United States’ standing in the world, without meaningfully serving the rule’s stated goals.

First, the fee does not fit its stated purpose. DHS justifies the rule as a way to strengthen program integrity, but a flat fee of this size applies equally to every student, and the overwhelming majority of OPT participants are doing exactly what the program intends: gaining practical experience in their field at universities, hospitals, laboratories, and companies. DHS already has oversight tools, such as training plans, employer reporting, and site visits, and the rule itself discusses extending these measures more broadly. That approach would strengthen oversight without making OPT unaffordable for the students it exists to serve.

Second, in practice the cost will fall on students. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the fee on to students or employers. $70,000 exceeds the annual stipend of most PhD students in the United States and the first-year salary of many new graduates. Few students could pay it, and few employers will pay it to hire an entry-level graduate. Universities will face the same pressure, so whether a student is recommended for OPT would depend on the institution’s budget rather than the student’s merit. Students at less wealthy institutions would be hurt most.

Third, the rule would undermine practical training as part of education. DHS expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT, because splitting OPT would cost $100,000. Pre-completion OPT is how many students gain internship and research experience while they study. Discouraging it makes American degrees less valuable and less competitive with programs abroad.

Fourth, comparing OPT to H-1B misunderstands the program. OPT is time-limited practical training directly related to a student’s field of study. It is an extension of education, not a substitute for a work visa. Setting fees to “align” with H-1B treats training as a labor loophole and ignores the long-standing recognition that practical experience is part of an education.

Fifth, the rule wastes public investment. Many international graduate students are trained with support from federal research grants, which U.S. taxpayers fund. OPT is often the main way the country gets a return on that investment: graduates apply what they learned in American labs and companies, pay taxes, start businesses, and often stay to fill critical roles. This rule would ensure that federally funded training mostly benefits other countries’ economies.

Sixth, the rule would weaken American leadership in science and technology. The best students choose where to study based partly on post-study work opportunities, and competitor countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia offer post-graduation work pathways without anything like this fee. If OPT becomes unaffordable, top talent will go elsewhere, and so will the research, patents, and companies they produce. The United States has also gained enormous soft power from generations of international students who trained and worked here and went on to become leaders in science, business, and government around the world. Closing that pathway gives up an advantage that cannot easily be regained.

Finally, the rule is unfair to students already enrolled. Current international students made multi-year commitments to American institutions based on a program that has existed for decades. Changing its terms this drastically, mid-degree, breaks faith with them.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. I support efforts to prevent fraud, but these fees are so high that they would effectively shut many qualified students out of a lawful program.

OPT is not a loophole. It is an established part of the F-1 system, with eligibility rules, school oversight, and government authorization. Students come to the United States legally, pay tuition, complete their degrees, and follow the rules with the understanding that they may apply for practical training in their field. OPT is not guaranteed, but people who meet the requirements should have a fair chance to apply. Making that chance depend on whether a school, student, or employer can come up with $70,000 is not reasonable enforcement.

It also makes little sense from the standpoint of American competitiveness. The U.S. spends years educating talented people from around the world. American employers and research teams then have a chance to benefit from the skills those graduates developed here. Why would we want to train these people and then put up a financial wall just as they are ready to contribute? Other countries are competing for the same talent, and they will be happy to welcome graduates who find the U.S. route too expensive.

Universities would pay a price as well. The chance to gain relevant work experience after graduation is one reason students choose to study in America. If OPT becomes financially unrealistic, some students will choose another country before they ever enroll. That means fewer tuition dollars for U.S. schools and less spending at local businesses. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. This proposal puts part of that value at risk.

What concerns me most is the weak connection between the size of these fees and the stated goal of fighting fraud. The proposed rule says the money would go into the U.S. Treasury and would not be specifically set aside for OPT investigations or enforcement. If the goal is to stop fraudulent employment, why not direct resources toward checking employers, verifying job arrangements, and investigating violations? A $70,000 charge does not tell us whether a job is legitimate. It mainly tells us who can afford to pay.

The burden on smaller institutions is especially troubling. DHS’s own analysis estimates that 98 small institutions could face annual fee costs exceeding 20% of their estimated revenue after the transition period. For some schools, that is money that could otherwise support teaching, student services, and research.

Fraud should be taken seriously. But legitimate students and the schools that educate them should not be priced out of OPT because of wrongdoing by others. I urge DHS to withdraw this fee proposal and pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement instead.

On behalf of Acron Aviation Academy, an FAA-approved flight training institution that enrolls international students in F-1 status, we respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations. 
As a flight school that prepares future professional pilots for careers in commercial aviation, we believe the proposed fee structure would have severe unintended consequences for students, educational institutions, and the broader U.S. aviation industry.
OPT is a critical component of aviation training for many international students as this is how pilot graduates build the flight hours necessary to qualify for airline employment. For international students, OPT provides a lawful avenue to gain this practical experience while contributing to the U.S. aviation training ecosystem.
Most importantly, the employment of international student graduates does not reduce opportunities for domestic graduates. Due to normal workforce turnover and continued industry demand, there is a significant and ongoing need for qualified flight instructors. As a Part 141 flight training provider training more than 1,000 students annually, Acron Aviation Academy prioritizes hiring its own graduates because they are already trained in our curriculum, operational procedures, and safety standards. To meet our instructional needs, we depend on both domestic and international graduates. The availability of OPT is therefore critical to maintaining our workforce and ensuring continuity of training operations.
The proposed fee of a minimum of $70,000 per student would effectively eliminate participation for institutions such as Acron Aviation Academy. Flight training organizations typically operate on narrow margins and are unable to absorb costs of this magnitude. While DHS notes that institutions may pass such costs on to students, this is not a realistic solution. Flight training already requires substantial financial investment due to aircraft acquisition, maintenance, fuel, insurance, and operational expenses. Neither schools nor students are positioned to absorb an additional fee of this size.
The practical effect of this proposal would likely be a significant decline in international student enrollment. This would have serious consequences for flight training institutions that rely on international students as an important component of their student population and future instructor workforce. For Acron Aviation Academy, reduced enrollment would directly impact business operations, growth, and sustainability.
Furthermore, the proposed fee would substantially reduce the number of graduates available to serve as flight instructors. Flight instructors are essential to the aviation training pipeline, providing the instruction necessary to prepare future commercial pilots and airline pilots. Restricting access to OPT would weaken the pilot training at a time when the aviation industry continues to require a strong and reliable supply of qualified pilots and instructors.
The proposed fee is extraordinarily high compared to existing immigration-related fees and appears disconnected from the actual administrative costs associated with reviewing and monitoring OPT participants. DHS states that the proposal is intended to combat fraud and protect U.S. workers. 
However, imposing a fee of this magnitude on every participating student, regardless of compliance history or field of study, penalizes legitimate educational institutions and law-abiding students rather than targeting specific instances of fraud. Enhanced compliance measures, targeted audits, and improved enforcement would be more effective and less disruptive alternatives.
We respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule or, at minimum, substantially reconsider the proposed fee amounts. If DHS determines that additional program oversight funding is necessary, any fee should be reasonably related to administrative costs and should not create barriers that effectively eliminate participation in OPT.
The proposed fees would impose an unsustainable financial burden on both flight training institutions and international students, effectively limiting access to lawful practical training opportunities. The resulting decline in international student participation would adversely affect flight schools' ability to maintain an adequate instructor workforce and support the aviation training pipeline. Ultimately, the proposal would undermine workforce development and pilot training capacity while providing little evidence that it would meaningfully advance the stated goals of fraud prevention, program integrity, or protection of U.S. workers.

I oppose approval of the proposed information-collection revision in its present form. The proposed OPT fee system would require designated school officials (DSOs) to confirm payments in SEVIS. Accurate reporting is important, but DHS has not adequately demonstrated the necessity, accuracy, or minimum burden of this additional requirement. 1. Unsubstantiated Five-Minute Estimate (Supporting Statement, Items 12 and 15)

DHS estimates 226,200 annual fee confirmations, five minutes per confirmation, and 18,850 hours of additional reporting. The Supporting Statement does not provide a time study or sufficient details of the tasks included in five minutes. It is unclear whether this figure covers identifying the correct payment, matching it to the student and OPT recommendation, verifying receipt, correcting errors, and updating records after cancellations or refunds.

The related proposed rule separately estimates additional DSO and administrator review and payment-processing time. DHS should clearly reconcile those estimates with the five-minute PRA figure, identify which activities are included in each, and avoid both omissions and double counting. 2. Internal Inconsistencies in Reported Burden Hours (Items 12 and 15)

The detailed student-data table on pages 11-13 lists annual hour subtotals of 240,346; 13,526; 192,575; 102,182; 16,622; 9,886; 12,350; and 18,850. These sum to 606,337 hours, while the table reports 611,649 hours, a difference of 5,312 hours. This discrepancy exceeds ordinary rounding.

Can the payment system transmit an authenticated payment status directly to SEVIS using a transaction identifier? What additional information would a separate DSO confirmation provide, and how would it improve accuracy or detect fraud?

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 | RIN 1653-AB01
I oppose DHS’s proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. The proposed OPT 1-year post-graduation work authorization pathway to further our training would become 149x more expensive than today. This proposal is disproportionate, poorly targeted, and risks restricting legitimate training while imposing unsustainable costs on students, institutions, and employers.
1. U.S. Workforce Capacity and Healthcare Access
The rule ignores critical healthcare workforce needs. The Commonwealth Fund reports that 43 million Americans live in rural areas with primary-care shortages, projecting that rural physician supply will meet just 68% of demand by 2037. Hospitals also face severe shortages of pharmacists, laboratory scientists, and imaging professionals. As a cancer research PhD and healthcare professional, I know OPT graduates in biomedical and health fields contribute significantly to clinical operations, research, and patient care. This fee narrows this vital talent pool without ensuring vacant positions are filled by U.S. workers. F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students do not have an open employment authorization document (EAD) to work anywhere. Every single job must be directly related to their major field of study. For the 24-month STEM OPT extension, the Form I-983 attestation is a safeguard against replacing existing domestic labor.
2. Economic Consequences for American Institutions
International students drive economic growth. NAFSA estimates they contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–25. With U.S. healthcare spending at an OECD-highest 17.2% of GDP in 2024, workforce capacity and research innovation are vital. DHS must assess the severe downstream impacts on enrollment, research recruitment, and local economies rather than assuming reduced OPT numbers automatically benefit domestic workers.
3. The Fee Does Not Address or Prevent Fraud
DHS identifies valid concerns like fictitious employers and false records, but levying an exorbitant fee on schools does not address them. It fails to verify that employment exists or relates to a student's major. In reality, F-1 students already undergo intense institutional oversight. To maintain status, they complete coursework mapped to Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and must regularly submit mandatory, structured employer evaluations to their Designated School Official (DSO). Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)–(11) and Wash. Alliance of Tech. Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), OPT is legally validated as limited training related to a student’s course of study. Enforcement should build on this framework, not create arbitrary financial walls.
4. Correcting Misconceptions on Tax Treatment and Equity
Commenters argue F-1 students hold a hiring advantage due to FICA exemptions. Per the IRS, certain nonresident F-1 students are exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes on authorized employment for their first five calendar years. However, they still pay full federal, state, and local income taxes. Crucially, they pay into these systems while being entirely excluded from the benefits they fund, including Federal Pell Grants, federal loans, Federal Work-Study, and ACA subsidies. They are also barred from incentive programs like Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), which forgives debt for U.S. citizens after 120 qualifying payments. Given that international students pay significantly higher tuition alongside steep SEVIS and visa fees that fund immigration worker jobs, the claim of a competitive advantage is groundless.
5. Fee Pass-Through and Institutional Burdens
DHS acknowledges schools may pass this fee to students or employers. A $70,000 or $30,000 fee would price out qualified talent, compounding existing tuition disparities. If schools absorb it, they will reduce student services or scale back vital academic programs. Furthermore, the 60-day implementation timeline completely disregards reliance interests. Students have committed tuition and structured their careers around the current framework. DHS must provide at least a 2-year transition window to protect current students.
6. Requested Action and Targeted Alternatives
DHS should withdraw this proposal and prioritize risk-based employer audits, worksite verifications, and penalties for confirmed violators. SEVIS data should prompt targeted investigations rather than justifying blanket fees.

I would like to raise a concern that seems to be missing from much of the discussion surrounding the proposed OPT fees: What happens to the jobs that the United States already struggles to fill?

There is a significant difference between protecting American workers from unfair competition and preventing qualified people from filling positions where workers are genuinely needed.

Education is one example. The United States has faced teacher shortages for years, particularly in special education, where recruiting and retaining qualified professionals remains a challenge. According to an analysis of state-reported teacher shortage data, 45 states identified special education as a shortage area during the 2024–2025 school year.

These shortages exist for reasons. Teaching can be demanding, salaries are not always competitive, and special education often requires additional training, patience, and professional responsibility. Not everyone wants to enter these fields, and many who do eventually decide to leave.

There is nothing wrong with Americans choosing other careers or seeking better opportunities. Everyone should have that freedom. But when schools cannot find enough qualified professionals, why should the government also make it harder for qualified international graduates who are willing to do this work?

The United States already recognizes the importance of attracting people into education. Federal programs such as Teacher Loan Forgiveness provide financial incentives for eligible teachers, including those working in special education. These programs reflect an understanding that teaching is essential and that certain positions can be difficult to fill.

It seems contradictory to recognize the need for more educators through one set of policies while introducing financial barriers that could prevent internationally educated professionals from entering the same workforce through lawful practical training.

I understand concerns about protecting employment opportunities for American citizens. American workers deserve fair wages, reasonable working conditions, and access to good jobs. However, protecting workers should not mean keeping necessary positions unfilled.

If an American citizen is qualified and willing to take a position, that person deserves fair consideration. But if a school has struggled to recruit qualified staff, preventing an eligible international graduate from working does not automatically create another qualified American applicant.

It may simply leave the position vacant.

I also believe we should question whether extremely high OPT fees would address the actual reasons behind workforce shortages. They would not improve teacher salaries, reduce workloads, or make difficult positions more attractive to American workers. International graduates should still be required to meet professional licensing standards, employment requirements, and immigration regulations. No one should receive a job simply because they are willing to take it. But people who are properly trained, qualified, and legally authorized should have a fair opportunity to contribute.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on a question the proposal never answers: why $70,000?

A fee is supposed to bear some relationship to a cost. DHS has published no study tying $70,000 to the expense of processing an OPT recommendation — because no such study could exist. The recommendation itself is a Designated School Official's verification in SEVIS, an administrative act that takes minutes. The government then adjudicates the student's employment authorization for roughly $500. At many public universities, $70,000 exceeds an entire year of in-state tuition. 1. Insufficient evidence of effectiveness (Section IV)

DHS identifies real instances of OPT fraud, which warrant enforcement. Yet these cases do not establish the prevalence of confirmed fraud across all OPT participants or show that universal fees would prevent it. The proposal does not estimate how many fraudulent applications the fees would deter relative to how many legitimate applicants would lose access. 2. Unjustified fee amounts (Section IV.C)

DHS partly justifies the fees by reference to H-1B-related costs and international students' educational expenses. Neither comparison establishes why $70,000 and $30,000 are necessary or proportionate for OPT. The proposal offers no persuasive analysis showing that substantially lower amounts would be ineffective. Moreover, the revenues would enter the U.S. Treasury rather than be directly retained by ICE for enforcement. DHS should provide an evidence-based justification for each fee and distinguish its asserted deterrent effect from actual investments in oversight.

3. Weaknesses in the economic analysis (Section VII.A)

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how institutions will respond but uses a primary participation estimate based on the average of two assumed scenarios. The low-participation scenario largely excludes students ineligible for STEM OPT extensions while assuming continued support for eligible students. Other plausible outcomes, including widespread reductions in STEM OPT recommendations, are insufficiently examined. The midpoint of two assumptions is not necessarily a reliable prediction.

DHS also uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity costs of lost participation. A government fee is not an empirical measure of the value of research, work experience, employer productivity, or future innovation. The analysis needs broader sensitivity testing, institution-specific behavioral scenarios, and independent estimates of forgone economic activity.

4. Harm to legitimate participation and U.S. institutions (Sections IV.C and VII.B)

An institution's ability to pay does not reliably indicate whether a student's OPT opportunity is legitimate. Financially constrained universities may be unable to support qualified graduates, while access to funding does not guarantee compliance. That is not a sufficient comparison of total costs and benefits. Risk-based employer audits, verification of worksites, improved use of SEVIS data, and stronger penalties for confirmed fraud could focus enforcement on documented vulnerabilities. DHS should compare these approaches against universal fees in terms of fraud reduction, economic costs, and effects on lawful participants.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule, substantiate the specific fee levels and expected fraud reduction, revise its economic analysis, and evaluate targeted alternatives. Re: DHS Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees
As a member of the Council of University Directors of Clinical Psychology (CUDCP), I oppose the proposed
$70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and the additional $30,000
fee for subsequent participation. CUDCP represents over 180 programs who provide doctoral
education in clinical psychology.
Clinical psychology requires extensive specialized training, often including a one-year
postdoctoral fellowship following doctoral education in many states, to prepare highly skilled
psychologists to enter the U.S. workforce. OPT is the key mechanism through which
international trainees can complete these required fellowships, and the proposed fees would
severely restrict access by imposing substantial financial burdens on CUDCP member programs’
universities, with the costs likely passed on to students or fellowship sites. This could
potentially lead programs to eliminate fellowship positions or exclude otherwise qualified
candidates, leading to even more imbalance in provider supply and demand than already exists.
Current research (Cicero et al., 2025) indicates that behavioral health care resources are in
decline, while demands for services are increasing. This mismatch will reach a peak by 2037,
when projected resources will be able to meet only 55% of anticipated demand.
Negative consequences of the proposed rule extend beyond individual trainees. International
professionals contribute to the U.S. workforce through clinical care and research, bringing
valuable scientific expertise related to psychological functioning that strengthens the quality of
psychological services, research, and patient care. Restricting access to specialized training
could further undermine already constrained workforce development and limit the availability
of clinical researchers equipped to advance the field and serve the needs of the U.S. population.
We urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, provide transparent justification for the
amounts, and explore less burdensome alternatives that preserve appropriate oversight
without creating prohibitive financial barriers to professional training.

Why does this proposal actually matter to the mission of CUDCP and our trainees?
OPT is the primary mechanism through which international trainees obtain authorization to
complete advanced training in the U.S. and is required for specialties such as
neuropsychology. The proposed rule would create a major systemic barrier to completing this
required training, as many programs would be unable to absorb the proposed fees and there
may not be an alternative visa pathway available to these trainees.
If the proposal is finalized, CUDCP member programs’ universities with international trainees
who match with programs through OPT would face the $70,000 fee, with the costs likely
passed on to students or fellowship sites. Of note, employers do not currently pay a fee for
OPT participation! An alternative is H1B/J1 sponsorship, but this is not a viable option for many
fellowship programs. Preliminary work conducted by the Asian Neuropsychology Association
suggests that during the most recent application cycle, only ~35% of fellowship programs 
accepted international trainees and either had a known visa mechanism in place or indicated
that some form of sponsorship might be possible but not guaranteed. So, international trainees
already face significant barriers under the current system, and this proposal would compound
these existing visa-related barriers, likely leaving trainees without a viable pathway to
complete our field's required training in the U.S.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Current participants should not face a five-figure charge, or the threat of one, in the middle of an authorization that was granted under different terms.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee schedule, or, at a minimum, substantially reduce the amounts, tie any fee to actual processing costs, exclude extensions and other OPT periods already authorized, and clarify how the rule would apply to students and graduates already in the OPT pipeline.

A Texas A&M University graduate on STEM OPT

Dear Homeland Security Department / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Document 2026-20660 / Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). As an F-1 graduate student currently conducting advanced research in STEM at a U.S. university , I believe this proposal is economically unviable, legally flawed, and severely detrimental to the competitive edge of American higher education and technology sectors.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule based on the following substantive grounds:

1. Arbitrary and Capricious Fee Assessment Beyond Statutory Authority
Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA, 31 U.S.C. 9701) and relevant immigration statutes, user fees imposed by federal agencies must be reasonably related to the actual cost of providing a specific service or administrative processing. The proposed imposition of exorbitant fees ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent/STEM OPT) far exceeds any legitimate cost-recovery mechanism for SEVP or USCIS administrative oversight. Imposing fees of this magnitude is functionally punitive rather than compensatory, rendering the rule arbitrary, capricious, and an abuse of agency discretion under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706).

2. Severe Economic Disruption to U.S. Universities and Employers
Shifting such massive financial burdens onto SEVP-certified institutions or F-1 students will have unintended, disastrous consequences for the U.S. economy:
- Financial Strain on Institutions: Universities cannot absorb these fees without drastically raising tuition for all students or cutting research budgets, directly undermining public higher education.
- Loss of U.S. STEM Competitiveness: High-skilled international graduates are vital to U.S. R&D, artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and biomedical innovation. Exorbitant fees effectively shut out top global talent, forcing critical research and employment to shift overseas to competing nations like Canada, Europe, and Asia.
- Small Business and Startup Harm: Employers who rely on OPT talent—especially mid-sized enterprises and early-stage tech startups—will be unable to subsidize these exorbitant fees or compensate for lost talent pools.

3. Disproportionate Impact on International Students and Equity
F-1 students already contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy while paying full tuition and living expenses without access to federal financial aid. Requiring students or institutions to pay tens of thousands of dollars just to receive temporary hands-on practical training directly linked to their degree renders OPT inaccessible to all but the wealthiest individuals, violating basic principles of educational access and equity.

4. Unsubstantiated Justification Regarding Integrity and Fraud
While program integrity is an essential goal, DHS has failed to provide empirical evidence demonstrating that imposing punitive financial barriers on schools or students is a targeted or effective method for preventing fraud. The existing regulatory frameworks (including SEVIS tracking, Form I-983 training plans for STEM OPT, and institutional reporting) already provide robust oversight. Enhancing compliance should be achieved through streamlined administrative audits, not by pricing legitimate international scholars out of practical training.

Conclusion
The proposed OPT fees will inflict irreparable harm on American universities, damage U.S. economic competitiveness, and unfairly burden global scholars who contribute significantly to the United States. 

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to rescind this proposed rule in its entirety.

Economic and Workforce Consequences:

International students contribute to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and industries such as artificial intelligence, healthcare, biotechnology, and semiconductor manufacturing. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. Making post-graduation employment opportunities prohibitively expensive risks reducing international enrollment, university revenue, and the availability of highly skilled graduates. It also places American employers at a disadvantage compared with competitors in countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Germany, which offer post-study employment pathways. The consequences would extend beyond international students to universities, American workers, research institutions, and local economies.

Less Restrictive Alternatives to Prevent Fraud:

DHS has legitimate reasons to protect the integrity of OPT. However, the proposed fees do not distinguish between legitimate students and fraudulent employers. Financial barriers are not reliable indicators of academic merit, employer legitimacy, or regulatory compliance.

Instead, DHS should:

Strengthen targeted investigations of employers and staffing agencies associated with fraudulent employment arrangements.
Use SEVIS data and risk-based monitoring to identify suspicious employer patterns and irregular student placements.
Increase employer accountability through audits and verification of training arrangements.
Establish reasonable administrative fees based on documented processing and enforcement costs, rather than imposing arbitrary amounts.

These measures would address fraud more directly without restricting legitimate participation.

Request for Reconsideration:

Given the significant economic, educational, and administrative consequences, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule in its current form. At a minimum, the Department should reconsider the proposed fee amounts, provide stronger evidence supporting their necessity, evaluate less restrictive alternatives, and allow sufficient time for universities, employers, and students to assess the implications. OPT is not simply an immigration benefit; it is an important component of the relationship between American higher education, workforce development, and national competitiveness. Policies intended to protect U.S. workers and prevent fraud should strengthen this system rather than undermine access to legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
I respectfully urge DHS to reject the proposed fees and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that preserve program integrity while protecting the interests of students, universities, American employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

DHS should withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

1. The Proposed $70,000 and $30,000 Fees Exceed DHS’s Statutory Authority and Constitute an Unlawful Revenue Tax
Congress authorized SEVP fees under Section 641(e) of IIRIRA (8 U.S.C. § 1372(e)) and the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (31 U.S.C. § 9701) solely to recover the reasonable costs of operating and maintaining the SEVIS information-collection system. Likewise, USCIS already recovers the full cost of adjudicating Employment Authorization Documents through the Form I-765 filing fee ($470 online / $520 paper) under 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m). Entering an OPT recommendation into SEVIS is a routine electronic record update performed by a university DSO that imposes virtually zero marginal cost on ICE. Charging $70,000 to $100,000 per student to collect an estimated $12.4 billion annually for deposit into the general U.S. Treasury bears no rational relationship to agency service costs. Under National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), an agency may not levy punitive, policy-driven taxes disguised as user fees without explicit congressional authorization.

DHS’s stated rationale—setting OPT fees “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” to deter employment—ignores the fundamental legal and economic reality of OPT. Post-completion OPT is limited to 12 months (with a 24-month STEM extension requiring a formal Form I-983 training plan). A $100,000 fee for 1 to 3 years of entry-level postgraduate training frequently exceeds the trainee’s entire annual compensation. Even more irrationally, under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), a student who completes a short summer internship on pre-completion OPT and later applies for post-completion OPT triggers both the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee—$100,000 total for a single 12-month statutory OPT allowance. This punitive structure effectively abolishes pre-completion OPT and hands-on experiential training.

3. Severe Harm to U.S. Innovation, Universities, Small Businesses, and Domestic Students
U.S. technological competitiveness depends on retaining graduates trained at American colleges and universities.
