RE: Comments on Proposed Rule – Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket ID: ICEB-2026-0100)   
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing as an international graduate engineering student at a major U.S. research institution to formally register my strong opposition to the proposed rule regarding substantial new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).   The primary motivation for many talented international students in choosing the United States—and rigorous, world-class research institutions—is the vital opportunity to connect classroom theory with hands-on, practical industry training. Working alongside leading industry experts, contributing to critical domestic infrastructure and technical projects, and exchanging diverse technical viewpoints provide indispensable professional grounding before returning to our home countries.   

Imposing an exorbitant fee structure ($70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for extensions) fundamentally disconnects regulatory policy from economic reality:  

Creates an Insurmountable Economic Hardship: International graduate students already bear immense financial commitments through non-resident tuition, institutional fees, and living expenses. A fee structure of this magnitude would force most early-career engineers and researchers out of practical training entirely, effectively closing off post-graduation employment regardless of merit or academic performance.   

Weakens U.S. Academic and Technological Competitiveness: Global talent drives research and industry development across STEM fields in the United States. Instituting prohibitive fees will divert top-tier prospective researchers, scientists, and engineers to competitor nations (such as Canada, the UK, or Germany) that offer accessible, structured post-study work authorization pathways, ultimately damaging U.S. university enrollment and innovation.

Contradicts the Purpose of Practical Training: OPT is inherently educational—an authorized extension of the learning environment meant to give graduates practical competency in their specialized field of study. Monetizing this authorization at tens of thousands of dollars per applicant transforms an educational training bridge into a punitive barrier that many qualified candidates simply cannot meet.   

Practical industry experience is essential for early-career professionals to synthesize their graduate learning and develop meaningful technical leadership. For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to withdraw or fundamentally restructure this proposal to ensure practical training remains accessible and fair.   

Thank you for your consideration of this public comment.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. Charging schools $70,000 per student for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT, would weaken the American economy, strain American universities, and hand our competitors talent the U.S. has already paid to train.

I work as a scientist in the biotech sector and help hire research staff. U.S.-trained international graduates are a real part of the talent pool that keeps our research moving.

It throws away an investment America has already made. International students are educated at American universities, often in labs funded by American research dollars. OPT is how that training becomes work here, in U.S. labs, startups, hospitals, and factories. A six-figure price tag on that step means the U.S. trains scientists and engineers and then sends them to Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, and China, all of which are actively recruiting the same graduates.

It hurts the American students it claims to protect. International tuition helps fund domestic students’ seats, financial aid, and graduate programs. DHS itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to international students, to all students, or to employers. Either way, the burden lands on Americans. Lower international enrollment means lost tuition revenue, and American families, taxpayers, and the college towns that depend on these institutions absorb that loss.

It is the wrong tool for protecting workers. If the concern is that OPT undercuts American wages, the answer is wage and training standards, not a flat fee. STEM OPT already requires employers to provide a formal training plan and pay comparable to similarly situated U.S. workers. A flat fee does not distinguish a well-paid PhD researcher from a low-wage placement. It simply prices out smaller schools, students without family wealth, and startups and small businesses that cannot absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per hire. That leaves the largest companies as the only ones able to compete for this talent.
It is the wrong tool for fighting fraud. If SEVP has found abuse, the right response is targeted enforcement against the specific schools and employers involved. A blanket fee punishes thousands of legitimate institutions for the conduct of a few. And DHS would not even keep the fee revenue to fund enforcement.

The analysis contradicts itself. The rule’s claimed benefits depend on substantially reducing OPT participation: fewer participants to monitor, and more jobs for U.S. workers. Yet DHS’s economic analysis assumes schools will largely keep recommending OPT. Both cannot be true. Suppose the fee shrinks the pipeline. Then the U.S. suffers the losses to innovation, growth, and university finances that DHS waves off as too speculative to weigh. Suppose instead that it doesn’t shrink the pipeline. Then the rule delivers none of its stated benefits while imposing billions of dollars in annual costs, as DHS’s own estimates acknowledge. A rule built on contradictory assumptions should not be finalized.

It weakens U.S. competitiveness where it matters most. Leadership in AI, semiconductors, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing depends on STEM talent, and international students make up a large share of U.S. STEM graduate programs. Many American companies, and the jobs they created, were founded by people who first came here as students. Pushing these graduates out just as they are ready to contribute hurts American competitiveness and national security.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fee. If DHS has specific integrity concerns, it should address them through targeted enforcement, wage and training-plan compliance, and school oversight. Those measures protect American workers without dismantling a program that keeps American-trained talent working for America.

I don't think DHS has provided sufficient evidence to justify imposing such enormous fees on all OPT participants.

DHS cites individual criminal cases and an investigation involving more than 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers. But suspected fraud is not the same as confirmed fraud. How many cases were confirmed? What percentage of all OPT participants actually committed fraud? And what is the measurable economic harm caused by these violations?

OPT is a legally authorized program. Using OPT according to its rules is not fraud simply because an employer might otherwise consider H-1B.

Charging $70,000 would not distinguish legitimate students from fraudulent ones. A legitimate student whose university cannot afford the fee would lose the opportunity, while someone with sufficient financial resources could still pay it.

Why not investigate fraudulent employers and institutions directly instead of creating a financial barrier for everyone?

I ask DHS to provide a reliable fraud rate, quantify the actual harm, and explain why targeted enforcement would be insufficient before considering such a drastic policy.

I think this change is unwarranted and counterproductive. This change will limit the academic talent that we have in the US and pose an undue burden on researchers in the United States. This program is designed to keep the talented academics trained in the US, where their work can enrich everyone. This change risks us losing that talent to bureaucratic waste and government overreach.

This is far more than it should cost to file paperwork (in the past, it seems like it has been less than $600.00) and is an example of government bloat as a way to extract value from F-1 visa holders and universities. In a time when the cost of living is already high, why are we making changes that raise costs and promote bureaucratic waste? 

I emphatically oppose this change and any other change that would push academic talent out of the United States.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. DHS has not provided a convincing economic justification for either the fee amount or its consequences.

DHS estimates that the proposal would collect approximately $12.4 billion annually. However, DHS itself classifies these payments as transfers, not new economic benefits. It also acknowledges that ICE cannot retain the money and that it will not be specifically allocated to OPT oversight or immigration enforcement.

If the purpose is preventing fraud, why charge such enormous fees without directing the revenue toward fraud investigations?

More importantly, where is the cost-benefit justification? A recent analysis by the Institute for Progress (October 2026) estimates that the proposed fees could reduce annual U.S. GDP by approximately $362 billion after ten years under its central model. This is almost 29 times DHS's projected annual fee collections, although these are different economic measures and the GDP estimate concerns the longer-term impact.

DHS estimates only $4.1 billion in annualized economic costs under its primary scenario. But the agency assumes that the lost economic value of an OPT opportunity is no greater than the unpaid fee, instead of independently estimating the economic contribution of these workers. How can DHS conclude that the fees are reasonable when it has not properly quantified what the United States could lose?

Collecting money for the Treasury does not automatically make the country richer. If the fees discourage productive workers, reduce university enrollment, and damage American businesses, the U.S. could lose far more than the government collects.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal until it can provide a credible cost-benefit analysis that includes long-term economic losses.

I oppose this proposal because there is substantial economic evidence that restricting OPT could cost the United States far more than the government would collect in fees.

DHS estimates approximately $12.4 billion in annual fee collections. In contrast, an October 2026 analysis by the Institute for Progress estimates that the proposed fees could reduce annual U.S. GDP by $110 billion to $744 billion after ten years under scenarios based on economic research by Michael Clemens, with a central estimate of $362 billion annually.

Even the lower-end projected loss is much larger than DHS's anticipated annual fee revenue. These are long-term projections, not measured losses, but DHS should explain why it does not adequately account for consequences of this scale.

There is also evidence that OPT benefits American workers. A February 2026 study by Kwon, Lee, and Monras examined the 2016 STEM OPT extension and found that retaining international STEM graduates increased firm creation and demand for native-born high-skilled workers.

This directly challenges the assumption that fewer OPT participants automatically means more jobs for Americans.

International students also support employment outside technology companies. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs in the 2024–2025 academic year. These estimates exclude contributions from students already working on OPT.

If the proposed fees discourage future international enrollment, the U.S. could lose tuition revenue, local spending, and future skilled workers at the same time.

Why should the United States accept these risks for a policy whose economic benefits DHS has not quantified?

I ask DHS to assess the long-term effects on GDP, American employment, business formation, and international student enrollment before proceeding.

As an international PhD student at an American university, I am especially concerned that DHS has underestimated how much this proposal could damage American higher education.

International students provide important revenue for universities. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024–2025, excluding people already on OPT.

For comparison, DHS expects to collect $12.4 billion annually in OPT fees. A hypothetical 30% reduction in the current economic contributions of enrolled international students would mean a loss of approximately $12.9 billion annually, already exceeding the projected fee collections. This is an illustration, not a prediction, but it shows how quickly the economic losses could become substantial.

And large enrollment declines are a real concern. A September 2026 economic study by Michael Clemens estimates that restrictions of this scale could reduce international bachelor's enrollment by 3–31% and master's enrollment by 5–58%, depending on who bears the cost. The study estimates that universities could lose hundreds of millions to over $4 billion annually in net margins.

The Institute for Progress further estimates that the proposed fees could result in approximately 46,000 fewer American students enrolling in bachelor's and master's programs each year, because universities would have less revenue to support their education.

This is not simply a problem for international students. It could mean fewer courses, less financial aid, fewer academic programs, and reduced educational opportunities for Americans.

For graduate research, the problem is even more serious. International PhD students are not simply paying tuition. They conduct research, teach courses, and contribute years of specialized work to American universities. Losing them would also damage research productivity.

DHS assumes universities can pay $70,000 for initial OPT and another $30,000 for an extension. But Clemens estimates that universities earn roughly $13,700 in annual net margins from an international master's student. Why would universities pay $100,000 for an OPT opportunity when that amount is several times the net revenue they receive from educating the student?

I ask DHS to properly account for lost tuition revenue, reduced domestic enrollment, and research productivity before imposing a policy that could seriously weaken American universities.

I get that this rule is to protect U.S workers and prevent fraud, but I think the fees are to high. I think the costs should be more reasonable and fair. The government needs to make sure this rule doesn't create any unnecessary problems from the people affected by it.

Instead, the proposal relies on selected cases and investigations without establishing a reliable program-wide fraud rate.

DHS also claims that OPT fraud harms American workers. What is the measured economic damage? How many American jobs were actually lost because of confirmed OPT fraud?

Charging $70,000 does not distinguish fraudulent students from legitimate ones. It distinguishes those who can afford the fee from those who cannot.

If DHS has evidence of fraudulent employers or universities, why not investigate them directly? Why should legitimate students and American institutions pay for misconduct they did not commit?

I ask DHS to publish reliable data on the prevalence and economic impact of OPT fraud, and explain why targeted enforcement would not be more effective.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). By pricing educational institutions and international students out of practical training, the U.S. will deter the world's most brilliant minds, driving them to competing nations with more accessible post-graduate training frameworks. This resulting "brain drain" translates directly to billions of dollars in lost tuition, diminished local economic spending, and a critical deficit in future innovation.

Second, the premise that OPT participants inherently displace U.S. workers ignores substantial economic data. Highly skilled international students complement the domestic workforce and act as catalysts for job creation. Studies consistently show that international students and highly skilled immigrants found startups, secure research funding, and drive technological advancements that generate proportional, high-paying employment opportunities for U.S. citizens.

The presence of top-tier global talent in U.S. research and labor markets pushes domestic students to maintain cutting-edge proficiency. Finally, while ensuring fair labor practices is a shared priority, creating arbitrary financial barriers to experiential learning contradicts the spirit of equal access and merit-based advancement. Rather than effectively targeting fraudulent “visa mills” or bad actors, a blanket $70,000 fee penalizes legitimate students and SEVP-certified institutions.

I urge the Department to withdraw this proposed fee structure and instead pursue targeted compliance and enforcement measures that do not jeopardize the United States' position as the premier destination for global talent.

May God bless the United States of America. 

Respectfully,

While I fully support the government's efforts to prevent immigration fraud and protect the integrity of the OPT program, these extraordinarily high fees are disproportionate and would create serious financial barriers for universities, international students and employers.

International students make valuable contributions to American universities through research, innovation, teaching and scientific advancement. Many graduate and doctoral students dedicate several years to their education and contribute directly to important research in engineering, technology, healthcare and other STEM fields. OPT provides a legitimate opportunity for these graduates to apply their academic knowledge, gain professional experience and contribute to the American workforce.

Although universities are required to pay the proposed fees, the financial burden could ultimately be transferred to students or employers. Universities may also become reluctant to recommend eligible students for OPT, while employers may hesitate to recruit highly qualified international graduates because of the additional costs. This could discourage talented students from choosing American universities and weaken the country's global competitiveness in research and innovation.

Legitimate students who have maintained their immigration status and completed demanding academic programs should not be financially penalized for fraudulent activities committed by others. A blanket fee does not adequately distinguish genuine students from those who misuse the system.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. Instead, the government should strengthen employer verification, institutional audits, compliance monitoring and enforcement against fraudulent participants. If additional administrative fees are necessary, they should be reasonable, transparent and proportionate to actual processing and compliance costs.

International students and their families make substantial financial, academic and personal sacrifices to pursue higher education in the United States. Preserving fair and accessible practical training opportunities is important not only for these students but also for American universities, employers, research institutions and the nation's future workforce.

As an international PhD student at an American university, I strongly oppose this proposal, especially its impact on students who are already studying in the United States.

The U.S. has already invested enormous resources in educating and training international students. In 2024 alone, the federal government funded $64.6 billion in university research, according to the National Science Foundation. International graduate students participate in this research, receiving specialized training while contributing to American scientific progress.

Many of these students spend five or more years completing their PhDs. By the time they graduate, they have developed specialized skills, research experience, and knowledge that American universities and companies can use.

According to NSF's 2026 report, approximately 73% of international science and engineering PhD graduates from 2017–2019 were still in the U.S. in 2023, around five years after graduation. Approximately 68% of an earlier cohort remained after ten years.

This means the U.S. has historically been able to retain much of the talent it trained. These graduates continue contributing through employment, research, innovation, and taxes.

However, the proposed $70,000 OPT fee could make it impossible for many students who are about to graduate to work in the U.S. What is the point of spending years training highly skilled researchers and then creating a financial barrier that drives them away just when they are ready to contribute?

DHS proposes only a 60-day transition period. But what about students who started their degrees three, four, or five years ago? Neither they nor their universities could have reasonably planned for a $70,000 fee when they began their education. How is 60 days sufficient to address years of educational and financial commitments?

There is also a long-term concern. Even if international students continue coming to the U.S. for education, making it difficult for them to stay afterward means they will take much of their American training and expertise back to their home countries or elsewhere.

Of course, international scientific cooperation has value. But why would the U.S. deliberately give up the opportunity to retain researchers it has already trained, especially when other countries would benefit from employing them?

OPT provides a way for the U.S. to receive a more direct return on its investment in international education. Graduates can apply their knowledge in American companies and research institutions, contribute to the economy, and help train the next generation of workers.

I don't understand how encouraging these graduates to leave would benefit the United States. It seems like an unnecessary waste of American educational resources and research investment.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. At the very least, students who have already enrolled in American universities under the existing OPT rules should not be subjected to these enormous new fees.

I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining and protecting Optional Practical Training (OPT) opportunities for international students pursuing higher education in the US. The proposed $70,000 initial fee per student creates an extraordinary financial burden for educational institutions, particularly smaller colleges, community-based institutions, and schools with limited operating budgets. Institutions could experience a financial impact that disrupts budgets, limits educational resources, and forces difficult decisions about which students they can afford to support.
A student who has successfully completed a degree and meets all eligibility requirements should not lose access to an essential career-development opportunity because their educational institution cannot absorb an extraordinary federal fee. The proposed fee also creates inequity among educational institutions. Larger, well-funded universities may have greater financial flexibility, while smaller institutions and schools will be unable to participate. 
International students participating in OPT bring specialized knowledge and valuable skills to American businesses, nonprofit organizations, healthcare systems, educational institutions, and other community services. OPT participants contribute to projects, help organizations address workforce needs, and bring fresh perspectives to complex challenges. Consider the contributions of international graduates working in healthcare, technology, education, business, and scientific research. Their practical experience strengthens organizations while allowing them to apply their academic preparation in ways that benefit the broader public. In smaller communities, where employers may have difficulty attracting individuals with specialized skills, international graduates can help fill important workforce gaps. 
I recognize that the federal government has a responsibility to prevent fraud, ensure compliance, and protect the interests of American workers. However, measures intended to address these concerns should be proportionate, targeted, and designed to preserve legitimate educational and professional opportunities.
A $70,000 initial fee per student is not a reasonable or sustainable mechanism for ensuring program integrity. It places the financial responsibility on educational institutions regardless of the individual student's circumstances, the quality of the educational program, or the legitimacy of the proposed employment experience.

The proposed fee structure threatens to turn an educational opportunity into a privilege available only to institutions with substantial financial resources and students whose employers or schools can absorb extraordinary costs.

I strongly oppose the proposed fee increase for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

OPT was designed to be a mutually beneficial program for international students, U.S. employers, and the country as a whole. Significantly increasing the cost of OPT would undermine the very purpose of this program. Raising fees to such an extent would effectively destroy the accessibility and value of OPT.

This would not only hurt international students. I urge DHS to withdraw the [proposed OPT fee rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/08/2026-20660/optional-practical-training-fees), including the fees in section V.A. Requiring schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, would create a severe barrier to legitimate practical training. Protecting American workers and preventing fraud are valid goals, but these fees would penalize compliant students and institutions while putting America's long-term economic competitiveness at risk.

The financial burden would reach students regardless of who formally pays. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass costs to students or employers. If students pay, access would depend heavily on family wealth and borrowing capacity. If schools absorb the fees, they could restrict recommendations, raise tuition, or divert resources from teaching, research, and student services. An institution recommending 100 students for initial OPT would face $7 million in fees. A student's eligibility and academic merit should not become secondary to the size of a university's budget.

Students already enrolled deserve particular consideration. They committed years of study, tuition, and living expenses under a framework that allowed eligible students to apply for practical training. The opportunity to seek relevant training can reasonably influence educational and financial decisions. Applying a prohibitive new condition to future recommendations for these students could strand investments they cannot recover. Section V.C should give greater weight to these reliance interests.

The policy could also harm U.S. higher education exports. Students comparing countries consider the complete educational experience, including opportunities to apply classroom learning. Restricting that experience could discourage future enrollment. [NAFSA's analysis](https://www.nafsa.org/policy-and-advocacy/policy-resources/nafsa-international-student-economic-value-tool-v2) estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-2025. These figures cover international students as a whole and show the economic activity at risk. Lower enrollment could hurt university budgets and businesses in college communities.

The longer-term cost is lost talent and innovation. America benefits when people trained in its universities can apply their skills in its laboratories and businesses. Making practical training unaffordable could encourage graduates to take those skills to competing economies. [NBER research](https://www.nber.org/papers/w30797) finds that immigrants represented 16% of inventors but accounted for 23% of patents in its sample. Although that study examines immigrants broadly, it illustrates why restricting skilled graduates' opportunities can carry consequences beyond an individual job opening. The United States risks educating talented people and then making it harder to benefit from their work.

Protecting U.S. workers requires evidence about job creation and displacement. Skilled colleagues can help teams develop products, expand operations, and support additional jobs. Some positions may go unfilled, projects may be delayed, and employers may move work elsewhere when needed talent is unavailable. Section VII.A should assess these potential outcomes. Small businesses, startups, and research organizations could be especially disadvantaged if they are asked to reimburse costs that larger employers can more readily absorb.

A large payment is also a poor substitute for verifying compliance. Ability to pay does not establish that training is legitimate, just as inability to pay does not establish fraud. DHS should target misconduct through employer verification, risk-based audits, checks that work relates to the student's degree, and meaningful penalties for fraudulent actors. If additional oversight funding is necessary, DHS should explain its costs and evaluate proportionate fees. A broad financial barrier could exclude honest participants while leaving the underlying methods of fraud insufficiently addressed.

Before imposing these fees, DHS should provide persuasive evidence that the amounts are necessary, assess effects on enrollment and research, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Fee revenue transferred to the government should not be confused with newly created economic value. The analysis must account for lost training, forgone earnings, reduced educational exports, and losses in innovation and business growth.

I respectfully request withdrawal of the $70,000 and $30,000 fees and preservation of accessible OPT for eligible students. Strong enforcement and worker protections can coexist with practical training that strengthens American universities, businesses, and long-term prosperity.

I am a Registered Architect, WELL Accredited Professional, and the Principal and CEO of Fisher ARCHitecture LLC, a small architecture firm in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, licensed in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Maryland. I also teach at Carnegie Mellon University’s School of Architecture. I oppose the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees (Sections IV.C and V.A).

My own path shows what temporary training programs are for. I came to the United States on a J-1 visa. It gave me twelve months to show an employer that I was worth investing in. I worked hard, earned that employer’s confidence, built a career here, and now run a firm that employs people and serves clients in three states. Programs like the J-1 and OPT work because merit is proven through work, and employers who value it can then choose to keep that talent here. DHS states that the fee will lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students” (Section IV.C). But a school’s willingness to pay $70,000 does not measure promise. The way to measure it is the one OPT already provides: a period of real, supervised work.

The fee does not reach the fraud DHS describes (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The rule’s evidence concerns employers: shell companies, staged worksites, and residential addresses with no employees. Yet the fee is triggered by a school’s recommendation and is not tied to any employer. A fraudulent employer pays nothing. A legitimate student at an accredited university loses access to OPT when the school cannot justify $70,000. DHS identifies roughly 10,000 students with highly suspect employers, out of more than 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. A fee charged to every participant is not a proportionate response to a problem concentrated among a small share of employers.

The fee does not fund the oversight DHS says it lacks (Section IV.C). DHS states that its compliance resources have not kept pace with the program, but the proposed fees would go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP or ICE. The rule would reduce participation without adding any capacity to find fraud among those who remain.

Impact on small firms and the architecture profession (Section VII.B.6). The small-entity analysis looks at schools but not at small employers like mine. Architecture graduates must complete supervised professional experience through NCARB’s Architectural Experience Program before they can be licensed. For international graduates of U.S. architecture programs, OPT is how they earn that experience. Architecture schools will not pay $70,000 per student to recommend graduates for entry-level design positions. As a result, the rule would effectively close OPT to the profession, even though DHS has made no finding that architecture graduates or firms are involved in fraud. Small firms like mine would lose access to talented designers whom U.S. universities have already educated.

Recommendations.

Withdraw the fee. Alternatively, reduce it to the actual cost of oversight and direct the revenue to SEVP compliance.
Target employers, not schools and students. Extend the Form I-983 training plan, E-Verify, and employer attestations to post-completion OPT, and require verification that the business and worksite exist before employment begins. DHS considered this option in Section IV.C and rejected it because of the administrative effort involved. Effort aimed at the actual source of fraud is a better trade than a flat fee charged to legitimate participants.
At minimum, exempt small employers and licensure-track professions with structured, supervised experience requirements, and include small employers in the Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis.

Conclusion. I support DHS prosecuting OPT fraud. But this rule charges the wrong party, adds no enforcement capacity, and would remove the very mechanism through which people like me proved their worth and went on to contribute to the U.S. economy. I urge DHS to withdraw the fee and adopt employer-focused safeguards.

Subject: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fee Rule (Docket ICEB-2026-0100)**

To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this public comment in respectful but strong opposition to the proposed rule introducing substantial new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extensions.

As an international student, choosing to pursue higher education in the United States represents a significant academic, professional, and financial commitment. Students invest years of their lives and considerable financial resources in American universities, often with the expectation that they will have a reasonable opportunity to apply their education through practical training after graduation.

OPT is not simply an employment benefit. It is a critical bridge between academic education and professional development, particularly in engineering, science, technology, and research, where practical experience is essential to developing industry-relevant skills.

I fully recognize and respect the government's responsibility to protect American workers, safeguard employment opportunities, and ensure immigration programs serve the national interest. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on OPT does not meaningfully address these objectives. Instead, it creates financial barriers that may ultimately harm American universities, employers, innovation, and economic competitiveness.

First, making OPT prohibitively expensive does not inherently protect American workers.A graduate's ability to participate in practical training should be based on qualifications, skills, and legitimate employment opportunities, not their ability to afford an extraordinary fee. If the objective is to prevent misuse of employment authorization programs, stronger compliance measures, wage protections, and enforcement of existing regulations would be more directly aligned with protecting American workers.

Second, these fees risk discouraging talented international students from choosing the United States. Students evaluate not only the quality of education but also the opportunities available after graduation. When practical training becomes financially inaccessible or unpredictable, talented individuals may increasingly choose countries offering more reasonable pathways from education to professional experience. The United States risks losing not only prospective students but also future researchers, engineers, entrepreneurs, and innovators.

Third, the proposal could undermine American innovation and competitiveness.American universities and industries have long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. International graduates contribute to research, technological development, engineering, and specialized industries. Creating an excessive financial barrier at the transition from education to practical training risks weakening this talent pipeline and encouraging skilled graduates to contribute their knowledge and abilities elsewhere.

**Fourth, the financial impact extends beyond individual students.** International students already bear substantial tuition, living expenses, and immigration-related costs. Introducing exceptionally high fees near graduation creates financial uncertainty after years of investment. If employers are expected to absorb these costs, smaller businesses, startups, and research organizations may be disproportionately discouraged from considering qualified international graduates.

Importantly, protecting American workers and attracting international talent should not be viewed as mutually exclusive objectives. The United States can prioritize its domestic workforce while maintaining a fair, accessible, and well-regulated practical training program. A policy that discourages qualified graduates solely through financial barriers does not necessarily create better opportunities for American workers; it may instead reduce the country's ability to attract talent and compete globally.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider the proposed fee structure, evaluate its economic and educational consequences, and pursue measures that directly address program integrity and worker protections without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on international students.

The United States has earned its reputation as a global leader in education, research, technology, and innovation partly because talented individuals from around the world have chosen to study and contribute here. Policies should strengthen that advantage rather than discourage future generations from making that choice.

Protecting American workers, supporting innovation, and attracting global talent are complementary goals. This proposal risks undermining all three without clearly demonstrating how such extraordinary fees would achieve their intended purpose.**

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule.

Respectfully submitted,

An International Student

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for universities to recommend international students for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT), and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.
Such a rule would place an undue financial burden on international students, universities, and employers, and would severely restrict international students' access to employment opportunities. OPT provides international students with a vital opportunity to gain professional experience in their fields of study following graduation, and for many, serves as an essential pathway to building a career in the United States. These exorbitant fees would make it increasingly difficult for universities and employers to recommend or hire international graduates, potentially forcing institutions to pass these costs onto students or discontinue OPT recommendations altogether.
Furthermore, international students make up a significant percentage of the workforce at American universities and research institutions, and contribute substantially to academic research, teaching, and innovation. Restricting their access to OPT would undermine the work of these institutions and the communities they serve, while discouraging employers from hiring qualified international graduates. These restrictions would also discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the U.S. and push international graduates to seek professional opportunities elsewhere, resulting in a loss of valuable talent and expertise from the national economy.
Overall, the proposed rule would place undue financial burdens on international students and American educational and research institutions, while restricting valuable employment opportunities and undermining the contributions of international workers. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and preserve accessible OPT pathways for international students and graduates.

OPT provides international students with a vital opportunity to gain professional experience in their fields of study following graduation, and for many, serves as an essential pathway to building a career in the United States. These exorbitant fees would make it increasingly difficult for universities and employers to recommend or hire international graduates, potentially forcing institutions to pass these costs onto students or discontinue OPT recommendations altogether.
Furthermore, international students make up a significant percentage of the workforce at American universities and research institutions, and contribute substantially to academic research, teaching, and innovation. Restricting their access to OPT would undermine the work of these institutions and the communities they serve, while discouraging employers from hiring qualified international graduates. These restrictions would also discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the U.S. and push international graduates to seek professional opportunities elsewhere, resulting in a loss of valuable talent and expertise from the national economy.
Overall, the proposed rule would place undue financial burdens on international students and American educational and research institutions, while restricting valuable employment opportunities and undermining the contributions of international workers. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and preserve accessible OPT pathways for international students and graduates.

OPT provides international students with a vital opportunity to gain professional experience in their fields of study following graduation, and for many, serves as an essential pathway to building a career in the United States. These exorbitant fees would make it increasingly difficult for universities and employers to recommend or hire international graduates, potentially forcing institutions to pass these costs onto students or discontinue OPT recommendations altogether.
Furthermore, international students make up a significant percentage of the workforce at American universities and research institutions, and contribute substantially to academic research, teaching, and innovation. Restricting their access to OPT would undermine the work of these institutions and the communities they serve, while discouraging employers from hiring qualified international graduates. These restrictions would also discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the U.S. and push international graduates to seek professional opportunities elsewhere, resulting in a loss of valuable talent and expertise from the national economy.
Overall, the proposed rule would place undue financial burdens on international students and American educational and research institutions, while restricting valuable employment opportunities and undermining the contributions of international workers. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and preserve accessible OPT pathways for international students and graduates.

Students currently in F-1 status applied, paid tuition, and in many cases took on debt under rules that promised 12 months of OPT, and 36 months for STEM graduates. They cannot go back and choose differently. A student graduating next spring who planned to apply for OPT will find that the opportunity has been priced at $70,000 with two months’ notice, through no fault of their own. Changing the terms after students have already committed years of their lives and their families’ savings is unfair and will damage the trust that international students place in U.S. institutions for years to come. If DHS proceeds at all, the fee should apply only to students who enroll after the final rule is published.

As an international graduate currently working under OPT, I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees.

International students have already invested significant time, effort, and financial resources in pursuing higher education in the United States. OPT provides a valuable opportunity to apply academic knowledge, gain practical experience, and contribute to American workplaces.

The proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial burden and effectively deny many qualified students access to these opportunities. Such excessive fees would not only harm international students but also discourage future students from choosing American universities and negatively affect U.S. employers who benefit from international talent.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. Access to practical training should be based on qualifications and compliance with immigration regulations, not financial privilege.

There should be no OPT fees and the government needs consider more reasonable alternatives. I don’t think we should put any fees on our international students or limit international influence in our country.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw the rule.

1. DHS lacks authority for what is functionally a tax. The fees would go to the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, ICE would not keep them, and DHS set the amount by reference to the H-1B fee rather than any cost (NPRM § IV.C). INA 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of a student's stay; it does not authorize a $109 billion, ten-year revenue charge on schools. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee for a skilled-worker program, it set one itself: $500, earmarked for fraud detection (INA 214(c)(12)). A federal court has already vacated the H-1B fee policy this fee is modeled on, holding among other things that such a payment needs clear authorization from Congress (California v. Mullin, D. Mass. 2026).

2. A student visa has never ended at graduation. Post-graduation practical training dates to 1947. Congress re-enacted the student-visa language in 1952 and has amended the statute many times without disturbing it, and the D.C. Circuit upheld OPT in 2022. In applied fields, supervised practice is part of education, just as residency is for physicians.

3. OPT does not take American jobs. The 360,078 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024 (§ IV.B) are about 0.2% of a 170.8 million-person labor force. DHS's own figure puts 2025 unemployment in computer occupations at 3.02%, below the 4.3% national rate. The two most recent studies of the 2016 STEM OPT extension found higher native employment and wages. A large Stanford payroll study links part of the recent decline in entry-level software jobs to AI, which the NPRM never mentions.

4. Restricting OPT sends jobs abroad. When H-1B visas were restricted in 2004, U.S. multinationals expanded hiring at foreign offices, particularly in China, India and Canada (Glennon, Management Science, 2024). India's 2,117 corporate "global capability centers" already employ 2.36 million people. The NPRM assumes lost OPT jobs go to Americans and never considers offshoring.

5. The fee misses the fraud. Most fraud DHS describes involves employers (shell companies, staged worksites), yet employers pay nothing, and the fee is paid before any employer is known. DHS's largest investigation flagged about 2.8% of participants; the fee hits all of them and selects for ability to pay, not merit.

6. DHS's math does not hold up. It projects up to $8.2 billion a year in costs and quantifies no benefits. Its method values a lost 24-month STEM extension at no more than the $30,000 fee, or $15,000 a year, less than a full-time federal minimum-wage job ($15,080). It compares 165,524 STEM OPT participants, a two-year group, with the 85,000 annual H-1B cap; its own annual figure, 95,384, is 12% above the cap, not "nearly double."

7. It breaks reliance. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), schools would owe $70,000, not $30,000, for graduates already working on OPT who apply for the STEM extension, as DHS's own Year 1 assumption confirms (§ VII.A.4.a).

8. The process is deficient. An economically significant rule received only a 30-day comment period, key fraud evidence is cited to a YouTube video rather than docketed data, and the UMRA and federalism analyses contradict themselves.

Fraud should be fought with employer verification, enforcement of existing unemployment limits, and a cost-based fee spent on oversight. I ask DHS to withdraw this rule or, at minimum, extend the comment period to 60 days, docket its underlying data, and protect students already enrolled or on OPT.

Additional point: an "anti-fraud" fee that funds no anti-fraud work is a tax. DHS justifies the fee as fraud prevention, yet concedes the money funds none: it goes to the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302), ICE "would not maintain or use" it, and DHS says only that Congress "could later" appropriate it (§ IV.C). No cost study supports the amount; DHS chose it to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas." A charge that pays for no service, ignores cost, and is designed to change behavior is a tax (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 1974), and taxing power belongs to Congress. Congress knows how to fund fraud prevention: for H-1B and L petitions it set a $500 fee and directed it to a fraud prevention and detection account (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12), 1356(v)). DHS proposes a charge 140 times larger that funds no detection at all. Even when the Supreme Court upheld an agency-collected charge in FCC v. Consumers' Research (2025), it relied on the statute limiting collections to what the program needs; INA 214(a) sets no amount, purpose or ceiling. If fraud is the concern, the logical remedy is enforcement paid for by a cost-based fee, not a revenue measure DHS cannot even spend.

I have attached as a PDF, a much more detailed analysis of these arguments, I urge this analysis be taken into consideration as it covers the effects this fee could have.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. DHS should withdraw this excessive proposal. International students are an economic asset. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–2025. These figures cover international education overall, rather than OPT alone, but demonstrate the economic interests threatened by policies that discourage studying here. American businesses and communities share these benefits. [2]
OPT helps turn education at American universities into skills available to American employers. Research published in the Journal of Public Economics found that international graduates contribute to the U.S. skilled labor supply and that transitions into employment were higher for STEM graduates following the 2008 OPT expansion. [3] Making practical training prohibitively expensive risks sending that talent elsewhere.
The stakes for technological leadership are substantial. NSF reports that temporary visa holders earned 62% of U.S. research doctorates in computer and information sciences, 56% in engineering, and 53% in mathematics and statistics in 2023. [4] NSF also found that 73% of temporary visa holders who earned U.S. science and engineering doctorates during 2017–2019 remained here in 2023. These are not estimates of OPT’s independent effect, but they demonstrate the lasting value of retaining internationally educated talent. [5]
DHS’s fraud rationale does not justify a blanket financial barrier. Documented misconduct deserves enforcement. However, Section IV.A’s criminal cases and investigations—including students associated with highly suspect employers—do not themselves establish a representative, adjudicated program-wide fraud rate. Suspicions, charges, and proven violations are different categories. [1]
“Fraud, waste, and abuse” cannot substitute for measurement. DHS should identify substantiated violations, relevant time periods and populations, actual losses, and the harm these particular fees would prevent. Available evidence does not establish that fraud is nonexistent or necessarily nominal. Equally, individual cases cannot establish that the entire program warrants prohibitive charges.
GAO’s 2014 OPT review identified weaknesses in risk assessment, employment information, and monitoring. Those findings support better oversight and reliable data. They do not establish that charging compliant institutions tens of thousands of dollars per participant is an effective remedy. [6]
A payment is not a verification system. Wealth does not establish compliance, and limited resources do not establish wrongdoing. An institution recommending initial OPT for 100 students would face $7 million in proposed fees alone. That arithmetic illustrates the proposal’s extraordinary scale; it does not demonstrate any corresponding enforcement benefit.
If DHS needs additional oversight resources, it should publish a transparent cost analysis and explain why targeted investigations, employer verification, improved reporting, and sanctions against proven violators would be insufficient. It should also distinguish fees collected from genuine net economic benefits: money transferred to the government does not automatically offset lost education, research, innovation, or productive employment.
I urge DHS to:
Withdraw the proposed fees.
Publish a transparent assessment of substantiated OPT violations and their prevalence.
Compare targeted enforcement alternatives with the proposed blanket charges.
Assess effects on enrollment, research, local jobs, talent retention, and competitiveness.
Support any alternative administrative fee with demonstrated costs and a proportionate justification.
America should enforce its rules while preserving a valuable training pathway. This proposal fails to demonstrate why its extraordinary charges are necessary or why their benefits would outweigh the damage. Pricing legitimate participation out of reach would surrender American economic advantages without establishing that misconduct will be prevented.

While supportive of reducing fraud and abuse of government programs, my comment is submitted in opposition Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, Cock N. ICEB-2026-0100. My opposition is based on the exorbitant level of the fee, failure to address the stated problem, internal inconsistencies within the proposed rule, and lack of legal authority for the fee. 

The proposed rule does not explain the logic behind the fee amount or adequately address the fee’s impact on educational institutions. At my institution, a small school with fewer than 100 students in F-1 status, the published cost of attendance is approximately $65,000 and our average discount rate is 60%, so almost no students pay the full cost of attendance, including international students. This places the fee well above what most students are paying for a single year of education. 

As many schools will be unable or unwilling to make payments in the amount of $70,000 for even the most promising international student’s OPT request, the cost will likely be passed to the student, should they recommend OPT at all. My entire office budget dedicated to international students is less than $15,000, making it impossible to pay such fees from the institution. I am not aware of any student in my current cohort that could pay an additional $70,000 to apply for OPT authorization. 

Each year, my small institution graduates 15-20 international students. Approximately 5-6 of them apply for OPT, often in healthcare roles with staffing shortages and in the business world. These students each meet the regulatory eligibility requirements for OPT and diligently report their employment. The proposed rule would require DSOs to discriminate between their students submitting OPT requests. Nowhere do the regulations provide for prioritizing students based on financial resources, employment prospects, or other criteria to discriminate between eligible students. 

The proposed rule does not address the problem DHS is trying to solve. This failure happens in three places:
1)	There is no evidence provided that students with fewer financial resources are more likely to engage in fraud. A student or school’s financial resources has no direct relationship to compliance in external employment. Such financial barriers may actually exclude students from participating in legitimate and valuable opportunities. 
2)	More effective means of countering fraud and abuse would be to increase employer checks, site visits, and training plans, all of which have been rejected without explanation by DHS. The anecdotal accounts of fraud cited by DHS all involved employers. There is no explanation of how placing an exorbitant fee on schools would reduce actions by fraudulent actors in the employment sector.
3)	The goal of lessening DHS’s oversight burden is in direct conflict with the proposed rule’s fees being deposited into the Treasury. Fees levied by DHS should be used for oversight and such fees are not available if they are deposited in the Treasury. 

The proposed rule also raises internal inconsistencies about implementation. As the proposed rule attaches the fee to the institution rather than the student, there is no way to determine if the $70,000 is to be paid once or twice should a student transfer between institutions. Additionally, the proposed fee is ambiguous regarding how many times the $30,000 would be paid; once for a second OPT application or multiple times at a rate of $30,000 for each additional application. 

The administrative and record keeping burden for both schools and DHS would be extremely high under the proposed rule. As noted, schools would likely pass these fees onto students. Therefore, DSOs and colleagues would need to build and maintain internal systems to process and make such large payments, collect funds from students, create liability and risk assessments, and develop ways to prioritize and weigh student OPT request applications. As the fees in the proposed rule are attached to the school rather than the student, DHS has not provided systems to tie fees to SEVIS records to prevent schools from having to pay the same fee multiple times. With the funds being directed to the Treasury, it seems this would be more difficult for DHS to track relative to SEVIS records. 

Finally, the proposed fee itself lacks legal justification. With funds to be deposited into the Treasury, such payments become a tax rather than a fee. DHS does not have the legal authority to levy a tax on international students. 

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee and instead pursue targeted measured to reduce fraudulent instances of employment that in such a way as to not undermine the benefits of the OPT program.

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I'm respectfully against the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations. I urge DHS to retract this fee structure and maintain reasonable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

My principal concern is that these fees would make access to practical training depend on financial resources rather than educational merit, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration requirements. Although the proposal places payment responsibility on educational institutions, it acknowledges that those institutions may pass the financial burden to students or employers. Shifting responsibility for payment does not eliminate the burden. I am concerned that institutions could decline to recommend otherwise qualified students, employers could withdraw legitimate training opportunities, and students could lose access to practical experience despite meeting all other eligibility requirements.

I support protecting American workers, preventing fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee is not evidence of compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of misconduct. DHS should justify why these particular amounts would effectively distinguish legitimate educational training from abuse. A reduction in participation should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that fraud has been prevented.

The proposal states that the fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury and would not be retained by ICE or specifically earmarked for immigration enforcement activities. I therefore ask DHS to explain how these fees would improve oversight beyond creating a financial deterrent. The agency should evaluate less burdensome alternatives, including targeted compliance reviews, verification of degree-related training, employer accountability, and enforcement of applicable worker protections. Measures directed at demonstrated misconduct would be preferable to a financial barrier affecting compliant participants.

I am also concerned about the proposed effective date of 60 days after publication of a final rule. DHS should meaningfully consider students who have already committed to educational programs, incurred substantial expenses, or accepted future training opportunities under the existing framework. Describing a requirement as prospective does not resolve its potential impact on decisions made years earlier. I request explicit protections for currently enrolled students and existing OPT participants, including those who would need a later recommendation or extension.

Before proceeding, DHS should assess the potential consequences for universities, teaching hospitals, veterinary services, scientific research, small employers, and underserved communities. The analysis should examine whether these fees could discourage legitimate clinical training, interrupt research, reduce educational opportunities, or limit access to essential services. It should also consider whether smaller institutions and modestly funded training programs would face disproportionate barriers compared with organizations possessing greater financial resources.

DHS should also evaluate whether shifting substantial costs to students could increase debt or dependence on employers willing to finance participation. A policy intended to protect workers should be examined carefully for the possibility that it could make participants more financially vulnerable.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure. Any alternative should be supported by transparent evidence, proportionate to its stated objectives, and designed to address demonstrated problems without making legitimate training financially unattainable. At a minimum, DHS should evaluate substantially lower fees, meaningful exemptions or waivers, and transition protections for students with existing educational commitments.

Protecting American workers and preserving immigration integrity are important goals. They should be pursued through effective oversight and evidence-based enforcement, not by making lawful, education-related practical training accessible only to those with exceptional financial resources.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee increases. I believe this policy fundamentally misunderstands how the labor market operates and risks undermining both America's economic competitiveness and its national security.

First, preventing qualified international graduates from working in the United States does not mean that their jobs will automatically go to American workers. Employment opportunities are not simply fixed positions that can be redistributed by restricting access to foreign talent. Employers hire individuals based on their qualifications, specialized knowledge, skills, and the needs of their organizations. If a qualified international graduate becomes unable to accept a position, there is no guarantee that another candidate will automatically fill it. An employer may leave the position vacant, reduce its operations, relocate the work overseas, or abandon the project entirely.

International students already face substantial disadvantages in the American job market, including immigration restrictions, limited employer sponsorship opportunities, and uncertainty about their long-term status. Those who successfully compete for positions often do so despite these barriers, not because they receive preferential treatment. Their achievements should be recognized as evidence of their capabilities rather than automatically interpreted as the displacement of American workers.

I fully support protecting American workers from unfair employment practices, wage suppression, and genuine labor exploitation. However, these problems should be addressed through appropriate labor protections, wage enforcement, and targeted investigations—not by imposing extraordinary financial barriers on an entire group of qualified graduates.

Second, I believe this proposal raises serious concerns from a national security perspective. Protecting national security is a legitimate and essential responsibility of the U.S. government. Risks involving sensitive technologies, intellectual property theft, foreign interference, and fraudulent immigration activities deserve serious attention. However, the appropriate response is evidence-based screening, effective oversight, and enforcement directed at actual risks.

A person's ability to pay an enormous fee is not a reliable indicator of whether that person represents a national security threat. Financial restrictions cannot replace meaningful security assessments. Such a policy risks excluding legitimate, highly qualified researchers and professionals without necessarily identifying individuals who present genuine security concerns.

Moreover, national security is not limited to preventing threats. It also requires maintaining America's leadership in science, technology, medicine, and innovation. International students contribute to American research institutions, laboratories, universities, and industries. Driving talented graduates away from the United States may ultimately strengthen competing countries while weakening America's own scientific and technological capabilities.

According to the National Science Foundation's 2026 Science and Engineering Indicators, foreign-born individuals accounted for 46% of employed doctoral-level scientists and engineers in the United States in 2023. This demonstrates the significant role that internationally sourced talent plays in America's advanced scientific workforce.

The United States should seek to attract and retain qualified individuals who contribute to its economy and research enterprise while maintaining rigorous and appropriate security safeguards. These objectives are not mutually exclusive.

Finally, the proposed fees would impose an extraordinary financial burden on universities, students, or employers. Financial resources are not a substitute for academic excellence, professional competence, or integrity. A policy that favors the ability to pay over the ability to contribute is neither an effective talent strategy nor a convincing national security measure.

**Restricting international talent does not automatically create opportunities for American workers, and imposing financial barriers does not automatically make America safer.**

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that genuinely protect American workers, strengthen program integrity, address national security risks, and preserve the United States' ability to attract the world's most capable individuals.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on the legal question at the heart of this proposal: where, exactly, does Congress authorize a fee of this size, imposed on this party, for this act?

Since the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, courts no longer defer to an agency's reading of its own statute merely because that reading is plausible. DHS must show that Congress actually granted the power it claims. For an action of this magnitude, the bar is higher still: under the major questions doctrine, an agency decision of vast economic and political significance requires clear congressional authorization. A fee that DHS itself estimates would extract roughly $12.4 billion a year from American universities — more than the annual budgets of many state higher-education systems combined — plainly qualifies. The proposal points to no statute that clearly authorizes it.

The fee provisions DHS cites allow it to set charges reasonably related to the cost of adjudicating immigration benefits. But the beneficiary here is the student, the adjudication is the employment authorization application, and the school is not even the applicant — it is a third party performing a certification act Congress assigned to Designated School Officials. Stretching a cost-recovery provision into a $70,000 levy on a non-applicant's routine attestation is not interpretation; it is invention. And Congress has repeatedly debated OPT and declined to end it. An agency may not accomplish by fee schedule what the legislature declined to do by law.

That is why federal courts blocked the administration's $100,000 H-1B fee earlier this year: a charge designed to deter participation, rather than recover costs, is a tax, and only Congress can levy one. The same reasoning applies with greater force here, where the fee is larger in aggregate and aimed at institutions Congress never authorized DHS to tax. If DHS believes OPT should end or shrink, it should make that case to Congress. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I am the Director of the Office of International Students and Scholars at the University of Pittsburgh where I oversee 14 staff, including 10 Designated School Officials, who advise approximately 3,000 F-1 students. I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. 

1. The rule would convert DSO’s from advisors into gatekeepers.
DHS states that the proposed fees would lead schools to recommend only the most promising students after a thorough review. In short, a school would have to decide which eligible students are worth $70,000. DSO’s are trained and designated to determine whether a student is eligible under the regulations, not to rank students by projected merit or value. DSO’s do not have the academic expertise to make judgment calls across such a wide range of academic fields and programs. Requiring DSO’s to choose ‘promising’ students will push institutions toward subjective, inconsistent, and potentially discriminatory criteria. 

2. The fees are wildly out of proportion to any cost of administering the OPT program.
The proposed dollar amounts do not align with the amount of work required by a DSO to make an OPT recommendation and/or advise the international student on all matters related to OPT or the work done at USCIS to approve an OPT application.  A DSO at our school typically spends about 2-4 hours per student on OPT casework and advising.  Because the amount collected would not just offset the work done by DHS to evaluate and approve OPT applications it cannot be considered a ‘fee’ and instead amounts to an OPT tax. 

3. The financial exposure would be unmanageable for the University of Pittsburgh and most other schools in the United States.
At our current volume, the fees would total approximately $39.5 million per year, which is untenable.  We would likely have to pass the cost onto the students, turning OPT into a pay-to-play system and excluding very qualified students from the US market.  Those highly educated students will then seek employment outside of the United States and help advance economies elsewhere.

4. The rule creates operational and compliance problems that DHS has not addressed.
Without clear answers to the following, schools cannot responsibly plan:
•	How and when would the fee be paid relative to the recommendation, and what happens to a student's application window if payment processing is delayed? OPT timing rules are strict, and a delay on the school's side could cost a student their eligibility.
•	Which school pays when a student transfers or changes degree level between OPT periods?
•	How would the refund process work, and why does it cover only a denial and not other circumstances, such as a student who withdraws or does not use the authorization?
•	How would the rule treat a student with a STEM extension recommendation after the effective date whose prior OPT predates the rule?

5. Alternatives
If DHS has specific concerns about OPT, such as employer compliance or program integrity, there are more targeted approaches.  
•	DHS could collect the Form I-983 (Training Plan) that schools are already required to keep on file for each STEM OPT applicant. 
•	DHS could target those known companies that do take advantage of the OPT program and penalize them accordingly.
DHS specifically asked for feedback about the option to apply the $70,000 fee again when a student begins OPT at a higher degree level.  All of the reasons stated above apply to an additional fee when applying for additional OPT, which make an additional fee undesirable, to say the least.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.  The damage done by a very small percentage of students and employers who take advantage of the OPT program is far outweighed by the huge benefits our country enjoys from having international graduates contribute to the US economy, our research capacity, and soft diplomacy worldwide.
