Reference: NPRM, sections III.D, IV.C, and V.A.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 4 of 10: University budgets.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed institutional payment obligation. Calling a school the payer does not create new resources. Administrators would have to choose among absorbing the cost, finding outside funding, transferring it, or declining otherwise legitimate recommendations.

For illustration only, 100 initial recommendations at the proposed $70,000 rate would require $7 million before subsequent fees and administrative expenses. This is arithmetic, not a claim about any specific university. DHS should evaluate such budget scenarios against unrestricted resources and operating margins, rather than treating gross revenue as freely spendable cash.

Section IV.C expressly allows costs to be passed to all students. That possibility deserves particular scrutiny: domestic students could bear higher charges or reduced services without having participated in OPT at all. It is unacceptable to treat this shifting of burdens as though it solves the underlying economic harm.

Please assess effects on tuition, aid, student services, and institutions with limited reserves. A policy intended to improve oversight should not force universities to ration lawful educational opportunities according to their capacity to finance a new charge. Withdraw the proposed fees.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 5 of 10: Employer planning.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose this proposal because it could disrupt legitimate recruitment without directly testing employer compliance. Section V.A makes payment depend on a school's OPT recommendation, rather than a particular employer. A careful, law-abiding employer could therefore lose access to a qualified candidate because of an independent institution's funding decision.

Section VII.A.5.b acknowledges possible productivity losses when employers cannot replace OPT participants with qualified workers. DHS should investigate that risk by occupation, location, recruitment lead time, and training needs. The existence of another lawful hiring category does not by itself establish that a suitable replacement is immediately available.

The practical cost of an interrupted placement may include delayed projects, repeated recruitment, and additional work for existing staff. These are potential mechanisms that require evidence, not personal experiences I am asserting.

I support meaningful verification of genuine jobs, supervision, and lawful working conditions. Those checks address conduct directly. A substantial payment imposed upstream does not demonstrate that a particular job is legitimate. DHS should withdraw the proposed fees and evaluate targeted oversight that preserves compliant employers' ability to plan and train responsibly.

Reference: NPRM, sections V.A, VI, and VII.A.5.b.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 6 of 10: Small-business access.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose a policy that could make lawful training opportunities depend on the financial strength of a school or potential employer. A small business can offer serious supervision and meaningful work while having far less cash available than a large corporation. Access to capital is not a reliable measure of compliance or training quality.

Although schools would formally owe the fees, section IV.C allows costs to be shifted to employers. If that occurs, smaller employers could face pressure to abandon a placement that a better-funded competitor could finance. Even without a direct charge, they could lose candidates when schools decline recommendations.

Section VII.B requests alternatives that minimize small-entity impacts. DHS should examine these financing constraints and downstream effects separately from its analysis of directly regulated schools. It should compare risk-based inspections, verification of genuine supervision, and enforcement against documented misconduct.

It is deeply concerning to create an entry barrier that may favor institutional wealth over a valuable learning opportunity. The agency should withdraw the proposed fee structure and develop an approach that tests integrity rather than purchasing power.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C, V.A, and VII.B.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 7 of 10: Public-interest training.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees because an educational placement's public value cannot be judged by its capacity to finance a large upfront payment. Legitimate degree-related training in community research, environmental work, public policy, or nonprofit services may produce benefits that are not fully reflected in a starting salary or an organization's available cash.

Section VII.A.5.b suggests that parties could share costs when the benefits exceed the fees. That reasoning needs a much more careful examination. A project can benefit the public without giving the student, school, or host organization a way to capture those benefits as money available for payment. Benefits spread across a community do not automatically become a funding source.

I find it troubling that financially constrained public-interest placements could be excluded even when their educational merit and compliance are clear. DHS should analyze these settings separately, including restricted funding and benefits received by people outside the paying parties.

Please withdraw the proposed fees. Preserve meaningful oversight while evaluating training through its educational content, supervision, and actual compliance, rather than its ability to produce an immediate payment.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.C and VII.A.5.b.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 8 of 10: U.S. workers and labor standards.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees and take the protection of U.S. workers seriously. Section IV.B should establish how this particular payment mechanism would improve wages and employment after accounting for different occupations, local conditions, and effects on employers' output.

A reduction in OPT participation does not, by itself, establish an equal increase in suitable jobs for U.S. workers. DHS should examine whether roles are filled, remain vacant, move elsewhere, or disappear when projects are reduced. It should also evaluate possible effects on U.S. colleagues whose work depends on a team's combined skills. I do not assume that every OPT placement is beneficial or that displacement never occurs; that is precisely why careful evidence is necessary.

Where exploitation, false employment, or unlawful working conditions are found, enforcement should address those practices directly. A large payment to the government does not by itself raise a worker's wage or improve supervision.

Workers deserve protections that can be shown to work. Please withdraw these fees and compare targeted labor-standard and anti-fraud measures using measurable outcomes and transparent assumptions.

Reference: NPRM, sections IV.B, VII.A.5.b, and VII.A.6.

Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Comment 9 of 10: Effective fraud prevention.
All ten topic-specific comments in this series come from the same anonymous individual. I do not claim to represent any institution or stakeholder group.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees while supporting serious enforcement against OPT fraud. Section IV.A identifies misconduct that deserves investigation. The critical question is whether a universal financial barrier detects or prevents it more effectively than direct, risk-based controls.

GAO-19-297 recommended improvements involving fraud-risk assessment, data analysis, school oversight, and DSO training. The report's online updates describe implementation of several recommendations and continuing work on training. These recommendations provide concrete oversight measures to evaluate; I am not claiming that every earlier deficiency remains unresolved.

Payment is not verification. A well-funded dishonest participant could still seek to evade requirements, while an honest participant with limited resources could lose access. DHS should show why the proposed amounts are necessary, compare less burdensome controls, and publish measurable criteria for success, such as confirmed violations detected and corrected.

It is profoundly frustrating to see legitimate educational access put at risk without a convincing demonstration that the chosen barrier addresses the actual misconduct. Withdraw the fee proposal and strengthen investigation, verification, and accountability directed at evidence of fraud.

References: NPRM, section IV.A; U.S. GAO, GAO-19-297, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297.

I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). This comment addresses a cost the NPRM never names: harm to U.S. foreign relations and to the exchange purpose that student visas have always served.

1. DHS's own history ties student visas to exchange.
Footnote 23 of the NPRM notes that the 1952 INA addressed the student visa and "amends the United States Information and Educational Exchange Act of 1948, 22 U.S.C. 1446." Congress built the student category alongside its public diplomacy law. The Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 states a goal of increasing mutual understanding between Americans and people of other countries through educational exchange (22 U.S.C. 2451). The NPRM lists "Cultural exchange program" among its CFR subjects. Yet its analysis treats OPT only as a labor and fraud issue.

2. DHS dropped its own exchange premise without discussion.
The NPRM quotes the 2016 STEM OPT rule, which rested on "the widely accepted proposition that educational and cultural exchange, a strong post-secondary education system, and a focus on STEM innovation are, on the whole, positive contributors to the U.S. economy and U.S. workers and in the overall national interest." The NPRM responds that participation grew. It never says the exchange benefit is false or smaller than DHS once thought. An agency that changes course must address the facts behind its earlier policy.

3. The F-1 design depends on graduates going home.
DHS stresses that F-1 students must have a foreign residence they do not intend to abandon (INA 101(a)(15)(F)(i), cited at footnote 122). That is the point. Most OPT participants are expected to return home. They take back a year or more of work inside U.S. firms, labs and agencies, plus colleagues, norms and contacts. Those ties are a long-term asset to the United States abroad. A $70,000 charge per student, and $30,000 more for STEM OPT, cuts that experience short or removes it. The rule pushes students toward the outcome DHS says it fears, which is study as a narrow path to a job, while removing the part of the program that builds lasting goodwill.

4. The cost analysis has no foreign-relations line.
DHS uses unpaid fees as a proxy for opportunity costs. It lists the value of labor to employers, contributions to the economy, educational outcomes and school enrollment revenue. It lists nothing for diplomatic or foreign-relations effects. It also assumes U.S. schools "remain highly attractive." In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court found DHS likely acted arbitrarily when it relied on a similar unsupported assumption in the companion Duration of Status rule. The same gap exists here.

5. The rule creates an unexplained gap with State Department exchange programs.
The fee applies only to F-1 students. J-1 students in State Department-designated exchange programs may receive academic training employment under 22 CFR 62.23(f), generally up to 18 months and longer for postdoctoral training, with no comparable fee. The NPRM does not mention J-1 academic training. It does not explain why one form of post-study training needs a $70,000 price screen and the other does not. Nor does it consider whether students and schools will shift to J-1 programs, which would move workload to State without any analysis.

6. No interagency foreign-relations review is described.
The NPRM notes that the State Department uses SEVIS data and cites Executive Order 14150, a foreign policy directive to the Secretary of State (footnote 84). It does not say whether DHS asked State to assess effects on exchange programs, alumni networks, or partner-government responses, including any measures affecting U.S. students and institutions abroad. A rule with 10-year transfers DHS estimates at $109.4 billion (primary estimate, 3 percent discount) should not skip that review.

7. Requests.
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS re-proposes any OPT change, it should (a) assess effects on foreign relations and exchange goals with the Department of State and publish that assessment; (b) explain the different treatment of F-1 OPT and J-1 academic training; (c) state whether it still accepts the 2016 exchange premise and, if not, give its evidence; and (d) address fraud through employer-focused enforcement that does not penalize the many students who use OPT as intended.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. A student could complete a demanding degree, follow every immigration requirement, and find a legitimate opportunity related to their education, yet still lose access because a $70,000 payment cannot be arranged. That is an unacceptable outcome.

Requiring the school to pay does not resolve the problem. If the school passes the cost to students, access depends on personal wealth. If the school absorbs it, access depends on the institution’s budget. Either way, a qualified student could be turned away for reasons unrelated to academic merit or compliance.

Students should be judged on whether they meet the requirements and whether their training is legitimate. The ability to produce an enormous payment tells us neither. DHS should withdraw this proposal.

The United States puts tremendous effort into educating talented people. This proposal could make it much harder for those graduates to apply what they have learned here through lawful practical training. I strongly oppose that direction.

A graduate’s skills do not become less useful because a university cannot finance an OPT fee. A promising research or engineering opportunity does not become suspicious because its funding is limited. Yet those are precisely the kinds of situations in which this policy could close the door.

DHS needs to consider what happens when capable graduates take their knowledge elsewhere because legitimate training becomes financially inaccessible. Their departure could also affect colleagues, unfinished projects, and future collaboration. These consequences deserve serious consideration before such a substantial barrier is imposed. Please withdraw the proposed fees.

What troubles me most is the possibility that a strong educational recommendation could become meaningless unless someone can finance the fee. A professor or supervisor might see clear value in a graduate’s continued training, while the institution’s finance office sees an expense it cannot approve.

Those are different judgments. One concerns whether the work is relevant, supervised, and educationally worthwhile. The other concerns available money. This proposal risks allowing the second judgment to override the first.

Research teams can spend considerable time developing specialized knowledge and working relationships. Interrupting that process could harm other researchers as well as the individual graduate. DHS should examine those consequences carefully. I strongly oppose charging institutions amounts that could prevent sound educational decisions from being carried out.

Saying that universities will pay these fees is not a satisfactory answer to concerns about affordability. Universities still have to find the money.

For illustration, just 100 initial OPT recommendations would mean $7 million in fees. A university facing that expense could restrict recommendations, seek reimbursement, or redirect money from other purposes. None of those choices is harmless. Nor should domestic students face higher charges or reduced services because their institution is trying to preserve training opportunities for international graduates.

The proposal places schools in a deeply uncomfortable position: support an eligible student’s educational plans or protect a limited budget. DHS should not create that conflict without a much stronger justification for the amounts involved. I strongly oppose the proposed fees and urge the agency to withdraw them.

An employer could offer relevant work, proper supervision, and fair treatment, and still lose a qualified graduate because the graduate’s school cannot arrange the required payment. I cannot support a policy that could produce that result.

The fee is triggered by the school’s recommendation, so a compliant employer’s careful planning would not necessarily protect the placement. Recruitment could have to start again. Projects could be delayed. Existing employees could be left carrying additional work while a replacement is sought.

It is reasonable to investigate whether a job is real and whether training requirements are being followed. Those checks should focus on the actual employer and placement. A large payment made by a university does not answer those questions. DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue oversight that examines compliance directly.

A small company may be able to offer a graduate close supervision, meaningful responsibility, and valuable practical experience. It may also have very little spare cash. This proposal could make that financial limitation decisive.

Although schools would formally pay the fees, the proposal allows costs to be shifted to employers. Larger organizations might be able to absorb that expense while smaller businesses abandon otherwise worthwhile placements. Even when employers are not charged directly, they could lose applicants whose schools decline to fund recommendations.

That would be a troubling way to determine who gets access to talent. A company’s bank balance does not establish the quality of its supervision or its respect for the rules. I strongly oppose a fee structure that could favor financial strength over the merits of a training opportunity.

Some worthwhile work does not generate much money. Community research, environmental projects, and nonprofit services can offer serious, degree-related training while operating within very tight budgets.

I strongly oppose making those opportunities harder to access through enormous OPT fees. A placement should not become less available simply because the work serves people who cannot pay much for it. Nor is it enough to suggest that everyone involved can share the cost. A community may benefit from a project without the student, university, or host organization having enough cash to finance the payment.

DHS should take that distinction seriously. Educational and public benefits do not automatically turn into available funding. This proposal could discourage valuable work for the wrong reason, and it should be withdrawn.

I am a Sociology PhD student at Portland State University, and I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule.

To whom it may concern,
 
I'm writing as a member of the public about one concern with this proposal: the cost to the U.S. economy.
 
I understand why DHS wants to protect the integrity of OPT, and I don't object to that goal. My worry is that a $70,000 fee for a first OPT recommendation, plus $30,000 for each one after that, would make U.S. schools much less attractive to international students, and the country would feel that loss well beyond OPT itself.
 
International students are a big part of the economy. NAFSA estimates they contributed $43.8 billion and supported 378,175 U.S. jobs in the 2023-24 academic year. Much of that money comes from tuition and everyday spending in college towns, and it exists because students expect to be able to gain U.S. work experience after they graduate. If OPT becomes too expensive for schools to offer, many students will simply study in other countries.
 
DHS's own analysis points the same way. It estimates the rule's primary annualized cost at $4.1 billion, with a range of $32 million to $8.2 billion, and it acknowledges that deterred students could mean lost enrollment. But the notice doesn't make clear how those losses are weighed against the fraud it hopes to reduce.
 
Because the downside could be large and the benefit is hard to measure, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and look at narrower ways to deal with fraud that don't put the whole program at risk.
 
Thank you for taking the time to read this.

To Whom It May Concern:
As a concerned U.S. citizen and resident invested in the long-term economic prosperity and technological security of our nation, I am writing to express serious concerns regarding and opposition to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Proposed Rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).
While regulatory modernizations and cost-recovery mechanisms are standard federal practices, this proposal, as structured, fails to balance administrative costs against the broader, indispensable benefits that OPT brings to the American economy, higher education system, and strategic innovation capabilities.
1. Threat to America’s Global Competitiveness in Critical Technologies
The Optional Practical Training program is not merely a non-immigrant benefit; it is one of the United States’ most effective instruments for retaining global, high-caliber talent in critical STEM disciplines. At a time when global competitors—such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union—are actively lowering barriers and expanding post-graduation pathways to capture international researchers and engineers, imposing additional fiscal barriers on OPT participants runs counter to our national interest. Diminishing the attractiveness of the U.S. as a primary destination for premier innovators directly compromises American leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing.
2. Adverse Repercussions on American Higher Education and Domestic Students
International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to local economies and higher education institutions across all 50 states. These students typically pay full tuition, which directly cross-subsidizes operational costs, STEM laboratory equipment, and financial aid packages for domestic American students. Cumulative administrative and financial hurdles erode the United States' competitive advantage in higher education, threatening university research budgets and ultimately shifting financial pressure onto domestic tuition-paying families.
3. Disproportionate Burden on American Startups and Small Businesses
While large multinational corporations possess the legal and financial resources to absorb regulatory fee increases, early-stage American startups, small enterprises, and academic labs rely heavily on cost-efficient access to recent graduates. By increasing the financial friction of hiring through OPT, this rule inadvertently penalizes the very entrepreneurial sector that drives domestic job growth and commercial innovation.
4. Failure of Economic Justification and Concerns of Duplicate Fees under the APA
Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency rulemaking must not be arbitrary, capricious, or unsupported by substantive economic modeling. OPT applicants already pay substantial fees to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for Form I-765 adjudication, in addition to upfront Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) fees. ICE has not sufficiently demonstrated that the proposed fee corresponds to an actual, distinct, and quantifiable administrative burden not already covered by existing federal fee structures. Without an auditable cost-accounting basis, this rule risks creating redundant bureaucratic extraction.
Conclusion
The U.S. government should be strengthening policies that attract, retain, and integrate top-tier talent into the domestic economy to safeguard American technological supremacy and fuel job creation. Imposing additional fees on the OPT pipeline creates immediate economic disincentives for minimal agency recovery.
I respectfully urge the Department and ICE to withdraw this proposed rule or conduct a comprehensive, independent economic impact assessment that thoroughly evaluates the secondary downstream costs to American industry and academic institutions.

To the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement:
As an American taxpayer and professional concerned with our national fiscal health and economic resilience, I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed fee imposition on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100).
Rather than serving public interest, this rule represents a counterproductive regulatory drag that undermines domestic tax revenue, strains American employers, and relies on an unsubstantiated fee structure.
1. Negative Net Fiscal Impact on Federal and State Tax Revenues
Participants in the OPT program work legally, contribute immediately to payroll taxes (FICA), federal and state income taxes, and inject substantial consumer spending into local communities—all while being ineligible for most public entitlement benefits. Artificially suppressing participation through compounding regulatory fees directly shrinks this tax-contributing workforce. The short-term regulatory revenue collected by ICE will be vastly outweighed by the long-term loss in broad-based tax revenues for both federal and local governments.
2. Misunderstanding of Domestic Job Creation and Innovation Multipliers
Extensive independent economic research confirms that high-skilled practical training programs do not displace American workers; rather, they serve as economic multipliers. STEM graduates participating in OPT provide the technical foundation that allows American firms to scale, secure patents, and subsequently create multiple downstream non-technical support, management, and operational jobs for U.S. citizens. Erecting financial roadblocks at the entry gate stifles business expansion, directly threatening job creation for domestic workers.
3. Inflationary Pressures on Crucial American Industries
American healthcare, engineering, and manufacturing sectors are already navigating chronic shortages of specialized technical personnel. Additional administrative and financial friction on OPT participation will exacerbate these shortages, creating unnecessary upward wage pressure in technical overhead and compounding broader inflationary strains across supply chains and critical domestic projects.
4. Administrative Redundancy and Lack of Cost Accounting Integrity
A core tenet of responsible governance is regulatory efficiency. Students participating in OPT already pay substantial fees to USCIS for employment authorization documents (Form I-765) and bear administrative overhead through their universities' SEVP reporting. ICE has failed to demonstrate a distinct, non-duplicative administrative service that warrants a separate fee assessment. Imposing multi-agency tolls on a single educational-to-practical transition pipeline creates bureaucratic inefficiency and fails the standard of reasoned decision-making required under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Conclusion
A forward-looking U.S. policy must prioritize economic growth, domestic innovation, and fiscal pragmatism. Disincentivizing global graduates trained inside American institutions from contributing to our domestic economy is economically self-defeating. I strongly urge ICE to withdraw this proposed rule.

An American Taxpayer and Resident

I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would undermine U.S. competitiveness: discouraging international enrollment, straining university finances, weakening research, and restricting employers’ access to U.S.-trained talent. DHS’s own analysis estimates $41.05 billion in costs over ten years without quantifying comparable benefits. DHS should withdraw the proposal.

1. DHS’s own estimates show substantial economic costs.

Table 10 estimates $41.05 billion in undiscounted monetized costs over ten years, with a primary annualized cost of $4.11 billion at a 3% discount rate. The accounting statement does not monetize the anticipated benefits. These are DHS’s estimates, not opponents’ projections. Unquantified benefits may exist, but DHS should demonstrate why they justify these costs and why targeted enforcement would be insufficient. Fee revenue is a transfer to the government, not automatically a net gain for the American economy. (public-inspection.federalregister.gov, public-inspection.federalregister.gov)

2. Universities face both direct financial burdens and lost enrollment.

At $70,000 per initial OPT participant, 100 participants would generate $7 million in fees; 1,000 would generate $70 million. These are illustrative calculations. Schools must either absorb the expense, pass it to students or employers, or restrict participation. Each option risks reducing resources for education or making American degrees less attractive. (public-inspection.federalregister.gov, public-inspection.federalregister.gov)

Students compare educational quality, total costs, and opportunities to apply their training. Making practical training prohibitively expensive could redirect enrollment abroad. Tuition-dependent universities could face serious budget shortfalls, while financially vulnerable institutions could experience deeper distress. Because facilities and instructional programs have fixed costs, lost revenue could lead to staff reductions, fewer courses, or higher tuition for American students.

3. Reduced enrollment threatens American jobs beyond universities.

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024–2025. Its methodology adjusts for U.S.-based financial support. (nafsa.org)

For scale, a hypothetical 10% decline in that contribution would equal $4.29 billion annually. This is an illustration, not a forecast. Nevertheless, it shows why enrollment effects matter: international students support housing, food services, transportation, and university employment. DHS should evaluate these potential losses when assessing whether the proposal protects American workers.

4. America cannot immediately replace its international research pipeline.

NSF reports that temporary visa holders earned 42% of U.S. science and engineering master’s degrees and 38% of doctoral degrees in 2024. Their shares reached 61% of computer and information sciences doctorates and 54% of engineering doctorates. These figures measure degree recipients, not OPT participation, but establish the scale of international talent in advanced American education. (ncses.nsf.gov)

Discouraging these students could weaken laboratories, delay research, and reduce opportunities for American students working alongside them. Expanding domestic STEM education is essential, but developing specialized researchers takes years. Restricting international talent does not instantly produce equally trained domestic replacements.

5. Employers could lose competitiveness rather than simply hire more Americans.

Specialized vacancies require particular skills and experience. An available worker is not necessarily an immediate substitute for a graduate trained in semiconductor design, scientific computing, or another technical specialty.

For illustration, a startup financing initial OPT fees for ten graduates would face $700,000 in additional expenses before salaries and benefits. It might reduce hiring, delay products, or move work abroad. None of these responses guarantees additional American employment. Delayed technical projects can also delay manufacturing, sales, and operational jobs.

NSF reports that approximately 73% of temporary visa holders earning U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2017–2019 remained in the country in 2023. Although this is not an OPT-specific statistic, it demonstrates that retaining U.S.-trained talent produces lasting domestic benefits. (ncses.nsf.gov)

DHS should withdraw these fees and prioritize targeted fraud investigations, genuine training verification, and enforcement against exploitation. Ability to pay is not evidence of compliance.

Protecting American workers requires strong universities, productive research, and competitive employers. This proposal risks damaging all three while transferring the benefits of American training to competing economies.

I oppose the proposed rule "Optional Practical Training Fees" (FR Doc. 2026-20660). DHS's statement that the rule would not affect health or safety.

1. The health and safety finding has no analysis behind it
The NPRM says the rule "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold in the first year" and provides a UMRA statement. UMRA section 202(a)(2) requires that statement to assess the mandate's effect on health and safety. The NPRM's answer is one sentence: "DHS does not believe that this rule would have impacts on health or safety." DHS gives no data, no reasoning, and no sign that it asked the Department of Health and Human Services.

2. DHS's own scenario removes OPT for most health graduates
In its low participation scenario, DHS assumes schools will pay the $70,000 fee "for only F-1 nonimmigrant students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension," and that "non-STEM OPT is no longer recommended." The STEM definition in footnote 49 covers the CIP two-digit series for engineering, biological sciences, mathematics and physical sciences, "or a related field." Most health professions degrees, including nursing and pharmacy practice degrees, sit in a different series (CIP 51) and are not on the STEM list. In that scenario, international graduates of those programs lose post-completion OPT. That is a direct effect on the health workforce, and the NPRM does not mention it.

3. The labor evidence is about computer jobs
The NPRM's labor-market case rests on computer occupations. The proclamation DHS quotes says computer science unemployment is "more than double the unemployment rates of recent biology and art history graduates." DHS cites nothing showing that OPT workers in nursing, pharmacy, public health or clinical research displace U.S. workers or depress wages. It also assumes "employers may find alternative workers." For clinical roles, that is a factual question about staffing, and DHS did not ask it. Where a hospital or clinic cannot fill a licensed position, the cost is measured in patient access, not only in payroll.

4. The refund rule fits licensed fields badly
Many health occupations require a state license, and graduates often sit for the licensing exam after the program ends. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1), the $70,000 fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document." If a graduate's license is delayed, the school loses the full fee even though no patient care was ever provided. A school pricing that risk will drop health students first. DHS did not consider this.

5. Biomedical research takes the STEM path, at full price
Biological sciences graduates do qualify for STEM OPT. That means $70,000 plus $30,000 for each graduate who moves into biotech, drug development, biostatistics or clinical trial work. The NPRM names "technology and critical infrastructure" as the high-risk sectors where abuse is "more likely." It cites no OPT fraud case in biomedical research or patient care. A flat fee charges these fields the same as the sectors DHS says concern it.

6. What DHS should have done
DHS has SEVIS data by program and employer. It could have reported how many OPT and STEM OPT participants hold health professions or biomedical degrees, and how many work for hospitals, clinics, health systems or clinical research sites. It could also have checked whether those employers sit in federally designated Health Professional Shortage Areas. It did none of this before concluding there is no health effect.

7. Requests
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS re-proposes any OPT fee, it should:
(a) complete the UMRA section 202(a)(2) health and safety assessment, in consultation with HHS, and publish it for comment;
(b) publish SEVIS counts of OPT and STEM OPT participants by CIP series and by health care employer type;
(c) exempt graduates of health professions programs and OPT employment with licensed health care providers, or at minimum allow a refund when a required license is not issued; and
(d) explain why a flat fee is needed in fields where DHS cites no fraud and no labor surplus.

I am an international graduate student pursuing an advanced degree in a STEM field at a U.S. university. My academic and professional experiences have shown me the importance of practical training opportunities in connecting higher education with industry innovation. I chose to pursue graduate education in the United States because of its world-class academic environment, research opportunities, and commitment to technological advancement.

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, protecting American workers, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, I am deeply concerned that the proposed fees would impose disproportionate burdens on legitimate students, educational institutions, and employers without adequately distinguishing lawful participation from fraudulent activity.

First, the proposed fees would undermine the accessibility and educational purpose of OPT.

Practical training is an important extension of academic education, enabling students to apply specialized knowledge in real-world settings. A $70,000 initial fee could make such opportunities financially inaccessible, regardless of a student's academic qualifications, professional potential, or compliance with immigration requirements. This financial barrier would disproportionately affect students with limited financial resources and could discourage talented individuals from pursuing advanced education in the United States.

Second, the proposed rule could weaken American technological competitiveness and innovation.

International graduates contribute specialized knowledge and skills to American research institutions and companies working in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, semiconductor technologies, and other strategically important industries. Practical training opportunities allow American employers to benefit from talent educated within the United States. Imposing substantial financial barriers could encourage highly skilled graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, potentially reducing America's ability to attract and retain international talent and weakening its long-term leadership in science and technology.

Third, placing the payment obligation on universities does not eliminate the financial burden on students and employers.

Although the proposed rule formally assigns payment responsibility to educational institutions, it explicitly allows institutions to pass these costs on to students or employers. Universities may also choose not to recommend otherwise qualified students because of the substantial financial obligation. Consequently, access to practical training could become increasingly dependent on financial resources rather than academic merit, professional qualifications, or legitimate educational objectives. This outcome would be particularly concerning for students who have already invested significant time and resources in their education based on the existing regulatory framework.

Fourth, more targeted alternatives could address fraud without disproportionately burdening legitimate participants.

I support stronger measures to prevent fraudulent employment arrangements and ensure that practical training remains directly related to students' academic fields. However, substantial fees imposed broadly on all participants are not necessarily an effective means of identifying or preventing fraud. I encourage DHS to consider alternative measures, including enhanced employer verification, risk-based compliance reviews, improved reporting mechanisms, and stronger enforcement against fraudulent institutions and employment arrangements. These approaches could strengthen program integrity while preserving legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Furthermore, I urge DHS to carefully evaluate the broader economic and educational consequences of the proposed fee structure, including its effects on university enrollment, international student recruitment, employer participation, and the competitiveness of the American research and technology ecosystem.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee structure and preserve accessible practical training opportunities for qualified international students. At a minimum, DHS should conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the proposal's impact on current students, educational institutions, employers, and American technological competitiveness before adopting such substantial fees.

Maintaining a fair, predictable, and accessible practical training framework is essential to ensuring that the United States remains a leading destination for education, research, and innovation.

I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it for the following reasons:
I. NO STATUTORY AUTHORITY: THE CHARGE IS A TAX
DHS relies on its general power to set "conditions" of nonimmigrant admission, INA 214(a). In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that a power to regulate does not include a power to tax. The charge is a tax under National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974): DHS admits it cannot keep the money, which goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302). The amount is tied to no cost of service, and its stated purpose is to deter OPT use. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee in INA 214, it enacted one expressly: $500 for certain H-1B and L petitions, earmarked for fraud detection (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12), 1356(v)). It has enacted no OPT charge. Washington Alliance v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT as a condition of status, not a power to raise revenue. With $109.4 billion in ten-year transfers, West Virginia v. EPA requires clear authorization, and Loper Bright gives DHS's reading no deference. On June 8, 2026, the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B charge as an unlawful tax, and the First Circuit denied a stay on July 24, 2026.
II. ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS: THE FEE DOES NOT FIT THE FRAUD
State Farm requires a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. DHS's largest figure, 10,000 students at "suspect" employers, is about 3% of 2024 participants (194,554 OPT plus STEM OPT), and DHS does not say how many cases were confirmed. Every case DHS cites involves employers or document vendors, and every one was found with existing tools: prosecutions, SEVIS data, site visits. Yet the fee is charged to schools, often before any employer exists, since students may apply up to 90 days before completion without a job offer. A change of employer triggers no new fee. A fee that never sees the employer cannot deter employer fraud. DHS also charges $30,000 on STEM OPT, the track that already requires I-983 training plans, E-Verify and site visits. DHS rejected extending those safeguards without estimating their cost, and never considered employer attestation, registration or debarment, or its existing power to withdraw SEVP certification.
III. FLAWED ANALYSIS AND IGNORED RELIANCE
DHS projects $12.8 billion a year by applying the fees to historic participation, while conceding that schools will decline to pay. If the fee deters, the revenue figure is wrong. If the revenue materializes, the fee has not deterred. DHS quantifies no effects on enrollment, tax revenue or research staffing. Its wage evidence relies on 2001 data, and it admits it cannot quantify OPT's labor impact. It concedes schools may pass the cost to "all students," meaning American students. DHS v. Regents requires weighing reliance interests. DHS calls them "far outweighed" without measuring any. Students now enrolled chose schools and took on debt in reliance on OPT carrying no school charge, and in the transition year even students moving into STEM OPT would face $70,000. 1,389 of 2,478 affected schools (56%) are small entities, yet DHS did not consider tiered fees, caps, phase-ins or exempting pre-completion OPT (5 U.S.C. 603(c)).
IV. BROKEN BENCHMARK AND INADEQUATE PROCESS
DHS set $70,000 to be "comparable" to an H-1B charge that a court has since held unlawful. A single summer internship would trigger $70,000, and $100,000 with later OPT. DHS gave only 30 days to comment on the rule itself but 60 days on paperwork burden. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 call for at least 60 days.

Supplemental opposition comment: The participation scenarios do not establish a reliable expected outcome

As an employee at a higher ed institution, I strongly oppose this rule. The rule is ambiguous in both its scope and application. If enacted, this rule will disrupt research teams, employer partnerships, and workforce pipelines, and it would impact learning, mentorship, and career opportunities for both international and domestic students. 

Crucially, the rule poses an existential threat to institutional financial stability at an exceptionally precarious moment. American higher education is currently navigating a severe "demographic cliff"—a sustained decline in the domestic college-aged population that has strained operating budgets nationwide. For years, international student enrollment has served as a critical counterweight to these domestic shortfalls. International students typically pay full non-resident tuition, providing essential revenue that supports departmental operations, student services, infrastructure, and institutional financial aid programs that directly benefit domestic students. Imposing a cost-prohibitive fee structure—whether passed on to students, shouldered by institutions, or transferred to employers—will inevitably divert international applications to competitor nations like China, European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. The resulting decline in international enrollment will decimate institutional tuition revenue at a time when colleges and universities can least absorb the blow. For many institutions already operating under razor-thin margins, this revenue shock will force severe budget cuts, the consolidation or elimination of degree programs, faculty layoffs, and diminished course offerings, ultimately hurting the entire academic community and American students.

I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. 

1. The fee raises revenue and is not a real condition of admission (Sec. IV.C). DHS says the fees would go into the general Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, and that ICE could not use them. DHS estimates annual collections of $8.4–16.5 billion. Yet it never ties the amounts to the cost of running OPT, and it does not rely on 31 U.S.C. 9701, which requires fees to reflect the cost or value of a service. A charge this large, unrelated to cost and paid into the general fund, works as a tax. INA 214(a)’s “time and conditions” authority does not clearly give DHS the power to raise billions in new revenue.

2. The fee does not target the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A). DHS’s evidence is about shell employers, staged worksites, and sold offer letters. The fee, however, is paid by the school before the DSO recommendation. DHS admits the fee is not tied to any employer, and initial OPT does not require a job offer at all. Paying $70,000 tells a school nothing about whether a future employer is real. Bad actors can pass the cost on to students, while legitimate students at schools that cannot pay lose access. Because the money goes to the Treasury, the fee also does nothing about the problem DHS itself names: compliance resources have not kept pace with the program.

3. DHS rejected targeted alternatives for its own convenience. DHS considered applying the STEM OPT safeguards (training plans, employer site visits, reporting) to all OPT. It chose a fee instead mainly because a fee needs minimal government resources. Saving agency effort is not a reasoned basis for moving billions in costs onto schools and students. Checking employers addresses the fraud DHS describes. A per-student fee does not.

4. The fee amounts are arbitrary. DHS says it picked $70,000 to match the H-1B fee and to be “on par with” one or two years of tuition. Neither benchmark measures fraud risk, harm to the labor market, or administrative cost. The same $70,000 applies to a part-time pre-completion internship, which is the form of training closest to OPT’s educational purpose. DHS itself expects pre-completion OPT to decline.

5. DHS quantifies the costs but not the benefits (Sec. VII.A). DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion (primary estimate $4.1 billion) and transfers of $12.8 billion per year. It gives no estimate of fraud prevented or U.S. jobs gained. It uses unpaid fees as a stand-in for lost value and does not estimate lost tuition, tax revenue, research output, or enrollment. Executive Order 12866 requires a reasoned finding that benefits justify costs, and this record cannot support one.

6. Small institutions are hit hardest (Sec. VII.B). By DHS’s own estimate, 841 of 1,389 small affected institutions would face transition-year costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 would face costs above 20%. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption because small entities make up 56% of regulated schools. That is exactly why the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires DHS to reduce the burden on them, not a reason to skip it.

7. DHS dismisses reliance interests and rushes the process (Sec. VI). Current students chose their programs, took on debt, and planned careers under the existing rules, and the fee would apply to them partway through their degrees. DHS also says schools may pass the cost to all students, which means U.S. students could end up paying for it. A rule with this much economic impact deserves the 60-day comment period that E.O. 12866 calls for, not 30 days.

8. The rule turns OPT into a privilege of wealth. Well-endowed schools and wealthy families can pay. Strong students at public, regional, and community institutions often cannot. The rule selects students by ability to pay, not by merit or integrity.

Recommendation: Withdraw the rule. To address fraud, DHS should pursue employer verification, more site visits, and enforcement against identified shell employers, and it should seek appropriations or a cost-based fee to fund SEVP oversight.

The proposed OPT fees could have consequences that extend well beyond the immigration system. They could undermine the competitiveness of American universities and research institutions, which play a critical role in the country's scientific and technological leadership.

International students are an important part of the academic and research ecosystem in the United States. They contribute to university revenues, participate in research projects, support teaching activities, and help laboratories maintain the skilled workforce needed to conduct advanced research. Their contributions do not end when they graduate. OPT provides a pathway for the knowledge and skills developed at American universities to be applied in businesses, research organizations, and other workplaces.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, particularly when they have limited financial resources. Even if universities do not directly pass these costs to students, they will have to make difficult decisions about allocating institutional funds. This could affect research budgets, hiring decisions, and the ability of smaller institutions to compete for international talent.

There is also a broader concern about America's position in global higher education. International students choose where to study based not only on academic quality but also on whether they can reasonably pursue professional opportunities after graduation. If the United States becomes significantly less accessible for practical training, talented students may choose universities in other countries. Once they establish academic and professional networks elsewhere, the United States may lose opportunities for future research collaborations, business development, and innovation.

This is not simply a question of international enrollment. It concerns the long-term return on America's investment in education and research. Scientific discoveries, new technologies, and successful businesses often emerge from the collaboration between universities and industry. Policies that weaken these connections could reduce the country's ability to translate academic research into economic value.

I urge DHS to carefully evaluate the broader institutional and economic consequences of this proposal, rather than focusing primarily on the number of OPT participants. Protecting the integrity of the immigration system should not come at the expense of the universities and research institutions that help maintain America's global competitiveness.

The proposed OPT fees appear to assume that reducing access to employment for international graduates will benefit American workers. However, this assumption overlooks how hiring decisions actually work.

Employment opportunities are not automatically transferred from one group of candidates to another. Employers hire based on qualifications, business needs, available budgets, and the expected value of a position. If an additional $70,000 fee makes hiring an international graduate financially impractical, the employer is not necessarily going to hire an American candidate instead.

In many cases, the position may simply remain unfilled. A company may cancel a planned hire, reduce its research activities, delay product development, or decide that a project is no longer financially viable. For startups and small businesses, one additional expense of this size can fundamentally change whether a hiring decision makes economic sense.

This distinction is important. A reduction in international hiring does not necessarily represent an increase in domestic employment. It could instead mean fewer jobs overall, less business investment, and reduced economic activity. American workers may ultimately lose opportunities when companies scale back or move their operations to other countries.

The proposed fee structure also raises questions about fairness and proportionality. It applies a substantial financial burden regardless of the size of the employer, the salary associated with the position, the nature of the work, or the actual risk of fraud. A small research organization and a large multinational corporation face the same fee, despite having very different financial capacities.

If the objective is to prevent fraudulent employment and protect U.S. workers, enforcement should focus on employers and arrangements that violate the rules. Stronger verification, targeted audits, and meaningful penalties for confirmed violations would address these concerns more directly.

Before adopting such a significant financial barrier, DHS should provide convincing evidence that it will actually improve employment outcomes for American workers rather than simply reduce legitimate hiring and economic activity.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposal and evaluate its effects on total employment, business investment, and the competitiveness of American companies, not merely the number of international graduates participating in OPT.

The proposed OPT fees raise serious concerns about economic inequality across different regions of the United States.

Not all universities, employers, and local economies have the same financial resources. Large corporations and well-funded universities may have the ability to absorb substantial additional expenses, while smaller universities, regional research institutions, nonprofit organizations, and early-stage companies may not.

This difference could create an uneven playing field. Institutions in smaller cities and less economically developed regions often rely on international talent to support research, fill specialized positions, and contribute to local economic development. If these institutions cannot afford the proposed fees, they may become less competitive in recruiting qualified graduates.

The consequences could extend to local communities. Universities are often major economic contributors in their regions. Their research activities support local businesses, create employment, attract investment, and contribute to the development of new industries. Smaller companies also depend on access to specialized talent to grow. Making that talent significantly more expensive to employ could disproportionately affect communities that already have fewer resources and fewer alternatives.

There is also a risk that opportunities will become increasingly concentrated in large metropolitan areas and institutions with substantial financial backing. This would run counter to broader efforts to encourage innovation, entrepreneurship, and economic development across different parts of the country.

DHS should evaluate the regional distribution of these costs and consider whether the proposal would create unintended disadvantages for smaller institutions, rural communities, and emerging technology sectors.

A policy affecting a national employment and training program should account for the diversity of the U.S. economy, rather than assuming that all schools and employers have comparable financial capacity.

I encourage DHS to conduct a more detailed assessment of these regional impacts before implementing a fee structure of this magnitude.

I strongly oppose and request the withdrawal of the proposed OPT fees. Fraud prevention is legitimate; financial exclusion is not evidence-based enforcement. The rule risks being "arbitrary, capricious" and "in excess of statutory ... authority" under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), (C).

WHERE IS THE SPECIFIC FEE AUTHORITY? DHS invokes general immigration and admission authority (8 U.S.C. 1103(a), 1184(a)), neither of which expressly authorizes these charges. Congress separately provided a student-monitoring fee based on "cost per alien" (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)(4)(A)). Under 31 U.S.C. 9701(b), government service charges must be "fair" and consider government costs and recipient value. In National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 341 (1974), the Court observed: "A 'fee' connotes a 'benefit'." DHS must explain why these deterrent charges are authorized fees, not exclusionary assessments. Under Loper Bright v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024), "courts must exercise their independent judgment" on statutory authority.

DHS ADMITS THE MONEY WILL NOT FUND ICE OVERSIGHT. The notice says "ICE would not maintain or use the funding" (91 FR 64576, IV.C): revenue goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. The deposit statute (31 U.S.C. 3302(b)) does not authorize imposing the fee. How do these payments remedy enforcement shortfalls? Reducing the number of lawful participants is not equivalent to identifying fraud. DHS must prove how these amounts prevent fraud, not merely exclude poorer applicants.

PAYMENT CANNOT VERIFY A JOB THAT DOES NOT YET EXIST. DHS admits a student "does not have to secure a training opportunity" before a school recommendation (91 FR 64569, III.D.1). How can advance payment verify an employer or worksite that may not exist yet? Wealthy bad actors can pay; compliant students may not. Wealth is not proof of compliance. DHS must publish confirmed fraud rates, denominators, and outcomes, not generalize from anecdotes.

THE ECONOMIC ANALYSIS IS CIRCULAR. DHS projects roughly $12.8 billion in annualized transfers and $4.1 billion in annualized costs (primary estimates, 3% discount; 91 FR 64579, VII.A.1). It says it "uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy" for lost OPT opportunities (91 FR 64588, VII.A.5.b). An agency-set fee cannot establish the value of lost wages, training, research, or enrollment. DHS also projects transition-year impacts exceeding 20% of revenue for 116 small institutions (91 FR 64595, VII.B.4). The rule does not quantify net U.S.-worker job or wage gains.

RELIANCE INTERESTS CANNOT BE DISMISSED BY A 60-DAY DELAY. Students committed years and substantial tuition to U.S. degrees under an established OPT system. The proposal could charge $70,000 even for an initial post-effective-date STEM extension where earlier OPT required no such fee. DHS must assess these commitments, not merely dismiss them. In DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), DHS was "required to assess whether there were reliance interests" (slip op. 26).

DHS REJECTS BETTER-TARGETED MEASURES WITHOUT COMPARABLE PROOF. Employer verification, risk-based site inspections, payroll audits, data-matching, penalties for sham employers, and stronger DSO accountability directly address the cited abuses. DHS dismisses these approaches without showing fees work better. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), requires the agency to "examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation." These fees treat lawful students as risks to be priced out.

Please withdraw the proposal. Alternatively, disclose precise authority, fee calculations, fraud data, economic/reliance analysis, and comparisons with targeted enforcement; reopen comments. Wealth is not compliance, and price is not proof.

I am a faculty member at the University of Florida, a public research university, where international graduate students and postdoctoral researchers make essential contributions to biomedical research, scientific education, and innovation.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation. These fees would impose an extraordinary financial burden on universities and could substantially undermine the ability of U.S. research institutions to attract and retain talented international researchers.

International students are an integral part of America's scientific workforce. In fields such as biomedical sciences, infectious diseases, biotechnology, and artificial intelligence, international graduate students and postdoctoral researchers contribute directly to research discoveries, technological innovation, and the training of future scientists. Their contributions benefit not only universities but also the broader U.S. economy, public health, and national scientific competitiveness.

The proposed fees would create several serious problems:

1. **Disproportionate financial burden on universities.** A $70,000 fee for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations is far beyond what most universities can reasonably absorb. Public universities operate under constrained research and educational budgets. These costs could force institutions to reduce international student opportunities, divert funding from research and education, or discontinue support for otherwise qualified graduates.

2. **Damage to U.S. scientific competitiveness.** The United States has long benefited from attracting talented students and researchers from around the world. International graduates who receive practical training contribute to American laboratories, universities, biotechnology companies, and the broader innovation ecosystem. Making OPT financially inaccessible would encourage talented researchers to pursue opportunities in other countries, weakening America's long-term leadership in science and technology.

3. **Negative consequences for biomedical research and public health.** Scientific research depends on continuity, specialized expertise, and collaboration. Restricting the ability of universities to retain international graduates could disrupt ongoing research programs, delay discoveries, and reduce the capacity of institutions to address important challenges in infectious diseases, cancer, and other areas of biomedical science.

4. **Lack of proportionality and demonstrated effectiveness.** While preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, the proposed fees do not appear reasonably connected to the actual administrative costs of processing OPT recommendations or the specific risks associated with individual students. A substantial financial penalty imposed on universities for recommending qualified students is not a targeted approach to identifying or preventing fraud. DHS should provide stronger evidence that these extraordinary fees would achieve the stated objectives and evaluate less burdensome alternatives.

I support reasonable measures to strengthen OPT program integrity, including improved institutional oversight, verification procedures, targeted audits, and enforcement against documented fraud. However, these objectives should be achieved without creating financial barriers that disproportionately harm legitimate students, universities, and the U.S. research enterprise.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. If additional oversight or administrative costs are necessary, DHS should consider reasonable, evidence-based fees that reflect actual administrative costs rather than imposing extraordinary financial obligations on educational institutions.

Maintaining the ability of U.S. universities to attract and train talented international researchers is an investment in America's scientific leadership, economic prosperity, and public health. This proposed rule risks undermining that investment.

I would strongly advocate against the proposed fee for OPT for international students in the U.S. in order to protect the economy in the United States and maintain its ability to be competitive globally.

For many international students, the U.S. is a priority destination because of its world-leading industries and the way that these are connected to a world-class higher education system.  International students contributed an estimated $42.9 billion dollars to the US economy in the 24-25 academic year and supported more than 355,000 U.S. jobs.  

Not only do international students make this direct contribution, they play a vital role in sustaining the United States’ global economic and technological competitiveness. By attracting talented students from around the world, American universities strengthen the pipeline of highly skilled graduates into strategically important fields such as engineering, artificial intelligence, computer science, biotechnology, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, and semiconductors. International students contribute directly to cutting-edge university research, scientific discovery, patents, and innovation, and those who remain in the United States after graduation provide critical talent to American employers and make disproportionately strong contributions to the creation of new companies and startups. At a time when countries around the world are competing aggressively to attract highly skilled students, scientists, and entrepreneurs, the ability of the United States to welcome, educate, and retain international talent is not simply an educational benefit. It is an important component of the nation's capacity to innovate, grow its industries, create jobs, and maintain its position as a global leader.

Introducing the proposed fee for OPT will cause many students to look at other country destinations for their opportunities.  This is a phenomenon that is already happening and it's estimated that the introduction of the new fee could reduce new student enrollments by anywhere between 50% and 70%.  The traditional 'big 4' destinations of the U.S., Canada, Australia, and the UK are declining in popularity due to non-friendly policies (or the threat of them) towards international students and their families.  This means the talent that would otherwise come to the U.S. is going to countries such as China, Singapore, Germany, the Netherlands, Malaysia, and Indonesia.  This will contribute to the swing of global industrial power away from the U.S.

The idea that U.S. students are losing out on jobs and university places to international students is a fallacy.  The contributions that international students make to the U.S. both financially and through industry grow the opportunities for domestic students and continue to keep the U.S. at the forefront of innovation, research and development.  Furthermore, most U.S. domestic students do not take advantage of study abroad opportunities and the presence of international students on campus and in classes provides a development opportunity for U.S. students who need to be competitive in what is now a global workplace.  If the OPT fee is implemented, U.S. domestic students will have less opportunity to work alongside international colleagues and thereby lessen their ability to obtain work in international companies.

The U.S. needs to keep moving forward.  In a global economy amidst worldwide competition, the U.S. must continue to attract the best talent from around the world regardless of nationality or risk becoming irrelevant.  The data tells us that with this OPT fee introduction, U.S. industry and innovation will decline, the number of startups and patents in the US will decline, and America's position in strategically important industries will decline.  It is vital for the health and well-being of U.S. industry that we look forwards not backwards.

For the sake of the U.S., reject the proposed fee.

Thank you.

Bob Gilmour

Re: Opposition to Proposed OPT Fees — DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01

Reference: 91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026; Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)

I am an international PhD student in engineering who has dedicated years to pursuing advanced education, conducting research, and gaining professional experience in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2).

1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Universities and Students (Sections IV.C and VII.A.4)

In Section IV.C (91 FR 64575), DHS explicitly acknowledges that educational institutions may pass the financial burden of these fees onto international students, other students, or employers. This raises a serious concern: even though universities are officially responsible for paying the fees, students could ultimately bear the costs.

Furthermore, DHS estimates in Section VII.A.4 (91 FR 64583, Table 3) that the proposed fees could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. These figures demonstrate the extraordinary financial scale of the proposal.

Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and publicly funded research universities, may be unable to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to practical training simply because their institutions cannot afford the fees.

2. Financial Ability Does Not Establish Academic Merit or Prevent Fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.

In Section IV.A (91 FR 64570–64571), DHS describes fraudulent employment arrangements, including shell companies and nonexistent workplaces. I recognize the seriousness of these concerns and support stronger enforcement against such activities.

However, Section IV.C (91 FR 64574) suggests that requiring substantial fees would encourage institutions to recommend only highly qualified students. Financial capacity is not an appropriate measure of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration regulations.

A student who has maintained lawful status, successfully completed an advanced degree, and secured legitimate training should not be denied an opportunity solely because their university cannot pay $70,000.

DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, compliance investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent entities rather than imposing financial barriers on all students.

3. Negative Consequences for Research and STEM Education (Sections VI and VII.A.5)

In Section VI (91 FR 64578), DHS recognizes that the proposed fees could affect institutions' existing budgets and suggests that universities could mitigate those impacts by transferring the costs to students or employers.

This approach does not eliminate the financial burden; it simply transfers it to another party.

For international graduate students in engineering and other STEM fields, practical training provides an opportunity to apply years of specialized education and research to real-world challenges. These experiences can benefit American businesses, infrastructure development, and technological innovation.

The proposed fees could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, limit access to professional training, and make the United States less attractive to talented international researchers.

4. Opposition to Repeated Fees at Higher Educational Levels (Section V.A)

In Section V.A (91 FR 64577), DHS specifically requests public comments on an alternative that would impose an additional $70,000 initial OPT fee whenever a student advances to a higher educational level.

I strongly oppose this alternative. Students who continue from bachelor's to master's or doctoral programs are investing additional years in education and developing specialized expertise. Repeatedly imposing such substantial fees would create an additional financial barrier to advanced education and professional development.

**Requested Action**

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), reject the alternative of repeating the $70,000 fee at higher educational levels, and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing OPT fraud.

Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate and important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement and oversight, not by imposing disproportionate financial barriers on legitimate international students, educational institutions, and employers.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I am not in favor of the proposed $70,000 fee for recommending OPT. While it is important to stop fraud in OPT and the student visa system, the reasoning in the notice is deeply flawed. It is comparing apples and oranges.

First, this would represent an increase of more than 14,700% over the current OPT application fee.

Any substantial fee increase should be decided by Congress after hearings and debate. If there are flaws in the OPT and student visa programs, those issues should be addressed by Congress. This exorbitant fee would discourage a vast majority of legitimate international students seeking practical training from applying for OPT, and it could have an even broader negative effect on international students choosing to study in the United States.

Several times in the notice, the justification for the fee increase is that DHS does not have the resources to monitor fraud. However, these students are graduates of U.S. undergraduate and graduate programs, and they are highly qualified individuals who are interested in furthering their academic qualifications. They are not students coming to the United States solely to seek employment.

The SEVP database already contains OPT employer information and could be used to identify suspicious employers. For example, the database includes the employer’s name, address, supervisor’s name, email, telephone number, and the job duties being performed by the student. The notice does not explain why this tool is not being used, or cannot be used, to identify employers and students who are out of compliance or committing fraud.

An ICE news release from October 21, 2020 stated: “ICE has a system of checks in place to mitigate fraud and is committed to protecting national security by ensuring that students, visitors, and schools comply with U.S. immigration laws,” and noted that ICE was actively targeting individuals who try to exploit the student visa system. That suggests ICE does have the ability to address fraud. In addition, the fee collected would go to the general fund, not directly to DHS, so DHS staffing would remain unchanged. It appears the purpose of the new $70,000 fee is simply to discourage colleges from recommending OPT and students from pursuing it.

ICE and DHS have also received major increases in funding in recent years. ICE has seen its budget increase more than threefold, jumping from about $10 billion in FY 2025 to over $85 billion total available resources following major federal spending bills.  The Big Beautiful Bill (2025), increased the DHS budget by 75 billion dollars.  Secure America Act (2026),  added nearly $39 billion more in multi-year funding.  Yet the notice continues to claim that the agencies do not have the resources to monitor fraud in the OPT program.

The argument also ignores the scale and importance of international students. In 2024–25, there were about 1.18 million international students in the United States, making up about 6% of total college enrollment. More than 57% of international students pursue STEM fields, which drive the vast majority of extended OPT utilization.
