Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an international PhD student in a STEM field at a U.S. research university. I write to oppose this proposed rule, in particular the $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), and the alternative of reapplying the $70,000 fee at each degree level. 

1. The fee would effectively close OPT as a path into U.S. academic research.
For international students who earn a PhD in the U.S., starting a postdoctoral appointment on F-1 OPT or STEM OPT is very common. J-1 and H-1B are alternatives, but OPT is usually preferred: the student applies for it directly, without needing the employer to file a job-specific petition with labor certification and fees, and it avoids the two-year home-residence requirement that can attach to J-1 status. The entry-level NIH Kirschstein-NRSA postdoctoral stipend for FY 2026 is $63,480. The proposed $70,000 fee exceeds a full year of a postdoc's pay. The school must pay before recommending OPT and may pass the cost to the student or employer, but academic labs pay postdocs from research grants with fixed budgets, and early-career scholars cannot pay it themselves. In practice, universities will stop recommending OPT or labs will stop hiring international graduates as postdocs.

2. The fee is not tailored to the fraud DHS describes.
The rule cites shell employers and "visa mills." Universities, national laboratories and nonprofit research institutes are not shell companies, and STEM OPT employers must already enroll in E-Verify and sign a Form I-983 training plan. A flat fee on every student penalizes legitimate employers and students alike; fraud is better addressed by enforcement against the bad actors DHS has already identified. The rule also states the fees go to the Treasury's general fund and will not be retained by ICE, so the money would not fund fraud prevention. A charge tied neither to the cost of administering OPT nor to the problem it claims to solve works as a barrier, not an integrity measure.

3. International researchers are central to U.S. science.
According to the NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, temporary visa holders earned 54% of U.S. engineering doctorates and 61% of computer and information science doctorates in 2024. NSF also found that 73% of temporary visa holders who earned science and engineering doctorates in 2017-19 still lived in the U.S. in 2023. These are researchers trained in U.S. labs, often on U.S. research funding, and most stay to contribute here. Since 2000, immigrants have won 40% of the Nobel Prizes awarded to Americans in chemistry, medicine and physics combined (45% in physics alone), according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Much of that leadership was built by people who came as students and stayed.

4. Talented students have other choices.
International students do not come to the U.S. because we lack opportunities at home. We come because U.S. universities have been the best place to do science, and because the path from PhD to postdoc to faculty or industry research has been open. That openness is already eroding. In a 2025 Nature poll, three-quarters of U.S.-based researchers who responded said they were considering leaving the country, including 548 of 690 postdocs. Other countries are recruiting them: the European Union launched a 500-million-euro "Choose Europe for Science" package for 2025-2027 to attract researchers from around the world. Established scientists are leaving too: in July 2026, Omar Yaghi, who came to the U.S. as a teenager and shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, left UC Berkeley to lead a new institute at Tsinghua University in Beijing. A $70,000 fee at the very start of an academic career would add to this pressure, telling the next generation of scientists to go elsewhere, and U.S. research will bear the cost.

5. Requests
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should at minimum:
- exempt OPT employment at institutions of higher education, their affiliated nonprofits, and nonprofit or governmental research organizations, consistent with how Congress treats these employers under the H-1B cap (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5));
- reject the alternative of reapplying the $70,000 fee at each degree level, which would fall hardest on PhD students who have earned several U.S. degrees;
- analyze the rule's effect on university research and postdoctoral hiring before finalizing it.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to submit a comment with respect to the Proposed Rule on optional Practical Training Fees (ICEB-2026-0100). 

I have 14 years of experience working in the international education sector, most recently with nearly 5 years of experience in graduate admissions for a U.S. university. Although I write in my personal capacity, and not for my employer, my past work experience and expertise in this field inform my view on this proposed rule.

A 2024 survey by Shorelight and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education showed that 79% of students responded to the question “If OPT were no longer available, would you still choose to study in the U.S.” with either “No” or “Not Sure” (Shorelight, https://shorelight.widen.net/s/8djqz7kpqc/sl_25-opt-in-focus-report_lr) This new rule would make OPT effectively nonexistent, with the $70,000 fee surpassing the tuition money that many universities bring in from a student in a year, therefore putting the program out of reach for universities and, by extension, students. A 79% decrease in international students would be catastrophic for U.S. higher education and for the U.S. student experience. It would also put hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs at risk as I will outline below.

My journey toward working in higher education started when I was an undergraduate student myself. A study abroad experience followed by subsequent friendships I formed with international students when I returned to the U.S. helped me to build my own skills and interest in intercultural competence and communication. I dedicated my career to making the world a more open and welcoming place through cultural exchange and educational programs. Over the years, in my work, I have seen the power of exchange programs, including the F-1 Visa program, to bring talented students to the U.S., giving them an opportunity to learn from U.S. educators and peers, as well as the opportunities for educators and peers to learn from them. 

The interactions and friendships formed between U.S. citizens (including students, faculty, staff, and community members) and international students are powerful and often enduring long after international students have graduated and even left the U.S. They return to their countries with a positive perception of the U.S., in addition to personal connections, with these programs contributing invaluably to U.S. soft power around the world at relatively little cost to U.S. taxpayers.

In fact, international students increase opportunities for U.S. students. In addition to offering connections and resources that help U.S. students develop their own intercultural competencies, international student enrollment supports a greater diversity of programs available to U.S. students. There are many graduate and undergraduate programs across the country that would not be able to maintain faculty and staffing levels without international student tuition dollars in play. According to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, “1.1 million international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2023-2024 academic year and supported more than 378,000 jobs” (NAFSA: Association of International Educators, https://www.nafsa.org/about/about-nafsa/international-students-contribute-record-breaking-level-spending-and-378000-jobs)

The rule purports to “to protect the interests of U.S. workers,” but does not account for the tremendous harm that would be done to institutions that employ the 378,000 individuals whose jobs are created or supported by international students, including mine. With fewer international students in the U.S., this would lead to colleges and universities cutting stuff, and does not even include indirect loss of income to businesses in college towns and cities where international students and students working through OPT live and work, including the landlords they pay rent to, restaurants and stores they frequent, and online businesses that they order from. The proposed rule does not contain an analysis of the harm to U.S. jobs and businesses and DHS needs to address that concern before implementing the rule.

It also does not account for the ways in which this loss of international students would make things more expensive for U.S. students, who would not have tuition-paying international students to shoulder the expenses required by colleges and universities, who would likely raise tuition for remaining students.

In summary, this proposed rule will substantially decrease the numbers of international students in the U.S., by up to 79%. This will cause harm to U.S. students, U.S. universities, U.S. university faculty and staff, and businesses supported by international students.

As an international educator at a private university, I respectfully express concern regarding the proposed fees for international students seeking post-graduate practical training.

While I recognize the importance of protecting our immigration system and preventing fraud, these fees create significant financial and operational burdens that undermine higher education, limit opportunities for international graduates, and may harm U.S. interests.

1. Misalignment with Statutory Intent

The proposed $70,000/$30,000 fee structure goes far beyond reasonable administrative cost recovery and creates a prohibitive financial barrier. When fees prevent eligible individuals from accessing legally established training opportunities, they function more as penalties than administrative charges.

Furthermore, if collected revenue goes to general Treasury funds rather than supporting OPT oversight, compliance, or fraud prevention, the connection between the fees and their stated purpose is unclear. Fraud prevention measures should be targeted, justified, and proportionate to the costs and risks they address.

2. Financial and Operational Impact on Higher Education

Assigning financial responsibility for these fees to institutions and employers creates an unreasonable burden, particularly for nonprofit, faith-based, and mid-sized institutions with limited resources. Absorbing these costs could negatively affect students, academic programs, and other institutional priorities.

Many valuable training opportunities are offered by nonprofit, religious, educational, and research organizations with limited budgets. Fees of this magnitude could make participation financially impossible, leaving opportunities primarily available through the largest and best-funded employers. This would disadvantage graduates pursuing careers in education, nonprofit service, humanitarian work, and other fields that provide substantial public benefit.

3. Institutional Oversight and Regulatory Responsibilities

Universities already fulfill significant regulatory responsibilities through Designated School Officials (DSOs), who maintain SEVIS records, report required information, and support compliance with student visa regulations. These responsibilities provide an established framework for monitoring international students and maintaining accountability.

While stronger oversight is appropriate, extraordinary financial burdens do not necessarily improve reporting accuracy or compliance. Institutional accountability should be reasonable and proportionate to actual responsibilities.

Post-graduate practical training is also a natural extension of higher education, allowing graduates to apply their knowledge, develop professional skills, and contribute to their fields. Creating substantial financial barriers between graduation and practical experience undermines this important educational connection.

4. Economic and Workforce Consequences for the United States

International graduates contribute to the U.S. workforce through research, innovation, specialized knowledge, and service in fields where qualified talent is needed. Practical training allows them to apply their education while contributing to American businesses, universities, research institutions, and nonprofit organizations.

Excessive fees risk diminishing the United States' ability to retain talent educated at its own institutions. International students consider career opportunities after graduation when choosing where to study. Prohibitive fees may encourage talented students to pursue opportunities in countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, allowing those nations to benefit from the educational investment and talent developed by American institutions.

Restricting these opportunities could reduce the pool of qualified workers, limit innovation, and weaken the competitiveness of American higher education.

Conclusion

I support responsible immigration administration and effective fraud prevention. However, these goals should be pursued through measures that are proportionate, financially reasonable, and consistent with U.S. educational and economic interests.

I respectfully urge the Department to reconsider the proposed $70,000/$30,000 fee structure and evaluate its legal justification, relationship to actual administrative and enforcement costs, and consequences for universities, employers, international graduates, and the American workforce.

Effective oversight should not require prohibitive financial barriers or unnecessarily restrict legitimate opportunities for graduates to apply their education. A balanced approach can protect our immigration system while preserving the valuable contributions international graduates make to American education, research, innovation, and service.

The proposed rule sounds flawed and would impose undue hardships on international students and may prevent them from studying in the United States. Furthermore, it is an added burden to institutions of higher ed.

University of Dayton comment on Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100. Cites are to 91 Fed. Reg. 64566.
The University of Dayton is a private Catholic research university in Ohio with 9,000 students, about 450 of them international, 270 of those graduate students, (17% of graduate enrollment). We are SEVP-certified and fall in the small-entity class analyzed in the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (64592). We share the Department's commitment to program integrity and urge reconsideration of this rule.
In FY 2026, 397 students began OPT. Under the Department's methodology—$70,000 per initial OPT, $30,000 per extension, and the 56% uptake rate (64583)—that single cohort carries a fee obligation to the university of about $34.5 million; the FY 2025 cohort of 230 starts would have cost $19.96 million. The obligation recurs each year and exceeds any reasonable level of support the University could provide.
The mitigation paths the rule suggests, passing costs to F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers (64578), are inconsistent with our values and do not hold up. Charging a nonimmigrant student $70,000 allocates a federal work authorization by family wealth. Charging all students raises tuition on domestic (including Ohio) students, to fund a federal fee—a transfer the rule never analyzes despite its American-worker rationale. Declining to recommend a student for OPT generates no fee and so appears costless to the Department, while imposing real costs on students, families, employers, and region. This would also make American higher education at our university unattractive to int’l students.
The rule states the fees are on par with one or two years of education (64575). Int’l graduate tuition at the university is about $20,000 a year, so the initial fee is equal to 3.5 years of tuition and the full obligation equals five.
The claim that only 20% of F-1 students use OPT (64,578) uses the wrong denominator of all 1.4 million F-1 students, including many who are not yet eligible. Since the fee is triggered by a DSO recommendation at program completion, the more relevant measure is OPT use among graduating internal students. In the most recent year, we conferred 393 degrees to int’l students and recorded 397 OPT starts—evidence that OPT use in our graduating cohort is far higher than 20%.
Participation is also not stable. Our starts rose 73% in one year, from 230 to 397, against the assumption of no change in recommendations (64582). Clemens projects a 79% decline in starts where institutions bear a $100,000 fee. NAFSA estimates a $102.3 million loss to Ohio in 2026-27 from falling int’l enrollment, and IIE projects up to $3.4 billion in lost revenue and 40,000 fewer jobs.
The administrative burden is understated. The rule estimates an hour of staff time per instance (64584, 64595), conceding it cannot estimate budgeting, recordkeeping, banking, or refund costs (64590). At our volume, roughly 397 payment events totaling $34.5 million a year, each needing finance approval, treasury handling, reconciliation, and audit records. Payment must precede the SEVIS recommendation (64599), which follows graduation timelines rather than our budget cycle, forcing unbudgeted rolling commitments. Refunds are discretionary, unavailable once an EAD issues, and carry no appeal, so they are not a reliable receivable.
The small-entity analysis does not support its conclusion. The rule reports 841 of 1,389 small institutions face impacts above 1% of revenue and 98 above 20% (64595-96), yet concludes the impact is minimized. Its rejection of an exemption counts institutions rather than participants or incidents of fraud (64596). The conduct described is employer-side—shell companies, staged worksites, residential addresses, third-party placements (64571)—not a function of school size. Targeting by compliance history or recertification outcome is a significant alternative under 5 U.S.C. 603(c) the analysis never addresses.
Less burdensome alternatives warrant analysis: adjust SEVP fees to fund fraud detection; use appropriated funds; pre-hire employer rules such as E-Verify, a valid EIN, and no residential worksites, self-employment, or third-party placement; extend STEM OPT safeguards to all OPT; and a risk-tiered fee. The only alternative fee discussed is a higher one (64577), which we oppose. The Department's own cost estimate is $4.1 billion/year, up to $8.2 billion (64579), while revenue goes to the Treasury and ICE may not use it (64576), so the fee funds none of the enforcement. The investigation tied suspect employers to about 3% (64571); why does the full fee reach the other 97%?
We ask that the Department reopen the comment period after further analysis of cohort-level participation, transaction and administrative costs,and where participant and fraud actually sit by institution type; address each alternative on the record; and reconcile the analysis with its findings.

Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees

I am an F-1 student pursuing dual master's degrees in Health Tech and Information Systems at Cornell Tech, expecting to graduate in May 2028. Before coming to the United States, I trained as a physician at Sun Yat-sen University in China. I chose to study in the United States, and pay full international tuition, in substantial reliance on the availability of Optional Practical Training (OPT), which would allow me to apply my clinical and technical training in the U.S. health technology sector. I respectfully oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for each subsequent OPT, for the following reasons.

1. The fees bear no relationship to the cost of administering OPT. An OPT recommendation is a SEVIS data entry by a school official, followed by the same Form I-765 adjudication for which students already pay a filing fee. Nothing in the proposal demonstrates that processing one student's practical training costs the government anything approaching $70,000. A charge of this size, deposited into the general Treasury, is a revenue measure directed at one group of students, not a fee calibrated to the cost of a service.

2. The flat structure is arbitrary. The same $70,000 would be triggered by a ten-week pre-completion summer internship as by twelve months of post-completion employment. There is no rational connection between the fee and the duration, value, or oversight burden of the training.

3. The proposal would end OPT in practice while claiming only to fund it. The Department itself acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or stop recommending OPT altogether. No student in my position could pay $70,000 on top of tuition and living expenses, and most schools cannot absorb such a cost either. Smaller institutions, and the hospitals, universities, and nonprofit health organizations that hire many OPT graduates, would be affected first and worst.

4. It would directly harm the U.S. healthcare workforce pipeline. My field, health technology and clinical AI, depends on people who combine clinical training with data science, and international students supply a large share of that pipeline. A $70,000 barrier will not protect U.S. workers in these shortage fields; it will move the talent, and eventually the employers and the research, to Canada, the United Kingdom, and other countries competing for the same graduates.

5. Fraud prevention does not justify a blanket fee on the compliant. Fraud in the F and M programs is properly addressed through SEVP school certification, site visits, and enforcement against bad actors. Charging every lawful student $70,000 because a small number of actors abuse the system punishes the compliant majority and the schools that follow the rules.

6. The rule disregards reliance interests. Hundreds of thousands of students, including me, selected U.S. institutions and committed years of study and substantial tuition in reasonable reliance on the longstanding availability of OPT. Raising the effective price of participation to $70,000 for students already enrolled is fundamentally unfair.

I respectfully request that the Department withdraw this proposal. If any fee is adopted, it should be capped at the demonstrable, per-student cost of administering the OPT recommendation, and students already enrolled in their programs should be exempt.

F-1 student, Cornell Tech, Class of 2028

I am a Designated School Official (DSO) at a large private university in the Midwest. I have worked as a DSO for nearly 15 years at multiple institutions in different states. At my current institution, we have about 4,600 enrolled international students and about 2,100 students on OPT and STEM OPT. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. My concerns relate to the rationale for the fee, its impact on institutions and students, and its broader economic consequences.

Lack of evidence supporting the fee

The proposed rule appears to be based in part on concerns about fraud within the OPT program. However, DHS has not provided evidence demonstrating widespread fraud that would justify imposing a substantial fee on all applicants. In my professional experience, international students are highly motivated to comply with immigration regulations because the consequences of status violations are severe. While some instances of fraud may occur, I have not observed evidence that fraud is so prevalent as to justify this broad financial burden. DSOs share DHS's interest in maintaining program integrity. Throughout my career, I have worked with colleagues who take their reporting and compliance responsibilities very seriously. If DHS believes additional oversight is needed, more targeted approaches are available. For example, SEVIS already contains extensive data that could potentially be used to identify patterns of noncompliance without imposing significant new costs on every OPT applicant.

Impact on institutions and DSOs

OPT is a long-standing benefit available to eligible F-1 students. Introducing a substantial financial barrier creates difficult questions for institutions, particularly if schools are expected to absorb any portion of the cost. Institutions could be forced to decide whether, and for whom, financial assistance should be provided. Such decisions might require schools to establish criteria based on financial need, academic achievement, or career prospects rather than immigration eligibility. These are not determinations DSOs are trained or authorized to make as part of the immigration advising process. The proposal has already increased advising demands on my office. International students often plan their coursework, internships, research activities, and graduation timelines years in advance. The uncertainty created by this proposal has made it more difficult for students to make informed decisions and for advisors to provide meaningful guidance.

Impact on students

Practical training opportunities are a critical component of the educational experience for many international students. Whether graduates remain in the United States or return to their home countries, OPT allows them to apply their education, gain professional experience, and contribute to the workforce. The uncertainty surrounding this proposal is already affecting student decision-making. I have worked with students who have modified academic plans, accelerated graduation timelines, or abandoned research interests because they are concerned that future access to OPT may become financially unattainable. It is disappointing to see students making major educational decisions in response to uncertainty surrounding an immigration benefit for which they are otherwise eligible. A decline in international student enrollment would also affect US students and institutions. International students contribute valuable perspectives to classrooms, research, and campus communities. These interactions are an important part of preparing students to succeed in an increasingly interconnected world.

Economic consequences

Even the proposal of this fee has created uncertainty that affects planning by students and employers. In conversations with students, I increasingly hear that they are considering opportunities outside the US because they are uncertain about future access to practical training, and that employers are cancelling interviews due to the uncertainty. OPT is an important bridge between higher education and participation in the US workforce, particularly in STEM fields. Adding a substantial new financial barrier risks making the US less attractive to talented students from around the world. Reduced international enrollment would have significant consequences for universities, research programs, local economies, and employers seeking highly skilled graduates.

Administrative process

Finally, I am concerned about both the process and timeline associated with this proposal. If DHS seeks to address fraud or program integrity concerns, it should pursue measures that are narrowly tailored to those objectives and that minimize burdens on compliant students, institutions, and employers. Given the significant impact this proposal could have on students, educational institutions, and employers, a longer comment period would have allowed for more meaningful stakeholder engagement and a more thorough evaluation of its consequences.

The proposed OPT fees are excessive, economically counterproductive, and inconsistent with America’s long-term interests in education, innovation, and global competitiveness.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal, preserve accessible OPT opportunities, and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures to address legitimate program integrity concerns.

The Institute of International Education reported declines in new international student enrollment in fall 2025. Although multiple factors affect enrollment, uncertainty about practical training can influence whether prospective students choose the United States or another country.

Employers may also face consequences. Some industries struggle to recruit people with specialized skills, language abilities, and international experience. Limiting the pool of qualified candidates can increase hiring difficulties and workloads for existing employees. In fields such as hospitality, staffing challenges can affect turnover, stress, and service quality. Businesses may also consider expanding recruitment or operations elsewhere if access to talent becomes more difficult.

International students have options. Other countries offer strong academic programs and pathways to professional experience. If studying and training in the United States becomes too costly or uncertain, students may choose to take their tuition, skills, and future contributions elsewhere.

After years of sacrifices, I am now questioning whether I will have a fair opportunity to use the education I worked so hard to earn. I am not asking for guaranteed employment or special treatment. I am asking for the chance to gain experience, compete fairly, and contribute.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed OPT fees, examine their effects on students and educational institutions, and consider how CPT restrictions compound these barriers. Immigration compliance and workforce protections matter, but so do the long-term interests of American universities, employers, communities, and students who have followed the rules.

Thank you for considering this perspective.

I strongly oppose the proposed imposition of additional fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This proposal risks undermining one of the United States’ greatest competitive advantages: its ability to attract, educate, and retain talented individuals from around the world.

International students already make substantial financial contributions to the American economy. They frequently pay higher tuition rates, face significant restrictions on employment while studying, and must navigate an expensive and complicated immigration system. Imposing additional fees simply for the opportunity to gain practical experience in their fields would create yet another financial obstacle for individuals who have already invested considerable resources in American education.

More importantly, OPT is not a privilege that benefits international students alone. It is a program that benefits the United States. International graduates contribute their knowledge, skills, innovation, and productivity to American businesses. They help fill specialized positions, support research institutions, and strengthen the country’s position in an increasingly competitive global economy.

The United States should be encouraging talented graduates to contribute to its workforce, not making that opportunity progressively more expensive.

There is also a fundamental issue of fairness. International students pursue their education under a system that offers limited opportunities for authorized practical training. Introducing additional financial burdens on access to that training risks disproportionately affecting students from lower-income backgrounds. A student’s ability to gain professional experience should not depend on their financial capacity to absorb an ever-growing series of administrative fees.

Furthermore, the agency should demonstrate that any proposed fee is necessary, proportionate, and supported by a transparent accounting of actual administrative costs. Regulatory fees should reflect legitimate administrative expenses, not function as financial barriers to lawful participation in an established immigration program. Without a convincing justification, additional fees risk appearing arbitrary and unnecessarily burdensome.

The long-term consequences deserve serious consideration. International students have choices about where to pursue their education and begin their careers. Countries around the world are competing to attract highly educated individuals. If the United States continues increasing the financial and administrative obstacles facing international graduates, it risks pushing talent, investment, and innovation toward competing economies.

This is not simply an immigration issue. It is an issue of economic competitiveness, educational opportunity, and the future of American leadership.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reconsider this proposal, provide a rigorous justification for any additional costs, and fully evaluate its potential economic and educational consequences.

The United States should not invest in educating the world’s brightest minds only to create unnecessary financial barriers when they are ready to contribute to the American economy.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the agency to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements.

I am an F-1 graduate who recently completed a master's degree in mechanical engineering at a U.S. university. I am currently employed in semiconductor equipment engineering under approved post-completion OPT, and I intend to pursue the 24-month STEM OPT extension in 2027.

I understand DHS's interest in preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, I am concerned that the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could create substantial barriers for students who are already complying with OPT requirements, as well as for universities and employers that support legitimate practical training.

I made significant academic, financial, and career decisions based on the OPT framework that existed when I enrolled and graduated. A major change to the cost of continuing authorized training could disrupt both my professional development and my employer's ability to retain trained engineering talent.

I am particularly concerned about the transition provisions in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)–(3). The regulatory impact analysis assumes a $70,000 initial fee for STEM OPT recommendations during the transition year when no prior fee has been paid. This appears to affect students whose initial OPT was approved before the new rule, even though STEM OPT is an extension of their existing training.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider these fees and explicitly protect students who received post-completion OPT authorization before the effective date, including their future STEM OPT extensions.

I also encourage DHS to consider more targeted fraud-prevention and compliance measures that would not impose the same financial burden on students and institutions participating legitimately in the program.

Thank you for considering these concerns.

I’m an international student here on an F-1 visa, and I came to the U.S. to study. Between tuition, rent, daily living and travel, I spend about $200,000 a year, and most of that money goes to my school and to small local businesses.

I agree that OPT fraud is a real problem and that the government should stop it. I’m also fine with OPT users paying a reasonable fee to cover the cost of enforcement.

This proposal doesn’t do that. Nowhere does it say what enforcement actually costs or how that cost turns into $70,000 per student, plus $30,000 for each OPT after that. It just picks a huge number meant to scare people away. A charge meant to discourage behavior rather than cover a cost is really a tax, and only Congress can create a tax.

It also doesn’t fit the problem. The fraud examples in the rule are almost all fake or shell employers, but this fee doesn’t check employers at all. It charges every student and every school the same amount. Fraud rings with money can still pay. Honest students mostly can’t, so many will simply choose another country. That means fewer students, less tuition and less spending in college towns, which hurts ordinary Americans and small businesses the most.

The problem is real, but this fix doesn’t match it. Please withdraw this proposal and replace it with a fee based on real enforcement costs, along with stronger checks on the employers who are actually committing fraud.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) - Oppose. The $70,000 initial fee is not a fee for a service. There is currently no school fee for an OPT recommendation, and a student already pays the USCIS Form I-765 filing fee ($470 online / $520 paper). DHS does not tie $70,000 or $30,000 to the actual cost of entering a recommendation in SEVIS, reviewing a file, or administering OPT. The NPRM itself says the money would be deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt under 31 U.S.C. 3302, that ICE would not retain or use it for SEVP or enforcement, and that deterrence is the point regardless of whether Congress later appropriates it. DHS estimates $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year, $12.4 billion as its primary estimate. A charge of that scale, untethered to cost and paid into general revenue, is a tax and a deterrent penalty, not a user fee. DHS should withdraw it and, if any fee is proposed, justify it with actual program costs.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) and the Legal Authority discussion - Oppose for lack of statutory authority. DHS relies principally on INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184(a), the power to prescribe the time and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld DHS authority to create OPT; it did not hold that DHS may impose a $70,000 charge on a third party, a school, as a condition of a recommendation, or levy billions of dollars for the general Treasury. Congress has set specific immigration fees elsewhere in the INA. It has never authorized this charge, on this payer, at anything near this magnitude. A decision of this economic and political significance - effectively pricing a national training program out of existence - requires clear congressional authorization, which INA 214(a) does not supply.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i) - Oppose because this is a de facto elimination of OPT, not regulation of it. A qualified student would lose practical training - training directly related to the degree the F-1 program contemplates - not because the student is ineligible, not because the job is unrelated, and not because of any misconduct, but because the institution will not pay $70,000. If the government wishes to end OPT, that choice belongs to Congress after open debate. It should not be achieved indirectly by pricing every recommendation beyond what schools can rationally pay.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees, Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis - Oppose because DHS's own analysis shows devastating, disproportionate harm to small institutions, and DHS rejected exempting them. Those are existential figures for small colleges, language schools, and specialized programs. A rule that its own author calculates could consume more than a fifth of a small school's revenue cannot be cured by telling the school to find outside funding or to stop recommending students. At minimum the impact on small entities alone requires withdrawal.

I am an international PhD student in engineering who has dedicated years to pursuing advanced education, conducting research, and gaining professional experience in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2).
1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Universities and Students (Sections IV.C and VII.A.4)
In Section IV.C (91 FR 64575), DHS explicitly acknowledges that educational institutions may pass the financial burden of these fees onto international students, other students, or employers. This raises a serious concern: even though universities are officially responsible for paying the fees, students could ultimately bear the costs.
Furthermore, DHS estimates in Section VII.A.4 (91 FR 64583, Table 3) that the proposed fees could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. These figures demonstrate the extraordinary financial scale of the proposal.
Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and publicly funded research universities, may be unable to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to practical training simply because their institutions cannot afford the fees.
2. Financial Ability Does Not Establish Academic Merit or Prevent Fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.C)
In Section IV.A (91 FR 64570–64571), DHS describes fraudulent employment arrangements, including shell companies and nonexistent workplaces. I recognize the seriousness of these concerns and support stronger enforcement against such activities.
However, Section IV.C (91 FR 64574) suggests that requiring substantial fees would encourage institutions to recommend only highly qualified students. Financial capacity is not an appropriate measure of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration regulations.
A student who has maintained lawful status, successfully completed an advanced degree, and secured legitimate training should not be denied an opportunity solely because their university cannot pay $70,000.
DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, compliance investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent entities rather than imposing financial barriers on all students.
3. Negative Consequences for Research and STEM Education (Sections VI and VII.A.5)
In Section VI (91 FR 64578), DHS recognizes that the proposed fees could affect institutions' existing budgets and suggests that universities could mitigate those impacts by transferring the costs to students or employers.
This approach does not eliminate the financial burden; it simply transfers it to another party.
For international graduate students in engineering and other STEM fields, practical training provides an opportunity to apply years of specialized education and research to real-world challenges. These experiences can benefit American businesses, infrastructure development, and technological innovation.
The proposed fees could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, limit access to professional training, and make the United States less attractive to talented international researchers.
4. Opposition to Repeated Fees at Higher Educational Levels (Section V.A)
In Section V.A (91 FR 64577), DHS specifically requests public comments on an alternative that would impose an additional $70,000 initial OPT fee whenever a student advances to a higher educational level.
I strongly oppose this alternative. Students who continue from bachelor's to master's or doctoral programs are investing additional years in education and developing specialized expertise. Repeatedly imposing such substantial fees would create an additional financial barrier to advanced education and professional development.
Requested Action
I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), reject the alternative of repeating the $70,000 fee at higher educational levels, and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing OPT fraud.
Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate and important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement and oversight, not by imposing disproportionate financial barriers on legitimate international students, educational institutions, and employers.
Thank you for considering my comment.

I am writing to express my concerns about DHS's proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations under 8 CFR 214.13.

While I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers, the proposed fee structure could create significant unintended economic consequences for American businesses, universities, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. Negative Impact on American Businesses and Workforce Development

OPT provides American employers with access to graduates who have received education and training in the United States. Many of these individuals develop specialized skills, gain familiarity with American industries, and are prepared to contribute immediately to the workforce.

If schools become unwilling or unable to pay the proposed fees, businesses could lose access to qualified candidates who are already educated and available in the United States. Recruiting replacements takes time and money, and suitable domestic candidates may not always be readily available for specialized positions.

This could increase hiring costs, delay projects, reduce productivity, and make it more difficult for American businesses, particularly small and medium-sized companies, to compete and innovate.

Restricting access to OPT does not automatically create an equivalent supply of qualified American workers. It could instead leave businesses with fewer qualified candidates and greater operational challenges.

2. Negative Impact on American Universities and the Education Sector

International students contribute significantly to American universities through tuition, research, academic collaboration, and innovation.

The availability of practical training opportunities is also an important consideration for many students choosing where to pursue higher education.

If universities face a $70,000 financial obligation for each initial OPT recommendation, they may become reluctant to support otherwise qualified students. This could discourage prospective international students from choosing American institutions, reducing university enrollment and revenue.

Over time, the United States could lose not only international tuition revenue but also valuable research talent and the economic contributions associated with international education.

3. The Proposed Fees Are Not a Targeted Approach to Preventing Fraud

I understand DHS's concerns about fraudulent OPT employment and abuse of the program. However, imposing the same extraordinary fee on every student does not distinguish between legitimate employment and fraudulent activity.

A student with a genuine job offer from a reputable American company should not face the same financial barrier as someone involved in a fraudulent arrangement.

DHS should prioritize targeted audits of high-risk institutions, investigations of fraudulent employers, and stronger verification of actual employment and training activities.

These measures would address the underlying problems more directly without unnecessarily restricting legitimate employment opportunities or imposing disproportionate costs on compliant universities and businesses.

4. The Economic Costs Deserve Greater Consideration

DHS's own regulatory analysis acknowledges that reduced OPT participation could result in productivity losses for employers, lower international student enrollment, and lost economic opportunities.

It also estimates annual fee collections ranging from $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion. However, the analysis acknowledges that there is insufficient data to precisely quantify the broader economic value lost when students cannot participate in OPT.

Government revenue should not be treated as an adequate measure of economic benefit. The long-term contributions of skilled workers, productive businesses, university research, and innovation must also be considered.

A policy that generates substantial fee revenue while reducing access to qualified talent may ultimately impose costs on the American economy that outweigh its intended benefits.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure.

If the objective is to strengthen OPT program integrity and protect American workers, DHS should pursue targeted enforcement, improved oversight, and risk-based compliance measures rather than imposing extraordinary financial barriers on every OPT recommendation.

The United States benefits when its universities educate talented individuals and its businesses have the opportunity to employ qualified graduates. OPT serves as an important connection between American higher education and the domestic workforce.

Protecting program integrity and maintaining America's ability to attract talent should be complementary goals, not competing ones.

Thank you for considering my comments.

First, I would like to clarify an important misconception regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT), as the process does not work as described in the proposed rule.

Designated School Officials (DSOs) do not select or determine which students are allowed to participate in OPT. Their role is to verify that international students have successfully completed, or are on track to complete, their academic program and meet the eligibility requirements to apply for OPT. USCIS is the agency responsible for reviewing, processing, and approving OPT applications.

Once USCIS approves an application and the student receives their Employment Authorization Document (EAD), the student can begin seeking employment directly related to their field of study. DSOs subsequently help ensure that the reported employment meets the regulatory requirements and is related to the student's academic degree.

The process is straightforward, and it is important to understand that receiving OPT authorization does not guarantee employment. Many international students are unable to secure jobs within their authorized period. As a result, some choose to pursue another academic degree, while others return to their home countries.

OPT is not a program designed to take jobs away from U.S. citizens. Rather, it provides international graduates with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to the education they received in the United States. Many of these graduates eventually return to their home countries, taking with them the knowledge, skills, and professional experience acquired through American higher education.

Furthermore, international students make significant contributions to the U.S. economy. They generate substantial economic activity through tuition payments, housing, transportation, groceries, retail purchases, and other everyday living expenses. According to Open Doors (Open Doors is sponsored by the U.S. Department of State with funding provided by the U.S. Government and supported in its implementation by IIE.), international students contributed nearly $55 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024 (https://opendoorsdata.org/services/research-special-reports-and-analyses/economic-impact-of-international-students/).

Approving this proposed rule could have consequences far beyond the international student population. It could negatively affect U.S. colleges and universities, reduce institutional revenue, discourage talented international students from choosing the United States as their destination for higher education, and ultimately weaken an important contributor to the American economy.

We must recognize that international education is not simply an immigration issue; it is also an educational and economic issue. International students contribute to our communities, support American jobs through their spending, strengthen our institutions of higher education, and help maintain the United States' global competitiveness.

Before implementing a policy that could significantly restrict OPT, it is essential to understand how the program actually operates and recognize the substantial educational and economic benefits it provides to the United States.

I am writing to express strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule introducing a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 extension fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. While maintaining program integrity and curbing fraud are critical objectives, this proposed fee structure is legally arbitrary, financially untenable for institutions and students, ineffective at preventing bad actors, and directly counterproductive to U.S. national security and economic priorities.

1. Lack of Statutory Justification and Cost-Accounting Basis
Under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and federal fee-setting guidelines (such as OMB Circular A-25), agency fees must be reasonably calculated to recover the administrative costs of providing a specific service.

Arbitrary Valuation: The proposed rule provides no transparent cost-accounting, empirical data, or mathematical framework explaining how DHS arrived at a $70,000 baseline or a $30,000 extension fee.

Regulatory Ambiguity: The proposed rule is dangerously vague regarding the operational application of the $30,000 extension fee—specifically whether it applies per attempt, per degree level, or sequentially across pre-completion, post-completion, and 24-month STEM OPT phases.

2. Untenable Cost Burden on Educational Institutions and Students. 
Imposing a cumulative $100,000 burden per student places an insurmountable financial barrier on both higher education institutions and participants:  

Higher Education Infrastructure: Higher education institutions cannot absorb multi-million-dollar annual fee liabilities to issue standard academic recommendations. Beyond the fees themselves, institutions will face substantial compliance costs to build payment collection mechanisms, hire operational staff, and manage software upgrades.   

Students and Employers: Students—whether on financial aid or self-funded—cannot afford a $70,000 to $100,000 access fee for practical training. Employers participating in standard entry-level post-graduate training programs cannot justify paying six-figure surcharges for short-term, entry-level training roles.   

3. Ineffective and Counterproductive as an Anti-Fraud Measure
The core rationale for this rule—using financial cost to deter fraud—is fundamentally flawed:   

Inability to Pay does not equal Non-Compliance: Ability to pay high fees bears no correlation to legal compliance or integrity. Wealthy bad actors can easily pay a fee, whereas law-abiding, highly qualified candidates will be priced out.   

Penalizing Compliant Students: The vast majority of F-1 students utilize OPT strictly within regulatory bounds to gain practical experience. This rule disproportionately punishes legitimate participants and restricts OPT availability almost exclusively to individuals securing immediate, high-paying corporate roles on an H-1B trajectory.

Socioeconomic Inequity: The fee creates a severe "have vs. have-not" system, restricting practical training to ultra-wealthy international students regardless of merit or academic achievements.

4. Severe Economic, Academic, and National Security Repercussions
Practical training is a key bridge between classroom learning and real-world innovation. Crushing this program damages broader U.S. interests:

Chilling Effect on U.S. Higher Education: Unprecedented fees will drive top international talent away from American universities toward competing nations (such as Canada, the UK, and Australia) with straightforward post-study work pathways.   

Undermining U.S. Talent Retention Goals: OPT represents the nation's premier talent retention pipeline for top scientists, researchers, and engineers, particularly in critical STEM fields. Most international graduates return home, but those who stay often launch careers, build startups, and drive domestic innovation.

Conflict with Administration Priorities: A key goal of the White House is "attracting and retaining top-tier global talent" in industries vital to national security and critical technologies. As President Trump has publicly noted, international talent often struggles with visa uncertainty when deciding whether to launch their careers in the U.S. Placing a $100,000 price tag on OPT directly undermines the policy goal of keeping the world's best minds in America.   

For these reasons, DHS should immediately withdraw the proposed $70,000 / $30,000 fee structure for OPT recommendations. The agency should instead focus on targeted, evidence-based compliance monitoring that preserves the vital role of practical training in American higher education and global competitiveness.

I strongly support the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for any subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions. These fees are a necessary step to protect American workers, reduce fraud, and restore integrity to a program that has grown into a large-scale, uncapped guest-worker pathway.

OPT has expanded dramatically, with roughly 294,000 participants in the 2024/25 academic year according to Open Doors data, and hundreds of thousands of authorizations in SEVIS. Unlike H-1B, OPT has no annual numerical limit, no comparable prevailing-wage requirement, and no labor-market test requiring employers to try hiring Americans first. It is concentrated in STEM fields, particularly computer science and related disciplines, where recent American graduates have faced elevated unemployment even as OPT participation in those same fields has grown substantially.

Employers receive a structural cost advantage when hiring OPT participants. Because these workers are generally non-resident aliens, both the employee and employer are typically exempt from FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare). This creates an estimated 7–15% payroll cost savings relative to hiring a comparable U.S. citizen or permanent resident. In competitive entry-level STEM roles, this tax subsidy systematically tilts hiring decisions against American graduates. The program’s concentration among large technology employers further concentrates competitive pressure on younger American workers seeking their first professional positions.

DHS and ICE have documented extensive fraud and abuse, including more than 10,000 potential fraud cases involving “pay-to-stay” schemes, shell employers, remote or offshore management of purported U.S. training, and worksites that do not provide genuine training. Schools currently face limited financial consequences for recommending large numbers of students, which weakens incentives for rigorous oversight by designated school officials. Placing a substantial fee on the recommending institution before the SEVIS recommendation and USCIS employment-authorization process creates accountability. It encourages schools to be more selective, improves program integrity, and reduces the volume of cases that exploit the system as a de facto work visa.

A $70,000 / $30,000 structure is meaningful relative to current practice, under which schools pay no OPT recommendation fee. However, given the scale of the program, the documented fraud, the multi-year duration of many OPT periods (especially STEM extensions), and the ongoing tax advantage conferred on employers, the fees may still be insufficient to fully internalize the costs imposed on American workers and the immigration system. Higher fees, or a structure that more closely tracks the economic value of the work authorization and the associated enforcement burden, would further deter marginal or fraudulent participation while preserving genuine, high-value training opportunities. Fees deposited to the Treasury also help offset the administrative and investigative costs of a program that has grown far beyond its original training purpose.

The proposal correctly places the fee on SEVP-certified schools rather than directly on students or tying it to a specific employer. This aligns incentives at the point of recommendation—the stage where institutional knowledge and control are highest—and avoids creating new barriers that could be easily gamed at the individual level.

I urge DHS to finalize the rule substantially as proposed and to consider whether modestly higher fees would better achieve the stated goals of combating fraud, strengthening system integrity, and protecting U.S. workers from unfair competition created by an uncapped program with a built-in tax subsidy. American graduates should compete on merit, not against a regulatory structure that systematically advantages foreign students through lower costs and fewer labor protections. This rule is a constructive step in that direction.

I urge DHS to withdraw it. I am a current student with experience receiving OPT multiple times in the past.

I recognize that DHS has legitimate interests in preventing fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and ensuring appropriate oversight of OPT. My objection is that this rule does not serve those interests. It is the wrong tool, set at the wrong price, with too little explanation.

1. The fees bear no relationship to any identified cost. Government fees ordinarily recover the cost of a service. A DSO’s OPT recommendation is an entry in SEVIS, and USCIS separately charges its own adjudication fee. A $70,000 charge for that entry cannot plausibly be cost recovery. If schools should contribute to the program’s integrity costs, that argues for a fee tied to actual administrative expense. The proposal also appears to direct revenue to the general treasury, and DHS should explain what statutory authority supports fees of this magnitude.

2. The rule would end OPT in practice, not merely regulate it. Few institutions can absorb a five-figure charge per student, and few students can pay it. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students, all students, or employers. A benefit available only to students who can pay $70,000 is a benefit in name only. If DHS or Congress intends to eliminate or sharply curtail OPT, that decision should be made openly and on its merits, not through a fee structure that achieves the same result.

3. Fraud concerns call for targeted enforcement. Fraud should be punished, but this rule charges every school and every student, including the overwhelming majority who comply. A $70,000 fee does not distinguish a legitimate university from a sham one; it mostly deters the compliant. DHS already has tools aimed at bad actors: SEVP can withdraw school certification, ICE can investigate and enforce, and employers have reporting obligations. Stronger use of those tools would address fraud directly without penalizing lawful participants.

4. Labor-market concerns should be answered with evidence. OPT is limited in duration and tied to the student’s field of study. If DHS believes OPT displaces U.S. workers or depresses wages, it should publish that analysis and propose measures matched to the findings. A prohibitive fee is not such a measure. Many employers report using OPT and STEM OPT to fill hard-to-staff technical roles, and international graduates frequently start companies that create U.S. jobs. 

5. The fee adds no worker protections. STEM OPT already requires a formal training plan and employer reporting. If DHS sees gaps in oversight, it can tighten those requirements directly. Charging schools does not change how employers treat workers or improve training quality.

6. Schools cannot simply absorb the cost, and many are not wealthy. DHS may view institutions as beneficiaries of international enrollment, but the fee would fall on public universities, regional colleges, and smaller institutions that have the least capacity to bear it. International tuition often helps sustain programs and research that benefit domestic students as well. For a benefit that primarily serves the student and the employer, schools have no practical way to recover this cost except by raising costs on students.

7. The rule is unclear on a critical point. The text is ambiguous about whether there is a cap on how many times a school must pay for the same student. Institutions cannot budget, set tuition, or advise students without knowing their potential liability. A rule imposing costs of this scale must be precise.

8. The broader harm falls on the United States. International students pay tuition, support research, and fill roles in fields facing shortages. OPT is a major reason they choose the United States over Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Making it unaffordable will redirect talent and economic activity abroad, and employers, especially small and mid-sized businesses without other visa options, will lose access to trained graduates.

9. The comment period is too short. A rule of this scale, affecting thousands of institutions and many thousands of students and employers, warrants more than 30 days. DHS should extend the period and publish the data and economic analysis on which it relies.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees to reflect actual administrative costs, clarify any cap on repeat payments, pursue its fraud and oversight goals through targeted measures, and provide an extended comment period.

The proposed OPT fee structure should be evaluated not only for its financial effects on educational institutions, but also for its administrative efficiency and enforcement value.

Three questions require particular attention.

1. What measurable compliance improvement is expected?

A substantial fee may reduce participation in OPT, but reduced participation is not equivalent to reduced fraud. The Department should distinguish between legitimate applications that become financially impractical and fraudulent arrangements prevented through enforcement.

2. Are the fees proportionate to the regulatory objective?

The Department should provide a transparent explanation of the relationship between the proposed payment amounts, administrative requirements, and anticipated compliance benefits.

Without that analysis, it is difficult to determine whether the fee structure is a cost-effective regulatory instrument.

3. Have less burdensome alternatives been adequately compared?

Employer verification, risk-based audits, improved reporting systems, and investigations focused on documented violations may address specific compliance problems.

These alternatives should be assessed against the proposed fees using consistent criteria, including enforcement effectiveness, administrative cost, institutional burden, and effects on lawful participation.

The proposed provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) raise important questions about whether financial barriers are being used in place of direct compliance oversight.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions and provide a more comprehensive comparison of regulatory alternatives.

Effective public administration requires demonstrating that a proposed intervention addresses the identified problem at a reasonable cost.

A regulation should be judged by its measurable outcomes, not simply by the magnitude of the financial obligation it imposes.

When people talk about OPT, the conversation usually focuses on engineers, scientists, and technology companies.

But what about the creative industries?

American businesses also employ people in animation, digital media, visual effects, interactive design, architecture, and other creative fields.

These careers depend heavily on practical experience. A student can learn design principles or animation software in college, but professional development involves collaborating with teams, meeting production deadlines, responding to client feedback, and understanding how creative projects are delivered.

OPT offers eligible international graduates an opportunity to develop those skills after completing their American education.

The proposed fees could make that transition considerably more difficult.

Smaller design studios, independent production companies, and creative agencies often operate with limited budgets. If universities become less willing to support OPT recommendations, these employers may face a narrower pool of qualified graduates.

I understand that immigration enforcement is necessary. However, I question whether imposing substantial fees on educational institutions is an effective way to identify fraudulent training arrangements.

The ability to pay does not demonstrate that a student is properly trained or that an employer is operating legitimately.

I also believe the economic analysis should recognize that American competitiveness extends beyond scientific research and traditional manufacturing.

Creative industries produce intellectual property, develop commercial products, and contribute to America's cultural influence internationally.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and consider more targeted compliance measures.

The economic consequences of this proposal should be examined across the full range of industries that rely on professionally trained graduates, including fields that are often overlooked in immigration policy discussions.

One group that deserves consideration in this discussion is America's military veterans.

Veterans returning to civilian life may need specialized services involving physical rehabilitation, mental health support, prosthetic technology, vocational training, and assistance with disabilities. Providing these services requires a broad network of trained professionals, researchers, and technical specialists.

American universities contribute to this work through programs in rehabilitation science, biomedical engineering, psychology, public health, and related disciplines.

For eligible international graduates in these fields, OPT can provide an opportunity to apply academic knowledge in professional environments. Practical experience is especially important when developing rehabilitation equipment, analyzing treatment outcomes, or designing technologies intended to improve independence and quality of life.

The proposed OPT fees raise concerns about whether universities will continue supporting these training opportunities at the same level.

Smaller research organizations and community-based service providers often have limited resources. If substantial fees reduce access to qualified graduates, some organizations may face additional challenges recruiting specialized personnel.

This does not mean that veterans' services depend entirely on international graduates. They do not. However, workforce policies can have indirect consequences for organizations that serve veterans and their families.

I also question whether the proposed fees are an appropriate response to immigration fraud. An institution's ability to make a substantial payment does not establish whether a training arrangement is legitimate.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and consider targeted verification and compliance enforcement instead.

Before implementing such significant financial requirements, DHS should evaluate potential effects on rehabilitation research, specialized workforce development, and organizations providing services to American veterans.

Supporting those who have served the country should include careful consideration of policies that may affect the professionals and institutions contributing to their care.

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. As an international student who has lived and studied in the United States for almost ten years, I believe this proposal would create substantial barriers to professional training, discourage international talent from contributing to the American workforce, and ultimately harm U.S. economic competitiveness.

I came to the United States nearly a decade ago to pursue higher education. Since then, I have completed undergraduate and graduate studies in chemical engineering and am currently pursuing a Ph.D. in environmental engineering at a U.S. university. Throughout these years, I have invested significant time and effort in developing technical expertise, conducting scientific research, and preparing to contribute to society through engineering. The opportunity to apply this training in American industries has been an important part of my educational and professional aspirations.

In engineering, classroom education and academic research alone cannot fully prepare students for professional practice. Curricular Practical Training (CPT) and OPT provide invaluable opportunities to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world industrial challenges, understand industrial operations, develop professional skills, and collaborate with engineers from diverse backgrounds. My own industrial experiences have helped me understand how engineering principles are translated into practical technologies and solutions, something that cannot be fully replicated in a classroom or academic laboratory.

For students in chemical and environmental engineering, such experiences are especially important. Our expertise directly supports industries addressing challenges in environmental protection, sustainable manufacturing, energy efficiency, and industrial innovation. Through practical training, international students can contribute specialized knowledge and fresh perspectives while developing the experience necessary to become effective engineers and researchers.

Although the proposed fees formally apply to educational institutions rather than individual students, their consequences would directly affect students like me. A $70,000 initial fee, potentially followed by another $30,000 for a STEM OPT extension, creates an extraordinary financial barrier. Universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs, and passing them on to students or employers would make practical training inaccessible for many qualified students. OPT is often the primary pathway for international graduates to gain professional experience and begin their careers in the United States. Without an affordable and accessible OPT program, students may lose employment opportunities despite having successfully completed years of education and training at American universities.

Personally, this proposal introduces significant uncertainty into my career planning. After spending nearly a decade building my education, research expertise, and professional connections in the United States, I hope to apply my skills to solving real engineering challenges in the American workforce. Under the proposed rule, my ability to pursue this goal could depend not on my qualifications, skills, or potential contributions, but on whether my university can justify paying an exceptionally high fee for my participation in OPT. This would be deeply discouraging for students who have devoted years to preparing for careers in the United States.

The consequences also extend far beyond individual students. American universities attract talented students from around the world, train them in advanced scientific and engineering disciplines, and prepare them to contribute to American industries. These students bring technical expertise, support research and innovation, contribute to local economies, and help American companies remain competitive internationally. OPT provides an essential bridge between this educational investment and its economic returns. Making that bridge prohibitively expensive risks encouraging talented graduates to pursue their careers in other countries instead.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and preserve accessible practical training opportunities for international students. The United States has invested in educating generations of international scientists and engineers. Allowing these individuals to apply their training and contribute to American industries benefits not only the students themselves, but also the U.S. economy, technological leadership, and society as a whole.

There are no protections for American workers who must compete with foreign students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed fee will deter use of the OPT program and prioritize deserving American students.

I am writing to oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) and to urge the Department to withdraw them.

International students are a proven economic engine for the United States. In the 2024-2025 academic year, international students at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs. For every three international students, one U.S. job is created or supported. That spending reaches local landlords, restaurants, retailers, and campus payrolls. It is also already declining. NAFSA estimates the U.S. economy lost $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs in Fall 2025 alone due to shrinking international student numbers. Adding new costs to OPT would deepen that lose.

OPT is not a side benefit of studying in the United States. For many students, it is the reason they choose a U.S. university over one in Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia. At the University at Buffalo, our office oversaw 4,631 students on OPT and STEM OPT in Fall 2025, more than the 3,820 F-1 and J-1 students enrolled on campus. These graduates are working for American employers right now.

The stakes are highest in artificial intelligence and technology. According to the National Foundation for American Policy, 70% of full-time graduate students at U.S. universities in AI-related fields are international students. The same research found that 42% of major AI companies in the United States have a founder who came to the U.S. as an international student. OPT is the bridge between those classrooms and those companies. Making that bridge more expensive hands an advantage to countries competing with the United States for AI leadership, including China, which would welcome the talent we discourage.

International students also shape what an American education is. Domestic students learn alongside peers from more than a hundred countries and graduate with the cross-cultural skills U.S. employers increasingly expect. International graduates who build early careers here through OPT often become long-term partners to American businesses and research institutions, whether they stay in the United States or return home.

These students and their families have already invested tens of thousands of dollars in U.S. tuition and living costs. A new fee at the point of graduation penalizes them for completing the education they came here to pursue, and it signals to future students that the United States is becoming more expensive and less welcoming than its competitors.

The proposed fees would harm students, universities, employers, and American workers who benefit from this talent. I urge DHS to withdraw them and preserve a fair and accessible OPT program.
