I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. Charging schools $70,000 for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each one after, including STEM OPT, would function as a near-ban on practical training for most international students. That would weaken the U.S. economy, cost American jobs, and push skilled people we have already trained to build their careers in competing countries.

International students strengthen the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, roughly one U.S. job for every three international students. In Illinois alone, that meant $2.4 billion and 22,479 jobs. These are jobs held by Americans in housing, retail, dining, transportation, and on campuses.

That contribution is already shrinking. NAFSA estimates that a 17 percent drop in new international enrollment in fall 2025 cost the U.S. economy over $1.1 billion and nearly 23,000 jobs. This rule would deepen that decline. Students choose where to study partly on whether they can gain work experience afterward: in a May 2026 IDP Education survey of nearly 6,000 international students, 66 percent said they would go elsewhere or consider going elsewhere without post-study work opportunities. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany will gladly take them.

DHS’s own analysis points the same way. In 2024, 194,554 students began OPT and 95,384 began STEM OPT. DHS’s low-end estimate projects a 56 percent decline in OPT participation under this rule, and it estimates tens of billions of dollars in economic costs over ten years while quantifying no offsetting benefits.

The rule’s premise, that OPT takes jobs from Americans, is not supported by evidence. A 2023 Niskanen Center study found that practical training for foreign STEM students is linked to more innovation and higher average earnings without displacing U.S. workers or lowering their wages. A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy analysis found no evidence that OPT reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. Talented graduates create jobs: they fill shortages, start companies, and make the teams around them more productive. If DHS is concerned about fraud by specific employers, it already has targeted tools, including SEVIS reporting and site visits. A six-figure fee charged to every school for every student is not a fraud measure. It punishes the many for the misconduct of a few.

International students also bring something harder to put a dollar figure on. They sit in classrooms with American students, work alongside American colleagues, and build lasting personal and professional ties between the United States and the rest of the world. That global understanding is a national asset, and it depends on students being able to stay, work, and contribute after graduation.

This issue is personal for me. My mother needed brain surgery. The neurosurgeon who saved her life came to the United States as an F-1 student, gained experience through OPT, and later stayed on an H-1B visa. Without OPT, that pathway would not have existed, and my mother would not be alive today. Behind the statistics are doctors, engineers, researchers, and entrepreneurs whose work directly protects and improves the lives of American citizens. Making it prohibitively expensive for them to begin their careers here does not protect Americans. It puts us at risk.

This proposal is shortsighted. It will cost American jobs, weaken American universities, and hand our competitors the talent we spent years educating. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the rule in its entirety and to keep OPT and STEM OPT accessible without these fees.

The OPT requirement of $70k then $30k is absurd and unfair to put onto institutions and students. Instead of welcoming international students to study in the U.S., this rule would make the pursuit of education very challenging. This feels antithetical to what this country stands for and I am fully against this.

I am a law student, and I write to oppose DHS’s proposal to charge schools $70,000 for a student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT extensions.

International students are part of American universities’ classrooms, labs, and clinics, and part of the legal profession. Under this rule, the decision about whether a student who meets every legal requirement can train in their field would no longer turn on merit or eligibility. It would turn on whether the student’s school decides to spend $70,000 on that student. DHS says outright that it expects schools to recommend only “the most promising” students. In practice, wealthy institutions and wealthy students would continue to have access, and everyone else would lose it.

OPT is one of the main reasons international students choose U.S. universities over competitors in Canada, the U.K., and Europe. A fee that can reach $100,000 per student would make U.S. programs much less attractive and would hit graduate and STEM programs hardest. Fewer international students means fewer research collaborators, fewer people to staff labs and teach, and less tuition supporting the programs that U.S. students attend as well. U.S. employers would lose access to graduates they have already spent time recruiting and training.

OPT and STEM OPT participants work in fields where the country needs talent: medicine and public health, engineering, computing, and scientific research. Pushing that talent to other countries weakens innovation and economic growth in the United States and gives competing countries an advantage in recruiting the world’s best students.

The rule is legally flawed. DHS relies on INA § 214(a). That provision lets DHS set conditions for nonimmigrant status. It does not let DHS raise revenue. The proposed amounts have no connection to what it costs DHS to process an OPT recommendation, and the money would go to the Treasury’s general fund. DHS’s own estimate is $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year. A charge like that is a tax, and only Congress can impose taxes. National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974). The NPRM also never explains how DHS arrived at $70,000 or $30,000. And it never explains how a fee paid before any employer is identified would address fraud, which typically involves sham employers. DHS already has targeted tools for that, including SEVIS reporting, employer attestations, and site visits. Finally, a 30-day comment period is too short for a rule with economic effects this large.

My request. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. If it does not, it should reopen the comment period for at least 60 more days.

The foundational strength of our nation lies in its history as a melting pot—a place where the best and brightest minds from across the globe come together to innovate, build, and drive our shared prosperity. Restricting overseas talent through steep, punitive financial barriers undermines this exact tradition and directly hurts our domestic economy.
The assertion that foreign talent harms local labor market outcomes is contradicted by economic data. High-skilled immigrants do not replace domestic workers; they expand the broader economic pie:

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on a contradiction at the center of this proposal: the administration has declared American leadership in artificial intelligence a national priority, and this rule taxes the very pipeline that produces it.

The United States does not lead in AI because it has a monopoly on talent. It leads because the world's most promising researchers come here to study, and OPT is the mechanism that keeps them here after graduation. A large share of the doctoral graduates in computer science and AI at American universities are international students, and a large share of the researchers staffing American AI labs — university labs, national laboratories, and private research groups — first worked in this country on OPT. The STEM extension, which this rule would surcharge by $30,000, is what gives a doctoral graduate the time to finish a research project, publish, and transition into the roles the country's AI strategy depends on.

Consider what happens when that bridge is priced out of reach. The graduate does not stop being an AI researcher. The graduate becomes an AI researcher in another country — in a lab in Toronto, London, or Shenzhen, working on the same problems, publishing the same papers, and building the competing systems that American policy is meant to outpace. The United States spent years and hundreds of thousands of dollars in educational investment training that person, and this rule would hand the return on that investment to its rivals. That is not a trade-off between immigration enforcement and innovation. It is a direct transfer of capability from the United States to its competitors.

The damage reaches beyond AI. The semiconductor workforce the CHIPS Act is trying to build, the biotech researchers, the engineers in advanced manufacturing — all draw on the same OPT pipeline. DHS estimates the fee would extract $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year from universities, and its own analysis concedes some schools would simply stop recommending OPT. When the recommendation stops, the graduate leaves, and the lab, the startup, or the national laboratory that would have employed them loses a worker it cannot easily replace.

A rule that claims to protect American workers while exporting the researchers who build American technology is working against its own stated purpose. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I oppose DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which proposes a $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee, and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. 

DHS proposes a $70,000 “fee” for the initial filing for OPT per student, and an additional $30,000 for every subsequent OPT application filed per student. DHS further proposes that “the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302” (p.64577). A fee is generally understood as payments charged to cover the costs of providing a good or service, charged specifically for the beneficiaries of those services (415 U.S. 352 (1974)), an example of this being the OPT filing fee and premium processing service fee that USCIS charges applicants. In contrast, a tax is a compulsory payment applied equally across populations and places for the purpose of funding the provision of public goods (112 U.S. 580 (1884)). The revenue earned from the tax being deposited in the General Treasury rather than DHS or ICE, and the parties bearing the expense of the “fee” being institutions rather than the OPT applicant directly imply that the amount will be treated as tax revenue rather than the cost of providing a specific service. We argue that this is a misrepresentation of the intended purpose of the fee, and does not serve to combat fraud or protect American workers as DHS claims it does.  

DHS also claims that “The financial costs would deter schools from recommending students with questionable qualifications for OPT, leading to higher program integrity. DHS anticipates that schools will consider adopting internal policies and procedures that prioritize quality and compliance over quantity of participants, stabilizing the number of OPT participants.” (p.64575). The proposed rule lays out no guidance on what DHS considers “questionable qualifications”, nor what parameters institutions are supposed to adopt. We are concerned that such an ambiguous instruction is encouraging schools to partake in actions violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, and national origin in programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. OPT is a training program available to every F-1 student that complies with the eligibility guidelines, and it is unfair and unjust to ask institutions to undertake discriminatory practices merely to issue recommendations for an authorization we do not grant.

Dear Acting Director David J. Venturella, 

I submit this comment letter in response to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (Department) proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), published October 8, 2026. 

We oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program remains intact.

DHS notes that “STEM OPT employers are subject to self-reporting requirements on the Form I-983, including certifying that the F-1 nonimmigrant student will not replace a U.S. worker...However, the employers for STEM OPT are not required to submit any business documents or supporting documents to DHS, such as tax records or proof of business.” (p.64574)

The need for greater transparency from employers and hiring practices is presented as a rationale for combating alleged OPT fraud. However, the fee imposed places a burden on institutions, despite no clear evidence that SEVP-certified institutions play any role in alleged OPT fraud. Furthermore, DHS provides no reasonable explanation for why it cannot update existing regulations and requirements for OPT employers as a measure against fraud. It also does not identify why the current information collected through SEVP, E-Verify, and the existing I-983 form is insufficient to investigate fraud, and why the additional information specified above is crucial to identifying fraud. We believe DHS has not made an attempt to explore less burdensome alternatives to the problem it poses in this proposal.

DHS presents the following statistic: “In fact, only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants participated in OPT in 2024 out of the 1.4 million F-1 nonimmigrants in the higher education system, which demonstrates that the vast majority of F-1 nonimmigrants choose to study in the United States for reasons other than to pursue work through OPT."” (p.64579). A September 2026 study examines the effects of this proposed tax on the price elasticity of demand for US degrees, university supply of OPT placements, and of employers’ demand for OPT workers. The results of this study showed that the nationwide count of international enrollment in the US responds with a price elasticity demand of -0.5 to -0.6, showing a fairly significant decline in enrollment in response to higher OPT taxes. It also demonstrated that when the $100,000 tax is offloaded onto students directly, the count for those starting OPT falls by a third of the no-tax baseline for OPT starters, and when the cost was borne by universities, OPT starts decline by four-fifths of the original baseline. This is preliminary evidence of the losses faced by universities and students with the imposition of this tax. [Source: https://docs.iza.org/dp18933.pdf]

One of the reasons presented by DHS as the basis of this rule is that OPT facilitates the undercutting worker wages and opportunities, go so far as to accuse the OPT program of “large scale replacement of American workers” (p. 64575). The Economic Innovation Group notes that international students transitioning to H-1B are more likely to add well-paying jobs to the US labor market, considering H-1Bs hired through outsourcing firms earn about $9,000 less than international students-turned-H-1B on average, despite being six years older than the latter group. [Source: https://agglomerations.eig.org/p/a-100000-tax-on-foreign-students]. A research study conducted by Seoyoung Kwon and Jongkwan Lee in March 2026 demonstrates that the increase in the supply of high-skilled immigrant workers as a result of the STEM extension program stimulates growth and innovation in start-ups and large companies alike, which in turn stimulates demand for domestic (American) high-skilled workers, as well as opportunities of local entrepreneurship. These findings disprove DHS’s argument with relation to the security and opportunity of American workers. [Source: https://bse.eu/research/working-papers/the-effect-of-retaining-high-skilled-international-graduates-evidence-from-the-stem-opt-extension]

These are just a portion of the concerns over this rule, and DHS has not done enough research into the hurt and damage that this will cause the higher education community.

As a DSO at a SEVP-certified institution, I oppose the proposed rule and urge that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program remains intact.

DHS states that “The OPT program instead relies heavily on DSOs, who are often overwhelmed by the program responsibilities and not fully trained, to be the initial gatekeepers for OPT authorization.” (p. 64575). It is important to note that DSOs do not have the authority to gatekeep or authorize OPT employment. DSOs issue OPT recommendation I-20s based on the eligibility requirements outlined by DHS as follows: 
"- The student has been a full-time student for one academic year in an SEVP-certified: College/University/Conservatory/Seminary
- The student is not studying English as a Second Language.
- The student’s proposed employment relates to the student’s major area of study
- The student has not used all optional practical training available at the current level of study.
- The student has not been authorized for 12 months or more of full-time Curricular Practical Training (CPT)." (Study in the States)

As per 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i), it is the student's responsibility to initiate the OPT application process, and the role of the DSO in pre-completion and post-completion OPT is limited to issuing the recommendation. The primary responsibilities of a DSO for post-completion OPT are outlined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(A), which states that "Prior to making a recommendation, the DSO at the educational institution of the student's most recent enrollment must ensure that the student is eligible for the given type and period of OPT and that the student is aware of the student's responsibilities for maintaining status while on OPT". No other additional responsibilities are listed for DSOs for post-completion OPT, especially with respect to alleged OPT abuse or employer fraud. The final authority for granting OPT authorization lies with USCIS, and once post-completion OPT is approved, the DSO's role in maintaining compliance is to updating the student's record with any changes in personal information or employment reported by the student (8 CFR 214.2(f)(12)(i)). DSOs are involved to the extent of ensuring compliance with existing eligibility and reporting requirements laid down by SEVP and DHS; if DHS holds the opinion that the current eligibility requirements require review, it is not clear why an enormous tax on SEVP institutions and additional burden on DSOs is the logical approach here. 

Given the limited role of DSOs and institutions in determining OPT eligibility, I believe the rationale for placing the burden of the “fee” and the enforcement of fee on DSOs and institutions is unfounded and should not be advanced.

I am a first-year student at Yale Law School and an Army veteran. I write to oppose the proposed rule requiring a $70,000 fee for a student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including the STEM OPT extension. DHS should withdraw it.
The fee has no connection to any cost DHS incurs. Federal user fees must be fair and based on the government’s costs and the value of the service (31 U.S.C. § 9701). Students now pay roughly $500 to apply for OPT work authorization. The rule raises that by about 13,900 percent without identifying any new adjudication or oversight cost a $70,000 charge would cover. A charge set far above cost and deposited into the general treasury is not a user fee. It is a tax, and only Congress may levy taxes.
DHS lacks the authority it claims. The rule rests on DHS’s general power to set “conditions” on nonimmigrant status. That provision is not a grant of power to impose a five-figure charge whose evident purpose is to make a lawful, decades-old program unaffordable. After Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), DHS receives no deference on its reading of its own statutory authority, and courts have already rejected a comparable theory used to justify the $100,000 H-1B fee. Congress, not an agency, decides whether to restrict post-study work.
The rule ignores serious reliance interests. Hundreds of thousands of students chose U.S. schools, paid tuition, and often took on debt with the reasonable expectation that OPT would be available on the terms that have existed for years. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires an agency changing course to weigh such reliance. The proposed grandfathering is largely illusory: because the $30,000 fee applies only where the $70,000 fee was already paid, a student already on OPT who seeks a STEM extension after the effective date would owe the full $70,000.
The cost will fall on those least able to bear it. Schools pay the fee, but the rule lets them pass it to students or employers. Wealthy universities may absorb some of it; community colleges, regional public universities, and smaller schools cannot. Startups and small businesses cannot pay $70,000 to hire a recent graduate. The practical result is that OPT becomes available only to the wealthiest students and largest employers, rewarding family resources rather than talent and effort, and forcing schools to decide which students are “worth” the fee.
The rule harms American competitiveness. Nearly 300,000 international students participate in OPT each year (Open Doors). Many work in science, engineering, medicine, and research, often in fields with persistent shortages, and many go on to found companies that employ Americans. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Germany all offer post-study work options and actively recruit these graduates. A $70,000 barrier hands that talent to our competitors. As someone who has served in uniform, I understand that national security depends on economic and technological strength; driving away people the United States has spent years educating weakens both.
DHS’s stated concerns call for targeted tools, not a blanket fee. DHS asserts that OPT should not be a “back door” into the workforce or a subsidy for cheap labor. If there is abuse, DHS already has SEVP oversight, employer reporting requirements, the STEM OPT training plan and wage protections, and its enforcement powers. It can strengthen those. A uniform $70,000 charge does not distinguish fraud from legitimate training; it simply prices out everyone who cannot pay, including the students who follow every rule. The rule also does not show that OPT participants depress U.S. wages, and the existing STEM OPT rule already requires wages commensurate with those of similarly situated U.S. workers.
The comment period is inadequate. A 30-day window is too short for a rule with consequences this large for universities, employers, and students across the country, many of whom are only now learning of it.
The proposed fees are unlawful, unsupported by any cost analysis, and harmful to students, schools, employers, and the national interest. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

Schools generally do not control employers’ operations, worksites, payroll, wages, or tax compliance, and cannot compel employers to provide business records. DHS notes that OPT and STEM OPT employers generally are not required to submit supporting documents, such as tax records or proof of business, and that employer attestations are not generally verified unless a site visit occurs. See Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64573. That supports improving employer verification—not making schools financially responsible for information they cannot obtain.

DHS should focus on the parties and conduct that present risk. Options include requiring relevant employer records, verifying information against available data, conducting targeted site visits, and investigating suspected shell companies and false submissions. A school’s payment of a fee cannot ensure employer compliance or prevent a student from providing false information. Schools cannot reliably assess whether a student is a “strong candidate”

The proposed rule calls DSOs “initial gatekeepers” and suggests schools may decline to recommend students they do not consider a “strong candidate” for OPT. Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64578. It does not define that standard or explain what evidence schools should use to apply it consistently and fairly. When making a recommendation, a DSO may not know the student’s future employer, worksite, duties, or the employer’s compliance history. DSOs confirm applicable requirements and maintain SEVIS information; they do not adjudicate Form I-765 applications, investigate employers, or inspect worksites. A DSO signing Form I-20 certifies under penalty of perjury that the information provided is true and correct. That should not make schools responsible for facts outside their knowledge or control. The Department describes SEVIS-USCIS data errors, correction requests, and communication problems that consume DSO time. DHS should address these capacity and information gaps before asking DSOs to make more consequential judgments.

DHS says the fee would reduce or stabilize participation and lessen enforcement burdens. Proposed Rule, 91 FR 64574–75. DHS considered broader reporting requirements, including approaches used for STEM OPT, but favored a fee partly because it could be implemented more quickly and require less government administration. Target investigations. Prioritize site visits and investigations using indicators such as unverifiable addresses, unusually high concentrations of OPT workers, inconsistent information, third-party placement arrangements, or prior compliance findings. DHS should assess whether SEVIS can identify patterns linking students to employers of concern and improve the system if needed.

Improve data and communication. DHS identifies SEVIS-USCIS data and communication problems, including issues involving the Computer-Linked Application Information Management System (CLAIMS). Use existing tools and build agency capacity. I am an international graduate student currently pursuing my master's degree in the United States. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," particularly the proposed fee requirements under 8 CFR 214.13(i).

Like many international students, I chose to study in the United States because of its outstanding educational opportunities, innovative environment, and the possibility of gaining practical experience related to my field of study. Pursuing graduate education here requires a significant investment of time, money, and effort. Optional Practical Training (OPT) is an important part of that educational journey because it allows students to apply their academic knowledge in real-world professional settings.

**First, the proposed fees would create unreasonable financial barriers.** Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions, could make it financially impossible for many universities to support their international students. Although these fees would formally be paid by institutions, students could ultimately bear the consequences through reduced OPT opportunities, additional financial pressure, or the inability to obtain school recommendations.

**Second, the proposal would undermine the value of American higher education.** International students contribute substantial tuition revenue, diverse perspectives, and academic talent to American universities. Practical training is often a major consideration when students decide where to pursue higher education. If OPT becomes inaccessible, future international students may choose to study in other countries, weakening the United States' ability to attract and retain global talent.

**Third, the proposed rule could negatively affect American businesses and innovation.** International graduates bring specialized knowledge, technical skills, and diverse perspectives to the workforce. Preventing qualified graduates from gaining practical experience could deprive American employers of valuable talent and reduce opportunities for collaboration and innovation.

I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and protect American workers. However, imposing extraordinarily high fees on educational institutions is not a reasonable or proportionate solution. Stronger compliance monitoring, targeted investigations, and enforcement against actual violations would be more appropriate alternatives.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fee requirements and preserve meaningful access to practical training for qualified international students.

International students come to the United States not only to receive an education, but also to develop skills, contribute to their communities, and participate in the country's academic and economic success. Policies should encourage these positive contributions rather than create unnecessary barriers.

I firmly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It relies on selective anecdotes, untested and faulty assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

International students are not asking for guaranteed jobs or permanent immigration benefits. We are asking for a fair and financially accessible opportunity to gain professional experience through an established program while complying with U.S. immigration laws.

In actuality, US research that keeps us continuously advancing in fields such as science, technology, and medicine is disproportionately driven by the tireless work of postdoctoral scholars, many of whom (in some fields, greater than 50%) came from outside the US to contribute their ideas, talent, passion, and labor that ensures the US remains a worldwide innovator in these fields. Ultimately, imposing this fee - particularly at such absurdly high levels - punishes a crime that has not been committed. If fraud is a concern, why then not consider measures that route it out specifically, such as via the imposition of fines or fees on institutions or individuals found to be acting in bad faith? I would urge the Department to consider measures that could support increased compliance with the protective measures already in place without punitive impositions on those who would otherwise seek to make our nation more innovative and robust.

Dear Department of Homeland Security,
I am an international Ph.D. student in applied physics, originally from Russia, currently studying in the United States on an F-1 visa. I strongly oppose the proposed rule introducing total 100,000$ fee for OPT authorization.
My opposition is based on two primary concerns: the questionable legal justification for these fees and their potentially devastating consequences for US scientific research and economic competitiveness.
1. The proposed fees raise serious questions about statutory authority and their distinction from taxation.
The proposed fees, totaling up to $100,000 per student, bear no reasonable relationship to the actual administrative costs of processing OPT applications. Indeed, DHS explicitly acknowledges in the proposed rule that the collected funds would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than directly used to fund OPT processing or immigration enforcement activities.
Furthermore, the proposed fees appear to be designed primarily as a financial deterrent rather than as compensation for administrative services. This raises a fundamental legal concern: when a government-imposed charge is not reasonably related to the cost of providing a service, but instead serves primarily as a deterrent or a means of generating government revenue, it may function more like a tax than an administrative fee.
Under the constitutional framework of the United States, the authority to impose taxes rests with Congress. I therefore question whether DHS possesses sufficient statutory authority to establish fees of this magnitude without explicit congressional authorization.
I urge DHS to reconsider the legal justification for this proposal and to explain why such extraordinary charges should be considered legitimate administrative fees rather than a form of taxation.
2. The proposed fees would undermine American scientific research, economic competitiveness, and national interests.
As a graduate student, I support myself entirely through my graduate research income. My family does not have the financial resources to assist me in paying fees of this magnitude. For students in circumstances similar to mine, a $100,000 financial burden is simply insurmountable.
The proposed rule would formally place the financial responsibility on educational institutions. However, my university, like many leading American research institutions, hosts a significant number of international graduate students. Requiring universities to pay up to $100,000 for each international student seeking OPT and STEM OPT would create an enormous financial burden.
In my view, this would lead to two particularly harmful outcomes.
First, universities may choose to cover these expenses using their existing budgets. In this scenario, substantial financial resources that could otherwise support scientific research, laboratory equipment, graduate education, and the employment of researchers would instead be diverted toward paying these fees.
This would directly reduce the resources available for scientific discovery and technological innovation in the United States. Ultimately, weakening the research capabilities of American universities would undermine the country's scientific leadership and long-term national interests.
Second, universities may be unable or unwilling to pay these fees. In this scenario, highly qualified international graduates, many of whom have spent years receiving advanced training and conducting scientific research in the United States, would be effectively forced to leave the country if they cannot obtain alternative work authorization.
The United States has already invested significant educational, institutional, and research resources in training these individuals. Allowing them to continue contributing to the American scientific and technological workforce would help the country benefit from that investment.
Instead, the proposed rule would encourage these highly trained researchers and specialists to pursue their careers in other countries. Those countries would gain access to an exceptionally valuable pool of scientific talent without having to bear the full costs of educating and training these individuals.
In effect, the United States would be investing in the development of highly qualified specialists only to transfer the benefits of their expertise, innovation, and future economic contributions to its international competitors.
I struggle to see how such an outcome could be considered beneficial to American national interests.
In summary, I believe the proposed rule raises serious questions about the legal authority to impose fees that appear disconnected from actual administrative costs. More importantly, it threatens to inflict substantial and lasting damage on American universities, scientific research, and technological competitiveness.
For these reasons, I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed rule.
Thank you for considering my comment.

Section IV.C explains that the revenue would be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and ICE would not retain it for OPT oversight or enforcement. They do not establish that every OPT placement benefits every worker, but they demonstrate why a simple job-displacement narrative is inadequate.

Third, existing STEM OPT regulations already address compensation and displacement. Under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C), duties, hours, and compensation must be commensurate with those of similarly situated U.S. workers. Employers must also attest that participating students will not replace U.S. workers. These requirements need effective verification and enforcement. - decertifying schools that misuse the program
- checking employer training plans (Form I-983)
- penalties for those who commit fraud

A flat fee on every recommendation falls equally on legitimate and fraudulent participants and cannot tell them apart. The NPRM does not explain why these narrower tools are not enough.

**3. The analysis contradicts itself.** The revenue estimate assumes OPT participation continues near current levels. Yet the rule aims to deter participation, and DHS admits schools may decline to pay at all. If participation collapses, the revenue estimate is wrong. If it doesn't, the deterrence rationale fails. - Charging F-1 students $70,000–$100,000 would put practical training out of reach for all but the wealthiest.
- Charging all students would raise tuition for U.S. students to pay an immigration fee.
- Charging employers would deter the startups, small businesses, hospitals, and research labs that rely on OPT graduates.

Many schools, especially smaller ones, will simply stop recommending OPT altogether.

I hope to continue contributing these specialized skills to U.S. research and industry. OPT provides an essential bridge between advanced academic training and practical work experience.

Under this proposal, universities would have to pay substantial fees before recommending students for OPT. Many institutions may be unable or unwilling to do so, regardless of a graduate's qualifications or the needs of potential employers. The rule could make access to practical training depend on institutional financial resources rather than merit, while discouraging scientific innovation and reducing access to specialized talent.

I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud and protect program integrity. However, these extraordinarily high fees are not a proportionate substitute for targeted oversight.

I oppose this rule. DHS says it wants to protect American workers from "cheaper and more pliable, visa-dependent" foreign labor. That phrase comes from a source DHS quotes in footnote 106. This comment shows that the fee design makes OPT workers more dependent on employers, not less, and so works against the labor goal DHS states.

1. DHS invites employers to finance the fee
The NPRM says schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." It also says the rule does "not propose the imposition of specific limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source the requisite funds," other than foreign gift reporting. The RIA assumes that where OPT is worth more than the fee, "affected parties could collectively cost share." So DHS expects employers to pay some fees and places no conditions on how they do it.

2. An employer who pays has a reason to lock the worker in
The fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and the NPRM says it "is not triggered by a change in employer." Once the EAD issues, the fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances." An employer that funds a $70,000 initial fee or a $30,000 STEM extension fee loses that money if the worker quits. The natural response is a repayment agreement, a training bond, or a promise to stay. Nothing in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i) bars these terms. A worker who owes $30,000 or $70,000 on leaving cannot bargain over pay or conditions, cannot report abuse safely, and cannot take a better offer. That is the "pliable" worker DHS says it wants to remove.

3. Students who pay are pushed toward any job
If the cost falls on the student, many will borrow. Post-completion OPT allows only limited unemployment before status is at risk (90 days, or 150 with a STEM extension, under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(E)). A graduate carrying a large fee-related debt and facing that clock will take the first offer at whatever wage. The fee raises the cost of saying no to a bad job.

4. DHS copied the H-1B price but not the H-1B worker protections
DHS says it set the $70,000 fee to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" and to "closely align with the H-1B fees" (citing Proclamation 10973). The H-1B program, though, also forbids an employer from making the worker reimburse the ACWIA training fee (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(9)), and Department of Labor rules bar penalties for leaving early and bar recovery of that fee from the worker (20 CFR 655.731(c)(10)). The NPRM adopts the price and leaves out the anti-recoupment rules that go with it. It never discusses the question.

5. The fee adds no wage floor
For initial OPT there is no wage or comparability requirement at all. For STEM OPT, the employer attests on Form I-983 to terms "commensurate" with similar U.S. workers, and the NPRM concedes DHS "does not generally verify the employer attestations unless and until there is a site visit." The rule changes neither. An employer that pays the fee can recover it through lower pay, which would add to the low-wage employment the RIA says the rule will reduce. The RIA never models fee recovery through wages or bonds.

6. The labor-protection claim is not supported
DHS's own footnote 103 quotes the CIS Ombudsman: OPT lacks "many of the customary protections that would have been legislated." Footnote 107 quotes testimony that OPT has "no protections for American workers or foreign workers." The fee adds none. It adds a large debt and a new reason for employers to control workers. An agency must consider an important aspect of the problem (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). DHS did not consider how a $70,000 charge shifts bargaining power between OPT workers and employers, or how that shift reaches the U.S. workers who compete with them.

7. Requested action
DHS should withdraw the rule. If DHS keeps any fee in a re-proposal, it should:
(a) bar any employer, school or third party from requiring a student to repay the fee, sign a training bond, or pay a penalty for leaving, modeled on 8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(9) and 20 CFR 655.731(c)(10);
(b) require the school to report in SEVIS who paid the fee and on what terms;
(c) provide a refund or credit when a worker leaves an employer because of a reported violation;
(d) analyze fee pass-through to wages, debt and job mobility in a revised RIA; and
(e) put enforcement where DHS's own evidence points: verification of employer attestations, with penalties on employers that underpay.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) / U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposed rule regarding new Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. While regulatory cost-recovery is a legitimate agency interest, imposing punitive, unprecedented fee structures on practical training fundamentally misunderstands the role of OPT as an integral educational component. If finalized, this policy will cause irreparable harm to the U.S. higher education ecosystem, undermine domestic scientific research, and diminish America's global technological edge.

1. Catastrophic Disruption to U.S. Higher Education and Institutional Solvency
International students contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support hundreds of thousands of domestic jobs. Full-tuition international enrollment directly subsidizes financial aid for domestic students, faculty compensation, and campus infrastructure. 

A primary driver for top global talent choosing American institutions over peer competitors (such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the EU) is the availability of post-graduation practical training. Imposing exorbitant fees on OPT—whether levied directly on students or on sponsoring academic institutions—serves as an effective tariff on American degrees. This will inevitably redirect prospective scholars to foreign competitor nations, devastating university operating budgets and disproportionately harming mid-tier and state universities that rely heavily on international graduate enrollment.

2. Severe Blow to the U.S. Scientific Research and STEM Talent Pipeline
OPT and the STEM OPT extension are not mere employment authorizations; they are vital extensions of academic pedagogy that feed the U.S. research and development (R&D) apparatus. 
- Critical Lab Operations: In fields such as artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, biotechnology, quantum computing, and clean energy, international graduate researchers, postdocs, and technical specialists conduct the heavy lifting on federally funded projects (supported by NSF, NIH, and DoD grants). 
- Institutional Attrition: Pricing these researchers out of experiential training creates an immediate personnel cliff for university laboratories. Pushing universities to absorb massive compliance fees will force institutions to cut research assistantships and shutter groundbreaking experimental projects.

3. Erosion of National Competitiveness and Induced "Brain Drain"
The proposed fees run counter to the United States' articulated national security and industrial policy objectives, such as the CHIPS and Science Act, which explicitly require expanding the high-skilled STEM workforce. Forcing early-career scientists and engineers to exit the U.S. ecosystem immediately upon degree completion guarantees an aggressive "brain drain." Competitor economies will readily welcome this U.S.-trained intellectual capital, allowing foreign industries to commercialize breakthroughs funded by American basic research.

Conclusion:
The proposed fee structure is economically counterproductive, arbitrary, and directly harmful to the U.S. educational and scientific enterprise. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve accessible, merit-driven practical training pathways that sustain American innovation.
The OPT program should be abolished.

Thank you for considering my comment.

As an international student, I believe it is deeply unfair to impose such enormous fees on the vast majority of students who follow the rules simply because a small minority may engage in fraud. The proposed fees appear excessive and unjustified, especially when more targeted enforcement measures could address the actual problems without punishing everyone. I am an international graduate student in a STEM field, currently on OPT, and I’m writing to oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. I ask DHS to withdraw the $70,000 initial fee and the $30,000 subsequent fee and to address fraud through targeted enforcement instead.

I understand why DHS wants to protect the program’s integrity and U.S. workers. People who abuse OPT should be investigated and penalized, and I have no objection to that. What I object to is charging a fee this large on behalf of every student and treating it as a substitute for enforcement.

My OPT position builds directly on what I studied in graduate school. It has been the part of my education where I found out how the methods I learned in class and in research actually hold up on real problems, and where I learned things no course could teach me. That is what practical training is supposed to do, and it is exactly what this rule would put out of reach for many students.

When I applied, I had to get my DSO’s recommendation, file with USCIS, pay the filing fee, submit supporting documents, complete biometrics, and wait for my EAD before I could start working. At each of those steps the government already verifies who I am, whether I’m in status, and whether my school stands behind me. If those checks need to be stronger, I’d support that. But whether my university can afford to spend $70,000 on me says nothing about whether I follow the rules. A compliant student at an underfunded school is no greater fraud risk than the same student at a wealthy one, yet under this rule their outcomes could be very different.

The fee is formally charged to schools, but DHS acknowledges that schools may pass it on to students or employers, or simply stop recommending OPT. In practice, access to OPT would come down to how much money a student’s school, employer, or family has. Small colleges, public universities under budget pressure, nonprofits, research labs, and startups would be hit hardest. DHS’s own analysis finds that 56 percent of affected institutions are small entities, that some may be unable to fund the fees at all, and that 60.5 percent of the small institutions it analyzed could face impacts above one percent of revenue (91 Fed. Reg. 64595–96). None of this separates legitimate training from fraud. It separates people by wealth.

The treatment of pre-completion OPT is especially troubling. Practical training during a degree is often where students first see how their coursework and research translate into real work. Yet a student who does pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000 in fees, and DHS itself expects pre-completion participation to drop. That pushes students and schools to plan training around avoiding a fee rather than around what makes sense for their education.

The costs also reach beyond students. We pay tuition, rent apartments, and spend money in our college towns; NAFSA estimates international students contributed about $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported roughly 355,000 jobs in 2024–2025. The chance to gain real work experience after graduation was part of why I chose to study in the U.S., and I know the same is true for many of my classmates. DHS acknowledges the fee could reduce F-1 enrollment and that it cannot precisely quantify the lost benefits (91 Fed. Reg. 64588–89). With projected collections of roughly $8.4 to $16.5 billion per year, this is not a cost-recovery fee. It is meant to change behavior, and those effects deserve much closer scrutiny than the proposal gives them.

DHS has better tools available: risk-based audits, site visits, closer review of employers with suspicious patterns, better data sharing among SEVIS, USCIS, schools, and employers, enforcement of the field-of-study requirement, and real penalties for those who actually violate the rules. The proposal notes that DHS considered some of these alternatives. If fraud is concentrated among certain actors, enforcement should be concentrated there too.

Finally, many students chose their programs years ago under the rules in place at the time, and a 60-day transition doesn’t reflect that, especially for PhD students. Protecting only those who already have a DSO recommendation or approved OPT before the effective date leaves out students who enrolled in good faith. If DHS moves forward, it should at minimum grandfather students who were enrolled before the proposal was published.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw these fees. If more oversight funding is truly needed, a much lower fee tied to actual costs, paired with targeted enforcement, would serve that goal without shutting out compliant students and smaller institutions.

I am an international student pursuing a master's degree in Computer Science at a U.S. university, with an expected graduation date in 2027. Like many international students, I have invested substantial time, effort, and financial resources in my education, with the reasonable expectation that I could apply for practical training under the existing regulatory framework.

**First, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier.** A $70,000 initial fee, followed by a potential $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extension, would make practical training financially inaccessible for many qualified graduates. Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, universities could pass these costs on to students or decline to recommend otherwise eligible students for OPT. **Second, the proposed fee amounts lack a sufficiently demonstrated connection to administrative costs.** The proposal does not adequately explain why charges of this magnitude are necessary to administer the OPT program. **Third, the proposal is poorly targeted toward its stated objective of preventing fraud.** Students who comply with immigration regulations and institutions that follow established procedures should not bear extraordinary financial burdens because of misconduct by a minority of participants. I ask the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. Section 214(a)(1) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes DHS to prescribe the time and conditions of a nonimmigrant’s admission. DHS reads that provision to authorize a $70,000 initial payment and a $30,000 subsequent payment by a separate party, the educational institution. The proposal does not explain why that is the best reading of the statute.
The question is who can be made to pay and under what authority
In Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), the court upheld DHS’s authority to permit practical training as part of the terms of F-1 admission. That decision supports DHS’s authority to prescribe substantive terms for training, including the role of a school recommendation. The power to recognize or require a school’s academic judgment does not by itself establish the power to charge the school for exercising that judgment. Nor does DHS’s authority to regulate SEVP-certified schools resolve which monetary exactions Congress authorized.
Congress has expressly prescribed immigration charges elsewhere in the INA. For example, 8 U.S.C. § 1184(c)(12) identifies liable parties and sets amounts for specified fraud prevention and detection fees. Congress separately provided for a charge supporting the foreign-student information collection program in 8 U.S.C. § 1372(e), with provisions governing the payer, calculation, and disposition of the proceeds. Those statutes illustrate the detail Congress used when it authorized payments in related settings. Section 1372(e) need not govern the proposed levy for that contrast to matter. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), a reviewing court independently determines the scope of the delegation.
DHS also has a reasoned decision-making problem
Even assuming DHS can impose some financial condition, the proposal does not adequately explain why a mandatory payment by the school before its recommendation is the appropriate instrument. DHS attributes potential fraud to students, employers, and schools, yet it attaches liability to every covered recommendation without distinguishing which party can detect or prevent the conduct. A school can assess whether training relates to the degree, but it may have limited ability to verify that an outside employer actually provides the promised supervision. DHS should explain why the recommending institution is the appropriate payer across those different circumstances and compare that choice with enforcing substantive duties on the actors who control the relevant conduct.
Finalizing this proposal would raise a statutory-authority objection under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C). Independently, failing to explain the choice of payer and its relationship to the stated problem would make the rule arbitrary and capricious under § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS proposes to collect $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation. The proposal justifies these amounts in substantial part by their deterrent effect and by reference to H-1B charges. It does not adequately identify what the school would receive for the payment or explain why these amounts are appropriate.
The purpose and design of the charge matter
DHS says the proceeds would go to Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. § 3302, and ICE could not retain them under the authority cited for the rule. Section 3302 governs the handling of money received by the government. It supplies no independent authority to impose the charge. Deposit in the Treasury is compatible with a valid fee, but here it is significant alongside DHS’s position that the charge would work even if Congress never appropriated the proceeds to support enforcement. The intended mechanism is the pressure the assessment places on participation.
In National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340–42 (1974), the Supreme Court distinguished charges for particular benefits from assessments imposed to advance broader public policies. That case interpreted the predecessor to 31 U.S.C. § 9701. Its reasoning is instructive by analogy here because DHS invokes general regulatory language to impose a large assessment that it expressly designs to deter conduct. DHS should identify the federal service or particular benefit conferred on the school, distinguish it from USCIS’s adjudication of the student’s separate employment authorization application, and explain how it values that benefit. If the assessment instead serves as a public-policy levy, DHS should identify the congressional delegation that authorizes it.
DHS needs to justify both prices

A comparison with H-1B charges does not establish the value of an OPT recommendation or the price needed to deter abuse. DHS should identify the data connecting each amount to the expected response of legitimate and fraudulent participants. It should also explain why the first recommendation warrants the higher amount when the fee can purchase access to training periods of very different lengths, and why two recommendations covering portions of the ordinary OPT period should produce a greater charge than one covering the entire period.
On this record, adopting the proposal would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) because the agency has not connected either price to the benefit or deterrent effect it invokes. The absence of an adequate statutory basis for a deterrent levy also raises a separate objection under § 706(2)(C). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

The transition fails to account for schools’ reliance on existing OPT rules

DHS should withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. The proposed transition generally turns on the date a designated school official recommends a student for OPT. That date may be administratively convenient, but it is a poor proxy for when schools, students, and employers made commitments in reliance on the existing framework.
Schools make commitments years before the recommendation
An institution can recruit an entering class, set tuition and aid, hire staff for career advising, and commit resources to employer partnerships well before any member of that class is eligible for a recommendation. A school may develop a multi-year degree program around a sequence of classroom instruction and training opportunities, even though a particular placement remains contingent on federal approval. An employer may budget for supervision and extend an offer before the recommendation date. The proposed cutoff can protect one recommendation while exposing a planned STEM extension for the same student to a $70,000 charge if the extension is the first recommendation subject to the fee.
DHS discusses reliance in § VI, states that the public interest outweighs it, and emphasizes prospective application. That answers when DHS would collect money. It leaves open what investments become difficult to recover and whether DHS could preserve them while addressing current risks. A student’s ability to depart the country or seek a different status does not address an institution’s staffing commitments, approved budgets, or agreements with training partners. Likewise, evidence of fraud in some placements does not establish how much enforcement benefit DHS would give up by adopting temporary protection for defined, existing cohorts.
DHS should evaluate alternatives tied to actual reliance
DHS should identify how many already-enrolled students and current OPT participants would be affected, using enrollment cohorts and SEVIS records where feasible. It should solicit information on existing institutional budgets, recruiting commitments, and training agreements, then compare the 60-day cutoff with at least three alternatives. Those include grandfathering students enrolled by a defined date through completion of their current program and associated OPT, protecting STEM extensions for students already on initial OPT, and delaying implementation until schools have completed a full budget and admissions cycle. DHS should estimate each alternative’s duration, scope, and effect on enforcement. Existing fraud and eligibility controls could continue to apply to protected cohorts.
DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1, 30–33 (2020), requires an agency changing policy to consider serious reliance interests and weigh them against competing concerns. A federal benefit can remain contingent while institutions reasonably rely on the existing process when making investments. Finalizing the proposal without grappling with those interests and plausible ways to accommodate them would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

DHS should reconsider the proposed fees and withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. The proposed regulatory text does not reliably tell a school which amount it must pay before recommending a student. This ambiguity concerns the central legal obligation and the data used to estimate the proposal’s effects.
The proposed paragraphs produce different answers on their face
Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(1) describes a one-time $70,000 payment for the first recommendation. Paragraph (i)(2) requires $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation if the student previously participated in OPT and paid the initial fee. Paragraph (i)(3) first appears to require $70,000 for any recommendation on or after the effective date, then provides for the subsequent $30,000 charge once the initial fee has been paid. The preamble suggests that DHS intends to collect $70,000 for the first recommendation subject to the rule and $30,000 for qualifying later recommendations. The text should implement that result explicitly, including which provision governs when the first recommendation preceded the effective date. It should also consistently identify the school as the payer rather than conditioning the later amount on wording that refers to payment by the student.
Three cases illustrate the practical problem. First, a student is already on initial OPT when the rule takes effect and then requests a STEM extension. Second, a student had a pre-effective-date recommendation, but the designated school official must issue a replacement recommendation after the cutoff. Third, a school previously paid $70,000, but a different school later recommends the student after a higher degree. The second case also requires DHS to distinguish a clerical correction from a new recommendation. In the third case, the later school needs an authoritative way to establish payment history before deciding whether to commit funds. The difference between fee tiers is $40,000 per recommendation.
The public needs an opportunity to evaluate the actual obligation
DHS should publish a decision table showing the fee and payer for each case, identify the precise triggering event, and specify how the school can verify the result before payment. It should reconcile the operative text with its participation, cost, and revenue estimates. If DHS pursues a revised rule, it should publish corrected text and updated estimates for comment under 5 U.S.C. § 553.
Finalizing the proposed text without resolving these issues would be arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS predicts that a large fee will discourage abuse and give schools a greater stake in screening recommendations. That prediction depends on who bears the fee and how legitimate and fraudulent participants respond. The proposal does not adequately test either link.
DHS should evaluate who leaves and who stays
A school or employer offering a genuine placement weighs the fee against the value of supervised training. That value can be substantial even when the placement brings in little revenue. An organized scheme could have different incentives. A broker might raise the price it charges students, pool financing, or concentrate its business in placements where it can recover the cost. The fee could make some schemes uneconomic. The record needs to explain which schemes would exit, which could adapt, and how those responses compare with the expected exit of legitimate programs.
For example, assume a program starts with 1,000 legitimate placements and 20 fraudulent ones. If a fee deters 500 legitimate placements and five fraudulent ones, the number of fraudulent placements falls, but their share rises from about 2 percent to about 3 percent. This illustration is not a forecast. It shows why total participation, fraud prevalence, and the number of violations prevented are different measures. DHS should assess all three and explain how their movement would affect investigative workload and the likelihood of identifying violations.
Pass-through also changes the screening incentive
The preamble predicts schools will screen more carefully because they bear a financial stake. The economic analysis also anticipates that schools may shift the charge to students or employers. A school that collects the full amount before it recommends a student still faces administrative and compliance risks, but it does not bear the same financial exposure as a school paying from its own budget. DHS should separately analyze school-funded, employer-funded, and student-funded recommendations and explain how each arrangement affects screening. It should compare the fee with controls directed at facts a broker cannot establish merely by producing payment, such as whether a worksite exists and whether it provides the training it claims to offer.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), finalizing the proposal would be arbitrary and capricious if DHS continues to assume that a smaller pool is a better-screened pool without examining these countervailing incentives. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees rule. DHS treats employer financing as a way schools might absorb the charge. The agency should also examine what happens when an employer agrees to fund a recommendation only if the student accepts conditions that make leaving or reporting abuse expensive.
Repayment terms could undermine the rule’s objectives
An employer that advances money might require a trainee to repay part or all of it upon resignation, through a contract, payroll deductions, or an arrangement with a staffing intermediary. For example, a trainee who discovers that promised supervision is absent might have to choose between continuing the placement and incurring a five-figure debt. Such a clause could also deter a worker from reporting inaccurate training records or wage violations. The proposal does not itself create a debt to an employer. The concern is the private arrangements that its financing model makes possible.
This issue directly concerns DHS’s stated goals. A rule intended to improve training integrity should consider whether workers will still report that their training is fictitious or has changed. A rule intended to protect U.S. workers should consider whether large repayment obligations could give employers extra bargaining power over OPT workers and affect working conditions for comparable employees. DHS’s STEM OPT rules already require commensurate terms and a non-displacement attestation. DHS should explain how it would assess those assurances where a worker’s effective compensation or ability to leave depends on a fee repayment agreement.
Congress addressed an analogous problem in the H-1B program by prohibiting early-cessation penalties and reimbursement of a specified statutory fee. See 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(2)(C)(vi). Those provisions apply to H-1B and offer a model for evaluating comparable risks in OPT. DHS should seek evidence on proposed financing terms and, if it pursues a replacement rule, evaluate prohibiting fee-related payroll deductions, repayment triggered by departure, and retaliation for reporting violations. It should address coverage of staffing intermediaries and explain how trainees could report violations confidentially.

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

The price difference can change how schools structure academic programs

DHS expects this to make schools more selective. It does not adequately explain how schools will allocate scarce funds or why those allocation decisions would identify the students whose training best meets federal requirements.
A school’s financial decision is separate from its assessment of eligibility
Under the current framework, a school already has a substantive role in recommending training. The proposal adds a separate decision over whether to commit institutional funds. Two students may present equally sound training plans, yet one department may have an employer partner willing to pay and another may have exhausted its discretionary funds. A campus might allocate a fixed number of recommendations at the start of the year, leaving a later graduating cohort without access despite equally strong qualifications. Those outcomes would follow from funding and timing even if school officials assess the quality of the training correctly.
The effect on access cannot be measured only by aggregate participation. DHS should assess which offices would control payment, how approvals would interact with federal filing deadlines, and what would happen when a finance office denies a request or makes a processing error. Because the payment comes before the recommendation, the student may lose the opportunity to have USCIS consider the application at all. Schools also may have recruited and advised current cohorts under existing practices. A short transition may leave them little time to develop consistent procedures or communicate material changes to students approaching graduation.
DHS should assess the allocation system it is creating
DHS should seek information on how schools would ration funds, including whether decisions would vary by department, graduating term, or availability of outside financing. It should compare that system with existing substantive eligibility and oversight tools. If it pursues a replacement proposal with an institutional payment, DHS should address published allocation criteria, timely written reasons for adverse decisions, and a means to correct payment or allocation errors before filing deadlines expire. It should distinguish an academic recommendation decision from a school’s decision about whether to finance it.
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), it would be arbitrary and capricious for DHS to rely on greater school selectivity as a program-integrity benefit while leaving the actual financial criteria, decision process, and consequences for eligible students unexplored. DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

In § IV.C, DHS suggests that existing disclosures of foreign gifts and contracts could help enforcement authorities identify foreign adversaries financing participation. DHS should show how the reporting system would reveal that link before crediting the proposed fee with this national-security benefit.
The existing disclosure system has a different unit of reporting
Section 117 of the Higher Education Act, 20 U.S.C. § 1011f, covers institutions that meet its statutory definition. Its gift and contract reporting trigger generally looks to $250,000 in transactions with a foreign source in a calendar year, and the statute also addresses foreign ownership or control. Many disclosures are reported in aggregate, with additional detail for specified restricted or conditional arrangements. A reported institutional gift can reveal a funding relationship. The report does not ordinarily establish that a particular dollar amount funded an OPT recommendation for a particular trainee.
For example, a $210,000 contribution would cover three initial fees. If it were the only qualifying transaction with that source in the calendar year and there were no foreign ownership or control, it would fall below the general gift and contract reporting trigger. At the other end, a reportable general-purpose gift could be fully disclosed while offering little evidence about whether it paid for any recommendation. DHS should distinguish institutional accounting records, reports to the Department of Education, and the payment records ICE would receive. The proposal should identify what information each system provides and what lawful data linkage would be needed to trace a payment.
DHS should test the mechanism against the baseline
Existing disclosure obligations operate without the new fees. DHS should explain what additional evidence the proposal would produce, how many affected institutions are subject to the statute, and which funding channels would remain difficult to trace. It should also examine the possibility that requiring large payments would encourage institutions to seek new external financing. Any benefit estimate should distinguish legitimate financing from risk indicators and compare the proposed fee with targeted financial inquiries or coordination under existing authorities where there is evidence of suspicious activity.
If DHS finalizes the proposal on the theory that existing disclosures will expose covert financing without demonstrating the link between the proposed payment and information the government can actually obtain, it would rely on a mechanism the record does not support.
