The Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a deeply flawed policy that functions as a de facto ban on experiential learning. While curbing immigration fraud is a legitimate government interest, these exorbitant fees will indiscriminately punish genuine international students, devastate U.S. university enrollment, and erode the United States' position as the premier global destination for higher education.

An Astronomically Unreasonable Price Tag
A $70,000 fee for a single year of practical training authorization is objectively unreasonable. For context, this figure exceeds the median annual income of a U.S. household and surpasses the total four-year tuition costs of many public universities. The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) explicitly states that these fees are designed as a "deterrent," but setting the cost at a punitive level untethered to actual administrative processing costs transforms the fee into a financial blockade. By forcing educational institutions to pay this upfront—which will inevitably be passed on to the students through specialized fees or tuition hikes—the rule ensures that only the ultra-wealthy, rather than the most academically talented, can afford to fully participate in the U.S. educational system.

Depriving Genuine Students of Crucial Educational Development
Practical training is not an ancillary loophole; it is a fundamental component of modern higher education. Genuine students rely on OPT to apply theoretical classroom knowledge to real-world environments, a requirement for mastery in fields ranging from engineering and medicine to business and the arts. By placing a $70,000 to $100,000 premium on this experience, the proposed rule deprives legitimate, law-abiding students of the hands-on training that makes U.S. degrees globally valuable. The rule unjustly punishes hundreds of thousands of legitimate students for the fraudulent actions of a localized minority of "visa mills" and shell companies. Punishing the entire student population with an insurmountable financial burden is a failure of regulatory precision, substituting targeted law enforcement and compliance audits with a blunt financial instrument.

A Devastating Impact on U.S. University Enrollment
The global market for international students is highly competitive. If the U.S. attaches a $70,000 penalty to post-graduate practical training, prospective students will simply take their talent, intellect, and tuition dollars to countries with welcoming, affordable post-study work policies, such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. This mass diversion of international students will trigger a severe enrollment crisis for U.S. universities.

International students contribute tens of billions of dollars to the U.S. economy annually, and their tuition often subsidizes academic programs, faculty salaries, and research facilities that directly benefit domestic American students. The NPRM's own Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis notes that 56% of regulated SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. A sudden, drastic collapse in international enrollment will force many of these small and mid-sized institutions into deep financial distress, leading to program cuts, layoffs, or closures.

Combating fraud requires precise school oversight, strict employer verification, and targeted investigations—not astronomical price tags that commodify access to education. Implementing a $70,000 OPT fee will not protect the integrity of the U.S. education system; it will hollow it out by driving away the world's brightest minds and plunging U.S. academic institutions into an entirely preventable financial crisis.

Tools that target fraud directly (training plans, employer attestations and site visits, as already used in STEM OPT) were set aside because a fee would be "immediate and effective." But a fee that funds no enforcement and cannot tell fraudulent employment from legitimate employment is "effective" only by suppressing participation across the board. That is not a "rational connection between the facts found and the choice made" (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 1983).

3. The worker-protection rationale does not support the amount. DHS cites the 7.65% employer FICA savings. For a graduate earning $80,000, that is about $6,100 a year; the $70,000 fee is more than eleven times that, and it applies equally to graduates who have been in the U.S. long enough to owe FICA. If FICA parity is the concern, the fix is legislation or a wage condition, not a flat charge.

4. Pre-completion OPT is priced irrationally. The initial fee applies "whether it is pre-completion or post-completion OPT." Both draw on the same 12-month entitlement, yet splitting it between a summer internship and post-graduation work would cost $100,000, or $130,000 with a STEM extension. DHS itself expects schools to shift away from pre-completion OPT, curtailing it through price rather than reasoned rulemaking. Pre-completion OPT should be exempt.

5. Reliance interests are dismissed, not weighed. Current students enrolled, paid tuition and borrowed money based on OPT as it has existed for decades. DHS concedes current students "are in a different position than prospective F-1 nonimmigrants," yet protects only those recommended before the effective date and simply declares that its concerns "outweigh any stakeholder's reliance interest." Conclusory statements do not suffice (Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 2016; DHS v. Regents, 2020). At minimum, DHS should exempt every student enrolled before the effective date.

6. DHS admits it does not know the rule's effects. Its annualized cost estimate ranges from $32 million to $8.2 billion, a more than 250-fold spread, and DHS "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation." It finds "a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities," with 841 small institutions facing impacts above 1 percent of revenue, yet rejects an exemption for small institutions. It also acknowledges that schools may pass the cost on to students generally, including Americans, through higher tuition.

7. The threat to end OPT is not a justification. DHS says that without the fees it "may shut down the program entirely." A rule must stand on its own reasoning; the possibility of a more drastic action does not make this one reasonable.

DHS should withdraw proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i). If it proceeds, it should (a) limit any fee to the documented cost of OPT oversight, (b) target employers with fraud indicators through site visits and attestations, (c) exempt pre-completion OPT, and (d) exempt all students enrolled before the effective date.

Subject: Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

As someone who understands the challenges international students face while pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal could create serious barriers to education, professional development, and economic opportunity.

1. Financial and Educational Impact

International students already make substantial financial investments in American education, including tuition, housing, health insurance, and living expenses. OPT provides an important opportunity to apply academic knowledge in professional environments. Introducing exceptionally high fees could discourage universities from supporting eligible students and potentially lead to additional institutional charges being passed on to students.

2. Negative Impact on American Universities

Universities, particularly smaller institutions, may struggle to absorb such substantial per-student fees. This could affect their ability to support international students and make American higher education less attractive to talented individuals worldwide.

3. Impact on American Businesses and Innovation

International graduates contribute to important sectors such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, healthcare, engineering, and scientific research. Startups and small businesses also benefit from access to qualified graduates. Making OPT participation financially difficult could reduce opportunities for employers to recruit skilled talent and weaken America’s competitive position in emerging technologies.

4. Disproportionate and Unjustified Financial Burden

Although these proposed fees are formally charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, their economic consequences could ultimately affect students and universities. DHS should provide clear evidence explaining how the proposed amounts were calculated and demonstrate why such substantial fees are necessary to achieve its enforcement objectives.

Fraud prevention and immigration compliance are legitimate government responsibilities. However, enforcement should target fraudulent institutions, employers, and employment arrangements rather than create excessive financial barriers for legitimate students.

5. Recommended Alternatives

I respectfully urge DHS to:

* Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure.
* Establish reasonable fees based on actual administrative and enforcement costs.
* Strengthen SEVIS monitoring and verification systems.
* Target fraudulent employers and institutions through evidence-based enforcement.
* Consider exemptions or reduced fees for financially disadvantaged institutions.
* Conduct a comprehensive economic impact assessment before implementing such a policy.

Conclusion

International students contribute to American universities, local economies, research, entrepreneurship, and technological innovation. OPT serves as an important bridge between education and professional experience.

The United States should continue attracting talented students and encouraging them to contribute their knowledge and skills to the American economy.

I support responsible immigration enforcement and the protection of American workers. However, these objectives should be achieved through proportionate, transparent, and evidence-based policies rather than exceptionally high fees that could undermine legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw or substantially revise this proposed fee structure.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I am qualified to comment because I have lived every stage of the pathway this rule would put out of reach. Over eight years in the United States, I studied as an F-1 undergraduate; worked full time at a U.S. firm on OPT, the STEM OPT extension, and then an H-1B; and have now returned on an F-1 visa for a graduate degree as I prepare to re-enter the U.S. job market.

My U.S. education opened the door to a career I loved, and OPT allowed me to walk through it. My employer selected me through the same competitive process as my American peers and invested in my growth. Over four years, I became a trusted contributor, co-authoring more than five research abstracts and three manuscripts with colleagues in health economics and outcomes research. Those collaborations also gave me lasting friendships and mentors who shaped who I am. None of this would have been possible without the work authorization that F-1 status provides.

Under the proposed rule, that same path would have required my school to pay $100,000 ($70,000 for my initial OPT and $30,000 for my STEM extension) before I could work a single day. Today, the only OPT-related cost is a filing fee of roughly $500. Because students typically request OPT before graduation, often before receiving a job offer, the $70,000 would be owed before a student knows whether, or where, they will work. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass this cost on to “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers.” For most international students, that would put OPT out of reach; for employers, it would make an international graduate far more expensive to hire than an equally qualified domestic candidate, regardless of merit.

This is not abstract for me. I am recruiting for internships and full-time roles right now. From my first job search in college, I know how long and uncertain the process already is for international students, and today’s market is tighter than the one I entered four years ago. A fee of this magnitude signals that they are not welcome to stay, and many will choose countries with post-study work pathways instead, taking with them tuition revenue that sustains programs and financial aid. And because the cost could be passed on to “all students,” American students could end up paying for this rule as well.

The consequences reach the broader economy and fields that serve the public. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-2025 academic year. In healthcare, my own field, international graduates contribute to research and innovation that improve patient care and public health.

I chose the United States eight years ago because it offered a world-class education and a real chance to put it to work. That choice paid off in both directions: I built a career, and my employer, colleagues, and community gained someone committed to contributing. This rule would close that door to the next student ready to do the same, and to students like me trying to walk through it again.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

An international graduate student

Re: Proposed Rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 FR 64566, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I am submitting this comment anonymously. I am a lawful permanent resident, yet I do not feel safe putting my name on it. I mention that because it matters to the record: many of the F-1 students this rule would affect have told me they’d like to comment but are afraid to do so. What DHS hears from them is probably much quieter than what they actually think.

Why this matters to me

I came to the United States in the late 1990s as an F-1 student. I picked a U.S. liberal arts education because it let me explore before committing to a path, which wasn’t an option where I grew up. OPT then let me spend three years working with children with special needs, in a field that couldn’t fill its jobs.

When I decided on graduate school, OPT was the deciding factor in choosing the U.S. I wanted a career in higher education administration, and I was counting on practical training to put my degree to work. A graduate degree without that wouldn’t have been worth the cost. CPT and OPT gave me the experience, and the professional network, that launched my career.

Today I am a designated school official at a large public university. I have spent two decades helping international students and scholars come here to study, do research, and contribute. That work depends on the same pathway that brought me here.

What our students are telling us

Our office recently surveyed our current F-1 students. About 600 responded, roughly 37 percent of those we reached. Around three-quarters are graduate students, and nearly three-quarters are in STEM fields.
77 percent said that if these fees had been in effect, they would not have chosen to study in the U.S.
98 percent said they would not be willing or able to pay.

This is a hypothetical, self-reported survey at one institution, so I offer it as one data point. But it comes from students who did choose the U.S. Those weighing several countries today may feel even more strongly. Many of the students who said the fees wouldn’t have changed their decision told us they would have looked at other countries first.

Below are select, lightly edited excerpts of their written feedback::

A doctoral student on a research stipend of about $25,000 a year put it plainly: “How can I possibly afford fees totaling $100,000?” Another wrote, “If I had $70,000, I would not have left my country.” A graduate student said, “Nobody who has access to the kind of money that is being asked for is in need of any kind of training.”

Others were thinking about the country’s loss. One PhD student in a highly specialized engineering field wrote that the fee “feels like getting taxed for having more skills than the rest.” Another said, “I would definitely go somewhere that appreciates my talent and hard work, because I will eventually contribute to the community and country where I live.” An undergraduate wrote, “With other developed nations having much better skilled working pathways I would never come here if this rule comes into play.”

Several also saw the effect on universities. One said the policy “limits the influx of international students,” which “reduces the vast amount of tuition that flows into schools.”

This isn’t just our campus

The national research points the same way. NAFSA’s comment letter summarizes much of it, so I’ll only touch on a few pieces:
Michael Clemens’s analysis (IZA Discussion Paper 18933) estimates that a $100,000 charge on OPT could cut OPT starts by roughly 80 percent in central scenarios where universities bear the cost.
The Institute for Progress projects large long-term GDP losses.
IIE’s Fall 2025 survey found that 92 percent of responding institutions expect many students would study elsewhere without OPT.
Hoover/Stanford research shows how heavily international graduates figure in U.S. STEM research and in founding leading AI firms.

These are projections, and projections carry uncertainty. But they all point in the same direction. The U.S. is competing for talent with countries offering clearer, more predictable paths after graduation, and fees this large would hand students to them.

What I’m asking

I respectfully ask the agency to:
Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees.
Reconsider the financial barriers these fees would create for international students.
Carry out a real assessment of the effects on international enrollment, U.S. universities, employers, and the country’s ability to attract talent.
Weigh the long-term economic, scientific, and societal contributions of international graduates, rather than treating OPT only as an immigration benefit.
Handle any legitimate administrative or program costs through reasonable, proportionate fees, not charges that shut out qualified students.

Respectfully,

An international education professional and former international student

Subject: Public Comment in Support of the Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Focus on Fraud and Domestic STEM Unemployment)
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit this formal comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The proposed framework—requiring a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions—is a critical, market-stabilizing measure needed to curb pervasive visa fraud, eliminate systemic displacement of domestic graduates, and protect American entry-level tech workers.
The critical need for this fee structure is demonstrated by the severe economic challenges facing American tech graduates alongside documented systemic issues within the program:
• Addressing High Unemployment Among Domestic STEM Graduates: While tech corporations frequently cite a lack of domestic talent, recent data reveals a stark contraction in entry-level hiring that has disproportionately harmed U.S. citizens. While the general national unemployment average is low, recent college graduates in computer science and computer engineering face an unemployment rate hovering around 7% to 8%. Flooding this already compressed labor market with hundreds of thousands of uncapped OPT guest-workers actively deprives qualified American graduates of the entry-level roles required to build their careers.
• Combatting Pervasive "Pay-to-Stay" and Shell Company Fraud: This proposed fee acts as a necessary firewall against the rampant fraud degrading the integrity of the F-1 visa system. In May 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and HSI exposed over 10,000 potential OPT fraud cases. Federal audits revealed extensive networks of fraudulent IT staffing agencies, vacant offices, residential "phantom addresses," and "pay-to-play" schemes where foreign nationals paid under-the-table fees to shell corporations simply to maintain visa status without performing legitimate work. By forcing a significant financial commitment up front, the proposed rule effectively dismantles the economic model underpinning these fraudulent networks.
• Preventing the Disenfranchisement of U.S. Citizens via Foreign Outsourcing: Recent DHS site visits confirmed that multiple alleged OPT employers were utilizing U.S. corporate addresses as a front while training and managing their OPT workers entirely via managers located overseas in places like India. This practice completely subverts the educational purpose of "practical training" within the domestic economy, effectively converting a student visa program into an unregulated offshore outsourcing pipeline that operates on American soil.
• Removing Arbitrary Cost Advantages and Corporate Incentives: Under current tax codes, employers are entirely exempt from paying the 7.65% FICA (Social Security and Medicare) payroll taxes on OPT workers. In fields like software engineering and computer science, this loophole makes hiring a foreign graduate thousands of dollars cheaper than hiring an American citizen graduate. The $70,000 and $30,000 fee structure properly offsets this financial distortion, neutralizing the systemic economic incentive for tech corporations to bypass domestic talent.
The OPT program has evolved far beyond a temporary training benefit into an institutionalized, cap-exempt labor system plagued by systemic exploitation. This proposed rule restores balance, encourages schools to stringently vet their corporate partnerships, and protects domestic grads during an incredibly difficult entry-level tech market.
Sincerely,

Subject: Public Comment in Support of the Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (Focus on Fraud, Healthcare, and STEM Workforce Impact)
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit this formal comment in strong support of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The proposed framework—requiring a $70,000 fee for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent extensions—is a critical, market-stabilizing measure needed to curb pervasive visa fraud, eliminate systemic displacement of domestic graduates, and protect American workers across highly specialized fields, including software engineering and healthcare.
While public attention frequently focuses on tech labor distortions, the current uncapped OPT framework has increasingly expanded into the medical and clinical sectors, introducing severe regulatory vulnerabilities and unfair competition that harm American medical graduates:
• Addressing Fraudulent Clinical Placement and "Ghost Residency" Schemes: The healthcare and medical research fields have seen a rise in regulatory exploitation mirroring the IT staffing fraud exposed by federal agencies. Unaccredited clinical research firms, fraudulent medical staffing agencies, and shell consulting companies have manipulated the OPT framework to orchestrate "pay-to-stay" schemes for foreign medical graduates (FMGs). In these arrangements, individuals pay under-the-table fees to shell corporations for fraudulent employment letters and falsified clinical hours to maintain immigration status. Requiring a significant upfront fee will effectively eliminate these illicit corporate actors by rendering fraudulent visa-brokering economically unviable.
• Protecting U.S. Medical Graduates from Structural Displacement: The traditional paths for foreign medical training in the U.S. (such as J-1 or H-1B clinical visas) are strictly regulated, requiring rigorous credential verification, ECMFG certification, and adherence to prevailing wage standards. In contrast, the expansion of OPT and STEM OPT in medical research, clinical laboratory, and healthcare administrative roles allows foreign graduates to bypass these standard vetting processes. This influx compresses employment opportunities for U.S. citizen medical students, pre-med graduates, and couples with a 7% to 8% unemployment rate facing recent domestic tech and STEM graduates who compete for essential clinical and technical research roles.
• Eliminating the Unfair Corporate Financial Incentive Over U.S. Doctors and Researchers: Under current tax codes, healthcare employers and private research facilities are entirely exempt from paying the 7.65% FICA (Social Security and Medicare) payroll taxes on OPT workers. This regulatory loophole provides medical groups, laboratories, and corporate healthcare chains an automatic financial incentive to hire foreign graduates over equally qualified U.S. citizen medical graduates. The proposed fee framework properly offsets this distortion, removing the financial benefit of bypassing domestic talent.
• Restoring Integrity to Medical Training Safeguards: Medicine requires the highest level of institutional oversight to protect patient safety and labor standards. Allowing a student visa program to operate as an unregulated, cap-exempt secondary guest-worker pipeline in medical and technical fields undermines the specialized visa pathways established by Congress.
The OPT program has evolved into an institutionalized labor system vulnerable to exploitation. This proposed rule restores structural balance, requires educational institutions to strictly vet their healthcare and technical partnerships, and ensures that the domestic workforce is not structurally disadvantaged.
Sincerely,

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposed rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The charge is a tax that Congress has not authorized. DHS projects $8.4 to $16.5 billion a year in collections, to be deposited in the general Treasury, not used for OPT oversight. DHS says it set the amount to “closely align with the H-1B fees,” not to recover any cost. A federal court has already held the $100,000 H-1B payment to be an unauthorized tax (State of California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 8, 2026), and the Supreme Court confirmed this year that the power to regulate does not include the power to tax (Learning Resources v. Trump, 2026). None of the statutes DHS cites authorizes a revenue charge on schools. DHS should explain which statute does, and why it did not use the cost-based fee authorities Congress provided (8 U.S.C. 1356(m), 1372(e); 31 U.S.C. 9701).

2. A flat charge does not prevent fraud. Every school pays the same amount for every student, whether compliant or not. The fraud DHS describes involves employers, yet a school must pay before a student may even have a job offer, so it cannot screen an employer that does not yet exist. No revenue funds investigators or site visits. DHS also contradicts itself: it says the charge is meant to “discourage” OPT use, but its revenue estimate assumes STEM OPT participation will not decline at all.

3. The rule ignores the reliance of students already enrolled. The fee applies to any recommendation made after the effective date, so students who enrolled under current rules would be fully subject to it. I am an international graduate student in computer science at a U.S. public university, expected to graduate in 2027, so any OPT recommendation for me would fall after this rule’s effective date. I chose to study here with the understanding that practical training was part of the educational path the regulations offer, and I have planned my coursework, finances and future around that understanding. Practical training is where what I learn in the classroom is tested against real problems, and I have already seen how much it adds to an education that coursework alone cannot provide. Nothing about my eligibility or my conduct would change under this rule; what would change is whether my university decides that I am worth $70,000. I do not believe that is a fair or rational way to decide who may complete their education. DHS calls these expectations “speculative.” They are not.

4. Better alternatives exist, and 30 days is not enough. DHS could extend STEM OPT safeguards (E-Verify, training plans, site visits) to all OPT, target the employers its own investigations flagged, or set a cost-based fee to fund oversight. It rejected these in conclusory terms. A 30-day comment period for an economically significant rule that was not on DHS’s regulatory agenda falls short of the 60 days Executive Order 13563 calls for. DHS should withdraw the rule, or at minimum reopen comment for 60 days and publish the data behind its fraud claims.

As a United States citizen, I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to establish a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT recommendation.

This rule is a necessary step to protect American workers, reduce fraud, and restore integrity to a program that has grown far beyond its original purpose.
Documented Fraud Requires Strong Action
In May 2026, ICE reported identifying more than 10,000 F-1 students linked to highly suspect employers—many involving phantom worksites, empty buildings, residential addresses listed as job sites, “pay-to-stay” schemes, and offshore management of purported U.S. training. These findings came from a review of only the top 25 OPT employers and were described by ICE officials as “only the tip of the iceberg.”
Earlier investigations have uncovered similar patterns, including shell companies and large-scale visa fraud operations involving thousands of students. The Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman has previously warned that the OPT program is especially vulnerable to fraud because compliance resources have not kept pace with its rapid expansion.
A substantial fee paid by the recommending school will create a real financial incentive for Designated School Officials to verify the legitimacy of proposed training before recommending students. Without such a cost, the current system continues to enable abuse.

OPT Has Become a Large-Scale Labor Pipeline

According to ICE’s 2024 SEVP data, nearly 195,000 foreign students held OPT work authorization and over 95,000 held STEM OPT authorization in a single year. The total number of foreign students with practical training authorization has grown into the hundreds of thousands. What began as a limited educational benefit has become a significant source of temporary foreign labor, particularly in STEM and IT fields, often competing directly with recent American graduates for entry-level positions.
When employers can access this labor at relatively low cost—or through third-party arrangements—the result is reduced opportunities and downward pressure on wages for U.S. citizens and permanent residents. The proposed fees help restore balance by ensuring that the privilege of multi-year work authorization carries a meaningful cost that reflects its impact on the domestic labor market.

The Fee Structure Is Sound

Charging the fee to the SEVP-certified school at the recommendation stage is administratively efficient and places responsibility on the institution best positioned to assess the legitimacy of the training. Depositing the fees into the U.S. Treasury is appropriate for a measure designed to protect program integrity and American workers.

The proposed effective date and grandfathering provisions provide a reasonable transition while preventing a rush of last-minute recommendations intended to circumvent the new requirements.
Conclusion

As a U.S. citizen, I believe American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been repeatedly exploited through fraud and that functions as a low-cost alternative to properly regulated employment visas. The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are a proportionate and necessary response.

I urge DHS to finalize this rule promptly and without reducing the fee amounts or weakening the requirement that payment precede any SEVIS recommendation for OPT.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment applies the Information Quality Act (section 515 of Pub. L. 106-554) and OMB's information quality guidelines (67 FR 8452, Feb. 22, 2002) to the evidence DHS disseminates in the NPRM. This one asks a prior question: can the public verify the evidence at all?

1. This is influential information
OMB's guidelines set a higher bar for "influential" information, meaning information with a clear and substantial impact on important public policy. That bar includes transparency about data and methods, so that qualified outsiders could reproduce the results. The NPRM projects 10-year transfers of $109.4 billion (primary, 3 percent). DHS says that without the fees it "may shut down the program entirely." The evidence behind that choice is influential by any reading.

2. The central fraud finding rests on a video
The headline finding is that an investigation "identified more than 10,000 F-1 nonimmigrant students" working for "highly suspect employers." Its only source is an ICE YouTube video of May 12, 2026 (footnote 67). Every listed key finding is cited to that video by timestamp (footnotes 68 to 74). The docket has no report, dataset or method behind it. DHS does not say how "highly suspect" was defined, what period was covered, how many cases were confirmed, or how many employers were cleared. Footnote 56 describes the same video as showing "10,000 highly suspected employers." A reader cannot tell whether the figure counts students or employers.

3. DHS relies on a news count of data ICE withheld
The figure of nearly 4,000 students at potential shell companies comes from a 2021 NBC Bay Area story (footnotes 64 and 65). That story's own title, as DHS cites it, says "ICE Keeping New Data Private." DHS holds SEVIS employer records. It could report how many OPT participants worked for employers later found noncompliant. It cites a reporter's estimate instead.

4. Labor-market figures are second-hand
The unemployment rates for computer science graduates, the growth in foreign STEM workers, and the foreign share of computer occupations all cite Presidential Proclamation 10973 (footnotes 91 to 93). Footnote 94, for the claim that STEM OPT "far surpassed" DHS's 2016 estimate, is also "Id." to that proclamation. The NPRM does not name the surveys, years or definitions behind these numbers. A proclamation restating figures is not a data source that outsiders can test.

5. Key inputs cannot be reproduced from the docket
Table 2, which drives every cost scenario, appears only as an image. Footnote 128 sources it to an ICE file titled "Total Number of Annual OPT, STEM OPT and CPT Authorizations." The NPRM does not say whether or how CPT was removed. The 56 percent STEM share is "Based on 2021-2024 data," but footnote 129 applies 56.11 percent to a 2022-2024 average, and neither calculation is shown. The small-entity tables use revenue from schools' I-17 filings in SEVIS, which the public cannot see. The NPRM does not say whether any of these inputs or models were peer reviewed, as OMB's Peer Review Bulletin (70 FR 2664, Jan. 14, 2005) contemplates for influential scientific information.

6. Undisclosed data also fails the APA
An agency must disclose the critical data it relies on so the public can respond. Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus, 486 F.2d 375 (D.C. Cir. 1973). In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court preliminarily postponed the companion Duration of Status rule. It found DHS likely acted arbitrarily, noting that on fraud the government "relies to a large extent on anecdotes." This NPRM repeats the pattern with less: some of its anecdotes are timestamps in a video.

7. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it re-proposes, it should first place in the docket:
(a) the HSI investigation's report or data, with its definition of "highly suspect," time period, counts of students and employers, and counts of confirmed violations, referrals and outcomes;
(b) the SEVIS extracts and code behind Table 2, the 56 percent STEM share and the small-entity tables, in machine-readable form;
(c) the primary sources for every labor-market figure now cited to the proclamation; and
(d) a statement of any peer review performed.
It should then reopen comment for at least 60 days. A $109.4 billion rule should rest on evidence the public can read.

Re: Comment on Proposed Rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026); DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01

I'm a data analyst working in the United States on an H-1B visa. I first came here as an international student and finished a master's degree here before starting work. I'm writing to ask the Department to withdraw the proposed $70,000 fee for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for later ones, or, at the very least, to do the analysis the law requires before finalizing anything. OPT is the bridge between a U.S. degree and a first job in your field of study. This proposal would price that bridge out of reach for most students and most schools, based on a fraud problem the proposal never measures and a fee amount it never justifies.

1. The fee has nothing to do with what OPT costs to run.
A fee should have some connection to the cost or the problem it's supposed to address. This one doesn't. The proposal says the initial fee was "designed to closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees." 91 FR at 64576.

2. The fraud case is asserted, not measured, and a flat price can't tell fraud from legitimate use.
I'm not saying OPT fraud doesn't exist. The proposal cites real enforcement actions, including Operation OPTical Illusion and Homeland Security Investigations' finding of 10,000 highly suspected employers. 91 FR at 64573-64576.

3. The proposal's own numbers show concentrated harm that it mostly leaves unmeasured.
The Department "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation due to these new requirements." 91 FR at 64583. In the low participation scenario, DHS assumes institutions will pay the initial fee only for students eligible for the 24-month STEM OPT extension, 88,374 students, against a 2024 baseline of 194,554 OPT authorizations, which means non-STEM OPT effectively disappears.

4. "The school pays" doesn't settle who actually pays, and the fee punishes the internships the program exists to provide.
The Department presents the fee as a charge on institutions, but its own text concedes the cost lands elsewhere: "schools may mitigate their budgetary impact by passing the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." 91 FR at 64578. A school that passes a $70,000 charge to a graduating student hasn't made the student more employable. It has made the student $70,000 more expensive to hire, with the cost landing on the party least able to bear it and least responsible for any fraud.

5. The reliance analysis is a conclusion, and the transition is too short for the students already here.
The Department's reliance discussion concludes that "the national interest in protecting American workers and program integrity far outweigh[s] any reliance interests of foreign students, employers ... or educational institutions," and that the F-1 visa "was never intended to provide a pathway to employment in the United States." 91 FR at 64578. That is a policy preference stated as a finding, not the assessment of the nature and extent of reliance that Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California requires. Students currently enrolled chose schools, programs, and financing under a framework in which OPT has existed since 1947 and the STEM extension since 2016; a majority of international students are in STEM fields, and 294,253 were on OPT in 2024-25.

6. The combined burden on the same students is never analyzed, and the alternatives were never genuinely modeled.
The same F-1 student faces, all at once: this fee; the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period (91 FR 57807); the $103,265 H-1B fee NPRM (91 FR 54817); the Department of Labor wage rulemaking; the duration-of-status final rule (91 FR 44976, currently postponed); and the August 2026 CPT broadcast messages restricting internships. The OPT proposal identifies no overlapping rule and performs no cumulative analysis. Each action on its own narrows the path from a U.S. degree to lawful U.S. employment; together, they close it for many students.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposal. If it does not, I ask at minimum for: (a) a published fraud-rate estimate and a cost basis for the $70,000 and $30,000 amounts; (b) a supplemental quantitative regulatory impact analysis with distributional effects by stakeholder, institution size, and field of study; (c) analysis of a genuine less-burdensome alternative; (d) grandfather and transition provisions for students already enrolled; and (e) a cumulative-impact analysis, each published for public comment before any final rule.

I support DHS’s proposal to establish substantial fees for Optional Practical Training, including the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee. OPT should provide genuine training directly related to a student’s field of study, not an inexpensive substitute for employment-based immigration or a mechanism for fraudulent employment arrangements.

Sections IV.A–C describe serious oversight concerns, including fictitious employment, nonfunctional worksites, and employer networks that obscure where students actually work. These findings justify stronger accountability. They do not establish that every participant is noncompliant, but they demonstrate why recommendations should require more than routine paperwork and unverified assurances.

I support placing the payment obligation on SEVP-certified schools before they recommend OPT, as proposed in Section V.A. Schools are responsible for evaluating eligibility and maintaining student records. A substantial financial obligation can encourage institutions to examine the educational value and legitimacy of recommendations more carefully rather than treating participation as an automatic benefit.

Protecting U.S. workers should remain an explicit objective. Legitimate practical training should not become a vehicle for replacing workers or avoiding the safeguards associated with employment-based visa programs. DHS should evaluate the fees alongside enforcement of existing training and worker-protection requirements; payment must never be treated as proof of compliance.

To strengthen the final rule, DHS should explain the evidentiary basis for the specific fee amounts and why they are preferable to lower fees or alternative safeguards. The agency should also address its acknowledged risk that schools will pass costs to students, employers, or the broader student body. Financial capacity alone is not a reliable measure of educational merit or lawful conduct.

DHS should also explore a legally authorized connection between SEVIS and IRS wage-reporting systems to help verify claimed paid employment and detect fabricated paystubs used to maintain student status. Where employment is represented as paid, supporting evidence should extend beyond an employer-generated paystub to independently verifiable wage reports and, where applicable, tax withholding and remittance records. DHS should coordinate with IRS and, where appropriate, the Social Security Administration to assess what matching is legally permitted and technically reliable, subject to tax-return confidentiality requirements and any necessary legislative authorization. Such checks should distinguish employee wages from other lawful arrangements and account for reporting schedules, corrected filings, applicable tax exemptions, and lawful unpaid training where permitted. A missing or delayed match, or the absence of tax due, should trigger an opportunity to provide documentation and correct errors—not an automatic finding of fraud or loss of status. Any system should minimize data sharing, restrict access, retain audit logs, and provide meaningful review before adverse action. Fees should complement this evidence-based verification, not substitute for it.
Finally, DHS should publish aggregate results on fraud findings, compliance, participation, and labor-market effects after implementation. Because Section IV.C states that receipts go to Treasury rather than directly to ICE, the agency should distinguish anticipated deterrence from any separately funded enforcement expansion.

I urge DHS to finalize a legally supported, evidence-based OPT fee framework that strengthens institutional responsibility, discourages abuse, and protects U.S. workers while preserving legitimate educational training.
Thank you,

In Docket ICEB-2026-0100, proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3) applies the fee to DSO recommendations dated on or after a date 60 days after publication of the final rule, and Section VI says institutions will not be required to pay it for OPT already approved or recommended before that date. That prospective design should be preserved in the final rule, and item 3 seeks a related adjustment for STEM extensions that follow pre-rule OPT.

1. Authority for the charge (Sections III.A, IV.C). Section IV.C describes the fee provisions as promulgated pursuant to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, says ICE would not retain the money because "the statute does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected," and says the fees go to the Treasury under 31 U.S.C. 3302. National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336, 340-42 (1974), describes heavy assessments meant to discourage an activity as in the nature of taxes traditionally levied by Congress, and Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212 (1989), reads that decision and its companion to require a clear congressional indication before an agency recovers administrative costs not inuring directly to regulated parties' benefit by imposing financial burdens on them. Both bear on review under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(C). Fix: Explain in Section III.A how the "time and conditions" text of INA 214(a), on which it relies, authorizes a mandatory payment of $70,000 or $30,000 to the Treasury.

2. Basis for the amounts (Sections IV.C, VII.A.6). Section IV.C compares the initial fee to the H-1B fee ("selected a fee amount for OPT comparable to the fee for H-1B visas") and the fees generally to "the educational costs" students incur for one or two years of study. Section VII.A.6 states the expected effect as a belief that the rule "would likely result in more scrutiny" of OPT recommendations. Fix: Docket the analysis that derives each amount and links it to an expected reduction in fraudulent OPT recommendations.

3. Transition fee for STEM extensions (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3); Sections V.A, VII.B.4). Section V.A classes a STEM OPT extension as subsequent OPT, and paragraph (i)(2) sets the $30,000 fee where the student "has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." Paragraph (i)(3) says schools "must pay the fee of $70,000 for each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT" dated on or after the effective date, and Section VII.B.4 states: "If an OPT fee has not previously been paid for an F-1 nonimmigrant, they are subject to the initial fee of $70,000." A STEM extension recommended after that date for a student whose initial OPT preceded it therefore draws $70,000, the same fee as a first recommendation. Fix: Add to paragraph (i)(3) a sentence providing that a recommendation for a STEM OPT extension for such a student is subject to the $30,000 fee.

4. Small-entity alternatives (Sections VII.B.4, VII.B.6). Of 1,389 small institutions, DHS reports that in the transition year 841 would experience impacts above 1 percent of estimated revenue and 116 above 20 percent. The alternatives discussed are no action, a full small-institution exemption (rejected because, with 56 percent of regulated institutions small, fraud could continue), a repeated initial fee, and expanded site visits or reporting. 5 U.S.C. 603(c)(1) names differing compliance requirements or timetables for small entities. Fix: Add to the final regulatory flexibility analysis a quantified alternative capping a small institution's annual OPT fees at 5 percent of its estimated annual revenue, with the effect on projected collections.

5. Refunds (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2); Section V.A). Both paragraphs say SEVP "may exercise discretion to grant a refund request from a school on a case-by-case basis." The school pays before the student may apply to USCIS, and Section IV.C says the refund provisions let schools "seek a refund if the student does not receive" an employment authorization document. A school meeting that condition still depends on discretion. Fix: In both paragraphs, replace "may exercise discretion to grant" with a statement that SEVP will grant the request, and delete the case-by-case qualifier.

6. Comment period (DATES; Sections VI, VII.A). OMB designated the proposed rule economically significant, and Section VI refers to a 30-day public comment period. The notice sets 60 days, to December 7, 2026, for information collection comments, and E.O. 12866 section 6(a)(1) provides that a comment period should in most cases be not less than 60 days. Fix: Publish a notice extending the comment period on the whole proposed rule to December 7, 2026.

A $70,000 fee for a school to recommend a student for Optional Practical Training — and $30,000 more for each later recommendation, including a STEM extension — is not a fee. It is a price that ends the program for nearly everyone it was built for. Schools cannot absorb a charge of this size across hundreds of students, and DHS itself acknowledges the cost will be passed on: to the F-1 student, to all students, or to employers. A student who has just finished a degree cannot pay $70,000 for permission to work, and most employers will not pay it for an entry-level hire either. The practical result is that OPT becomes available only to the wealthy — or to no one.

That defeats the purpose of OPT. It is the bridge between a U.S. education and skilled work in the United States: the year or three in which a graduate applies what they studied, and an employer evaluates them before sponsoring an H-1B. Under this rule, no company will be willing to sponsor international talent at all — the cost of the pipeline becomes so high that employers will simply stop hiring international graduates, no matter how talented they are. That is the opposite of a merit-based system: it selects on ability to pay, not on skill or contribution. A graduate's future here would depend on whether someone can afford a $70,000 fee, not on what they can do. The result is that engineers, data scientists, and researchers educated at American universities go to Canada, the United Kingdom, and every other country competing for them, along with the tuition, research, and tax revenue they bring.

The STEM extension fee is the sharpest contradiction in the proposal. STEM graduates are the workers the United States says it most needs, and this rule would charge $30,000 extra precisely for keeping them here longer.

DHS's own estimate puts the fees at $12.4 billion a year. That is not cost recovery; it is a wall. I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep OPT accessible to the students and employers it serves.

I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. DHS suggests schools can pass the cost along, but that suggestion assumes a payer exists. I want to ask a practical question the proposal never answers: who actually writes the check, and through what channel?

Start with the student. A university bursar's office charges fees tied to enrollment — tuition, housing, lab fees. There is no billing code for a federal immigration charge triggered by a SEVIS entry, and no mechanism to put a $70,000 levy on a student's account at the moment a Designated School Official clicks "recommend." Nor could the student pay it if there were: international students are barred from federal student loans, private lenders generally require a U.S. co-signer and do not lend against a fee assessed to a third party, and the charge falls due before the student has a job, an offer, or a paycheck. Asking a graduating student to produce $70,000 on the spot for a document that does not yet exist is not cost-sharing. It is a demand with no payer behind it.

The employer is no better. A company hiring through ordinary campus recruiting has no contract with the graduate's university, no purchase order, and no vendor relationship to invoice against. A school would have to send a $70,000 bill to a stranger and hope it gets paid — and when the employer declines, as any procurement department would, the recruiter simply hires the candidate who carries no surcharge. Universities are not debt collectors, and employers are not parties to a SEVIS recommendation.

That leaves the school itself, and here the mechanics fail too. Public universities set tuition and mandatory fees through boards and regents, typically a year in advance; a mid-year levy of millions cannot simply be invented. The international office that runs OPT is a cost center, not a revenue center — it has no income stream from which to pay $70,000 per student, and no grant or appropriation covers it. And the fee is due before the employment authorization document even exists, non-refundable once it issues, so the school pays first and learns later whether the authorization survives.

A fee with no payer is not a fee. It is a shutdown wearing a price tag. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. The $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees exceed DHS's authority, do not address the fraud DHS describes, and rest on an incomplete analysis.

1. IT IS A TAX, NOT A FEE (Sections III.A, IV.C)
DHS admits the money would go to the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt and that ICE cannot keep it. Under 31 U.S.C. 9701 and National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), a fee must reflect the cost of a service; a charge set to raise revenue and deter activity is a tax, which only Congress can impose. DHS chose $70,000 to match H-1B costs, not any cost of processing OPT. WashTech v. DHS (D.C. Cir. 2022) upheld OPT itself, not revenue charges attached to it, and after Loper Bright (2024) DHS's reading of its authority gets no deference.

2. IT DOES NOT FUND OVERSIGHT (Section IV.A)
DHS's central finding is that compliance resources have not kept pace with OPT. Yet the rule adds no investigators, site visits, or SEVIS improvements. A remedy that adds nothing to the stated problem is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

3. IT TARGETS THE WRONG PARTY (Sections IV.A, V.A)
Every fraud example DHS cites involves employers: shell companies, fake worksites, phantom employees. But the fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and for initial OPT schools must pay before the student even has a job, so they cannot screen employers at all. DHS links about 10,000 students to suspect employers, under 3 percent of roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The other 97 percent bear the cost.

4. BETTER ALTERNATIVES WERE REJECTED FOR CONVENIENCE (Section IV.C)
DHS rejected site visits and training-plan requirements mainly because a fee costs DHS less. Mandatory E-Verify and verified worksite data for OPT employers, risk-based site visits, or a cost-based fee retained by SEVP would target fraud directly.

5. THE ANALYSIS IS FLAWED (Section VII)
DHS estimates up to $8.2 billion a year in costs and $12.8 billion in transfers but quantifies no benefit at all. It finds 116 small institutions would lose over 20 percent of revenue, yet offers no relief. Its UMRA section says both that the rule does not exceed the $100 million threshold and that it does.

6. THE STRUCTURE IS ARBITRARY (Section VII.A.5.d)
Fees apply per recommendation, so the same 12 months of OPT costs $100,000 if split for a summer internship and $70,000 if not. DHS's own low scenario assumes non-STEM students lose OPT entirely, with no finding that those fields are more fraud-prone.

7. RELIANCE INTERESTS ARE IGNORED (Section VI)
DHS v. Regents (2020) requires serious weighing of reliance. DHS concedes current students are differently situated (fn. 124) yet calls their interests "speculative." Students who enrolled, paid tuition, and relocated families under existing rules should be exempt.

8. THE COMMENT PERIOD IS TOO SHORT
An economically significant rule with up to $69.9 billion in ten-year costs received 30 days; E.O. 12866 calls for at least 60.

I respectfully submit this comment opposing the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

My concerns focus on three fundamental deficiencies in the proposed rule.

1. The Proposed Fees Raise Serious Questions About Statutory Authority and Regulatory Purpose

DHS principally relies on its general authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act, including INA Section 214(a), to establish conditions governing nonimmigrant admissions.

However, authority to regulate immigration status does not necessarily establish unlimited authority to impose extraordinary financial obligations on educational institutions.

The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 charges are not calculated primarily by reference to the administrative cost of processing OPT applications or providing immigration services. Instead, DHS expressly intends these charges to discourage participation.

Moreover, DHS acknowledges that the resulting revenue would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury rather than retained by ICE for fraud detection or program oversight.

These features raise substantial questions regarding the legal and regulatory character of the charges.

I request that DHS identify the specific statutory language authorizing fees of this magnitude, explain whether these charges function as regulatory fees or economic deterrents, and establish the limiting principle governing their amount.

DHS should also explain why an OPT fee benchmarked against costs associated with the H-1B program is appropriate when OPT and H-1B operate under distinct statutory and regulatory frameworks.

2. DHS Has Not Adequately Demonstrated That Financial Exclusion Prevents Fraud

The proposal assumes that imposing substantial financial costs will discourage fraudulent participation and incentivize educational institutions to exercise greater scrutiny.

However, the ability to pay $70,000 does not establish whether a student, institution, or employer complies with immigration requirements.

A legitimate research institution with limited financial resources may be unable to finance the proposed fees, while a well-funded noncompliant participant may remain capable of paying them.

The proposed fee therefore risks distinguishing participants according to financial capacity rather than compliance.

DHS should provide empirical evidence demonstrating that the proposed fee amounts would reduce fraud, including the expected relationship between payment capacity, misconduct, and program participation.

The Department should separately estimate how many legitimate OPT opportunities would be eliminated for each anticipated reduction in fraudulent participation.

Without such analysis, it is difficult to determine whether the proposal addresses misconduct or merely reduces participation in an otherwise lawful educational training program.

3. DHS Has Not Adequately Justified Rejecting More Targeted Alternatives

The proposal acknowledges alternatives such as employer site visits, training plans, expanded reporting, and enhanced verification, but largely rejects them because they may require additional governmental resources.

Administrative convenience alone does not establish that a substantially more restrictive measure is preferable.

Reasonably available alternatives include risk-based audits, enhanced employer verification, targeted enforcement against repeat violators, improved information-sharing, and expanded safeguards modeled on existing STEM OPT requirements.

These approaches could potentially address misconduct directly without conditioning legitimate educational training on exceptionally large payments.

I request that DHS conduct and disclose a meaningful comparative assessment of these alternatives, including their expected costs, effectiveness, and consequences for lawful participants.

DHS should also explain why a uniform $70,000 fee is necessary rather than a lower amount, a graduated fee, or a risk-based compliance framework.

Conclusion

The proposed rule raises serious concerns about the scope of DHS's statutory authority, the evidentiary basis for its deterrence rationale, and the adequacy of its consideration of less burdensome alternatives.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. At a minimum, DHS should disclose the evidence supporting its fee amounts, meaningfully evaluate alternative measures, and provide a reasoned explanation addressing these concerns before adopting any final rule.

Safeguarding immigration integrity is essential, but regulatory measures should distinguish actual misconduct from lawful participation rather than treating financial exclusion as a substitute for effective oversight.

I respectfully oppose DHS's proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees. I support effective fraud prevention, but the proposal does not adequately justify its economic assumptions, treatment of reliance interests, or implementation burdens. I request that DHS address the following issues in any final rule.

1. Economic Analysis and Opportunity Costs

DHS estimates annual fee collections of $8.4–$16.5 billion across its modeled scenarios. For foregone OPT participation, it uses unpaid fees as a proxy for opportunity costs while acknowledging that actual costs may be higher or lower. Yet a government-imposed price is not a demonstrated measure of the economic value of lost practical training.

DHS should explain why this proxy reasonably represents lost educational and economic benefits, rather than merely reflecting the fee DHS has chosen. The analysis should distinguish transfers to the Treasury from real resource costs and foregone benefits, and test sensitivity to different assumptions about students' willingness and ability to pay, institutional budget restrictions, and employer cost-sharing.

Reduced OPT access may also affect international enrollment, tuition-supported academic programs, research continuity, employer partnerships, and opportunities available to U.S. students and workers. I request scenario analyses of these indirect effects, with assumptions and uncertainties disclosed rather than treated as negligible.

2. Institutional Burdens and Reliance Interests

DHS estimates 30 minutes of DSO review and 30 minutes of administrator processing per recommendation, but six-figure or near-six-figure commitments across multiple students may require budget approvals, legal review, financing decisions, system changes, accounting controls, and refund administration. DHS acknowledges that certain transaction and refund costs cannot be quantified.

The agency's own small-entity analysis estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small entities (about 61%) would face transition-year impacts exceeding 1% of annual revenue; 116 (8.4%) would exceed 20%. DHS should explain how affected institutions could finance payments, especially where public funding or donor restrictions limit allowable expenditures, and whether its administrative-cost assumptions capture the approval process in practice.

DHS also should meaningfully address reliance interests. Students already enrolled, universities maintaining degree programs and research collaborations, and employers coordinating training opportunities may have made long-term commitments in reliance on existing OPT rules. Prospective application to later OPT recommendations does not eliminate these effects. What alternatives, grandfathering provisions, or transition periods did DHS consider, and why were they rejected? Why would 60 days after publication of a final rule be sufficient for institutions to adapt?

3. Unclear Fee Triggers, Unequal Effects, and Public Participation

The NPRM contemplates separate charges for pre-completion and post-completion OPT and further charges for STEM OPT. It also raises questions about additional OPT at higher degree levels and across institutions. DHS should specify, with worked examples, when each $70,000 or $30,000 fee is due, whether a second institution must pay another initial fee, how prior participation is tracked, and when refunds are available. Absent clarity, similarly eligible students may face different barriers based on institutional resources and academic pathways rather than program compliance.

I also request analysis of less disruptive approaches to institutional oversight, including risk-based audits and targeted verification. A 30-day comment period is especially restrictive for institutions needing to gather budget data and consult students, researchers, and employers. DHS should extend the comment period and provide a renewed opportunity to comment if material provisions change.

Conclusion

DHS should withdraw the proposed rule or, at minimum, provide a more rigorous economic analysis, assess reliance interests and less burdensome alternatives, clarify the fee triggers and refund procedures, and allow meaningful public participation. Program integrity should be advanced through evidence-based oversight, not inadequately evaluated barriers to lawful practical training.

I'd ask DHS to apply the fee only to students who begin a program after the final rule takes effect, or at least to exempt students who were already enrolled when the proposal was published on October 8, 2026.

DHS also says schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers," and that this would discourage misuse. I don't think a fee can really tell which students are misusing OPT, though. A student with a real job offer and a student gaming the system would owe the same $70,000, so it basically comes down to who can afford it. I really doubt most small schools could cover that for each of their students, so in practice it would fall on the student or the employer. A lot of international graduates are hired by small and mid-sized businesses, not large tech companies. Under this rule a small business would have to come up with $70,000 before a graduate's first day, while a large company with a big immigration budget could probably just pay it. I think that ends up deciding which employers get to hire international graduates at all, and smaller businesses would mostly lose out.

The size of the fee is the other thing I wanted to point out. Filing the I-765 costs a few hundred dollars today, and DHS's own analysis estimates these fees would bring in $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion a year. Students in STEM fields can also apply for the 24-month STEM extension, which adds the $30,000 fee and makes the real cost $100,000 for us (DHS uses that same total in its analysis). DHS says the rule would lead schools to recommend "only the most promising students," but at that price I think schools would end up recommending the students whose families or employers can pay, and I don't think that's the same group.

DHS says it considered exempting small institutions and decided against it because 56 percent of SEVP-certified schools are small entities. I read that the other way. If most certified schools are small, then most schools are the ones least able to pay. If the fraud DHS describes is coming from specific schools or employers, I think the tools DHS already has, like SEVP recertification reviews and employer site visits, would get at those directly, without charging every student at every school the same amount.

Practical training is a big part of why a lot of us chose to study in the US. I'd ask DHS to withdraw the fee. If it does go forward, I'd at least ask that students who are already enrolled be exempt, and that the STEM extension not carry a second fee on top of the first. Thank you so much for reading this.

I am a graduate student worker studying neurodegeneration in the Department of Neuroscience at Yale University. I have worked in both academic and industry-based research, and I am submitting this comment on the basis of that experience. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, which would charge $70,000 for an F-1 student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that.

Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are diseases of aging, and they are difficult to model. No single model fully reproduces human disease, so researchers often combine several models and approaches to build a reliable picture. Mouse models are central to this work, but the pathology we study develops slowly. Mice must be bred, often across multiple genetic crosses, and then aged for many months before the disease features we want to study appear. Only then can behavioral testing, tissue analysis, and molecular experiments begin, and those need to be repeated and validated. A single well-controlled study can take well over a year from the first breeding to usable data. Because the experiments themselves are slow, training in this field takes longer. A PhD student, like me, studying neurodegeneration often reaches the point of collecting key data late in their program, and the work that follows (replication, analysis, writing, and publication) frequently extends beyond graduation. OPT is what allows an international trainee to stay and complete that work as a postdoctoral researcher. Without it, projects that took years to set up would be left unfinished, aged animal cohorts would be wasted, and the training invested in the scientist who ran them would be lost. 

A fee of this size would break the link between training and employment. Few employers, whether a university lab or a small biotech startup, can justify a five-figure surcharge to hire a single early-career scientist, and no trainee can pay it out of pocket. Having worked in both academic and industry settings, I have seen how a discovery travels from the bench to the clinic. Findings typically begin in university labs and are then developed by biotech and pharmaceutical teams. The people who carry that work across are often early-career scientists who trained in one setting and were hired into the other. OPT is a major part of that handoff for international researchers. If these researchers never begin U.S. training or leave once they finish, the expertise and the public investment in their education leave with them.

Neurodegenerative diseases affect millions of American families, and the work to treat them is slow and cumulative. Narrowing the pool of people allowed to do that work will slow it further. It would also weaken the biotechnology sector and the jobs it creates, and it would encourage the strongest applicants to choose other countries that actively recruit international scientists, eroding U.S. leadership in biomedical research.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees [1, p. 64566] and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. It would weaken the U.S. economy, punish honest students for the fraud of a few, and hand the world's best young talent to America's competitors.
 
1. It harms the U.S. economy (Section VII.A). International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,000 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year [2]. Most of that money comes from abroad [3], and DHS itself acknowledges that schools could lose enrollment if students are deterred by the fees [1, p. 64588]. DHS's own primary estimate is $4.1 billion in costs every year, about $35 billion over ten years, yet DHS lists the rule's monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" [1, Tables 1 and 10]. A rule with tens of billions in costs and no quantified benefit should not be finalized.
 
2. It punishes honest students instead of fraudsters (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The fee is the same for every student and is not tied to any employer or fraud indicator [1, p. 64577]. DHS cites more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers [1, p. 64571]; that is a small fraction of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT authorizations in 2024 alone [1, Table 2]. Fraud should be fought by targeting fraudulent employers and schools through site visits, E-Verify, and employer vetting. And because the fees go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP, not one dollar would fund fraud investigations [1, p. 64576].
 
3. It selects by wealth, not talent (Sections IV.C and VI). DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to students [1, p. 64575]. A STEM student could face $100,000 [1, p. 64583], or $130,000 with pre-completion OPT [1, p. 64577]. A brilliant young engineer from a modest family would be priced out, while a wealthier but less qualified student would not. That is the opposite of choosing "the most promising students" [1, p. 64574]. Small schools would be hit hardest: DHS estimates 98 small institutions would face costs above 20% of annual revenue [1, Table 15].
 
4. It gives our talent to competitors, including China. Other countries are competing hard for exactly the students this rule pushes away. In October 2025 China launched its K visa, which lets young foreign STEM graduates come and work without an employer sponsor [4]. If the United States charges $70,000 for one year of practical training, why would a top student not choose China or another competitor instead? Those graduates would then build their companies there. Today, 24% of U.S. billion-dollar startups have a founder who first came here as an international student [5]. If America wants to lead in AI, semiconductors, aerospace, and biotech, it must compete for this talent, not tax it.
 
5. It breaks faith with current students (Section VI). Many students already enrolled, including those in multi-year PhD programs, chose the United States expecting OPT to be available. Calling that expectation "speculative" [1, p. 64579] ignores real decisions about years of study and money already invested here.
 
 
American universities train these students with American resources. OPT lets that investment pay off here, through skilled work, research, and new companies, instead of sending it to our competitors. I urge DHS to withdraw this rule and fight fraud through targeted enforcement against the actual bad actors.
 
Respectfully

I oppose the proposed rule imposing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation. The proposal is poorly targeted. If DHS has identified fraud involving employers, staffing firms, or improper training arrangements, enforcement efforts should focus on those actors. Instead, the rule imposes substantial costs on all participating institutions regardless of their compliance history. As a result, schools and students who follow the law would bear the costs of misconduct committed by others. 

The proposed fees would likely discourage participation in OPT and reduce international student enrollment. This would have economic consequences far beyond higher education. International students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy during the 2024-25 academic year and supported more than 355,000 American jobs. NAFSA reports that roughly one U.S. job is supported for every three international students. 

International students support local economies through spending on housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and other services. Recent enrollment declines have already been associated with an estimated $1.1 billion reduction in economic activity and nearly 23,000 fewer jobs nationwide. The proposed rule risks worsening these losses by making the United States a less attractive destination for international students.  

The rule would also undermine research, innovation, and workforce development. More than half of international students pursue STEM-related fields, and many contribute to research laboratories, graduate programs, and high-skill industries. Research has found that international researchers account for more than 30 percent of U.S. patents and approximately one-third of U.S. Nobel Prize recipients. Restricting access to OPT threatens an important pathway through which the United States attracts and retains highly skilled talent.  

DHS has not demonstrated that these unprecedented fees will meaningfully reduce fraud. More targeted alternatives exist, including enhanced oversight of high-risk employers, increased penalties for proven misconduct, risk-based audits, and improved verification of training arrangements. Such measures would directly address abuse without imposing broad costs on compliant institutions and law-abiding students. 

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule or substantially revise it to focus on enforcement against employers and entities engaged in misconduct rather than imposing sweeping financial burdens on educational institutions and students.

Imposing steep fees directly onto universities or employers forces smaller institutions out of the recruiting pipeline, depriving local U.S. economies of key talent.

Catastrophic Financial Impact on U.S. Higher Education Institutions Requiring SEVP-certified institutions to shoulder or process $70,000 and $30,000 payments will force many smaller colleges and universities to abandon participating in practical training recommendations altogether. This threatens institutional budgets, compromises international academic partnerships, and reduces overall funding for campus facilities that benefit American students.
10. Arbitrary Policy That Undermines Economic Growth and Innovation Studies consistently show that international graduates participating in OPT contribute significantly to U.S. GDP, spur local consumer spending, fund payroll taxes, and fuel domestic patent creation and entrepreneurship. Shutting down or crippling OPT through prohibitive fees stifles domestic innovation and harms American workers by shrinking the overall economic footprint generated by top global talent.
