The Consumer Technology Association appreciates the opportunity to submit the attached comment on Optional Practical Training Fees.

OPT is an important opportunity for international students to gain practical experience, apply what we have learned, and contribute to the U.S. workforce. We have invested so much financially and personally in our education, and we should not face additional barriers when trying to begin our careers. I urge policymakers to reconsider these changes and take into account the financial realities and contributions of international students.

I write as the founder of OPT Global, an international career coaching consultancy — and I should start by saying plainly that this rule would be good for my business. If OPT disappeared, students would need my help more, not less, and I would probably make a lot of money. I am opposing the rule anyway, because the value of OPT to the United States, to our competitiveness, and to the students we invited here is worth far more than what my company would gain. I also work at a large research university, but these comments are my own, not my employer's.

DHS says this rule targets fraud and protects American workers. Take that at face value, then do the math: the current I-765 filing fee for OPT is $470. This proposal sets it at $70,000. Is fraud really 150 times more expensive to prevent than to commit?

And be clear about who pays: the university does. This is a fee on the school for recommending a student for practical training — $70,000 per initial recommendation, $100,000 for a student who uses post-completion OPT and then a STEM extension. It is not a fee on a student, and it is not a fee on fraud. It is a fee on the institution that educated the student and is asked to vouch for them.

American universities are the engine of scientific progress, and that has been America's leading strength. This rule taxes that engine directly. A university facing $70,000 per recommendation will recommend fewer students, ration access, or cut elsewhere to absorb the cost. In every version, the university does less of what made it valuable, and the student loses the training that was part of why they came.

That is how American competitiveness falls behind. In 2024, 165,524 foreign students participated in STEM OPT, according to ICE's 2024 SEVIS by the Numbers report. Those are the engineers, researchers, and technologists American employers hire because the domestic pipeline does not yet produce enough of them. Every recommendation a university cannot afford is one fewer STEM graduate working here — and the countries competing with us for the same talent will take the ones we turn away.

DHS also expects schools to "steer students toward post-completion OPT only" under the fee structure. The agency's own proposal predicts it will distort student decision-making away from pre-completion OPT, which exists because early work experience helps students land. When your rule needs a disclaimer about the behavior it will cause, that is the rule telling you what it costs.

There is a promise at stake, too. We brought these students to this country, and in doing so we entered into a social contract with them: an American education came with practical training attached. That was the value of our education to the world — not just the degree, but the chance to do the work. A $70,000 price on the university's recommendation breaks that promise after students have already invested years and tuition. The world notices when America's word on its own education does not hold.

Here is what $70,000 buys the American economy under this rule: nothing. The fees go to the general Treasury, not to the SEVP system that administers OPT. American workers, whose protection is the stated goal, gain no jobs from a rule that makes universities poorer and hiring new graduates more expensive.

If fraud is the problem, price the enforcement at the fraud. At $70,000, this isn't enforcement. It's a velvet rope — hung across the university door.

Withdraw the proposal.

Respectfully submitted,
Richard Spicer
Founder & CEO, OPT Global

Legal Critique: Statutory Overreach and Unconstitutional Taxation
The proposed fee faces substantial vulnerability in federal court under administrative and constitutional law.
Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Under the APA, agency actions cannot be "arbitrary and capricious." DHS has not demonstrated how a $70,000 charge—more than 130 times the existing $520 USCIS filing fee—is rationally connected to the actual administrative cost of adjudicating an application or investigating fraud.
Unlawful "Tax" vs. Permissible "User Fee." Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA) and established Supreme Court precedent, executive agencies may charge user fees only to recover the cost of providing a specific benefit or service. Because the proposed revenue is routed directly to the general U.S. Treasury for unspecified purposes rather than earmarked for SEVP or USCIS processing, legal scholars and groups like NAFSA argue the charge functions as an unconstitutional revenue-raising tax, a power reserved exclusively for Congress.
De Facto Repeal of a Statutory Program. By setting a financial barrier that few universities or students can afford, DHS is effectively terminating the OPT program through executive fiat rather than through congressional legislation or transparent rulemaking.
Economic Critique: Self-Inflicted Harm to U.S. Innovation and Higher Education
Rather than protecting the domestic economy, the proposal risks triggering severe financial contraction across U.S. universities and key industries.
Collapse of International Enrollment. International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and frequently pay full out-of-state tuition, which subsidizes financial aid and research programs for domestic students. According to the American Immigration Council, the fee could trigger a 35% drop in international graduate applicants, resulting in billions in lost university revenue and potential tuition hikes for American students.
Loss of Global STEM Competitiveness. OPT—and particularly the two-year STEM OPT extension—serves as the primary talent pipeline for U.S. research labs, healthcare systems, and technology startups. Pricing graduates out of post-completion training pushes U.S.-educated scientists and engineers directly into competing economies like Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.
Disproportionate Impact on Small Businesses and Nonprofits. While mega-cap corporations might occasionally absorb exorbitant sponsorship costs for select hires, public universities, rural hospitals, non-profit research institutes, and early-stage startups cannot pay $70,000 to $100,000 per graduate, consolidating talent exclusively among the wealthiest corporate employers.
Humanitarian and Equity Critique: Socioeconomic Exclusion and Precarity
From a human impact perspective, the rule undermines educational equity and destabilizes the lives of compliant students.
Wealth-Based Gatekeeping. Practical training is designed to be an experiential extension of a student's academic curriculum, evaluated on merit and academic alignment. Attaching a $70,000 price tag transforms educational opportunity into an auction, ensuring that only students from ultra-wealthy backgrounds—or those backed by affluent institutions—can access hands-on training in their fields.
Punishing Compliant Students for Institutional Oversight Gaps. DHS justifies the fee as a mechanism to force universities to police fraud. However, shifting a massive financial penalty onto the recommendation process punishes hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students who have already invested life savings and years of hard work into accredited U.S. degrees under existing rules.
Sudden Disruption of Life Plans. F-1 students make multi-year financial and personal commitments to study in the United States with the legitimate expectation of gaining practical experience before returning home or pursuing further sponsorship. Abruptly erecting an insurmountable financial wall mid-degree leaves students stranded with heavy educational debt and no viable pathway to apply their training.
Having supervised students on OPT, I can attest to the value this program generates for employers and students alike.
Thank you for your consideration.

I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT. These fees are excessive, financially prohibitive, and counterproductive to the interests of American universities, employers, and the U.S. economy.

1. Unreasonable Financial Burden on International Students

A $70,000 fee for initial OPT is an extraordinary financial burden for international students, many of whom have already invested substantial personal and family resources in pursuing higher education in the United States. Most students do not have the financial means to pay such an amount, particularly when transitioning from student status to their first professional employment.

This proposal would effectively make OPT accessible only to individuals with significant financial resources rather than those with strong educational qualifications and professional merit. It would disproportionately disadvantage students from lower- and middle-income backgrounds and undermine the accessibility and fairness of American higher education.

2. Harm to American Universities, Research, and Employers

International students are essential contributors to the U.S. academic and research community. They participate in scientific discoveries, laboratory research, technological advancement, and innovation. Many graduate students spend years conducting research at American universities, contributing to research projects and advancing knowledge in critical fields.

Preventing these graduates from participating in OPT would disrupt the transition from academic research to professional employment. American universities, research institutions, and companies would lose access to a substantial pool of highly educated and trained talent. This would ultimately weaken the country’s research capacity and economic competitiveness.

3. Disproportionate and Ineffective Fraud Prevention

Preventing immigration fraud and protecting the integrity of the immigration system are legitimate government objectives. However, imposing fees of $70,000 and $30,000 on students is neither a reasonable nor a targeted solution.

An individual’s financial resources have no meaningful relationship to whether they comply with OPT requirements. High fees do not establish the legitimacy of employment or prevent fraudulent reporting. If fraud prevention is the objective, the government should strengthen employer verification, conduct targeted compliance audits, improve oversight of participating institutions, and enforce existing regulations against fraudulent employment arrangements. These measures would address potential abuse without indiscriminately penalizing legitimate students.

4. Undermining America’s Global Competitiveness

International students choose the United States because of its world-class universities, research opportunities, and professional development prospects. The opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation is an important consideration when deciding where to pursue higher education.

A $70,000 OPT fee would send a message that international graduates are no longer welcome to contribute their expertise unless they can afford an extraordinary financial payment. Other countries actively compete to attract international graduates and skilled professionals. This proposal risks driving talented scientists, engineers, researchers, and entrepreneurs elsewhere, resulting in lost innovation, research capacity, and economic opportunities for the United States.

5. Unfair Treatment of Law-Abiding Students

International students have made significant commitments to their education in the United States. They have complied with visa requirements, maintained their legal status, paid substantial tuition, and contributed to their universities and communities. They should not be collectively subjected to financially prohibitive fees based on generalized concerns about potential fraud. Immigration enforcement should target actual violations rather than penalize students who have consistently followed the rules.

Conclusion and Request

I urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and reject the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee.

If the government identifies weaknesses in the OPT program, it should pursue evidence-based, narrowly tailored enforcement measures that target fraudulent actors rather than impose financially prohibitive fees on all international students.

This proposal would undermine those goals.

I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment addresses a question DHS asked the public about: how the fees work when a student earns degrees at more than one educational level, often at more than one school. Under the rule, the fee depends on the student's OPT history, not on the school making the recommendation. That breaks the rule's own logic.

1. One student, two schools, two different prices
OPT "can be authorized for up to 12 months at each educational level." Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) charges $70,000 "the first time" a student is recommended for OPT. Paragraph (i)(2) charges $30,000 for any later recommendation. Nothing ties either charge to the school. So the first school to recommend OPT pays $70,000. Any later school pays $30,000 for its own, separate recommendation. A college that recommends OPT after a bachelor's degree pays the full amount. The university that later recommends the same student after a master's degree pays less than half, though it makes its own decision about a new degree, job and OPT period.

2. The stake DHS wants schools to hold does not follow the decision
DHS says the fee gives schools "a direct stake in the integrity of the OPT program" and makes them "more selective and deliberate." If that is the theory, each school's stake should match its own decision. Under this rule, a graduate school's stake shrinks by $40,000 because a different institution paid years earlier. The first school's payment buys nothing for its own oversight of the later OPT, which it does not recommend or monitor.

3. The price runs opposite to DHS's vetting rationale
DHS sets the initial fee higher because students "may not have been vetted by the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa." A student finishing a second degree has usually been in the United States longer, and further from that visa vetting, than a first-time OPT applicant. Under this rule that student is cheaper to recommend. A master's student who came straight from a bachelor's program abroad costs the school $70,000. A master's student who already used OPT in the United States costs $30,000. The fee schedule tracks payment history, not the vetting gap DHS names. Footnote 115 points to extension-of-stay vetting under the Duration of Status rule, which was postponed in Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026).

4. It distorts admissions and pushes the largest charge to the first school
A graduate program weighing two equal applicants can see that one costs $40,000 less to recommend for OPT. The rule also gives each school a reason to let a later school pay the $70,000. The first school in the chain is often a smaller college, and sometimes a community college recommending OPT after an associate degree. Those schools have the least money and the shortest relationship with the student, yet they would carry the largest charge.

5. DHS did not model any of this
The regulatory impact analysis "applies the initial fee of $70,000 to the OPT participation data and applies the subsequent fee of $30,000 to the STEM OPT participation data." It never counts students who use OPT at more than one educational level, never says which schools would pay which fee, and never estimates the admissions or recommendation shifts described above. DHS cannot judge the alternative it asks about without that count.

6. The alternative DHS floated would make it worse
DHS asks for comment on charging $70,000 again at each new educational level. That would remove the cross-school discount, but only by charging $140,000 or more to students who earn two degrees here and $30,000 more for any STEM extension. It would hit hardest the students who invest most in U.S. education. DHS offers no evidence that second-degree students commit more fraud. DHS should reject this alternative.

7. The text leaves cross-school questions open
Paragraph (i)(2) applies if "the alien has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee." The alien does not pay; a school does. The rule does not say how a second school confirms another school's payment, or what happens if the first school later received a refund. DHS states the rule meets E.O. 12988's standard of "a clear legal standard for affected conduct." On this point it does not.

8. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. If it re-proposes any fee, it should (a) reject the repeat $70,000 alternative; (b) stop making one school's charge depend on another school's past payment; (c) publish SEVIS counts of students with OPT at more than one educational level and at more than one school; and (d) explain how any fee schedule fits its stated vetting and school-accountability goals for these students.

In response to Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis. As a PhD student in the humanities at an Ivy League institution, with many colleagues in the arts, I believe that this legislation, contrary to section IV.B would not 'ensure that only highly qualified eligible F-1 students participate in OPT and the labor market is not oversaturated with low-paid foreign workers' so much as render OPT prohibitively expensive and result in an exodus of highly skilled practitioners in the arts and humanities from the United States.

Sec. IV.A provides a scattered portrayal of the existence of fraud on a small scale relative to the number of students engaged in OPT. DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Regardless of these inconsistencies, 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

(Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers, rather than penalising students and institutions who wish to apply highly specialised knowledge gained from US institutions within the United States.

I am a graduate student in speech-language pathology (SLP), a healthcare field that diagnoses and treats disorders related to language, communication, voice, and swallowing. I am opposed to ICEB-2026-0100 because of the negative effects it will have on my profession and on healthcare as a whole. 

Many of my fellow graduate students hold F-1 visas and hope to practice SLP in the US after graduation, which they can only do if they complete a year of fellowship training (i.e., an OPT). This proposed financial barrier will keep my classmates from contributing the demonstrated skill and expertise that only they can bring to this field, at a time when demand for healthcare workers is increasing faster than we can keep up with as a country. 

In order to practice as an SLP, one must complete a clinical fellowship year, which qualifies as an OPT for international students holding an F-1 visa. In this sense, it is not an "optional" training period as Section D1 of the proposal describes; yet, these positions fall into this wide category (1). Our field needs more practitioners than are graduating into the field each year, and international students help meet this growing demand. In addition to their labor, international students' diverse perspectives and backgrounds help the field grow, and ensure culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all people who need it. This proposal will reduce the number of qualified professionals across healthcare disciplines in what is a growing shortage of healthcare professionals nationwide. 

US healthcare is facing dire staffing shortages across disciplines (2), and SLP is no exception (3). Because of the US's aging population and the over-twofold increase in childhood language delays since the COVID-19 pandemic (4), the demand for SLPs is skyrocketing, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics predicting that SLP as a field will grow by over 15% over the 2024–2034 decade (5). Meanwhile, SLP graduate programs are already failing to keep up with current demands, with 55% of surveyed SLPs reporting that job openings exceeded applicants in their area in 2025 (3). More people need more SLPs than are graduating into the workforce each year, and that is only going to worsen as the population continues to age and children continue to experience COVID-related language consequences. We need international students to help fill these gaps.

International healthcare workers have bolstered the healthcare workforce in the midst of growing professional shortages, and are historically more willing to take on lower-paying jobs in underserved areas when compared to their US-born counterparts (6). International SLP students take on a special commitment to practicing in the US, as an SLP certificate is not valid in other countries. 

In a field as demographically homogeneous as SLP, international students are key to ensuring culturally and linguistically appropriate care for all Americans. 80% of SLPs identify as white, and over 90% are women (7). A 2021 report found that less than 10% of SLPs are bilingual (8), while nearly a fifth of all Americans are bilingual (9). People who speak languages other than English and come from other racial and ethnic backgrounds need care that is culturally and linguistically appropriate, and it will only become harder for them to find it if fewer international students enter the workforce in the coming years. A diverse SLP workforce is key to the growth and health of the field, and including international students will help us meet these demands.

International students in healthcare fields train to fill the growing gaps in our healthcare system, and are a vital piece of ensuring that Americans receive the care they need. The passage of ICEB-2026-0100 would keep the American healthcare system from accepting help that it badly needs, and throw a wrench in the lives of people working to provide it.

On behalf of the Van Andel Research Institute (VARI), we write in opposition to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS)'s proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. While we share DHS's interest in preserving the integrity of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, this rule would impose severe burdens on small, independent research institutes like ours and place the cost of OPT misuse on institutions and students who follow the rules, rather than on those who violate them. We urge DHS to withdraw the rule.

The proposed fees would either divert funding from research or end OPT access for our students. VARI is a nonprofit biomedical research institute in Grand Rapids, Michigan with a doctoral program. Our PhD students pay no tuition and receive a fixed stipend. Over one third of our PhD students hold F-1 status, and we expect one to five OPT recommendations per year over the next five years. If each graduate uses the STEM extension, fees for 15 new graduates between 2027 and 2031 ($1,050,000) and 11 extensions ($330,000) would total over $1.3 million in five years. With no tuition revenue, this cost would come from research funds; students living on stipends cannot bear it. DHS's small-institution analysis measures revenue by tuition, room, and board, overlooking tuition-free doctoral programs like ours. DHS acknowledges some small institutions "may be unable to secure such funding." For students at compliant, tuition-free programs, the fee would not ensure "that legitimate participants continue to benefit from its opportunities"; it would end their access.

We also oppose a second initial fee for students who completed OPT at a prior institution. DHS asks for comment on charging a new $70,000 initial fee when a student begins OPT at a higher degree level. Some of our F-1 students completed OPT at another U.S. school; under this rule, VARI would owe $70,000 for a student whose initial fee was already paid, though neither school violated any OPT requirement. One student's practical training should not trigger more than one initial fee.

Additionally, a flat fee does not target fraud; it penalizes compliant institutions. Before recommending OPT, we meet with each student to verify continuity between their degree, training, and planned employment. For STEM OPT, we review each training plan to confirm it is genuine, and that the employer will provide appropriate training. Under the proposed rule, an institution that meets every OPT requirement would pay the same fee as one that knowingly misuses the program. This is unfair and does little to deter bad actors who can pay. A fairer alternative is to increase penalties, with due process, on schools and employers found to have knowingly violated OPT requirements, including substantial monetary penalties and loss of OPT eligibility in confirmed fraud cases.

To our knowledge, no accredited college or university, academic medical center, or nonprofit research institute has failed to comply with OPT requirements. DHS's evidence of noncompliance includes "highly suspect employers," staged worksites, and shell companies selling job letters. The school-related cases DHS cites are F-1 visa fraud prosecutions, largely involving for-profit and language schools, not cases of OPT noncompliance. Targeted enforcement may be more burdensome to administer than uniform fees, but it is far fairer to compliant institutions.

Finally, the fees would interrupt research at VARI, which employs 12 researchers on OPT or STEM OPT who trained at other U.S. universities. Their work spans cancer, including pediatric cancer; Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and other neurodegenerative diseases; structural biology; metabolism; and epigenetics. If these scientists' former schools declined to pay, these projects could face major delays or elimination. Research continuity at VARI should not depend on the budget decisions of other institutions.

Recommendations. Alongside increased penalties for noncompliance, we urge DHS to:
1. Adopt risk-based enforcement that directs audits and penalties toward schools and employers with documented noncompliance, treating nonprofit research institutions, tuition-free doctoral programs, and low-volume schools with strong compliance records as low-risk.
2. Apply new penalties or requirements only to conduct occurring after the effective date and allow at least one academic year before they take effect for schools and employers to update their procedures.
3. Strengthen STEM OPT oversight through existing tools, such as Form I-983 review and employer site visits, and penalize employers that fail to provide certified training.
4. Assign any penalty solely to the school or employer responsible for a violation.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Jonathan D. Licht, M.D.
President and Chief Scientific Officer, Van Andel Research Institute

The result will be devastating: schools will stop recommending OPT, students like me will lose the critical work experience our STEM degrees are meant to lead to, and U.S. businesses will lose the highly trained graduates they need to stay competitive in fields like AI and data analytics.
DHS has not demonstrated that $70,000 bears any relation to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation. A fee of this magnitude punishes legitimate F-1 students and will push talented graduates to study and work in competing nations instead of the United States. If a fee is needed, it must be set at the actual administrative cost with a full justification in the record. The proposed $70,000 / $30,000 fees should be withdrawn immediately.

CSET submits the attached comment in response to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security's notice of proposed rule on Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket Number ICEB-2026-0100).

I oppose the proposal of the new fees to OPT.

This fee does not bring labor protection back to the U.S. nor does it guarantee that students who can reliably pay the fee are any more talented than those who couldn’t. This rule, therefore looks more like a shadow ban on the program due to the U.S.’s own grievances with immigrants, especially immigrants of color (as most international students in the U.S. are people of color) than to truly protect the citizens of the States. Below I would like to demonstrate why I make this statement.

OPT as a system is oftentimes utilized (and in many cases, crucial) by graduates or degree-seekers to be able to work as interns, off-campus resesrch assistants, medical scribes, EMTs, and more as the acquisition of these positions can demand students work more than 20 hours per week which would be pass the CPT limit. However, if that is to be the argument then DHS must fix how H-1B can be sponsored and how easily can it be filed because under current rules, H-1B filing simply doesn’t happen quickly enough. This means that for fields where an H-1B is in play, the loss of OPT will result in a loss in international workforce across the board, harming institutions that rely on these talents.

OPT is even more crucial in healthcare. In this argument, I will use the example of the nursing track. Nurses don’t tend to use H-1B; they use EB-3. Unlike EB-1A (which tend to require a PhD) and EB-2NIW, nurses cannot self-petition for an EB-3. This will simply deter students enough to significantly exacerbate the aready existing nursing shortage in the U.S. I would like to remind DHS and the federal courts that all healthcare positions must be staffed for the system to function.

These two arguments above point to how this proposal hurts both industries and international students but doesn’t address how it fails at wage and labor protection for U.S. citizens. RE: Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100, RIN 1653–AB01, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
The fee bears no relationship to the cost of the service it purports to fund. DHS’s own Regulatory Impact Analysis estimates the actual cost of reviewing and processing each OPT application at roughly $50–$90 per application (Section VII.A.5.a(2), Table 5) — a few dollars, not tens of thousands. A fee set at 1,000 times the administrative cost of the transaction functions as a tax or a bar to entry, not a service fee, and DHS does not explain how a figure “comparable to” the H-1B fee (rather than tied to OPT’s own costs) is a lawful basis for setting it.
The fee is not targeted at the fraud DHS describes. DHS’s own fraud examples (Section IV.A) involve a relatively small number of shell companies and bad-faith employers. Rather than pursuing the alternatives DHS itself identified and rejected. expanded site visits, stronger DSO training, employer vetting (Section VII.B.6), the rule imposes a blanket, six-figure cost on all 194,554+ lawfully participating students and the institutions that sponsor them. This is not narrowly tailored; it punishes the overwhelming legitimate population to reach a small set of violators.
The fee does not fund fraud enforcement. By DHS’s own description, collected fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and are not earmarked for SEVP oversight (Section IV.C). DHS cannot credibly claim the fee strengthens its enforcement capacity when the revenue is not directed to that purpose.
The agency’s own cost-benefit analysis cannot justify the rule. For an “economically significant” action under E.O. 12866, DHS lists annualized monetized benefits as “Not Estimated” (Table 1) while estimating transfers as high as $17 billion annually and total 10-year costs up to $69.9 billion (Section VII.A.1). An agency cannot reasonably conclude that unquantified, qualitative benefits outweigh quantified costs of this magnitude.
The rule falls hardest on small and under-resourced institutions. DHS’s own data show 56% of affected SEVP-certified schools are small entities, and that under the post-transition period, over 280 small institutions would see fee impacts exceeding 10% of annual revenue (Table 15). DHS considered and rejected a small-institution exemption, meaning this rule will disproportionately push smaller, often non-profit, schools out of OPT sponsorship altogether - concentrating opportunity at the wealthiest institutions, which has nothing to do with fraud prevention.
The fee effectively creates a shadow visa-cap/fee regime that Congress did not authorize. Congress set specific numerical and fee limits for the H-1B program by statute. Using INA 214(a)’s “time and conditions” authority to impose a fee explicitly designed to be “comparable to” and to “closely align with” H-1B fees (Section IV.C) functions as an end-run around Congress’s statutory scheme for employment-based nonimmigrant visas, which DHS has no delegated authority to replicate through a fee on a different, uncapped visa category.
DHS undervalues reliance interests and the fee’s chilling effect on legitimate students and institutions. Many current F-1 students selected their programs years in advance, in part because of OPT availability, yet the rule applies to anyone without a DSO recommendation as of the effective date — including students already mid-program. DHS also does not meaningfully grapple with the fee’s likely effect on U.S. international-student enrollment and the significant economic contributions those students make, dismissing this impact as merely “speculative” (Section VI).

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure, or at minimum, substantially reduce the fee to an amount reasonably related to actual administrative costs, and pursue the fraud-specific enforcement alternatives it already identified instead of a blanket fee on the entire legitimate OPT population.

I am an Assistant Professor at an R1 institution studying neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric diseases and am an American citizen. I am strongly against adding additional financial barriers to OPT, which has been an invaluable tool for students studying in the US to contribute to the American research enterprise. These students often end up staying on as permanent resident scientists. Adding a $70,000-100,000 cost to OPT would remove this stream of highly educated, highly capable young scientists, as universities would not be able to afford the new proposed OPT cost (typical post-undergraduate salary of a research assistant is ~$50,000). One of the things that has made American research so strong is the influx of global talent that then chooses to stay in the US and grow the US economy. The proposed change to OPT would be a huge hindrance to American research efforts.

I strongly oppose this proposed rule. Imposing a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent filings is not a reasonable regulatory fee—it is a punitive tax that acts as an outright prohibition on practical training.
Neither educational institutions nor students can absorb costs of this magnitude. Rather than combating fraud, this rule will force many schools to scale back or abandon their international programs entirely, severely damaging the skilled talent pipeline that American STEM industries rely on.
If the objective is program integrity, the Department should pursue targeted enforcement against bad actors rather than pricing qualified graduates out of the workforce and handing global talent to competitor nations.

A university education is one of the largest financial commitments a person can make. For international students, that commitment often begins years before they arrive in the United States.

Students compare academic programs, tuition costs, living expenses, and opportunities for practical training before deciding where to study. OPT is an important part of that decision because it allows eligible graduates to apply what they have learned in a professional setting.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee could significantly change those expectations.

My concern is not that immigration regulations should never change. Governments have the responsibility to review programs and address problems. The concern is whether major changes should take effect without meaningful protection for people who made long-term commitments under the existing framework.

The proposed 60-day transition period under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(3) appears particularly inadequate.

A student who is approaching graduation cannot realistically recover years of tuition payments, transfer an entire degree program, or develop an alternative career plan within two months.

Even if the payment obligation formally falls on educational institutions, students may bear the consequences if their schools cannot afford to support OPT recommendations.

This creates uncertainty that could affect confidence in American higher education.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee under § 214.13(i)(1). If any substantial changes are adopted, DHS should provide meaningful grandfathering protections for students already enrolled before the final rule takes effect.

Regulatory predictability matters. Students and institutions need reasonable notice when government decisions affect educational commitments made years in advance.

Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees"

I write as an F-1 international student at a large public university, graduating in spring 2027 with majors in computer science, data science, and economics, planning to use post-completion OPT and, if eligible, the STEM OPT extension. I submit this comment anonymously.

Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i), my school would pay $70,000 before a designated school official may enter my first OPT recommendation, and $30,000 for each later recommendation. DHS openly acknowledges schools "may pass the financial obligation" to F-1 students, all students, or employers. For a 2027 graduate like me, the initial fee is not abstract: it would attach to my first OPT recommendation in my first months out of school, when I have the least bargaining power and would be asked to absorb — through tuition surcharges or employer pass-through — a $70,000 cost, rising to $100,000 with a STEM OPT extension. The school's decision whether to pay, pass through, or stop recommending OPT would be made per student; students at budget-constrained public universities bear the most risk.

DHS justifies the figure as "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas." But for a new graduate, OPT is not an alternative to the H-1B lottery — it is the bridge employment that lets an employer evaluate a graduate before sponsoring them. Pricing a new graduate's first year of U.S. work at $70,000–$100,000 does not deter fraud; it prices entry-level hiring of international graduates out of reach for most employers, especially small and mid-size companies, and punishes students for timing they cannot defer — post-completion OPT must be filed within 60 days of program end.

I ask DHS to: (1) withdraw or substantially reduce the initial $70,000 fee; (2) not apply the $30,000 subsequent fee to STEM OPT extensions, which cover the graduates the United States most wants to retain; (3) reject the alternative floated in the proposal of charging $70,000 again at each higher degree level; and (4) if any fee survives, cap total per-student liability and set explicit limits on pass-through to students, since the proposal itself anticipates schools shifting the cost to students who cannot pay it.

Accounting and financial compliance are essential functions for American businesses, yet they are often overlooked in discussions about workforce policy.

Small companies need professionals who understand financial reporting, internal controls, audit preparation, taxation, and accounting systems. These responsibilities require practical experience as well as academic training.

OPT can allow eligible international graduates with accounting, finance, or information systems degrees to develop professional skills in American workplaces.

The proposed fees could make that pathway more difficult if universities become unable or unwilling to support OPT recommendations.

For smaller accounting firms and businesses, staffing constraints can be particularly challenging during tax season, financial reporting periods, or regulatory audits.

A reduced pool of qualified candidates may result in longer processing times, increased workloads for existing employees, and higher operating costs.

This does not mean international graduates are the only available source of accounting talent. However, restricting legitimate training opportunities could create additional recruitment difficulties without necessarily improving compliance.

There is also an important distinction between financial capacity and regulatory integrity.

A university's ability to pay a substantial OPT fee does not establish whether an employer maintains appropriate records or whether a graduate is participating in legitimate training.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and examine their potential effects on accounting workforce development and small business compliance.

Targeted verification of employers and training arrangements would provide a more direct method of addressing documented immigration violations.

What should determine whether a graduate qualifies for practical training?

Their education? Their compliance with immigration rules? Whether the training is related to their degree?

Or whether their university can afford an enormous fee?

That is the question I keep coming back to when reading about this proposal.

OPT is intended to connect academic education with practical professional experience. Students spend years completing degree requirements, developing specialized knowledge, and preparing to enter their chosen fields.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could introduce a financial obstacle that has little connection to those educational objectives.

Two graduates with identical qualifications could face very different outcomes simply because their universities have different financial resources.

I find that difficult to justify.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud. But legitimate students should be evaluated according to clear eligibility and compliance requirements. A large payment does not demonstrate honesty, professional competence, or the legitimacy of a training opportunity.

I am also concerned that these fees could disproportionately affect students attending smaller institutions, including those that serve communities with fewer financial resources.

The Department should explain why a uniform financial requirement is necessary instead of strengthening verification of individual training arrangements and investigating institutions with documented compliance problems.

I request withdrawal of the proposed provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

A fair regulatory system should distinguish between legitimate participants and actual violations. Financial resources should not become a substitute for that distinction.

RE: Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100, RIN 1653–AB01, “Optional Practical Training Fees”
The “transition period” fee structure is punitive and procedurally unfair to students already enrolled. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), any student receiving a DSO recommendation on or after the effective date pays the full $70,000 “initial” fee — including students who are already mid-degree and chose their program years ago, in part because OPT was an expected, affordable benefit of F-1 status. DHS acknowledges this reliance interest exists (Section VI) but dismisses it by asserting, without real evidentiary support, that OPT availability is merely “one of many factors” in a student’s enrollment decision. That conclusion is not supported by data DHS itself collected; DHS did not survey students or institutions on this question, it simply asserted the conclusion it needed to reach.

DHS’s own numbers undercut its “widespread fraud” premise. Section VI states that only about 20% of F-1 nonimmigrants participate in OPT at all, and the fraud examples DHS cites (Section IV.A) — a handful of shell-company prosecutions spanning over a decade, plus one 2025–2026 investigation — amount to a small fraction of the 194,554+ students who used OPT in 2024 alone. Imposing a fee on the entire remaining population to address conduct DHS itself describes as concentrated among identifiable bad actors (shared addresses, fake worksites, specific employer clusters) is not a proportionate response; DHS has the tools to target those employers directly (site visits, SEVIS data matching) without a blanket fee on all students and schools.

The pre-/post-completion fee differential ($100,000 vs. $70,000) is arbitrary and not explained by any fraud-prevention rationale. DHS admits (Section V.A, VII.A.5.d(3)) that this structure exists only because of how DHS chose to define “initial” vs. “subsequent” fees — not because pre-completion OPT carries more fraud risk than post-completion OPT. DHS even states it expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT specifically to avoid the extra $30,000, which is a $30,000 regulatory distortion with no integrity-related justification.

The 30-day comment period is inadequate for a rule of this magnitude. DHS designated this an “economically significant” action under E.O. 12866 with a primary cost estimate of $35.1 billion and a high-end estimate near $70 billion over 10 years (Section VII.A.1) — yet gave the public just 30 days to review a rule built on dozens of tables, cost models, and regulatory impact assumptions. For a rule of this fiscal scale affecting over 1.4 million F-1 students and 2,478 institutions, a comment period this short limits the public’s meaningful ability to identify errors in DHS’s modeling (e.g., the participation-scenario assumptions in Table 3) before the rule is finalized.

The rule does not address the stated FICA-exemption “incentive” problem it blames for part of the harm. Sections IV.B and footnote 108 attribute some of the alleged wage suppression to the FICA tax exemption for F-1 nonimmigrants, not to OPT itself. If that exemption is the actual driver of any hiring incentive, a six-figure OPT fee does nothing to fix it — DHS is imposing a massive cost on students to address a problem its own analysis attributes to a separate provision of the tax code that this rule does not touch.

The proposed OPT payment requirements raise significant operational questions for educational institutions.

Universities already maintain administrative systems for international student advising, immigration reporting, academic eligibility verification, and compliance with federal regulations.

Introducing substantial payments as a prerequisite for OPT recommendations would create additional financial and administrative responsibilities.

These responsibilities should not be underestimated.

Institutions would need to determine how payments are authorized, which departmental budgets are responsible, how eligibility decisions interact with financial approvals, and how payment disputes or processing delays are resolved.

Such requirements may be especially challenging for universities with decentralized administrative structures or limited international student services staffing.

The proposed payment conditions under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and (iii) also raise questions about whether administrative delays could prevent otherwise eligible students from obtaining timely recommendations or employment authorization.

An institution may have a legitimate student and a qualifying training opportunity but still experience internal delays in approving an extraordinary financial obligation.

That would create a problem unrelated to the student's academic qualifications or immigration compliance.

Before implementing the proposed requirements, DHS should provide a detailed assessment of institutional implementation costs, administrative processing times, and potential effects on students approaching OPT application deadlines.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fee provisions and reconsideration of the related payment requirements.

If DHS identifies specific compliance weaknesses, those problems should be addressed through clearly defined oversight procedures rather than a payment system that may introduce additional administrative barriers.

Effective regulation should improve compliance without unnecessarily complicating the lawful processes it is intended to oversee.

I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. DHS's own numbers show the cost falls mainly on students and schools. DHS estimates that the fees would transfer $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion per year from schools to the federal government, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion (Section VII.A.4). Over ten years, the primary transfer estimate is $109.4 billion at a 3 percent discount rate. DHS also estimates annual opportunity costs of about $8 billion to $9 billion from lost OPT participation (Section VII.A.5.b). The rule's stated alternative is a blanket charge on a population of roughly 195,000 to 290,000 students, yet DHS acknowledges it "cannot confidently predict" how much participation will fall.

2. The fee is not tied to any service. A DSO's OPT recommendation is an administrative act. The rule admits that the fee is "not nominal," that it is "on par with the educational costs... for one or two years" of study, and that the fee was chosen to be "comparable" to H-1B fees (Section V.A). It does not tie the $70,000 to the cost of processing a recommendation. The rule also states that the proceeds will go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts because the statute "does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds." A charge that is not cost-based, not retained by the agency that administers the program, and justified by deterrence is a revenue measure. DHS should explain its authority for that approach, and I question whether the INA's conditions-of-admission language in § 214(a) supports it.

3. The fraud rationale does not match the remedy. The rule cites real abuse, including a 2020 prosecution involving thousands of students and an HSI investigation that identified more than 10,000 students working for "highly suspect" employers. The 10,000 figure is about 5 percent of the 194,554 students who held OPT authorization in 2024. A targeted response aimed at those employers and the schools that recommended them would address the identified fraud. A fee on every recommendation charges the other 95 percent of students for the conduct of a small minority. The rule itself acknowledges that "enforcement activity" could address the problem, and it rejects that option because a fee is "quicker" and "minimal[ly] burdensome" for the agency, not because it is more effective.

4. The STEM extension is penalized most heavily. Each STEM OPT extension triggers a $30,000 subsequent fee. The rule's own projections assume that schools will steer students toward post-completion OPT to avoid the $100,000 that split OPT would cost. That is a predictable behavioral response, and the rule does not quantify its effect on STEM graduates or on employers in fields with documented shortages. The rule's own data shows 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, and the fee would apply to all of them.

5. The benefits are not quantified. The rule quantifies costs and transfers. Its benefits discussion (Section VII.A.6) is qualitative. It does not estimate how many fraud cases the fee would prevent, how many U.S. jobs it would create, or what wage effects it would have. Executive Order 12866 and Executive Order 13563, which the rule cites, require agencies to weigh quantified costs against quantified benefits. Without a benefit estimate, the rule cannot show that its benefits justify roughly $35 billion in ten-year costs.

6. The small-business impacts are severe. DHS estimates that 1,389 small institutions would be affected in the post-transition period. Of those, 98 would face costs above 20 percent of their annual revenue, and 82 more would face costs of 10 to 20 percent. In the transition year, 60.5 percent of affected small institutions would exceed a 1 percent revenue impact (Section VII.B.4). DHS rejected a small-institution exemption because "fraud could still continue given the majority are small entities." That reasoning treats the regulatory burden as a feature rather than a cost the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires DHS to minimize.

7. The reliance analysis is inadequate. DHS dismisses reliance interests of students, employers, and institutions, but the rule's own text acknowledges that schools may have to "alter [their] budget that was prepared without consideration" of this fee (Section VI). Many students already admitted under existing OPT rules would face changed costs with only 60 days' notice, and the proposed 30-day comment period is short for a rule of this size.

Recommendation: Withdraw the proposal. If DHS is concerned about OPT integrity, it should use targeted enforcement against employers and schools shown to be engaged in fraud, publish the benefit analysis the rule currently lacks, and address the authority question before any fee is imposed.

I made significant financial sacrifices to pursue a world-class education in the United States as a first-generation student. The OPT program serves as a critical bridge between academic education and professional experience, allowing international students like me to apply what we've learned in real-world settings.

I have personally benefited from the OPT program, which allowed me to gain valuable research experience, contribute to scientific publications, and strengthen my academic credentials. These opportunities were instrumental in preparing me to apply to competitive PhD programs at some of the leading research institutions in the United States. Without the opportunity to work in a research laboratory through OPT, I would not have had the same pathway to advance my academic and scientific career. Making this process financially inaccessible would disadvantage talented international graduates but would also deprive their respective fields of the important contributions they make.

I support effective immigration enforcement. I also believe that any regulatory measure should be proportionate to the problem it is intended to solve.

The proposed OPT fees raise serious questions under that principle.

A substantial payment may reduce the number of institutions willing to recommend students for OPT. However, reduced participation should not automatically be interpreted as improved compliance.

A legitimate student who loses access to practical training because a university cannot afford the fee is not an example of fraud being prevented.

Similarly, an institution capable of paying the fee is not necessarily free from compliance problems.

The proposed structure therefore requires a clear explanation of how the payment amounts were determined and what measurable enforcement outcomes they are expected to produce.

Several questions deserve answers:

What specific categories of OPT abuse are these fees intended to address?

What evidence connects the proposed payment amounts to reductions in those violations?

Have employer verification, targeted audits, and enhanced reporting been evaluated as alternatives?

How will DHS distinguish reduced legitimate participation from actual improvements in compliance?

These questions matter because regulatory costs can produce consequences beyond the intended enforcement objective.

The Department should demonstrate that the expected benefits justify the financial burdens imposed on educational institutions and the potential indirect effects on students and employers.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) until a transparent assessment of proportionality and less burdensome alternatives has been completed.

The effectiveness of immigration enforcement should be measured by whether violations are detected and prevented, not by how expensive lawful participation becomes.

I am a Ph.D. student in the United States and am planning to pursue a post-graduation opportunity through the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. This opportunity is vital for both international scholars like myself and for U.S. colleges and universities.

However, imposing a $70,000 fee on the OPT program would severely harm this mutually beneficial arrangement. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed fee structure and preserve reasonable access to legitimate, degree-related practical training.

Participation in OPT would allow me to apply the knowledge and skills I have developed through years of academic training in both teaching and research settings. Such opportunities enable international scholars to continue contributing to the academic community while further developing their professional expertise. In addition, American educational institutions have long benefited from the knowledge, perspectives, and specialized expertise of international students and scholars.

To use myself as an example, one college has invited me to teach a Korean Language and Culture course due to the growing number of students interested in Korea. In fact, dozens of students voluntarily created and signed a petition requesting that the college offer the course. The same institution has also asked me to teach a course titled Philosophical Perspectives, through which I would introduce students to a variety of philosophical traditions, including non-Western philosophical and religious perspectives. Both the World Languages and Cultures Department and the Philosophy and Religious Studies Department have expressed a need for an international scholar who can help meet their curricular needs.

Beyond teaching, OPT provides important opportunities for research and scholarly collaboration. International scholars often participate in research projects, contribute specialized knowledge and language skills, engage in interdisciplinary collaboration, and help expand the global reach of American scholarship. These contributions strengthen the research missions of U.S. institutions while allowing scholars to advance their own academic and professional development. In an increasingly interconnected world, such exchanges enhance innovation, cross-cultural understanding, and intellectual diversity across the American higher education system.

In conclusion, OPT has enabled both international scholars and U.S. educational institutions to benefit from one another. International scholars gain opportunities to further develop their research, teaching, and professional skills through practical training experiences, while U.S. colleges and universities enrich their curricula, strengthen their research programs, and broaden their academic perspectives through the contributions of international scholars. However, DHS's recent proposal to impose a $70,000 OPT fee would significantly hinder these valuable academic and research exchanges and deprive U.S. institutions of the substantial benefits that international scholars provide. Preserving affordable access to OPT will help ensure that American higher education continues to attract talented scholars and maintain its global leadership in both teaching and research.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee structure, particularly the $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and the $30,000 fee for subsequent recommendations under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i).

While preventing fraud and abuse within the OPT program is a legitimate and important objective, the proposed fee structure is disproportionate, unfair to compliant participants, and potentially counterproductive. Although the fees would formally be imposed on SEVP-certified educational institutions, their economic consequences would extend directly to international students. Institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial costs, potentially passing financial burdens to students or declining to recommend otherwise eligible students for OPT. In either case, students who comply with immigration requirements could lose valuable opportunities because of misconduct by unrelated individuals or institutions.

A fair and effective regulatory system should focus enforcement resources on identifying and holding actual violators accountable rather than imposing extraordinary financial barriers on compliant participants. The proposed fees do not appear to be sufficiently justified by evidence demonstrating that charging $70,000 or $30,000 per recommendation would reduce fraud more effectively than targeted verification, improved oversight, enhanced reporting, or enforcement against fraudulent employers and institutions. Simply making legitimate participation prohibitively expensive does not necessarily address the underlying vulnerabilities that enable misconduct. DHS should provide stronger evidence that the anticipated compliance benefits justify the proposed financial burden and explain why less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient.

Furthermore, these fees could significantly undermine U.S. competitiveness in STEM education, research, and technological innovation. OPT provides an important pathway for international graduates to apply their education through practical experience, contribute to U.S. employers, and participate in the nation's scientific and technological workforce. Making that pathway financially inaccessible could discourage talented prospective students from choosing American universities and encourage them to pursue education and career opportunities elsewhere. This could weaken the research talent pipeline, reduce opportunities for university-industry collaboration, and ultimately harm American innovation.

Importantly, DHS's own regulatory impact analysis acknowledges that reduced OPT participation could lead to lost work experience and earnings for international students, productivity losses for employers, and declining international student enrollment at U.S. institutions. These consequences deserve serious consideration when evaluating whether the proposed fees would produce benefits proportionate to their costs.

I therefore urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed OPT fee structure and pursue more targeted, evidence-based, and proportionate measures to combat fraud. Protecting the integrity of the OPT program should not come at the expense of compliant students, American educational institutions, and the nation's long-term competitiveness.

The College of St. Scholastica opposes the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) applications and asks the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed rule. This proposed fee structure would negatively impact our students, the US and local economy, our employer partners, and our institution. Attracting international students is in our nation's best interest. The US economy benefits directly when international students choose to study, stay, and work through Optional Practical Training (OPT). Research consistently refutes claims that OPT harms domestic opportunities:

Niskanen Center research shows experiential learning through OPT increases innovation and average earnings without reducing U.S.jobs or wages. (Esterline, 2023)
A National Foundation for American Policy found no evidence that STEM OPT participation reduces job opportunities for U.S. workers. (Zavondy, 2019).
“The Economic Impact of Curbing the Optional Practical Training Program” (2018) report by the Business Roundtable illustrated significant negative effects on the U.S. economy if OPT were curtailed.

Research has shown that Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a vital part of the student experience and that over 66% of international students report they would not come to the United States without the opportunity to gain professional experience through OPT (NAFSA). Losing international students would have a negative impact on the US and local economies. NAFSA reports that international students studying at U.S. colleges and universities contributed $42.9 billion and added 355,736 jobs to the U.S. economy during the 2024-2025 academic year.

Proposed DHS OPT Fee Rule: Institutional Impact Statement
Institution: Kansas State University
Date: November 9, 2026
Summary
Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a longstanding benefit of the F-1 student regulations that allow eligible F-1 students to apply for and receive permission to engage in employment directly related to their major field of study. The program serves as a key connection between academic learning and professional application. Limiting access to OPT may reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education in an increasingly competitive global market.
The current proposed rule would require Kansas State University when recommending the OPT to pay the applicable fee prior to recommending the OPT benefit. The proposed rule includes a fee of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. 
The proposed fees would create severe financial, enrollment, operational, and other economic consequences. The rule would significantly reduce access to practical training opportunities, diminish the attractiveness of U.S. higher education to international students, and negatively affect employers who rely upon highly skilled international graduates.  This letter is written to express strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing fees of $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent Optional Practical Training recommendations.
Financial Impact
International student populations would generate potential Kansas State University institutional liabilities, reaching millions of dollars annually under the proposed fee structure. The magnitude of these fees far exceeds current administrative costs associated with OPT advising and compliance responsibilities.
Universities would be faced with difficult choices:
1.	Absorb the costs through institutional budgets.
2.	Pass costs directly to students or employers.
3.	Restrict or eliminate OPT participation.
Kansas State University currently has 232 students on OPT and STEM OPT. Given that number, and the proposed fee, it would cost more than $12 million dollars just to provide the practical training recommendation in SEVIS and issue the I-20. 
Impact on Students- Recruitment, Access, Retention, and Success
The opportunity to engage in OPT is a critical component for international students when deciding where to pursue their studies. Any policy that would limit access to these opportunities will reduce the appeal of studying in the U.S. and Kansas State. Therefore, if the current cohort of students on OPT/STEM OPT had chosen not to enroll at K-State because of the additional fees required to participate in OPT, Kansas State University would be negatively affected by at least $6.63 million annually. 
Administrative Concerns
The proposed fee levels appear disconnected from the actual administrative costs associated with Kansas State University compliance, OPT recommendation processes, and government oversight activities. The proposal would create significant administrative complexity and institutional risk.  As a public University, any fee that will be collected from a student will need to go through the University process as well as the Kansas Board of Regent’s approval process.  
Request
For the reasons outlined above, Kansas State University respectfully requests that DHS:
1.	Withdraw the proposed OPT fee rule; or
2.	Substantially reduce the proposed fees; or
3.	Revise the rule with other eligibility criteria to assist with oversight;
4.	Conduct a comprehensive economic impact analysis involving institutions, employers, and students;
5.	Engage stakeholders from higher education before proceeding with implementation.
Proposed ideas to add additional layers of oversight and program integrity:
a)	Require a job offer with the OPT recommendation. Making the authorization employer specific. This would then require more reporting and touchpoints throughout the authorization period. Each new employer would need at the very least a new I-20 prior to completing the I-9.
b)	Activate the termination in SEVIS for those who do not report timely or exceed unemployment days. 
c)	Require paid experiences only. Do not permit unpaid experiences to meet eligibility requirements for maintenance of status.
d)	Consider a registration by employers to employ those on OPT. Like the registration process for Hs.  
Conclusion
We urge DHS to withdraw the proposal or substantially revise the fee structure. The proposed 30-day comment period does not provide adequate time for stakeholders to fully evaluate a proposal.
Please see attachment for full public comment, discussion, calculations, and methodology.
Submitted by Stacey Bailey, Director of International Student and Scholar Services and Grant Chapman, Associate Provost for International Programs – Kansas State University

The United States invests public money and years of its scientists’ time in training doctoral researchers. We have a national interest in putting that expertise to work here, particularly when an American laboratory has already identified a graduate as the best person for the job.

Consider a physicist who develops a more sensitive way to measure a weak electromagnetic field. A U.S. laboratory may recruit that physicist both to build a detector and to teach American graduate students how to operate it. Publishing the method makes it available worldwide. But learning how to build the instrument, recognize sources of noise, and improve its sensitivity takes time working alongside the person who developed it. Where that scientist works matters to everyone who hopes to learn from them.

The first appointment may also shape where the scientist spends the next thirty years. A physicist who takes a postdoctoral position here may choose to remain in the United States, establish a research group, and continue making discoveries and developing new technologies here. The detector that prompted the original offer may turn out to be a small part of that scientist’s contribution to this country. If the fee leads the physicist to accept an offer abroad, another country may gain decades of scientific work from someone whose training American taxpayers helped support.

DHS reasons that when a placement is worth more than the fee, the parties can pool their resources to preserve it (91 Fed. Reg. 64588–89). A fee charged to universities before a student even has an employer does not reach them. Verifying employers and penalizing those that fail compliance checks would. Public universities would pay from state funds and tuition, moving money from labs and assistantships into general federal revenue. Schools that refuse to pay will lose international doctoral students, who make up much of the U.S. STEM research workforce. DHS never estimates that loss.

IV.C).** The rule states: "DHS acknowledges that the schools may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F–1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers." I am deeply concerned about the growing dependence of major U.S. technology companies, including Microsoft and Google, on the H-1B visa program.

When major American technology companies employ large numbers of H-1B workers, particularly when their workforce becomes heavily concentrated in particular foreign-nationality groups, an important question must be asked: What meaningful employment opportunities are being left for American citizens?

The United States has invested generations of resources in building its education system, universities, research institutions, infrastructure, and technology industry. American taxpayers help support this foundation. American students spend years studying engineering, computer science, and other technical disciplines, often taking on substantial student debt, with the expectation that they will have a fair opportunity to pursue careers in their own country.

Yet American graduates and experienced professionals increasingly face intense competition for technical positions at major U.S. companies. It is reasonable to question whether employers are making a genuine effort to recruit, train, and retain American workers before relying on foreign labor.

I recognize that immigration and international talent have contributed to America's economic and technological development. Qualified foreign professionals can bring valuable skills. However, the H-1B program was intended to address genuine labor shortages, not to provide companies with an alternative workforce strategy that disadvantages American workers or suppresses wages.

I urge the government to consider the following reforms:

Prioritize American workers: Require employers to demonstrate meaningful recruitment efforts and explain why qualified American applicants were not selected before sponsoring H-1B workers.

Increase transparency: Require large technology companies to disclose their H-1B workforce numbers, job categories, salary levels, and the proportion of their workforce represented by visa holders.

Prevent workforce displacement: Strengthen protections against replacing American employees with lower-cost foreign workers, including through outsourcing arrangements and subcontractors.

Enforce fair wages: Ensure that H-1B employees are paid competitive wages and that the program cannot be used to undercut compensation for American workers.

Encourage investment in American talent: Require companies that rely heavily on H-1B workers to demonstrate meaningful investment in training, internships, apprenticeships, and career development for U.S. citizens.

Review excessive concentration: Examine whether a small number of employers or recruitment networks are using the program in ways that limit fair access to employment opportunities and create unfair advantages in hiring.

American citizens should not have to wonder whether they have become second priority in their own country's technology industry. U.S. companies benefit from America's education system, infrastructure, legal protections, and economic environment. They should also have a responsibility to invest in the American workforce.

The purpose of the H-1B program should be to fill genuine skill shortages, not to replace the responsibility of American companies to develop and employ American talent.

I respectfully urge the government to strengthen oversight of the H-1B program and ensure that American workers receive fair consideration, fair compensation, and genuine employment opportunities.
