I am an F-1 student in the fifth year of my PhD in Computer Science at an R1 University. I strongly oppose the proposed rule and urge that the DHS withdraw it for the following reasons.

First, the rule contains inconsistent numbers and contradictions to itself. The UMRA section says the rule "would not result in" a $100 million expenditure, but the next paragraph says that it "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold" (64597). The federalism section finds no "substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments" (64598), but 1,044 of the 2,478 affected schools are state-run (64592), and DHS "did not consult with elected representatives of
the affected State, local, and tribal governments" (64597). The Paperwork  eduction Act section counts 226,200 annual responses (64598). while footnote 143 counts 289,938. Section IV.B cites 65,524 STEM OPT participants for 2024 (64573); the economic analysis uses 95,384 (64583). The reliance section says "only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants participated in OPT in 2024" to show students do not depend on it (64578), counting every enrolled student rather than graduates, while the same rule says OPT growth has "exponentially outpaced" DHS's capacity (64571) and the program is "flooded with participants" (64570) -- how can it be both marginal and overwhelming? The DHS should reconcile these statements, conduct the state consultation it admits it skipped, and publish a corrected analysis with the underlying data before it can proceed.

Second, the DHS offers no cost basis for the proposed fee. It says that the figure was chosen to be "comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" and to deter use (64575). The general fee statute, 31 U.S.C. 9701, requires agency charges to be based on the cost to the government and the value of the service to the recipient, and the Supreme Court has held that statute authorizes a fee, not a tax, because taxation is a legislative function (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). The one fee Congress authorized for F-1 students, the SEVIS fee, must be "based on" the cost per alien (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)). The H-1B payment that DHS refers to was vacated by a federal court in June 2026 as a tax, but the rule does not mention that ruling. DHS should address that decision and explain how a general-fund receipt with no service behind it satisfies 31 U.S.C. 9701. If there is to be a fee, it must be cost-based, set by a published cost study of SEVP's OPT oversight, collected with Form I-765, and retained for enforcement  just like the SEVIS fee.

Third, DHS claimed that the no-action alternative "does not provide enough accountability for schools" (64596) without saying what accountability schools lack. SEVP certification, recertification every two years, DSO training, SEVIS reporting, site visits and withdrawal of certification already exist (64568, 64571-64572), DHS launched DSO fraud training in November 2025, and it reports implementing five of seven GAO recommendations on school fraud risk (footnote 81). The rule does not evaluate this functioning oversight system, which casts into question why this fee would be the measure to improve things. Before any fee can be imposed, the DHS must evaluate that baseline system and use the tools it already has, treating a high rate of a school's students at flagged or debarred employers as a recertification trigger under 8 CFR 214.3-214.4 and auditing OPT recommendations during the two-year review already required by Congress.

Given insufficient evidence of any need for this proposed rule, I request that the DHS withdraw it.

New York University (NYU) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100), which would establish a fee of $70,000 per F-1 student for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation. 

The NYU community is concerned that the proposed rule would limit our country’s ability to attract and retain the best and brightest minds to study, conduct research, and contribute to fields critical to our nation’s prosperity. International students who study at U.S. universities and subsequently join the American workforce have contributed greatly to overall economic growth, driving scientific discovery, innovation, and medical breakthroughs. For example, in 2023, the Nobel Prize winners in the categories of Physics, Chemistry, and Medicine each included a U.S. university faculty member that was born outside of the country. In addition to these invaluable scientific contributions, according to NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the approximately 1.1 million international students who attend U.S. colleges and universities each year generate an estimated $44 billion in economic activity and support more than 378,000 jobs nationwide.

Talented international students are attracted to American universities in part because of the opportunity to participate in OPT, which allows eligible graduates to gain valuable practical work experience in their fields of study. This is certainly true at NYU. For example, during the 2024-25 academic year, some 51.1% of our OPT-eligible students were approved for post-completion OPT. In that same year, 54% of our STEM students eligible for OPT were approved for the STEM-OPT extension.

Increasing the OPT fee from approximately $500 to $70,000 for initial participation, with additional fees for subsequent periods, would place participation beyond the reach of virtually all students, employers, and universities, and thus would effectively serve to end the program. Without OPT, many talented international students will undoubtedly choose to enroll at universities in other countries, benefiting competing economies and industries at the expense of American businesses and research institutions.

NYU maintains a rigorous process to ensure compliance with all federal regulations governing OPT. International students must first complete a training module outlining OPT rules and requirements, and then submit a request to NYU’s Office of Global Services (OGS). OGS coordinates with the appropriate NYU department to confirm academic progress and the anticipated program of study completion date. Following departmental approval, an OGS advisor verifies the student’s F-1 status and OPT eligibility before issuing an updated I-20 (the official government document certified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program) with the OPT recommendation. The student then submits their OPT application directly to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

While we are proud that the U.S. has made strides in recent years to increase the number of domestic students graduating from American universities in the STEM and health care fields, the technology and health care workforce remains reliant on recruiting top international talent. Policies designed to increase the number of American STEM students should complement existing federal programs, such as OPT, that successfully attract top international talent. If we don’t focus on both policy goals, we make it more difficult for U.S. employers to recruit highly skilled graduates, potentially slowing innovation, limiting research opportunities, and undermining economic growth.

For the reasons outlined above, the NYU community respectfully urges DHS to rescind the proposed “Optional Practical Training Fees” rule, and work with the higher education sector and other stakeholders to identify alternatives that address the Department’s concerns without imposing prohibitive financial burdens on talented international students and their prospective employers. Preserving access to OPT is essential to ensuring that U.S. businesses have access to the world’s most highly skilled graduates so they can continue to contribute to our country’s economy and long-term prosperity. 

Thank you for your consideration.

New York University

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and an additional $30,000 fee for a subsequent OPT recommendation. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

As an international student preparing to pursue graduate education in the United States, I have chosen this country because of its world-class universities, research environment, and opportunities to contribute to society. Like many international students, I am making a significant investment in the hope of developing skills that can benefit both my future career and the United States.

I recognize the government's responsibility to prevent immigration fraud and ensure that OPT operates lawfully. However, these proposed fees are disproportionate and could seriously undermine the educational, economic, and technological interests they should serve.

1. OPT Benefits the U.S. Economy and Workforce

OPT connects American higher education with the U.S. labor market. It allows eligible international graduates to apply the knowledge and skills gained at American universities in practical employment related to their studies.

International students already contribute substantially through tuition, housing, consumer spending, research, and support for local businesses. Their contributions also support jobs and economic activity in communities across the country.

These benefits continue after graduation. Through OPT, qualified graduates can contribute to American companies, laboratories, and research institutions. They can help address skill shortages, improve productivity, develop new technologies, and support business growth.

The proposed fees could discourage universities from recommending eligible students and employers from hiring them. This would reduce the economic contributions of international graduates and potentially push talented individuals toward countries with more accessible post-graduation employment pathways.

2. The Fees Could Weaken U.S. Technological Competitiveness

The United States is competing globally for talent in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, energy, and other strategic industries.

International students contribute to American research and education in these fields. OPT allows eligible graduates to apply their training in the U.S. workforce, supporting innovation, entrepreneurship, and technological development.

A $70,000 initial fee and an additional $30,000 fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier. Universities, startups, small businesses, and research institutions may be unable to absorb these costs. Even employers interested in hiring qualified graduates may reconsider because of the added expense.

Talented graduates could instead pursue opportunities in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, or other countries. The United States would risk losing not only skilled workers but also future research contributions, business investment, innovation, and tax revenue.

At a time when technological leadership is essential to national security and economic strength, the United States should attract global talent rather than create unnecessary barriers to retaining it.

3. OPT Does Not Automatically Displace American Workers

International graduates do not necessarily replace American workers. Their specialized skills can complement the existing workforce, help companies expand, and support the creation of additional jobs.

OPT employment must be related to a student's academic field. STEM OPT also includes additional safeguards, including E-Verify participation and Form I-983 training plans. These requirements provide a framework for monitoring employment and ensuring that practical training meets program standards.

If DHS identifies labor exploitation, fraudulent employment, or program abuse, it should address those specific violations through targeted enforcement. Imposing extremely high fees on all participating institutions and indirectly affecting all eligible students is not a proportionate solution.
4. Recommended Alternatives

I respectfully recommend that DHS:

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees.

Preserve reasonable access to existing OPT and STEM OPT pathways for eligible graduates.

Strengthen risk-based oversight and enforcement against actual fraud and noncompliance.
Improve employer verification and monitoring of training requirements.
Set any necessary fees according to documented administrative costs.
Assess the effects of regulatory changes on universities, students, employers, research, and U.S. competitiveness.
These measures would protect program integrity without unnecessarily undermining the benefits of international education and skilled employment.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT authorization, as outlined in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (2). I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal.

1. Disproportionate financial burden on universities

Requiring educational institutions to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each international graduate seeking practical training would create a substantial financial burden. Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and those with limited resources, would be unable to support these costs. This would effectively restrict access to OPT based on institutional financial resources rather than students’ qualifications or the relevance of their employment.

2. Damage to American research and innovation

International students make important contributions to scientific research, engineering, medicine, and technology in the United States. OPT provides an essential bridge between academic training and professional research. Imposing such substantial fees would discourage talented international students from studying in the United States and could push highly trained graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries. This risks weakening the American research ecosystem and reducing the country’s ability to attract and retain scientific talent.

3. Negative consequences for American competitiveness

U.S. universities invest significant resources in training highly skilled researchers and engineers. Preventing these graduates from gaining practical experience in the United States would reduce the country’s ability to benefit from that investment. American businesses, research laboratories, and universities would lose access to specialized talent, potentially slowing innovation and economic growth.

4. Disproportionate fees are not a targeted solution to fraud

I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud and protecting the integrity of the OPT program. However, the proposed fees do not appear reasonably connected to the administrative costs of processing OPT recommendations or to the specific risks associated with individual applications. More targeted enforcement, institutional oversight, and verification procedures would better address these concerns without broadly restricting legitimate participants.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed fees, provide stronger justification for their magnitude, and evaluate less restrictive alternatives that preserve legitimate OPT opportunities while addressing documented compliance concerns.

I am an international PhD candidate at Yale University, finishing my degree in the coming months. My research studies extreme heat and how it affects people’s health. My publication record is among the strongest in my peer group, including first-author papers in leading journals.
DHS states that this rule would lead schools to recommend only “the most promising students” for OPT. I am the kind of student DHS describes. But because of this rule, I am already struggling in my job search, and my spouse and I are seriously considering leaving the United States.
This is not just about the amount of money, or about who would be willing to pay that out of their own pockets. This is about trust. When a research group chooses between two strong candidates, the decision is often finely balanced. This rule places a weight on one side of that scale, turning a close call into a foregone conclusion. It does not matter whether the weight is $30,000 or $70,000. Once it is there, the decision tips against the international candidate almost every time.
My own case shows how this works. I am currently being considered for a two-year postdoctoral research position. I would rely on 12 months of initial OPT, followed by the 24-month STEM OPT extension. Until now, this has been the simplest path for both sides: my employer would not need to sponsor a J-1 visa, which takes time to process and carries the risk of delays or denial. For this reason, research employers have generally preferred candidates who can start on OPT. However, under the proposed fees [proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2)], my school would have to pay $30,000 before recommending my extension, or possibly $70,000, since the rule is unclear for students whose first OPT came before the rule took effect. My extension would fall about one year into the position, after the rule could take effect. My employer therefore cannot be sure I can stay for the full project. A two-year project cannot be built around someone who might have to leave after one year.
The effect goes beyond any single fee or any single case. Once employers learn to see international graduates as a risk, they will stop treating them as a first choice even if some of them are excellent matches. The rule would change how academic employers hire, and that change would outlast the rule itself. The result would not be fewer fraudulent students, but fewer of the strongest researchers trained at American universities choosing to stay. Many of us want to stay because, through years of academic work here, we have come to see the United States as the place where the pursuit of knowledge is most consistently protected and respected, free from disruption. This rule would undermine that. Its effect would not take decades to appear: it would quickly reduce the appeal of the United States to talented researchers worldwide, and that loss would hurt the United States itself, seriously.
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. At minimum, DHS should not charge any fee for the STEM OPT extension of students whose initial OPT was recommended before the rule takes effect.
Thank you for considering this comment.

1. It would effectively end OPT in the social sciences and humanities

The employers that hire international affairs graduates (universities, think tanks, research institutes and nonprofits) cannot absorb that cost, and neither can most students. 

2. It would cost the United States expertise it needs 
My international classmates bring language skills and regional knowledge, of Russia, Eastern Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere, that U.S. research and policy institutions depend on. In these specialized roles, knowledge of a particular language or region is the qualification, and it is scarce in the domestic workforce. OPT is often the only way these graduates can contribute that knowledge here, and the professional ties formed during that year connect American institutions with counterparts in allied countries long afterward. Pricing them out will push this talent towards UK, Canada and Europe, and make it harder for U.S. universities to recruit strong international students in the first place.

3. It would penalize students who enrolled relying on current rules 
Current international students chose U.S. programs and took on substantial costs expecting access to OPT under the existing fee structure. Because the fee would apply to any recommendation issued on or after the effective date, many would be charged in the middle of their degrees.

Policy rationality (Section IV). The fraud documented in the NPRM centers on shell employers and nonexistent worksites. Yet the fee applies uniformly to every school and student, regardless of compliance history. The fees would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than funding SEVP oversight, so they add no investigative capacity. Reliance interests (Section VI). DHS concedes that current students are differently situated from prospective ones, yet it protects only those already recommended for OPT. Western Technical College urges the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw its proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees, published October 8, 2026. The proposal would require a Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP)-certified institution to pay $70,000 before a student’s first Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and $30,000 before any subsequent recommendation, including for pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, or a STEM OPT extension. (91 FR 64566, 64576–77.)
Western is a public technical college serving students and employers across western Wisconsin. Our mission connects education with applied learning and workforce preparation. OPT can give F-1 students field-related experience during or after their studies.
THE FEE WOULD PLACE ACCESS AT RISK
A $70,000 payment for one student, followed by $30,000 for a later OPT recommendation, is not a routine administrative charge. The payment must be made before a designated school official can enter the recommendation in SEVIS, and the rule would prevent employment authorization if the fee has not been paid. (91 FR 64576–77.) For a public technical college, each payment would require a consequential use of institutional funds. The cost could lead a college to decline to recommend an otherwise eligible student, regardless of the training’s educational value or the student’s compliance history.
Access would depend on an institution’s ability and willingness to absorb the charge. Students at institutions with greater financial resources could retain an opportunity that equally qualified students elsewhere lose. This financial screen does not identify which students or institutions present a compliance risk.
THE CHARGE IS NOT A TAILORED INTEGRITY MEASURE
Western supports a lawful, well-administered OPT program and appropriate efforts to investigate fraud and enforce program requirements. But the proposed fee does not distinguish between institutions or students with compliance concerns and those with strong records. An institution’s ability to pay does not show that a recommendation is legitimate, and inability to pay does not show fraud. The proposal would screen access by financial capacity rather than compliance or educational purpose.
DHS should explain how it set these amounts in relation to oversight costs or risks, and how collecting the fees would reduce fraud or protect U.S. workers. The rule also creates financial uncertainty because fee refunds would be decided case by case, at DHS’s discretion, with no appeal. (91 FR 64577.)
THE PROPOSAL NEEDS A FULLER IMPACT ANALYSIS
Administering the fees would require institutions to find funding, obtain financial approvals, verify a student’s OPT history and applicable fee, coordinate payment with the designated school official, track payments and recommendations, and manage refund requests. These steps add staff time and create the possibility of delays or errors beyond the fee itself. DHS should fully assess these institutional costs and burdens.
The rule also needs clear procedures for students who progress to a higher degree, change institutions, or seek more than one type of OPT. DHS should explain how it would prevent duplicate initial fees and how institutions can determine the correct fee before making a recommendation. A 60-day transition period would not resolve these questions or ensure institutions can establish compliant processes.
REQUESTED ACTION
Western asks DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS pursues changes to OPT oversight, it should consult with colleges, students, and employers; consider less burdensome alternatives that target specific compliance risks; analyze the full costs and operational impacts; and clarify how the requirements would work in common circumstances. Any final approach should preserve access to legitimate, field-related practical training for eligible students.
Thank you for considering Western’s comments.

**Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Sections V.C and VI (Transition Period and Reliance Interests)**

I am a current F-1 graduate student. I recognize that Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a temporary, discretionary benefit—not an entitlement to employment or a guarantee of authorization. I am not asking DHS to preserve OPT unchanged or arguing that the agency cannot regulate the program. I ask DHS to distinguish future students, who can make informed decisions under new rules, from current students, who have already made substantial commitments in reliance on the framework in place when they began their studies.

For many years, eligible F-1 students have been able to seek up to 12 months of post-completion OPT, with an additional 24-month extension for graduates of qualifying STEM programs. This was not a promise of a job, but a known part of the academic-to-professional pathway that students could reasonably consider when deciding to study in the United States and planning their careers. Students already here have committed years of their lives and substantial resources to tuition, housing, relocation, and living expenses. Many have left jobs, paused careers, and moved away from their families. These commitments cannot be undone by giving students 60 days' notice after a new rule is finalized.

The proposed rule would impose a $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. Although the institution would formally pay the fee, the proposal allows schools to pass the cost to students, the student body generally, or employers. It also allows a school or DSO to decline to recommend a student for OPT rather than pay the fee. In practice, OPT could become inaccessible to students who planned their education around the existing framework, even if the fee is not billed directly to them.

This is especially important for STEM students. Practical training is not simply an opportunity to remain in the United States or obtain a job after graduation; it bridges academic learning and professional practice. It allows graduates to learn how scientific and technical knowledge is applied in workplaces, how projects and teams operate, and how research and technical skills become practical solutions. For students who intend to return home, this experience can be essential to applying their education in local industries, developing new ventures, or becoming entrepreneurs. University coursework alone cannot always provide the same exposure to professional methods and practical constraints.

I am particularly concerned that the proposed transition rule uses the date of the DSO recommendation—not the date a student began the degree—as the trigger for the new fees. A student who began a multi-year degree before the rule was proposed could therefore face this new financial condition simply because they will not be eligible to request OPT until after it takes effect. This is prospective only in a formal sense: it imposes a new condition on students whose educational decisions and substantial investments were made under the prior framework.

DHS acknowledges in Section VI and footnote 124 that current F-1 students who have already moved to the United States are in a different position from prospective students. That difference should have practical consequences. OPT need not have been the sole reason a student chose to study in the United States for its established availability to have been an important part of their academic and professional planning. The fact that not every F-1 student ultimately uses OPT does not diminish the reliance of those already enrolled who planned their path around it.

I respectfully ask DHS to revise Sections V.C and VI so the proposed fees apply only to students who begin a new degree program after the final rule's effective date. F-1 students enrolled in their current degree programs before publication of this proposal on October 8, 2026, should remain under the existing OPT framework for that program, including initial post-completion OPT and any eligible 24-month STEM OPT extension—even if their DSO recommendation is issued after the new rule takes effect. They would remain subject to existing OPT eligibility, training, and oversight requirements; this request is only for protection from the newly proposed fees.

This approach would allow DHS to implement a new policy for future cohorts while treating current students fairly. Students enrolling after the effective date can assess the changed conditions before committing years of time and substantial resources. Those who have already made these commitments should not have the terms of their educational pathway changed midway through their studies.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I am writing to submit my formal comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule regarding **Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees** (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01).

While the rule intends to address administrative and program integrity concerns, the imposition of an excessive fee structure—such as a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions—will introduce severe, unintended negative consequences for U.S. higher education, technological competitiveness, and local economies.

---

### Key Areas of Concern

1. **Destabilization of Higher Education Finance**
* International students are a vital financial cornerstone for American colleges and universities. Because the vast majority pay full, out-of-state tuition without access to federal financial aid, their enrollment heavily subsidizes institutional infrastructure, research laboratories, and financial aid packages for domestic students.
* A prohibitive post-graduation fee wall will cause a sharp decline in international student enrollment, resulting in severe budget shortfalls for higher education institutions nationwide.


2. **Impact on Local Consumer Economies**
* International students do not exist in an economic vacuum. Throughout their studies and practical training periods, they contribute billions of dollars annually to local communities through housing, utilities, transportation, retail, and professional services.
* Decreasing the viability of the OPT program drains critical consumer capital out of college towns and metropolitan areas, directly hurting small businesses.


3. **Loss of Tax Revenue and Fiscal Contributions**
* Graduates participating in OPT and STEM OPT contribute directly to federal, state, and local tax bases through income taxes on their professional earnings.
* Transitioning OPT into an economically prohibitive financial burden cuts off these steady tax streams and stifles the economic multiplier effect generated by skilled professional spending.


4. **Stifling Critical STEM and Technology Talent Pipelines**
* The United States faces ongoing specialized skill shortages in high-tech sectors, including software engineering, artificial intelligence, and critical infrastructure management.
* Imposing an insurmountable barrier will not protect domestic jobs; instead, it risks compelling multinational companies to shift high-value technical projects, engineering hubs, and research operations overseas to more competitive global jurisdictions.



---

### Conclusion

The proposed fee structure is economically prohibitive and counterproductive to maintaining American leadership in global talent and innovation. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposal and maintain an accessible framework for the OPT program.

Dear Secretary Mullin and Acting Director Venturella: 

This letter is regarding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to increase fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. The OPT program is a critical pathway for states like Michigan to retain our skilled international students after they graduate and plays a huge role in maintaining our global leadership across Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields. DHS’s proposed increase in OPT fees has the potential to wipe out this program and deter future international students from studying in the United States, endangering a key talent pipeline for the country. 
 
This proposed rule would establish a $70,000 fee for universities to recommend international students on F-1 visas for OPT and a $30,000 fee for OPT users to access the 24-month STEM extension. Michigan alone is home to over 40,000 international students who bring a global perspective to our campuses and communities, contribute $1.4 billion every year to the state economy, creating thousands of jobs, and advance research and innovation.  The OPT program is a much-needed talent pipeline in the state of Michigan, which is facing smaller high school graduating classes at the same time as it faces increasing demand for high-skilled STEM workers.  Over the last decade international students using OPT have filled 97,000 jobs in Michigan, helping plug critical talent gaps and drive scientific research forward. Michigan has become a leader in international student retention, and we value the important role these students will play in supporting Michigan’s growth for decades to come. Disrupting the OPT program with these proposed fees would destroy the substantial long-term investments we have made to keep the students who study at our world-renowned universities in Michigan and would threaten our ability to remain a leader in cutting edge scientific research. 

Across the country, nearly 300,000 international students enter the U.S. workforce each year through the OPT program. These international students on nonimmigrant visas account for 46% of graduates from American STEM master’s programs and 45% of STEM PhD programs.  These students are a major source of scientific talent that our country has come to rely on across the public, private, and non-profit sectors. DHS’s proposed fee will make the U.S. a less attractive place for international students to study at a time when other nations are increasing their recruitment of such talent. Our ability to attract and retain top students from around the globe has historically been one of our greatest accomplishments and a driver of our economic success. 

If these proposed fees were to go into effect, the anticipated decline in OPT participation will shrink the US economy by between $110 billion and $744 billion per year after a decade.  DHS should withdraw this proposal, given the financial burden these fees would place on our communities and the harm they would cause by discouraging international students and limiting international engagement. 

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

Sincerely,
 
Debbie Dingell
Member of Congress

In industry, physics PhDs are hired into roles in technology, finance, engineering, and data science precisely because of the quantitative and computational skills developed during doctoral research. In 2023, 22 percent of the U.S. STEM workforce was foreign born. International and domestic talent are complementary: the same labs, departments, and companies that train and employ international graduates also train and employ American students.

I am submitting this formal public comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to establish an initial $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for STEM OPT extensions. While the Department frames these fees as measures to enhance program integrity and prevent domestic worker displacement, an empirical analysis of the U.S. technology sector demonstrates that imposing a combined $100,000 regulatory burden per graduate will severely damage American tech leadership, compromise national security goals in Artificial Intelligence (AI), and force high-value engineering operations offshore.

---

### 1. Severe Disruption to Critical AI and High-Tech Talent Pipelines

The United States faces acute talent shortages in specialized technical domains, including AI model development, semiconductor design, cybersecurity, cloud architecture, and quantum computing. A substantial portion of advanced STEM degrees awarded by American research universities go to international students who utilize OPT and STEM OPT extensions to enter the domestic workforce.

Imposing a $100,000 barrier on post-graduate training effectively severs this critical bridge between American higher education and the U.S. tech economy. Facing prohibitive costs, top-tier international researchers and engineers educated at U.S. universities will be priced out of remaining in the country. This self-inflicted bottleneck will directly weaken U.S. capability to maintain leadership in frontier technology standards.

---

### 2. Offshoring of R&D, Tech Jobs, and Venture Capital

Rather than protecting domestic tech workers, an economically prohibitive OPT fee will compel technology companies to restructure their operational footprints.

* **Corporate Offshoring:** Multinational technology enterprises will shift entry-level engineering hubs, R&D labs, and AI research units to foreign jurisdictions with competitive high-skilled immigration pathways—such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, or India.
* **Loss of High-Growth Startups:** International graduates have historically founded a significant percentage of U.S. technology startups and unicorn companies. Eliminating viable post-graduate training options will cause future technical founders to launch their ventures in alternative global tech hubs, taking venture capital investment and job creation with them.

---

### 3. Net Harm to Domestic Tech Employment and Innovation Multipliers

Economic literature demonstrates that high-skilled foreign-born engineers act as force multipliers for domestic employment rather than replacements.

In technology and software development, skilled OPT workers enable tech firms to scale projects, expand product lines, and build out infrastructure. This scaling creates complementary roles for U.S. workers in project management, product design, sales, marketing, and legal compliance. By artificially reducing the supply of specialized technical talent, the proposed fee will slow software release cycles, reduce corporate R&D output, and ultimately shrink net hiring for domestic tech workers.

---

### 4. Flawed Regulatory Rationale and General Fund Diversion

DHS asserts that high fees are necessary to curb program misuse, yet the rule specifies that collected funds will not be dedicated to enhanced verification, enforcement, or fraud detection tools within the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). Instead, revenues are directed to the general Treasury fund.

Imposing an exorbitant financial exaction that functions as a general revenue-raising tax—without providing administrative or program enhancements—is arbitrary, capricious, and counterproductive to maintaining a secure, efficient immigration framework for high-skilled talent.

---

### Conclusion

At a pivotal moment when global economic leadership hinges on technological dominance, imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 STEM OPT extension fee will paralyze the nation's high-tech workforce pipeline. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety to safeguard American technological innovation, national security, and economic resilience.

---

On behalf of the State University of New York at Oneonta (SUNY Oneonta), we respectfully submit the following comments regarding the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule, New Fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) (026-20660 (91 FR 64566)), published on October 8, 2026.

SUNY Oneonta supports the Department’s efforts to combat fraud, uphold the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers. As a member of the SUNY system, our institution already adheres to stringent compliance and reporting requirements in partnership with federal and state agencies, including through the Department’s Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS). We remain committed to working collaboratively with DHS to strengthen the immigration system while preserving the nation’s ability to attract and educate talented students from around the world.

However, we are deeply concerned that the proposed rule would adversely affect international students, diminish the richness of our campus community, and create negative economic consequences for both New York State and the nation. The proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT application and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT authorization would effectively place participation in OPT out of reach for most students and discourage prospective international students from pursuing degrees at U.S. institutions like ours. The opportunity to gain practical, time-limited professional experience through OPT is one of the primary factors that draws international students to study in the United States.

International students make meaningful contributions to SUNY Oneonta and the surrounding community through their academic engagement, cultural perspectives, and economic impact. A decline in international enrollment would result in significant losses for our local and regional economies. Imposing substantial new fees that are costly, burdensome, and time-intensive will not advance the goals of preventing fraud, strengthening immigration integrity, or protecting U.S. workers. Instead, these requirements would create unnecessary barriers for students and institutions alike, while discouraging future enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities.

For decades, the United States has benefited academically, economically, and culturally from its position as a leading destination for higher education. We urge the Department to reinforce that legacy by enhancing existing standards and processes rather than implementing new requirements that are unnecessary, prohibitively expensive, and likely to increase bureaucratic inefficiencies. Maintaining the nation’s reputation as the premier destination for international education and research is essential to sustaining our global competitiveness.

Accordingly, we respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed rule. We stand ready to work with the Department on policies that both strengthen the immigration system and preserve our ability to attract outstanding students from around the world who contribute to our campuses, communities, and the continued success of the United States. Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

OPT provides international students with a vital opportunity to gain professional experience in their fields of study following graduation, and for many, serves as an essential pathway to building a career in the United States. These exorbitant fees would make it increasingly difficult for universities and employers to recommend or hire international graduates, potentially forcing institutions to pass these costs onto students or discontinue OPT recommendations altogether.
Furthermore, international students make up a significant percentage of the workforce at American universities and research institutions, and contribute substantially to academic research, teaching, and innovation. Restricting their access to OPT would undermine the work of these institutions and the communities they serve, while discouraging employers from hiring qualified international graduates. These restrictions would also discourage talented international students from pursuing education in the U.S. and push international graduates to seek professional opportunities elsewhere, resulting in a loss of valuable talent and expertise from the national economy.
Overall, the proposed rule would place undue financial burdens on international students and American educational and research institutions, while restricting valuable employment opportunities and undermining the contributions of international workers. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposal and preserve accessible OPT pathways for international students and graduates.

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. I understand and support the government's objectives of preventing immigration fraud and protecting employment opportunities for American workers. However, imposing such extraordinarily high fees on universities and potentially international students is not an appropriate or proportionate way to achieve these goals. Fraud should be addressed through targeted investigations, stronger employer verification, university compliance audits, and meaningful penalties for those who violate the law, rather than imposing a financial burden on legitimate students who have followed immigration regulations and invested significantly in American education. If widespread OPT fraud is the justification for these fees, DHS should provide transparent, independently verifiable statistics establishing the percentage of OPT participants involved in confirmed fraud, along with evidence demonstrating that these fees would meaningfully reduce such violations. Similarly, protecting domestic employment is important, but DHS should demonstrate how many American jobs are actually displaced by OPT participants rather than assuming that every international graduate represents a lost opportunity for an American worker. International students also make substantial contributions to the United States. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported approximately 355,736 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. Beyond tuition and living expenses, international students contribute to scientific research, technological innovation, entrepreneurship, and the growth of American businesses. Many students choose the United States specifically because its universities offer opportunities to apply their education through practical training, and they make substantial financial and personal commitments based on the programs available when they enroll. Introducing fees of this magnitude would undermine those expectations, potentially discourage talented students from choosing American universities, and weaken the country's ability to attract skilled professionals. A policy intended to protect American workers should also consider the American jobs and economic activity supported by international students. I urge DHS to reconsider these proposed fees and instead pursue evidence-based, targeted enforcement measures that address actual fraud and labor abuses without penalizing legitimate international students and the universities that educate them.

I am a faculty member in geology and environmental science at Utah State University in Utah. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw this rule. The views presented here are my own, and not of the institution I work for.
The fee does not fit the fraud DHS describes (Section IV.A).
DHS's largest recent investigation found about 10,000 OPT students working for suspect employers. DHS's own 2024 data show about 290,000 to 360,000 students in OPT and STEM OPT. That is less than 4% of participants. A fee on every student punishes the 96% or more who follow the rules.
The fee does not pay for oversight (Section IV.C).
The fees go to the US Treasury, and ICE cannot keep them. DHS considered targeted tools, such as site visits and training plans, but chose a fee because it needs fewer government resources. Targeted tools address fraud but a flat fee does not.
DHS expects legitimate students to lose OPT (Sections VII.A.3–4).
In its low scenario, DHS assumes schools will pay only for STEM students. DHS also assumes students will stop using OPT during their degree. DHS estimates 10-year costs of up to $69.9 billion and gives no dollar value for any benefit. Also, Section IV.B reports 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, but Section VII.A.3 uses 95,384 for the same year. DHS should explain this difference before it finalizes a rule based on these numbers.
This rule harms Utah.

In 2024–25, 10,343 international students studied in Utah. They contributed $316.3 million to the state economy and supported 2,427 jobs (NAFSA; Open Doors 2025). NAFSA estimates Utah lost $8.2 million in 2025–26 as new international enrollment fell. Utah's public universities would have to pay these fees from their budgets or pass the cost to students.
The rule harms research and teaching in my field as our international students and collaborators bring much rigor and a variety of perspectives specific to the various earth systems and ecosystems we work within.  
In geology, earth and ecosystem science, international students and postdocs collect field data, run lab analyses, build computational models, and maintain monitoring networks. This work helps Utah, for example to manage its water quality and quantity, prepare for earthquakes on the Wasatch Fault, understand the Great Salt Lake ecosystem and water levels and managment, find critical minerals and geothermal energy]. 

If these people need OPT or a STEM OPT extension after this rule takes effect, the school would have to pay $70,000 or $30,000 before they could continue. DHS says schools may pass this cost to employers, but the federal grants that fund these positions were not budgeted for it and cannot cover it. They may be forced to leave the US, and their work would stop or move abroad. Section VI says the rule protects people already on OPT, but it does not protect people who need the next step.The rule trains people for work that protects the nation, then forces them out (Section V.A).

Federal agencies such as NSF, USGS, DOE, and NASA fund graduate students and postdocs to study earthquakes, water supply, energy, and natural hazards. This research protects lives, infrastructure, and national security. The US invests years of funding and training in these students. OPT is often the step where that investment starts to pay off, because it lets them apply their skills here. A $70,000 to $130,000 fee at that step means the US pays to train these s    cientists and then pushes them, and their skills, to other countries. The alternative in Section V.A, which charges the $70,000 fee again at each degree level, would make this worse. It targets the students who earn both a master's and a PhD in the US, who are the students most likely to enter research careers. 

I urge DHS to reject this alternative.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS wants to reduce fraud, it should use targeted tools that do not punish students who follow the rules.

Kelly K. Bradbury

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees because they would disproportionately harm graduates pursuing research, nonprofit work, and other socially valuable opportunities that do not necessarily offer high salaries.

OPT is not exclusively used by graduates entering large technology companies or financial institutions. Eligible students may pursue practical training in university laboratories, research assistant positions, nonprofit organizations, public-interest projects, and early-stage startups.

These opportunities can produce significant benefits for American society despite limited financial resources.

A research laboratory may have sufficient grant funding to support a junior researcher but not an additional $70,000 institutional charge. A nonprofit may provide valuable training in education, public health, or community development while operating on a constrained budget. A startup may offer opportunities to develop innovative technologies without possessing substantial financial reserves.

Because the proposed fee is imposed at the institutional recommendation stage rather than based on the student's salary or the employer's resources, these opportunities may become inaccessible regardless of their educational or social value.

The proposal could therefore distort students' career choices toward higher-paying positions while discouraging research, public service, and entrepreneurship.

It also creates unequal access based on institutional wealth. Students with identical academic qualifications and legitimate employment opportunities could face different outcomes depending on whether their universities can afford the fee.

DHS should examine these distributional effects and assess whether the proposed policy would reduce research productivity, nonprofit capacity, and opportunities for graduates at less wealthy institutions.

The Department should also consider that the value of practical training cannot be measured solely by immediate wages. Research and nonprofit work can generate long-term benefits that extend well beyond the individual participant.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and implement targeted compliance measures that protect program integrity without excluding students from legitimate research and public-interest opportunities.

I am a graduate student pursuing a degree in Speech-Language Pathology (SLP), a healthcare profession dedicated to the assessment and treatment of communication, voice, and swallowing disorders. I am writing to express my opposition to ICEB-2026-0100 because of the significant consequences this proposal could have on my profession and the broader healthcare workforce.

Throughout my graduate education, I have had the opportunity to learn alongside many international students holding F-1 visas who hope to remain in the United States and contribute to the healthcare system after graduation. To practice as an SLP, graduates must complete a clinical fellowship year, which international students complete through Optional Practical Training (OPT). Although Section D1 of the proposal characterizes this training as "optional," it is an essential requirement for entering independent clinical practice. The proposed financial barriers could prevent qualified international graduates from completing this necessary training and contributing to a workforce already struggling to meet growing patient needs.

Speech-language pathology is experiencing an increasing demand for services that exceeds the number of clinicians entering the profession. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment in SLP to grow by more than 15% between 2024 and 2034. Additionally, in 2025, 55% of surveyed SLPs reported that job openings in their area exceeded the number of applicants. With an aging population and increasing demand for pediatric communication services, our profession cannot afford to lose qualified individuals who are prepared to enter the workforce. International graduates are an important part of addressing these shortages and expanding access to care, particularly in underserved communities.

Beyond their clinical knowledge and skills, international students bring valuable cultural and linguistic perspectives that strengthen healthcare delivery. Speech-language pathology remains a relatively homogeneous profession, with approximately 80% of clinicians identifying as White and more than 90% identifying as women. Furthermore, a 2021 report found that fewer than 10% of SLPs were bilingual, despite nearly one-fifth of Americans speaking more than one language. International students can help address this disparity by bringing multilingual abilities and cultural experiences that support more individualized, culturally and linguistically appropriate care. Restricting their ability to enter the profession could further limit access to essential services for individuals and families from diverse backgrounds.

International students have already invested significant time, education, and clinical preparation into pursuing careers in the United States. For many, American SLP credentials do not automatically transfer to professional practice in other countries, making their commitment to completing their training here especially meaningful. Creating additional financial obstacles could discourage these future clinicians from entering a profession that needs their contributions.

Ultimately, international students are not simply completing their education in the United States; they are future healthcare professionals who can make meaningful contributions to patients, families, and communities nationwide. Implementing ICEB-2026-0100 could prevent qualified graduates from completing the clinical training necessary to practice, worsen existing healthcare staffing shortages, and further limit the diversity of our healthcare workforce. I urge consideration of the long-term impact this proposal could have not only on international students but also on the American patients and communities who depend on accessible, qualified, and culturally responsive healthcare.

Pureflight Aviation Training formally urges the reconsideration of the proposed rule introducing new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). International flight students are already among the most heavily vetted, biometrically screened, and continuously tracked individuals in the entire U.S. educational system. Imposing these prohibitive fee requirements will do little to curb intentional fraud; instead, it will directly deter prospective international flight students from attending Pureflight Aviation Training, drain essential global talent from the aviation pipeline, and inflict financial harm on American flight training institutions. 

The climate surrounding international education in the United States is already under severe strain. As research by Marbang et al. (2020) highlights, shifting immigration policy environments create widespread uncertainty and anxiety among F-1 visa holders, directly influencing their decisions regarding whether to remain and contribute to the U.S. workforce post-graduation. The opportunity to work following graduation through OPT provides U.S. institutions and companies with access to high-caliber, globally competitive applicants. Rather than threatening U.S. workers, international graduates foster healthy competition and innovation. Furthermore, Obinna (2026) notes that international students are increasingly viewed through a restrictive national security lens rather than celebrated for their talent, leaving them facing potential loss of status daily. Compounding these existing pressures with exorbitant fees signals an adversarial posture toward non-citizens, directly echoing Caty's (2019) observation that "individuals in countries across the world are now dealing with increased uncertainties in working in America. It is becoming increasingly more difficult for legal immigrants holding J-1 and F-1 visas to enter the United States, which is having a profound effect on the United States’ ability to recruit talent and increase innovation" (p. 1).

Imposing severe financial barriers on OPT candidates is economically counterproductive. Academic research by Bound et al. (2021) demonstrates the immense economic footprint of international scholars, noting that "in 2019 foreign students poured nearly $44 billion into the US education system (Bureau of Economic Analysis, 2020), and that international student flows also help generate a ready supply of high-skilled foreign workers for the US labor market" (p. 164). This issue is particularly acute in specialized STEM fields such as aviation. As Chen (2026) emphasizes in the American Journal of STEM Education, restrictive post-graduation regulations compromise the stability of the U.S. as a primary destination for global talent, driving prospective STEM graduates away from domestic flight programs and post-education opportunities. In specialized industries like aviation—where training already demands significant capital investment—international students will not choose to train in the United States for an FAA license if required to absorb tens of thousands of dollars in added OPT fees.

Instead of penalizing legitimate international students under the rationale of "combating fraud," the government should focus enforcement resources directly on bad actors. Protecting the integrity of the OPT program should involve punishing deceptive entities rather than placing insurmountable financial barriers on law-abiding students. Pureflight Aviation Training strongly encourages the agency to rescind the proposed fee structure and collaborate with aviation education leaders to refine anti-fraud mechanisms that protect program integrity without harming legitimate educational institutions and their students.



References

I am an F-1 student in year 4 of a PhD program in Biomedical Engineering at Yale University, a private nonprofit institution. My research develops custom three-photon microscopes with adaptive optics to image deep inside the living brain and spinal cord. I respectfully oppose the proposed fee and ask DHS to withdraw it.

The fee would price me out of training my degree depends on. I am applying for summer industry internships in optical system engineering. For a doctoral student in a program without a CPT-eligible course for such work, pre-completion OPT is the only lawful route. Under the rule, one summer internship would trigger the $70,000 initial fee. It would also turn later post-completion OPT into a $30,000 “subsequent” fee, for $100,000 in total (64577). DHS expects pre-completion OPT to decline by an amount it “cannot reasonably predict” (64591), and it counts that loss as zero. Pre-completion OPT should be exempt.
Nothing in the record concerns students like me. Every fraud example in Section IV.A involves employers at IT consulting or staffing worksites: fabricated offer letters, shell companies, and “phantom employees” at residential addresses (64570-64571). DHS offers no case involving a PhD graduate, a postdoctoral researcher or a research university. A fee that cannot tell a neuroscience postdoc from a phantom employee is not “targeted” (64576). DHS already runs employer-side safeguards for STEM OPT, including E-Verify, the Form I-983 training plan and site visits. It should extend those safeguards instead of charging schools.
There is no cap to circumvent in research. DHS says OPT is used “to circumvent employment visa caps” (64573). Universities and nonprofit research institutes, however, are H-1B cap-exempt (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)). If a university paid $70,000 so its own graduate could stay on as a postdoc, money would simply move from research to the Treasury, with no integrity effect. Doctoral graduates and employment with cap-exempt institutions should be exempt.
The fee is paid before there is anything to evaluate. For initial OPT, a student “does not have to secure a training opportunity before the DSO can recommend OPT” (64569). When the school pays, it knows nothing about the employer, the worksite or the job. The payment therefore cannot ensure “genuine educational value” (64574). In practice, schools will fund students whose employers can reimburse them. That favors high-paying placements over research, nonprofits and startups, a selection that has nothing to do with fraud risk.
The amount has no cost basis. DHS chose it to be “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” and to deter use (64575). Under 31 U.S.C. 9701, a fee must rest on the cost to the government and the value to the recipient. A charge that funds no service and goes to the general fund is a tax, which only Congress may levy (National Cable Television Ass’n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). DHS should identify clear statutory authority or withdraw the rule.
The rule ignores current students’ reliance. The transition rule protects only students who already hold a DSO recommendation (64577-64578). I committed years to a U.S. PhD knowing OPT existed. Footnote 124 concedes that current students “are in a different position” and then offers them nothing. NSF data show that most temporary-visa science and engineering doctorates with definite plans stay in the United States, so relying on OPT is the norm, not “speculative” (64579). Every student enrolled on the effective date should be grandfathered.

I also ask DHS to publish the underlying data for Tables 2-17 and its per-institution fee analysis (64593-64594). I further ask it to quantify the fraud it expects to prevent and the effect on U.S. workers, as Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 require, rather than relying on “would likely,” “could” and “may” (64591).

As an alternative, DHS could match SEVIS employer names and EINs against IRS and state business records and hold employers with no filings. That would catch the shell companies it describes at no cost to students or schools. DHS could also pilot any new measure in the IT services and staffing sector it identifies and expand it only if the data justify doing so.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee. Any integrity measure that follows should act on employers, where the evidence lies. It should rest on a cost basis if it is a fee, exempt pre-completion OPT, doctoral graduates and cap-exempt employment, and protect every student enrolled on the effective date. Thank you for considering this comment.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — the proposed OPT fees are a tax DHS has no authority to impose

This comment challenges the proposed rule on one ground: the charges in proposed 8 CFR 214.13 are not fees, and the Department has not shown it has authority to levy them.

A fee is a charge tied to the cost of a service provided to the payer. The NPRM states that these collections would be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury. The money does not fund OPT oversight, SEVIS, fraud investigation, or any service connected to the recommendation being charged for. A charge that raises general revenue is a tax, and the power to tax belongs to Congress. The NPRM identifies no statute in which Congress authorized DHS to raise $12.4 billion a year — the Department's own estimate — from schools and students through OPT recommendations.

The stated justification does not fill this gap. The rule says the fees are meant to combat fraud, yet it reports no fraud rate among OPT participants and cites no data showing that fraud is widespread, or that a per-recommendation charge of $70,000 would reduce whatever fraud exists. Program integrity for OPT is already enforced through SEVIS reporting, the Form I-983 training plan, and DSO and site-visit oversight. Charging every compliant school and student $70,000 per recommendation does not target fraud; it prices a lawful program out of reach and calls the proceeds integrity.

Before this rule can be finalized, the Department should be required to answer two questions on the record. First: what specific statutory provision authorizes DHS to impose a revenue-raising charge that is untethered from the cost of any service? Second: what evidence shows that OPT fraud occurs at a rate that a fee of this size could plausibly address?

If the Department cannot answer both, the proposed fees should be withdrawn.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees because their consequences would extend far beyond international students. The policy could undermine the financial stability of American universities, reduce educational resources available to domestic students, and threaten employment in college communities.

The Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report documented approximately 1.18 million international students in American higher education during the 2024-2025 academic year. Importantly, 59% attended public institutions.

International education is therefore not merely a concern for wealthy private universities. It is closely connected to the financial health of public higher education institutions serving American students.

The proposed fee would require universities to pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation. Consider an institution with 500 students seeking initial OPT annually. Supporting all 500 would require $35 million in fees, before accounting for subsequent OPT recommendations.

For many institutions, this would represent an extraordinary financial obligation. Universities could respond by limiting OPT recommendations, reallocating existing budgets, or seeking additional revenue.

Each response carries potential consequences for American students.

First, international students contribute tuition revenue that supports university operations. Although the extent of cross-subsidization varies across institutions, reduced international enrollment can place pressure on budgets supporting academic departments, instructional facilities, student services, and financial assistance.

If universities lose this revenue, domestic students may face higher tuition, reduced course offerings, larger classes, or diminished access to academic resources.

Second, universities employ American faculty, administrators, laboratory technicians, teaching assistants, maintenance workers, and student-service personnel. Financial pressures caused by reduced enrollment could lead institutions to freeze hiring, eliminate positions, or reduce academic programs.

Third, international graduate students contribute to research and teaching. Their participation can support laboratories, faculty research projects, and instructional activities that also benefit domestic students. Reduced international enrollment may therefore affect research productivity, course availability, and undergraduate research opportunities.

Fourth, universities are major economic anchors for their surrounding communities. International students rent apartments, purchase groceries, visit restaurants, use transportation, and support local businesses.

NAFSA estimated that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs during the 2024-2025 academic year.

In fall 2025, declining international enrollment was associated with an estimated $1.1 billion reduction in economic contributions and nearly 23,000 fewer supported jobs.

These findings illustrate that international student enrollment supports American employment outside university campuses as well.

Fifth, the proposed fee structure could exacerbate inequality between universities. Wealthy institutions may be better positioned to absorb extraordinary fees, while smaller universities, regional public institutions, and financially constrained schools may have little practical ability to do so.

The result could be a system in which access to practical training depends increasingly on institutional financial resources rather than academic qualifications or compliance.

DHS should also examine the potential effects on university competitiveness. If students increasingly choose universities in other countries because post-graduation training in the United States becomes financially uncertain, American institutions could lose tuition revenue, research talent, and international standing.

These risks deserve rigorous economic analysis.

For example, DHS should evaluate scenarios involving 10%, 20%, and 30% declines in new international enrollment and estimate the resulting effects on institutional revenue, domestic tuition, university employment, financial aid, and local economic activity. These figures should be treated as hypothetical stress scenarios, not assumed forecasts.

Protecting American workers and taxpayers is a legitimate policy objective. However, the Department must also consider whether its proposed measures would impose substantial costs on those same Americans.

A policy that reduces university employment, weakens public institutions, limits educational resources, and damages college-town economies may undermine the very interests it claims to protect.

I am a graduate student studying engineering in Oregon and concerned US citizen. I am writing to oppose the proposed rule on Optional Practical Training Fees. We want to have the best skilled workers in the United States, and imposing restrictive fees will ensure that they go to the competitors of the United States. The rule claims to be protecting American workers, when in fact, it would do the opposite. For example, the rule cites that "workers in computer occupations jumped from an average of 1.98 percent in 2019 to 3.02 percent in 2025." While they attribute this to foreign workers, this can be attributed to the investment in AI by many companies. In fact, here is an example of one of many articles that shows that companies are laying off workers due to investments in AI: https://www.forbes.com/sites/karadennison/2026/06/17/companies-are-firing-workers-to-fund-ai-that-isnt-working-yet/. Here are some reasons why the proposed rule should be rescinded:

1. The fees do not fund the enforcement DHS says it lacks (Sec. IV.A, IV.C). The rule justifies itself by citing understaffed oversight: roughly 60 SEVP field representatives for 6,186 schools, and compliance resources “not scaled” to the program. Yet the fees would be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, and the rule concedes ICE has no authority to retain them. DHS states it “cannot operate OPT” without these fees, but the fees add nothing to its capacity to operate it. That DHS lacks authority to retain the funds also raises serious doubt that INA 214(a) authorizes a charge of this size, which is unrelated to any cost of service.
2. The fee does not target the fraud described (Sec. IV.A, V.A). Every fraud example in the rule involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. The fee is charged to schools and is explicitly “not tied to a specific employer.” A student whose fee is paid may still work for a fraudulent employer. Worse, DHS’s own low-participation scenario predicts schools will pay mainly for STEM students, the population where the cited HSI worksite findings occurred. The rule concentrates participation where the fraud was found.
3. The fee selects for wealth, not merit (Sec. IV.C, VI). DHS says the fee will limit OPT to “the most promising students,” but it also expressly allows schools to pass the cost to students or employers. A fee paid by students screens for family wealth. “Pay-to-stay” schemes already involve paying for fraudulent employment; a larger payment does not deter them.
4. The rule uses inconsistent figures for the same year (Sec. IV.B vs. VII.A.3). Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024 to argue STEM OPT is “nearly double” the H-1B cap. The economic analysis uses 95,384 as its high-end 2024 STEM OPT figure. The larger number also appears to be a count of everyone currently participating, compared against an annual cap on new H-1B visas. Using DHS’s own 95,384 figure, the 2016 projection of about 92,000 participants by year 10 was accurate, not “far surpassed.”
5. The H-1B rationale does not apply to cap-exempt employers. Universities, nonprofit research organizations, and government research organizations are not subject to the H-1B cap, so OPT employment there cannot circumvent it. The fee applies anyway, burdening university research with no connection to the stated goal.
6. Benefits are unquantified while costs are $4.1 billion per year (Sec. VII.A). DHS criticizes the 2016 rule for not quantifying effects on U.S. workers, then quantifies no benefits of its own: no jobs, wages, or fraud reduction. The opportunity-cost method assumes lost OPT is worth no more than the unpaid fee, which builds the conclusion into the premise. It also omits lost tuition and income-tax revenue while counting FICA gains as a benefit.

7. The statutory findings contradict each other (Sec. VII.D, VII.F). The UMRA section states the rule “would not result in” a $100 million expenditure, then states it “exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold.” The Federalism section finds no substantial direct costs to states, yet the RFA analysis treats all 1,044 public institutions as state-run. State universities would pay a large share of the fees, and DHS admits it consulted no state governments.
8. DHS rejected targeted alternatives without adequate reasoning (Sec. IV.C). Extending STEM OPT safeguards (training plans, employer site visits, E-Verify, reporting) to all OPT would target employer fraud directly. DHS rejected these as resource-intensive, but the fee provides no resources either.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule. At minimum, it should reissue the rule with a corrected economic analysis and a 60-day comment period.
