I submit this comment in my individual capacity on the Optional Practical Training Fees proposal, DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I oppose the proposed rule and request that DHS withdraw it.

1. Transition and reliance interests

Sections V.C and VI describe a 60-day transition that DHS says accounts for reliance interests. Under proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(3), a STEM OPT recommendation from a designated school official (DSO) dated on or after the effective date could trigger a $70,000 charge to the school if the initial fee was never paid for that student. This would reach students who already received initial post-completion OPT authorization and began degree-related training under the existing rules. By the time the fee applies, those students may have accepted jobs, begun supervised training, and worked with their employers to prepare Form I-983.

The current filing windows show why advance notice alone leaves some students exposed. Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C), a student may file for the STEM extension up to 90 days before the current employment authorization expires and must file within 60 days of the DSO entering the recommendation in SEVIS. For a student whose authorization expires more than 150 days after the effective date, a recommendation entered before the effective date would already be too old when the filing window opens. Please assess this group's reliance interests separately. If DHS proceeds, it should amend § 214.13(i)(3) to exempt otherwise eligible STEM OPT extensions for students whose initial post-completion OPT was authorized before the effective date, regardless of the date of the extension recommendation.

2. School prepayment and interrupted training

Under Section V.A, school payment is a prerequisite for the DSO to enter the recommendation. A school might decline to pay, pass the charge on to the student or employer, or need more time to approve payment than the filing window allows. If the recommendation is delayed past the filing deadline, a student who otherwise meets the eligibility requirements could have to stop training when the current authorization expires.

Section VII.A's low-participation scenario assumes schools would pay for the STEM-eligible group and attributes lost participation to non-STEM students. Please add scenarios in which schools decline to pay for STEM extensions, pass through the charge, or delay payment. Estimate how many students already on initial OPT would miss the extension filing window or have to interrupt their training under each scenario.

3. Evidence for the fee levels and targeted alternatives

Sections IV and V.A cite fraud prevention and reference H-1B payments in selecting the initial fee. Please disclose the number of confirmed fraud cases and the corresponding number of participants for initial OPT and STEM OPT separately. Explain the basis for expecting $70,000 and $30,000 to reduce fraud and estimate how the proposed amounts and lower amounts would affect both fraudulent and compliant participation.

DHS recognizes existing STEM OPT safeguards, including Form I-983, E-Verify, reporting, and employer site visits. Please compare the cost and likely effectiveness of the proposed fees with audits and site visits targeted at employers or schools flagged by existing reporting or compliance records. Evaluate that alternative specifically for STEM extensions, where these safeguards already apply.

4. Statutory authority for the charge

Section III.A relies in part on INA § 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1), which addresses the terms and conditions of nonimmigrant admission. Section V.A cites 31 U.S.C. § 3302 for depositing the receipts in the U.S. Treasury. I question whether the cited authority extends to requiring a school to pay $70,000 or $30,000 as a condition of making an OPT recommendation. Please identify the statutory text that authorizes DHS to impose this charge on schools and explain how that authority supports the proposed amounts.

Please address these objections and alternatives in any final rule and make the supporting data and methodology available in the public docket. If DHS relies on materially new data or analysis, please provide an opportunity to comment before finalizing the rule.

Regarding Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees
Protecting the wages and job prospects of American workers, especially recent graduates, is a legitimate goal. I oppose the proposed OPT fees because the proposal does not show that they would serve that goal. Keeping OPT with no new fee is better for American workers than a rule whose benefits DHS has not measured, and I ask DHS to withdraw it. This comment addresses Section IV.B (Protecting American Workers) and Section VII.A (regulatory impact analysis).
The proposal does not measure the benefit it claims. Table 1 lists monetized benefits as Not Estimated and lists effects on wages and effects on growth as N/A. A rule that DHS estimates would move about $12.8 billion a year and impose about $4.1 billion a year in costs should rest on at least a rough estimate of how many jobs or how much wage growth American workers would gain. Without one, neither the public nor the agency can judge whether the rule helps the workers it names.
The evidence cited is not about OPT. Section IV.B relies on a proclamation concerning the H-1B program, on unemployment rates for recent computer science graduates, and on a study of the computer science labor market in 2001. None of these isolates the effect of OPT participants on wages or hiring. Unemployment among recent graduates may have many causes, including changes within the technology sector, and the proposal does not try to separate them.
A flat fee does not target low pay. DHS says the aim is to prevent a labor market oversaturated with low-paid foreign workers. The fee is the same whether a graduate is paid well above the market wage or below it. If underpayment is the concern, the direct tools are a wage floor or the attestation that pay match that of similar American workers, which already applies to STEM OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C).
The payroll tax concern belongs to Congress. Section IV.B describes the FICA exemption as an incentive to hire F-1 students. That exemption is set by statute at 26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19). If it distorts hiring, Congress can amend it, and DHS can recommend that. A $70,000 charge is many times larger than the 7.65 percent employer share on an entry-level salary and is not a tailored response.
The proposal may also cost American jobs. Section VI assumes that employers will replace OPT participants with American workers. Some will. Others, particularly firms that operate in several countries, can move the work and the team abroad, and the American jobs connected to that team move with it. Graduates who are turned away may start companies in other countries instead of here. The analysis in Section VII.A does not consider either outcome.
I recommend that DHS leave OPT without the proposed fee and, if it believes OPT harms American workers, do the following.
1. Publish data specific to OPT on wages, occupations, and employers, and estimate the effect on American workers before choosing a remedy.
2. Extend the wage and non-displacement attestations from STEM OPT to all OPT and enforce them.
3. Refer the payroll tax question to Congress.
American workers are better served by rules that address underpayment and displacement directly than by a fee that makes no distinction between good and bad employers.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, ICEB-2026-0100, concerning the imposition of extraordinarily high fees on international students participating in Optional Practical Training (OPT).

Students should not be financially punished for pursuing legitimate educational and professional opportunities in the United States.

2. The proposal would negatively affect U.S. employers and the economy.

OPT allows U.S. employers to recruit graduates who have received education and training from American universities. These graduates contribute valuable knowledge, technical skills, research capabilities, and professional expertise.

Imposing such high fees would discourage employers from hiring international graduates, particularly small businesses, startups, research institutions, and organizations with limited financial resources.

Rather than strengthening the American workforce, this proposal could reduce access to qualified talent and negatively affect innovation, productivity, and economic growth.

3. The proposal would harm American universities and higher education.

International graduates contribute significantly to fields such as science, technology, engineering, mathematics, healthcare, and other specialized professions.

International students make major educational and financial decisions based on the existing immigration and educational framework.

Students commit years of hard work, significant financial resources, and personal sacrifices to earn degrees from American institutions.

6. Fraud prevention should not come at the expense of legitimate students.

However, addressing fraud should involve targeted oversight, stronger compliance measures, effective enforcement, and appropriate penalties for violations.

Imposing fees of $70,000 and $30,000 on the OPT process is an unnecessarily broad approach that could penalize legitimate students and employers who follow the rules.

The government should pursue measures that address actual misconduct without creating unreasonable financial barriers for the entire international student population.

Re: DHS Docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01, Optional Practical Training Fees

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and address documented abuse through targeted oversight. Legitimate OPT is a bridge between U.S. education and practical training. A price barrier of this size would screen for ability to pay, not whether a student, school, or employer complies with the law.

Section V.A would require a school to pay before its designated school official can recommend an otherwise eligible F-1 student. The fee applies even when the school has no identified fraudulent conduct, and DHS acknowledges that schools may pass it to students, other students, or employers (section VI). Schools with fewer resources may decline to recommend qualified students. Students with modest means could lose opportunities even when their training is directly related to their degree. The proposal contains no showing that a $70,000 fee distinguishes a legitimate placement from a fraudulent one better than verification and enforcement would.

The near-term effects reach beyond the student. DHS acknowledges in section VII.A.5.b that reduced OPT participation could mean lost earnings and training, employer productivity losses when replacements are unavailable, and reduced international enrollment and university revenue. Its low-participation scenario assumes non-STEM OPT is no longer recommended. DHS estimates up to $8.07 billion annually in post-transition opportunity costs in that scenario, while warning that its fee-based proxy cannot precisely measure the true loss. Those are not projected GDP losses; they are a reason to take the risk seriously and improve the analysis before imposing the rule.

The proposal would also distort educational choices. Under section VII.A.5.d, a student who uses pre-completion and then post-completion OPT could trigger $100,000 in fees, compared with $70,000 for post-completion OPT alone. DHS expects pre-completion participation to decline. That would deny some students practical experience during their studies for a reason unrelated to the training's quality.

Longer term, a less credible path from a U.S. degree to practical experience may make American universities less attractive, weaken their finances, and reduce the pool of graduates available to U.S. employers and research teams. The Institute of International Education counted 294,253 international students on OPT in 2024/25. The National Science Board reports that 46% of U.S. science and engineering workers with doctoral degrees were foreign born in 2023. These figures do not prove that every OPT participant produces a net economic benefit, but they show why DHS must analyze consequences for talent, research, and competitiveness rather than assume workers are interchangeable.

I recognize DHS's stated concerns about fraud, program integrity, and opportunities for U.S. workers (section IV.C). Fraud should be investigated and punished, and OPT training should be genuinely related to a student's field. But a fee collected from every compliant school does not directly inspect a placement or prove that a U.S. worker was displaced. DHS itself considered site visits, training plans, and reporting requirements (section IV.C). The notice rejects those approaches in part because they require government resources, yet the fee revenue would go to the Treasury and is not earmarked for OPT enforcement. That choice needs a much stronger explanation.

Before any final rule, DHS should publish evidence on the frequency and sources of OPT abuse; explain how the proposed fee amounts were derived and how they would prevent abuse; estimate how many students, schools, and employers would leave the program; assess tuition, research, labor-market, and regional effects; and compare the fee with targeted audits, employer verification, training plans, and enforcement against repeat violators. It should also analyze who would ultimately pay the fee and whether smaller institutions and lower-income students would bear disproportionate costs. The rule should not be finalized without a demonstrated net benefit and a serious assessment of less restrictive alternatives.

Please withdraw this fee proposal and pursue evidence-based oversight that preserves access to legitimate training while protecting workers and enforcing the law.

Sources: DHS NPRM, 91 FR 64566, sections IV.C, V.A, VI, VII.A.5; IIE Open Doors 2025, International Students (opendoorsdata.org/annual-release/international-students/); National Science Board, The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026 (ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsbsep20261/executive-summary).

I write from the employer-and-practitioner side of the U.S. STEM talent pipeline that Optional Practical Training sustains — the pipeline through which American companies hire early-career engineers in data infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and open-source software. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

**1. The fee levels would functionally end OPT for all but a handful of students.**

The proposal requires SEVP-certified schools to pay $70,000 for a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including the 24-month STEM OPT extension — against a current cost of roughly $500 per student, an increase of approximately 13,900%. A student who uses pre-completion OPT and then post-completion OPT would cost their school $100,000. No plausible university budget absorbs this. The result is not a "fee" — it is a de facto elimination of the program for ordinary students, which no statute authorizes DHS to do through a fee rule.

**2. DHS's own proposal concedes the burden falls on students and employers.**

The proposal expressly states that schools may pass the cost on to the F-1 students, to all students, or to employers, and sets no limits on how a school collects or sources the money. In practice this means the fee becomes either a $70,000 surcharge on young graduates who already invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in U.S. tuition and living expenses, or a hiring tax on the American employers who recruit them. Neither outcome is consistent with the rule's stated worker-protection rationale.

**3. The rule harms the U.S. technology sector and American competitiveness.**

OPT and STEM OPT are the principal lawful path by which U.S. employers — including the data-platform and AI teams I work with daily — bring international graduates of American universities onto their engineering staffs. These are graduates of U.S. institutions, trained in U.S. labs and classrooms, who build the data infrastructure and AI systems American companies depend on. A $70,000 entry fee will not redirect these graduates to American employers; it will redirect them to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries competing for the same talent — while American companies lose access to the pipeline and American universities lose the enrollment that sustains STEM programs and research. This proposal punishes rule-following students and the employers who hire them, not fraud. Fraud and program-integrity concerns should be addressed through targeted enforcement and the existing compliance framework, not a blanket fee that makes the program unusable.

**4. The agency's own estimates confirm the rule's disproportionate scale.**

DHS estimates 2,478 affected schools and $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion in annual fees. A rule imposing tens of billions of dollars in annual costs on higher education — with fees deposited into the general Treasury rather than tied to program administration costs — demands far more than a 30-day comment period and a cost-benefit analysis that treats a 13,900% fee increase as routine. The proposed alternative of charging the $70,000 fee again each time a student advances to a higher degree level would compound the harm and should be rejected outright.

**5. Request.**

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. At a minimum, DHS should (a) reject the alternative of re-charging the initial fee at each degree level, (b) set any fee at a level tied to the actual administrative cost of processing OPT recommendations, and (c) provide a comment period commensurate with the rule's multi-billion-dollar annual impact before any re-proposal.

For me, this fee is not $70,000 or $30,000 in isolation. It is $70,000 for my first OPT recommendation plus $30,000 for my STEM extension: $100,000 for one student, one degree, one training path. My school is the legal payer, but the proposal itself says schools may pass the fee on to students, and a school that cannot pay or will not risk $100,000 per student will simply recommend fewer students, or none. That would make OPT effectively unavailable to me, even though I have done everything the program asks: studied full time, kept a 4.0, and taken degree-related internships.

OPT is not optional for me in any real sense. It is the supervised, degree-related work experience my program is designed to lead into, and the only lawful way for me to do that work after graduation. Without it, the training the United States has already invested in through my degree is cut off at graduation, and the employer pipeline from OPT to H-1B to PERM that my whole plan depends on breaks at its first step.

The current Form I-765 adjudication fee is about $500; this proposal is roughly 140 times that, and the proposal contains no cost analysis linking $70,000 or $30,000 to any government cost. The proposal admits the amounts are meant to deter, stating that passing the fee on "would further discourage misuse of OPT," and concedes the money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to the fraud enforcement the rule claims to serve. DHS's own evidence shows fraud concentrated among a small minority: its 2026 probe identified roughly 10,000 suspect participants out of about 194,554 OPT employment authorizations in 2024, around 5 percent. This fee punishes the other roughly 95 percent across every field, and treats compliant universities identically to bad actors. Targeted tools such as site visits, training plans, and employer verification were considered and rejected as too administratively burdensome. New international student enrollment fell 17 percent from fall 2024 to fall 2025, a loss estimated at more than $1.1 billion in revenue and about 23,000 fewer jobs. International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,736 American jobs in 2024-25. Skilled immigration complements rather than displaces U.S. workers: research cited by ITIF found H-1B immigration raised native non-STEM workers' incomes by about 15 percent in computer systems design. Driving away U.S.-trained graduates harms, rather than helps, the domestic workers DHS claims to protect. STEM OPT already requires formal training plans, employer reporting, and site visits; extending verification to post-completion OPT would target fraud directly, at its actual source.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule.

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I strongly support the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations. However, I believe these amounts are too low and encourage DHS to consider significantly higher fees.

My position is straightforward: American immigration policy should serve American citizens, not provide corporations and universities with an inexpensive pipeline into the domestic labor market.

1. If these are truly the world’s best and brightest, the fees should reflect that.

We repeatedly hear that foreign workers and international graduates possess extraordinary skills that American employers supposedly cannot find domestically.

If these individuals are genuinely the next Einsteins, groundbreaking innovators, and irreplaceable scientific minds, why should a $70,000 or even substantially higher fee be considered unreasonable?

Truly exceptional talent should be capable of demonstrating extraordinary economic or scientific value. Institutions and employers claiming that such talent is indispensable should be prepared to substantiate those claims.

The United States has no obligation to subsidize corporate access to international labor simply because employers prefer a larger applicant pool.

2. OPT should not function as an alternative employment visa program.

F-1 status exists primarily for education. OPT has expanded opportunities for foreign students to participate in the American labor market beyond their academic studies.

DHS itself identifies concerns involving fraud, program integrity, and the potential use of OPT to circumvent H-1B fees and requirements.

These concerns deserve meaningful regulatory action.

The United States should not allow temporary educational status to become an inexpensive substitute for employment-based immigration procedures.

3. American graduates deserve priority.

American students invest considerable time and financial resources in obtaining degrees, particularly in engineering, computer science, technology, and other technical disciplines.

Their employment prospects should matter when federal agencies evaluate programs that increase the supply of available labor.

Employers claiming domestic talent shortages should demonstrate that they have offered competitive compensation, invested in training, and made meaningful efforts to recruit qualified Americans.

Expanding access to foreign labor should not become a substitute for developing the domestic workforce.

4. Corporate inconvenience is not sufficient justification for low fees.

Universities and employers may argue that these costs discourage international recruitment or limit participation.

That is not necessarily a defect in the policy.

If the objective is to discourage routine reliance on OPT while preserving access where institutions can justify the substantial expense, the fee should be high enough to influence institutional decisions.

DHS should evaluate higher initial and subsequent fees, with a transparent economic and legal justification.

Importantly, the proposed rule places payment responsibility on educational institutions. DHS should also examine whether schools might transfer these costs to students or receive indirect reimbursement from employers, and establish appropriate disclosure and enforcement safeguards.

5. Protecting the domestic labor market is a legitimate national objective.

The economic interests of universities, multinational corporations, and immigration beneficiaries are not automatically identical to those of American workers.

The relevant questions are whether OPT delivers measurable benefits to the United States, whether program participants fill genuinely unmet needs, and whether the program affects domestic hiring, wages, and career opportunities.

Those questions should be evaluated using evidence rather than assertions that foreign labor is inherently indispensable.

Conclusion

I support finalizing the proposed OPT fee rule, but recommend increasing the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

If institutions and employers truly believe these candidates possess rare, extraordinary, and economically indispensable abilities, they should be able to demonstrate that value.

If substantially higher fees make routine OPT recruitment uneconomical, that outcome should prompt serious examination of whether the program was being used for exceptional talent or simply convenient access to additional labor.

American workers should not be expected to compete against an international labor pipeline structured around the convenience of employers and educational institutions.

American workers first. Domestic workforce development first. Corporate convenience last.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule because DHS has not shown that the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee bear a reasonable relationship to the cost of administering OPT. More importantly, the NPRM makes clear that deterrence is not merely incidental. DHS expects the fees to reduce OPT participation, discourage the use of OPT as an alternative to H-1B, and cause schools to be more selective in making recommendations.[1] A charge deliberately set at a level expected to prevent otherwise eligible students and institutions from using the program is fundamentally different from an administrative fee calibrated to program costs.

1. DHS does not derive the proposed amounts from administrative cost.

The NPRM does not derive the $70,000 amount from the cost of reviewing an OPT recommendation, maintaining SEVIS, conducting compliance checks, or investigating fraud. Instead, DHS compares the proposed amount with its proposed H-1B fee and with the cost of one or two years of U.S. higher education.[1] Those comparisons may explain why DHS believes $70,000 is large enough to alter behavior, but they do not establish that administering an OPT request costs anything close to $70,000.

The contrast is striking in DHS's own regulatory analysis. Under its primary scenario, DHS estimates recurring fee transfers of about $12.4 billion per year after the first year.[1] Separately, DHS estimates that the additional annual institutional review and payment-processing costs created by the rule would be about $15.7 million.[1] These figures are not the same category of cost, and $15.7 million is not the total cost of administering OPT. However, the roughly 790-fold difference reinforces the need for DHS to explain what governmental costs, risks, or programmatic burdens justify fees of $70,000 and $30,000 per student.

2. The proposed STEM OPT fee is even harder to justify on an incremental-cost basis.

A STEM OPT extension is not the first review of a student's practical training eligibility. The student has already completed a qualifying U.S. degree, obtained a DSO recommendation for post-completion OPT, received employment authorization, and participated in an existing period of practical training.

STEM OPT adds safeguards, including Form I-983, E-Verify participation, employer attestations, reporting requirements, and possible site visits. But the relevant question is the additional governmental cost created by extending an already approved OPT period. The NPRM does not demonstrate that these activities create a governmental cost remotely approaching $30,000 per student.

The transition structure makes this problem even clearer. DHS's first-year analysis treats certain students already on OPT who later seek STEM OPT as subject to the full $70,000 initial fee because the new fee had not been paid when their original OPT began.[1] Such a student may already have spent close to a year in lawful, monitored practical training. It is difficult to identify what new administrative event at the STEM-extension stage could suddenly justify a $70,000 charge.

3. Requiring the school to pay does not make the economic cost disappear.

The rule formally places the payment obligation on the SEVP-certified educational institution, but changing who writes the check does not eliminate the burden. For a public university, a large transfer to the Federal Treasury may simply move resources from a state-supported public institution to the Federal Government. Those resources could otherwise support instruction, research, student services, or other public purposes.

This point is secondary, but it illustrates why describing the payment merely as a "transfer" can obscure its real consequences. Someone ultimately bears the cost, whether it is the university, a department, an employer, other students, or the affected international student indirectly.

If DHS needs additional resources for SEVIS administration, fraud investigations, employer monitoring, or compliance enforcement, it should identify those costs and establish a proportionate fee. It could also expand targeted audits and verification measures. The proposed rule instead uses an exceptionally large financial barrier to reduce participation. DHS should explain why deterrence of otherwise eligible practical training is an appropriate use of the statutory authority cited for this rule and why narrower, cost-related alternatives would be inadequate.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule because it risks causing the United States to permanently lose highly trained Ph.D. graduates after U.S. universities, research institutions, and funding agencies have already invested years and substantial resources in training them.

I earned my Ph.D. in physics from the University of Maryland, College Park, and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher at Duke University. My own path is directly relevant to this proposal: the United States invested years in training me as a scientist, and I am now continuing to contribute to research at another U.S. university. A policy that makes post-graduation practical training prohibitively expensive risks breaking exactly this kind of training-to-research pipeline.

1. A research Ph.D. represents a large investment before OPT even begins.

NSF data show that physics Ph.D. recipients spend a median of approximately 6.3 years from the start of graduate school to the doctorate, and about 90 percent receive tuition remission.[1] Even using a modest illustrative graduate stipend of $40,000 per year, six years of stipend support alone amounts to approximately $240,000.

But stipend support is only one part of the investment. A research Ph.D. also requires tuition support, faculty and staff time, laboratory space, equipment, consumables, computing resources, administrative support, and research infrastructure. Experimental STEM programs can require particularly expensive laboratories and equipment. The actual institutional and research resources invested in producing a Ph.D. can therefore readily exceed $500,000.

The proposed OPT fee would create its largest barrier at exactly the point when this investment begins producing its greatest return. After roughly six years of training, a newly graduated Ph.D. is becoming capable of independent research and highly specialized technical work. If a $70,000 OPT barrier causes that person to leave the United States, the loss is not merely several years of OPT employment. The United States risks permanently losing the researcher together with the return on the much larger training investment already made.

2. The lost return can extend over decades.

NSF data show that among temporary-visa holders who received U.S. science and engineering doctorates, approximately 73 percent were still in the United States about five years after graduation, and approximately 68 percent of an earlier cohort remained after about ten years.[2]

These figures show that post-graduation practical training is often the beginning of a much longer U.S. career. A person who leaves because the initial post-graduation path becomes economically inaccessible may instead spend the next ten, twenty, or thirty years conducting research, developing technology, teaching students, starting companies, and building institutions in another country.

This matters because temporary visa holders constitute a large share of the U.S. doctoral talent pipeline. In 2024 they earned approximately 61 percent of U.S. doctorates in computer and information sciences, 54 percent in engineering, and 52 percent in mathematics and statistics.[3] Policies affecting whether those graduates remain can therefore materially affect the U.S. scientific and technical workforce.

The proposed policy creates a poor economic tradeoff. After the United States has spent years and potentially several hundred thousand dollars producing highly specialized human capital, a $70,000 to $100,000 OPT-related barrier may cause that human capital to move to another economy just as it becomes most productive. The receiving country may then obtain decades of future economic and scientific benefit without having borne the original cost of training that researcher.

For these reasons, I urge DHS not to finalize the proposed fee structure. At minimum, DHS should conduct a serious analysis of the long-term human-capital loss associated with reduced retention of U.S.-trained Ph.D. graduates.

I am an F-1 international student at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, opposing the proposed OPT fees. Having worked at an early-stage technology startup building production software, I have seen how practical training lets international students apply their American education while contributing to U.S. businesses.

1. Financial Capacity Does Not Establish Merit or Compliance

The proposal does not adequately demonstrate that a substantial fee will distinguish legitimate OPT participants from those seeking to abuse the program. A university's ability to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation says little about a student's qualifications, whether their work relates to their degree, or whether their employer will comply with the law. Conversely, inability to pay does not indicate fraud.

Reducing participation is not the same as reducing fraud. DHS should distinguish benefits arising from lower participation from measurable improvements in compliance and explain why these fee amounts would deter fraudulent activity more effectively than legitimate training.

2. Repeated Fees Penalize Pre-Completion and STEM OPT

Under the proposal, a school could pay $70,000 for initial pre-completion OPT, $30,000 for subsequent post-completion OPT, and another $30,000 for a STEM OPT extension—a cumulative $130,000.

As a student approaching graduation, I have considered lawful options for degree-related engineering work while still enrolled, including pre-completion OPT. The proposed structure could make this pathway substantially more expensive solely because training begins before graduation. Even DHS acknowledges the fee differential may discourage pre-completion OPT.

Students should not be discouraged from legitimate training simply because of when it occurs. DHS should explain why each successive fee is justified.

3. Existing Students' Reliance Interests Warrant Stronger Protection

I pursued my education and professional opportunities under a framework permitting eligible F-1 students to seek degree-related practical training. OPT is not a guarantee of employment or immigration status, but its availability is a meaningful factor in academic and career planning.

The proposal's transition depends on whether a student receives a dated Designated School Official recommendation before the rule takes effect. That offers little protection to students who have already committed years and resources to U.S. education but are not yet ready to request OPT. With my anticipated graduation in May 2027, a rule finalized before then could materially alter the opportunities available to me.

DHS cites approximately 20% OPT participation among higher-education F-1 students in 2024. But a single year's participation rate cannot show how many students eventually use OPT or their enrollment motives. Current undergraduates anticipating post-graduation training would not necessarily appear in that statistic. Nor must OPT be a student's sole motivation for enrollment to create a reliance interest.

I urge DHS to grandfather students enrolled in eligible programs before the effective date, rather than relying only on the date of an OPT recommendation.

4. The Economic Analysis Understates Lost Opportunities

The regulatory impact analysis should separate changes in baseline enrollment from participation changes caused by the fees. When both vary at once, the scenario difference cannot all be attributed to the fees. DHS should provide a common no-rule baseline and sensitivity analyses.

Forgone fee payments are also an inadequate proxy for the value of opportunities lost. An engineering role's value is not limited to what a school, student, or employer can pay. Legitimate OPT work can strengthen teams, support technological development, and spread knowledge within U.S. companies.

Finally, the historical computer-science labor-market research cited by DHS does not directly measure the effects of these fees or isolate economic harm from OPT fraud. Potential harm to particular worker groups deserves consideration, but DHS should also acknowledge the research's limits and offsetting effects.

Conclusion

I support immigration enforcement, employer accountability, and prevention of OPT abuse. But the proposed fees would place enormous burdens on legitimate students and universities without adequate evidence that they improve compliance. My experience shows that practical training can be a genuine extension of an American education and a meaningful contribution to American businesses.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees, protect currently enrolled students, and pursue targeted, evidence-based alternatives.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule because its effects would extend far beyond students who eventually apply for OPT. By making post-graduation practical training substantially more difficult or expensive, the rule would make U.S. higher education less attractive to prospective international students and reduce the broader economic contribution of international education.

1. International students already make a large economic contribution to the United States.

According to the Institute of International Education, U.S. institutions hosted approximately 1.18 million international students in the 2024-25 academic year, including 357,231 undergraduate students, 488,481 graduate students, and 294,253 students participating in OPT.[1]

NAFSA estimates that international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25.[2] Their spending supports universities as well as housing, food, transportation, insurance, retail, and other local industries. Importantly, NAFSA's economic-impact calculation excludes students participating in OPT.[2]

International students also provide important tuition revenue to many U.S. institutions, particularly in undergraduate and master's programs.

2. The economic contribution continues after graduation.

NSF reports that among 2024 U.S. doctorate recipients with definite domestic commitments, median expected salaries in the physical sciences were approximately $65,000 for postdocs and $120,000 for industry employment. Engineering industry positions had a median of approximately $125,000, and computer and information sciences industry positions approximately $180,000.[3]

At $65,000 per year, three years of postdoctoral employment represents approximately $195,000 in labor income. At $120,000 per year, three years represents approximately $360,000. These figures exclude research output, intellectual property, tax revenue, technological development, business formation, and other spillover benefits.

For many graduates, OPT is the beginning of a much longer U.S. career. Over ten or twenty years, the economic contribution can be many times larger than the proposed OPT fee.

3. The proposed rule can affect enrollment years before any OPT fee becomes due.

Students compare the United States with Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe, Australia, and other destinations before deciding where to spend several years obtaining a degree. The possibility of gaining practical experience after graduation has value even for students who ultimately do not use OPT.

In my academic circle, many international students explicitly considered post-graduation OPT when deciding whether to study in the United States. In my experience, roughly half regarded the OPT framework as an important factor in that choice. This is a personal observation rather than a national estimate, but it illustrates why actual OPT usage does not measure the value prospective students place on having that option.

The United States therefore faces two separate losses: it may lose graduates who have already been educated here, and it may lose future students who decide from the outset to take their tuition, living expenditures, and eventual professional careers to another country.

DHS's own regulatory analysis acknowledges that the proposal may reduce international enrollment but does not quantify that effect with confidence.[4] Given the scale of international education, this uncertainty is economically significant.

For these reasons, I urge DHS not to finalize the proposed fee structure without a fuller analysis of its likely effects on international enrollment, university finances, local economies, and the long-term economic contribution of international graduates.

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule because DHS has not adequately explained why its authority to regulate the "time" and "conditions" of F-1 status permits a $70,000 monetary condition designed in part to deter otherwise eligible participation. I also believe the proposed 60-day transition does not adequately address serious reliance interests created by the longstanding OPT framework.

1. Authority to regulate practical training does not automatically authorize a $70,000 deterrent payment.

DHS relies in significant part on INA section 214(a)(1), codified at 8 U.S.C. section 1184(a)(1), which authorizes the Government to prescribe the "time" and "conditions" of a nonimmigrant's admission.[1]

In Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), the D.C. Circuit relied on this authority when it upheld OPT and STEM OPT as permissible practical training connected to F-1 status.[2] But that case did not decide whether section 1184(a)(1) permits a $70,000 monetary condition deliberately designed to reduce participation.

This distinction matters because DHS states that the fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than retained by ICE as OPT program revenue.[3] DHS should explain why authority over F-1 conditions extends to a monetary exaction of this magnitude and purpose.

2. OPT has been legally sustained as practical training connected to education.

Washington Alliance treated OPT as practical training related to the educational purposes of F-1 status.[2] Existing regulations also require OPT employment to be directly related to the student's major area of study.

If DHS believes fraud or inadequate supervision requires stronger enforcement, it can use employer verification, reporting, audits, site visits, or other training-related conditions. DHS should explain why a very large financial payment is reasonably connected to practical training rather than functioning primarily as a barrier to participation.

3. The proposed 60-day transition does not adequately address reliance interests.

In Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the Supreme Court held that when an agency changes a longstanding policy, it must consider serious reliance interests created by the existing framework.[4]

For international students, the relevant reliance decision often occurs years before an OPT application. A Ph.D. student may choose the United States five or six years before graduation and complete nearly the entire degree under a system that includes post-completion OPT and STEM OPT. Those years cannot be recovered or shifted to another country's educational system during a 60-day transition.

In my academic circle, many international students explicitly considered post-graduation OPT when deciding whether to study in the United States. In my experience, roughly half regarded the OPT framework as an important factor. This is anecdotal, but it illustrates why reliance cannot be measured only at the moment of an OPT recommendation.

4. Students already on OPT present an especially strong transition case.

Under the proposed rule, a student who lawfully began post-completion OPT under the existing framework may later face the full $70,000 fee when seeking STEM OPT because no new-rule initial fee had previously been paid.[3]

That student chose the U.S. degree, completed it, entered OPT, and began the practical-training sequence under the prior rules. Treating the STEM recommendation as a new event does not eliminate those earlier reliance interests.

The Administrative Procedure Act directs courts to set aside agency action that is arbitrary or capricious or exceeds statutory authority. 5 U.S.C. section 706(2)(A), (C).[5]

At minimum, DHS should consider grandfathering students already enrolled in F-1 degree programs before publication of the final rule. A narrower alternative would be to grandfather students who had already graduated or begun post-completion OPT, including allowing them to complete an otherwise eligible STEM OPT extension under the existing fee structure.

Arbitrary and Capricious Flaws in the Proposed OPT Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program. As a Master’s graduate from the University of California, San Diego, currently employed as a Software Development Engineer at Amazon, I urge the withdrawal of this rule due to its severe logical flaws, factual inaccuracies, and arbitrary nature under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Specifically, the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) contains three major loopholes:

1. Contradictory Funding Logic (The "Miscellaneous Receipt" Flaw)
The NPRM claims that the fees are necessary because DHS lacks the compliance resources to scale its anti-fraud efforts. However, in Section IV.C, the NPRM admits that ICE has no legal authority to retain these funds, stating that the fees "would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt." It is inherently arbitrary and capricious to justify a massive fee by claiming a lack of agency resources, while simultaneously acknowledging that not a single dollar of the collected fee will actually go toward funding ICE's investigative or administrative operations. This transforms the proposed "fee" into an unauthorized, punitive tax.

2. Factually Incorrect Justification for the $70,000 Amount
The NPRM attempts to justify the exorbitant $70,000 initial fee by claiming it was "selected... comparable to the fee for H-1B visas" to deter employers from bypassing H-1B costs. 1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

DHS also says a main purpose is to discourage OPT use, and receipts would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, not to ICE. A charge meant to deter conduct and raise general revenue is a tax, and only Congress can tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. U.S., 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). INA 214(a) says nothing about fees. A federal court struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee on exactly this ground in June 2026, the First Circuit refused to stay that ruling, and a second court blocked the fee in September. Pegging the OPT fee to it invites the same result.
(2) It does not fit the fraud problem. DHS's evidence is a few prosecutions, a news report, and a figure sourced to a YouTube video, against 194,554 OPT participants in 2024. A $70,000 charge screens by ability to pay, not legitimacy, and because the money goes to the general Treasury it funds no investigators or site visits. Congress's own anti-fraud fee for H-1B and L petitions is set by statute and dedicated to fraud detection.

DHS projects $8.4-$16.5 billion a year in fees and costs ranging from $32 million to $8.2 billion, yet says it "cannot confidently predict" the drop in participation, the rule's central effect. Studies of a $100,000 charge (what a STEM student would face here) project 35% fewer international graduate applicants (Economic Innovation Group), 80% of students reconsidering staying (Institute for Progress), and up to $4 billion a year in lost university revenue (Clemens). DHS also ignores reliance interests of students who enrolled and paid tuition under current rules (DHS v. Regents, 2020).
(4) Americans would pay. DHS admits schools may pass costs to "all students." International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25 (NAFSA). 56% of affected schools are small entities, and DHS estimates 98 would pay fees above 20% of revenue. Startups and small employers could not compete for U.S.-trained graduates.

Yet the fee falls on schools, and Section V.A states it is not tied to any employer. Paying $70,000 to a school does nothing to verify that a job is real. Targeted measures DHS already uses for STEM OPT, such as Form I-983 training plans, E-Verify, and employer site visits, address employer fraud directly. The rule harms university research without serving its own goals. One stated purpose is preventing OPT from being used to circumvent the H-1B cap. Universities and nonprofit research institutions are cap-exempt, so OPT employment there circumvents nothing. Yet the fee still applies, raising costs for academic research and early-career researchers. The rule also expects schools to steer students away from pre-completion OPT to avoid paying twice (Section VII.A.5.d). The economic analysis is internally inconsistent.

Section IV.B cites 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024. Section VII.A.3 uses 95,384 as its high estimate for the same year.
The paperwork analysis (Section VII.E) estimates 226,200 responses at 5 minutes each. Its own footnote cites 289,938, and the cost analysis assumes a full hour of staff time per application.

I am an international student studying in the United States on an F-1 visa, and I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions.
Start with the scale. The current federal filing fee for an OPT work permit application is $470. This proposal would attach a $70,000 charge to the school's recommendation alone, roughly 150 times the existing fee and more than the entire first-year salary of many entry-level jobs. A fee bears no relationship to the actual cost of processing a recommendation, and no relationship to any service provided. It is not a user fee. It is a price on participation itself.
The Department justifies these fees partly as a tool against fraud. But a blanket fee is not an anti-fraud measure. Fraud is committed by a small number of bad actors, and a fee does not screen them out; if anything, well-funded fraudulent schemes are the ones best able to pay. The people a $70,000 fee actually screens out are ordinary, compliant students and the schools that follow the rules, complete SEVIS reporting, and verify employers and training plans. Punishing the compliant majority for the conduct of a few is not program integrity. Targeted enforcement against the institutions and employers that abuse the program already exists, and it addresses fraud directly without ending the program for everyone else.
The practical effect of this rule would be to end OPT for all but a small, wealthy minority. Most universities, especially public ones, cannot absorb $70,000 per student, and the Department acknowledges schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Students who cannot pay will lose access to the practical training that has been part of the F-1 program for more than three decades. Employers, faced with a five-figure charge tied to one candidate, will simply hire a different one. The rule would divide otherwise equally eligible graduates into two classes: those who can buy access to work experience, and those who cannot.
The damage would extend well beyond the students affected. In a recent survey of 734 international students, 87 percent planned to use OPT, but 80 percent said they would be less likely to stay and work in the United States if this fee were adopted, and 69 percent said they would not have enrolled in a U.S. program at all had it been in effect. The United States educates much of the world's top STEM talent and then, under this proposal, would charge it out of the country, while Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia actively recruit the same graduates. Fewer than 200,000 students participate in OPT in a year; they are not a threat to the American workforce. They are part of its research labs, hospitals, and technology sector, and this rule treats them as a revenue source instead.
Finally, I ask the Department to respect reliance interests. Students choose schools, sign leases, turn down opportunities in other countries, and plan their lives around the rules in place when they enroll and when their schools recommend them for OPT. At a minimum, no fee should apply to any recommendation issued before a final rule takes effect, and no $30,000 fee should be imposed on a STEM OPT extension for a student already in post-completion OPT.
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. If the Department's concern is program integrity, the answer is targeted oversight of bad actors, not a fee that prices legitimate students out of a program that has served the United States well for over 30 years.
Thank you for considering this comment.

I am an early-career software engineer with a U.S. master's degree in computer science, on post-completion OPT at a technology company in the San Francisco Bay Area, paid at market rate. I ask DHS to withdraw this rule, or at minimum to fix the transition provision described in point 1.

1. The rule penalizes students already on OPT, and its transition text is internally inconsistent (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3); Sec. V.C, VI).

Under 214.13(i)(2), the $30,000 fee applies only to a student who "has previously paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." A student whose initial OPT began before the effective date never paid that fee, so the STEM extension would cost $70,000. A student who starts OPT after the effective date would pay $30,000 for the identical extension. The RIA confirms this reading: its Year 1 model assumes STEM OPT participants pay $70,000. DHS gives no reason for charging more to the students with the strongest reliance interests.

Those interests are concrete. Students on initial OPT accepted jobs, signed leases, and declined other options in reliance on the 24-month extension under the 2016 rule; employers invested in I-983 training plans. Calling these interests "outweighed" in one sentence is not the weighing required by DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020).

My own STEM OPT recommendation will likely be dated after the proposed effective date. My school would owe $70,000, likely passed to me or my employer, for work I already perform lawfully. No fraud is involved.

Request: exempt from all fees any STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT EAD was approved before the effective date.

2. The fee is a revenue measure, not a condition of admission (Sec. IV.C).

DHS states that the fee is not based on processing cost, will be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, will not fund ICE or SEVP, and was set to be "comparable" to H-1B fees. DHS projects $12.8 billion in annual transfers. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service and paid into the general fund is a tax. INA 214(a) authority over the "time and conditions" of admission is not taxing power (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). A federal court vacated the $100,000 H-1B payment on this ground (California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 8, 2026).

3. The fee cannot address the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A, IV.C).

DHS cites about 10,000 students tied to suspect employers. In 2024, 194,554 students were on OPT and 165,524 on STEM OPT. The fee falls on all of them. It is also paid before the DSO recommendation and, in DHS's words, "would not be tied to a specific employer." The fraud described occurs at the employer and worksite; a fee paid before an employer is known cannot screen for it, and because the money goes to the Treasury it adds no investigative capacity. DHS set aside targeted tools (site visits, training plans for all OPT, employer verification) mainly because they take resources, which is not a reasoned basis for choosing a measure that does not reach the problem (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

NAFSA projects up to 111,000 fewer international students this fall, costing about $3.4 billion and nearly 40,000 U.S. jobs. This rule would deepen that loss.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers instead of a blanket fee on all students.

I submit this comment as a Designated School Official (DSO). I advise F-1 and J-1 students on federal regulations, including Optional Practical Training (OPT). These comments reflect my professional experience administering the F-1 program.

I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. DHS should instead integrate practical training into the academic experience, remove financial barriers, and give schools an appropriate role in authorizing eligible students.

1. The proposal makes schools fiscal intermediaries for an individual benefit

Under current regulations, F-1 students who meet eligibility requirements may apply for OPT. The DSO verifies eligibility (one completed academic year, valid F-1 status, timely filing) and provides the recommendation in SEVIS. USCIS makes the final determination on employment authorization.

The proposed rule would require schools to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one, including STEM OPT. This makes schools financially responsible for a benefit that belongs to the student. Students need not have an employer when they apply, so reliance on employers as a funding source does not reflect how OPT operates.

2. The proposal assigns schools responsibilities that belong to the government

Investigating employers. Identifying fraudulent employers is an enforcement responsibility of DHS, including HSI. DSOs lack the authority and information to do it.

Ranking programs. Faced with these fees, schools would have to decide which students or fields justify the expense. Nothing in the regulations or the DSO’s role supports ranking fields of study by perceived value.

Assuming others’ decisions. If schools limit recommendations based on perceived fraud risk or program value, they take on judgments that belong to federal agencies and invite claims of unequal treatment. The alternative is absorbing costs they have no obligation to pay.

Either outcome undermines the DSO’s role as a source of accurate, consistent guidance.

3. The fee is not tied to fraud prevention and restricts access to OPT

The fee applies regardless of risk. Every recommendation is charged whether or not there are indicators of fraud. It is a barrier to participation, not a measure against misconduct.

The revenue is not dedicated to enforcement. As I understand the proposal, it would go to the general Treasury, not to oversight or investigations.

It restricts a benefit through regulation. Congress has considered changes to practical training and has not enacted them. Fees that make participation financially impossible for most institutions achieve a similar result through rulemaking.

4. The proposal would undermine the international student experience

Tran and Soejatminah (2017) describe how work-integrated learning helps international students develop the skills and attributes employers seek. (Ly Thi Tran & Sri Soejatminah, “Integration of Work Experience and Learning for International Students: From Harmony to Inequality,” Journal of Studies in International Education, 21(3), 261-277.) Making OPT inaccessible would create inequality between students based on their institution’s finances rather than their qualifications.

5. Recommended alternative

Integrate practical training into the academic experience. Rather than treating OPT as an entirely separate process after completion of academic coursework, DHS should explore ways to incorporate practical training into the student's overall degree experience. Planning with academic departments, establishing appropriate learning objectives, and documenting relevant training expectations would provide schools with a legitimate academic basis for oversight. This would also encourage students to view practical training as an extension of their education rather than simply an employment benefit.

Eliminate the application fee. Remove the per-recommendation fee, and reconsider the separate employment authorization application fee for OPT, so that the cost of access does not determine who can use a benefit the regulations grant.

Make the DSO’s recommendation the operative authorization. Schools already verify eligibility and enter recommendations in SEVIS. Treating the recommendation as authorization, subject to DHS oversight and audit authority, would remove a duplicative adjudication step while DHS retains enforcement authority.

Target fraud directly, don't dance around the issue and have your agencies do their job, not the schools. 

Conclusion

The proposed rule shifts substantial financial responsibility to schools, pressures DSOs into decisions outside their authority, and would make OPT inaccessible at many institutions regardless of student eligibility. I urge DHS to withdraw it.

OPT should remain an opportunity based on student eligibility and regulatory compliance, not on an institution's ability to pay an extraordinary fee.

To the Department of Homeland Security:
As an F-1 student in the U.S., I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee and $30,000 subsequent fee (91 Fed. Reg. 64566) and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. OPT access was vital to my decision to study in the U.S.; 69% of F-1 students would not have enrolled—and 37% definitely would not have—under these fees (Institute for Progress, Oct. 6, 2026).  
1. Wealth Replaces Merit and Compliance
These fees tie training access to wealth rather than merit, qualifications, or compliance. Most entry-level jobs pay under $70,000/yr, so a 12-month fee exceeds a graduate's annual salary in nursing, teaching, research, pharmacy, and agriculture. DHS's claim that $70,000 is "on par" with 1–2 years of tuition (91 Fed. Reg. 64575) lacks data: public non-resident tuition is often $20,273–$25,938/yr ($70,000 is 86% of $81,090 4-year tuition), and campus OPT fees are ~$150.  
2. The "Pass-Through" Premise Fails
The rule charges 2,478 schools—including 1,044 public schools (42%) excluded from DHS's institutional analysis (91 Fed. Reg. 64593)—assuming they can pass the $8.4B–$16.5B/yr cost ($109.4B/10 yrs, 91 Fed. Reg. 64583–84) to students or employers (91 Fed. Reg. 64575). All 3 options fail:  
 Schools Cannot Pay: State anti-donation clauses (Tex. Const. art. III, §§ 50–52; La. Const. art. VII, § 14), fee rules (UNC Policy Manual 1000.1.2.1[R]), and budgets bar using public funds for private fees.  
 Students Cannot Pay Upfront: Students apply 90 days before to 60 days after graduation (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)), usually before a job offer. Because payment precedes SEVIS recommendation (Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii)) and refunds end once an EAD issues (Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(1)–(2)), students risk $70,000 upfront with no offer or refund right, driving debt and employer dependence. Foreign-exchange caps (China's $50,000/yr limit) also block payments.  
 Employers Cannot Pay: Most applicants lack an employer when applying. Even with offers, $70,000 payments exceed $50,000 state procurement limits, trigger foreign-gift reporting ($250,000 under 20 U.S.C. § 1011f; $50,000 under CHIPS Act § 10339B), and exceed Pay.gov's $24,999 card cap and $5,000 state p-card limits—far beyond DHS's 5-min to 1-hr burden estimate (91 Fed. Reg. 64585, 64598).  
3. No Statutory Authority and Flawed Fraud Deterrence
I support protecting U.S. workers and stopping fraud, but ability to pay does not prove compliance and lower participation is not proof of prevented fraud. Because fees go to the general Treasury (31 U.S.C. § 3302; 91 Fed. Reg. 64576) rather than ICE oversight, this is an unauthorized tax under INA § 214(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(a)(1) (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229 (2026)). DHS also benchmarked the fee to a vacated $100,000 H-1B fee under Proclamation 10973 (91 Fed. Reg. 64575; California v. Mullin, 833 F. Supp. 3d 50 (D. Mass. 2026); Global Nurse Force v. Trump (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2026)) and contradicted its Aug. 2026 H-1B rule exempting universities from a $103,265 fee (91 Fed. Reg. 54817, 54831). DHS should use targeted compliance and employer enforcement instead.  
4. Penalties on Pre-Completion OPT, Transfers, and Higher Degrees
The rule penalizes pre-completion OPT—capped at 20 hrs/wk (8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(A)) with zero cited fraud—charging $100,000 ($70,000 + $30,000) if a student does an internship before post-completion OPT (91 Fed. Reg. 64590), even after Aug. 18 & 24, 2026 SEVP CPT limits forced healthcare, pharmacy, and business students into pre-completion OPT. It also risks duplicate $70,000 transfer fees, and I oppose charging $70,000 again at each higher degree level ($140,000–$170,000 total, 91 Fed. Reg. 64577).  
5. Retroactive Impact and Harm to Critical Sectors
A 60-day effective date and 30-day comment window on a $12.8B/yr rule (91 Fed. Reg. 64579; E.O. 12866 § 6(a)(1)) harm students who committed to degrees years ago. Worse, under Proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.13(i)(3), current OPT holders seeking a STEM extension after the effective date owe $70,000, not $30,000 (91 Fed. Reg. 64583). F-1 students add $42.9B and 355,736 jobs (NAFSA & JB Int'l, Aug. 11, 2026), founded 25% of U.S. $1B+ startups (NFAP, June 2026), cross-subsidize domestic courses (Shih, 156 J. Pub. Econ. 170 (2017)), and staff labs, hospitals, and rural clinics, where curbing OPT risks 443,000 jobs over 10 yrs (Business Roundtable).  
Requested Actions: Please withdraw this rule. At a minimum, DHS must set far lower fees, grandfather all current F-1 students and active OPT holders (including STEM extensions), exempt pre-completion OPT, reject repeat fees for transfers or higher degrees, and refund fees whenever no EAD issues.  
Thank you for considering this comment.

Respectfully submitted,

As a scientist working in biomedical research for over a decade, I have met many incredible international scientists who started their careers pursuing an education in the United States. These scientists are frequently as talented and competent as, if not necessarily moreso than, some of the American researchers I have worked alongside during that same period of time. Their skills are sufficiently niche and valuable that it naturally makes sense for American industry and academic labs to retain their labor beyond the period of time provided by their training visas. It therefore follows that regulations crafted with a clear intention to reduce the number of OPT participants is a direct attack on the productivity of our biomedical output. Long-term, this change will cripple the strength of our biomedical research system by discouraging international students from applying for OPT, and downstream, less likely to apply to our advanced educational programs to begin with.

In our current academic environment of government-imposed research austerity, the requirements for a successful academic career domestically and abroad have shifted towards a de facto need for post-baccalaureate or postdoctoral research experience. OPT, then, is a practically required element of advanced education for international students. Adding the undue burden of up to $100,000 in personal expenses to pursue institutional recommendations for an OPT or STEM OPT extension is very blatantly an attempt to discourage applications in the first place. While the regulations offer the institution to bear the cost of the recommendation, they suggest that they could shift the cost to "F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers". Often times, STEM OPT's employers are the same or another academic institution. The practical effect of this is that universities will refuse to put up $100,000 for each of their international students, and that will kill the OPT system for all but the wealthiest international students. 

Frequently, the academic workers on OPT (and especially STEM OPT) will opt to continue working in the United States after their extended visa, requiring tedious additional efforts to obtain a J-1 or H1B visa that include necessary time away from work back in their home countries. This additional time results in a decrease in research productivity for their employers, and a reduced quality of life for the employee caused by the interruption in employment. The fact that so many OPT visaholders proceed with these costly and personally destabilizing bureacratic processes is proof of their desire to continue contributing to our nation's research efforts.

These regulations are justified as "strengthen[ing] the integrity of the immigration system, and protect[ing] U.S. workers". They accomplish neither of these claimed purposes.

The rationale proposed by DHS's SEVP in this docket involves a convoluted fantasy where F-1 visaholders are contracting the services of illicit shell companies en masse to stay in the United States without having to pursue relevant work. These reports are based entirely on the claims of an out-of-control agency that has provably attempted to cover up the deaths of both nonimmigrant residents and American citizens at the hands of their agents. 

Even if ICE is to be believed that there exists such a problem, how is this solved by increasing the cost of OPT application fees? In effect, DHS is arguing that the reasonable way to fix a problem that they tenuously claim exists with 10,000 OPT participants *in total* is to financially destroy the prospects of applications for over 200,000 OPT participants *every year*. The suggestion that this fee is to cover processing OPT visas is ludicrous on its face - DHS's discretionary budget has ballooned from $46 billion to $65 billion dollars over the course of the two Trump administrations. In no way does attempting to rip more money away from productive nonimmigrant workers strengthen the integrity of a system that has grown one-and-a-half-fold in scale in the last decade.

The inability of academic institutions to host more students than they currently do is a direct result of austerity in government funding of scientific research. In the absence of more science funding, US workers are not being protected in any way by their coworkers being forced out of employment roles that require niche skilled labor. If DHS Secretary Mullin truly wanted to address the existing problems with academic labor, he would instead lobby his boss to propose substantially larger operating budgets for the NSF and NIH.
