Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 — Optional Practical Training Fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2))

I am an F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT, interning at a tech company as an AI/ML engineer, doing work directly related to my degree. I write about a part of this proposal that has received little attention: the fee is non-refundable, and the school must pay it before the recommendation is even made. I ask the Department to withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, a fee of this size must be refundable when the training it pays for does not happen, and refund decisions must be appealable.

Under the proposal, the school pays $70,000 before the designated school official recommends the student for OPT. The payment comes first; the recommendation, the adjudication, and the employment authorization document all come after. Under the proposal's refund rules, a refund is available only if the student never received the employment authorization document and the school removes the recommendation. Once the document is issued, the fee is non-refundable under any circumstances, and refund decisions cannot be appealed.

That means the school — and, if the cost is passed on, the student — pays $70,000 for an outcome that is not guaranteed, and bears all of the risk if it does not happen. If the employment authorization is denied, the money is gone. If the student cannot find qualifying work in time — and on post-completion OPT, a student has only 90 days of unemployment — the money is gone, and the student loses the OPT as well. If the employer withdraws the offer, the money is gone. In every one of these cases, the government keeps $70,000 for a training period that never took place, and no one can appeal.

That is not how a fee for a government service should work. A fee should pay for a service that is provided. Here the government takes the money first, controls every step that follows, and keeps the money even when the service is not delivered. For a fee of a few hundred dollars, that might be a nuisance. For $70,000 — more than many families earn in a year — it is a serious financial risk that no school or student can plan around. A small college that pays $70,000 for a student whose authorization is then denied has lost money it cannot recover, for nothing.

The Department should explain why a fee of this size is non-refundable and why refund decisions are unappealable. If the Department proceeds, the fee should be refunded whenever the OPT does not happen — when the employment authorization is denied, when the recommendation is withdrawn, or when the student is unable to use it. Refund decisions should be appealable like any other decision involving this much money. Better still, the fee should be charged only after the employment authorization is issued, so that no one pays for a training period that never begins.

A rule that asks schools and students to pay $70,000 in advance, keeps the money when the training never happens, and offers no appeal, is not a fee. It is a gamble that only the government can win. Please withdraw it.

Respectfully submitted,
An F-1 master's graduate on post-completion OPT

I oppose the proposed OPT fee rule. Beyond its extraordinary price, the NPRM contains four analytical and design flaws requiring a specific response. These comments address Sections V, VI, and VII (91 FR 64566).

1. Financial deterrence is not evidence of fraud detection.

In Section VII.A.5.b(2), DHS estimates an additional 0.5 hours of DSO review per OPT application, including SEVIS fee updates, and 0.5 hours of administrator time to process payment. These are incremental workload estimates, not evidence of more effective fraud investigations. Yet DHS predicts that the fees will improve scrutiny and deter abuse.

What evidence links a $70,000 payment by a school to better detection of fraudulent employment? How would DHS distinguish improved compliance from schools simply refusing to recommend eligible students? DHS should compare the fee approach against targeted audits, employer verification, and risk-based reviews using measurable enforcement outcomes. A financial barrier is not a substitute for evidence of effectiveness.

2. The opportunity-cost model confuses social value with ability to pay.

In Section VII.A.5.c, DHS uses unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the opportunity cost of lost participation. DHS acknowledges that true costs could be higher or lower, but assumes stakeholders can share costs whenever OPT's benefits exceed the fee.

This assumption ignores liquidity constraints and coordination failures. OPT can generate value for a student, employer, university, and the broader economy without any single party having the cash, budget authority, or mechanism to fund $70,000 up front. Benefits may accrue over years, while payment precedes the DSO recommendation. Inability to pay does not establish that an OPT opportunity is worth less than the fee.

DHS should test alternative estimates using wages, enrollment sensitivity, institutional financing constraints, and uncertainty ranges rather than treating its proposed charge as a proxy for lost social value.

3. The structure discourages the training it claims to safeguard.

Section VII.A.5.d(3) acknowledges that dividing the same maximum 12-month ordinary OPT allowance between pre-completion and post-completion training can cost $100,000, versus $70,000 if used only after graduation. DHS even anticipates that schools will discourage pre-completion OPT due to this fee differential.

This is a perverse incentive. Two students may use the same total authorized training time, yet the one gaining earlier degree-related experience creates an extra $30,000 obligation. DHS should explain how discouraging legitimate practical training during enrollment advances program integrity. The same aggregate OPT entitlement should not be penalized merely for being used in two stages.

4. The transition rules penalize lawful prior participation.

Sections V.C and VI describe prospective application, yet the transition analysis in Section VII.B assumes a $70,000 initial fee for a STEM OPT recommendation when no initial fee was paid previously. Someone already lawfully authorized for post-completion OPT could thus face the initial fee when seeking an extension, solely because the fee did not exist at the time of their first authorization.

This is not equivalent to a first-time OPT applicant. Existing students, schools, and employers have made commitments under prior rules. A 60-day delay after publication may not allow a school to budget $70,000 per affected student; STEM extension applicants cannot simply choose an earlier eligibility date. Nor should access to the $30,000 subsequent fee depend on payment of a fee that could not previously have been paid.

DHS should grandfather students who received initial OPT authorization or a DSO recommendation before the effective date. Otherwise, it should explain why previously authorized students are treated as first-time fee payers and quantify the impact on existing cohorts.

Based on the above reasoning, I urge DHS to withdraw this rule. At minimum, it should substantiate the anti-fraud mechanism, replace the unsupported opportunity-cost proxy, eliminate the pre-/post-completion penalty, and establish explicit grandfathering. Regulation should distinguish actual compliance from financial exclusion and economic value from ability to pay.

Thank you for considering my comments.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee and urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw the proposal.

DHS has a legitimate responsibility to prevent fraud and protect OPT's integrity. However, a universal fee of this magnitude is not a targeted response. It risks burdening universities, restricting the educational value of practical training, and weakening the U.S. technical and scientific talent pipeline.

1. Impact on educational institutions:
Under the proposal, an SEVP-certified institution must pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT. The fee is not tied to a particular employer or evidence of noncompliance.
Recommending 100 students for initial OPT would create a $7 million fee obligation; 500 students would create a $35 million obligation.
Smaller public and regional institutions may be unable to absorb these costs. DHS's analysis recognizes that reduced OPT participation could affect international enrollment and university revenue.
Institutions may therefore limit or stop recommending students because of financial constraints, regardless of their academic qualifications or the legitimacy of their training. Access to practical training should not depend primarily on a university's ability to pay this fee.

2. Impact on students and OPT's educational purpose:
OPT allows eligible students to apply theoretical knowledge gained through academic study in a practical, application-oriented environment. In engineering, semiconductor technology, computer science, biotechnology, and research, practical experience reinforces theory and develops applied problem-solving skills.
The proposed fees could make this training inaccessible to students whose institutions cannot afford the payments. Students may lose opportunities to apply classroom knowledge to real engineering systems, research, and technical challenges. This can limit practical skill development and create unequal outcomes for equally qualified students based on their institutions' resources.
STEM OPT already includes structured training requirements through Form I-983, including learning objectives, supervision, and evaluation. DHS should strengthen training verification and compliance rather than impose a universal financial barrier that also affects legitimate students and institutions.

3. Impact on the U.S. technical and scientific talent pool:
International graduates are an important part of the U.S. science and engineering pipeline. The National Science Board's 2026 Science and Engineering Indicators reports that temporary visa holders earned 42% of science and engineering master's degrees and 38% of doctoral degrees awarded by U.S. institutions in 2024. They earned 54% of engineering doctorates and 61% of computer and information sciences doctorates.
Restricting practical training could disrupt the transition from advanced U.S. education to applied technical expertise. The country risks losing the benefit of educating highly qualified individuals if they cannot continue their practical development here. This matters in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, electrical engineering, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, and computer science.
The National Science Board also reports that approximately three-quarters of temporary visa holders who earned science and engineering doctorates remained in the United States five years after graduation. If the proposed fees discourage students from pursuing U.S. education and practical training, the country could weaken its ability to attract, develop, and retain specialized technical talent, while other countries may benefit.

4. Request for withdrawal:
DHS has identified legitimate concerns about fraudulent OPT arrangements. However, the same substantial fee for every institution does not distinguish fraud from legitimate training at compliant institutions.
DHS should prioritize targeted audits, verification of employers and training sites, improved training for Designated School Officials, and enforcement against actual violations.
DHS acknowledges uncertainty in estimating the effects of reduced OPT participation, including losses of student experience, enrollment, and revenue. A fee of this magnitude requires a transparent, proportionate justification showing that it is necessary and effective.
I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. Protecting program integrity should not undermine legitimate educational training, impose disproportionate costs on universities, or weaken the U.S. technical and scientific talent pipeline.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Conflating documented, law-abiding F-1 visa holders with undocumented populations, introducing punitive financial barriers, and compressing procedural windows transforms a legitimate educational bridge into an exclusionary wealth test. Beyond the initial arguments regarding legal status distinctions and unrealistic application windows, several critical dimensions expose why a massive financial levy on OPT is fundamentally unfair, economically counterproductive, and legally unsound.  
1. The False Equivalence with Undocumented Populations and Criminalization of Legal Status
A foundational flaw in the justification for heavy-handed OPT restrictions is the rhetorical conflation of legal international students with unauthorized immigrants or individuals lacking status. F-1 students undergo rigorous consular vetting, maintain continuous SEVIS compliance, pay full-price non-resident tuition, and operate under strict federal oversight. Labeling or treating legal, tax-paying graduates as a population requiring financial deterrence ignores the rule of law. Using an exorbitant six-figure price tag to "filter" international talent treats legitimate students as regulatory liabilities rather than lawful, authorized participants in the American academic and economic ecosystem.
2. Impractical Time Constraints and Mismatch with Administrative Realities
The push to compress procedural timelines—such as shortening transition and application windows or tightening post-completion rules—divorces policy from administrative reality. Normal OPT processing through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) frequently spans multiple months. Forcing strict, compressed deadlines onto a system notorious for agency backlogs creates an impossible trap for graduates. Rather than streamlining the process, arbitrary time restrictions penalize students for bureaucratic delays that are entirely outside of their control.  
3. Economic Discrimination and the Death of Meritocratic Innovation
Imposing a $100,000 fee—whether levied on institutions or trickling down to students—fundamentally converts work authorization into a pay-to-play scheme. This shifts the selection criteria from academic merit, technical skill, and market demand to raw generational wealth. Brilliant engineering, science, and arts graduates from modest socioeconomic backgrounds worldwide will be systematically priced out of the U.S. labor market. Consequently, American innovation pipelines in critical sectors like technology, health, and visual arts will lose top-tier global talent simply because candidates cannot afford an arbitrary entry toll.  
4. Institutional and Regional Economic Destabilization
U.S. colleges and universities rely heavily on international graduate enrollment to fund advanced research, sustain department budgets, and maintain global competitiveness. If universities are handed the financial or administrative burden of absorbing or managing these exorbitant fees, many institutions—particularly regional or mid-tier universities—will be forced to curtail their international programs. This sudden contraction triggers a cascading economic loss for local communities, campus economies, and regional housing markets that benefit directly from international student spending.
5. Undermining Established Reliance Interests and Predictability
For decades, OPT has served as the predictable, legally sanctioned bridge connecting academic study to professional training. Multinational corporations, mid-sized startups, and non-profit institutions build their recruitment pipelines around this predictable transition. Introducing a retroactive or sudden six-figure penalty shatters the legal certainty and reliance interests of both employers and students who entered the U.S. education system under clear, established federal guidelines. Breaking this compact damages the global reputation of the United States as a predictable, stable destination for higher education.
Conclusion
The proposal to install prohibitive six-figure fees and unrealistic structural constraints on OPT is a counterproductive policy that injures America's competitive edge. By penalizing legal compliance, pricing out talent, and ignoring the operational realities of federal immigration processing, this approach replaces a functioning bridge of global exchange with an exclusionary barrier. Preserving the integrity of the F-1 program requires honoring the legal framework already in place, rather than turning professional work authorization into an exclusive luxury item.

I am an F-1 student in year 4 of a PhD program in Biomedical Engineering at Yale University. I comment on the information collection supporting the proposed OPT fee rule, and I ask that DHS not submit, and OMB not approve, this collection. Under 44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A), DHS must show that a collection is necessary and has practical utility, that its burden estimate is accurate, and that burden has been minimized. This collection fails each test.

1. It has no practical utility for fraud prevention. Schools must document payment before a DSO recommendation, yet for initial OPT no employer or job needs to exist at that point (64569). Proof that a school paid says nothing about whether a training opportunity is real.
2. The burden estimate is internally inconsistent. The PRA section counts 226,200 annual responses (64598), while footnote 143 counts 289,938. The rule also gives 165,524 STEM OPT participants for 2024 (64573) but uses 95,384 in its economic analysis (64583). OMB cannot evaluate a burden that the agency states two different ways. DHS should reconcile these figures and explain how it derived them.
3. Cost burden is left unestimated. DHS says it is “unable to estimate” the budgeting, banking, IT and refund costs the rule creates (64590). Schools must build payment, confirmation and tracking processes, and 1,044 of the 2,478 affected schools are state-run (64592). A supporting statement that omits these costs does not meet the PRA’s cost-burden requirement.
4. The refund collection has no instructions. Refund requests are decided “case-by-case,” are not appealable, and are governed by guidance SEVP “may” post later (64600). Respondents cannot know what information to submit. The forms and instructions for this collection should be published now, so the public can comment on them.
5. The burden on students appears to be uncounted. The rule expects schools to pass costs to students or employers (64575, 64578). Schools deciding whom to fund will need financial information, repayment agreements or employer sponsorship letters from students. Before recommending me for a summer internship, my school could require such documents from me. That is an information burden on individuals that the estimate should include.
6. Less burdensome sources already exist. Form I-765, SEVIS reporting and Form I-983 already hold employer and worksite information. DHS could verify employers against IRS and state business records and require employers to confirm start and end dates in SEVIS within 10 days. That would yield more useful integrity data at far lower burden.

This collection exists only to implement a fee that should be withdrawn, and OMB should not approve it. If DHS proceeds, it should republish a corrected supporting statement with a new comment period. That statement should reconcile the response counts, estimate the full cost burden, publish refund instructions, and count the burden on students. Thank you for considering this comment.

OPT provides a structured opportunity for U.S.-educated graduates to apply their knowledge in the American workforce and gain professional experience. 1. The Policy Could Harm the American Economy Rather Than Protect It

A 2019 study in Labour Economics found that increased foreign STEM labor supply was associated with a 4.67% increase in average wages for existing U.S.-born STEM workers, largely through productivity and innovation spillovers.

Reducing international employment does not automatically create jobs or increase American wages. DHS has not demonstrated that this fee will benefit American workers.

2. Eliminating OPT Would Make These Problems Worse, Not Solve Them

Eliminating OPT would remove an established pathway for American-educated graduates to contribute to U.S. businesses.

Employers could lose access to qualified graduates, making it harder to fill specialized positions, conduct research, develop technologies, and expand operations.

Eliminating OPT does not guarantee those positions will go to Americans. Employers might reduce operations, relocate overseas, or outsource work to countries with lower labor costs.

Meanwhile, international graduates may take their skills to competing economies, transferring economic benefits away from the United States.

3. The United States Risks Exporting Its Own Educational Investment

International students pay tuition to American universities, spend money in local communities, and contribute to research and economic activity. After investing years and substantial resources in American education, many seek to apply their skills to American businesses through OPT.

If financial barriers prevent them from working here, they may take their expertise elsewhere, transferring skilled labor, innovation, and future economic growth to competing countries.

Why should the United States educate international talent only to create barriers that encourage graduates to contribute their skills and productivity elsewhere?

Lower-income graduates could be particularly disadvantaged if universities pass the costs to students or employers, making employment opportunities depend increasingly on family wealth rather than ability.

4. Individual Job Competition Stories Do Not Establish That OPT Harms American Workers Overall

American graduates' frustration with unemployment deserves to be taken seriously. However, individual hiring experiences cannot establish OPT's overall economic impact.

Employers generally seek qualified American candidates. When they cannot find available Americans who meet their requirements, hiring qualified international graduates allows businesses to fill positions and continue operating.

Claiming that an international student stole an American's job requires evidence that a qualified and available American worker was actually passed over. Without evidence of discrimination or unlawful hiring, an individual hiring decision does not establish that OPT harms American workers.

Blaming international graduates without establishing the actual cause of unemployment does not solve the problem. The question is whether restricting OPT creates more opportunities for Americans or simply makes American businesses less competitive.

5. Neither Charging an Extraordinary Fee Nor Eliminating OPT Is an Appropriate Way to Prevent Fraud

Even if DHS has concerns about OPT fraud, a $70,000 fee is not an effective or targeted solution. It does not distinguish legitimate students from those involved in fraudulent employment. Compliant students face the same financial barrier.

Paying $70,000 does not make employment legitimate, and being unable to afford it does not indicate fraud.

Eliminating OPT is no better. It does not identify fraudulent employers, distinguish legitimate employment from sham arrangements, or improve fraud detection. It simply eliminates the pathway for everyone, including students, universities, and employers that fully comply with the law.

The existence of fraud does not justify abolishing an entire program. DHS should investigate employers, verify employment arrangements, conduct audits, and penalize proven violations.

Preventing fraud should mean targeting misconduct, not financially punishing legitimate participants or eliminating an entire employment pathway.

I am a tenure-track assistant professor from a public university in Iowa. I write in my personal capacity, not on behalf of my employer. I share DHS's goal of stopping fraud in OPT, and I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees or revise them as suggested below.

1. MY EXPERIENCE

I earned a Ph.D. at a public university in Texas. My degree was conferred and my faculty appointment began in the same month, so I started on post-completion OPT while my cap-exempt employer prepared my H-1B petition. Since then I have taught seven course sections and about 225 Iowa undergraduates. New students have named me a Student Advocate in both of my years, and a student-athlete selected me as a Faculty Appreciation Honoree. I also serve on the committee building a new business major. None of this would have started on time without OPT.

Section VI suggests that students can instead use "the H-1B visa following graduation." In academic hiring that is rarely possible, because the degree is completed in summer and classes begin weeks later. OPT is the bridge. Under the proposal, my Texas university would have owed $70,000 so that a university in another state could hire me on time. It would have had little reason to pay, and neither a new Ph.D. living on a stipend nor a regional public university could readily have covered the cost. My students would have started the semester without their instructor.

2. FEE DESIGN (Sections IV.A and IV.C)

The fee does not appear to reach the fraud DHS describes.

- Section IV.A describes shell employers and staged worksites. The fee falls on schools, which do not control employers. For initial OPT, no employer needs to be identified when the DSO makes the recommendation, so a school cannot screen an employer it does not yet know.

- Section IV.C states that the fees go to the Treasury and are not available to SEVP, so the rule adds no investigative capacity.

- The amount is aligned with the H-1B fee to deter cap circumvention. Employment at a cap-exempt university circumvents no cap.

- The fee is the same for a compliant public university as for a "visa mill," and for a verified faculty appointment as for a questionable placement.

- No refund is available once the EAD is issued, even if OPT lasts only a short time before a change to H-1B status.

- Section VII.B.3 treats all 1,044 public institutions as not small because States run them. A regional public university's budget is not its State's budget. I ask DHS to analyze public institutions individually.

Section VII.D also states both that the rule would not exceed the unfunded mandates threshold and that it does. I ask DHS to reconcile these statements and consult the States.

a. Extend the STEM OPT safeguards discussed in Section IV.C (identified employer, E-Verify, training plan, site visits) to all OPT, and focus enforcement on employers that show risk indicators.

b. If a fee is retained, set it at the actual cost of oversight.

c. Exempt OPT with cap-exempt employers: institutions of higher education and nonprofit or governmental research organizations.

d. Provide a pro-rated refund when OPT ends early through a change of status or departure.

Policies that create extreme financial barriers to practical training risk weakening that reputation and reducing the country's long-term competitiveness.

A more effective approach would involve strengthening compliance measures, improving monitoring procedures, and addressing specific instances of misuse without penalizing the broader international student community.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT-related fees. Thank you for taking the time to consider my concerns and for recognizing the importance of maintaining accessible practical training opportunities for international graduates.

DHS unwisely assumes that this alternative achieve the goal of reducing fraud with the least administrative burden on the government. I am an international graduate student at a U.S. university. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee rule and urge DHS to withdraw it in its entirety. OPT is an important part of American higher education, allowing international students to apply academic knowledge through practical experience while contributing to U.S. research, innovation, and workforce development. The proposed fees would severely restrict these opportunities, unfairly harm currently enrolled students, and undermine American universities.

1. The proposed fees resemble unauthorized taxation.

The $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee appear designed to deter participation rather than recover administrative costs. In National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), the Supreme Court distinguished regulatory fees from taxes. DHS has not adequately demonstrated congressional authorization to impose charges of this magnitude for deterrent purposes.

2. The revenue would not directly support anti-fraud enforcement.

DHS acknowledges that the collected fees would enter the U.S. Treasury rather than directly fund ICE investigations or OPT oversight. This disconnect between the stated purpose and the use of funds undermines the proposal's justification. Making lawful participation prohibitively expensive does not itself prevent fraud.

3. The proposal burdens the wrong parties.

DHS identifies fraudulent employers and fictitious employment arrangements as major concerns, yet universities must pay the fees, potentially passing the costs to students. Students may not even have employers when receiving initial OPT recommendations. Financial responsibility should target actual misconduct, not legitimate universities and students.

4. The proposal unfairly harms current students and universities.

International students make substantial educational and financial commitments based on existing regulations. Imposing extraordinary fees after enrollment disregards these reliance interests, particularly for students who have not yet received OPT recommendations. Universities may be unable to absorb the charges, while declining international enrollment could reduce tuition revenue and damage research programs.

5. Less burdensome alternatives were inadequately considered, and the comment period is too short.

DHS dismissed measures such as enhanced employer verification, site visits, and reporting requirements partly because of administrative burdens. Government convenience cannot justify shifting enormous costs onto students and universities. A roughly 30-day comment period is also insufficient for a proposal with such significant consequences.

6. The economic analysis relies on circular reasoning.

DHS uses hypothetical unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for economic losses from reduced participation. But those fee amounts are determined by DHS, not independently measured economic values. Raising the fees could mechanically increase estimated losses without changing actual economic harm. A credible analysis should independently assess effects on employment, education, and research.

Conclusion

I strongly oppose this proposal because it lacks adequate legal and economic justification and would cause disproportionate harm to international students, universities, and American innovation. These fundamental problems cannot be resolved merely by reducing the fees.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

Sonoran University of Health Sciences strongly opposes the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation fees. We support DHS efforts to prevent fraud and maintain program integrity, but these charges would disproportionately burden smaller institutions and could effectively eliminate lawful postgraduate training opportunities for otherwise eligible international graduates. Our attached letter provides supporting evidence and recommendations.

Institutional financial impact: Sonoran is a specialized health sciences university in Tempe, Arizona, enrolling 15 F-1 students as of October 26, 2026. Over 30 academic years, 64 graduates pursued OPT. At $70,000 per initial recommendation, an equivalent number would cost $4.48 million, excluding subsequent fees. This illustrates scale, not retroactive charges. In four of the last five years, Sonoran's net income was below $100,000. A single $70,000 recommendation would represent a major financial obligation, while three would cost $210,000. Based on Sonoran's financial results, applying such fees would have produced reported losses in each of those four years.

The proposal requires the educational institution to pay before its Designated School Official may recommend OPT. Employer or graduate reimbursement cannot be assumed. An eligible student could complete a rigorous professional degree and secure legitimate, field-related employment or training, yet be unable to access OPT solely because the institution cannot afford the recommendation fee. DHS should evaluate whether smaller nonprofit and specialized institutions would reduce or discontinue OPT recommendations rather than assume historical participation will continue.

Healthcare training and enrollment: OPT can facilitate eligible graduates' transitions into field-related employment, supervised clinical training, research, and other professional experiences. Naturopathic medical residencies and other health sciences training opportunities may involve small practices, nonprofit organizations, or educational settings without resources to offset tens of thousands of dollars in institutional charges. They may also discourage international students from enrolling in U.S. health professions programs: students make substantial educational and financial commitments years before becoming eligible for OPT, and uncertainty about their institution's future ability to pay is consequential. DHS's economic analysis should address changes in institutional, student, and employer behavior, not merely the theoretical revenue generated by the fees.

Disproportionate effects on small institutions: A uniform $70,000 fee does not reflect differences in institutional size, financial capacity, or compliance history. Even one or two recommendations could affect operating budgets and student services. DHS should assess whether the rule would make OPT effectively unavailable at smaller compliant institutions and examine alternatives or accommodations for nonprofit and specialized schools.

Fee justification and uncertainty: DHS should explain the evidence linking these particular fee amounts to demonstrated fraud or compliance risks; how the $70,000 and $30,000 figures were calculated; how the revenue would advance program integrity; and why less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient. Uniform charges are not targeted oversight. DHS should also specify when the $30,000 subsequent fee applies, including employment or training-site changes, corrections, extensions, and transfers; whether multiple fees could be imposed for one student; whether cumulative charges would be capped; and whether fees would be refunded if an application were denied or withdrawn. Without clear rules, institutions cannot budget or reliably advise students.

Requested action: Sonoran urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue evidence-based, proportionate measures, such as risk-based monitoring, targeted investigations, employer and placement verification, clearer reporting standards, improved guidance for Designated School Officials, and administrative fees reasonably related to actual program costs. At minimum, DHS should reassess small-institution impacts, realistic participation and enrollment responses, cumulative financial exposure, and less burdensome alternatives before finalizing any fees.

OPT eligibility and compliance, not an institution's ability to absorb an extraordinary charge, should determine whether an international graduate can pursue lawful field-related training. Please consider this comment and Sonoran's attached formal letter together as our complete response to the proposed rule.

Submitted on behalf of Sonoran University of Health Sciences by Melissa Winquist, MA, Primary Designated School Official and Vice President of Student Affairs.

I oppose applying the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees to graduates of U.S. doctoral programs, particularly PhD recipients working in research and development (R&D). The proposal would do far more economic harm than good and would work against its stated purpose of protecting American jobs.

A PhD researcher is not an entry-level hire. Doctoral training takes years of highly specialized work, much of it supported by U.S. universities, federal grants, national laboratories, and American companies. OPT is how employers keep that expertise and convert the investment into technologies, patents, competitive products, and jobs for U.S. workers. When a laboratory loses a researcher, it loses more than one person. Project continuity suffers. Research partnerships weaken. Funding opportunities can disappear, along with the ability to hire the engineers, technicians, and other staff who work alongside that researcher.

University laboratories, startups, and small R&D firms would be hit hardest. Consider a $70,000 payment due before an OPT recommendation is even made: that money might otherwise pay for experiments, equipment, or an additional employee. Grant-funded research groups frequently cannot redirect their funds to cover such a cost at all. Large companies may absorb the fee. Smaller innovators will more likely forgo a critical hire, delay a project, or move the research overseas, and none of those outcomes secures a job for a U.S. worker. Reduced R&D capacity can also eliminate the complementary jobs that new research and commercialization would otherwise generate.

Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, and I do not dispute them. But charging legitimate doctoral researchers the same extraordinary fees as potentially abusive participants is poorly targeted. Research employment at accredited universities and bona fide research organizations can be verified through other means, including employer documentation, training plans, targeted audits, and meaningful enforcement of the existing wage and non-displacement requirements.

I therefore urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees. At a minimum, graduates of accredited U.S. PhD programs engaged in bona fide research employment, including those on STEM OPT extensions, should be exempt. Before finalizing any rule, DHS should separately assess its effects on doctoral researchers, R&D productivity, small businesses, federal research investments, and net American job creation. A policy meant to protect U.S. jobs should not drive U.S.-trained researchers, their projects, and the employment opportunities that follow them to competing countries.

I support establishing a meaningful fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT) as one part of protecting the program from sham employment. DHS proposes a $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent recommendation, paid by the school before it recommends the student. I urge DHS to pair any fee with checks that distinguish actual training from employment reported only to avoid accruing unemployment days. I also urge DHS to explain how the chosen amounts will deter fraud without excluding legitimate training.

- **Verify unpaid and campus research roles independently.** A legitimate research appointment or volunteer role should remain possible under ordinary OPT. But a title or letter alone should not establish that work occurred. For an unpaid role, require a named supervisor, a description connecting the duties to the degree, contemporaneous records of hours and work performed, and periodic confirmation by a school official who is **not** the sponsoring professor. Audit a sample of these records. ICE already says unrelated volunteering does not stop the unemployment clock; this would make that rule easier to enforce.

- **Disclose who ultimately pays the fee and whether anyone paid for the job.** The proposal permits schools to pass the fee to students or employers. Require disclosure of reimbursement arrangements and investigate payments from a student to a purported employer or intermediary for an offer letter, placement, or continued listing as employed. A school-paid fee alone may not deter a “pay-to-stay” business that shifts its costs to students.

- **Check networks of purported employers, not just individual records.** ICE has reported empty worksites, students who never appeared for work, and employers operating from residential addresses. Link employer identifiers, worksites, supervisors, and related business entities across SEVIS records to prioritize verification when many students are reported at the same site or under the same supervisor. Such patterns should trigger review, not an automatic finding of fraud.

- **Watch for displacement into CPT.** The proposed rule covers OPT, not Curricular Practical Training (CPT), and DHS acknowledges fraud concerns in CPT. After implementation, compare school-level changes in OPT and CPT participation and investigate abrupt shifts concentrated at particular schools or employers. This would help determine whether a fee reduces abuse or moves it to another category.

- **Measure whether the fee works.** Publish annual figures for confirmed fraud findings, results of employer checks, and effects on legitimate participation, using consistent denominators. Reassess the fee amounts against those results. The proposal says fee receipts go to the Treasury and are not retained by ICE for oversight, so the fee should not be treated as a substitute for verification.

As an alternative or complement, DHS should consider requiring evidence of actual compensation comparable to similarly situated workers for paid roles, while allowing carefully verified, lawful unpaid research or public-interest training under ordinary OPT. A single nationwide income threshold could exclude genuine opportunities without proving that a reported job is real. For employment reports presenting concrete fraud indicators, prompt targeted verification would be more precise than a blanket pause of OPT.

By DHS's own analysis, the fee would put OPT out of reach for most students. DHS says it "cannot confidently predict" how far participation will fall; its low scenario assumes OPT ends entirely for non-STEM students, and it simply assumes schools will keep paying $100,000 for every STEM student. The fee is about 150 times today's $470 online application fee. DHS calls it "on par with" one or two years of educational costs, so if schools pass it on, as DHS says they may, it could roughly double the price of a degree. US degrees are a heavy investment for students from almost every country, and OPT gives them a chance to recoup at least part of that cost, including those who then return home.

I began preparing for US graduate study months before this proposal was published, relying on OPT rules that have existed for decades. If the rule is finalized, it would likely apply to me by the time I graduate.

DHS argues OPT is not central to student choices because only about 20% of all 1.4 million F-1 students used it in 2024. That counts students years away from graduating. Among F-1 graduates, about 54% use OPT (SEVIS data via the Institute for Progress). In a 2025 Institute for Progress and NAFSA survey, a majority of international students said they would not have enrolled without OPT.

I agree OPT has been abused, and those responsible should be stopped and punished. But DHS says the fee is not tied to a specific employer. A student hired by a legitimate robotics company triggers the same fee as one attached to a shell company, and the money goes to the Treasury, not to oversight. The more than 10,000 students DHS flags as working for "highly suspect" employers are about 3% of 2024 OPT and STEM OPT participants.

Better options exist: require E-Verify, training plans and site visits for all OPT employers, not only STEM OPT employers; ban residential worksites and require employers to have a real operating history; require accreditation for all OPT; debar employers and officials who commit fraud; and fund oversight through cost-based SEVP fees, as DHS did in 2019.

OPT participants are not a drain on federal benefit programs: they are generally barred from federal public benefits and pay federal income tax. They are US-trained graduates, many at the master's level and heavily in STEM. Not every one is exceptional, and OPT was never meant only for prodigies; the US has long benefited from drawing not just the most exceptional people from around the world, but many of the best. OPT is also how many graduates lawfully move into the employment visas Congress created; most international STEM graduates who stay to work used OPT first. As I understand it, this administration has no quarrel with legal immigration, and OPT is one of the cleanest lawful pathways there is.

This rule may look like a quick win in the short term, but its long-term cost to the United States would be far larger. DHS estimates this rule's costs at $4.1 billion a year and lists its monetized benefits as "Not Estimated." I am an F-1 student in my 4th year of PhD program in Biology at Yale University. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule for the following reasons.
1. The proposed fees are excessive and place a significant financial burden on academic research
The proposed fees are far beyond what many graduates can afford, especially those pursuing careers in academia. For example, the minimum annual salary for a first-year postdoctoral researcher at Yale is $68,500, less than the proposed initial fee alone. Yale's minimum annual compensation for postgraduate trainees, laboratory associates, and visiting fellows is even lower, at $45,600. Although universities would formally pay these fees, neither individual graduates nor many academic employers could realistically afford them. Research laboratories often operate on limited grant funding, and these additional costs could make hiring international researchers unaffordable. This would particularly affect graduates who are interested in pursuing academic and nonprofit positions (e.g. professors/researchers/lecturers) over higher-paying industry jobs. 
2. The proposed fees would drive highly trained talent away from the U.S. and hurt scientific research
U.S. universities invest years of resources in educating and training international students at the bachelor's, master's, and doctoral levels. Many of these graduates go on to contribute to scientific research, technological development, and other fields in the U.S. If universities and employers cannot afford the OPT fees, many graduates would have little choice but to seek opportunities elsewhere. The U.S. would lose highly trained professionals who have already spent years studying here. This would also make it harder for research laboratories to recruit and retain qualified researchers, affecting ongoing research and future scientific progress.
3. The proposed fees do not adequately address the fraud DHS identifies
The fraud examples in Section IV.A of the proposed rule largely involve fraudulent employers, fabricated employment arrangements, and staged worksites, rather than legitimate academic research institutions. DHS also cites circumvention of H-1B visa caps as a justification, even though universities and qualifying nonprofit and government research organizations are exempt from those caps. Charging the same fees across all institutions does not distinguish legitimate research employment from the fraudulent activities DHS is concerned about. DHS should instead focus on more targeted employer verification and enforcement measures.
4. The proposed fee amounts lack sufficient justification
DHS has not adequately explained how the $70,000 and $30,000 fees relate to the actual costs of administering OPT. Instead, DHS partly justifies the initial fee by comparing it to the $100,000 H-1B payment, which remains subject to litigation. Using another extraordinarily high and legally disputed charge as a benchmark does not explain why these OPT fees are necessary or reasonable. DHS should provide a clear, evidence-based justification for these amounts rather than relying on such a comparison.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. Any alternative measures should focus on addressing actual fraud risks without placing unreasonable financial burdens on international graduates, universities, and research institutions.

I submit this comment as a concerned citizen with extensive professional experience interpreting and applying F-1 student regulations and advising international students regarding immigration compliance, employment authorization, and practical training benefits.
I strongly oppose the proposed fee structure establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. While DHS states that the proposal is intended to strengthen program integrity, deter fraud, and protect U.S. workers, the proposed rule does not adequately demonstrate how fees of this magnitude are reasonably connected to those objectives.
The proposed fees would function not as administrative charges, but as substantial barriers to participation. 
Of particular concern is the rule's limited discussion of the extensive compliance infrastructure already embedded within the F-1 program. In my experience, OPT and STEM OPT are not programs lacking oversight. Rather, they are benefits subject to multiple layers of monitoring, reporting, review, and enforcement involving students, employers, educational institutions, SEVP, USCIS, and DHS.
Throughout the post-completion OPT period, including the 24-month STEM extension period, universities already perform significant compliance functions that support the integrity of the OPT and STEM OPT programs at no cost to DHS. DSOs review training plans, evaluate regulatory eligibility, maintain records, monitor reporting obligations, counsel students regarding compliance requirements, and update SEVIS records accordingly. The proposed rule does not account for these substantial institutional investments, which effectively supplement federal oversight efforts and contribute to program integrity on a daily basis.
In this regard, universities effectively serve as partners in the administration of this benefit. The work performed by Designated School Officials provides an important layer of review that supports program integrity. Yet the proposed rule does not meaningfully address this  or explain why such measures are insufficient to address the concerns identified by DHS.
The likely effect of this proposal is not merely increased program integrity. Rather, it appears to discourage participation by otherwise eligible students, reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education, and diminish the ability of U.S. employers to recruit graduates who have been educated U.S. institutions. Students weighing educational opportunities increasingly compare options across multiple countries. Policies that significantly restrict access to practical training opportunities may influence enrollment decisions and redirect talented students elsewhere.
Access to practical training should be based on eligibility, compliance with regulatory requirements, and educational objectives. In my experience, compliance challenges are best addressed through education, advising, monitoring, targeted enforcement, and data-driven oversight. Broad financial barriers imposed on all participants are a blunt policy instrument that risks substantial unintended consequences while offering limited evidence that they will achieve the agency's stated goals.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule or substantially revise it. At a minimum, DHS should provide additional evidence supporting the proposed fee levels, conduct a more robust analysis of the consequences for students, educational institutions, and employers, and evaluate less restrictive alternatives capable of advancing program integrity without effectively eliminating access to practical training opportunities.

I strongly believe that imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent OPT fee is a disproportionate and counterproductive response that would harm legitimate students, American educational institutions, and the broader U.S. economy.

1. The proposed fees create an unreasonable financial barrier
Optional Practical Training is an educational opportunity designed to allow international students to apply their academic knowledge in a professional environment. It is not a guarantee of employment, permanent residency, or an exemption from existing immigration requirements. Requiring an educational institution to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation, followed by another $30,000 for subsequent training, would make this opportunity financially inaccessible for many qualified students. Although the proposed rule formally places the payment obligation on universities, institutions may be unable or unwilling to absorb these costs. Consequently, students could lose opportunities because of financial considerations rather than their qualifications, academic achievements, or compliance with immigration laws.

2. The proposal risks undermining American higher education and economic competitiveness
International students make significant financial investments in American universities through tuition, housing, transportation, and other living expenses. They also contribute to university research, academic collaboration, and local economic activity. Many students choose American institutions because of their educational excellence and opportunities to gain practical experience in their fields.
A financial barrier of this magnitude could discourage talented students from choosing the United States, reducing international enrollment and weakening the competitiveness of American universities.

3. Financial barriers should not substitute for effective fraud prevention
I fully support stronger oversight, verification of legitimate employment, and appropriate enforcement against individuals or institutions engaging in immigration fraud. However, the ability to pay an extraordinary fee is not evidence of legal compliance, and the inability to pay is not evidence of fraudulent intent.
The proposed fees risk penalizing legitimate students and responsible universities without necessarily addressing the individuals or organizations responsible for actual violations. DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, improved reporting mechanisms, risk-based compliance audits, investigations of suspicious employment arrangements, and meaningful penalties for proven misconduct.
These approaches would more directly address the underlying problems while preserving opportunities for students who follow the law.

4. The proposed rule could disproportionately harm smaller educational institutions
DHS's own regulatory analysis estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small institutions could experience financial impacts exceeding 1 percent of their estimated annual revenue. These institutions may lack the financial resources to pay substantial OPT fees or obtain external funding. As a result, access to practical training could become dependent on the financial capacity of a student's university rather than the student's academic preparation or eligibility. Such an outcome would create an uneven system that disadvantages students attending smaller institutions, including those serving communities outside major metropolitan areas.

5. DHS should reconsider the proportionality and economic justification of these fees
The proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees are extraordinarily high relative to the administrative purpose of recommending a student for practical training.
Furthermore, the proposed rule states that the collected fees would be deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts rather than retained by ICE to directly fund OPT oversight. This raises an important policy question: How would imposing these extraordinary financial obligations more effectively prevent fraud than targeted enforcement measures? I respectfully request that DHS provide a clearer evidence-based justification demonstrating that these specific fee amounts are necessary, proportionate, and more effective than less burdensome alternatives.

6. The United States should protect both American workers and legitimate educational opportunities
Protecting American workers and supporting international education should not be treated as mutually exclusive objectives. America's strength has long depended on its ability to educate talented individuals, encourage innovation, and create opportunities through institutions that uphold high academic and professional standards. International students who comply with immigration requirements should be evaluated based on their qualifications, conduct, and eligibility, not on whether their university can afford an extraordinary government fee.

I am a faculty member in earth science at an R1 university in Utah. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw this rule. The views presented here are my own, and not of the institution I work for.

1. The fee does not fit the fraud DHS describes (Section IV.A).
DHS's largest recent investigation found about 10,000 OPT students working for suspect employers. DHS's own 2024 data show about 290,000 to 360,000 students in OPT and STEM OPT. That is less than 4% of participants. A fee on every student punishes the 96% or more who follow the rules.

2. The fee does not pay for oversight (Section IV.C).
The fees go to the US Treasury, and ICE cannot keep them. DHS considered targeted tools, such as site visits and training plans, but chose a fee because it needs fewer government resources. Targeted tools address fraud but a flat fee does not.

3. DHS expects legitimate students to lose OPT (Sections VII.A.3–4).
In its low scenario, DHS assumes schools will pay only for STEM students. DHS also assumes students will stop using OPT during their degree. DHS estimates 10-year costs of up to $69.9 billion and gives no dollar value for any benefit. Also, Section IV.B reports 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, but Section VII.A.3 uses 95,384 for the same year. DHS should explain this difference before it finalizes a rule based on these numbers.

4. This rule harms Utah.
In 2024–25, 10,343 international students studied in Utah. They contributed $316.3 million to the state economy and supported 2,427 jobs (NAFSA; Open Doors 2025). NAFSA estimates Utah lost $8.2 million in 2025–26 as new international enrollment fell. Utah's public universities would have to pay these fees from their budgets or pass the cost to students.

5. The rule harms research in my field. 
In geophysics and seismology, international students and postdocs run lab experiments, deploy seismic networks, and build models of fault behavior. Personnel in our group who are on OPT or about to apply for it study earthquake hazards on the Wasatch Fault, which runs beneath Utah's most populated cities, and on the San Andreas Fault. If they need a STEM OPT extension after this rule takes effect, the school would have to pay at least $30,000 before they could continue. DHS says schools may pass this cost to employers, but the federal grants that fund these positions were not budgeted for it and cannot cover it. They may be forced to leave the US, and their work on hazards that affect millions of people in Utah and California would stop or move abroad. Section VI says the rule protects people already on OPT, but it does not protect people like them who need the next step.

6. The rule trains people for work that protects the nation, then forces them out (Section V.A).
Federal agencies such as NSF, USGS, DOE, and NASA fund graduate students and postdocs to study earthquakes, water supply, energy, and natural hazards. This research protects lives, infrastructure, and national security. The US invests years of funding and training in these students. OPT is often the step where that investment starts to pay off, because it lets them apply their skills here. A $70,000 to $130,000 fee at that step means the US pays to train these scientists and then pushes them, and their skills, to other countries. The alternative in Section V.A, which charges the $70,000 fee again at each degree level, would make this worse. It targets the students who earn both a master's and a PhD in the US, who are the students most likely to enter research careers. I urge DHS to reject this alternative and withdraw the rule.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS wants to reduce fraud, it should use targeted tools that do not punish students who follow the rules.

Formal Opposition to the Proposed $70,000 Initial OPT Fee and $30,000 Subsequent OPT Fee

Docket No.: ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. While I recognize the importance of protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system, these extraordinarily high fees are disproportionate and could create serious unintended consequences for the U.S. economy.

International students come to the United States, pay substantial tuition, contribute to universities, support local businesses, and invest years of their lives preparing to contribute professionally. OPT provides a pathway for graduates to apply their education, develop practical skills, and contribute to American innovation and economic growth.

Implementing fees of this magnitude would create significant financial barriers for employers and graduates. In particular:

Harm to American businesses and employment: Small businesses, startups, and even established employers may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial fees. This could discourage legitimate hiring, limit business growth, and reduce opportunities for American workers who benefit from productive businesses and expanding industries.
Loss of skilled talent and global competitiveness: International graduates contribute to critical fields, including technology, engineering, healthcare, research, and entrepreneurship. If the United States makes it financially impractical to hire qualified graduates, competing countries will become more attractive destinations for skilled talent, research, and investment.
Unfair financial burden on students and families: International students already pay significant tuition and living expenses, often without access to the same financial assistance available to domestic students. Such excessive fees could undermine years of educational investment and place additional financial pressure on families who have sacrificed considerably to support their children's education.
Disproportionate impact on innovation and economic growth: International graduates do not simply compete for jobs; they also create businesses, contribute to research, pay taxes, purchase goods and services, and support American communities. Restricting their employment opportunities could have broader economic consequences beyond the individual student.
I support strong immigration enforcement and efforts to prevent fraud. However, enforcement should be targeted toward fraudulent employers, unauthorized practices, and violations of immigration regulations—not achieved through excessive fees that penalize legitimate students and employers.

I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to:

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.
Establish reasonable and proportionate fees based on actual administrative and enforcement costs.
Conduct a transparent economic impact assessment, including the effects on small businesses, American employment, universities, and local communities.
Prioritize targeted fraud prevention and employer compliance rather than imposing excessive financial barriers.
Conclusion

The United States has built its position as a global leader through education, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the ability to attract talented individuals from around the world. International graduates who study here and contribute their skills are part of that strength.

Protecting American workers and maintaining immigration integrity are important goals, but policies should strengthen the American economy rather than unintentionally discourage investment, innovation, and legitimate employment.

A fee structure of $70,000 and $30,000 risks turning an opportunity for economic contribution into an unreasonable financial barrier. I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to reconsider and withdraw this proposal and pursue a fair, practical, and economically responsible alternative.

Please protect American competitiveness, support legitimate employers, and preserve opportunities for talented graduates who want to contribute to the United States.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Subject: Strong Opposition to the Proposed $70,000 Initial OPT Fee and $30,000 Subsequent OPT Fee

Docket Number: ICEB-2026-0100

I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. Although I understand the government's responsibility to protect American workers and prevent immigration fraud, imposing fees of this magnitude would create an unreasonable financial barrier for legitimate international graduates and the employers seeking to hire them.

International students make substantial investments in the United States by paying tuition, living expenses, and other educational costs. They contribute to universities, local businesses, research institutions, and the broader economy. OPT allows these graduates to apply the knowledge and skills they have developed through their education while contributing to American businesses and industries.

The proposed fees could have several serious consequences:

Negative impact on American employers: Many startups, small businesses, and research organizations cannot afford an additional $70,000 or $30,000 expense to hire a qualified graduate. Employers may choose not to hire international candidates, even when they are highly qualified. This could limit business growth, reduce innovation, and indirectly affect employment opportunities for American workers.
Loss of skilled talent and economic competitiveness: International graduates contribute to important sectors such as technology, engineering, healthcare, finance, and scientific research. Excessively high fees could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in countries with more reasonable employment policies. The United States risks losing skilled individuals, future entrepreneurs, researchers, and potential job creators to global competitors.
Unfair burden on students and families: International students already face significantly higher educational expenses and often have limited access to financial assistance. Many families make substantial financial sacrifices to support their children's education in the United States. These additional fees could make it extremely difficult for graduates to secure employment and benefit from the education they have worked so hard to obtain.
Broader consequences for American communities: International graduates contribute through taxes, consumer spending, entrepreneurship, and professional services. Their participation supports local economies and creates opportunities for businesses and communities. Restricting legitimate employment through excessive fees could negatively affect more people than just the international students themselves.
I strongly support protecting American workers, preventing fraudulent employment practices, and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, these objectives can be achieved through stronger employer verification, targeted investigations, compliance monitoring, and reasonable administrative fees. Excessive financial penalties should not become a barrier to legitimate employment.

I respectfully urge DHS and ICE to:

Withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees.
Establish reasonable fees that reflect actual administrative and enforcement costs.
Conduct a comprehensive economic impact assessment before implementing such a significant policy.
Consider the effects on American employers, domestic workers, universities, international graduates, and local communities.
Focus enforcement efforts on fraudulent employers and violations rather than placing disproportionate financial burdens on legitimate participants.
Final Statement

The United States has become a global leader because it attracts talent, encourages innovation, supports entrepreneurship, and provides opportunities for people to contribute through education and hard work.

International graduates who study in the United States are not simply seeking employment; they are also potential innovators, researchers, entrepreneurs, taxpayers, and future job creators. Policies that make it financially impractical for American employers to hire them could weaken the very economic competitiveness the country seeks to protect.

I urge DHS and ICE to reconsider and withdraw this proposal. Immigration integrity and the protection of American workers should remain priorities, but they must be balanced with economic growth, fairness, and America's long-term global competitiveness.

Please do not turn legitimate educational and professional opportunities into financial barriers that ultimately hurt American businesses, workers, families, and communities.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It relies on selective examples, unsupported assumptions, conflicting data, and a flawed cost-benefit analysis. As a current PhD student at a research university, I see firsthand how critical OPT is to advancing research and bringing incredible minds to work in this country. 

**1. Selective evidence (Sec. IV.A)**
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests that year, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video. The text says the video identified 10,000 students working for suspicious employers, while footnote 56 says 10,000 suspicious employers. Either way, suspicion is not proof, and 10,000 is only about 3% of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. Most cited cases involve employer fraud uncovered through existing site visits and prosecutions, yet DHS says the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." There is no evidence this fee would have prevented the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

**2. Conflicting data**
DHS claims STEM OPT has "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of roughly 92,000 participants by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, citing 165,524 participants. But its own analysis reports 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, consistent with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study using 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not an analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires comparable wages (Form I-983).

**3. High fees do not prevent fraud (Sec. IV.C)**
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students," but a high fee measures ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Employers already selling job letters can build the fee into their prices, while honest students who cannot afford $70,000 are excluded. DHS provides no evidence that any fee level would reduce fraud.

**4. This is a tax, not a fee**
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, generating an estimated $8.7–16.9 billion annually. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must cover program costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no costs; it is modeled on an H-1B fee to discourage participation. That makes it an unauthorized tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). INA 214(a)'s authority over "time and conditions" cannot justify a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources failing to keep pace with the program, yet none of this money would fund compliance. DHS also suggests it may end OPT without the fees, while admitting it cannot keep the revenue.

**5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)**
DHS leaves benefits unquantified while estimating costs of up to $8.2 billion annually. It caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee, arguing parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. This is circular: much of OPT's value, including innovation, taxes, and local spending, benefits the public, not just whoever pays. DHS also fails to model enrollment losses, an omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

**6. Alternatives dismissed**
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as too slow or costly, despite relying on those tools to uncover the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, also cited by DHS, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative convenience is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

**7. Reliance and unintended consequences**
DHS calls reliance speculative because only about 20% of F-1 students use OPT. That still represents roughly 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt based on the program. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000, versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, penalizing students who combine work and study. Refund denials also cannot be appealed.

**8. Small institutions and states**
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS offers no relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then says it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, despite requiring 1,044 state institutions to pay.

**9. Process and baseline**
DHS allows 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days for a paperwork change estimated to take five minutes. It also relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) as its baseline and vetting rationale without noting that the rule has been postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.

I am an international Graduate Student, in my fourth year of Computer Science PhD, at an Ivy League university.

Dear Officers and Regulatory Specialists,

I am writing to respectfully offer my public comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees. As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States under an F-1 visa, I deeply respect the Department’s ongoing commitment to safeguarding national security, maintaining the integrity of our immigration framework, and protecting the American workforce. However, I am compelled to voice my profound concern regarding the proposed assessment of a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee. While I appreciate the intent to deter bad actors and fraudulent entities, imposing such an unprecedented financial burden creates immense personal hardship for law-abiding students while inadvertently harming American higher education and the broader domestic economy.

From a personal perspective, the opportunity to participate in practical training is a vital extension of the academic journey rather than a financial privilege or an employment loophole. International students and their families make extraordinary sacrifices, often liquidating life savings or securing substantial loans, to afford full tuition and living expenses at American universities. Entering an academic program with the understanding that post-graduation training would allow us to apply our classroom knowledge in real-world settings forms a core part of the decision to study in the United States. Assessing a $70,000 fee places an insurmountable barrier before students who have meticulously followed every immigration rule. For the vast majority of scholars, a fee of this magnitude far exceeds an entry-level annual salary, effectively pricing dedicated graduates out of the very training opportunities their education prepared them to fulfill.

Beyond individual hardship, this policy threatens the vitality and global competitiveness of American higher education institutions. U.S. colleges and universities rely heavily on international scholars to foster vibrant, diverse academic communities and to drive cutting-edge research. Because smaller non-profit institutions and public universities cannot absorb these multi-thousand-dollar transfers on behalf of their students, the proposed fees will inevitably lead to a sharp decline in international enrollment. Prospective scholars will increasingly redirect their talents to nations with more welcoming post-study work frameworks, such as Canada, Australia, or members of the European Union. Over time, the loss of international student tuition and intellectual contributions will undermine campus operations, force reductions in academic programming, and diminish the collaborative research environment that benefits domestic students.

Furthermore, dismantling the practical training ecosystem runs counter to the long-term economic interests of the United States. International graduates, particularly those in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, serve as crucial catalysts for technological innovation and economic growth. Restricting their access to temporary practical experience deprives American industries of specialized talent and diminishes the nationwide potential for research and development. While curbing fraudulent shell companies and bad actors is a necessary objective, achieving it through financial exclusion risks penalizing legitimate scholars and eroding the aggregate productivity of the national economy. Fraud is best combated through heightened administrative verification, focused employer site visits, and targeted enforcement against bad actors, rather than an extraordinary fee structure that renders the entire program inaccessible.

In conclusion, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw the proposed OPT fee schedule. Upholding the integrity of the immigration system does not require closing the door on legitimate international talent. By pursuing balanced, targeted oversight measures rather than prohibitive financial demands, the Department can maintain robust security standards while preserving the immense mutual benefits that international scholars bring to American campuses and communities. Thank you for your time, consideration, and dedication to serving the public interest through open dialogue.

Respectfully submitted,
