I am a current F-1 graduate student. I recognize that Optional Practical Training (OPT) is a temporary, discretionary benefit—not an entitlement to employment or a guarantee of authorization. I am not asking DHS to preserve OPT unchanged or arguing that the agency cannot regulate the program. I ask DHS to distinguish future students, who can make informed decisions under new rules, from current students, who have already made substantial commitments in reliance on the framework in place when they began their studies.

For many years, eligible F-1 students have been able to seek up to 12 months of post-completion OPT, with an additional 24-month extension for graduates of qualifying STEM programs. This was not a promise of a job, but a known part of the academic-to-professional pathway that students could reasonably consider when deciding to study in the United States and planning their careers. Students already here have committed years of their lives and substantial resources to tuition, housing, relocation, and living expenses. Many have left jobs, paused careers, and moved away from their families. These commitments cannot be undone by giving students 60 days' notice after a new rule is finalized.

The proposed rule would impose a $70,000 fee for an institution's initial OPT recommendation and a $30,000 fee for a subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. Although the institution would formally pay the fee, the proposal allows schools to pass the cost to students, the student body generally, or employers. It also allows a school or DSO to decline to recommend a student for OPT rather than pay the fee. In practice, OPT could become inaccessible to students who planned their education around the existing framework, even if the fee is not billed directly to them.

This is especially important for STEM students. Practical training is not simply an opportunity to remain in the United States or obtain a job after graduation; it bridges academic learning and professional practice. It allows graduates to learn how scientific and technical knowledge is applied in workplaces, how projects and teams operate, and how research and technical skills become practical solutions. For students who intend to return home, this experience can be essential to applying their education in local industries, developing new ventures, or becoming entrepreneurs. University coursework alone cannot always provide the same exposure to professional methods and practical constraints.

I am particularly concerned that the proposed transition rule uses the date of the DSO recommendation—not the date a student began the degree—as the trigger for the new fees. A student who began a multi-year degree before the rule was proposed could therefore face this new financial condition simply because they will not be eligible to request OPT until after it takes effect. This is prospective only in a formal sense: it imposes a new condition on students whose educational decisions and substantial investments were made under the prior framework.

DHS acknowledges in Section VI and footnote 124 that current F-1 students who have already moved to the United States are in a different position from prospective students. That difference should have practical consequences. OPT need not have been the sole reason a student chose to study in the United States for its established availability to have been an important part of their academic and professional planning. The fact that not every F-1 student ultimately uses OPT does not diminish the reliance of those already enrolled who planned their path around it.

I respectfully ask DHS to revise Sections V.C and VI so the proposed fees apply only to students who begin a new degree program after the final rule's effective date. F-1 students enrolled in their current degree programs before publication of this proposal on October 8, 2026, should remain under the existing OPT framework for that program, including initial post-completion OPT and any eligible 24-month STEM OPT extension—even if their DSO recommendation is issued after the new rule takes effect. They would remain subject to existing OPT eligibility, training, and oversight requirements; this request is only for protection from the newly proposed fees.

This approach would allow DHS to implement a new policy for future cohorts while treating current students fairly. Students enrolling after the effective date can assess the changed conditions before committing years of time and substantial resources. Those who have already made these commitments should not have the terms of their educational pathway changed midway through their studies.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Failing to weigh important aspects of the problem is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Targeted enforcement against bad actors would address the concern without penalizing compliant students and schools.

The proposal is also ambiguous. It does not clearly state whether a STEM extension would cost $30,000 or $70,000 for a student whose first OPT began before the rule takes effect. DHS itself anticipates that charging separately for pre-completion and post-completion recommendations could discourage pre-completion OPT. Combined with fees of this size, the rule will push schools to limit OPT access and weaken the pipeline of international talent that U.S. employers and universities depend on.

For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS proceeds, it should substantially reduce the fees, tie them to documented costs, and publish a full analysis of the impacts on students, schools, and employers.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to Bureau’s proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees," published on October 8, 2026.

I submit these comments from a critical and deeply personal perspective: I am on an H4 visa. I have paid taxes, and raised my family here. Currently, I have one child attending an American university and another who has recently "aged out" of dependent status. While this rule is framed as a regulatory adjustment for educational institutions, its real-world impact is a devastating financial and humanitarian blow to lawful, high-skilled immigrant families who have followed every rule to contribute to this country.
I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal based on the following severe consequences:

1. Critical Threat to "Aged-Out" Children and Family Unity
Children of long-term H-1B visa holders who grow up in the United States face a precarious future when they turn 21 and "age out" of their dependent H-4 status. For these young adults, transitioning to an F-1 student visa and subsequently utilizing the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program is the primary legal pathway to maintain status, remain with their families, and enter the workforce in the only country they call home. By levying an astronomical $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for extensions, this rule effectively destroys the only viable survival pipeline for aged-out children. It forces unnecessary separation of legal immigrant families, punishing children who have grown up as part of the American fabric.

2. Extreme Financial Duress on Immigrant Households
Universities will be forced to pass these massive new institutional OPT fees directly down to students, this rule creates an insurmountable financial penalty. For a family already managing the high costs of higher education, an unexpected $70,000 to $100,000 surcharge just for a child to gain post-graduation practical training is a financial impossibility. 

3. Destruction of the Career Entry Pipeline for the Next Generation
My child currently in college deserves a predictable, fair, and merit-based landscape upon graduation. If universities are forced to restrict OPT recommendations, or if the financial barriers prevent students from applying, the entry-level career pipeline for foreign-born graduates will effectively die. Legitimate students who have worked hard in American classrooms will be barred from gaining the practical experience required to launch their careers, leaving them stranded despite their family's legal status and immense financial investment in American higher education.

4. Misaligned Enforcement and Economic Harm
While the agency’s stated goal is to enhance oversight and curb fraud, punishing compliant, world-class American universities and lawful student applicants is an arbitrary mechanism. It does nothing to target actual bad actors. Instead, by crippling the STEM OPT pipeline, the rule will starve the very American industries—such as technology, engineering, and healthcare—that rely on high-skilled talent. This harms the long-term economic stability of the companies that sponsor legal workers, ultimately damaging the broader American economy.

This proposed rule introduces unprecedented, disproportionate financial barriers that target the most vulnerable segment of the legal immigration community: the children of high-skilled workers. It forces family separation and imposes impossible financial burdens on families who have acted entirely in good faith. I respectfully urge to withdraw this harmful proposal in its entirety.
Thank you for your time and consideration of these comments.

1. Contradictory Financial, Federalism, and Statistical Analyses
The rule contains unresolved contradictions. DHS states both that the rule would not generate $100 million in expenditures and that it exceeds the $100 million threshold (64597). It also denies substantial state and local compliance costs (64598), despite 1,044 affected schools being state-operated (64592), while admitting it skipped consultation with affected governments (64597). Further discrepancies include 226,200 versus 289,938 annual responses and 165,524 versus 95,384 STEM OPT participants. DHS also minimizes OPT reliance using total enrollment rather than graduates, contradicting its claims that participation has overwhelmed administrative capacity (64570–64578). DHS should reconcile these figures, conduct the required consultation, and publish corrected analyses before proceeding.

2. Regulatory Burden Misplaced on Educational Institutions
All fraud examples cited by DHS involve employers, including fabricated offer letters, shell companies, staged worksites, and phantom employees (91 FR 64570–64571). None implicates universities, yet they bear the proposed fee. DHS already applies employer safeguards to STEM OPT, including E-Verify, training plans, and site visits, but declined to extend them to all OPT because of administrative costs (64576). DHS should withdraw the fee and extend these existing safeguards to all post-completion OPT rather than penalize students and institutions for employer misconduct.

3. No Meaningful Refund or Appeal Rights
Once an employment authorization document is issued, the fee is nonrefundable, even if a student never finds employment, is laid off, changes status, or leaves the country (64577). Exceptions depend on SEVP's discretion, with no administrative appeal and standards potentially published later through website guidance (64600). If retained, the fee must include pro rata refunds for early OPT termination, clear regulatory eligibility criteria, and a right of appeal.

4. Universal Fees Instead of Targeted Fraud Enforcement
DHS acknowledges that fraud is concentrated in high-risk sectors (64574) but proposes a fee applying uniformly to all participants (64576). The approximately 10,000 students associated with suspect employers represent only 3% of ICE's 340,066 OPT authorization holders in 2024. DHS should disclose the evidence behind these allegations, including resulting charges and terminations, particularly given its reliance on a video (footnotes 55, 56, and 67). Rather than charging all students, DHS should use SEVIS data to identify suspicious employers through indicators such as excessive student registrations at one address, residential worksites, and shared corporate officers.

I ask DHS to quantify the rule's benefits, including the number of fraudulent authorizations it
expects to prevent and the effect on U.S. workers, as Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 require,
rather than relying on "would likely," "could" and "may" (64591).

I ask DHS to state in regulatory text which fee applies to a student already on OPT who later
seeks a STEM extension, since proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) by their terms cover neither
(64600).

I ask DHS to publish the underlying data for Tables 2-17, which appear only as images, and the
per-institution fee analysis the rule says it ran in Python (64593-64594), so that the public can
check the figures.

I suggest replacing the fee with a wage rule: require every OPT employer to attest to paying the actual or
prevailing wage for similarly situated U.S. workers, as STEM OPT employers already must on
Form I-983 (64570), with referral to the Department of Labor for violations. This addresses
"depressed wages" (64574) directly; a fee passed to the student lowers the student's pay and
makes the problem worse.

For these reasons, I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fee. Any integrity measure that follows
should act on employers, where the evidence of abuse lies; should rest on a cost basis if it takes the form
of a fee; should exempt pre-completion OPT, doctoral graduates and employment with H-1B cap-exempt
institutions; and should protect every student enrolled on the effective date. Thank you for considering
this comment.

Comment on Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — information collection aspects of "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566

I am an F-1 student completing a master's degree in computer science at Northeastern University, graduating in May 2027. I plan to apply for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and, as a STEM graduate, the 24-month STEM OPT extension. I am writing about the new information collection this proposed rule would create, and about its practical utility and burden.

First, the collection appears to have little practical utility. Every OPT recommendation is already recorded in SEVIS by the Designated School Official; DHS already holds complete, real-time data on who is recommended, when, and for what employer. The proposed rule would layer a second, per-recommendation payment and reporting collection on top of a data set the agency already owns. A collection that duplicates existing SEVIS records does not improve program integrity; it only adds a payment checkpoint.

Second, the burden is understated. The fee is charged to schools per recommendation — $70,000 for an initial recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one, up to $100,000 for a student like me who uses OPT and STEM OPT. Processing, reconciling, and keeping records for per-student payments of this size is not a minor administrative task for a school with thousands of F-1 students; it is a major new financial operation. And because no school can absorb $70,000 per student, the predictable outcome is that schools will stop issuing recommendations altogether. The burden estimate should account for this: a collection attached to a process it effectively shuts down serves no one.

Third, if DHS proceeds at all, the burden should be minimized by using existing SEVP fee and SEVIS channels rather than creating a new per-recommendation collection.

The timing matters for students graduating in 2027. Under the proposal, the fees would apply to recommendations made on or after the final rule's effective date — which, on the proposed 60-day timeline, could fall exactly in the semester when my cohort's DSOs make our OPT recommendations. Students who chose U.S. graduate programs years ago, in reliance on the existing OPT framework, would have the terms changed at the finish line.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees. At minimum, the information collection should not be approved in its current form: it duplicates SEVIS data, its burden is significantly underestimated, and its practical effect is to end OPT participation for the students the program exists to serve.

Yuchen Zhang
F-1 student, Northeastern University (Seattle)

Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100

I strongly oppose the proposed fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT, including a STEM extension. These fees could total $100,000 for a student pursuing initial OPT and a STEM extension. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

HARM TO AMERICAN EMPLOYERS

These fees could prevent American employers from hiring qualified graduates educated at U.S. universities. Small businesses, startups, nonprofit organizations, and research institutions may be especially unable to absorb these costs.

A substantial fee could make hiring an otherwise suitable graduate financially impossible, leaving positions vacant, delaying projects, and limiting growth. Reducing OPT participation does not automatically create jobs for American workers. Employers may eliminate positions, reduce operations, or move work elsewhere instead. DHS should evaluate these potential consequences rather than assume that every lost OPT opportunity would produce a replacement hire.

RISKS TO AMERICAN RESEARCH AND INNOVATION

International students and researchers help strengthen American universities, laboratories, and businesses. Their knowledge and ideas contribute to scientific discovery, technological progress, and economic competitiveness.

Making practical training financially inaccessible could drive talented graduates toward other countries. The United States would educate these students and then make it harder for American institutions and employers to benefit from their skills.

The proposal could also discourage future international students from choosing U.S. universities. DHS should assess the potential effects on enrollment, research funding, ongoing projects, and America’s ability to attract and retain talented researchers.

UNAFFORDABLE COSTS FOR UNIVERSITIES AND STUDENTS

International students already invest substantial time and money in their American education. Many families make significant sacrifices to support tuition, housing, and other expenses. An additional financial barrier of this magnitude could place practical training beyond their reach.

Universities also operate within limited budgets. Requiring them to pay substantial fees for individual students could force institutions to restrict OPT participation. Passing costs to students or employers would shift the burden without resolving the affordability problem.

Access to practical training should depend on eligibility, educational relevance, and compliance with program requirements—not the ability to absorb a $70,000 or $100,000 expense.

FRAUD REQUIRES TARGETED ENFORCEMENT

I support preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers. However, DHS should demonstrate how fees of this size would effectively achieve those goals.

Charging legitimate participants more does not establish that shell companies, fictitious employment, or false reporting will be detected or prevented. A reduction in participation is not, by itself, evidence of a reduction in the fraud rate.

DHS should prioritize employer verification, accurate reporting, review of suspicious employment arrangements, and enforcement against those responsible for misconduct. These approaches would address abuse more directly without placing overwhelming costs on compliant students, universities, and employers.

The Department should also distinguish immigration fraud from actual job displacement. Fictitious employment is a serious compliance concern, but its existence alone does not establish that an American worker lost a job. DHS should explain the specific harms identified and provide evidence that the proposed fees would address them.

REQUEST TO WITHDRAW THE PROPOSAL

DHS should provide compelling evidence connecting these fees to fraud prevention and improved employment opportunities for American workers. It should evaluate less burdensome alternatives and fully assess the consequences for universities, research institutions, students, employers, and local economies.

America benefits when talented students choose its universities and apply their education through lawful practical training. These fees risk discouraging that talent, weakening research, and limiting opportunities for American businesses.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and pursue targeted, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity and American workers while preserving educational opportunity, scientific leadership, and economic competitiveness.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee-related information collection requirements.

DHS estimates that each payment verification and SEVIS reporting response will take only five minutes. I believe this estimate overlooks the actual administrative work involved. Universities may need to verify payments, coordinate between departments, resolve errors, and handle questions from students. These responsibilities take time and resources away from education and student support.

I also question whether this additional reporting is necessary. Universities already maintain detailed international student records through SEVIS. Adding another layer of verification without clearly demonstrating its practical value creates more bureaucracy rather than meaningful oversight.

If preventing fraud is the goal, DHS should focus on improving existing verification systems, using automated checks, and targeting actual cases of misconduct instead of placing additional administrative burdens on every participating institution.

This proposal also risks delaying legitimate OPT applications, disrupting students' employment plans, and creating unnecessary complications for American universities and employers. These consequences should be considered when evaluating the true cost of the information collection.

The United States benefits from attracting talented students who contribute to American research, businesses, and innovation. Making the process more complicated and expensive does not strengthen that advantage.

I urge DHS and OMB to reconsider these information collection requirements, provide a more realistic assessment of their administrative burden, and pursue simpler, more effective alternatives.

Thank you for considering this comment.
